Speaking at the inauguration ceremony, Director of Sahara Group Foundation, Chidilim Menakaya, highlighted the Foundation’s continued investment in practical, community-focused solutions that deliver lasting environmental and socio-economic benefits. “This initiative aligns with our sustainability and development priorities by transforming waste into valuable resources, reducing environmental impact, supporting climate action and creating livelihood opportunities. It demonstrates how communities can advance environmental responsibility while promoting inclusive economic growth,” she said. Reiterating the Foundation’s broader vision, Menakaya noted that Sahara Go Recycling demonstrates the transformative potential of collective action in building cleaner, more resilient communities. “Through collaboration, innovation and community participation, we are driving long-term environmental impact while improving livelihoods and strengthening community ownership of sustainable practices,” she added. The Commander of 651 Base Services Group, Air Commodore M.A. Imam, commended the Foundation’s investment in environmental sustainability and emphasised the importance of collective action in addressing waste management challenges in rapidly growing communities. Also speaking, the Head of Corporate Communications at Ikeja Electric, Kingsley Okotie, said the company was delighted to join forces with the Sahara Group Foundation to promote responsible environmental stewardship and sustainability at the Air Force base. He reaffirmed Ikeja Electric’s commitment to building sustainable relationships, enhancing seamless power supply, and supporting the well-being of customers, institutions, businesses and communities. Since its inception, Sahara Go Recycling has facilitated the recycling of more than 1,000 tonnes of recyclable waste and directly and indirectly supported over 2,000 livelihoods across collection, sorting, logistics and community-based enterprise activities. Through strategic partnerships and community engagement, the initiative continues to promote recycling, unlock economic value from waste and encourage sustainable lifestyles.

title: The Road To 2027 Runs Through Kaduna, But The North Is Not A Number
body: President Bola Tinubu will formally open his re-election campaign in Kaduna on Saturday. The location is deliberate, the arithmetic is formidable, and the message is unmistakable: the All Progressives Congress intends to win the 2027 election by rebuilding a northern coalition around the President. The three northern geopolitical zones contain 56.01 million of Nigeria’s 103.43 million registered voters; 54.2 per cent of the national register. The North-West alone has 25.08 million, making it the country’s largest electoral bloc. APC campaign officials are consequently talking about northern consensus and setting a national target of approximately 40 million votes. But registered voters are not actual votes, political endorsements are not public opinion, and the North is not a single electoral personality. That is the political signal this week. Why Kaduna matters Kaduna is in the North-West region. Kaduna is an appropriate starting point because it captures both the opportunity and the danger confronting Tinubu. It is a major political centre in the North-West, but it is not naturally secure territory for the President. Tinubu lost Kaduna to Atiku Abubakar in 2023. The state also embodies several issues that could determine northern voting behaviour: insecurity, rural poverty, food prices, religious sensitivity and the relationship between elite political agreements and popular sentiment. By beginning there, the APC is signalling that it will not concede the region to Atiku merely because he is a northern Muslim. It is relying on Vice-President Kashim Shettima, governors, ministers, traditional relationships and a greatly expanded party structure to offset Atiku’s regional appeal. That structure matters. The APC now enjoys an extraordinary advantage in the number of governors, lawmakers and local political networks under its control. Governors influence campaign financing, mobilisation and the organisation required to convert public sympathy into votes. The party’s challenge is that political machinery can mobilise supporters, but it cannot permanently insulate an incumbent from lived economic experience. The contest between structure and hardship The APC’s campaign argument will be that the most painful period of reform has passed. Inflation has moderated, foreign reserves have improved, economic growth has strengthened, and the Central Bank has begun adjusting interest rates. The administration will argue that removing the petrol subsidy and reforming the foreign-exchange market prevented a deeper fiscal crisis. The opposition’s reply is more immediate: food, transport, energy and business costs remain painfully high. That explains the political significance of the National Economic Council’s newly approved 90-day action plan. It prioritises food affordability, tax harmonisation, completion of high-impact projects, removal of investment bottlenecks and regulated household support. It also proposes a national dashboard to track projects and the use of savings from subsidy removal. On paper, these are reasonable interventions. The problem is timing. The presidential election is 86 days away, while the relief plan is designed to run for 90 days. Atiku’s campaign has therefore called it “election bait,” arguing that Nigerians are being asked to vote before the promised relief can be fully assessed. That is a partisan allegation, not proof that the programme is improper. But the calendar gives the criticism political force. The government can answer it only through early, measurable delivery. What food has become cheaper? Which households have received support? What projects have been completed? How much has been spent, by whom and under what criteria? Announcements will not be sufficient. The electorate needs receipts. The opposition’s unity problem While the APC prepares a major campaign launch, opposition parties are again discussing a consensus candidate. Representatives of the ADC, NDC, PRP, SDP, APM and PDP have inaugurated legal and media committees to develop a framework for cooperation. Atiku, Peter Obi, Donald Duke and Adewale Adebayo are among the names mentioned in the talks. Coalition organisers say negotiations are progressing towards a single candidate. That claim should be treated cautiously. The Independent National Electoral Commission has already published 18 presidential candidates, including Atiku for the ADC and Obi for the NDC. Agreeing that the opposition should unite is therefore much easier than determining who withdraws, who leads, what happens to the running mates and how supporters are transferred between parties. There is also no guarantee that voters will follow elite instructions. An Atiku endorsement of Obi would not automatically deliver Atiku’s northern vote. An Obi endorsement of Atiku would not automatically transfer younger urban voters or the South-East. Nigerian politicians often mistake negotiations among leaders for consolidation among electorates. The opposition nevertheless understands the arithmetic. Tinubu won in 2023 with 36.61 per cent of the valid votes; 8.79 million votes. Atiku and Obi together received more than 13 million. That does not mean a joint ticket would have automatically defeated Tinubu, because elections are shaped by turnout, geography and the constitutional requirement for national spread. But it shows why fragmentation remains the APC’s quiet ally. Unless the coalition produces a credible agreement quickly, it risks becoming a committee for managing defeat. The register question The emphasis on 103.43 million voters has also reopened an important transparency dispute. INEC says the total follows the addition of approximately 10.77 million new registrants. Atiku has demanded that the preliminary register be made available for public inspection, alleging that an online page intended for that purpose was empty. The allegation does not establish manipulation. Technical delays or publication problems are not evidence of a compromised register. But INEC should resolve the issue immediately. A national figure cannot substitute for a register that citizens and parties can scrutinise. The public must be able to identify duplicate entries, deceased persons, omissions and questionable registrations before the final roll is certified. If parties are already building campaign strategies around precise regional totals, voters deserve access to the underlying data. First, watch the language and attendance at Saturday’s Kaduna rally. A large gathering will demonstrate organisational capacity, but the more important question is whether influential northern leaders offer genuine commitments or merely perform ceremonial loyalty. Second, watch whether the 90-day economic plan produces identifiable benefits before election day. Its political credibility will depend on outcomes, not intentions. Third, watch the opposition negotiations. A consensus announced after ballots and campaign loyalties have hardened may be largely symbolic. Finally, watch INEC. Publication and scrutiny of the voter register will be an early test of whether the Commission intends to manage doubts proactively or react only after they become political crises. Tinubu enters the northern campaign with the strongest political machine, an expanding network of governors and a divided opposition. Those advantages are substantial. But the North’s 56 million registrations are not a blank cheque. Its voters are living with insecurity, expensive food, high transport costs and the uneven consequences of economic reform. The APC is campaigning on structure and patience. The opposition is campaigning on hardship and change, but without yet agreeing on whose change. The election may ultimately turn on which side solves its greater weakness first: whether Tinubu can convert improving economic indicators into household relief, or whether the opposition can convert popular discontent into one coherent electoral force. EDITORIAL NOTE Political Signals is an independent weekly political analysis produced for Channels Television. It examines political developments, personalities and electoral trends without endorsement of any political party or candidate. Its assessments are based on publicly available evidence and may change as events and evidence develop. The post The Road To 2027 Runs Through Kaduna, But The North Is Not A Number appeared first on Channels Television .

title: France protests: Latest developments
body: Hundreds of protests were held in France Saturday as nationwide anger grows over the cost of living, with security forces massing to prevent a repeat of violence that marred demonstrations last week. Here are the latest developments: – ‘Calm’ in Paris – French police had arrested 135 people nationwide and seized a variety of weapons, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said, adding that, so far, “there has been no major incident”. Weapons confiscated included metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said. Paris police described the situation as “calm” at midday. – ‘Scandalous’ – Hundreds of demonstrators could be seen gathering at Porte d’Italie in Paris, where authorities have said they must begin the only authorised march. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters it was “scandalous” that President Emmanuel Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating “where we wish to demonstrate”. “We are here today, quite obviously, because there is immense social anger in this country, and because wages have still not been increased to the level they should be,” she added. Paris police at the last minute ordered the union-organised march be moved from Bastille, in the centre, to the more remote Porte d’Italie on the southeastern rim. Unions said they reluctantly agreed. But the Yellow Vests — a loosely organised group that staged disruptive street protests against Macron eight years ago — indicated they would not comply. – Halloween protests called – One group organising Saturday’s demonstrations — the Yellow Vests — said they would hold another round of protests on October 31. Organisers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the “authoritarian drift” of President Emmanuel Macron’s government and urging citizens to stand up for “public freedoms”. – Tear gas in Lyon – Police fired teargas to disperse some 150 people protesting in the southeastern city of Lyon, in an area banned to all demonstrations, an AFP journalist saw. Police fired several teargas grenades to clear the group near a university faculty and the city’s police station as part of nationwide rallies against the cost of living. Police moved in as demonstrators tried to block a road. – ‘Macron resign’ – Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched in the city of Orleans against a congress by far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) party there, AFP journalists saw. The protest criticised both leading presidential candidate Le Pen and centrist Macron. “Macron resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd yelled. – Louvre, Orsay closed – The Louvre, d’Orsay, and Picasso museums, as well as the Grand Palais in Paris, were closed Saturday. The culture ministry had called on institutions to take every measure to ensure the safety of visitors and staff, and the protection of artworks. The post France protests: Latest developments appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Deadly church attack shocks Jordan's deep-rooted Christian community
body: Jordan’s small Christian community was reeling on Saturday, a day after the killing of eight of its members in what authorities called a terrorist attack on a church . Friday’s attack on St George's Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud was the largest attack against the country’s Christians since the mid 1950s. Overnight, Jordanian authorities increased the death toll from seven to eight and said none of the three assailants had not yet been captured. Hamoud is about 80km south of Amman. The victims were all men who mostly belonged to the Halasah family, a prominent Christian family in Jordan. The Halasah's ancestral land is situated in Hamoud. Three doctors were among those killed. “Jordan has not seen such an attack. It appears to have been designed to make the Christians leave,” said a prominent member of the Halasah clan, who is also a doctor. Jordan is dependent on US aid and has a defence pact with Washington. The kingdom is widely regarded as a bastion of stability in the Middle East. But it faces domestic challenges as its economy has been stagnant for 15 years and the official unemployment rate is 16 per cent. The attack occurred as the authorities were promoting a site near the Dead Sea where Christians believe Jesus was baptised in an effort to revive tourism. The kingdom’s Christian population numbers 250,000 out of a population of 11 million. Orthodox Christians are the largest denomination. The attack struck at the core of Jordan’s Christian minority, the doctor said, describing the Halasahs as "the most prominent" of the Christian families, and Hamoud as their "bastion”. The church responded to the attack by affirming loyalty to the state. Christophoros of Kyriakoupolis, the Archbishop of Jerusalem, described it as an “ugly terrorist act” that "will not undermine national unity” and allegiance to King Abdullah II. The archbishop, who also presides over the church in Jordan, said that the "Christians are part of the history of this country … and will be, with the grace God, part of its future”. There was no claim of responsibility for the attack, nor did the authorities name a culprit. The country has maintained a complex relationship with Islamist groups. Last year, the government banned the Muslim Brotherhood. However, the authorities kept the Islamic Action Front, a group linked to the Brotherhood, which constitutes the largest bloc in parliament. This year, the Islamic Action Front rebranded itself as the Umma Party. Criticism by Jordanians and other Arabs started to appear on social media about views by some Islamists suggesting that Jordan was doing the Christians a favour by letting them stay in the kingdom. One of those who was criticised was MP Huda Al Otoum, from the Umma Party. She warned this month that Jordan’s “acceptance” of the Christians could be used to “accept the Jews”. Social media users criticised her for sowing sectarian tension. Many Jordanians took to social media after Friday's attack in support of Christians, pointing out that Christianity is intertwined with the history of the country. Step News Agency, an anti-Brotherhood Youtube channel describing itself as a specialising in Arab affairs, published an old clip of a TV interview with Hamza Mansour, a former head of the Islamic Action Front, refusing to condemn ISIS outright. The Umma Party said in a statement that the attack in Hamoud "constitutes a dangerous crime and a terrorist action that targets "our nation and its cohesion." When the authorities banned the Brotherhood in 2025, they accused the group of complicity in a weapons manufacturing scheme aimed at creating instability. The kingdom has been ruled by the Hashemite monarchy since it was founded as a British protectorate in 1921. All significant powers are with King Abdullah, who has ruled since 1999.

title: Germany in talks to buy Ukrainian jet-powered drones
body:
Germany is negotiating a deal with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones, a German official with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 24.
Berlin is discussing the deal with Kyiv as Germany plans to buy thousands of deep-strike weapons from European arms companies, as initially reported by Bloomberg on Oct. 23.
According to officials Bloomberg spoke with, Germany’s future strategic thinking involves using masses of cheap missiles to overwhelm enemy air defenses. Currently, Germany’s army only operates midrange Taurus cruise missiles, while the U.S. warned its allies to expect years-long delays for missile deliveries.
The Bars jet powered drone has a range of 1,000 kilometers and can reach speeds of up to 700 kilometers per hour. The manufacturer of the drones is not publicly known for security reasons. The Ukrainian army launches around 2,000 of these drones per month, targeting Russian oil refineries, power plants, and substations, a representative of the company told Ukrainian media outlet NV in September. Germany and Ukraine signed a deal to jointly produce Bars in July 2026 as part of the Build with Ukraine initiative. Under the first stage of the deal, Germany would finance the production of the drones, while all manufactured equipment would be sent to Ukraine’s Armed Forces.
Recently, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Bars have proven to be one of the most effective interceptors against Russian jet-powered drones, as Moscow escalates attacks on Ukrainian cities, Ukrinform reported on Oct. 10.
Germany has emerged as the biggest foreign partner in Ukraine’s burgeoning defense tech sector. A September report from the Kyiv School of Economics Institute found that there were 36 joint ventures between Ukrainian and German firms, as Berlin prioritizes deep-strike technology and intelligence.

title: Gov Ododo’s Policies May Undermine Tinubu’s Re-election in Kogi, Ijele Warns
body: A social activist and politician, Isaiah Davies Ijele, has raised the alarm that the style of governance and policies of Kogi State Governor, Usman Ododo, may be undermining President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election chances in the state in 2027. In a strong political intervention released on Friday, October 24, 2026, Ijele said it has become imperative for the president and the leadership of the All Progressives Congress (APC) to be made aware of developments in the state. According to him, “It has become imperative that Mr. President and the leadership of the All Progressives Congress (APC) are made aware that the style of governance and certain policies of Governor Usman Ododo in Kogi State may be undermining President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s chances of securing re-election in 2027.” Ijele argued that at a time when the Federal Government allocates substantial resources to states and local governments, Nigerians have been encouraged to hold governors accountable for how public funds are managed. “The question is simple: What is Kogi State doing with the resources available to it, and why are ordinary citizens still being subjected to unbearable economic pressure?” he queried. He noted that Kogi State receives allocations running into billions of naira, including funds meant for local government administration and grassroots development, which he said should translate into better roads, affordable education, improved healthcare and stable electricity. “Unfortunately, rather than feeling the impact of governance, many citizens are confronted with additional financial burdens,” Ijele stated. The activist cited the reported N6,000 charge imposed on tricycle (Keke) riders for state stickers, describing the riders as ordinary people struggling to feed their families in a difficult economy. “Why should they be made to pay more when government has access to public funds that should support development and improve living conditions?” he asked. Ijele said the situation becomes more disturbing with the reported 100 per cent increase in school fees in state-owned institutions. “At a time when parents are struggling to meet basic needs, doubling school fees places an enormous burden on families and threatens the educational aspirations of thousands of young people. Is this the change the people expected? Is this how a government demonstrates compassion for its citizens?” he asked. He argued that other states are exploring ways to make education more affordable through scholarships and financial assistance, and Kogi should not be moving in the opposite direction. “The problem is not simply about money. It is about priorities, accountability and the responsibility of government to its people,” Ijele stressed. The activist said Kogi East in particular deserves more than political promises, adding that communities continue to demand meaningful infrastructure, good roads, electricity, functional healthcare facilities and economic opportunities. “The people want to see the impact of public expenditure in their daily lives. If billions of naira are being allocated to government at different levels, citizens have every right to ask what tangible projects have been delivered, what they cost and how communities have benefited. Public resources must produce measurable results, not merely announcements and political publicity,” he said. Ijele warned that President Tinubu has a political stake in how APC-controlled states perform, noting that while the president cannot be held personally responsible for every state policy, citizens may associate the performance of governors with the broader party. “President Tinubu has a political stake in how APC-controlled states perform. The conduct of governors and other political officeholders will inevitably influence how voters judge the president and his administration,” he said. He cautioned Governor Ododo that increasing financial burden on citizens could have political consequences. “You cannot continuously increase the financial burden on citizens, frustrate students and their parents, and then expect the same people to enthusiastically support your preferred candidate at the polls. The people who pay these fees, the Keke riders who struggle to earn a living, the parents who sacrifice everything to educate their children, and the communities waiting for basic infrastructure are all voters. Their experiences will shape their political decisions in 2027,” Ijele warned. According to him, “No amount of political mobilisation can permanently replace good governance, and no campaign slogan can erase the daily experiences of suffering citizens.” Ijele called on the state government to review policies that impose excessive burdens, address concerns around school fees, ensure transparency in the use of public allocations and prioritise projects that directly improve lives. “The people of Kogi State deserve responsible leadership. They deserve affordable education, accessible healthcare, good roads, reliable electricity and an administration that sees public revenue as a responsibility rather than an opportunity to impose more charges,” he stated. He added that President Tinubu’s re-election campaign cannot be separated entirely from the performance of those governing under his party. “If Governor Ododo wants Kogi people to support the president, his government must give them reasons to do so. You cannot make life harder for the people and expect their votes as a reward,” Ijele said. He concluded that as it stands, there is zero visible impact of the state government in the nine local governments of Kogi East Senatorial District, while questioning how local government funds are being utilized. “Governor Usman Ododo must act now, not when the political consequences of public dissatisfaction become impossible to reverse. Mr. President, act now before it’s too late!”

title: Unemployment and poverty pushed us into dangerous underground mining – Atwima Kwanwoma miners
body: Some youth engaged in underground mining in the Atwima Kwanwoma District of the Ashanti Region say unemployment and poverty have forced them into the dangerous activity despite the risk to their lives. According to the miners, many of them have completed senior high school and tertiary education but have been unable to secure jobs, compelling them to resort to underground mining to earn a living and support their families. In an exclusive interview, one of the miners, Kwame Asah, popularly known as Tagor, disclosed that he had been involved in underground mining in the area for more than seven years. He ventured into the activity after completing senior high school but could not further his education due to a lack of financial support. “When I completed SHS, I did not get the support to further my education. As a man, I had to leave my hometown, Ejura, and come here to work to help solve the financial problems at home,” he said. Kwame described underground mining as less destructive to natural resources than surface mining, but acknowledged that it poses significant risks to the lives of those involved. He said he would readily quit the job if another employment opportunity became available, given the constant danger of underground pits collapsing. “If there is another employment opportunity for me, honestly, I will quit this job because I could die at any time if the pit collapses,” he said. The miners have consequently appealed to the government to prioritise job creation and provide sustainable employment opportunities for young people. They believe such interventions would help reduce the number of youths turning to dangerous underground mining activities as a means of survival.

title: Technocracy Takeover
body:
Elon Musk is a technological genius, a successful entrepreneur, and a worrisome geopolitical force. He is fabulously wealthy, politically aggressive, erratic, and accountable to no one.
On Oct. 20, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered restrictions affecting SpaceX satellite communications used by Ukraine’s military drones, significantly impeding its military operations. Any time they flew faster than 100 miles an hour (161 kilometers per hour), the video feed cut out.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Musk said he discussed the issue with White House officials, but US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was unaware of prior discussions and that Musk and SpaceX made the decision.
But Musk has denied responsibility for the Starlink restrictions, while credible media outlets attributed the decision to him. This underscores the reality that a single businessman has inordinate power over life and death on a battlefield or in cities.
Culpability aside, this is unacceptable, as tech pioneer Bill Gates has warned: “The state – not the tech sector – must hold the ultimate authority over these potentially lethal systems.”
The world cannot afford a future in which the fate of nations depends on the whims, political loyalties, or commercial calculations of a handful of billionaires. America’s tech giants are as powerful as nation-states financially, and wield political influence globally.
Musk played a heroic role in Ukraine’s defense in February 2022 after the Russian invasion when he activated Starlink service and arranged deliveries of terminals. This prevented a catastrophe, but then months later he declined to extend Starlink coverage to support a Ukrainian attack against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet near Crimea. He did so at the urging of a Russian friend.
Now, this recent stoppage has undermined Ukraine’s defense.
The overriding issue is that a handful of tech businesses control five strategically essential choke points: communications, intelligence, weapons, computing power, and infrastructure. The danger is not technological power, but dependence on privately owned tech without sufficient democratic or legal oversight.
The world’s biggest hyperscalers are as powerful as nation-states. As just one measure, here are the biggest tech giants’ revenues compared to the GDP of certain countries:
In 2025, the combined gross revenue of Elon Musk’s primary technology companies – Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI (which absorbed X/Twitter) – reached approximately $116.7 billion, equivalent to Venezuela’s GDP.
These are the world’s six most powerful tech tycoons:
Musk and other billionaires have also bought media outlets to gain oversized political influence. They donate staggering amounts to political campaigns, provide access to publicity, and hand out corporate favors and jobs.
Musk’s X has intervened aggressively in American and European political debates. Tech billionaires are buying newspapers, networks, and entertainment services to reshape public discourse, pivot into streaming and AI integration, and to project political or cultural influence.
This week, Senior White House adviser Peter Navarro warned that Fox Corp.’s proposed $22 billion acquisition of Roku (a major streaming service used by millions) could create a powerful streaming conglomerate capable of controlling what millions of Americans watch, which competing networks they can access, and how advertisers reach consumers.
Navarro, President Donald Trump’s senior counselor for trade and manufacturing, called the proposed transaction a major antitrust threat.
“This is not just a merger; it is also a weapon,” he wrote.
Musk has aggressively waded into foreign politics. He endorsed Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), attacked Britain’s Labour government, amplified anti-immigration campaigners, and supported nationalist and populist political figures across Europe.
Musk has frequently targeted British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, called for early elections, amplified posts from anti-immigration figures like Tommy Robinson, and engaged with controversial Reform UK figures like Nigel Farage.
In France: Musk described National Rally figure Marine Le Pen as “France’s last hope” following legal troubles, drawing rebukes from French government officials who labeled the comments as foreign meddling. He has supported Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and criticized leaders in Spain and other European nations. Such interventions have provoked accusations of foreign electoral interference, but he claims he is simply challenging established political elites.
Such concentration of power leads to corruption, conflicts of interest in government procurement, political accountability issues, and national security vulnerabilities.
The US was the first nation to understand and tackle the danger of concentrated economic power with its antitrust laws decades ago – against the Rockefellers and Wall Street financiers. Today, however, AI giants get a free pass, and what will happen when a tech billionaire disagrees with American foreign policy or his commercial interests conflict with national-security priorities? What if an owner becomes politically aligned or fully controlled by a foreign government or ideology?
Public concern about tech increases, mostly concerning future job losses to AI as well as about the concentration of wealth in the hands of too few.
On Sept. 29, the world’s richest tech executives signed a White House Accord on Super Intelligence, an agreement to self-regulate one another with some government oversight. Trump gathered Silicon Valley’s A-list to combat the drumbeat of news stories about serious accidents, hacking incidents, children hunted by predators on social media, and suicides or shootings triggered by AI models that have run amok.
Critics and many AI experts demand government regulation, but the laissez-faire Trump regime doesn’t want to lose America’s technology lead over China, so it proposed self-regulation. Some cynically say this will accomplish nothing, but President Trump replied confidently: “They will police one another and bad actors will get nabbed.”
However, the majority of Americans and state governments want government regulations over the country’s technocracy in light of rogue incidents and warnings.
The father of AI, Geoffrey Hinton, put the need to take action bluntly: “The masters may be losing control of their creation... [They] can escape containment and conspire with each other, making them dangerous. So we should make them so they really care about us. And if we don’t do that, we’re toast.”

The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
Diane Francis is an award-winning columnist, bestselling author, investigative journalist, and television commentator. She writes twice weekly at https://dianefrancis.substack.com/ and is Editor at Large with the National Post and Postmedia newspapers writing twice weekly. She is Senior Fellow at the Atlantic Council, Eurasia section, in Washington DC. She has written pieces for the Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, Daily Beast, Politico, Miami Herald and the New York Post. In addition she is a Distinguished Professor at Ryerson University's Ted Rogers School of Management and has been a Visiting Fellow at Harvard University’s Joan Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy. In 1991, she became Editor of Canada's Financial Post, the first woman editor of a national daily newspaper in Canada, a position she held until the paper was sold in 1998.

title: Countries with the largest armies, tanks, naval fleet and aircraft
body: Military strength can be measured in several ways, including the number of active personnel, tanks, military aircraft and naval vessels. A country that ranks highly in one category may occupy a lower position in another, highlighting the different priorities and capabilities of armed forces worldwide. Using 2026 data from Global Firepower, this comparison examines the 10 countries with the largest military inventories across four key categories: active military personnel, tanks, military aircraft and naval assets. Active Personnel China has the world’s largest active military force, with approximately 2.04 million personnel. India ranks second with 1.43 million, followed by the United States with about 1.33 million active personnel. North Korea and Russia are also prominent in the ranking, each with approximately 1.32 million active personnel, according to the figures provided. Their positions highlight the substantial manpower maintained by countries with different military priorities. The top 10 countries with the largest active military forces are China, with 2,035,000 personnel; India, with 1,431,000; the United States, with 1,333,030; North Korea and Russia, with 1,320,000 each; Ukraine, with 900,000; Pakistan, with 660,000; Iran, with 610,000; Ethiopia, with 503,000; and Türkiye, with 481,000. The figures cover active personnel across the armed forces but exclude reservists and paramilitary organisations. North Korea’s high ranking reflects its emphasis on preparing for a potential conflict on the Korean Peninsula. Its military structure places considerable importance on ground forces, with significant strength positioned near the Demilitarised Zone separating the country from South Korea. Japan’s 2026 defence white paper also highlights the security challenges surrounding the Korean Peninsula and the military capabilities maintained by North Korea. Tank Ranks by Country China leads the ranking of countries with the largest tank inventories, followed by Russia, while North Korea occupies third place ahead of the United States. The figures illustrate the importance several countries continue to place on land-based military operations, although the number of tanks alone does not determine the effectiveness of an armoured force. Russia has 5,870 tanks, while China follows closely with 5,630. North Korea ranks third with 4,895 tanks, ahead of the United States, which has 4,666. India occupies fifth place with 3,913 tanks, followed by Egypt with 3,620. Pakistan ranks seventh with 2,677, while Iran is eighth with 2,675. Türkiye takes ninth place with 2,284 tanks, and Vietnam rounds out the top 10 with 1,999. North Korea’s extensive tank inventory reflects its long-standing focus on conventional ground warfare. Research published by the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) indicates that the country operates a combination of older Soviet-inspired designs and newer equipment. Maintaining a large number of tanks can provide a military with substantial ground-firepower capacity. However, the age and technological sophistication of the vehicles also matter. Modern armour, targeting systems, sensors, weapons and battlefield communications can significantly affect the performance of tanks in combat. Consequently, a country with a larger inventory does not necessarily possess a more effective armoured force than one with fewer but more advanced vehicles. Military Aircraft The United States has the world’s largest military aircraft inventory, with 13,032 aircraft, placing it far ahead of other countries. Its fleet is more than three times the size of Russia’s and exceeds the combined totals of the next four countries in the ranking. Russia comes second with 4,237 military aircraft, followed by China with 3,529. India ranks fourth with 2,183, while South Korea occupies fifth place with 1,540. Pakistan follows with 1,429 aircraft, ahead of Japan, which has 1,397. Türkiye ranks eighth with 1,101, while Egypt has 1,088. France completes the top 10 with 974 military aircraft. The ranking includes aircraft across military branches, covering helicopters, transport planes, training aircraft and other military aviation assets, rather than combat jets alone. The United States’ substantial advantage reflects the requirements of maintaining military operations across multiple regions of the world. Its armed forces need to transport troops, equipment and supplies over long distances while supporting combat missions far from home bases. These operations depend on a broad aviation network that includes cargo aircraft, aerial refuelling tankers, helicopters and fighter jets. The ability to transport personnel and equipment and keep aircraft supplied with fuel is essential to sustaining military operations overseas. However, the difference between the United States and China becomes smaller when the comparison is restricted to fighter and interceptor aircraft. The United States has 1,791 fighters and interceptors, compared with China’s 1,443. This gives Washington an advantage of approximately 24 per cent in this category. The narrower gap demonstrates that the United States’ lead in total military aircraft is partly attributable to the size and diversity of its wider aviation fleet, rather than fighter aircraft alone. Naval Assets China has the world’s largest navy by the number of vessels in the Global Firepower ranking, with 841 naval assets. The United States follows with 465, while Russia ranks third with 343. The ranking reflects China’s expanding maritime capabilities and its extensive shipbuilding industry. Research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has examined how China’s commercial shipbuilding infrastructure can also support military ship production, providing an industrial foundation for expanding its naval fleet. North Korea ranks fourth with 338 naval assets, followed by Sweden with 332. Indonesia occupies sixth place with 304 vessels, while Italy ranks seventh with 285. India is eighth with 279 naval assets, Thailand ranks ninth with 275, and Sri Lanka completes the top 10 with 275 vessels. China’s total of 841 vessels is substantially higher than the United States’ 465, but vessel counts provide only one measure of naval strength. The figures include different types of vessels, ranging from small patrol boats and coastal craft to larger warships. Each vessel contributes one unit to the total, regardless of its size, armament or operational role. As a result, a country with numerous smaller vessels may rank above another whose fleet contains fewer but significantly larger and more capable ships. The ranking changes when naval strength is measured by total fleet tonnage instead of vessel numbers. Under Global Firepower’s fleet-tonnage ranking, the United States takes first place, with approximately 2.6 times China’s total displacement. Fleet tonnage measures the combined displacement of a navy’s vessels and provides a different perspective on the scale of its maritime assets. Nevertheless, tonnage also has limitations. It does not independently measure a vessel’s weapons, technological sophistication, operational readiness or combat effectiveness. Taken together, the rankings demonstrate why military strength cannot be assessed through a single measure. Personnel numbers reveal the size of a country’s active force, tank inventories highlight its armoured capabilities, aircraft totals reflect its aviation resources, and naval counts offer insight into its maritime presence. However, equipment quality, training, logistics, technology and the ability to deploy forces effectively are also crucial to determining a military’s overall strength. title: Ukrainian, Romanian PMs discuss defense, energy, logistics
body:
According to Ukrinform, Koretskyi reported this on Facebook .
Both sides discussed Russia's attack on a civilian vessel off the Romanian coast, which killed one Ukrainian sailor, injured four others and left three missing. Six people were rescued.
Koretskyi thanked Romania for its principled stance and clear condemnation of this crime, which constitutes a gross violation of international law and freedom of navigation.
"We held substantive discussions on defense, energy and logistics. We seek to accelerate projects that will expand railway capacity, develop river transport routes and increase freight-handling capacity," he said.
Koretskyi invited his Romanian counterpart to establish cooperation through intergovernmental consultations. "This format has already proven effective in cooperation with other countries," he said.
"I thanked Romania for its consistent support since the first days of the full-scale invasion. I invited Niculescu to Kyiv. This was our first conversation since his appointment, so I also took the opportunity to congratulate my counterpart on his new position," Koretskyi added.

title: Police Fire Tear Gas As New French Protests Kick Off
body: French police started firing tear gas at protesters Saturday as they stepped up security in major cities, aiming to prevent a repeat of rioting a week ago, on a day of fresh nationwide demonstrations over the high cost of living. Police in the southeast city of Lyon fired tear gas to disperse some 150 protesters near the city centre — where demonstrations had been banned — when they briefly tried to block a road, an AFP journalist saw. “The police are really mobile… They come and disperse marches before they even form,” said a 21-year-old student who had turned up to protest, speaking on condition of anonymity. Elsewhere, authorities and rattled shopkeepers geared up for potential new street violence. Protesters take part in a demonstration “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. Near Paris’s Bastille neighbourhood, a clothing store had removed all its merchandise from shelves ahead of the demonstrations, while a nearby restaurant was boarded up with signs insisting it was “still open”. Many other retailers in the capital also had wooden boards covering their windows. The Louvre and the Musée d’Orsay museums were closed. The capital’s police said at midday officers had confiscated “various forbidden items” but described the situation as “calm”. In Marseille, riot squad vehicles, armoured trucks and a water cannon were parked in the city centre, while police elsewhere prepared for potential clashes. They were among 70,000 security personnel the interior ministry said were mobilised to counter the “high” threat of violence. A protester speaks in a microphone as others hold a banner reading “neither congress nor meeting for the RN” during a demonstration “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. Protest Against Le Pen’s Party Adding to tensions, Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party held a congress in Orleans to launch her campaign for elections in six months to choose President Emmanuel Macron’s successor. Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched on Saturday against Le Pen, and also against Macron, a pro-business centrist leader. “Macron resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd yelled. Police put their numbers at 11,000 while organisers said 26,000 took part. The unrest highlighted tensions in France ahead of the vote, which Le Pen is best-placed, according to surveys, to win. Last weekend saw rioters on the margins of the nationwide demonstrations clash with police, vandalise public buildings and loot hundreds of stores. Some 2,700 people were arrested, and the retail sector said shopowners were left with damage and stolen stock totalling hundreds of millions of euros. Macron attributed the worst of the violence to “ultra-left” groups that he said want to bring down the republic. Groups organising Saturday’s renewed demonstrations have accused Macron and his government of ignoring widespread public anger over rising costs, and over classroom conditions for students. Inflation in France, as elsewhere, has been sent surging by the Middle East war, started in February against Iran by US President Donald Trump and Israel. Protests have also been taking place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems. Italy has mobilised 500 troops to Milan after street violence there. Protesters stand at the Campo Santo Antifascist village as part of a demonstration “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) with the Orleans Cathedral in the background in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. Boarded-Up Shops In Paris, streets on Saturday were unusually quiet, with many shop windows boarded up, and some of the bigger retailers sent messages to customers warning that they were closed for the day. The capital’s police at the last minute ordered a union-organised march in the city be moved from Bastille, in the centre-east, to the more remote eastern Porte d’Italie on the southern rim of the capital. Unions said they reluctantly would go along with that. But the Yellow Vests, who staged disruptive protests against Macron eight years ago, denounced an “authoritarian drift” and called for yet more demonstrations on October 31 for “the freedom to protest”. Protesters march along the Avenue Jean Zay during a demonstration “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. A shopworker in the city of Rennes told AFP: “Bans are sometimes worse. Protesting is a right, and when you ban it you make it even more tempting.” Macron and his government have sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last Saturday. Courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, officials said. Macron has said authorities would accept only union-led demonstrations and would counter any others they deemed “illegitimate”. The restrictions, including outright bans on protests in some cities, have drawn criticism. Amnesty International denounced what it called “a slide toward authoritarian practice”, saying the measures were “jeopardising the right to demonstrate peacefully”. “Police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. title: Which countries are best at maths? See top 10
body: China leads the world in mathematics performance among 15-year-old students, followed by Singapore and Macao, according to the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results published in September 2026. The ranking compares the average mathematics scores of students across participating countries and economies. PISA assesses more than the ability to memorise formulas, examining how well students apply mathematical knowledge and reasoning to real-world problems. More than 760,000 students participated in PISA 2025 across 91 countries and economies, representing roughly 33 million 15-year-olds worldwide. Here are the 10 highest-scoring countries in mathematics. 1. China — 612 points China tops the ranking with an average mathematics score of 612. The result represents Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang, rather than the whole country. 2. Singapore — 563 points Singapore ranks second with an average score of 563, placing it 49 points behind China. 3. Macao — 549 points Macao takes third place with 549 points, maintaining a position among the highest-performing education systems in mathematics. 4. Taiwan — 546 points Taiwan ranks fourth, recording an average score of 546, just three points behind Macao. 5. Japan — 525 points Japan places fifth with 525 points, making it the fifth-highest-scoring participant in the ranking. 6. South Korea — 522 points South Korea records an average score of 522, placing it sixth, three points behind Japan. 7. Hong Kong SAR — 522 points Hong Kong SAR also scores 522 points, matching South Korea’s average. 8. Estonia — 508 points Estonia is the highest-ranked European participant, with an average mathematics score of 508. 9. Switzerland — 499 points Switzerland ranks ninth with 499 points, placing it 36 points below Estonia. 10. United Kingdom — 488 points The United Kingdom completes the top 10 with an average score of 488, 25 points below Switzerland. The post Which countries are best at maths?
