title: Britain and France to lead Hormuz transit mission
body: Britain is co-leading planning with France for a Multinational Military Mission intended to give commercial shipping safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, and has an autonomous mine countermeasures capability already working in the region, according to an answer given in Parliament. Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, had asked how the United Kingdom is contributing to multinational maritime security task forces in the Red Sea and Gulf. Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The UK remains steadfast in its commitment to maritime security in the Middle East and to supporting regional stability alongside our regional partners. “The UK is supporting multinational maritime security efforts in the Red Sea and Gulf regions, working alongside international partners including US-led Combined Maritime Forces. “The UK is also co-leading planning efforts with the French on the Multinational Military Mission that will support safe transit for commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. As part of this, the Royal Navy’s modernisation programme has delivered an autonomous mine countermeasures capability operating in the region, which continues to innovate at pace.” The Royal Navy withdrew its last Sandown class minehunters from the Gulf and replaced crewed mine warfare vessels in the region with uncrewed systems operated from a support ship, drawing on the work done through the Maritime Mine Counter Measures programme developed jointly with France. The post Britain and France to lead Hormuz transit mission first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Obuasi SHTS sexual abuse: Headmaster has no right to use accuser’s motherhood to justify alleged rape – NETRIGHT
body: Convener of the Network for Women’s Rights (NETRIGHT), Professor Akosua A. Adarkwa, says the suspended Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS) headmaster Zakaria Abdulai has worsened his position by publicly referring to the age and parental status of the student who accused him of rape. She said his comments, in which he disclosed that the accuser was between 20 and 21 years old and had a child, raised further concerns about attitudes towards women and the justification of sexual abuse. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 24, Prof Adarkwa said the remarks suggested a troubling attitude towards female students and the circumstances in which they could be vulnerable to abuse. “But actually, he’s made his case worse because it means he’s sitting at the school and he’s trying to figure out which of these girls he should go and abuse. That’s what he’s saying to us,” she said. Prof Adarkwa stressed that a woman’s character or personal circumstances could never justify sexual assault, insisting that even if the student had a reputation for misconduct, that would not give the headmaster the right to abuse her. “And you, the headmaster, does that give you a right then? Even if she was the chief of the bad girls association, not just the Ghana version, international. She is the lead of the bad girls association international. Does that give you the right to sexually assault her? And then stand in public and use it as justification,” she asked. Read also: Obuasi SHTS headmaster says rape accuser is 20 to 21 years old and has a child She also criticised what she described as a lack of respect for women in Ghanaian society, arguing that the absence of strong public condemnation of such remarks could embolden people to express attitudes that excuse sexual violence. “Because part of this is also that we have no respect for women in this country. So, he can boldly say something like that. He doesn’t get a reaction that makes him think, ‘Wait a minute, maybe I shouldn’t, even if I’m thinking this, I shouldn’t have the nerve to open my mouth and say this,’” she said. Prof Adarkwa expressed concern about reactions to the case on social media, saying some comments appeared to trivialise the allegations or suggest that the student’s circumstances could be used to judge her credibility. She urged the public to reflect on the controversy and examine the social attitudes that allow the mistreatment of girls and women to be defended or normalised. “If you go on social media, you’ll be sick. Because sometimes I read and I’m wondering, is this person being contrarian just to have a laugh? Do they really, honestly, truly believe this? And if they do, how come we’ve created a society where we think it is acceptable to treat girls like this. We need to use this as a learning moment for all of us,” she added. Background Mr Abdulai, who has been suspended amid allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi SHTS, made the comments in an interview with radio host Blakk Rasta while responding to reports surrounding the case. “I know she’s given birth. She has a child. She’s 20 to 21 years. But I cannot judge her; whether she’s bad or good. I cannot. But I have my story,” he said. He also disclosed that he had been cautioned by the police following a complaint lodged by the student and her parents, and that he had been granted self-recognisance bail while awaiting court proceedings. “I have been cautioned because one girl and her parents said I have raped her. So, they reported, I was cautioned, and as a headmaster I was given self-recognisance bail. I’m waiting for court days,” he said. Mr Abdulai maintained that he had his own account of the events and said the committee that investigated the matter had heard both his account and that of the student and her relatives. The allegations remain subject to investigation, and the claims against the suspended headmaster have not been established in court.

title: Obuasi SHTS scandal: Investigate all schools where headmaster previously worked – Akosua Manu
body: The Adviser on Gender and Social Protection to former Vice-President Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, Akosua Manu, has called for investigations into all schools where the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School, Zakaria Abdulai, previously worked, following allegations of sexual abuse involving female students. Her comments follow allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School, brought to public attention through investigative journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni’s documentary, Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow. Appearing on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 24, Ms Manu said investigations should extend beyond the current allegations to examine how complaints were handled at the headmaster’s previous institutions and whether officials responsible for student protection fulfilled their duties. “Now, what I want us to do is to call for an investigation. Every school that he has been in, we have to look at everybody who was a safety protocol officer there,” she stated. She also demanded scrutiny of Ghana Education Service (GES) officials who may have received complaints but allegedly failed to take appropriate action. “We need to see who is in charge, even at GES, who receives these complaints and flips the paper over and says that it’s normal,” she added. Ms Manu expressed concern about the power imbalance between school authorities and students, particularly girls from economically disadvantaged backgrounds who depend on the Free Senior High School (Free SHS) policy to continue their education. According to her, some students may remain silent about sexual abuse for fear of losing their educational opportunities or facing retaliation from influential school authorities. “Now, when you go to school and this happens to you, do you not fear that you may not complete your education? So you’d rather keep quiet and finish school,” she said. She argued that such vulnerabilities could expose students to exploitation, especially where effective reporting and safeguarding systems are absent. The former adviser also questioned the institutional oversight that allowed the reported transfer of at least 38 teachers from the school without, in her view, sufficient scrutiny. “What audit process at GES says, ‘Hold up, how have 38 people been transferred from your institution in the last couple of years? What is going on?'” she questioned. Ms Manu further raised concerns about alleged attempts to influence complainants and their families, citing reports that some had been approached with offers of educational support in exchange for withdrawing complaints. She disclosed that, of the 19 girls reportedly linked to the allegations, only four had physically come forward to give accounts of their experiences, while one complainant had reportedly withdrawn her police complaint. She commended the efforts of a parent who reportedly involved the local Odikro to document an alleged attempt to persuade the family to abandon its complaint. Ms Manu also criticised attempts to discredit alleged victims through claims about their personal backgrounds, insisting that such narratives could never justify sexual abuse. “It doesn’t matter. You do not have a right to abuse her,” she stressed. Turning to the political controversy surrounding the allegations, she criticised the handling of the matter by the National Democratic Congress (NDC), questioning its reported decision to clear the headmaster to contest a party position before subsequently changing its stance following public criticism. She argued that political considerations should not overshadow the protection of children or the need for accountability. Ms Manu also called for stronger institutional safeguards, stressing that school authorities, education officials and law enforcement agencies must be held accountable where investigations establish failures in their responsibilities.

title: Starlink returns to working order in Ukraine, the private power behind a modern war
body: Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version, Starshield, were again operating at high speeds after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned systems came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.Ukrainian officials said the restrictions hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations."Ukraine's Ministry of Defense monitoring systems are officially recording the restoration of Starlink/Starshield operating speeds," the ministry said on the Telegram app."Connectivity remains stable at speeds exceeding 400 km per hour," it added.The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems' maximum operating speeds, and the defense ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored. When limitations were in place, Ukraine experienced problems trying to operate at speeds over 160 kph.Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, but Starlink is vital for frontline communications, and Starshield is used for military operations in occupied territories.The sudden disruption of satellite communications used by Ukrainian forces on October 14 has exposed a growing vulnerability in modern warfare: Military operations increasingly depend on privately operated technology whose availability can be restricted without warning.Renewed questions over private influence on military operationsThe limitations imposed on services provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX interrupted Ukrainian drone missions, including operations intended to counter Russian attacks. The incident has triggered a dispute over who authorized the restrictions and renewed questions about the influence commercial satellite providers can exert over military operations.The implications extend beyond Ukraine to the Middle East, where Starlink technology has played a role in US military operations against Iran while also providing civilians with a way to circumvent government-imposed internet restrictions.Ukrainian officials reported that satellite terminals had stopped maintaining reliable connections when mounted on equipment traveling faster than approximately 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph). Some military units experienced disruptions at lower speeds, forcing them to cancel or interrupt drone missions.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that the restrictions had impaired Ukraine's ability to intercept faster Russian drones. Although some services were subsequently restored, limitations on high-speed operations remained in place as Kyiv sought a resolution.On October 22, The Wall Street Journal reported that President Donald Trump had called Musk a day earlier and asked him to lift the restrictions. US and Ukrainian officials said the system was operating more normally on Thursday, although some Ukrainian officials reported that full functionality had not been restored.The disruption came during heightened tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil facilities. However, whether those disagreements influenced the restrictions has not been established.The question of responsibility has produced conflicting accounts.On October 15, Reuters reported, citing two American officials and a Western official familiar with the matter, that the order to slow the military satellite service originated inside the White House.On October 20, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, citing US officials and people familiar with the decision.President Trump denied involvement in the original restrictions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently said that decisions about the speed and permitted use of SpaceX services were governed by commercial arrangements rather than White House directives.Rubio also said Ukraine did not have access to Starshield, SpaceX's military-oriented satellite service, contradicting Ukrainian officials and US senators who said the service had been restricted.The conflicting explanations have drawn scrutiny from Congress. On October 15, a bipartisan group of senators called for a Pentagon inspector general investigation into the disruptions. Four Democratic senators followed on October 19 with a letter demanding that SpaceX clarify its role in restricting Ukraine's access to satellite services.Beyond the immediate political dispute, the episode has exposed the risks of building military capabilities around infrastructure controlled by an outside provider.Ukraine is over-reliant on Starlink technologyPatrick Bolder, a strategic adviser at the Hague Centre for Strategic Studies who specializes in European defense, NATO, and military space operations, told The Media Line that Ukraine's reliance on Starlink has grown far beyond what its developers originally envisioned.“Starlink wasn't designed for military operations because it was designed for civil use,” Bolder said.Nevertheless, the network has become integral to Ukrainian military operations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.John King, founder of Q Advisory, described the technology's appeal to military planners.“Starlink has become a major source of military advantage because it connects people, sensors and commanders when conventional communications are damaged or unavailable. Its low Earth orbit network provides broadband with relatively little delay. The strategic value is the speed with which information can move between those who observe a threat and those responsible for responding.”For Ukrainian forces, satellite internet has become part of an interconnected command system rather than simply a backup means of communication. King illustrated what that means during a military operation.“Losing a connection can interrupt several activities at once: receiving video, sharing a warning, coordinating units or controlling a connected platform.”The October incident also brought attention to the distinction between two SpaceX services whose names have sometimes been used interchangeably.Who controls Starshield systems - Musk or the US government?Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite broadband service, originally developed for civilian and business customers. Starshield, which builds on Starlink technology, is designed for government and national security applications, including secure communications, Earth observation, and specialized satellite payloads.Although the systems share technological foundations, they do not necessarily provide identical capabilities or operate under the same contractual arrangements.King said the distinction is important when interpreting claims about what Ukrainian forces have lost.“Ukraine's communications service should therefore not be confused with every intelligence capability associated with the Starshield name. Carrying intelligence over a network is different from collecting that intelligence.”Musk has argued that Starshield systems fall under US government control, while Rubio has described decisions about commercial service restrictions as matters for SpaceX. Ukrainian officials, meanwhile, have reported disruptions affecting services they identify as Starshield.The precise division of technical, contractual, and operational authority remains disputed.For Bolder, the situation raises broader concerns about Washington's approach to Ukraine. He argued that restricting military assistance and communications capabilities could increase pressure on Kyiv to accept unfavorable terms in negotiations with Russia.King was more cautious about drawing broader strategic conclusions from the disruption.“A restriction on Ukrainian connectivity can benefit Moscow by weakening Ukraine's ability to coordinate operations and defend against attacks. The scale of that benefit depends on the affected services, duration, and availability of backups. It does not follow that losing one network automatically determines the outcome of the war. The sound conclusion is that dependence creates leverage and additional vulnerability, even when disruption is temporary.”Accusations that Starlink has been improperly used in the Middle EastSimilar questions have emerged in the Middle East, where Starlink technology has served both military and civilian purposes during the war involving the United States, Israel, and Iran.In May, Reuters reported that American LUCAS one-way attack drones operating against Iran had used Starlink-related connectivity, prompting disagreements between SpaceX and the Pentagon over service pricing.According to the report, SpaceX sought to increase the monthly connectivity fee from approximately $5,000 to $25,000 per terminal, arguing that the drones were using a service comparable to its more expensive aviation tier. Pentagon officials objected to the proposed pricing but ultimately agreed to the higher fees, Reuters reported.Musk disputed the Reuters report, saying that civilian Starlink services had been improperly used for military purposes. The Pentagon also challenged the report, although neither provided detailed evidence contradicting its central findings.The disagreement highlighted the complications that can arise when military capabilities depend on commercial technologies governed by contractual terms and pricing arrangements.Starlink helps Iranian dissidents communicate during imposed blackoutsIn Iran itself, Starlink has played a different role.Iranian authorities have repeatedly restricted internet access during periods of political unrest, leaving satellite connections among the limited means available to some residents seeking to communicate with the outside world.The authorities have responded by confiscating unauthorized terminals and attempting to disrupt satellite connections.In October, a senior Iranian official claimed that the government had successfully disabled Starlink terminals during protests earlier in the year. The extent of those efforts has not been independently established.King cautioned against drawing conclusions about the military uses of Starlink from evidence of its availability to Iranian civilians.“Separately, satellite internet has helped some Iranians communicate during state-imposed blackouts, while authorities have confiscated terminals and used jamming. Civilian access and military connectivity must be assessed separately; evidence of one does not establish a particular targeting or intelligence mission.”Bolder also discussed proposals to supply Starlink terminals to Iranian opposition groups. Such initiatives, he suggested, could extend a commercial provider's influence well beyond the communications industry.“Should they be responsible for such a thing? Shouldn't there be some rules on this? I wonder.”European governments, defense systems rely on US systemsFor European countries, Ukraine's experience has added urgency to a longstanding debate about dependence on American military and technological capabilities.Other satellite communications providers are developing services for government and defense customers, but there is no straightforward way to substitute one network for another in the middle of an armed conflict.King said the problem is more specific than a lack of competition.“I would describe SpaceX's position as an acute concentration of operational dependence, rather than a proven monopoly over all military satellite communications. Other providers exist. The difficulty is replacing the particular combination of network capacity, suitable terminals and integration into existing operations.” Bolder focused on the political consequences of Europe's relationship with the United States.“We trusted the US, and we did a lot of business with the US, and we depended on the US, and now you see that the trust is gone but the dependency is still there and we've maneuvered ourselves in a position where we can be blackmailed,” he warned.European governments have begun pursuing greater independence through programs such as IRIS², the European Union's planned secure satellite communications constellation.Under an agreement announced in August, the project will expand to 348 satellites, with initial launches planned for 2029 and services introduced progressively thereafter.The constellation is intended to provide secure communications for European governments, defense forces, and emergency services. However, its development cannot immediately replace the capabilities Ukraine currently needs.Bolder argued that Europe must diversify its strategic dependencies, even if doing so requires substantial investment.Militaries should be prepared for communications network failures King placed greater emphasis on building resilience into existing arrangements. Governments, he said, should establish clear rules determining who may authorize changes to services, how emergency restrictions are handled, and what obligations providers have to maintain connectivity during military operations.Independent communications systems should also be available and regularly tested so that military operations can continue if a primary network becomes unavailable.The debate reflects a broader shift in military planning. NATO recognized space as an operational domain in 2019, acknowledging the importance of satellite systems for communications, intelligence, surveillance, and military coordination.Ukraine's experience has demonstrated that possessing advanced military technology is not enough when the communications infrastructure supporting it can be restricted by another party.King said the disputes surrounding Starlink should prompt governments to reconsider how they measure military readiness.“For future conflicts, the measure of strength will be whether a force can keep making decisions when its preferred network becomes unavailable. Starlink has shown the extraordinary value of commercial innovation. Governments now need to match that innovation with dependable agreements, practical alternatives, and accountable public decisions.”

title: FIFA: Infantino says backed by ‘vast majority’ in bid for re-election
body: FIFA president Gianni Infantino has said he has the backing of the “vast, vast majority” of member associations in his bid for re-election despite criticism of his aborted World Cup selloff plan. The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) rallied behind Infantino on Friday in a significant boost to the 56-year-old’s hopes of winning a fourth term in charge. Infantino’s future in the role was in doubt two months ago when he faced a furious backlash to his plan to sell off a portion of the commercial rights of competitions run by football’s world governing body to private investors. The heads of European football’s governing body UEFA, the AFC and CONCACAF, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter saying football “belongs to no individual”. But Infantino, who apologised last week for the failed private investment project, is now in a strong position to secure re-election in March. “I think what is important is that in an organisation like FIFA, there can be different views, different points of view,” Infantino told the BBC on Saturday. “But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority. “I’m just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all African countries have endorsed me. I’m speaking to all associations everywhere in the world.” No other candidate has yet come forward to oppose Infantino with the deadline to do so less than a month away on November 18. He added: “There are different points of view it’s not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the FIFA member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want FIFA to be run.” The post FIFA: Infantino says backed by ‘vast majority’ in bid for re-election appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Police in Lyon disperse student protest with tear gas
body:
PARIS, October 24. /TASS/. Police in Lyon (central France) used tear gas to disperse students who attempted to hold a demonstration near Lyon 3 University despite a government ban, the Actu.fr news portal reported.
Around 150 people attempted to stage a protest, but law enforcement officers arriving at the scene ordered them to clear the area in front of the university. In response, several youths began shouting insults at the officers, who then moved to forcibly disperse the crowd using tear gas during the confrontation.
Earlier, the prefect of the Rhone department banned all public gatherings for October 24 to prevent unrest similar to the riots on October 17. Enhanced security measures were implemented across the city, featuring an expanded presence of police and gendarmes on the streets. The prefect also imposed a curfew from 11:00 p.m. Saturday until 6:00 a.m. Sunday.

title: Sheikh Khaled meets Emirati military students on official visit to Greece
body: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed , Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, met Emirati military students honing their skills in Greece as part of his official visit to the country. He hailed the young citizens as ambassadors for the UAE owing to their diligence, excellence and dedication and called on them to embody Emirati values and represent their nation and its armed forces with honour. Sheikh Khaled wished the students well on their academic and professional journey during discussion held at the Technical Training and Qualification Centre. Sheikh Khaled conveyed the greetings of President Sheikh Mohamed to the prospective military personnel, emphasising the UAE's commitment to following their well-being and progress abroad. The military students expressed their thanks to Sheikh Khaled for the visit and extended their gratitude to the country's leadership for its continued support and care. The technical training centre offers specialised training programmes combining theoretical knowledge and practical applications across various technical fields. خالد بن محمد بن زايد، ولي عهد أبوظبي، يزور مركز التدريب والتأهيل الفني في اليونان، ويلتقي عدداً من الطلبة العسكريين الإماراتيين الدارسين في المركز، حيث أكّد سموّه حرص القيادة الرشيدة على متابعة دراستهم وتدريبهم وتوفير الدعم لهم لتحقيق التميز وأداء واجباتهم الوطنية بكفاءة واقتدار. pic.twitter.com/1rLCtE3EAw — مكتب أبوظبي الإعلامي (@ADMediaOffice) October 24, 2026 Those programmes form part of military co-operation between the Emirates and Greece aimed at enhancing the readiness of UAE Armed Forces members for duty. The military meeting was held before Sheikh Khaled concluded his official visit on Friday, which took place at the invitation of Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis. Sheikh Khaled had on Thursday held talks with Mr Mitsotakis as major deals were agreed on between the countries. Discussions at the Prime Minister's Office centred on efforts to bolster collaboration across sectors including energy, infrastructure, health care, advanced technology and health care. Sheikh Khaled emphasised the UAE's desire to strengthen long-standing relations with Greece to support the aspirations of both nations. It was also announced during the visit that the UAE is to invest a further €15 billion ($16.8 billion) in Greece as part of a joint initiative between the countries. Sheikh Khaled also toured two of Greece's leading cultural attractions on Friday. Sheikh Khaled viewed the extensive collection of artwork at the National Gallery of Greece and also visited the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. He was briefed on the creative works at the gallery that reflect the rich history and heritage of Greece and the evolution of its art scene.

title: CIA Continues Intel and Warning Feeds to Ukraine
body:
The US Central Intelligence Agency ( CIA ) continues to provide Ukraine with critical military intelligence despite political friction between US President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky, The Atlantic reported.
Citing a senior military officer who regularly travels to Ukraine, the publication reported that the CIA plays a “leading role” among US institutions supporting Kyiv’s defense posture.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The officer noted that coordination with US intelligence agencies has substantially upgraded the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s ability to plan and execute precision strikes against Russian military targets.
An intelligence official from a Baltic nation collaborating with the US to counter Russian regional threats told The Atlantic that CIA field and tactical operations have become “significantly more aggressive” under current agency leadership compared to parameters maintained during Joe Biden’s administration.
The report highlights the complex position occupied by CIA Director John Ratcliffe. While Ratcliffe directly advises a president who has repeatedly sparred with Ukrainian leadership in public forums, he concurrently leads an intelligence apparatus that remains vital to Ukraine’s air defense coordination and battlefield survival.
According to The Atlantic, Ukrainian officials do not regard Ratcliffe as an unconditional ally. Because the CIA director ultimately answers to Trump, Kyiv recognizes he would execute an executive directive to suspend intelligence flows should the White House formally condition data access on a cessation of Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian oil refineries.
Officials and interlocutors cited by the magazine indicated that Ratcliffe recognizes the security hazards Moscow poses not only to Ukraine, but to the US and European allies.
Sources suggested that similar strategic awareness is shared by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , even as both cabinet officials have publicly echoed Trump’s political messaging in recent weeks.
The report also disclosed that the CIA director has previously offered informal counsel to Zelensky regarding communication strategies for engaging with the American president.
The intelligence continuity follows recent technical friction that complicated air defense notifications across Ukraine, including disruptions to SpaceX’s Starlink network and temporary interruptions in US early-warning missile launch data.
While US data streams have experienced operational friction, Washington has not formally terminated intelligence sharing with Kyiv. However, sources familiar with agency workflows noted that Trump retains statutory authority to order a complete intelligence cutoff at any time.
People familiar with Ratcliffe’s interactions indicated that if Trump were to issue an executive order halting intelligence cooperation with Ukraine, the CIA director would likely comply without attempting to reverse the president’s determination, notwithstanding internal concerns within the intelligence community.
The reporting on intelligence flows aligns with statements delivered earlier in the week by President Zelensky, who confirmed on Tuesday, Oct. 20, that early-warning tracking cooperation had resumed following high-level diplomatic discussions in Oslo, Norway.
Prior to the Oslo summit, Kyiv had endured days without advance notifications regarding incoming ballistic strikes, during which kinetic impacts damaged capital utility networks.
Following talks with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff, Zelensky noted that intelligence pipelines were functioning again and expressed optimism regarding follow-on technical agreements on Patriot interceptors and Starlink connectivity.
The diplomatic movement in Oslo preceded travel by Witkoff to St. Petersburg to present prospective peace frameworks to the Russian leadership , even as Kremlin officials publicly ruled out political concessions.

title: Khmara discusses procurement and production development with defense industry representatives
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry reported this on Facebook .
"Equal rules for all defense industry enterprises are important to us. Manufacturers must understand the state's needs and future demand and plan their work accordingly. In turn, we expect the defense industry to realistically assess its production capabilities, continuously develop and seek new technological solutions. Russia adapts quickly. We must be faster. We must stay one step ahead. We must respond to a threat that exists only as an enemy plan," Khmara said.
The ministry stressed that the main criterion for the development of the defense industry must be whether it meets the needs of Ukraine's Defense Forces. The ministry is also working on mechanisms for the controlled export of Ukrainian defense products.
"The focus must not be on sales, but on the needs of our military. We must have a clear understanding of how much weaponry the front needs and guarantee its delivery. Only after that can export opportunities be considered. Exports should open up new markets for Ukrainian manufacturers, help them expand production and generate resources for further investment," the minister said.
Khmara also underlined the importance of reinvesting profits in enterprise development and increasing production volumes. He said this was necessary to ensure that Ukraine's defense industry could respond promptly to changing frontline needs.

title: MK May Golan questioned for 10 hours over allegations of stealing thousands from charities
body: MK May Golan was questioned by police for 10 hours on Thursday over allegations that she pocketed donations intended for a nonprofit she founded.During questioning at Lahav 433, Israel Police's national crime investigation unit, Golan denied the allegations and said she had documents showing where the money had gone. When investigators cited evidence provided by employees in her ministry, she asked to hear the recordings herself.One part of the investigation focuses on whether Golan used funds from the nonprofit she founded and managed for personal expenses. Investigators told her they had a witness who alleged she had taken approximately $22,000 in donations for herself.Investigators say Golan's employees provided documents and recordingsGolan called the claims lies and said she had documentation supporting her account. “I have documents that can show that all the money was donated to activities providing food baskets and helping homeless people in south Tel Aviv," she said.Investigators also questioned Golan about allegations that she used public funds for personal purposes. One investigator told her that employees in her ministry had provided evidence supporting that allegation.Golan asked to examine the evidence. “Play me the recordings. I am prepared to confront them," she said, according to Walla. The questioning ended for the day after 10 hours. Investigators say they have documents and recordings, some provided by Golan's employees. Golan maintains that her own documents will show the donations were used to help people in need.The investigation is ongoing, and Golan denies the allegations against her.

title: Abuja High Court Rules in Favour of Halkin E&P Over Eunisell
body: The High Court of the Federal Capital Territory in Abuja has delivered judgment in favour of Halkin Exploration and Production Limited (Halkin E&P) in a suit brought by the company against Eunisell Limited over a disputed contractual provision. The dispute centred on Clause 10.4 of a service agreement between Halkin E&P and Eunisell, which the court ruled was unenforceable, having found it to be a penalty clause designed to terrorise the claimant. Under Clause 10.4 of the agreement, Halkin E&P was required to pay a late payment charge of 0.5 per cent daily, equivalent to approximately 177 per cent annually on a compound interest basis, on outstanding payments. The provision resulted in Eunisell claiming millions of dollars in accumulated charges, reportedly exceeding ten times the underlying debt. In its judgment, delivered by Justice S.B Belgore on October 22, 2026, the court held that “Clause 10.4 of the Service Agreement between Halkin Exploration and Production Limited and Eunisell Limited dated 20th January 2022, which imposes an annual default fee of 177% (equivalent of 0.5% per day), is null, void, and of no legal effect whatsoever.” In addition, the court ruled that it was “setting aside, quashing, nullifying and invalidating all late payment/default invoices, bills and/or assessments, howsoever described, predicated on Clause 10.4 of the Service Agreement between Halkin Exploration and Production Limited and Eunisell Limited dated 20th January 2022 issued by the Defendant against the Claimant.” Commenting on the ruling, counsel to Halkin E&P, Chikaosulu Ojukwu, SAN, said “This decision is a victory for the rule of law and vindicates the consistent position maintained by our client, Halkin E&P, that the impugned clause in the agreement was contrary to public policy and therefore unenforceable. “Our client maintains that Eunisell Limited sought to use that clause to secure an unjustified financial windfall. The defendant Eunisell Limited withdrew from the oil well in the middle of the night, without notice, causing damage to the wellhead, according to our client. Our client will pursue a US$50 million claim against Eunisell Limited through the appropriate legal proceedings. This is a classical case of get rich quick” .

title: Kidnappers kill Abuja victim after collecting N16.2m ransom, suspects arrested – Police
body:
The police say seven suspected kidnappers abducted four members of a family in Abuja, collected N16.2 million ransom for the release of one of the victims, and demanded an additional N50 million before eventually killing her.
Victor Godfrey, the commander of the Force Intelligence Department, Special Tactical Squad (FID-STS), disclosed this to journalists on Friday, while parading the suspects, in the presence of the deceased’s family.
Mr Godfrey, an assistant commissioner of police, said the deceased, Oluwadamilola Adedayo, 14, was murdered after resisting an attempt by her abductors to sexually molest her.
He said that Oluwadamilola was abducted alongside her mother, Nancy, her 12-year-old brother, David, and their housemaid, Jennifer David, at gunpoint on 23 August.
Her decomposing body was recovered from a forest in Tukuba, Kuje, Abuja, on 19 October, following an intelligence-led operation by operatives of the FID-STS.
Twelve-year-old David recounted how the kidnappers broke into their homes at midnight, herded them into the forest and held them captive in the mountains.
David said Jennifer collapsed while trekking and was thrown into a stream, where the kidnappers covered her with leaves, believing she was dead.
The police said Jennifer survived and found her way back home.
David revealed that his sister was killed after she injured one of the kidnappers.
“She now cut the hand of one of them. Then, from there, they got angry. They beat her. They threw rocks at her. Unfortunately, she died. They threw her off the cliff, and nobody can survive that kind of fall,” he said.
One of the suspects, Alidu Lawal, 18, told reporters that the deceased attacked him with a cutlass, showing the wound on his right wrist. Mr Lawal denied attempts by any member of his gang to sexually assault the deceased.
David said he was later tied to a tree by the kidnappers.
“They tied me to a tree, saying that they want to go and buy coke, but they will soon come back. So, I managed to untie myself from the tree,” he said.
David said he climbed down the mountain and spent the night near a stream. The following day, he encountered a “Fulani” herdsman, whom he repeatedly told, “Kuje, Kuje.”
The herdsman led him to hunters, who took him to a village chief. Vigilantes subsequently took him to a hospital in Danfara, Kuje, where his uncles found him, he said.
The police commander said the boy escaped before any ransom was paid by the family, who did not know their daughter had been killed.
The victim’s father, Mr Adedoye, has called for justice, expressing appreciation to the Inspector General of Police (IGP) and the operatives involved in the investigation.
“The kidnapping and murder of our beloved daughter, Oluwadamilola, at this time has left our family in deep pain. However, the support and assurance from the leadership of the police force has given us strength and hope that justice will prevail,” he said.
“We continue to appeal to the police, with the help of Almighty God, to get to the root of this matter and ensure that all those responsible for this wicked act are brought to book.”
According to the police, the commando-style abduction occurred on 23 August 2026 in Kuchiyako, Kuje.
The deceased’s mother was released about an hour after the abduction to coordinate ransom payment,
The family subsequently paid N16.2 million for the release of their children. However, the kidnappers demanded another N50 million.
Mr Godfrey, the police commander, did not disclose whether any further payment was made.
The police commander said further investigations linked the same syndicate to the abduction of a businessman, John Ali, in Kuje on 24 September.
Mr Ali, an indigene of Benue State, was released after the kidnappers collected N3 million and recharge cards worth N100,000, he said.
The suspects were arrested after the Inspector-General of Police’s Secretariat endorsed a petition on 15 October, prompting an intelligence-led investigation.
Two suspects were arrested in Rijana community, Kaduna State , while five others were apprehended in Sagbon Lugbe, Abuja, through a joint operation involving police operatives, vigilantes and other security agencies.
On 19 October, operatives led by Mr Godfrey searched the gang’s camp in Tukuba Forest, where they recovered the deceased’s decomposing body.
Her remains were taken to a hospital mortuary for preservation and a possible autopsy, Mr Godfrey said.
He identified the remaining suspects as Ishaka Abdullahi, 27; Abdullahi Dabo, 42; Abubakar Jibrin, 20; Barahu Ibrahim, 24; Sani Mohammed, 24; and Yakubu Abubakar, 28.
Mr Godfrey said the suspects were found with four AK-47 rifles, a locally made revolver pistol, 63 rounds of live ammunition, a motorcycle, N400,000 and a mobile phone said to have been used for ransom negotiations.
“Investigation is ongoing, while efforts are being intensified to arrest other fleeing members of the syndicate and recover additional weapons,” he said, adding that the IGP has reaffirmed his unit’s efforts to “sustain aggressive operations against all forms of criminality across the nation.”
Mr Godfrey urged citizens to remain security-conscious and promptly report suspicious persons or activities to the nearest police station.
He vowed that such coordinated operations will be sustained and replicated across all states of the federation.

title: Russian Drone Hits Sumy Farm, 1 Dead, Child Injured in Dnipro
body:
A Russian drone struck a cattle-breeding agricultural enterprise in the Konotop district of Sumy region on Saturday, Oct. 24, killing a 31-year-old female farm worker and injuring four other people, regional authorities reported.
Head of the Sumy Regional Military Administration Oleh Hryhorov confirmed that the victim was located at the epicenter of the blast when the drone struck the civilian facility. The woman would have turned 32 in several days, Hryhorov stated in an official dispatch.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Medical responders evacuated the injured from the facility grounds, hospitalizing two victims whose injuries were preliminarily assessed as non-critical. The strike also killed and wounded livestock housed at the agricultural facility, prompting emergency veterinary and municipal civil defense units to deploy to contain the damage.
“The enemy struck a civilian cattle-breeding enterprise in Konotop district,” Hryhorov stated.
“Russia continues to strike civilian enterprises, destroy farms, and take the lives of people who were simply carrying out their work.”
Concurrently on Saturday, Russian forces launched an aerial drone attack against the Pokrovske community in the Nikopol district of Dnipropetrovsk region, injuring four civilians, regional officials confirmed .
Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha reported that the wounded included a 14-year-old boy. Emergency medical teams stabilized the boy at the scene before transferring him in critical condition to a regional pediatric hospital in Dnipro .
A 46-year-old man was also hospitalized in serious condition, while medical personnel treated two other wounded adults. Emergency response detachments initiated structural inspections across surrounding residential neighborhoods to assess blast impacts and repair severed local utilities.
The Saturday daytime drone strikes across Sumy and Dnipropetrovsk regions followed separate missile bombardments targeting civilian infrastructure in northeastern and southern Ukraine earlier in the day.
In Kharkiv region, a Russian missile hit a commercial warehouse in the city of Lozova , killing a 45-year-old man and wounding two others aged 26 and 43. Emergency medical crews attempted resuscitation at the scene, but the victim died of severe blast trauma as specialized firefighting units worked to extinguish a fire that engulfed the storage facility.
Concurrently in Zaporizhzhia , Russian tactical strikes engaged an infrastructure installation, wounding two civilians and setting adjacent passenger vehicles ablaze.

title: Alake’s attack on Atiku won’t cut food prices, ADC campaign fires back
body: By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja The African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Campaign Council has fired back at Information Minister Dele Alake over his allegations against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, saying no amount of political propaganda can shield President Bola Tinubu’s administration from public anger over rising living costs. The council argued that Nigerians were more concerned about the cost of food, fuel and transportation than allegations of artificial intelligence manipulation and deepfakes, challenging Alake to produce evidence linking Atiku or the ADC to the alleged fabricated letter and video. In a statement on Saturday, Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, described Alake’s intervention as an attempt to divert attention from the government’s record, insisting that the economic hardship confronting Nigerians was real and undeniable. “Until then, his ‘fake news alert’ is an empty political stunt,” Shaibu said, challenging the minister to provide names, dates and forensic findings to substantiate his allegations. Citing petrol prices of about ₦1,400 per litre, diesel prices above ₦2,000 and food inflation hovering around 20 per cent, Shaibu said the economic pressures facing households could not be dismissed as fabricated information. The council also cited a World Bank poverty estimate reported by Reuters, arguing that the administration’s economic direction had left millions of Nigerians struggling to make ends meet. Turning to Tinubu’s campaign rally in Kaduna, Shaibu questioned the explanation that a vehicle seen near an APC billboard was on routine patrol, asking why a campaign billboard required such protection. He also raised concerns over reports that supporters had travelled from distant states and were left sleeping on Kaduna’s streets. The statement further referred to reports of accidents involving APC supporters travelling from Sokoto and Abuja to the rally, although details remained unconfirmed. Shaibu urged the APC to account for the safety of those travelling to its campaign events, condemning what he described as the exploitation of supporters for political optics. “Making citizens endure long, hazardous journeys and sleep outdoors simply to create rally optics is political exploitation, not leadership,” he said. The ADC campaign council also questioned Tinubu’s reported decision to campaign in only 12 states, alleging that supporters were being moved from one rally to another to project an impression of widespread popular backing. “You can hire buses, assemble a crowd and plaster the streets with billboards. You cannot hire consent,” Shaibu said. He maintained that the APC’s economic record, rather than its attacks on the opposition, would shape its electoral prospects, insisting that Nigerians enduring high prices and shrinking incomes would ultimately judge the administration at the polls. “Alake’s attack on Atiku will not reduce the cost of a meal by one naira,” Shaibu added. The council expressed confidence that voters would reject the APC, promising a different economic direction under Atiku. “Bola made life expensive; Atiku will make Nigeria affordable again!” Shaibu declared. The post Alake’s attack on Atiku won’t cut food prices, ADC campaign fires back appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Seen And Heard At France Protests Today, As Police Arrest 135 People
body: AFP has deployed reporters, photographers and video journalists in cities across France to document nationwide cost-of-living protests on Saturday. Here is a round-up of what they are witnessing as security forces seek to prevent a repeat of violence and looting that erupted on the sidelines of similar demonstrations last weekend. ‘Distressing’ At Porte d’Italie, the alternate point that authorities have ruled Paris protesters must begin their demonstration, police surrounded a young man with bleached blond hair, emptied his bag on the ground and began going through his belongings piece by piece. At Porte de Vincennes, where the march is to finish, few businesses had been barricaded, though many had their shutters down. “It’s distressing. I don’t know where we’re heading,” said Dominique, an employee of a car rental company who preferred not to give her full name. “I don’t hold it against the people who are demonstrating. My grievance is with the rioters — those who come specifically to smash things and to steal.” France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu (R), France’s Decentralisation Minister Francoise Gatel (L), France’s Culture Minister Catherine Pegard (2nd-L) and the Mayor of Limoges Guillaume Guerin (C) listen to explanations from police commissioner Yannick Sallabert (3rd-L) during a visit of the damaged premises of the City Hall of Limoges in the context of security and reconstruction efforts at the police station in Limoges on October 23, 2026, after a group of individuals forced entry into the building during last weekend’s protest action against the “high cost of living”. (Photo by Pascal LACHENAUD / POOL / AFP) | Pascal LACHENAUD / POOL / AFP Police Are ‘Faster’ A 21-year-old student protester in Lyon, where demonstrators were tear-gassed on Saturday, said police were “highly mobile”. “As a result, I haven’t been able to find a march all morning. We keep moving around, but since the police have vehicles, they’re faster; they manage to break up the groups before they can even really form,” he said. “Last week, the police weren’t nearly as mobile. We didn’t run into any issues; the atmosphere was very friendly and good-natured. Today, things are much more complicated … We end up exchanging information like criminals. We’re in small groups — sometimes just pairs — trying to share updates and find other people, but it’s extremely difficult.” People gather with city hall employees and elected officials outside Lille’s town hall as part of a day of rallies called by the French Mayors’ Association (AMF) to condemn the “very serious and premeditated acts” following October’s 17 violence at town halls and calling for “a change to the police’s operational doctrine”, in Lille, north of France, on October 17, 2026. ‘Still Open’ Near Paris’s Bastille square, a clothing store removed all its merchandise ahead of the demonstrations, while a nearby restaurant was boarded up despite signs insisting it was “still open”. Many retailers in the capital had wooden boards covering windows. A heavy police presence could be seen in Place de la Bastille, along with many journalists, but few protesters. Police used a megaphone to tell the crowd that the demonstration had been banned from the area, telling protesters to go to the alternate route near Porte d’Italie “immediately”. Saint-Denis Mayor Bally Bagayoko (bottom C) attends a demonstration “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. – Not ‘Just One Grievance’ “I don’t think the French people have just one grievance,” said Aliyah, 22, sitting with her mother Ludovine on a cafe terrace near the Old Port in Marseille as they waited for demonstrations. She said people’s primary concern was rising costs. “The people are growing poorer, the people are unhappy, so they take to the streets to protest,” she said, adding that bans on the demonstrations in some cities “only makes us more determined to show up”. ‘Curiosity’ Protests were prohibited in the city of Grenoble, with shops and restaurants open mid-morning — though a curfew was in place in parts of the city and several shopping centres from 6:00 pm (1600 GMT). Francois-Xavier Chambron, who works at a bar on the city’s Place Grenette, said they planned to stay open at least for lunch, noting that they already had reservations and that people will be around “out of sheer curiosity”. Protesters stand at the Campo Santo Antifascist village as part of a demonstration “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) with the Orleans Cathedral in the background in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. ‘Hotter Than Fascists’ Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched in the city of Orleans against a congress by the far-right National Rally (RN) party of Marine Le Pen. The protest criticised both leading presidential candidate Le Pen and centrist President Emmanuel Macron. “Macron resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd yelled, while carrying placards that read “The Youth say ‘screw you’ to the National Rally” and “Hotter than fascists”. Tear Gas In Lyon Police fired tear gas to disperse about 150 protesters in the southeastern city of Lyon, in an area banned to all demonstrations, an AFP journalist saw. Police fired several tear gas grenades to clear the group gathered at a university building and the city police station. Police moved in as protesters tried to block a road. Earlier, a police helicopter could be seen flying over the city, with security forces patrolling and armoured vehicles and riot police vans parked nearby. Shops were boarded up, with private security guards in front of some. Calls to defy the bans on protests in the city centre had circulated on social media. ‘Improvise’ Shopkeepers in boarded-up Paris said they were unsure what to expect. “It feels like we’re all just going to have to improvise a bit… We’ve secured everything as best we can, we’ll likely close at 1:00 pm and then stay in the vicinity to keep an eye on things,” Armelle Gueganton, a bookseller in the 12th arrondissement, told AFP. She worried about the route that authorities had mandated for the main Paris rally, pointing out that parts of it were “extremely narrow” and that it passed by a petrol station. “I have to wonder if they even have Google Maps at the prefecture when they authorise routes like this.” ‘Break Things’ Shops were also boarded up in the southwestern city of Bordeaux. “Boarding up five storefronts like ours … costs us nearly 5,000 euros ($5,600),” Margaux Rey, manager of the Altermundi shop, told AFPTV. “There is a high demand for securing shops ahead of the upcoming demonstrations,” confirmed Joseph Fernandez, a tradesman who was “scrambling” to meet the requests — though, he added, if individuals “want to break things, they will”. A protester speaks in a microphone as others hold a banner reading “neither congress nor meeting for the RN” during a demonstration “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. On Patrol Numerous riot police vans could be seen in Marseille, along with armoured vehicles and water cannon. Philippe Mamelli, 64, said he was “patrolling” the southern port city’s thoroughfares armed with a truncheon at his waist and pepper spray in his pocket before heading to a demonstration later. He said he was part of a group called “Citizen Revolution” which sought to support the student protesters, adding: “The rioters are undermining” the student demands. Protesters take part in a demonstration “against racism, fascism and imperialism” on the sidelines of the Congress of the Far-right party Rassemblement National (RN) in Orleans, central France on October 24, 2026. – Not ‘At Ease’ – Employees of barricaded shops in Rennes said they were worried about Saturday’s events despite a ban on protests. “Sometimes a ban makes things worse. Protesting is a right — it’s like with children, when you forbid something, it becomes even more tempting,” one employee told AFP. Another said people did not know what to expect. “Last week, it was kids doing the smashing, even while people were still inside the shops. They were highly organised — they even piled up paving stones along the street before using them.” Police Arrest 135 People, Seize Weapons French police on Saturday arrested 135 people and seized a variety of weapons as they deployed for nationwide demonstrations with orders to prevent renewed street violence, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.Weapons confiscated included metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said, while adding that, so far, “there has been no major incident”. The post Seen And Heard At France Protests Today, As Police Arrest 135 People appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Obuasi SHTS scandal: State has failed alleged victims – Akosua Manu
body: The Adviser on Gender and Social Protection to former Vice-President Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, Akosua Manu, has criticised state institutions over what she describes as their failure to adequately protect female students allegedly sexually abused by the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School. Her comments follow allegations involving 19 female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School, brought to public attention through Manasseh Azure Awuni’s investigative documentary, Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 24, Ms Manu said the Ghana Education Service (GES), Ministry of Education and Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection should have taken immediate steps to identify and protect the alleged victims, preserve evidence and prevent further abuse. She stressed that although the headmaster, Zakaria Abdulai, is entitled to due process and the presumption of innocence, authorities do not need to wait for a criminal conviction before implementing measures to safeguard students. “First of all, Zakaria and whatever due process he’s entitled to is the law. He should experience it, no problem,” she stated. “Now, protective measures do not require a criminal conviction. I’m saying this because Zakaria does not need to go to court to be found guilty before the state, from GES, Ministry of Education, Gender Ministry, for them to trace the victims,” she added. Ms Manu argued that the response of state institutions had been inadequate, particularly following the allegations and accounts presented in investigative journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni’s documentary. “And this is where I believe the state failed, especially in light of the overwhelming evidence that has been presented in the last week,” she said. She also expressed concern about reports of individuals allegedly approaching families of complainants, stressing the need for authorities to protect potential witnesses and preserve relevant evidence. According to her, the controversy should not be reduced to political disagreements, as the welfare of the affected students must remain the priority. “I’m going to focus on the girls, and it’s important that we do. Because it goes beyond the politics at this point,” she emphasised. Highlighting the global prevalence of sexual violence, Ms Manu cited UNICEF’s 2024 estimates indicating that more than 370 million girls and women alive today experienced rape or sexual assault before the age of 18, representing approximately one in eight. She noted that the global estimate rises to about 650 million when non-contact forms of sexual violence are included, while approximately 79 million girls and women in sub-Saharan Africa have experienced contact sexual violence during childhood. Ms Manu further raised concerns about the unequal power relationship between teachers and students, arguing that some girls may feel compelled to comply with inappropriate demands because of fears about punishment or their academic performance. “What does this tell you? It tells you there is a certain power dynamic as far as the school is concerned,” she said. She warned that sexual abuse could have lifelong psychological consequences, including trauma and school dropout, particularly where effective protective measures are absent. The former adviser also questioned why media interviews with the headmaster had not sufficiently examined whether similar allegations had arisen during his previous postings at Juaben, Toase and Nsawam. She disclosed that a woman who had previously attended school at Juaben sent her a private message alleging that the headmaster had made inappropriate advances towards her and treated her harshly after she rejected them. “Once he makes advances towards you and you decline, you are dead. He will hit you with passion. He hated me so much, and I hated him back and avoided him like the plague,” Ms Manu quoted the woman as saying. She further relayed the woman’s claim that the number of potential complainants at Juaben could exceed 100, although that allegation has not been independently established. Ms Manu criticised sections of the media for what she described as insensitive reporting on sexual abuse, warning that sensational coverage could discourage victims and their families from seeking justice. Ms Manu maintained that protecting students, supporting complainants and ensuring a thorough investigation must take precedence over political considerations, while respecting the legal rights of everyone involved.

title: Iran’s “Noghreh” advances to 39th Tokyo Intl. Film Festival
body:

The poetic drama " Silver ," directed by Soheil Karimi and produced by Mohammad Gharakhanlou, will be screened in the "Asian Future" competition section at the Tokyo International Film Festival, according to Mehr news agency.

title: Two Filipino SF-260 Training Aircraft Collide Mid-Air 4 Pilots Killed
body:
Four Philippine Air Force pilots were killed on October 23 when two SF-260 single-engine propeller aircraft collided during a training flight at Fernando Air Base in Batangas province, south of Manila.
The crash occurred at 3:51 p.m. local time. “Both aircraft went down within the base perimeter, with no other casualties reported,” Air Force spokesman Colonel Alvin Capinguian said on Saturday.
The military has launched an investigation to determine the cause and temporarily grounded its SF-260 fleet as a precaution. It is also coordinating with the deceased pilots’ families to provide assistance.
The accident follows other fatal SF-260 crashes in the Philippines. In May 2026, two pilots died when a trainer aircraft crashed in a mountainous area in the north. Another SF-260 TP Marchetti crashed during a training flight in 2023, killing two pilots.
The military also used SF-260 aircraft during months of air strikes on Marawi City in 2017, after Islamic State-linked militants seized parts of the southern Philippine city.
The cause of Friday’s collision remains under investigation, and no date has been announced for the fleet’s return to service.
