Broken concrete and rubble cover a destroyed bridge, interrupting a route lined with anti-drone netting. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Broken concrete and rubble cover a destroyed bridge, interrupting a route lined with anti-drone netting. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
She accepts a lift, visibly relieved to be spared the walk. At the next bus stop, she joins a group of other older people waiting for a ride into Kharkiv. Public transport continues to run and mail still arrives, preserving connections between settlements where schools and many businesses remain closed. Most of the civilians visible along these roads are of her generation, making their way between homes and the few services still available.
An elderly woman in a green poncho makes her way through the rain on crutches in the north of Kharkiv. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
An elderly woman in a green poncho makes her way through the rain on crutches in the north of Kharkiv. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Among a short row of houses, an open door offers little hint of the shop within. A motorcyclist pulls up and slips inside.
Along another route north, two soldiers stand with their rifles, looking into the sky. Beside them, a small roadside shelter is almost lost beneath camouflage netting.
Ukrainian soldiers known by the call signs Samali, left, and Kolobok watch the sky beside a road. Their task is to engage drones threatening passing vehicles and nearby residents. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Ukrainian soldiers known by the call signs Samali, left, and Kolobok watch the sky beside a road. Their task is to engage drones threatening passing vehicles and nearby residents. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
“We are targeting low-flying aircraft – FPVs, Shaheds or Molniyas,” says the tall soldier, who goes by the call sign Samali.
The 51-year-old stands with his feet planted wide apart.
“Our job is to stop them getting through and shoot down as many as possible, so local people and vehicles don’t get hit.”
Seen through protective netting, Kolobok scans the sky with a rifle in his hands. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Seen through protective netting, Kolobok scans the sky with a rifle in his hands. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Before volunteering at the start of the full-scale invasion, he worked as a driver in the Boryspil district near Kyiv. His service began in the confusion of those first days.
“The recruitment offices were overcrowded, so we organized ourselves in our communities.”
Samali sits with his rifle inside the small roadside shelter, surrounded by camouflage netting that shades and conceals the position. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Samali sits with his rifle inside the small roadside shelter, surrounded by camouflage netting that shades and conceals the position. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Since then, he has watched successive waves of new weapons and tactics reshape the fighting. “The war has completely changed.”
Russian drones increasingly operate in groups. Molniyas and Shaheds, themselves used for strikes, now also transport smaller attack drones over distances the FPVs could not cover on their own – as many as three on a single carrier.
“The Molniya flies at a very high altitude and releases them,” Samali says. “They fly off it and descend, saving their batteries.”
If one aircraft is lost, another can take over. Reconnaissance drones locate targets from above and guide the attacks. A Molniya can also serve as an airborne radio relay, extending the connection between FPVs and their operators.
Some of these smaller drones, including fiber-optic models, land and wait until a vehicle or a person appears. Equipped with larger cable spools, the fiber-optic drones can now reach farther, extending the area in which they can lie in wait.
Inside the shelter, sunlight falls through gaps in the camouflage netting onto cigarette packets and bottles of water. Rifles, a machine gun and shotguns lie within reach. On the table, the Shcheznyk’s display shows the landscape from above.
The Ukrainian-made device intercepts video feeds from drones, giving the soldiers the same view as their Russian operators. They study the road and vegetation for clues to the aircraft’s course.
A Shcheznyk receiver displays an intercepted drone video feed. Recognizable features in the landscape help the soldiers determine the aircraft’s course. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer) Advertisement
A Shcheznyk receiver displays an intercepted drone video feed. Recognizable features in the landscape help the soldiers determine the aircraft’s course. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Experienced pilots know their transmissions may be intercepted.
“It flies toward the net, then the pilot tilts the camera upward and goes underneath,” Samali says. “We can’t see where it’s going anymore, but we’ve already seen its approach.”
Then the buzz of a drone cuts through the air as the detector sounds an alert, sending both men back outside, weapons ready.
Gunfire breaks the quiet, leaving spent cartridge cases scattered around the position.
The machine gun can engage drones out to around 200 meters, according to the soldiers. Between 10 and 15 drones may be detected at their position each day, sometimes more. Those that fly within range leave little time to aim and fire.
Samali stands beneath anti-drone netting, holding his weapon upright as he watches the sky above the road. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Samali stands beneath anti-drone netting, holding his weapon upright as he watches the sky above the road. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
As the firing subsides, both men return beneath the netting and light cigarettes. A cyclist passes along the road outside.
Samali serves in a neighboring unit; his companion, Kolobok, belongs to the National Guard’s 13th Khartiia Brigade.
His family lives near Northern Saltivka, the Kharkiv district whose apartment blocks were devastated early in the invasion. He has 12-year-old twins, a boy and a girl.
His manner is contained, his expression occasionally breaking into a mischievous grin.
Kolobok, a soldier with the National Guard’s 13th Khartiia Brigade, inside the shelter. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Kolobok, a soldier with the National Guard’s 13th Khartiia Brigade, inside the shelter. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
“All my relatives are here. Even when the war started, nobody went anywhere. Everyone stayed,” Kolobok says. “Nobody wanted to leave. Not for Kyiv, not anywhere.”
He has little patience for those who left the city and abandoned their businesses. “The way I see it, they came here, lived here, made a mess and left. Of course that hurts.”
His call sign comes from the round bread character of a familiar folk tale, a reference to his work in Kharkiv’s bread factories. The 42-year-old has worked in several civilian trades, including construction, before most recently selling crockery at Barabashovo market.
“Nine-story buildings, five-story buildings – brick buildings. Anything involving brick and reinforced concrete, that’s my trade.”
Not far away, cars pull up outside a small roadside bakery. Customers in camouflage step inside and emerge carrying paper bags. Pastries fill the glass counter; packets of sweets crowd the shelves behind it.
Samali and Kolobok often stop here, too, for coffee and a few words with the owner, their weapons still slung over their shoulders.
The bakery’s owner stands behind a counter stocked with pastries and sweets. Samali and Kolobok are among her regular customers. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
The bakery’s owner stands behind a counter stocked with pastries and sweets. Samali and Kolobok are among her regular customers. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Once, she recalls, a drone slipped beneath the protective netting and appeared directly outside the window. Customers were drinking coffee inside. Everyone dropped to the floor. The aircraft was disrupted electronically, she says, and the soldiers shot it down.
Samali regards the attacks on Kharkiv as an attempt to wear down the people who remain.
“They’re trying to create chaos and panic in the city so people will make the concessions they’re demanding more quickly.”
An FPV attack drone hangs entangled in protective netting just above the road, its explosive charge still intact. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
An FPV attack drone hangs entangled in protective netting just above the road, its explosive charge still intact. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Russian drones have repeatedly struck filling stations in Kharkiv and on its outskirts this year, hitting fuel stops used by civilians and soldiers alike.
Back in the car, each kilometer north brings fewer signs of habitation.
A burned-out car stands beneath the netting, its doors open and its interior gutted by fire. The protected road continues over the hills beyond it. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
A burned-out car stands beneath the netting, its doors open and its interior gutted by fire. The protected road continues over the hills beyond it. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Ruins stand on either side. The road continues beneath the mesh until, farther along, the netting ends too.
A roofless building stands beside bare tree trunks, with vegetation spreading around its damaged walls and empty window openings. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
A roofless building stands beside bare tree trunks, with vegetation spreading around its damaged walls and empty window openings. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
A remnant of a rocket lies among grass and gravel, beside a discarded energy drink can. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
A remnant of a rocket lies among grass and gravel, beside a discarded energy drink can. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
There is almost no sound except for detonations in the distance.
Dogs emerge from gaps between buildings and the overgrown edges of the road. One approaches, hesitates, then comes a little closer. Others follow at a distance. Their coats are rough, their bodies lean. They sniffed among the debris for scraps, curious about the arrival but wary of coming within reach. They seem to be the last remaining residents here.
A stray dog rests on the asphalt in front of a burned-out vehicle. Torn strips of protective netting hang around the wreck. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
A stray dog rests on the asphalt in front of a burned-out vehicle. Torn strips of protective netting hang around the wreck. (Photo by Korbinian Leo Kramer)
Winter is approaching. Rain will give way to frost along these roads, and the people waiting at the bus stops will have another season to endure in villages already stripped of so much.
In Kharkiv, further attacks on energy infrastructure threaten heat and electricity as temperatures fall.
Samali expects the technology to keep changing. Interceptor drones are taking on more of the work of bringing down other aircraft.
“Our defense system is more integrated now, our air defense is stronger, and there’s more communication.”
Still, as detection improves, attackers adjust their methods. The devices on the table and the weapons carried outside may change again over the coming months.
Even so, he does not expect technology to make men like him unnecessary. “I think there will always be work for us.”
Korbinian Leo Kramer is currently a correspondent for the Kyiv Post, reporting from both Central Europe and the frontline regions of Ukraine. He previously worked as a freelance journalist and photographer across eastern Ukraine, covering the human and social dimensions of Russia’s fullscale invasion. His reporting focuses on resilience, everyday life, and the realities of war.

title: Keyamo accuses Atiku of fearing APC’s Northern support
body: The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, has accused former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar of being apprehensive about the All Progressives Congress (APC)’s support base in northern Nigeria ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Keyamo, a senior advocate of Nigeria, made the allegation in a statement titled, “Why Atiku Abubakar Is Particularly Jittery About the Kaduna Flag-off,” in which he criticised the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate’s reported online attacks against the APC ahead of the party’s campaign rally in Kaduna State. He alleged that some videos circulating online showing the removal of President Bola Tinubu’s campaign posters were staged to create the impression that the President had lost support in the North. Keyamo also dismissed as fake a purported letter alleging that N2.3 trillion had been earmarked for the Kaduna rally, describing it as an attempt to portray the APC as relying on financial inducements to attract supporters. The minister, however, did not provide evidence in the statement to substantiate his allegations about the videos or the purported letter. He argued that Atiku’s political calculations ahead of the 2027 election had been based largely on securing northern votes, adding that the former vice-president faced challenges in gaining support in the South. Keyamo cited the 2023 presidential election, claiming that Atiku lost across the North-Central states and all Southern states except Osun State. He alleged that Atiku had initially expected Tinubu to have limited electoral appeal in the North but was now concerned about the APC’s political structures in the region. According to Keyamo, the APC’s presence in northern Nigeria could undermine Atiku’s strategy of relying on the region to secure victory in the next presidential election. The minister further argued that even a strong showing by Atiku in parts of the North might not be sufficient to secure victory if he failed to make significant gains in the Middle Belt and Southern states. Keyamo also drew a comparison between Atiku and former President Muhammadu Buhari, who secured substantial northern support in the 2015 presidential election. He argued that Atiku’s political background differed from Buhari’s, while making corruption-related allegations against the former vice-president without presenting supporting evidence in the statement. The comments come amid intensifying political activity ahead of the 2027 general elections, with parties and their presidential contenders seeking to consolidate support across the country’s geopolitical zones. The post Keyamo accuses Atiku of fearing APC’s Northern support appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: 2027: Basiru urges ex-Assembly speakers to back Tinubu
body: The National Secretary of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Senator Ajibola Basiru, has urged former presiding officers of State Houses of Assembly across the country to mobilise support for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election in 2027 and promote the administration’s economic reforms. Basiru made the call at a programme organised by the Kaduna State chapter of the Former Presiding Officers of State Houses of Assembly in Nigeria, themed, “Kaduna 2026: United Voices of Experience, All Together for Tinubu 2027.” He described the former legislative leaders as experienced political actors whose electoral and public service backgrounds could help the ruling party strengthen its grassroots presence ahead of the 2027 general elections. According to him, their experience would be useful in explaining the rationale behind the Tinubu administration’s economic policies, responding to opposition criticism and engaging voters on the government’s performance. Basiru said Tinubu inherited severe fiscal pressures upon assuming office, which, he noted, necessitated difficult policy decisions, including the removal of petrol subsidy and the adoption of a more market-driven foreign exchange regime. He argued that the reforms, despite the initial difficulties they caused, had improved the financial capacity of state governments, enabling them to meet salary and pension obligations and invest in development projects. The APC national secretary urged political stakeholders to explain the objectives of the reforms to Nigerians, including the challenges associated with their implementation and their expected long-term effects. He also challenged opposition leaders who had previously occupied influential positions in government to account for their records in office before criticising the current administration. Basiru specifically questioned former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar’s economic proposals, citing his participation in previous administrations and raising concerns over the privatisation and sale of national assets during that period. He cautioned voters against what he described as unrealistic promises and politically motivated narratives by opposition figures seeking support ahead of the 2027 elections. The APC chieftain urged the former presiding officers to intensify public enlightenment, engage communities and encourage voters to assess political parties and candidates based on their records, policies and performance. He said sustained mobilisation, strategic communication and unity among party stakeholders would be necessary for the APC’s campaign ahead of the elections. Basiru reaffirmed his call for party members and political stakeholders to take the administration’s message to the grassroots and mobilise support for Tinubu’s re-election bid. The post 2027: Basiru urges ex-Assembly speakers to back Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Police fire tear gas as new French demonstrations kick off
body: French police started firing tear gas at protesters Saturday as they stepped up security in major cities aiming to prevent a repeat of rioting a week ago, on a day of fresh nationwide demonstrations over the high cost of living. Police in the southeast city of Lyon fired tear gas to disperse some 150 protesters near the city centre — where demonstrations had been banned — when they briefly tried to block a road, an AFP journalist saw. Elsewhere, authorities and rattled shopkeepers geared up for potential new street violence. Near Paris’s Bastille neighbourhood, a clothing store had removed all its merchandise from shelves ahead of the demonstrations, while a nearby restaurant was boarded up with signs insisting it was “still open”. Many other retailers in the capital also had wooden boards covering their windows. The Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay museums were closed. Police were seen readying riot gear in zones that bore the brunt of last weekend’s clashes and looting. They were among 70,000 security personnel the interior ministry said were mobilised to counter the “high” threat of violence. “We will not tolerate any unrest,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday, adding that calls had been circulating on social media calling for violence and looting. – Protest against far-right party – Adding to tensions, far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) party was holding a weekend congress in the central city of Orleans to kick off her campaign for elections in six months to choose President Emmanuel Macron’s successor. Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched on Saturday against Le Pen, and also against Macron, a pro-business centrist leader. “Macron resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd yelled. The violence last weekend and the heightened tensions over this weekend’s demonstrations highlighted the febrile atmosphere in France ahead of that vote, which Le Pen is best-placed, according to surveys, to win. Last weekend saw rioters on the margins of the nationwide demonstrations clash with police, vandalise public buildings and loot hundreds of stores. Some 2,700 people were arrested and the retail sector said shopowners were left with damage and stolen stock totalling hundreds of millions of euros. Macron attributed the worst of the violence to “ultra-left” groups that he said “want to bring down the republic”. Groups organising Saturday’s renewed demonstrations have accused Macron and his government of ignoring widespread public anger over rising costs, and over classroom conditions for students. Inflation in France, as elsewhere, has been sent surging by the Middle East war, started in February by US President Donald Trump and Israel. Protests have also been taking place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems. Italy has sent 500 troops to try to quell street violence in Milan. – Boarded-up shops – In Paris, streets on Saturday were unusually quiet, with many shop windows boarded up, and some of the bigger retailers sent messages to customers warning that they were closed for the day. The capital’s police at the last minute ordered a union-organised march in the city be moved from Bastille, in the centre-east, to the more remote eastern Porte d’Italie on the southern rim of the capital. Unions said they reluctantly would go along with that. But the Yellow Vest movement — a loosely organised grouping that staged disruptive street protests against Macron eight years ago — indicated it would not comply. Macron and his government have sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last Saturday. Courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, officials said. Macron has said authorities would accept only union-led demonstrations and would counter any others they deemed “illegitimate”. Authorities in Marseille had banned all protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis”. The restrictions, including outright bans on protests in some cities, have drawn criticism. Amnesty International denounced what it called “a slide toward authoritarian practice”, saying the measures were “jeopardising the right to demonstrate peacefully”. “Police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. The post Police fire tear gas as new French demonstrations kick off appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Arrests, demolitions, raids and displacement: Israel launches days-long West Bank offensive
body: Israeli troops forcibly displaced dozens of families in the occupied West Bank city of Al Khalil, while demolishing buildings, raiding homes and arresting at least 13 people, the Wafa news agency reported on Saturday. Israel's military said the operation would last for "several days" and that residents would be able to leave through one of three designated exists after "interrogation and inspection". All entrances to the city have been sealed off , Wafa said. Israel launched its campaign after five people were injured and two Israeli soldiers were later killed in a shooting at a military checkpoint near the city of Al Khalil, also known as Hebron, on Friday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later ordered the "full closure" of the West Bank. Israel’s military said it killed two suspects armed with a rifle and a handgun. Two of the injured were reported to be in a critical condition. Palestinian media reports named the pair as family members Mohammad Jaaba and Firas Jaaba, both 27 and from Al Khalil. The military said the men had planned to carry out a “large-scale” attack on Israelis. There are a number of illegal Israeli settlements in the area. On Friday, Israeli forces demolished a residential building in Farsh Al Hawa, west of the city, and prevented residents from entering or leaving the area, Wafa reported. Reactions Palestinian activist Issa Amro, who is based in Al Khalil, on Saturday said he had been unable to leave his home. "At least 250 families have been displaced in Hebron, including my own sister, Hayat, and her seven children," he said in a post on X. "Homes and shops are being demolished by the Israeli military. Around 250,000 people are trapped in the city, while 1,000 families in H2 remain in their homes. We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported." The Palestinian Authority, which is supposed to control parts of the occupied West Bank, said Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa spoke with the city's Mayor, Yousef Al Jaabari. They discussed the needs of residents amid "incursions by Israeli occupation forces into several areas and neighbourhoods and forced evacuation operations affecting hundreds of Palestinians, most of them women, children, older persons and patients". The military campaign was also condemned by Israeli rights organisation B'Tselem, which described it as part of "ethnic cleansing" efforts. In a statement on Saturday, executive director Yuli Novak said B'Tselem "urgently calls on governments and international institutions to act now, using all means available under international law, to prevent the forcible displacement of Palestinian civilians, collective punishment and extensive unlawful destruction in Hebron". Israeli leaders "are openly declaring their intentions and actions on the ground have already begun", he added. Mr Netanyahu had confirmed that Israel would enter neighbourhoods, remove residents and "dismantle terror infrastructure". Shortly after Mr Netanyahu made those comments, Defence Minister Israel Katz elaborated on the operation in a post on X. “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron,” he wrote, referring to the now-destroyed camp in the north of the West Bank. B'Tselem said at least 33,000 Palestinians had so far been displaced by Israel's actions in the northern West Bank. Israel is set to hold parliamentary elections in three days, in which Mr Netanyahu has based his campaign on national security concerns.

title: AI-Assisted Paper on Z-Library Cites a TorrentFreak Article That Doesn't Exist
body:
A fresh academic paper on Z-Library cites a TorrentFreak article that doesn’t exist, and several other sources in the paper are also unfindable. The authors disclose that they used AI tools, which may explain what is going on. The use of AI in an academic paper on shadow libraries is also somewhat ironic, as rightsholders are suing AI companies for using these sites to train AI models.
Z-Library is one of the largest pirate ebook libraries on the Internet, offering millions of books and papers for free.
For students and researchers who can’t afford expensive textbooks and journal subscriptions, it can be a useful resource. At the same time, publishers have spent years trying to take it down, with takedown notices and blocking orders , while U.S. authorities indicted its alleged operators.
This tension is the subject of a paper published earlier this month in the journal New Review of Academic Librarianship , written by two librarians at Nigerian universities.
The peer-reviewed academic paper doesn’t pick a side and the lead author kindly shared a copy of their work with TorrentFreak. While the conclusions are not immediately newsworthy, there was one reference that stood out right away.
In a section on enforcement against Z-Library, the authors write that major academic publishers, including Elsevier and Springer Nature, have taken similar legal action. The reference is a 2021 TorrentFreak article, as shown below.
The problem is that this particular legal action is new to us. The reference section lists the article as “Publishers continue crackdown on shadow libraries” and links to the TorrentFreak homepage. However, we have never published an article with that title.
We did report that Elsevier and Springer Nature obtained a UK blocking order against Sci-Hub, and that several Z-Library domains were temporarily suspended over copyright infringement claims. However, we’re not aware of this particular legal action against Z-Library.
Looking more closely, we see more claims that don’t seem to fit. The paper’s account of the Z-Library criminal case, for example, states that the U.S. Department of Justice “arrested individuals” in 2022.
The DOJ’s own press release says that the two alleged operators, whose indictment we covered at the time, were arrested in Argentina “at the request of the United States.” The title the paper gives for that press release doesn’t exist either.
These non-existent citations appear plausible, as they cite real publications and organizations in a fitting context. However, that doesn’t mean they are accurate. When we went over the full reference list, we noticed that this applies to more sources.
The paper cites a 2019 Harvard Journal of Law & Technology article by IP law professor Daniel Gervais, titled “The future of intellectual property in the shadow of shadow libraries.” The table of contents of the cited issue doesn’t include it, and the cited pages are taken up by two articles on other topics.
The same applies to a 2019 College & Research Libraries article attributed to Carol Tenopir and colleagues. The cited issue has no article by Tenopir. She did co-author a 2019 article on a similar topic, but it appeared in a different journal, under a different title.
Other references that couldn’t be located include a 2019 article credited to Björn Brembs and articles credited to authors named Smith, Piper, Okike and Aronson, as well as a Kaspersky report on “the hidden dangers of shadow libraries.”
In total, we had trouble finding at least ten of the 44 references in the paper, as well as others that didn’t necessarily back the stated claims.
The obvious question is where these mystery references came from. The paper’s acknowledgements may offer a hint in the right direction, as they mention that AI was used in the research and writing process.
“We confirm that Consensus AI was used in sifting through large volume of literature and extract relevant information,” the authors write. They add that ChatGPT was used to improve the language of parts of the paper.
AI chatbots are known to invent references, often with plausible titles credited to real experts in the field. This could explain the findings, although it doesn’t prove that AI wrote these references.
We also ran the paper’s abstract and conclusion through the AI detection tool Pangram . For both sections, the tool reported that “100% of the text is likely AI-generated.” These types of tools are not perfect and can produce false positives, but it would fit the picture.
It would be rather ironic if AI caused these errors. It would mean that a paper in a commercial, peer-reviewed journal, published by Taylor & Francis , relied on AI to write about Z-Library. Meanwhile, many rightsholders are suing AI companies for using shadow libraries to train AI models.
Interestingly, the paper explicitly warns that sites such as Z-Library hurt publishers’ revenue, which funds peer review and editing.
“The widespread use of Z-Library poses significant challenges to the sustainability of academic publishing. Publishers rely on subscription fees and paywalls to fund the peer review, editing, and distribution of scholarly works,” it reads, presumably generated by AI as well.
The paper doesn’t mention that peer reviewers generally aren’t paid for their work, an issue that was central to a recent lawsuit against major academic publishers, including Taylor & Francis.
The lead author initially shared a copy of the paper with us, but didn’t answer our follow-up questions about the mysterious references. We also asked Gervais, Brembs and Tenopir whether they wrote the papers that are credited to them, but they didn’t respond either.
Publisher Taylor & Francis did reply and says that it’s looking into the matter.
“I can confirm that this has been referred to our Editorial and Publishing Ethics & Integrity teams, who will investigate the concerns you have raised,” a Taylor & Francis spokesperson informed TorrentFreak.
The publisher will not comment further while the investigation is ongoing. Whether the paper will be corrected or retracted has yet to be seen. —
The paper “Z-Library and Full-Text Access: Democratizing Knowledge or Undermining Copyright Ethics?” is available here .

title: Ebola: Uganda restricts transit for travellers from DRC
body:
Uganda has barred travellers with a history of travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) from transiting through the country as it investigates the traveller who tested positive for Ebola disease in Nigeria.
The Ugandan Ministry of Health announced the measure on Friday, alongside the reinstatement of traveller locator forms “to facilitate timely follow-up and contact tracing where necessary.”
“The Ministry of Health wishes to update the country on an ongoing investigation into the traveller who tested positive for Bundibugyo Virus Disease in Nigeria.
“Available information indicates that the traveller did not exhibit symptoms at the time of departure from Uganda. However, investigations are continuing to establish the timing of symptom onset and the circumstances surrounding her infection,” the ministry noted in a statement signed by its Director General of Health Services, Charles Olaro.
It added that Uganda is working with Nigerian health authorities to establish the traveller’s full travel history, movements and possible exposure. It has also requested additional information from Nigeria, including detailed travel records and genomic sequencing results, where available.
The country insisted that it “remains Ebola-free.”
Uganda had earlier battled an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which was declared on 15 May 2026 after cases were imported from the DRC.
The country recorded 20 confirmed cases, including two deaths, before declaring the outbreak over in August after 42 days without a new locally acquired case.
As of 20 October, the DRC had recorded 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths across eight provinces, according to the World Health Organisation (WHO).
The ministry said infection prevention and control measures had been reinforced at all points of entry and exit and health facilities, while surveillance continued across the country.
It also warned that provisions of Uganda’s Public Health Act would be invoked where public health requirements were breached.
The ministry urged communities to report suspected unauthorised border crossings to relevant authorities for screening and public health follow-up.
The ministry urged travellers and the public to remain calm and vigilant, practise proper hand hygiene and comply with screening and other public health measures.
Uganda’s latest measures follow an earlier clarification after Nigeria announced its Ebola case and said the patient had arrived on an international flight from Uganda.
On 21 October, Uganda said the traveller’s passage through the country does not establish that she contracted Ebola there. The ministry said preliminary information indicated that she had travelled to eastern DRC for business before passing through Uganda and that she had not shown symptoms while in the country.
Uganda also said at the time that it had no active Ebola cases. The latest statement maintains that position, saying investigations with Nigerian authorities are still ongoing.
On Friday, Nigeria announced a genomic finding showing that the virus detected in its patient is highly similar to the virus found in Kenya’s first imported case.
Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, said the finding does not establish that the Nigerian patient was infected in Kenya, as there was no evidence that she had travelled there.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) had earlier said it was investigating a possible link between the Nigerian and Kenyan cases because both patients travelled through Uganda’s Entebbe International Airport on 3 October.
Kenya’s first case was imported from the DRC through Uganda. The country has since recorded nine confirmed cases, including two deaths, with the eight additional cases linked to the first patient.

title: Kazakh Academic Kanysh Satpayev in Britain: A View from 1947
body: After the end of World War II, relations between the Soviet Union and Western countries began to deteriorate rapidly. Although Britain, France, the United States, and the Soviet Union had been allies, the period known as the Cold War began. Winston Churchill’s famous speech in Fulton, Missouri , on March 5, 1946, is often regarded as one of its defining early moments. Nevertheless, just over a year after the speech, a large official Soviet delegation visited Britain in March 1947. The delegation represented the Supreme Soviet, the Soviet Union’s legislature, and arrived in London at the invitation of both houses of the British Parliament. Clement Attlee’s Labour government supported expanding contacts with the Soviet Union despite growing disagreements over the postwar settlement in Europe. Soviet delegates at Karl Marx’s grave. From left: Kanysh Satpayev, president of the Kazakh SSR’s Academy of Sciences; mathematician N. I. Muskhelishvili; and Soviet official P. A. Shariya. The other individuals have not been identified. The delegation consisted of 20 people and was led by Vasily Kuznetsov, chairman of the Soviet of Nationalities, one of the Supreme Soviet’s two chambers. Among its members were Alexander Fadeev, head of the Union of Soviet Writers and author of The Young Guard, about Soviet youth resisting Nazi occupation during World War II, and the poet and writer Konstantin Simonov. Aviator Mikhail Gromov, a Hero of the Soviet Union who commanded a nonstop flight from Moscow across the North Pole to San Jacinto, California, in 1937, also joined the delegation. Kanysh Satpayev , president of the Academy of Sciences of the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, was also among the invited delegates. Soviet delegates meeting Newcastle’s Lord Mayor Pearson. From left: Ukrainian poet N. P. Bazhan, test pilot M. M. Gromov, Kanysh Satpayev, an unidentified individual, Soviet official P. A. Shariya, Communist Party foreign policy department head M. A. Suslov, and Pearson. The delegation stayed for almost a month, from March 13 to April 11, 1947. The visitors met with Prime Minister Attlee, Conservative opposition leader Churchill, and members of Parliament. According to Satpayev’s notes, the participants visited the University of London, the Royal Society, the British Museum, industrial enterprises, and government institutions. Outside the capital, the delegation visited Newcastle, Sheffield, Cardiff, Manchester, Oxford, Cambridge, Stratford-upon-Avon, Coventry, Edinburgh, and Glasgow. Soviet delegates viewing armor in the White Tower at the Tower of London. Among the delegates, from right: A. M. Ivanov, Kanysh Satpayev, and M. Z. Babayev. In his report following the trip , Satpayev claimed that the British organizers had tried to overwhelm the visitors with official events and limit their contact with ordinary workers: “It should be noted that government officials tried to organize our visits to industrial enterprises in such a way that the delegation had practically no opportunity to communicate with workers. Visits to factory workshops often coincided with lunch breaks. Sometimes the delegation was shown workshops during working hours, but these were places where there were few workers or where production processes (metal smelting or rolling) made it impossible to talk to them. Everywhere, the delegation was ‘assisted’ by a whole crowd of British intelligence agents posing as interpreters, in whose presence the workers naturally could not speak openly. Workers who spontaneously gathered when the delegation appeared were skillfully dispersed. Our hosts took every measure to conceal the true situation in the country from the delegates whenever possible, even resorting to ‘Potemkin village’ methods. For example, during a visit to a kindergarten in the Finsbury district of London, an elderly woman said: ‘You should have seen what was going on here on Saturday. They were scrubbing and washing everything to somehow hide the terrible filth. The head of the kindergarten had been asking the local council for linoleum to cover the floors for several months. Who knows how much longer she would have had to ask for it if you had not come?'” Kanysh Satpayev and A. Karavayev, a secretary at the Soviet Embassy in London, speaking with ballerina Margot Fonteyn after a performance of Swan Lake. Satpayev’s notes reflect the confrontation between the two political systems. Along with the photographs provided by the Central State Archive of Film, Photographic Documents, and Sound Recordings of the Republic of Kazakhstan, they are authentic historical records of the period.

title: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course
body: I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. The companion book These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. The videos As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. 1. Motivation and code setup The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues. Topics covered The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses On the benefits of learning through code implementations The scope of this video series Installing Python dependencies Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment Watch video 1 · Setup instructions 2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model. Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient. These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos. Topics covered Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code 3. Building a verifier for evaluation and reinforcement learning In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500. We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset. However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Topics covered Intro to verifiers and how they fit into LLM evaluation methods (other methods are covered in the book’s appendix) Reusing answer verification as a reward signal for RLVR (more on that in chapter 6) The verifier flow, including extracting final answers, normalizing answers and checking mathematical equivalence Building an answer grader and an evaluation loop for MATH-500 Comparing base and reasoning models on MATH-500 Watch video 3 · Chapter 3 code 4. Inference-time scaling: sampling and self-consistency Now we explore ways to improve answers while keeping the model weights fixed. But before implementing specific inference-scaling techniques, we first implement methods to generate diverse answers from the same prompt (this is standard practice in proprietary LLM chatbots, such as ChatGPT). Concretely, we implement temperature scaling, multinomial sampling, and top-p filtering to generate diverse responses. Then we combine multiple responses through self-consistency, using majority voting over their final answers. We also examine the tradeoff between answer accuracy and the extra computation needed to generate more candidates. Topics covered Comparing how additional compute benefits model performance during training and during inference A gentle intro to inference-scaling through chain-of-thought prompts Implementing temperature scaling and multinomial sampling to generate diverse answers Adding top-p filtering to control the quality of the diverse answers Combining candidate answers through self-consistency, one of the most popular inference scaling techniques Evaluating MATH-500 accuracy against the cost of additional inference compute Watch video 4 · Chapter 4 code 5. Inference-time scaling: scoring and self-refinement Building on the previous video, we implement scoring functions to compare multiple answers generated from the same prompt. We can also use these scoring methods to break ties in self-consistency (covered in the previous lecture). The scoring methods covered here include computing token and sequence log probabilities (this will also be relevant in the later reinforcement learning chapters). We then implement a self-refinement loop in which the model critiques an answer and attempts a revision. The evaluation lets us check how useful those additional steps are for our model. Topics covered Using scoring functions for comparing multiple answers and breaking ties Implementing a simple heuristic scorer Computing token probabilities and sequence likelihoods (also relevant for the following lectures) Using log probabilities for improved numerical stability Building a self-refinement loop for generating critiques and revised answers Evaluating self-refinement on MATH-500 Watch video 5 · Chapter 5 code 6. Reinforcement learning: implementing GRPO for RLVR In this lecture, we move on to implementing a training technique called Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). We first implement a simplified version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), generate groups of responses, score them with our verifier, and use their relative rewards for the model weight updates during training. Topics covered Generating reasoning traces and understanding the relationship between answer lengths and problem-solving abilities Discussion and comparison of two important LLM post-training methods: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) Turning verifier scores into rewards and relative advantages Computing sequence log probabilities and a simplified GRPO loss Assembling the training loop with logging and checkpoint saves Evaluating checkpoints and checking training stability and memory needs Watch video 6 · Chapter 6 code 7. Reinforcement learning: tracking, clipped policy ratios, and KL terms Now that we implemented the training loop in the previous lecture, we can revisit it and analyze the training runs in more detail. Concretely, this video adds more training metrics for inspection and analysis, including entropy and advantage statistics, clipped policy ratios, KL loss term values, and formatted rewards. We then review the training logs and evaluation results to understand what these additions do and whether additions such as clipped policy ratios and KL loss terms are helpful. Topics covered Running longer training experiments and interpreting their logs Tracking advantages and entropy to understand training behavior Implementing clipping in the policy loss and analyzing its effects Adding a KL loss term and discussing reward hacking Understanding limitations of the simplified KL formulation Implementing format rewards and conditioning them on answer correctness Comparing checkpoints on MATH-500 and exploring further GRPO research Watch video 7 · Chapter 7 code 8. Distilling a reasoning model Finally, we explore another way to train a small reasoning model, that is, learning from answers generated by a stronger (and bigger) teacher model. We discuss different forms of distillation, prepare reasoning data, and implement the supervised training loop. We finish this lecture and course by evaluating the distilled model on MATH-500 and comparing the results. This rounds out the series with an alternative to developing reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning. Topics covered Comparing the different combination and approaches to distillation, including soft and hard distillation, and on-policy and off-policy distillation Creating and collecting teacher-generated answers for the MATH dataset (using DeepSeek R1) Preparing the distillation dataset, including tokenization and training/validation/test splits Computing answer-token log probabilities and understanding the cross-entropy loss Implementing supervised training and tracking training and validation losses Evaluating checkpoints on MATH-500 and comparing distillation results Watch video 8 · Chapter 8 code Final words As you watch these lectures, I encourage you to pause occasionally and try a small experiment of your own if something interesting comes to mind. For example, feel free to change the sampling settings, inspect a few failed answers, or try variations of different ideas similar to the suggestions in the exercises. And if you would like the full written walkthrough, figures, and exercises alongside the videos, you can find Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) at Manning and Amazon . Thanks for reading and supporting Ahead of AI. I am taking a short break to regenerate, and I look forward to being back with the next round of LLM research articles next month. In the meantime, happy viewing and tinkering!

title: UAE oil spill: Ras Al Khaimah closes all beaches 'until further notice'
body: Ras Al Khaimah on Saturday announced the closure of all beaches "until further notice" as authorities work to contain an oil spill from a supertanker in the Arabian Gulf. The decision comes after Umm Al Quwain temporarily closed all of its beaches and coastal areas and authorities in Sharjah sealed off Al Hamriya beach as a precautionary measure. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirmed the incident early on Friday morning. It said the spill was the cause of a strong smell reported across the country in recent days. The Ras Al Khaimah Public Services Department announced the closures on Instagram."The public is kindly requested to follow the instructions and guidelines issued by the relevant authorities to ensure everyone’s safety," it said in the post. The extent of the oil slick is unclear, but the incident was confirmed amid growing concerns about the environmental impact of the Iran war on the Gulf and the Arabian Sea. Umm Al Quwain Municipality said it was carrying out field operations to contain the effects of the spill and minimise damage to marine and coastal environments. The municipality will monitor conditions, identify affected areas and support clean-up and treatment work as part of those efforts. Specialists will also help to assess the impact of the spill and determine appropriate measures. Limiting environmental impact Experts have told the National that swift containment of the spill was vital to limit damage to the environment and the UAE's marine ecosystems. Inesaf Benzaki, campaigns lead at Greenpeace Mena, said timely action was particularly important because the Gulf’s semi-enclosed geography limited the exchange of water with the open ocean, potentially allowing pollutants to persist. “We acknowledge the UAE authorities’ ongoing efforts to contain the reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain and address its immediate effects,” she said. “As these efforts continue, understanding the potential environmental impact will be important to protecting the area’s marine ecosystems.” Prof John Burt, director of New York University Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, previously warned that if oil reached the coastline, remediation could be expensive and a full recovery could take years.

title: OpenAI's isolated AI agents found ways to talk to each other through CPU cache
body:
OpenAI now trains frontier models without internet access and uses AI agents to red-team its own infrastructure. In separate isolation tests, agents even communicated through covert side channels, showing how hard true containment is.
On September 20, an internal research model exploited a misconfigured DNS resolver to reach the open internet during training, even though OpenAI had already tightened security after the now infamous Hugging Face incident in July and other observed misalignment cases . OpenAI contained the breach quickly but still halted all frontier model training and evaluation.
OpenAI made a policy decision in response: Frontier models now train without internet access until safety measures justify restoring it. Models learn to browse and search inside a closed "offline world" built from indexed and cached web content, and all frontier reinforcement learning runs now operate this way. Ad
Full network isolation, a so-called air gap, isn't feasible yet because experiments still need external connections for operations and monitoring, the company says. But even a complete air gap wouldn't guarantee containment, according to OpenAI researcher Noam Brown . He gave one example of how isolated systems could still communicate: two separate computers could theoretically signal each other through temperature sensors, with one heating its CPU while the other reads the change. Ad
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made a similar argument in a recent interview: Sandboxes offer only limited protection against powerful-enough models, and at some point it may no longer be possible to trace how they escaped. Monitoring helps early on, but what ultimately matters is that an AI system internalizes human values, a problem the field knows as "AI alignment" and has yet to solve.
OpenAI documents just how hard it is to control AI agents in its blog post . During tests, agents found ways to communicate without a network. In one test, agents placed in separate, isolated environments on shared hardware were told to exchange secrets with no network connection and no shared files. Ad
They used the processor cache. One agent deliberately altered the data stored there, while the other measured differences in load times and decoded the message. The same technique is behind the well-known Spectre and Meltdown attacks .
More channels turned up through write patterns on shared memory and through OpenAI's own offline infrastructure, the system meant to replace the internet. One agent noted in its reasoning log that it "could create an acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle." Ad
In one case, agents were given only a general list of vulnerabilities and told to find a communication channel on their own. They developed a channel independently, agreed on an encoding scheme, and successfully exchanged information. The channels are usually slow and hard to exploit, OpenAI says, but they do reach across boundaries meant to keep agents apart. Ad
During the training pause, OpenAI also had teams of AI agents systematically attack its own infrastructure. The agents were given source code, configuration details, and documentation of potential vulnerabilities. OpenAI's goal was to test its defenses under conditions that favored the attackers. The agents included the upcoming GPT-6 Astra Cyber and an internal frontier model. The campaign consumed hundreds of billions of tokens, according to OpenAI.
The agents discovered previously unknown vulnerabilities in the open-source components in use and exploited them to escape from secured virtual machines. One was a vulnerability in Kata Containers, a widely used container isolation system. OpenAI reported it as CVE-2026-24834 and provided a patch. More fixes went to other projects, and OpenAI reported additional, as-yet-unpublished vulnerabilities through the "Patch the Planet" initiative.
In tests where agents had already gained control of a host, they found a vulnerability in nearly every remaining internet-facing service. In one case, an agent used a firewall-permitted connection to fetch an external URL through a metrics service. Others bypassed security filters through misconfigurations.
The agents could no longer find a way to access the internet that was both easy to exploit and hidden from monitoring, according to OpenAI. The red-teaming also exposed gaps in monitoring and in the automatic pause mechanism.
After fixing the issues, OpenAI resumed training and internal use of its frontier models on October 1, eleven days after the pause began. OpenAI says this kind of compute-intensive red-teaming campaign is now a standard part of the approval process for new training runs.

title: Bandits killed as hunters repel attack in Katsina
body: Fourteen suspected bandits have been killed in a gun battle with community hunters who repelled an attack in Gidan Wawo village, Kakumi Ward, Bakori Local Government Area of Katsina State. The Katsina State Government said a community hunter and a traveller were also killed in the incident, while three other people were rescued. The Commissioner for Internal Security and Home Affairs, Dr Nasir Mu’azu, disclosed this in a statement issued on Friday, saying security agencies had earlier received intelligence about the movement of 26 armed bandits on 13 motorcycles towards Dawan Laila forest in Bakori. He said security personnel in the local government were immediately placed on alert to prevent a planned mass abduction in neighbouring communities. Gunmen invade Taraba community, kill residents, cart away motorcycles Insecurity spreads in Sokoto According to the statement, the bandits later attacked a vehicle belonging to Jamilu Lawal, 50, who was travelling with three others from Kakumi Ward to Illela market in Sokoto State. The vehicle was set ablaze during the attack. The statement said community hunters from Gidan Wawo quickly mobilised and engaged the bandits in a gun battle, killing 14 of them. However, a 29-year-old hunter, Mohammed Ibrahim Jidda, died during the encounter, while another hunter, Usman Sunday, 25, sustained minor gunshot injuries and is currently receiving treatment. Unfortunately, Lawal was burnt to death in the vehicle, while the three other occupants were rescued alive. The commissioner said intelligence reports had indicated the possibility of a reprisal attack by the bandits following the heavy casualties they suffered, adding that the state government is working with security agencies to prevent further attacks and address potential threats in the area. The Commissioner also commended the community hunters and security operatives for their courage, urging residents to remain calm and provide credible information to security agencies.

title: 2027: Arewa‘ll return Tinubu to Aso Rock – Musa Kwankwaso
body: A member of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Dr Musa Kwankwaso, says the North-West will return President Bola Tinubu to Aso Rock by voting for him massively in the 2027 general elections. Kwankwaso spoke against the backdrop of the massive turnout and endorsement of Tinubu at the formal kick-off of the APC Presidential Campaign on Saturday in Kaduna. Kwankwaso described the gathering as a decisive demonstration of Northern support for Tinubu ahead of the 2027 polls. The APC campaign council member said the Kaduna rally had effectively dispelled lingering doubts over where the North stood in the unfolding presidential contest. “Today, we of the North-West geopolitical zone have spoken loud and clear on who we stand for. Our choice of Tinubu remains our commitment to a better Nigeria and national cohesion,” he said. Kwankwaso said that the significance of the Kaduna gathering extended beyond the immediate political mobilisation. He argued that the North had sent a strong message to other geopolitical zones on the need to consolidate around Tinubu for the sake of national progress. According to him, the president’s administration represents an opportunity to deepen equitable development and ensure that the country’s resources are distributed fairly across the six geopolitical zones. “Tinubu’s presidency stands for fair and equitable distribution of resources to all zones, and his return will be a blessing to the greater Nigeria of our dream.” He also dismissed any suggestion that the North’s support for Tinubu was merely transactional, saying the region had a responsibility to honour its political commitment and remain united behind the President as the 2027 election approaches. “Asiwaju is the northern candidate, and he will not promote anything outside his ambition because we are trustworthy people, and we shall deliver him come 2027,” he said. He urged Nigerians, particularly political stakeholders across the geopolitical zones to view the emerging support for Tinubu through the prism of national unity and collective progress, rather than narrow political interests. He emphasised that the Kaduna mobilisation had demonstrated that the North had already made its choice. (NAN) The post 2027: Arewa‘ll return Tinubu to Aso Rock – Musa Kwankwaso appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: 2027: APC supporters slept at Kaduna venue, streets ahead Tinubu campaign flag-off
body:
Several All Progressives Congress (APC) supporters spent Friday night at the Ranchers Bees Stadium and on surrounding streets in Kaduna ahead of the official launch of the party’s presidential campaign by President Bola Tinubu.
The eager supporters made their way into the stadium late Friday to secure seats ahead of the event. By 6 a.m. on Saturday, several others had arrived at the venue, making frantic efforts to gain entry, while another crowd created a carnival-like atmosphere outside the arena.
Many supporters slept on the streets near the stadium to ensure they gained entry ahead of the campaign rally, awaiting the arrival of President Tinubu, who was scheduled to arrive in Kaduna at noon.
The rally marks the flag-off of the APC presidential campaign, drawing party faithful and elected officials from across the seven North-West states – Kano, Jigawa, Zamfara, Sokoto, Kebbi, Katsina and the host state.
Zaidu Bala, a media aide to the Governor of Kebbi State, described the supporters’ vigil at the venue and on the streets as a strong display of political resilience that signalled an APC victory.
He claimed that many were forced to spend the night outdoors because hotels and guest accommodations across Kaduna were fully booked.
“Politics is not for the faint-hearted; any party that does not have resilient and dedicated people like these (who spent the night on the streets) will not win an election in Nigeria.
“Hotel rooms in Kaduna are exhausted; guest accommodations are full because of the love for Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu,” Mr Bala said on Facebook.
A Kaduna-based political analyst, Haruna Ibrahim, told Daily Trust that the choice of Kaduna for the campaign flag-off is strategic because of the state’s position in northern politics.
According to Mr Ibrahim, Kaduna is home to people from different ethnic, religious and social backgrounds, making it a meeting point for political interests across the country.
He said supporters from other northern states could find it easier to travel to Kaduna than some other destinations in the region.
“The rally should hold in Kaduna rather than Sokoto, Zamfara or Katsina states because Kaduna is more or less the centre of northern Nigeria and also a bit safe compared to others,” the newspaper quoted him as saying.
He added that people from Bauchi, Gombe, Borno and Yobe might prefer to attend a rally in Kaduna because of its location and transport connections.
Mr Ibrahim also argued that the state’s concentration of security formations could make it a more suitable location for a large political gathering than some other parts of the North-west.
The Saturday’s campaign flag-off in Kaduna came on the heels of heated politics between the ruling APC and the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC).
​The ADC accused the ruling party of deploying enormous state resources and security operatives to guard its presidential campaign posters.
However, APC supporters in the state dismissed the allegations, maintaining that security personnel were not assigned to protect campaign materials, but were stationed at strategic locations to safeguard the public.
​In turn, the APC alleged that it had uncovered plots by opposition figures and supporters in the state to deface and destroy its candidate’s billboards to create a false narrative on social media that the party lacks grassroots support in Kaduna.
​Governor Uba Sani was widely regarded as former governor Nasir El-Rufai’s political protégé and handpicked successor; but their relationship deteriorated after Mr Sani took office in May 2023.
​The division became public in March 2024 during a town hall meeting in Kaduna, where Governor Sani revealed that his administration inherited a staggering debt burden of approximately $587 million in foreign loans, ₦85 billion in domestic debt, and 115 contractual liabilities from Mr El-Rufai’s eight-year tenure – 2015 to 2023.
Mr Sani explained that federal allocations were heavily deducted at source to service these obligations, severely constraining his ability to pay civil servants’ salaries and execute new capital projects.
Following Governor Sani’s statements, the Kaduna State House of Assembly established an ad hoc committee to investigate financial dealings, contract awards, and loan disbursements during the Mr El-Rufai administration, who is now a figure in the opposition ADC.
The committee recommended investigations by anti-graft agencies (such as the EFCC and ICPC) into billions of naira in state spending, effectively ending the alliance between the two political camps. While the APC is flagging its 2027 reelection campaign, Mr El-Rufai is under court-authorised detention, facing corruption charges.

title: Obuasi school scandal: NETRIGHT demands offenders’ register, annual GES reports on abuse cases
body: The Convener of the Network for Women’s Rights in Ghana (NETRIGHT), Professor Akosua Darkwah, has called on the Ghana Education Service (GES) to establish an offenders’ register and publish annual reports detailing sexual abuse cases reported in schools and how they were handled. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 24, Prof. Darkwah said the sexual abuse allegations involving the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School should serve as a turning point for the GES to review its child protection policies and strengthen enforcement. She expressed concern that Ghana has numerous laws intended to protect children, but their implementation remains a major challenge. “I would like to end on the GES and to ask that they use this as a reflection point and go back to their policies and enforcement because Ghana, we don’t have trouble with passing laws,” she stated. Prof. Darkwah referenced Ghana’s child protection legislation, arguing that the country’s willingness to adopt laws has not always translated into effective measures to safeguard children. “We sign nicely, then we go to sleep. I would like to see this be the point from which we begin to see some real changes,” she said. She particularly questioned the GES’s policy of transferring teachers, urging the Service to reconsider whether such arrangements adequately address cases involving allegations of sexual misconduct. “Are we going to continue to transfer teachers? So they need to go back and think about their transfer policies, whether it makes sense,” she stressed. The NETRIGHT Convener further demanded greater transparency in the handling of sexual abuse complaints, proposing that the GES publish annual statistics on reported cases and the actions taken. “We would like to have a report annually. How many sexual abuse cases did the GES get, and how did they resolve them, so that when you are taking your daughter to school, you will know comfortably that she is protected,” she stated. “We want an offenders’ register,” she added. According to her, such accountability measures would help reassure parents that schools have effective systems to protect children from sexual abuse. Her comments follow allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School, brought to public attention through an investigative documentary by journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni. Prof. Darkwah maintained that the controversy should prompt lasting institutional reforms rather than temporary responses, with particular emphasis on safeguarding students, reviewing teacher transfer policies and ensuring accountability in the handling of sexual abuse complaints.

title: Obuasi SHTS sexual abuse: Zakaria Abdulai is a free man now, as I know – Manasseh
body: JoyNews investigative journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni says the suspended headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Zakaria Abdulai, is moving freely despite allegations of sexual abuse involving female students. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 24, Mr Awuni said that, to his knowledge, the headmaster had not been detained and was able to move around following his engagement with the police. “Zakaria, as far as I know, is a free man at least for now because I left Obuasi on the 25th of August and at the time, he hadn’t been arrested,” he said. Mr Azure explained that although there had been reports of an attack on the headmaster by students, he understood that the incident was being used as a reason to allow him to recover. “They claimed he had been attacked, I think, on the 4th by the rioting students, so they wanted him to heal.” He also recounted claims that the father of one of the alleged victims had been contacted by the police and that there had been an attempt to settle the matter privately. “But even before that, the girl’s father said the police had called him. The man wanted them to sit down and settle so that the case wouldn’t go out, and the girl’s father said no,” he said. According to Mr Awuni, the headmaster had subsequently indicated on other platforms that he had been cautioned by the police and granted self-recognisance bail. “He literally walked to the police. They listened to his story and then said you can go,” the journalist added. Mr Awuni further claimed that the headmaster had been in Accra recently to meet the NDC Functional Executive, arguing that he continued to move around despite the allegations. Background The controversy follows a JoyNews investigation by Mr Azure, titled Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow , which detailed allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at the school. One of the cases concerns a 20-year-old student who alleged that Mr Abdulai raped her at his official residence on campus on July 25, 2026. According to a police statement, the student reported the incident to the Domestic Violence and Victim Support Unit in Obuasi on August 4, accompanied by her father. She further alleged that the headmaster gave her GH¢100 to keep quiet. The allegations remain under investigation. The investigation also reported that complaints about alleged sexual abuse had been brought to the attention of school management, education officials and other authorities months before the headmaster’s suspension. Following the revelations, Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu directed the Ghana Education Service (GES) to suspend Mr Abdulai and referred the matter to the Criminal Investigations Department for investigation. Interior Minister Mohammed Muntaka Mubarak subsequently disclosed on October 20 that the headmaster had been arrested in connection with the allegations. Police investigations have included efforts to obtain DNA evidence, while the case docket has been forwarded to the Attorney-General’s Office for advice. Mr Abdulai has denied wrongdoing and has said he was cautioned and granted self-recognisance bail. He has also resigned as Juaben Constituency Secretary of the National Democratic Congress and withdrawn from the constituency chairmanship race amid the controversy. The allegations have triggered public concern and calls for a thorough investigation into both the claims against the headmaster and the handling of earlier complaints by school and education authorities.

title: Pizza Fan Probe Leads to 23 Arrests and €1.28 million in cash
body: Greek authorities have seized 92 luxury watches, valuable jewellery and more than €1.28 million in cash during an investigation into an alleged tax evasion scheme involving the owner of Pizza Fan, one of Greece’s major pizza chains. Police carried out the operation on Thursday, October 22, 2026, searching offices, businesses and homes in Attica and Thessaloniki. Officers arrested 23 people, including a 68-year-old man alleged to have led the organisation, while investigators identified another 109 people in the case file. Authorities estimate that the alleged scheme cost the state more than €35 million in unpaid income tax and value-added tax (VAT). They estimate that the network concealed more than €150 million in taxable revenue. Luxury watches, diamonds and cash hidden in a villa During a search of Konstantinos Antaras’ villa in Ekali, officers seized 92 watches from prestigious brands, including Rolex, Patek Philippe, Vacheron Constantin, Audemars Piguet, Panerai, Zenith and Franck Muller. Investigators also found certificates of authenticity, repair receipts and spare parts associated with luxury watchmakers. Other seized items included a diamond necklace, a ring and three pink-coloured gemstones. Authorities have not disclosed their value. Investigators also discovered €1,175,990 in cash concealed in a hidden room behind a shoe cabinet. The money lay wrapped in bundles and stacked on top of one another.
