title: Top U.S. Navy Fighter Gains Major Air-to-Air Combat Boost with Very Long Range Missile Configuration
body: The release of an image showing a U.S. Navy F/A-18F Super Hornet fighter carrying both the AIM-174B and AIM-260A Joint Advanced Tactical Missile has provided an indicator of significant progress in efforts to transform the air-to-air combat capabilities of the ageing combat jets. The aircraft, assigned to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 31 was photographed flying over Ridgecrest, California, on October 14, and all integrated an IRST21 infrared search-and-track system. Where U.S. combat aircraft have for years been significantly outranged by their Russian and Chinese counterparts, the AIM-174B and AIM-260A provide a distinct advantage over the Russian R-37M missile, and may provide parity with the more advanced Chinese PL-17. The AIM-174B and AIM-260A are designed to provide complementary capabilities. The AIM-174B, derived from the Navy’s ship-launched Standard Missile-6, is a particularly large air-to-air weapon intended to engage targets at very long ranges. Its potential targets include airborne early warning and control aircraft, aerial refuelling tankers and bombers. The AIM-260A, meanwhile, is being developed as a next-generation successor to the AIM-120, providing improved range and performance against increasingly capable adversary fighters and other airborne threats. Its development is closely associated with efforts to counter advanced Chinese air-to-air missiles, including the PL-15, while maintaining a sufficiently compact form to allow internal carriage by stealth aircraft such as the F-22 and F-35. The appearance of both weapons on the same aircraft is significant because it demonstrates the potential for the Super Hornet to carry missiles suited to engagements at different distances and against different categories of targets. This mirrors the Chinese J-16 fighter’s integration of the PL-17 and PL-15/16 for much the same complementary benefits. The AIM-174B’s size and range make it particularly relevant to engaging China’s fast expanding and increasingly world leading fleet of AEW&C systems such as the KJ-500 and KJ-3000 , which are expected to contribute to providing Chinese forces with an overwhelming situational awareness advantage. It is expected that the newer AIM-424 will also enter service in the early 2030s to provide a significantly superior long range targeting capability, potentially as a direct successor to the AIM-174B. The presence of the IRST21 system is also noteworthy. Unlike conventional radar, infrared search-and-track equipment detects the heat signatures of airborne targets, allowing aircraft to search for and track potential threats without necessarily emitting radar signals that could reveal their position. This passive detection capability is particularly valuable in contested environments where fighters must manage their electromagnetic emissions, although successful long-range missile engagements may still depend on additional sensor data and communications networks. Integrating passive sensors with long-range weapons could help the Super Hornet detect and engage threats while reducing its reliance on its own radar. Such systems are also valuable due to their ability to lock on to stealth aircraft at potentially longer ranges than is possible for radars.

title: This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
body:
New speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., holds the gavel during the opening session of the 116th Congress at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 3, 2019. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.
But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.
That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.
These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.
Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.
But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.
The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.
All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.
Because this is a decade with three presidential cycles (2020, 2024 and 2028), it is also a decade with just two midterms. One went by in 2022. Some expected at the time that a "big red wave" would sweep then-President Biden's majorities out of Congress.
It did not happen. Democrats held on in the Senate, and the House shifted from barely Democratic to barely Republican. That did bring an end to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's second (and last) turn with the Big Gavel. But the GOP would spend much of the next two years struggling to unite behind a speaker of their own.
That's a far cry from the big midterms that have at times rivaled presidential elections for responding to the mood of the times and rearranging the landscape.
If we take the last hundred years as our sample, we can start with the midterms that followed the Wall Street "Crash of 1929." That financial panic set off a sequence of events that would be called the Great Depression, and the collateral damage included the closing of an era of Republican dominance in Washington.
That era ended with the midterms of 1930, which cost the GOP eight Senate seats and 52 seats in the House in November 1930. Although the GOP initially retained small majorities in both chambers, they lost it in the House with the results of a few special elections early in 1931.
The "Democratic New Year's Eve Cheer" cartoon from Dec. 31, 1931, reflects the Democrats' win of the House that year after special elections. National Archives hide caption
The Senate remained nominally Republican but featured a working majority of Democrats and progressive Republicans. A page had been turned, and Democrats would take control outright in 1932 and hold that majority through World War II.
After that war had ended, the period of Democratic hegemony under President Franklin Roosevelt also ended, and abruptly, with the results of the midterm of 1946.
Republican numbers in Congress had fallen so far in the FDR years ( below 100 at one point in the 435-seat House ) that it seemed impossible for them to return to power. But in 1946 they stormed back to majority control of both House and Senate in a single midterm cycle.
Midterms have continued to serve as political regulators in the generations since. Dwight Eisenhower won two landslide elections as president in the 1950s, but he lost the House in 1954 and needed the vice president to break ties in the Senate.
In his second term, the re-elected "Ike" did not control Capitol Hill, and in the 1958 midterms saw his party drop to just 35 seats in the Senate .
The Senate Democrats first elected in 1958 established a critical mass that would later drive the bipartisan super-majorities needed to break the filibuster and pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
In the same era, Democrats in Congress enacted a raft of social programs that would become part of the language, such as Medicare and Medicaid. It was all part of President Lyndon Johnson's "Great Society" program.
Demonstrators carrying signs against the war in Vietnam march in front of the White House in April 1965 in Washington, D.C. AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption
But by the midterm year of 1966, much of the energy from LBJ's landslide election in 1964 had been expended — and much more had been siphoned off by his escalation of the war in Vietnam.
Right on time, the midterm arrived, and while the Democrats only took a haircut in the Senate elections they lost a painful 47 seats to the GOP in the House. It gave the party a new lease on life and encouraged its new emphasis on winning in the South . The redirection would guide the party's 1968 presidential candidate, Richard Nixon, and remain a focus for the onetime "Party of Lincoln" for decades to come.
Also in the midterm of 1966, out on the West Coast, a first-time candidate named Ronald Reagan won the governorship of California. People were starting to use the term "Sunbelt."
But what the midterms of 1966 gave the GOP, the midterms of 1974 would largely take away. Nixon had been elected president in 1968, pursuing what was called a Southern Strategy, and was reelected in a resounding 49-state landslide in 1972.
But by 1974 it had all gone the other way for Nixon. The "Watergate" scandals emerged from his 1972 campaign's use of burglary and electronic surveillance among other unsavory tactics. An attempt to cover it all up blew back on the White House and forced Nixon to resign on the brink of impeachment in August of 1974 – just three months before the midterm for his second term.
The result was a crushing defeat for the GOP, the loss of 48 seats in the House and several more in the Senate (where the Democrats already had more than 60 votes).
While it is tempting to attribute these losses to Nixon's downfall, the country had — to some extent — rallied behind his vice president and successor, Gerald R. Ford. The underlying vulnerability of the GOP was the state of the economy, which was suffering from inflation and the hangover from the oil embargo of 1973 by Arab members of OPEC, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.
That embargo, a side effect of the Arab-Israeli "Yom Kippur War" of 1973, temporarily raised the price of crude oil from $3 to $12 and introduced Americans to the phrases "oil shock" and "energy crisis."
President Ronald Reagan waves beside his wife, Nancy Reagan, after being sworn in as 40th president of the United States by Chief Justice Warren Burger on Jan. 20, 1981, at the Capitol in Washington, D.C. Consolidated News Pictures/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Reagan became the dominant political personality of the 1980s, defeating incumbent President Jimmy Carter in 1980 and winning a 49-state landslide reelection in 1984. He was able to carry in a majority for Republicans in the Senate and establish a kind of working majority in the House with the aid of conservative Democrats in that chamber.
On the strength of those elections, restrained only marginally by the midterm elections of 1982, Reagan began his second term on top of the world. But he soon learned how hard that height can be to hold. As he neared his second midterm, Democrats were on the march nationally and restoring their strength in the more populous Southern states.
In 1986, Democrats defeated six GOP senators who had been elected with Reagan in 1980. The net gain of eight Senate seats gave them a 55-45 majority. In the session of Congress that followed, the Senate would override Reagan's veto of a highway bill and reject his nomination of Robert Bork to the Supreme Court. Reagan was a spent force.
Reagan was able to see his vice president, George H.W. Bush, take the White House in 1988, but the party's hopes for momentum into the 1990 midterms were largely unfulfilled. The presidency was also lost in 1992, when Democrat Bill Clinton won a three-way race with just 43% of the popular vote, defeating Bush and independent candidate H. Ross Perot.
Clinton's lack of a majority and list of frustrations in his first term set the stage for a bruising first midterm election in 1994. But what came was beyond bruising. Republicans stormed to their first majority in the House (54 seats net) in 40 years and recaptured the Senate with eight new seats there as well.
The new GOP speaker, Newt Gingrich of Georgia, was a hard-driving partisan who had portrayed the chamber as a House of Ill Repute, the title of a book he and other House Republicans had published.
The use of a "Contract with America" theme promised lower taxes, less corruption and a healthier economy in a compact agenda that had voter appeal as well.
Gingrich explicitly rejected the go-along-get-along attitude of previous GOP leaders in the House and advocated confrontation. The strategy proved less fruitful once he had the Big Gavel, however, and Gingrich spent much of his time as speaker making deals with Clinton. Internal dissatisfaction with him forced him out late in 1998.
In the new century that followed, parties have continued to prosper when their presidential candidates win and give ground in the midterms. George W. Bush was an exception as the president after the terror attacks of September 2001. In his first midterm the following year, the GOP made gains across the board.
But the larger dynamic caught up to him in 2006, when he and his party took what he called "a thumpin'" in elections at all levels. Bush had initially gained popularity with his "War on Terror" and won a second term. But thereafter, his invasion of Iraq had become an albatross. And in 2006 he paid the historic price, losing both his party majorities in the House and Senate. The new majority in the House made Pelosi the first woman speaker in history.
That created an atmosphere of optimism for Democrats, who elected Barack Obama president in 2008 and gave him majorities in the House and Senate (the latter briefly reaching 60 seats). But Obama felt the sting of the midterms early — much as Clinton had. Republicans in 2010 capitalized on an economy still experiencing the recession that had aided Obama's win in 2008. The GOP also capitalized on fears and confusion surrounding the enactment of the Affordable Care Act, or "Obamacare," in 2010.
Echoing his predecessor, Obama called this setback "a shellacking," and settled in to work with a much diminished Senate majority and a Republican-dominated House under Speaker John Boehner.
President Barack Obama is greeted by House Speaker John Boehner and Vice President Joe Biden prior to delivering his State of the Union address in January 2011 at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Obama managed to thread the needle well enough to win a second term for himself in 2012, but the House remained Republican and the Senate followed suit in Obama's second midterm election in 2014.
That second midterm revealed continuing GOP strength across the South and Midwest and to some degree augured the Electoral College majorities that would make Donald J. Trump president in 2016 and 2024.
If the 2020s are to have a midterm with the kind of impact others have had, roughly once a decade for a century, the last opportunity for that to happen is Nov. 3.
If the once-a-decade rhythm has any rationale, in fact, the pressure for a meaningful midterm ought to be building substantially. And in fact most pollsters, pundits and other prognosticators now predict Democrats could flip control of the House and even the Senate as well.
Just as in the previous 10 cycles, the current cycle combines economic concerns (including energy prices) and negative stories about incumbents in various offices. It is the party perceived as being in power that is exposed in a midterm, and it pays a price when voters perceive that party to have lost its mandate — or at least its momentum.

title: Ukraine Confirms Hits on Proton Plant, Tolyatti and Yeysk Airfield
body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces struck key military-industrial facilities and an aviation base inside Russia overnight Friday-Saturday, confirming direct hits on the Proton-Elektroteks plant in Oryol, the Tolyattikauchuk industrial plant in Samara region, and an aircraft stationed at the Yeysk airfield, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported .
According to an official dispatch released by the General Staff and reported by state news agency Ukrinform, the operations were conducted within Ukraine’s inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter to degrade Russian military manufacturing and aerial strike capacity.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Damage has been confirmed to the main production building of JSC Proton-Elektroteks in the city of Oryol, Oryol region of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff announced.
“This complicates the production of components for cruise and ballistic missiles used by the adversary to strike Ukrainian cities.”
Military authorities identified Proton-Elektroteks as a leading Russian enterprise providing a full manufacturing cycle for optoelectronic equipment and power semiconductor devices, spanning from raw crystal processing to finished modules.
The General Staff noted that the Oryol facility produces specialized modules integrated into Russian S-71 “Kover” air-launched cruise missiles, alongside inverter-switches utilized in 9M723 ballistic missiles deployed by the Iskander-M mobile theater system.
Under inter-industry cooperative agreements, the plant also supplies critical electrical components integrated into combat vehicles of the Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft missile-gun system and its modern variants.
The confirmed impact follows visual evidence indicating British-supplied Storm Shadow air-launched cruise missiles penetrated the industrial perimeter in Oryol on Oct. 23, causing upper-floor collapses and extensive structural damage across main assembly workshops.
In the city of Tolyatti, located in Russia’s Samara region, Ukrainian units struck the Tolyattikauchuk chemical complex overnight into Saturday, Oct. 24, with military observers registering an explosion and a major industrial fire across the facility’s perimeter.
The General Staff emphasized that beyond commercial petrochemical products – including monomers, hydrocarbon fractions, and high-octane gasoline additives – the enterprise manufactures synthetic rubbers that serve as a foundational raw material for producing solid rocket propellant utilized in Russian tactical and ballistic missile systems.
The overnight drone assault in Tolyatti also prompted Russian authorities to order the precautionary evacuation of shifts at the neighboring AvtoVAZ automotive plant, Russia’s largest carmaker.
Ukrainian forces also targeted the Russian military airfield in Yeysk, located in the Krasnodar region along the Sea of Azov littoral.
The General Staff confirmed that an aircraft stationed at the air base was struck during the operation, adding that the extent of the airframe’s operational degradation and secondary damage remains under technical assessment.
The Yeysk airfield functions as a major staging and operations base for Russian naval aviation and tactical strike aircraft engaged in combat missions against Ukraine.
The kinetic strikes inside Russia coincided with a systemic blackout that plunged large swathes of Russian-occupied Crimea into darkness overnight into Saturday, Oct. 24.
Ukraine has sustained targeted interdiction operations against rear military-industrial facilities , rocket fuel synthesis hubs, and front-line combat aviation bases to constrain Moscow’s operational stamina and diminish the volume of standoff strikes targeting Ukrainian municipal networks ahead of winter.

title: Khmara: Starlink and Starshield speeds above 400 km/h have resumed
body:
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara told reporters this.
“The Ministry of Defense’s monitoring systems are recording that Starlink/Starshield has resumed its speed. We are recording speeds exceeding 400 km/h, and the connection is stable,” he noted.
According to the minister, restoring satellite communication speeds is of critical importance to the Ukrainian military, particularly for the operation of drones, logistics, and maintaining communications on the front lines.
“This is yet another example of how direct dialogue and the President of Ukraine’s firm stance at the highest level yield results. And this result is, above all, important for our front lines, for the military, for the operation of drones, logistics, and communications,” Khmara emphasized.
He stressed that the Ministry of Defense continues to monitor the operation of satellite systems and track their performance metrics.
As reported by Ukrinform, as of the morning of October 24, the Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems are operating at speeds exceeding 161 km/h.

title: Samson’s Take: One country, different standards of justice?
body: Something is troubling about how our criminal justice system treats suspects and offenders. The law sometimes appears merciful to the powerful, merciless to the poor, and remarkably swift against those accused of offensive speech, especially in recent times. Consider the Obuasi school scandal. At least 19 girls, helpless girls, have reportedly alleged sexual abuse involving their headmaster. He denies wrongdoing and enjoys the presumption of innocence. I’m a lawyer, I should say that. But why has the police response appeared so restrained compared with the speed and force sometimes deployed against suspects accused of misdemeanor speech offences? Yes, just upon the suspicion and arrest, they get locked up. They spend weeks in custody. Must frightened schoolgirls formally report before the police vigorously investigate credible allegations of sexual abuse? Then consider the Northern Development Authority case. Three former executives and a businessman were convicted of corruption-related offences yesterday, but they received fines rather than imprisonment. Fines, GH¢4,000. The court considered mitigating circumstances, including the prevention of financial loss; that is legally permissible. But compare their treatment with that of poor offenders in prison for stealing food, sometimes because they cannot afford fines or legal representation. If it’s messy being administered equally in this country, I’m not demanding imprisonment for the NDA convicts or unlawful detention of the Obuasi suspects. I’m demanding consistency, fairness, and equal justice. The law must protect every suspect’s rights while ensuring that serious allegations receive serious attention. And judicial mercy must never appear to depend on wealth, status, or influence. Attorney General Dominic Ayini’s proposal to deploy lawyers to police stations is therefore important. But legal representation alone cannot cure inconsistent enforcement. People are watching. Dear police, people are watching. Dear executives, the wielders of power, people are watching. The schoolgirls are watching. The poor are watching. And when justice appears harsh against the weak, but accommodating towards the powerful, confidence in the law suffers. Justice must be fair without being cruel, merciful without being selective, and equal without regard to status. One country, one constitution, one standard of justice. That’s the title of my take. And that is my take.

title: Sokhumi, Tskhinvali, Moscow Digest – October 16-22, 2026
body: Below is the weekly digest of key developments and discourses in and around the occupied regions of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia , as well as those concerning Tbilisi–Moscow relations. Sokhumi Police Cooperation Agreement with Moscow Sparks Heated Debates in Abkhazia A cooperation agreement between the de facto Abkhaz and Russian interior ministries has sparked public debate in Abkhazia, with critics raising concerns about “sovereignty,” information sharing, and the potential use of law enforcement cooperation against political opponents. The controversy followed the publication of cooperation plans for 2024-2025 and 2026-2027 by the Telegram channel Aiashara . The latter was signed by Russian Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev and his de facto Abkhaz counterpart, Robert Kiut. Particular concern has focused on provisions concerning the exchange of information about individuals capable of “destabilizing the situation in the border region.” The public movement Apsuaa Rymch warned that these arrangements could facilitate external pressure on Abkhaz public figures and called for a legal review and the publication of the agreements in full. Although de facto interior minister Robert Kiut did not directly respond to the investigation published by Aiashara , he subsequently gave an extensive interview to local television channels defending the cooperation with Russia. He maintained that the plans introduced no new obligations and were based on existing agreements signed in 2009 and 2014. Kiut stressed that Abkhaz “legislation” remained paramount and highlighted what he described as the practical benefits of cooperation, including the dismantling of approximately four major drug-trafficking networks in 2025-2026. He also cited the reclassification of around 400 Abkhaz residents suspected of illegally cashing out Russian maternity capital benefits as witnesses, claiming that this had effectively shielded them from criminal prosecution. The controversy has renewed calls for greater transparency and scrutiny of agreements with Russia. Some de facto Abkhaz lawmakers have called for “parliamentary hearings” to assess whether the documents comply with Abkhazia’s “constitution.” Abkhaz Delegation to Participate in Russia-Africa Forum De facto representatives of Abkhazia will participate in the Russia-Africa Forum scheduled for late October, according to so-called foreign minister Oleg Bartsits. He announced the planned participation during a meeting with de facto Abkhaz leader Badra Gunba and said the invitation had been secured thanks to the support of Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. According to Bartsits, Abkhazia continues to expand its international contacts, including with countries in Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. “I think that during this large-scale summit, we will establish some very interesting new contacts, which I will certainly inform you about,” he said. Abkhaz De Facto Foreign Ministry Confirms Difficulties Crossing into Russia The de facto foreign ministry of Abkhazia has acknowledged cases in which Abkhaz residents holding “dual” Abkhaz and Russian citizenship have encountered difficulties at the so-called “border” when presenting their Abkhaz passports. The agency said it was holding consultations with the relevant Russian authorities, taking into account existing “bilateral agreements.” It urged citizens who encounter similar difficulties to formally report them to the de facto ministry, providing detailed information about the circumstances. In 2025, Russia introduced new regulations under which Russian citizens holding multiple passports are treated exclusively as Russian citizens and are therefore required to enter the country using their Russian passports. Since then, the de facto Abkhaz authorities have been consulting with Russian counterparts in an effort to restore the possibility for Abkhaz residents holding “dual citizenship” to cross the so-called Russian border using their local documents. Abkhaz Activist Calls on Russian “Ambassador” to Address Case Against Irakli Bzhinava Kadir Argun, a member of an initiative group supporting Irakli Bzhinava, has appealed to the so-called Russian Ambassador Vyacheslav Gladkov over the case against Bzhinava, expressing concern about the charges brought against him in Russia. In his appeal, Argun argued that Bzhinava’s public statements, including his criticism of certain agreements, were part of Abkhazia’s public and political debate and did not indicate an intention to threaten Russia’s security. “The charges brought against Bzhinava set a dangerous precedent by treating legitimate public debate as a threat to state and legal security. This raises serious concerns within Abkhaz society and creates risks for the legal status of Abkhaz citizens,” the statement said. Argun called for the case to be resolved in accordance with the principles of justice and proportionality, as well as the close allied relations between Sokhumi and Moscow. Abkhaz national Irakli Bzhinava was arrested in Rostov-on-Don in February 2026. A criminal case was initially opened against him over alleged public calls for activities directed against Russia’s security. A second case was subsequently brought against him on charges of publicly justifying terrorism online. Over 965,000 Crossings of ABL Recorded in Nine Months A total of 965,423 crossings by individuals and 52,780 vehicle movements were recorded at crossing points along the ABL connecting with Georgia proper during the first nine months of 2026, according to the de facto state security service. Rustam Latipov, head of the de facto border directorate, provided the figures during a meeting with the Abkhaz leader Badra Gunba, where the operation of crossing points was discussed. Meanwhile, the de facto security service also reported continued detentions along the Enguri River for alleged violations of the so-called border regime. Those detained are transferred to the service’s district offices, where decisions on liability are made in accordance with established procedures. The statement did not specify the number of people detained along the Enguri River during the first nine months of 2026. However, according to statistics released by the de facto authorities for the first half of the year, more than 130 people were held liable for violating the so-called border regime in the area, while four criminal cases were opened over alleged illegal border crossings. Abkhaz ‘State University’ Students Complete Academic Program in Istanbul Sixteen fifth-year students from the Department of History and Theory of International Relations at the so-called Abkhaz State University participated in an academic program in Istanbul. The program included a series of lectures on global affairs and world history, covering Turkish foreign policy, counterterrorism, geopolitical developments in the contemporary Middle East, and economic history. The program was organised at Istanbul Medeniyet University with the support of the de facto Abkhaz Representative Office in Turkey. Tskhinvali Kambolov Appoints Members of De Facto Government Marat Kambolov appointed Soslan Margiev as de facto “prime minister” of the occupied Tskhinvali/South Ossetia on October 22, culminating a series of appointments in the region’s executive branch after Kambolov was declared a winner in the region’s early “presidential vote” in September. Kambolov signed a relevant “decree” after the de facto parliament unanimously approved Margiev’s candidacy on the same day. According to the region’s so-called “constitution,” the “president” appoints the “head of government” with the consent of “parliament,” while the “president” can independently appoint and dismiss members of the “government” and heads of executive bodies. Read about the appointments in detail here. 135th IPRM Meeting Held in Ergneti The 135th meeting of the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism (IPRM) took place on October 22 in the village of Ergneti, near the occupation line in Georgia’s Russia-occupied Tskhinvali region. The meeting, which brought together the representatives of Georgia’s central government and de facto authorities of Tskhinvali/South Ossetia, was co-facilitated by Bettina Patricia Boughani, Head of the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia (EUMM), and Christoph Späti, Special Representative of the OSCE Chairperson-in-Office for the South Caucasus. The next IPRM meeting is set to take place on December 15. Read about the meeting in detail here . Two Illegally Detained Georgian Citizens Released After 2 Years Two Georgian citizens who were detained on September 16, 2024, near Mejvriskhevi, a village in Gori municipality adjacent to the Tskhinvali occupation line, have been released and returned to the Tbilisi-controlled territory, the State Security Service of Georgia (SSSG) said on October 22. Details here. Tskhinvali Announces Lifting Ban on Entry into Russia for Three Former “MPs” The “parliament” of the occupied Tskhinvali Region announced that the ban on entry into Russia has been lifted for former “MPs” David Sanakoev, Gari Muldarov, and Dzambolat Medoev. They had previously been stripped of their Russian citizenship, after which restrictions on their entry into the Russian Federation were imposed. According to “parliament” speaker Alan Margiev, the issue was repeatedly raised and discussed with Marat Kambolov while he was still serving as acting “president.” Subsequently, the “MPs” sent an official request asking for assistance in resolving the issue. The “parliament” claims that after reviewing the appeal, appropriate steps were taken, resulting in the lifting of the restrictions. Res Analytical Piece Notes Crisis of Legitimacy at International Criminal Court An analytical article by Res, the local news agency of the occupied Tskhinvali region, claims that the International Criminal Court (ICC) is experiencing a profound crisis of legitimacy and is increasingly perceived as a politicized institution. The authors note the limited number of states parties to the Court, the withdrawal of several countries from the Rome Statute, and the refusal of certain states to comply with ICC rulings. Much attention is devoted to criticizing the Court’s activities in the context of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as the events of August 2008. The authors believe that the ICC takes a selective approach to investigating crimes and operates under the influence of Western states. Examples cited include arrest warrants for Russian and Israeli officials, as well as the investigation into the events in Georgia and the occupied Tskhinvali region. Separate sections address the court’s effectiveness, its legal status, personnel scandals, and the enforcement of its rulings. In conclusion, the authors express support for the position of Russia and China, which oppose the politicization of international justice, and characterize the ICC as an instrument of political pressure rather than an independent judicial body. Head of Russian House in Tskhinvali Notes High Level of Russian Language Proficiency in Occupied Region Sergey Komissarov, head of the Russian House in Tskhinvali, stated that the level of Russian language proficiency among schoolchildren in the occupied Tskhinvali region is comparable to that in regions of Russia. According to him, this is confirmed by the results of academic competitions that Armavir State Pedagogical University has been holding in the region for several years. Komissarov noted that these educational projects are implemented with the support of Rossotrudnichestvo and the region’s “Ministry of Education.” In addition to language competitions, the university participates in the work of the Open Education Center in occupied Akhalgori and the “Russian Teacher Abroad” program. In his view, participation in the contests promotes in-depth study of the Russian language, fosters motivation, and expands opportunities for local schoolchildren. Contest winners are given the opportunity to visit educational institutions in Russia. “Foreign Ministry” in Tskhinvali Slams OSCE Chairperson’s Visit to Occupation Line The “Foreign Ministry” of the occupied Tskhinvali region criticized the visit by the OSCE Chairperson-in-Office, Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, to the occupation line during his trip to Georgia . The agency called such trips by Western politicians “political tourism” and stated that they contribute to promoting Georgia’s position on security issues. The statement asserts that such visits call into question the OSCE’s objectivity and Switzerland’s neutral status. The region’s “Foreign Ministry” also emphasized that issues of security and the settlement of relations should be discussed within the framework of the Geneva Discussions. The agency called on international organizations to adhere to the principles of neutrality and urged the Georgian side to move toward a practical dialogue on border delimitation and demarcation. “Foreign Ministry” in Tskhinvali Slams Kobakhidze’s Statements on Non-Recognition The “Foreign Ministry” of the occupied Tskhinvali region responded to remarks by Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze regarding the work of the new special representative for relations with Russia. The agency drew attention to his statement that Tbilisi does not intend to recognize the independence of occupied Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region or to conclude any agreements with them. In its commentary, the “Foreign Ministry” characterized this position as a sign of disrespect toward the residents of both regions and their political choice. The agency also criticized the Georgian authorities’ use of the terms “so-called Republic of South Ossetia” and “so-called Republic of Abkhazia.” The statement calls on the Georgian side to engage in dialogue on an equal and respectful basis within the framework of existing negotiation formats. Moscow-Tbilisi First Deputy FM Zurabashvili Becomes Prime Minister’s Special Representative for Russia First Deputy Foreign Minister George Zurabashvili has been appointed Prime Minister’s Special Representative for Relations with Russia while retaining his current position, Irakli Kobakhidze announced on October 21. The position has been vacant since December 2025. Details here. Zurabashvili’s Appointment Draws Concerns of Upgrade in Tbilisi-Moscow Relations The appointment of First Deputy Foreign Minister George Zurabashvili as the Prime Minister’s Special Representative for Relations with Russia has drawn concern among Georgian former diplomats about the “dangerous trend” of it being a “form” of restoring diplomatic relations with Moscow and of widening the post’s mandate. More here . Rosselkhoznadzor, Georgia’s National Food Agency Discuss Expanding Trade in Agricultural Products Representatives of Rosselkhoznadzor and Georgia’s National Food Agency held a meeting in Tbilisi on the sidelines of a regional seminar organized by the World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) on strengthening regulatory systems for veterinary products, Rosselkhoznadzor stated in a press release. The parties discussed expanding bilateral cooperation, increasing mutual shipments of livestock products, and allowing new types of goods into the markets of both countries. The Russian side announced that, starting in November 2026, two Georgian dairy processing plants will be able to supply products to Russia following the completion of the necessary approval procedures within the framework of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Rosselkhoznadzor also confirmed its readiness to conduct inspections of six Georgian fish and seafood producers interested in exporting to the Russian market. According to the Russian side, in 2026, exports of live pigs and onions from Russia to Georgia increased, while exports of dairy products and veterinary vaccines continued. At the same time, imports of Georgian fruits and berries into Russia have increased, including nectarines, apples, blueberries, plums, mandarins, figs, and watermelons. Zakharova on Restrictions on Georgian Beverages Russian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Maria Zakharova commented on the suspension of sales and imports of beverages from a number of Georgian producers, stating that there is no political motive behind the restriction on Georgian beverages, RIA Novosti news agency reports . Late last week, as reported by RIA Novosti citing a source among retailers, Russian stores began removing beverages from a number of Georgian manufacturers from circulation, following an order from Rospotrebnadzor. “There is no political motive behind this. I think these are all just speculations,” Zakharova said during her briefing. title: Trump says end of Russia-Ukraine war nearing, suggests 200% tariffs could be imposed on both countries
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump stated on Friday that the Russia-Ukraine war is nearing its end, while noting that the use of trade tariffs to compel Kyiv and Moscow toward peace would be largely ineffective, given the small volume of American imports from both nations.

“We're close to ending, I hope, the Russia-Ukraine catastrophe. I hope we're ending that,” Trump said.

According to the head of the White House, the threat of imposing 200% import tariffs has previously helped the United States halt five out of eight armed conflicts around the world. Trump suggested the possibility of immediately applying a similar approach to Ukraine and Russia, though he noted that the USA does not import a sufficient volume of goods from either country for such tariff-based pressure to be effective.

Furthermore, the American president once again drew attention to the massive human toll of the Russia-Ukraine war, which averages 25,000 casualties per month.

title: Bodies of three victims discovered after missile strike in Oryol
body:
ORYOL, October 24. /TASS/. The bodies of three victims have been discovered during debris clearance operations following a Ukrainian missile strike on a facility in the city of Oryol, Regional Governor Andrey Klychkov reported on his Max channel.
"In Oryol, efforts continue to address the aftermath of a terrorist attack by the Kiev regime on a civilian site, carried out using missiles manufactured by NATO countries. It is with deep sorrow that I must report that the bodies of three individuals have been found during the debris clearance. My sincere condolences go out to the families and loved ones of the victims. The entire Oryol region mourns with you," he wrote.
According to the governor, emergency services remain at work on the scene. The Oryol city administration has begun inspecting affected apartments to assess damage for subsequent compensation. "The families of those who died or were injured will receive all necessary assistance," Klychkov added.
On October 23, the Ukrainian military launched a missile strike on a facility in Oryol’s Sovetsky District. Eight people sought medical attention, receiving all necessary care and undergoing required surgical procedures, the governor previously reported. A fire at the site was extinguished before crews began clearing the debris. The regional head also refuted reports regarding any chemical hazard.

title: Concerned Ho Zongo Youth demand permanent resolution to Volta Regional Chief Imam impasse
body: Concerned Ho Zongo Youth are demanding a lasting resolution to the Volta Regional Chief Imam impasse and objecting to the “knee-jerk” approach to resolving the issue. They raised concerns about alleged political interference, urging political players to stay out of the issue, which is fueling violent among members of the community. The Concerned Ho Zongo Youth spokesperson, Abdul Razak Abubakar, entreated the Volta Regional Minister, James Gunu, the Volta Regional Security Council and other relevant institutions to endeavour to bring closure to the Chief Imam impasse. He warned of the consequences should the governing National Democratic Congress pick sides in the impasse or fail to restore peace in the Ho Zongo community. “The youth reserve the right to express their political disappointment through peaceful and lawful democratic means, including at the ballot box. No political party should take the support of any community for granted while legitimate concerns remain unresolved”, said Mr Abubakar. Shooting incident unresolved He recounted how the impasse was marked by a violent incident in December 2025, which resulted in the injury of scores of believers who had gathered at the Central Mosque for Salat al-Jumu’ah prayers. He explained that the victims were yet to receive justice, as the culprits had not been prosecuted. He therefore entreated the Interior Ministry to relaunch investigations into the shooting incident and ensure that those found culpable were brought to book to appease grieving hearts. “We also call on the Minister for the Interior to take urgent interest in the reported shooting incident, ensure a thorough investigation and help prevent any further violence. The safety of worshippers and residents must be paramount”, he said. Closure of mosque Following the shooting incident, the mosque was closed to the public to avert further clashes, forcing believers to worship on the premises. It was, however, opened briefly for the National Chief Imam, His Eminence Sheikh Dr Osmanu Nuhu Sharubutu, accompanied by the Volta Regional Minister, James Gunu, to perform some prayers two weeks ago. The mosque has since been locked to worshippers. Mr Abubakar warned that the Zongo youth would launch a series of demonstrations until an amicable solution to the Volta Regional Chief Imam impasse was found and the Ho Central Mosque reopened for its intended purpose. “The reopening of the mosque must be pursued through lawful coordination with the relevant authorities, with the safety of worshippers and the wider community fully protected. We expect the Minister to act urgently and demonstrate genuine leadership before tensions escalate further”, he said.

title: Emacs finally folds to my liking
body:
I’ve been slowly turning my Emacs config into something I actually enjoy using, not just something that works, and folding was the last place where that wasn’t true.
Every mode had its own idea of what folding is: treesit-fold in Tree-sitter modes, Hideshow in the Lisp-ish ones, Outline in everything that resembles text, Org with its own invisible text that no one else’s commands can undo.
So every buffer had different keys, a different look, and worst of all different performance characteristics. Folding a big file sometimes felt like holding my breath.
I’m running Emacs 32.0.50 from master (built from source, as one does), and it’s finally one system.
kirigami doesn’t fold anything itself. It dispatches : it keeps a list of folding engines, checks which one is actually active in the buffer, and forwards to it. Tree-sitter, Hideshow, Outline, Org, Vdiff â all behind one interface.
So on top of it I put one set of keys, the same in a Kotlin buffer, YAML, a Scheme or ELisp buffer and an Org file:
That sounds small. It is not small. The number of times a day I used to think “wait, what does TAB do in this mode again” is now zero, and the muscle memory transfers across an entire polyglot config.
One wrinkle worth mentioning: kirigami answers with the first engine in its list whose mode is on, and outline-minor-mode is on in nearly every buffer I have. In the buffers where I deliberately turned on Hideshow â Scheme, for instance â that choice has to win, otherwise C-c v c folds “headings” a Scheme file doesn’t have. So I reorder kirigami-fold-list to put Hideshow first instead of rewriting it; engines kirigami adds later still get used wherever Hideshow is off.
Most of my programming buffers are *-ts-mode , so treesit-fold does the work there â bash, C, C++, CMake, CSS, Dockerfile, Elixir, Go, HTML, Java, JS/TS/TSX, JSON, Kotlin, Lua, Nix, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, Scala, TOML, YAML. Line counts are shown inline, which I find genuinely useful when deciding whether to open a fold.
The indicators took the most fiddling. treesit-fold-indicators draws a block’s guide with a bitmap 23 rows tall, centered in the line beside it. A line in my config is 29 pixels â the font’s 23 plus six of line-spacing â so every row of the guide was a 23-pixel dash with three pixels of nothing above and below it. A folded block looked like a dotted line running down the fringe. Not subtle, just wrong.
There’s no setting for that, so I replaced the bitmaps: a single-row bitmap that define-fringe-bitmap repeats down however tall the line is (no spacing can introduce a gap), plus a +=/ -= box and an end-elbow cut to the exact height of a line, so the guide runs from the marker into the row below and turns toward the text where the block ends. It’s an advice on the function that builds the string for each line. It looks like a bracket now, not a perforation.
And the colour: the indicators inherited shadow , which most themes make as bright as a comment. Fine for one marker on one line, wrong for a marker on every line of a block â the grey became a rule drawn through the code. They’re now shadow blended 50% toward the theme’s background, recomputed on every theme and scale change, so it fades correctly on light themes too and no theme needs a special entry.
Not everything has a grammar, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise:
Hideshow’s own fringe indicators ( hs-show-indicators + hs-indicator-type 'fringe ) are on in all of these, so it doesn’t feel like a downgrade from the Tree-sitter buffers.
The rule I enforce per buffer is exactly one set of indicators : Tree-sitter buffers get treesit-fold and Hideshow is turned off; Hideshow buffers get Hideshow and Outline’s clickable buttons are turned off so the two don’t double up; outline-only buffers (Markdown, diff) keep the buttons. Nobody ends up with two markers per block.
Org folds with text properties, not overlays, so neither Tree-sitter nor Hideshow nor Outline’s buttons can draw a marker for it. So I wrote its own indicators: a fringe triangle pointing down for an open heading, right for a folded one, clickable with mouse-1 to toggle exactly like TAB . Folding itself is untouched â TAB , S-TAB and the C-c v keys all still work.
The performance part is where the real win is. A naive “redraw indicators after every command” implementation is a disaster in a large file, because it re-searches the buffer and rebuilds every overlay on every pause. Mine is driven by the text instead:
Folding changes text properties rather than characters, so folding alone takes the cheap path. Fold state is read back from Org on each redraw rather than remembered, so external folding can never leave a stale marker.
Two config choices matter just as much: org-fold-core-style is text-properties (so a visibility cycle doesn’t re-parse the file), org-element-use-cache is on, and Org starts with showeverything â which is both what I want (a note is read, not consulted) and the cheaper state, because it skips the visibility passes that walk every heading on open. I also removed a org-restart-font-lock that was re-fontifying the whole buffer a second time on open; JIT-lock handles what’s on screen.
The end result is that folding is boring now. C-c v c in Kotlin, Scheme, Elisp, Org, XML, YAML, Markdown. Guides that look like brackets. Indicators quiet enough to ignore until you need them. No pause on a 3000-line Org file. No two competing markers.
It honestly changes how much I collapse and expand while reading code. I used to avoid folding because it felt fiddly; now it’s free and mouse friendly.
If you want to read the actual code: it’s in dev-folding.el for the engines and indicators, the heks/fold-* wrappers in heks-emacs.el for the keys, and the Org indicators live in org.el . Everything is GPL-3.0, and it’s tested: maak verify asserts a fold actually covers a whole definition and that the documented keys are bound, and maak keys fails on a key that does two jobs or names a command that doesn’t exist.
Happy to answer questions about any of it, especially if you’ve fought the treesit-fold-indicators bitmaps yourself, because that one cost me an evening and I’d love to know if there’s a cleaner way.

title: Moldova Expels Russian Diplomat After Drone Crash
body:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Moldova declared a staff member of the Russian Embassy in Chișinău persona non grata after an explosive-laden Russian strike drone crashed on Moldovan sovereign territory, the ministry announced on Friday, Oct. 23.
In an official diplomatic declaration, Moldovan authorities described the incident as a direct infringement on national sovereignty and public safety resulting from Moscow’s ongoing hostilities against neighboring Ukraine.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“This incident is a serious violation of the sovereignty and security of the Republic of Moldova and poses a direct threat to the safety of citizens. Such actions are unacceptable and once again demonstrate the risks associated with the aggressive war of the Russian Federation against Ukraine,” the ministry stated.
The diplomatic body demanded that Moscow immediately halt cross-border aerial incursions and activities that undermine regional security.
“In this context, as a retaliatory measure, an employee of the Embassy of Russia in Chișinău will be declared persona non grata,” the ministry added.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu confirmed that the downed munition was identified as a Russian-operated Geran-type loitering munition that breached Moldovan airspace before falling in proximity to civilian residential quarters and a utility facility.
Writing on X, Sandu criticized the recurring hazards posed to Moldovan non-combatants.
“Russia’s war keeps putting Moldovan lives at risk,” Sandu stated.
“Today, a Russian Geran attack drone violated our airspace and fell near family homes and an energy facility. We condemn this latest dangerous act. In response, we have declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata.”
Moldovan law enforcement agencies and specialized explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) detachments secured the impact area to neutralize remaining ordnance and conduct forensic evaluations on the wreckage.
Russia's war keeps putting Moldovan lives at risk. Today, a Russian Geran attack drone violated our airspace and fell near family homes and an energy facility. We condemn this latest dangerous act. In response, we have declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata.
The diplomatic expulsion coincides with discussions between Chișinău and Kyiv to reorganize joint border administration to protect personnel and travelers from Russian standoff strikes along the Moldovan-Ukrainian frontier.
Moldovan Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin confirmed that Chișinău has withdrawn its customs officers and border police from four joint border posts situated on Ukrainian territory. Misail-Nikitin announced that Moldova is negotiating with Ukrainian authorities to relocate Ukrainian personnel onto the Moldovan side of the border to maintain joint customs inspections while minimizing physical exposure.
“Arrangements have already been reached with Kyiv for two crossings, and others will be assessed in the medium term depending on the risk of incidents,” Misail-Nikitin told television network Moldova 1.
Ukraine’s Deputy Minister for Communities and Territories Development Serhiy Derkach stated earlier in October that operational plans for several pilot relocation projects are projected within three months, supported by existing bilateral border agreements.
In September, the Moldovan Customs Service recalled operational personnel from three joint border posts, including the Giurgiulești-Reni crossing, relocating them to Moldovan territory for an initial 90-day window.
The defensive adjustments follow kinetic strikes by Russian loitering munitions against Ukrainian border infrastructure across the Odesa region.
On Sept. 9, a Russian drone strike on the Starokozache crossing killed two civilians and wounded three others roughly one kilometer from Moldovan territory.
Earlier on Aug. 21, Ukrainian border installations at the Tabaki crossing sustained structural damage from drone impacts, prompting a temporary operational closure. On Oct. 5, drone debris struck a commercial bus at the Palanca crossing, inflicting minor injuries on a Moldovan border guard.
While Russian authorities have asserted that border crossings facilitate weapon transfers into Ukraine – an allegation rejected by Chișinău – Moldovan officials have emphasized that recurring airspace breaches and debris falls endanger neutral border zones.

title: CAF Club Competitions: Late goals send Rangers, El-Kanemi crashing out
body:
Nigerian clubs Rangers International and El-Kanemi Warriors suffered painful exits from continental competition on Friday after late goals overturned their hopes of progressing against Algeria’s MC Alger and Morocco’s Raja Club Athletic, respectively.
Rangers surrendered a two-goal first-leg advantage to lose 3-0 in Algiers, crashing out of the CAF Champions League 3-2 on aggregate, while El-Kanemi Warriors conceded twice late in Casablanca to suffer a 4-2 aggregate defeat in the CAF Confederation Cup.
Both Nigerian sides had given themselves promising opportunities to advance after their first-leg results, but their continental campaigns ended in frustration as their North African opponents produced decisive performances when it mattered most.
Rangers’ hopes of reaching the CAF Champions League group stage were shattered after MC Alger scored three second-half goals to overturn the Nigerian champions’ first-leg advantage and secure a dramatic qualification victory.
The Flying Antelopes travelled to Algeria with a 2-0 lead from the first leg in Abeokuta, where they had demonstrated remarkable resilience despite playing with 10 men for most of the encounter following goalkeeper Lucky Jimoh’s dismissal in the 13th minute.
Kenneth Igboke converted a penalty before James Emo struck late to give Rangers a significant advantage heading into the return fixture.
However, the Nigerian champions could not reproduce that defensive resistance in Algiers, where MC Alger gradually turned the contest around to keep their continental ambitions alive.
Chahreddine Boukholda reignited the hosts’ hopes in the 58th minute, cutting Rangers’ aggregate lead to 2-1 and giving the Algerian side the belief that a comeback was possible.
With the pressure mounting, Mohamed Bangoura struck in the 84th minute to restore parity on aggregate, leaving Rangers desperately trying to hold on as the tie edged towards a possible penalty shootout.
But the visitors’ resistance finally collapsed in stoppage time when Soufiane Bayazid found the net in the 92nd minute, completing MC Alger’s remarkable turnaround and sending the Nigerian champions out of the competition.
For Rangers, the defeat represents a bitter disappointment after putting themselves in a strong position to progress. Having secured a two-goal advantage in the first leg, the Enugu club needed to protect that lead but were unable to withstand the late pressure from their opponents.
The elimination also revives memories of a painful chapter in Rangers’ continental history. In 1976, the Nigerian club suffered a similar setback against MC Alger, losing the return leg 3-0 after winning the first encounter 2-0. MC Alger subsequently went on to claim the continental title.
Rangers must now redirect their attention to domestic football following their Champions League disappointment, while MC Alger advance to the next stage with their ambitions of another continental triumph intact.
El-Kanemi Warriors also suffered a heartbreaking continental exit after two late goals handed Moroccan giants Raja Club Athletic a 2-0 victory in Casablanca, sealing a 4-2 aggregate triumph for the hosts in the CAF Confederation Cup.
The Nigerian side had entered the return leg with renewed confidence after holding Raja to a 2-2 draw in the first leg in Ikenne. With the tie delicately poised, El-Kanemi knew that a goalless draw would be enough to secure their place in the group stage.
For much of the encounter, the Nigerian representatives remained disciplined and frustrated their more experienced opponents, keeping Raja at bay as the hosts searched for the breakthrough that would swing the tie in their favour.
However, El-Kanemi’s defensive resistance was finally broken in the 88th minute when Aymen Barkok stepped up to convert a superb free-kick, giving Raja the lead on the night and shifting the aggregate scoreline to 3-2 in favour of the Moroccan club.
The goal left El-Kanemi facing an uphill task in the closing stages, with their hopes of forcing the tie back in their favour fading as Raja pushed forward to secure qualification.
Portuguese defender Marian Huja then delivered the decisive blow in the fifth minute of stoppage time, finding the net to make it 2-0 and complete Raja’s 4-2 aggregate victory.
The late double proved devastating for El-Kanemi, who had held their own for much of the contest but could not withstand Raja’s pressure in the closing moments.
For the Nigerian side, the defeat brings an end to their hopes of reaching the 2026/27 CAF Confederation Cup group stage. Their first-leg draw had kept the tie finely balanced, but they were unable to produce the performance required to finish the job in Morocco.
Raja, meanwhile, have secured their place in the group stage as they continue their pursuit of a third Confederation Cup title. The Moroccan club, two-time winners of the competition, will now turn their attention to the next phase of their continental campaign.
El-Kanemi Warriors must return their focus to domestic football after missing out on qualification, joining Rangers in an unfortunate evening for Nigerian club football on the continental stage.
The exits of Rangers and El-Kanemi Warriors underline the challenge facing Nigerian clubs when competing against experienced North African opposition over two legs.
Both teams travelled for their respective return fixtures with realistic hopes of progressing, having secured results in the first legs that kept qualification within reach. Yet late goals proved decisive, turning promising positions into painful eliminations.
Rangers’ collapse in Algiers was particularly damaging, given their two-goal advantage, while El-Kanemi’s resistance in Casablanca lasted until the closing stages before Raja struck twice to settle the contest.
With both continental campaigns now over, the Nigerian sides must regroup and focus on their domestic commitments, while MC Alger and Raja Club Athletic move forward in their respective competitions.

title: Russian drone attack on Zhytomyr leaves nine people injured, damages civilian infrastructure – National Police
body:
Russian forces attacked Zhytomyr with strike drones on Thursday, leaving nine people injured and causing damage to civilian infrastructure, the Patrol Police of Ukraine reported on Friday.

"Yesterday, the enemy attacked Zhytomyr with drones. As a result of the strike, nine people sustained injuries, including two children... Civilian infrastructure facilities were damaged," the agency stated on its Telegram channel.

According to law enforcement, there were no fatalities from the enemy strike. The victims received necessary assistance from emergency services.

title: Polish FM refutes Musk’s claim that Ukrainian elites profiting from US aid to Ukraine
body:
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has refuted a claim by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk that Ukrainian elites are allegedly enriching themselves through the multi-billion-dollar aid provided by U.S. taxpayers. Sikorski pointed out that the USA ceased funding for Kyiv last year, and that purchases of American weaponry are now being financed by European states.
“No, Elon, the U.S. stopped funding Ukraine last year. In fact, U.S. companies make money on American weapons for which we Europeans pay. The more you meddle in our politics and the more you play politics with your products, the more you damage your brand,” the minister said on X.
Meanwhile, Musk posted on the social media platform X, highlighting a significant disparity in motives between Ukraine’s elites and its ordinary citizens. He alleged that those in power have enriched themselves through hundreds of billions of dollars in foreign aid, even as the general population is being mobilized for the military. The American billionaire further suggested that a portion of U.S. taxpayer funds may be finding its way back—via money-laundering schemes—to finance political campaigns within the United States, which he posited as an explanation for why certain American politicians continue to support Ukraine.
At the same time, ABC News chief international correspondent James Longman reported on X, citing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the current performance of Starlink terminals remains insufficient to support the operation of Ukrainian defense drones. According to the journalist, the United States has provided Ukraine with only 24 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems over the past three months, whereas Russian forces launched 80 ballistic missiles into Ukrainian territory in the last week alone.

title: Ukraine strikes factory in Russia's Tolyatti, airfield in Krasnodar Krai, General Staff says
body:
Ukrainian forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, as well as an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai, Ukraine’s General Staff said on Oct. 24.
The General Staff said it recorded an explosion and a fire in the area of the Tolyattikauchuk plant. The plant produces synthetic rubbers, monomers, and high-octane gasoline additives. According to the General Staff, the synthetic rubbers are used to make solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.
"Damage to such objects affects the supply chain of raw materials for the Russian missile program," the General Staff added.
Telegram monitoring channels reported earlier in the day that fires broke out at several plants and factories in Tolyatti amid a wave of drone attacks overnight.
Videos filmed by locals show smoke billowing over the city in the early morning, with reports claiming that the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant was attacked and that evacuations took place at the AvtoVAZ car manufacturing factory.
Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ also claimed that a "military-purpose plant" was on fire, although without specifying what the plant produced.
Located around 1,300 kilometers from Kyiv, Tolyatti has been targeted by Ukraine on several occasions, including attacks on the Tolyattikauchuk rubber plant on Sept. 12 and the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant and KuibyshevAzot chemical plants on April 4.
Ukrainian forces also struck an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield, the General Staff said, while the extent of the damage is still undetermined clarified. The General Staff did not specify the type of aircraft damaged in the attack.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.
In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up attacks on businesses and enterprises. Kyiv’s long-range drone campaign has targeted numerous companies helping Russia’s war effort, while Moscow has taken a no-limits approach, destroying food logistics hubs, postal services, and public transport, killing numerous civilians in the process.

title: Fire extinguished in Kyiv’s Obolon district following Russian attack
body:

According to the State Emergency Service, on the morning of October 24, the enemy struck the Obolon district of Kyiv. Two people were injured as a result of the Russian attack on a residential area.
In addition, a single-story residential building was destroyed and a fire broke out after a strike hit a private estate. During the rescue operation, one victim was found and handed over by firefighters to medical personnel for hospitalization. Another victim did not require hospitalization.
“The minor fire caused by the attack was quickly extinguished,” the State Emergency Service reported.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 22, a strike was recorded at a transportation infrastructure facility in the Darnytskyi district.

title: Death toll from terror attack in Jordan rises to eight
body:
BEIRUT, October 24. /TASS/. A Jordanian woman who sustained injuries during a terrorist attack on an Orthodox church in Al-Karak has died in a local hospital, the kingdom’s Health Ministry reported. According to the ministry, this brings the death toll from the terror attack to eight.
Health Minister Ibrahim Al-Baddour stated that 27 injured people remain in medical facilities. "Eight of the wounded have been transferred to the Prince Ali bin Al-Hussein Military Hospital. Doctors assess the condition of two of them as critical," he noted.
According to the Al Mamlaka television channel, Jordanian security services have not yet managed to apprehend the members of the terrorist cell that carried out the attack on the church. The search for the perpetrators is ongoing. Security measures have been tightened in Amman and other cities.
On Friday, three terrorists opened fire near the St. George Orthodox Church in the Hammoud area of the Al-Karak Governorate. The attack, which took place during a funeral, left eight people dead and 34 injured.
King Abdullah II of Jordan personally visited the victims in hospitals and vowed to respond to the terrorist raid with an "iron fist.".

title: 2027: Mutfwang rallies Plateau indigenes in Kaduna for Tinubu
body:
Plateau State Governor Caleb Mutfwang has urged indigenes of the state living in Kaduna to back President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid, citing federal backing for infrastructure projects in Plateau.
Mr Mutfwang made the appeal on Friday while addressing members of the Plateau community in Kaduna ahead of the official flag-off of the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign on Saturday.
He said continued cooperation between Plateau and the federal government would accelerate development, urging the community to help secure another term for Mr Tinubu.
“Let us join hands to support President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for another term in 2027 so that the Renewed Hope Agenda can continue to deliver tangible benefits to our people and our nation,” he said.
The governor also described the emergence of Nentawe Yilwatda as APC national chairman as an opportunity for Plateau to strengthen its influence in national politics.
Recalling the late Solomon Lar’s role in national party leadership, he said Plateau’s representation at the national level should help advance the interests of its people.
Mr Mutfwang thanked members of the Kaduna-based community who travelled to Plateau to vote for him in the 2023 governorship election, saying their contribution to his emergence would not be forgotten.
He pledged to maintain the relationship as the 2027 elections approach and urged the indigenes to participate actively in the democratic process while maintaining peaceful relations with their host community.
Highlighting his administration’s performance, the governor cited ongoing road projects across Plateau’s 17 local government areas, reforms in education, improvements to healthcare facilities and collaboration with security agencies.
He also mentioned the Tin City Metro bus service and federal approval of major road corridors linking Plateau with other states, saying the projects would improve transportation, facilitate trade and expand economic opportunities.
Earlier, Deputy Governor Josephine Piyo, Secretary to the State Government Samuel Jatau and Director-General of the Mutfwang/Piyo Campaign Council Joseph Ari urged the community to remain engaged in Plateau’s affairs ahead of the 2027 elections.
The chairman of the Plateau community in Kaduna, John Nanpe, thanked the governor for the visit and pledged the community’s backing for his re-election.
A patron of the community, Peter Dasat, also commended the administration and urged Mr Mutfwang to remain focused on his development agenda.

title: Cabinet appoints Svyrydenko as rep to US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund
body:
The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has appointed former Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko as its authorized representative to the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF).
According to Directive No. 1116, dated October 23, the Cabinet of Ministers has recalled Yehor Perelyhin, former Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment, from his role as the Ukrainian government’s authorized representative to the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (structured as a limited partnership). In his place, the Cabinet has appointed Yulia Svyrydenko, former Prime Minister, who currently serves as Vice-Rector for the Development of Business Education at the private institution Kyiv School of Economics (KSE) University to act as the authorized representative (with her consent).
The U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF) is a joint U.S.-Ukrainian investment fund, established via an intergovernmental agreement in May 2025 to mobilize capital and attract investment for the reconstruction, economic development, and strategic sectors of Ukraine. The Fund focuses, in particular, on projects that facilitate Ukraine’s recovery, strengthen supply chains, and bolster the overall economic security and prosperity of both Ukraine and the United States.
As previously reported, on October 13, 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers accepted the resignation of Yehor Perelyhin from his position as Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment.
Yulia Svyrydenko served as Prime Minister for exactly one year, from July 2025 to July 2026. In September, she was appointed President of the KSE Business School.

title: USS McFaul completes 11-month deployment after combat operations with three carrier groups
body: The Arleigh Burke-class destroyer departed Norfolk on Nov. 25, 2025, and its deployment covered the U.S. 5th and 6th Fleet areas, where it defended U.S., allied and partner interests. While integrating with the USS Abraham Lincoln, USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington carrier strike groups, McFaul provided anti-air warfare, surface warfare and naval surface fire support. It used its Aegis Combat System both during the buildup to the operation and during its execution. “The Sailors of the USS McFaul have performed exceptionally well during this demanding combat deployment, proving themselves as a true warfighting powerhouse. Operating in a highly volatile region, this crew has repeatedly demonstrated the grit, technical mastery, and resilience required to protect our strike group and execute complex missions under pressure,” said Cmdr. Adam Samson, McFaul’s commanding officer. McFaul, designated DDG 74, is a Flight II Arleigh Burke-class destroyer capable of anti-air, anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare. Its vertical launching system and radar network enable it to track and engage multiple threats simultaneously. The ship is designed to operate independently or as part of a carrier strike group or amphibious readiness group. “I could not be more proud of their unwavering dedication and the quiet professionalism they bring to the watch every single day,” Samson said. “The true strength of this warship is, and always will be, its people.” Commissioned on April 25, 1998, in Savannah, Georgia, McFaul was the 24th destroyer of its class and the 11th built at Ingalls Shipbuilding in Pascagoula, Mississippi.

title: Ukraine Received Only 24 US Patriots in 90 Days
body:
Ukraine has received 24 surface-to-air interceptors for its Patriot air defense systems from the US over the past three months, despite requiring approximately 350 missiles per month to defend against Russian ballistic strikes, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
In an interview with ABC News broadcast he outlined munition shortfalls as Russian forces continue standoff strikes targeting municipal infrastructure ahead of winter.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Zelensky noted the difference between domestic interceptor stockpiles and incoming aerial strikes, stating that Russian forces launched more than 20 ballistic missiles against Ukrainian territory during strikes on Oct. 22 alone .
“Over the last 90 days, I have received 24 missiles from our strategic partner,” Zelensky said. “We don’t cry, and we don’t scream, but this is very important. I am just trying to say that every missile matters.”
The Ukrainian president compared Western munition deliveries to Ukraine with the expenditure of allied interceptors in the Middle East .
Zelensky stated that during the first 84 hours of armed escalation in that region, forces fired roughly 2,000 partner-supplied interceptors to defend airspace.
“In the first 84 hours, they launched about 2,000 missiles received from partners,” Zelensky said, pointing to the disparity in munition transfers.
Ukrainian defense officials have expressed concern over the allocation of US-manufactured Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors to Middle Eastern operational theaters.
The allocation of production lines and existing inventories has affected deliveries coordinated through NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program, leaving Ukrainian municipal centers and energy distribution facilities reliant on limited interceptor stocks.
The interview with ABC News follows appeals made by Zelensky to EU leaders in Brussels and defense specialists at Washington’s Hudson Institute.
In his address to the European Council on Oct. 16, Zelensky requested a winter air defense package of 300 Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors , stating that deliveries of two to four missiles every few months remain insufficient to counter coordinated strike waves.
The president described a plan under which transfers from European nations holding Patriot inventories – including Greece, Spain, and Germany – would bridge the gap until bilateral German procurement contracts and the 10-nation FREYJA anti-ballistic project become operational.
However, allied efforts to secure interceptors from Southern European inventories have met with reservations. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis stated on Oct. 16 that while Athens supports Ukraine, it will not transfer missiles from its PAC-2 batteries if doing so affects Greece’s own defense posture in the Eastern Mediterranean.
