title: The trouble with loving Russia: Evan Gershkovich's memoir seeks sentimentality in a lost country
body:
By the end of his pre-trial detention at Moscow's infamous Lefortovo Prison, American journalist Evan Gershkovich had developed a curious rapport with the FSB investigator tasked with proving he was a spy.
"Most people break after four months or so, but you're still holding strong — a year in," the investigator told him, and the two raised their cigarettes in a toast to "having tried to find common ground."
Gershkovich writes about many such moments in "This Cursed Beautiful Land: A Russian-American Story," his memoir of nearly 500 days in a Russian prison. His ability to capture them without artifice is one of the memoir's most distinctive qualities. It is also where the book becomes most troubling.
Read from Ukraine , these interactions raise a question that extends beyond Gershkovich's captivity: What does it mean to recognize the humanity of people who help uphold — even passively — a system of brutal repression?
Gershkovich was arrested in April 2023 while reporting in Yekaterinburg for the Wall Street Journal on Russia's military-industrial sector. The Federal Security Service (FSB) accused him of espionage, claiming he was collecting information on behalf of the American Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). The charges were baseless, and the Russian authorities provided no credible public evidence to substantiate them.
Gershkovich admits that before his arrest, he had felt "protected" and "immune" from the authoritarian system taking shape around him. He had mistaken the relative freedom afforded to a foreign correspondent for security. As with the detentions of Marine veteran Paul Whelan and basketball player Brittney Griner before Gershkovich, the Russian state demonstrated with his arrest its willingness to imprison Americans and turn their freedom into a bargaining chip in international negotiations.
After 16 months in captivity, Gershkovich was released as part of a major international prisoner exchange in the summer of 2024, which also included Russian opposition figures Ilya Yashin and Vladimir Kara-Murza. His release came shortly after the conclusion of his sham trial, which saw him sentenced to 16 years in prison for a crime he did not commit.
Much of "This Cursed Beautiful Land" details those nearly 500 days of Gershkovich waiting to regain his freedom. He learns the rules of prison conduct from cellmates; he watches momentous events, like the Wagner Mercenary Group's short-lived uprising against the Kremlin in June 2023, on television, frustrated that he cannot cover them as a journalist; he dreams and longs for his loved ones.
The relatively humane treatment he receives from his captors at the onset of his imprisonment confirms the obvious: the international attention given to his case made him a high-value hostage. At the same time, he did not have to live through the terror of being tortured for the circumstances to weigh on him.
This distinction matters. Gershkovich does not claim that his experience represents the Russian prison system as a whole, and he repeatedly refers to himself in the book as a "voyeur" among actual prisoners. He has also used his press tour for the book to draw attention to Ukrainian prisoners, including journalist Viktoria Roshchyna , who died in Russian captivity. Her body was returned to Ukraine in 2025 bearing signs of torture and evidence of mutilation, including the removal of some internal organs.
The contrast between Gershkovich's experience and that of prisoners like Roshchyna is jarring. It also exposes the limits of what the memoir can tell us about the true machinery of the Russian prison system — a system that ensnares not only those in Russia brave enough to speak out against the state, but also Ukrainians terrorized under occupation.
Yet the book is not simply an account of how an American journalist got swept up in the Kremlin's political circus. By detailing interactions with prisoners, security service officers, and prison employees, Gershkovich attempts to understand how the country descended into a state of madness. One of the reasons is that contemporary Russia, in many respects, inherited the Soviet police state — a system where widespread suspicion, political entrapment, and the presumption of guilt were instruments of power.
One of the best examples of this is the cult of personality surrounding Felix Dzerzhinsky, the founder of the Soviet secret police and an architect of the Red Terror, a period of state-sanctioned violence from 1918 to 1922 against perceived internal enemies of the Soviet Union. Gershkovich calls Dzerzhinsky an "avatar for the convulsions of modern Russian history," adding that he was "trapped in (Dzerzhinsky's) world, and so was the country."
As if to reinforce his point, in September 2023 — while Gershkovich was still in prison — Russian authorities erected a statue of the secret police chief at the headquarters of Russia's foreign intelligence service. That was more than three decades after the original monument outside the feared KGB headquarters was dismantled amid the collapse of the Soviet Union.
But the memoir's understanding of Russia becomes less convincing when it shifts its attention from the foundations of the country's authoritarianism to interactions with those who operate within it.
Gershkovich repeatedly tries to maintain a semblance of civility with the prison employees who control his life. Some, he notes, even commend his politeness despite the circumstances. Such exchanges suggest that the boundaries between captor and captive are not always expressed through open hostility. They also reveal how ordinary social conventions can survive inside a profoundly abnormal system.
At the same time, these interactions are not inherently compromising. A prisoner's willingness to converse with a guard does not amount to an endorsement of the guard's employer. Under extreme coercion, interpersonal ties can be essential to preserving one's sense of self. Gershkovich's steadiness reflects strength of character, coupled with the curiosity of a good journalist — not political endorsement.
But when kindness is presented alongside state violence, does it help us understand how repression works, or does it offer an emotional refuge from that reality?
Ukrainian writer and filmmaker Oleh Sentsov's account of his own imprisonment between 2014 and 2019 offers a useful comparison. During his hunger strike in a Russian penal colony, Sentsov also recalled moments of civility with his captors. Yet his observations are dry, sardonic, and openly contemptuous not only of the prison system but also of those who uphold it. Even a passing observation about their habits — like their listening to Russian chansons, a genre of music that glamorizes criminals — is part of a broader indictment of Russia's political and social decay.
The point is not that Sentsov was morally superior, or that Gershkovich should have responded to imprisonment by also going on a hunger strike as well. Their experiences and circumstances were radically different — Sentsov took a stand against the occupation of his native Crimea; Gershkovich was a hostage used as a bargaining chip. Rather, Sentsov's account more effectively shows that a system of brutality does not require every person within it to be sadistic — just enough people willing to perform their roles and look away from the violence and senselessness that sustain it.
The Ukrainian poet and dissident Vasyl Stus , who died in a Russian penal colony in 1985, offers another perspective. Declassified KGB records show that he cursed his captors at every opportunity he had, refused to obey basic tasks, and was so defiant that even fellow political prisoners worried that his actions would invoke collective punishment. His unyielding stance came at a great personal cost, but for him, they were the human face of the system that sought to punish him for his pro-Ukrainian stance.
Gershkovich's instinct is different. He tries to understand the people around him, including those implicated in his persecution. That instinct aligns with the work of a journalist, whose task is often to look beyond familiar categories and discover how people understand themselves — no matter how repulsive the truth might be.
This is where the memoir's emotional generosity becomes politically ambiguous. Gershkovich's encounters offer a means to distinguish individual Russians from the state that imprisoned him, preserving a connection to the country of his immigrant family's roots. That distinction is both understandable and important. Russia is not entirely reducible to its government, and Russian culture cannot be understood solely through the crimes committed in its name.
But the state's violence cannot be separated entirely from the society in which it operates. The question is how to distinguish between those who resist, those who are coerced, and those who willingly serve an authoritarian power.
Our introduction to Gershkovich's thoughts on Russia also draws on his fond memories of being raised by post-Soviet immigrants in the U.S. and of getting his footing as a young reporter in his family's homeland. There's an enduring sentimentality throughout the book, which conveys that the traumatic experience of being held hostage for over a year has not completely turned him against Russia. Indeed, he admits that the thought of never returning to Russia in his life, or at least for the foreseeable future, drives him to tears.
Even the title — portraying a country that is both beautiful and cursed — suggests a desire to see Russia in a better light. The idea of a "cursed" country evokes a dreamlike folktale: a curse, after all, can be reversed. But Russia's history, so deeply entwined with the suffering of its own people and the subjugation of its neighbors, resists such narrative neatness. To call Russia a "cursed" land is to risk sentimentalizing it.
Russia occupies an unusually privileged place in the Western cultural imagination. The insistence on its depth, including its literature and supposedly unfathomable soul, is often indistinguishable from the violence that permeates its history.
That romantic tradition can make the recognition of Russian suffering feel like a moral achievement while leaving the suffering inflicted on Russia's neighbors at the margins. It can also turn the enduring popularity of Russian culture into an argument for the country's essential goodness, as though cultural achievement were an argument against condemnation.
Gershkovich's memoir is more thoughtful than that. It is clear that he knows that the state that imprisoned him is dangerous, and he does not confuse his comparatively privileged captivity with the experience of Ukrainian prisoners. His continued attachment to Russia is not, in itself, an apology for its government. But the book enters a cultural tradition in which personal affection can too easily obscure political judgment.

title: Marine from Mykolaiv region returns from Russian captivity after more than four years
body:
The marine’s mother, Hanna Ivanivna, told a Ukrinform correspondent about this.
“When they called me yesterday and told me that Yevhen had returned… We had been waiting for this for so long that I was both overjoyed and in disbelief. I was overwhelmed with emotions that are hard to put into words,” the woman said.
His mother added that she never doubted her son’s return. Just two days ago, she sent him a letter—one she had been putting off writing for some reason, perhaps sensing something on a subconscious level.
Yevhen Uimanov had been held captive since April 12, 2022. In civilian life, he was a construction worker, but on the first day of the full-scale invasion, he went to the military registration and enlistment office, just like three other members of his family—his father, his sister’s husband, and his father-in-law. He was assigned to the 36th Marine Brigade.
“On February 28, he called home and said he was in the Donetsk region, near Volnovakha. Later, we found out that they were defending Mariupol. Then there was another call—on the night of March 17. To call us, he had to climb onto the roof of a high-rise building. That’s when the connection was lost,” said the Marine’s mother.
Lilia, Yevhen’s sister, constantly searched the internet for any news about her family. After all, her husband, Oleksandr Shepelya, and her father, Hennadii Uimanov—who served in the 79th Airborne Assault Brigade and were also defending the Donetsk region—went missing at the same time as her brother. She found a video of our marines who had been taken prisoner near the Ilyich Mariupol Metallurgical Plant and recognized her brother by the backpack that Yevhen had taken from his son when he went to war. Later, Lilia found a photo online of the prisoner holding a tag with his last name and date of birth. Although he looked very gaunt and was wearing dirty clothes, his family was certain it was Yevhenii.
“The first message from him came as early as 2023. We wrote him many letters, but they took 7–9 months to arrive, and not all of them made it. At first, his messages were very short, but lately he’s started writing a little more. He said he missed us very much and wanted chocolate and condensed milk. And in one of his most recent letters, he even wrote that he already had a business plan, and when he returned home, he would need my help to put it into action,” said Anna Ivanivna.
Her son-in-law and husband, as it turned out later, were also taken prisoner in April 2022. Her husband returned home as a result of a prisoner exchange in June 2025; her son-in-law remains in captivity.
The fate of another relative, Arkady, Yevgeny’s father-in-law, remains unknown; he is considered missing in action.
As reported by Ukrinform, 270 Ukrainians returned to Ukraine on October 23 as a result of a prisoner-of-war excha nge.

title: This Bicolano theater group brings grassroots stories — and disaster relief — to communities
body: ALBAY, Philippines – Sining Banwa (SB) began in 2011 as a free space for budding Albay artists to create art and stage progressive productions outside the classroom. Since then, this homegrown collective has evolved into a powerhouse of Bicol culture — using performance not just to entertain, but to bring communities together. Veteran theater artist Julie DM Vega emphasizes that SB’s soul is rooted in original, grassroots theater that were breathed to life through deep community immersion. For 15 years, the troupe has unearthed and amplified raw, multi-cultural stories that capture the true pulse, pain, and resilience of the region. (READ: 8 plays, 1 reality: Bicol theater unpacks hard-hitting local issues ) “SB is a home for the very communities whose lives we put on stage,” said Vega. “It gives artists the space to sharpen their craft while anchoring every performance to the real, urgent lives of the people they serve.” Built entirely from the ground up, Sining Banwa was powered by volunteer actors and a crew who personally bankrolled their early productions. In return, some communities they helped gave them harvested rice, sweet potatoes, and fresh vegetables to keep the troupe fed and afloat. “In those early years, our volunteer members kept the lights on,” recalled Vega. “When we brought our plays to the communities and stood with them in their struggles, strong networks were forged. Grateful locals would send us crops which sustained us through our toughest moments.” VLF BIKOL. Julie DM Vega performs in the 2026 Virgin Labfest Bikol, portraying a drag artist-activist who is the child of a desaparecido. Photo by Reinnard Balonzo/Rappler Remembering SB’s leanest years, Vega highlighted the sheer grit that kept them moving forward when funding was nonexistent. “We once reached a point where no one had money for a decent meal,” Vega added. “We gathered wild leaves we weren’t even sure were edible just to have something to go with our rice. It’s funny to look back on now, but those extreme sacrifices remind us of our roots and keep us deeply motivated.” Art relief programs Extending its impact beyond performance art, Sining Banwa launched programs such as Pagtugdon , a Bicolano term for a bird landing or perching, symbolizing the collective’s deep rootedness in the communities it serves. “By our fifth year, we reflected on our core identity as a community theater,” Vega explained. “We knew we had a responsibility to step up, especially during times of crisis.” ART HEALING. Sining Banwa helped numerous calamity-stricken communities across Bicol through its art relief programs following Super Typhoon Rolly in 2020. Photo by Sining Banwa In 2016, the theater company started providing art relief programs for calamity-stricken communities, particularly as Bicol is regularly battered by storms . In 2020, when Super Typhoon Rolly (international name: Goni) left Bicol with at least 20 people dead and almost P1.1 billion in agricultural damage, SB was among the first groups to respond amid government delays. “When Rolly hit, lahar heavily impacted our partner community in Busay, Daraga,” Vega said. “The actors and crew were on their feet to save whatever we could salvage from houses that were almost covered in lahar.” REBUILDING COMMUNITIES. Alongside creative disaster response initiatives, Sining Banwa members collected supplies and provided manual labor to rebuild storm-damaged homes in Bicol in 2020. Photo by Sining Banwa When the group launched a donation drive to help more people, contributions unexpectedly surged to over P400,000 in cash donations, allowing the project to expand to nearby communities, neighboring towns, and adjacent provinces. The group also assisted in relief operations in Tabaco City and Catanduanes province . “After providing relief goods and hot meals in Busay, we also helped in some areas of Tabaco City and gave victims construction materials to rebuild their homes. It continued until we reached Catanduanes, where we helped a community that couldn’t be reached immediately by other relief groups due to its geographically isolated location,” she added. GRASSROOTS RELIEF. Walking for more than half an hour through difficult terrain, Sining Banwa members brought assistance to isolated communities cut off from immediate government aid. Photo by Sining Banwa After trekking for nearly an hour on foot to reach their target communities, the volunteers worked with residents to help process trauma through art and community-building (READ: Bicol artists bring art relief to traumatized Kristine survivors ). “We weren’t there to pretend or act as if we would save them from what they experienced, so we partnered with them to help them realize their own strength despite going through so much. While the residents were packing relief goods, we had time to conduct art relief programs for children — something the government rarely provides after disasters,” Vega pointed out. Beyond typhoon recovery, SB also mounted several productions in 2025 to help a village engulfed by fire in Pilar, Sorsogon. That same year, all proceeds from their PedXing: Collab series were donated to disaster victims in the town of Tiwi in Albay (READ: Higit sa Pag-ibig: The Musical’ reveals the pain of Bicol’s flooded, red-tagged communities ). GIVING LIGHT. As Christmas approached in the aftermath of Super Typhoon Rolly, Sining Banwa distributed lamps to disaster-stricken families. Photo by Sining Banwa Bigger stage Fresh off acclaimed shows and expanding productions, Sining Banwa is setting its sights on a bolder ambition: forging a unified regional stage by embedding theater and community arts directly into the Bicolano educational system (READ: Why Bicol theater revived a century-old epic ). “Our vision is to see theater fully woven into the academic curriculum, and brick by brick, that dream is taking shape,” Vega proudly told Rappler. “Our school networks have rallied behind us — bringing their students to our plays and opening their gates for us to perform. Theater is no longer just an extracurricular; it is becoming a vital engine for learning.” ELECTION EDUCATION. Sining Banwa actors stage a play about elections during the 2025 Pista nin Teatrong Bikolnon as part of their voter education drive. Photo by Zachary Oliver Gonzales Looking back on SB’s journey, Vega envisions a future where local theater doesn’t just survive, but thrives. She urged local leaders and communities to address the chronic shortage of creative spaces for grassroots artists. “What we are truly fighting for is the creative freedom and physical space to hone our craft,” she emphasized. “It is high time that local governments and communities invest in their artists, empowering us to bring art directly to the masses.” Reaffirming their ties to the grassroots communities that have always been their lifeline, SB vows to continue staging fierce, truth-telling stories that inspire a stronger, more resilient Bicol. – Rappler.com

title: Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms
body:
Editor's note: This article was updated with additional comments by U.S. Billionaire Elon Musk, former Defense Ministry Adviser Serhii Sternenko, and Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Starlink and Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk's satellite internet system, Starlink, was working at full speed as of the morning of Oct. 24, after it had previously been limited to 161 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour).
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelensky said. "I thank all Americans and all our partners who took this seriously and truly helped us. I thank members of Congress , senators, all the media, the State Department, and the President."
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again.
"We record a speed of more than 400 kilometers per hour, the connection is stable," the ministry said.
The ministry continues to monitor and record the work of Starlink and Starshield, according to Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
"This is another example of direct dialogue and the persistent position of the President of Ukraine at the highest level yielding results. And this result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," the ministry added.
Musk later said that Ukraine's military violated the terms of service for Starlink, adding that the "loophole" has now been closed.
Ukraine's "military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," he said in a post to X.
"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is not a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk said.
He also claimed that SpaceX has done more than any other company to help Ukraine in its fight against Russia's war.
Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser Serhii Sternenko denied that Ukraine violated Starlink's terms of service.
"As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true. In February of this year, whitelists were introduced. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians," he said in a post to X.
"But for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work," Sternenko added.
Using Starlink for drone missions has been "technically impossible" since all drone campaigns that require satellite communications would only work with the military Starshield service, he said.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov also denied Musk's claims, saying that all Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90 kilometers an hour and do not work on Russian territory.
"Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said in a post to Facebook. "It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
Since mid-October, Starshield had been operating at limited capacity. With speed limit caps, Kyiv's ability to defend from deadly Russian jet-powered drones and coordinate strikes against Russian targets is hindered. Despite Ukrainian and U.S. officials apparently engaging in discussions to resolve the disruptions, nobody has publicly taken credit — or blame — for making or implementing the decision. However, the Trump administration officials continue pointing fingers firmly at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions, saying the president was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 160 kilometers (100 miles) an hour."
Trump said he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but might do so if the problems persisted.
"I have not spoken to him," Trump said. "I might have to, but I have not... I've heard it's fixed. If it's not, I will speak to him.... If there's a problem, I will get it straightened out." On Oct. 23, Zelensky confirmed that issues with Starlink continued to plague Ukrainian forces. "The speed restrictions for Starlink and Starshield are still in effect," Zelensky said. "The speed has not been restored. And the supply of interceptor missiles to protect against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed." On Oct. 23, U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal announced that he is opening a probe into the Starlink disruption. Blumenthal's investigation asks the Pentagon to clarify who ordered the restrictions and to provide information on the U.S. military's own reliance on Starlink.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also brought up the issue with Trump on Oct. 23, underlining the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves, according to a press release from the minister's office.

title: A Misguided Narrative: The Dangerous Implications Of Punch’s Editorial
body: Biodun Ajiboye The Punch Editorial Board’s October 16, 2026 piece on the political participation of chief executives of federal parastatals is far worse than merely flawed. It is an ill-fated, ill-informed overreach. It stands as a textbook example of journalism attempting to dictate law without basic comprehension. The editorial’s central argument collapses under an elementary error in political science: conflating the civil service with the public service. In basic public administration (Public Administration 101), the civil service is recognised strictly as a subset of the larger public service framework. It constitutes the permanent, tenured bureaucracy within ministries and operates under its own distinct civil service rules. By failing to grasp this foundational distinction, the editorial builds its thesis on a fundamentally flawed premise. The public service spans a far wider scope than the core civil service, incorporating political appointees, commission heads, and leaders of extra-ministerial departments whose offices exist at the president’s pleasure. Federal parastatal chief executives operate as political appointees and public servants rather than career civil servants. To equate a presidentially appointed director-general, governing under a specific statutory Act, with a career Level 8 civil servant in the Ministry of Works is either profound intellectual laziness or deliberate mischief. If we are to accept Punch’s distorted logic from its, then federal ministers—who are also presidential appointees—must similarly be barred from political engagement. Would Punch ever dare to publish an editorial claiming the Minister of Information cannot campaign for his own government? The absolute absurdity of that premise exposes the emptiness of their entire argument. The foundation of this debate is not the opinion of Punch . It is Section 40 of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, as amended, which the newspaper conveniently ignored. Section 40 guarantees every person, including public officers, the right to assemble freely and associate with other persons, including forming or belonging to any political party. This right is not a privilege granted by any media organisation. It is constitutionally guaranteed. Any restriction on that right must be justifiable under Section 45—meaning that it must be reasonably justifiable in a democratic society in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality, or public health. Where is the public danger in a director-general mobilising support for the president who appointed him? There is none. Punch writes as if the Supreme Court has not spoken on this matter. It has, and authoritatively so. In INEC v. Balarabe Musa & 7 Ors (2003) 10 WRN 1, the apex court demolished the very argument Punch is now recycling. Justice Emmanuel Ayoola (JSC) delivered a definitive blow to restrictions on civic freedoms, ruling that barring public and civil servants from political party membership is entirely indefensible in a democratic society. The apex court explicitly rejected the argument that public safety, order, morality, or health could justify such a ban, declaring that any attempt to weaponise Section 45(1)(a) to undermine the fundamental political rights guaranteed under Section 40 of the Constitution is fundamentally erroneous. The Supreme Court explicitly branded it erroneous, yet the newspaper—in a blatant characterisation—upheld it as law. In his landmark concurring judgment, the former Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN), Justice Mohammed Lawal Uwais, dismantled any ambiguity. He declared that the provisions of Section 40 of the 1999 Constitution are absolute: every citizen, including civil servants and public office holders, possesses the fundamental right to assemble freely and associate with any political party, trade union, or association to protect their interests. Justice Uwais underscored that the constitution makes zero exceptions and enforces no restrictions on public officers. Where the highest law of the land refuses to draw lines, Punch has arbitrarily invented them. Even the Head of Service circular, upon which Punch’s argument implicitly relies, was clarified by the Supreme Court judgment. After her office was inundated with requests for clarification on the apex court’s ruling, the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation issued a memo dated May 5, 2022, attempting to enforce the 2008 Public Service Rules regarding partisan politics. That clarification is exactly what the newspaper missed. The Public Service Rules cannot override the constitution. Because the rules are merely subsidiary legislation, the constitution remains supreme. Where the PSR conflicts with Section 40 (as interpreted by the Supreme Court), it becomes void to the extent of that inconsistency. This is the core principle of constitutional supremacy under Section 1(3)—something paper should well know. We are arguing for legal precision, not anarchy. The law draws a sharp line between the right to belong to a political party and the act of partisan mobilisation on official duty. This distinction is anchored in explicit terms of appointment, strict codes of conduct, and enabling statutes. It cannot be erased by a blanket editorial lumping everyone into a single category. A chief executive retains every lawful right to be a committed member, supporter, and mobilizer for the All Progressives Congress (APC), provided these activities are conducted within legal boundaries and outside official functions. The law does not demand political neutrality; it demands structural integrity. What it strictly forbids is the weaponisation of the office—specifically, the diversion of public funds, the exploitation of official hours, and the use of coercive power to compromise subordinates. By issuing a sweeping, lazy ban, Punch completely bypassed this crucial legal nuance, mistaking legitimate association for institutional abuse. This editorial is a masterclass in legal illiteracy and political alarmism. It is a transparent attempt to intimidate appointees legitimately driving the re-election campaign of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. Let there be no mistake: momentum is firmly on our side, and the opposition is visibly feeling the heat. Recent media commentary has drifted into fiction, yet our resolve remains unshaken. We will continue to consolidate our gains and sustain the momentum of our strategic political engagement. Moving forward, our actions will remain strictly within the law, guided exclusively by our official mandates and the constitution—not by outside noise. The law is settled and the Supreme Court has cleared the air. All Nigerian workers, whether civil or public servants, possess the constitutional right to participate in politics. No media editorial can rewrite the constitution. The Punch is simply late to class. * Otunba Ajiboye is Chairman, Media & Publicity Committee of FORCEPA, and Executive Secretary/CEO, National Institute for Cultural Orientation (NICO)

title: Wahala App, NIIA Forge Alliance to Deploy AI for Security Intelligence, Business Risk Management
body: Nigerian technology company, Wahala App Ltd, has partnered with the General Leo Irabor Early Warning Systems Centre (GLIC) of the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs (NIIA) to deploy artificial intelligence (AI) and real-time data analytics for security intelligence, operational risk management and business continuity. The partnership is expected to strengthen early warning capabilities by integrating citizen-generated incident reports with AI-powered analytics to identify emerging threats, monitor security trends and provide businesses, government institutions and other organisations with information to support timely decision-making. In a statement issued in Lagos, the company said the collaboration would give the Centre access to its Wahala Network, a digital platform that aggregates incident reports from individuals, businesses and participating organisations to provide insights into security risks and potential operational disruptions. The initiative comes amid growing demand for technology-driven solutions to security challenges, particularly as businesses seek to minimise exposure to threats affecting logistics, supply chains, personnel and other critical operations. According to the company, the platform’s analytical capabilities enable organisations to identify recurring incidents, detect previously overlooked vulnerabilities and assess the potential impact of security developments on their operations. It explained that AI-powered analysis could also establish connections between seemingly unrelated incidents, providing insights into wider security and socioeconomic risks affecting industries and communities. The Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Wahala App Ltd, Oriekaose Agholor, said the partnership represented an important step towards integrating citizen participation with institutional early warning systems and expanding the commercial application of real-time security intelligence. “Safety is a shared responsibility, and timely information can help people make more informed decisions about their surroundings. Our partnership with GLIC is an important step towards connecting citizen participation with wider early warning efforts,” Agholor said. He added that the company was seeking further partnerships with government agencies, corporate organisations and other institutions to expand the reach of its technology and improve access to actionable security information. Under the arrangement, businesses connected to the Wahala Network would be able to receive information on incidents that could affect their operations, including developments requiring adjustments to transportation routes, logistics planning and personnel safety measures. The company said its technology could also support preventive risk management by identifying patterns of incidents that might otherwise develop into larger operational or security crises. Agholor noted that wider adoption of the platform could strengthen information sharing across sectors and help organisations respond more effectively to emerging risks. “We invite Nigerians, businesses and institutions to join us in building a more informed and safety-conscious society,” he said. Also speaking, Acting Head of the General Leo Irabor Early Warning Systems Centre, Dr Omotola Ilesanmi, said technology and reliable information were increasingly important to effective risk management and institutional preparedness. “Effective early warning depends on the timely identification of risks and the availability of reliable information to support informed decision-making,” Ilesanmi said. “Technology and citizen participation can contribute to this process by strengthening awareness of emerging risks and supporting preparedness.” Beyond institutional collaboration, Wahala App said it was expanding public engagement through its Ambassadors Against Wahala programme, which encourages responsible incident reporting and safety awareness across workplaces, educational institutions, religious organisations and communities. The company explained that its digital platform enables users to report incidents, receive location-relevant alerts and send emergency notifications to designated contacts, while its broader technology offerings provide organisations with data-driven insights for security planning and operational resilience. It emphasised that the platform was intended to complement the responsibilities of government security agencies and emergency response institutions rather than replace existing security structures. Wahala App said the partnership formed part of its broader strategy to deepen collaboration with public institutions and private sector operators, expand the application of AI in risk intelligence and strengthen the role of technology in Nigeria’s security and business environment. The company, which specialises in real-time crisis awareness and management, operates a digital network connecting citizens, businesses and institutions through incident reporting, emergency alerts and AI-powered risk analysis.

title: Nigeria Shows Global Tech Giants Are Not Beyond Reach, Says Luminate CEO
body: The Chief Executive Officer of Luminate, Melanie Hui, has praised Nigeria as a leading example of how African countries can shape the global artificial intelligence economy rather than simply consume it. She pointed to the country’s regulators, workers and innovators as proof that the continent is already setting its own terms. Hui gave the keynote address at the Build 2026 Conference in Abuja on Wednesday. The audience included the Honourable Minister of Communication, Innovation and Digital Economy, heads of government parastatals, members of the diplomatic community and members of the Nigeria AI Collective. She said research Luminate commissioned this year on the continent’s AI landscape “found not only patterns of extraction and inequality. It found imagination and leadership.” “Here, there are important reasons for optimism,” she said. Hui cited the action Nigeria’s competition authority took against Meta over data exploitation and discriminatory practices. She said this showed that “global tech companies are not beyond the reach of national institutions.” She also praised app-based drivers in Nigeria for securing government recognition for Africa’s first e-hailing trade union. She said innovators across Nigeria are “using locally built, practical technology to serve the underserved: from bringing reliable banking for rural communities to tackling massive crop losses.” Her examples from elsewhere on the continent were litigation in Kenya establishing that global technology companies can be brought before Kenyan courts civil society coalitions in South Africa challenging bulk surveillance at the Constitutional Court AI-assisted learning materials in local languages helping children in Mali drones extending healthcare to remote islands in Uganda “They are not merely enduring technology,” she said of Africa’s technologists, teachers, climate advocates, feminists, trade unions, youth movements and public interest lawyers. “They are shaping and reshaping it.” “These examples matter because ownership is also about power: the power to negotiate, regulate, organise and secure remedy,” she added. Hui’s speech was titled “Africa in the Global AI Order: Towards Equitable Ownership and Shared Prosperity.” She made clear that Luminate stands behind Africa’s ambition to be a full participant in the AI economy. “My African friends tell me they will not be confined to the role of consumer, supplier of raw data, source of critical minerals or provider of low-paid labour in somebody else’s AI economy,” she said. “And Luminate will stand with them in securing a better digital age.” She said equitable ownership “means moving beyond participation alone.” It means having “meaningful influence over the infrastructure, the institutions, the partnerships, the choices that will determine Africa’s digital future.” She also said Africa’s young and growing population, along with its markets, languages and cultures, “will be enormously valuable to the development of future AI systems.” Hui rejected the argument, made by some in the tech industry, that regulation holds innovation back. She offered a more hopeful view of how growth and fairness can go together. “Those of us who promote tech justice must not lend credence to some in the tech industry who would paint regulation as a brake on progress. I disagree,” she said. “Safeguards are the allies of progress. Inclusion is the engine of meaningful scale. Sovereignty means being stronger together.” “Prosperity is not shared automatically,” she added. “It is shared because workers have bargaining power. Because markets can compete. Because regulators and courts have resources and authority. Because people can seek remedy when they are harmed.” To show what successful AI deployment needs, Hui described how India’s Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare used AI to predict the start of the monsoon for 40 million farmers. She credited African expert Rose Mutiso with the insight that AI “was the last piece of this breakthrough, not the first.”

title: Israel has not invested enough resources into hasbara, and now we are paying the price - opinion
body: As we approach Israel's forthcoming election, to what extent do we recognize the significance of this period? Yes, we have become accustomed to wars and the reality that Jews – both here and abroad – are not the flavor of the month. Yet I cannot recall a period such as this, where we in Israel are consistently considered the aggressor. What is particularly reprehensible is that on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led invasion of Israel on Oct. 7, 2023 – the day when the world witnessed the barbaric slaughter of 1,200 Israelis, the sexual abuse of countless women, and the abduction of 251 people who were taken hostage – we witnessed some 40 countries holding large demonstrations against us, the victims of the barbarism. This year, on Oct. 7, US House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries attacked Israel and called for “a dramatic shift in Middle East policy, demanding the establishment of a Palestinian state and work to end the settler violence.” While I concur that we need a government to address the unacceptable settler violence, yet Jeffries – on this, of all days – did not have one word of condemnation for those responsible for an attack on Jews that has seen no precedent since the Holocaust.We are experiencing a situation that just a few years ago we would have thought was impossible. I refer not only to those who refuse to accept that Jews have a right to live in their historic homeland, or those who have chosen not to recognize the UN Partition Plan of 1947, to which Israel adhered but the Arabs did not.I also refer to the countries in Europe and the free world who, with each passing year, find reasons to condemn us rather than condemn those who wish to destroy us – and them.If only they would open their eyes. How tragic that their non-acceptance of the Jewish people's right to their historic homeland appears more important than what, ultimately, might be the end of their respective countries.Some will argue that we Jews have no need to worry; in spite of the above, America is on our side. True, it would appear so at this moment.However, the wind is blowing in a different direction with the forthcoming midterm elections to be held on November 3. There are predictions that the Republican majority might be eliminated in both houses of Congress. This possibility, together with the election of a new US president in 2028, does not bode well for Israel.As if this were not enough, far too many American Jews of all ages are turning away from Israel. In recent elections, for instance, AIPAC did not have the same influence as it had in previous years. We are told that the anti-Israel mayor of New York, Zohran Mamdani, was elected with the help of many young Jews. In addition, the country my grandparents referred to as “The Goldener Medina,” where Jews felt completely at home, is now experiencing antisemitism. We need to find a way to project the factual reality of the one Jewish stateTHERE IS also the worldwide negative perception of Israel that seems to worsen every day. We need to find a way to project the factual reality of the one Jewish state; currently, we are paying the price of not recognizing the significance of the battle of the word.Yes, we have won military battles but, tragically, consistent Israeli governments have ignored the prime battle: to ensure that our side of the story is projected rather than leaving our enemies to present their distortions and lies. Our leaders have also ignored the reality that the world now receives its information 24/7 online.As a vital part of hasbara (public diplomacy), we must recognize the important part that should be played – but is not – by our embassies throughout the world. Unfortunately, during the past decade-plus, the government has severely reduced the Foreign Ministry's budget. This has resulted in the closure of Israeli embassies, the loss of several potentially excellent diplomats, as well as severely restricting the vital activities of embassies abroad. In addition to ensuring the truth, rather than the lies projected worldwide, the embassies should reach out to young Jews – many of whom have adopted the Palestinian narrative. Hasbara is vital if we wish to receive the support of the younger generation of world Jewry. The government's unbelievable financial allocations to the haredim would be better spent ensuring we create a society with correct values. It requires a far greater investment in our education system which, according to official surveys, finds Israel's education strategy at an all-time low – a dangerous phenomenon for a country that relies heavily on its brainpower.We need to invest more in public relations and find funds for additional medical training schools based in Israel. This would stem the flow of medical students who are forced to study abroad and, in many cases, do not return here after their studies.It means improving the lives of our hard-working doctors, to ensure they remain in Israel rather than find work in other countries, as did 1,370 doctors during the past three years.What are the priorities for the parties that want to form a government?WITH THE ELECTION for a new Knesset just days away, we must recognize the challenges Israel and the Jewish people are facing. What are the priorities for the parties that want to form a government? Three years after Oct. 7, the time is long overdue for a full state commission of inquiry to investigate how Israel's leaders were caught by surprise when our enemies – apparently with the greatest of ease – simply crossed over from Gaza to murder men, women and children. This attack must have been planned for months, if not years. If we fail to learn from our mistakes, a similar disaster could be repeated. The government we elect must urgently redirect the state's resources. No more financial benefits to haredi schools that do not teach core subjects. No more funds to enable some 80,000 haredi men of enlistment age to avoid conscription, at a time when we are told the IDF is dangerously short of soldiers. It is four days to the election of a new Knesset. Before entering the cubicle to vote on October 27, we must ask ourselves which party, and which leader, chooses to rely solely on extremist parties to form a government. It is the extremists who continue to demand exemption from conscription for haredim, resulting in too many of our soldiers returning home, exhausted, overwrought, and psychologically damaged. The country does not have sufficient psychologists, psychiatrists, and counselors to deal with the fallout of this ongoing war, where too few bear the responsibility of ensuring a tomorrow for our beloved state. Let us never forget those prepared to give their lives in defense of Israel and its citizens. They deserve a far better leadership than those who have been steering the country in recent times.The bottom line: We should be voting for leaders who comprehend the priorities facing Israel and the Jewish world rather than those whose prime aim is to stick to their seats. It is incumbent on us, the electorate, to appreciate the urgent necessity for change at this most challenging time for Jews since the Holocaust. The time for new leadership is now. We – who are privileged to live in the one Jewish state – must live up to our responsibility to ensure its continuity as the strong and vibrant Israel we love. Am Yisrael chai!  ■The writer is the president of Israel, Britain, and the Commonwealth Association, and has chaired public affairs organizations in Israel and the UK. The views expressed here are her own.

title: Drones Hit Tolyatti Plant, Missiles Strike Oryol Defense Site
body:
An overnight Ukrainian drone attack hstruck the “Tolyattikauchuk” petrochemical facility in Russia’s Samara region, igniting a major industrial fire and prompting the evacuation of workers at the neighboring AvtoVAZ automotive plant, open-source monitors and local residents reported early Saturday, Oct. 24.
According to the Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) project Exilenova+, strike drones hit the industrial grounds of Tolyattikauchuk in the city of Tolyatti, triggering an intense blaze as additional unmanned aerial vehicles were spotted maneuvering across different sectors of the municipality.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Local residents reported that assembly-line workers at the adjacent AvtoVAZ automobile manufacturing plant – Russia’s largest carmaker – were evacuated from their shifts amid the incoming drone alerts.
Tolyattikauchuk operates as one of Russia’s largest specialized petrochemical manufacturers, producing synthetic rubber, hydrocarbon fractions, monomers, polymers, organic and inorganic synthesis goods, and performance additives for commercial and military vehicle fuel.
The industrial strike in Tolyatti follows a precision standoff missile strike conducted on Friday, Oct. 23, against the “Proton” defense manufacturing complex in the western Russian city of Oryol.
Visual evidence published by Exilenova+ showed British-supplied Storm Shadow air-launched cruise missiles penetrating the airspace of the industrial perimeter before detonating within the facility.
Open-source imagery confirmed that at least one major production and assembly workshop sustained catastrophic damage, resulting in the structural collapse of upper floors, outer masonry facades, and roof framing, rendering primary manufacturing lines fully inoperable.
Defense consultancy Defense Express reported that the struck facility shares its industrial complex with two affiliated defense-electronics enterprises: ZAO Proton-Impuls and AO Proton-Elektroteks.
All three entities function as suppliers for the Russian military-industrial base, producing specialized microelectronics, optoelectronic equipment, power semiconductors, and sub-assemblies for high-tier combat platforms.
Defense analysts identified the complex’s output as critical components integrated into Russian T-90 and T-14 Armata main battle tanks, Pantsir-S1 mobile air defense gun-missile systems, Iskander-M short-range ballistic missiles, and S-71 “Kover” cruise missiles, alongside specialized military electronics.
Military specialists noted that while destroyed production equipment and industrial workshops might eventually be replaced, the degradation of proprietary manufacturing tools and the scarcity of qualified technical specialists pose severe, prolonged hurdles for Moscow’s defense manufacturing capacity.
The kinetic strikes inside Russia coincided with a massive systemic blackout that plunged large swathes of Russian-occupied Crimea into darkness overnight into Saturday, Oct. 24.
According to monitoring group Crimean Wind and Exilenova+, coordinated drone strikes targeted key electrical transmission nodes and distribution substations across the occupied peninsula, precipitating simultaneous blackouts in Sevastopol, Simferopol, Yalta, Feodosia, Dzhankoi, Alushta, and Yevpatoria.
Residents across the peninsula reported that Russian mobile air defense detachments engaged incoming aerial targets near Baherove in the vicinity of Kerch, while at least four detonations were logged in the Pervomaiske district.
Sevastopol’s Russian-installed occupation governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, confirmed widespread power cuts across the naval port , attributing the outage to structural damage sustained by power installations situated elsewhere on the peninsula.
Razvozhayev stated that municipal emergency services and healthcare infrastructure were transferred onto backup diesel generators while regional energy dispatchers operated under emergency contingency protocols.

title: Would ousting Netanyahu cure Israel's chronic public relations failures? - opinion
body: Among the most cited stories I ever wrote for The Jerusalem Post was the series of polls taken during US president Barack Obama's administration asking whether his policies were more pro-Israel or pro-Palestinian.In June 2019, only 6% of Israelis said they considered Obama more pro-Israel. Two months later, the figure fell to only 4%.I thought of those polls this week, when Obama made headlines with new false accusations against Israel and current President Donald Trump intervened in next Tuesday's election by endorsing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, which he also did when I interviewed the then-businessman for the Post ahead of our election in 2013.Needless to say, Trump fares far better than Obama here.A June Pew Research Center poll of 36 countries found that his highest favorability rating is in Israel, at 81%, which is obviously much higher than in the US ahead of the midterm elections there.That admiration is not reciprocated, however, considering how our prime minister is perceived in the US.Americans have little to no confidence in Netanyahu to do the right thingAn April Pew poll found that 59% of Americans have little to no confidence in Netanyahu to do the right thing regarding world affairs, including 76% of Democrats and 44% of Republicans.A poll taken by the National Opinion Research Center at the University of Chicago in July found that 20% of Americans view Netanyahu favorably, 38% unfavorably, and 41% admit that they do not know enough about him to have an opinion.Those numbers raise an interesting question ahead of Tuesday's vote: Would a change in power in Israel significantly impact the perception of the Jewish state in America?Could we just tell the world that the defeated Netanyahu was responsible for anything they did not like about Israel and that there is no reason to not like us anymore?The most obvious answer is that no one knows. But that's no fun, so let's speculate anyway.There are historical precedents for a country's international perception improving dramatically following the departure of a leader who was not liked abroad, and there are historical precedents of it making little difference.One example of the former is what has happened to Zambia since Hakainde Hichilema replaced Edgar Lungu as president.Hichilema's administration initiated major reforms that reshaped how the global community views Zambia, including restructuring the poor country's debt, restoring press freedom, and broadening public transparency of the work of the government. An example of the latter is Zimbabwe, following the ouster of long-time authoritarian president Robert Mugabe in 2017.Mugabe left the country globally isolated as a pariah state due to hyperinflation, intense political violence, and severe human rights abuses. When he was forced to resign following a military intervention in November 2017, the global community felt a brief wave of optimism.'Zimbabwe is Open for Business'His successor, Emmerson Mnangagwa, immediately launched an aggressive international public relations campaign.Using the slogan “Zimbabwe is Open for Business,” Mnangagwa promised a clean break from the autocratic past, pledging to implement democratic reforms, revive the economy, and re-engage with Western nations.But according to the Council on Foreign Relations, Zimbabwe's international standing failed to recover because its underlying governance structures remained completely unchanged, which enabled continued human rights abuses and entrenched authoritarianism, resulting in Western sanctions remaining.No one should compare Israel to Zimbabwe or Netanyahu to Mugabe. But what Netanyahu and Mugabe have in common is that they are their country's longest-serving leaders who have made plenty of decisions without taking into account how they would be perceived abroad.AS I POINTED out in my new book, in a 60 Minutes interview five months ago, Netanyahu blamed antisemitism's resurgence on “a concerted effort by several states to vilify Israel primarily on social media and the standard media, too, and we have not fought back yet.”“We have not done well on the propaganda war,” Netanyahu said in the interview. “We have to fight back against these lies, this propaganda, with the only weapon we have, which is the truth.”“I am trying to do that now, and we will try to do that with much greater effort, because we have left the battlefield to our enemies, and boy do they lie – all the time,” he continued.If Netanyahu keeps that promise and devotes his next government to the narrative war that he himself admits his governments have not engaged in before, perhaps international perception of Israel will improve with him remaining in power.But for that to happen, he would need to muzzle MKs in his political bloc, who were quoted in an Associated Press piece that ran in The Washington Post this week, titled: “In their own words: Israeli politicians' extreme speech surges ahead of elections.”The article features the number two candidate on the Religious Zionist Party and Zehut list, Moshe Feiglin, saying that Gazans “must be expelled by all possible means, such as cutting off their water, and whoever wants to drink a bottle will leave. Killing them all would be incredible.”Otzma Yehudit's Yitzhak Kroizer is quoted as saying, “In Jenin, there are no innocent civilians. In Jenin, there are no innocent children.”And MK Amit Halevi from Netanyahu's own Likud is quoted about produce from the West Bank, saying, “The bottom line is that the salad you are eating contains a great deal of Palestinian poison.”The next Knesset could include MKs who care deeply about improving Israel's public image. I purposely won't single out a candidate four days before the election, but the forum on Israel's relationship with the Diaspora hosted this week by the ANU museum (available on YouTube) gives hope.Maybe too much of the world will hate us no matter who is in the Knesset.At my election briefing at Shivtei Yisrael synagogue in Ra'anana this week, Australian Jewish leader Danny Lamm, who recently made aliyah, recalled how hard a time he had getting meetings with left-wing leaders for then-Labor Party leader Merav Michaeli when he brought her down under.And maybe a relationship with the US president matters more than the rest of America.Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu was vigorous, and Gadi Eisenkot and his prospective foreign minister Yair Lapid admitted that they tried and failed to persuade the American administration to prevent the endorsement.The beauty of democracy is that all voters get to decide this big question for themselves if it's a factor for them when they cast their ballots.No matter who wins, let's hope that the polls about Israel and its leadership are better soon – in America and worldwide.■The writer is the author of The Blood Libel Machine: Exposing the Anti-Israel Hate Network and How to Fight Back, which can be ordered from Amazon or Pomeranzbooks.co.il

title: Israeli researchers use ancient stone tools to trace hunter-gatherer migrations
body: Fragments of ancient stone tools found within a cave in the Armenian Highlands have revealed new insight into the complex nomadic lifestyles of Middle Paleolithic hunter-gatherers, according to a recent study. The study was conducted by a team of international researchers, headed by Dr. Ariel Malinsky-Buller and PhD students David Nora, Ioannis Oikonomou and Dominik Rogall from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Published in the journal Quaternary Science Reviews, the study analyzed an assemblage of 1,770 stone artifacts spanning five distinct layers in Ararat-1 Cave in Armenia in order to trace how early humans adapted their technology in order to survive harsh and changing environments.The study focused specifically on the late Middle Paleolithic period, roughly between 33,000 and 52,000 years ago, when ancient hunter-gatherers attempted to navigate intense environmental shifts in the South Caucasus region.Studying the tool fragments, researchers found a distinct difference in how such prehistoric groups used the stone resources available to them.Obsidian was transported from afar, local stone used as neededWhile high-quality obsidian tools were transported across long distances to be used, some originating from olcanic sources up to 200 kilometers away, tools made from local chert reflecting the hunter-gatherers' resourcefulness.Researchers found that the obsidian tool fragments bore evidence of continuous reshaping and maintenance, indicating that they had been specifically designed to survive use by mobile groups moving through areas of extreme altitude.In contrast, the chert tool shards show signs of benign produced on-site where they were found, pointing to early hunter-gatherers utilizing nearby resources for short-term tasks when staying at a specific location.By adopting an analytical framework to track tiny fragments smaller than 20 millimetres in size, researchers were able to identify near invisible evidence of tool repair, even when the tools tthemselves had been removed from the site.The findings challenge traditional methods classifying ancient cultures solely by static tool shapes found in their camps.Instead, the study showed that Ararat-1 Cave functioned mainly as a maintenance-and-rest station within a network of seasonal migration routes."Our study demonstrates that ancient hunter-gatherers were highly flexible and strategic thinkers," said Malinsky-Buller. "They did not rely on a single way of doing things. Instead, they carefully balanced portable, long-distance toolkits with immediate local resources, treating caves like Ararat-1 as critical hubs to rest, repair their gear, and plan their next move across a challenging landscape."The project received support from the European Research Council and the Fritz Thyssen Foundation.

title: “You cannot act as if it is not wartime when you are at war”
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 24 (MNA) – Referring to the US aggression waged against Iran, Judiciary Chief Gholamhossein Mohseni-Ejei has said, “You cannot act as if it is not wartime when you are at war.”
Speaking at a get-together meeting with the economists of the country in Tehran on Saturday, the Judiciary head pointed to the significance of identifying problem in the realm of economics, noting, “The purpose of holding such expert-level meetings is not merely to assist the government but to serve the country as a whole, especially in economic terms.”
Today, addressing urgent economic issues, crises, and quasi-crises is a top priority that must be taken into serious consideration, Ejei underlined.
“We should bear in mind that our current conflict with the enemy is an existential war,” he said, adding, “The savage and criminal Zionist regime is not even satisfied with the fragmentation of Iran; it seeks the total destruction and annihilation of Iran. For our part, we consider the very existence of this occupying regime to be a danger to humanity."
Elsewhere in his remarks, the head of the Judiciary elaborated on how to strengthen social capital during wartime, stating, "Social capital, and the issue of public trust is of paramount importance. The people are the foundation of the Islamic Establishment, so, the question of how to preserve and bolster this social capital is a critical matter.”
He described enhancing public resilience and resistance during wartime as a highly significant and strategic matter, noting that the enemy, in its hybrid warfare, seeks to infiltrate the social, psychological, and economic structures of society and turn the minds and collective will of Iranian people into a target.
Under such circumstances, increasing the level of public resilience is a critical imperative and must rank among the top priorities for any government, the Judiciary chief underlined.

title: Hellenic Navy Conducts Inaugural SPIKE Missile Firings During Joint Drills with Israel
body: Greek surface and special operations craft validated their new Rafael-made missile systems, while a coordinated submarine torpedo strike sent the decommissioned frigate Bouboulina to the bottom of the Cretan Sea. On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, acceptance firings of SPIKE NLOS and SPIKE ER guided missiles were conducted in the wider northern Cretan Sea area. The firings were attended by Hellenic National Defence General Staff Chief General Dimitrios Choupis, Israeli Navy Commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel, Hellenic Navy Chief Vice Admiral Dimitrios-Eleftherios Kataras, and Hellenic Fleet Commander Vice Admiral Christos Sasiakos. Greek and Israeli warships in formation in the northern Cretan Sea during the joint live-fire exercise. Hellenic Navy photo. The exercise involved ships from the Hellenic Navy’s Frigate Command, Submarine Command, Fast Attack Craft Command, Surveillance Ship Command, and Underwater Demolition Command, as well as helicopters from the Hellenic Naval Aviation Command and Hellenic Air Force assets. They were joined by two fast attack missile craft from the Israeli Navy, which also conducted undisclosed missile firings during the drills, further enhancing operational interoperability between the two forces. Rafael SPIKE NLOS and SPIKE ER2 missiles were successfully fired from a Machitis -class patrol vessel and a Mark V Special Operations Craft (SOC), respectively. The firings clearly demonstrated the effectiveness and operational value of the newly installed weapon systems. SPIKE NLOS missile launch SPIKE NLOS missile launch SPIKE ER missile launch The decommissioned Hellenic Navy Elli -class (Kortenaer/S-type) frigate Bouboulina (F463) served as the target ship. Following the missile strikes, she was subsequently sunk by an SUT torpedo fired from a Hellenic Navy Papanikolis -class (Type 214HN) submarine. Before her Hellenic Navy service (2001-2013), Bouboulina served with the Royal Netherlands Navy as HNLMS Pieter Florisz (F826). Commissioned in 1983, she was the final Kortenaer -class frigate to be built. The decommissioned Hellenic Navy Elli-class (Korternaer/S-type) frigate Bouboulina (F463) served as the target ship. Hellenic Navy photo. As part of the exercise, the Hellenic Navy Chief and the Israeli Navy Commander held a bilateral meeting aboard the Hellenic Navy Hydra -class (MEKO 200HN) frigate Psara . They exchanged views on matters of mutual interest, focusing on contemporary maritime security challenges, freedom of navigation, and developments across the wider Eastern Mediterranean. Video of the missile firings. Credits to Hellenic Navy. Both navies emphasized the need to further strengthen their cooperation to promote regional stability and security, reaffirming their commitment to expanding partnerships in naval operations, innovation, and new technologies. The exercise took place amid renewed tensions in the Eastern Mediterranean, following the decision by Libya’s eastern-based parliament on October 20 to ratify the controversial 2019 maritime memorandum with Turkey. This development comes amid growing Turkish-Israeli tensions and closer Greek-Israeli defense cooperation, adding to the region’s increasingly complex security environment. SPIKE Missiles in Hellenic Navy Inventory Greece has equipped eight vessels of two different types with Rafael’s SPIKE fire-and-forget missile systems , significantly enhancing their operational capabilities. Machitis-class patrol vessel launching a SPIKE NLOS missile. Hellenic Navy photo. Four Machitis -class patrol vessels are fitted with the Typhoon MLS-NLOS system. Each system is capable of carrying eight SPIKE Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) missiles with a range of 32 km. The sixth-generation electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) multipurpose missile system enables both sea-to-shore fire support and sea-to-sea engagements. The upgrade included the installation of the Typhoon MLS-NLOS launcher, replacing the aft-mounted 40 mm L/70 Breda-Bofors gun fitted on a Type 520R naval mount. Mk V SOC with its Typhoon MLS-ER launcher fitted SPIKE ER missiles visible on the aft deck area. Hellenic Navy photo. The other f our vessels are Mk V Special Operations Craft (SOC) , fitted with the Typhoon MLS-ER system on their stern decks. Integration required significant modifications to the main cabin, mast, and aft deck area. Each craft carries four SPIKE Extended Range (ER) 2 missiles, with a range of 10 km. The post Hellenic Navy Conducts Inaugural SPIKE Missile Firings During Joint Drills with Israel appeared first on Naval News .

title: Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. arrested for alleged cyber libel
body: MANILA, Philippines – Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested by the Quezon City Police Department (QCPD) under the leadership of acting district director Police Brigadier General (PBGEN) Christopher Olazo on Saturday, October 24, for alleged cyber libel. The Kamuning Police Station 10’s warrant section and the Quezon City District’s anti-cybercrime team both facilitated the arrest. Lustre, 72, is the author behind Kill, Kill, Kill : Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines, a book about former president Rodrigo Duterte’s deadly war on drugs. He had been attending the House of Representatives’ Saturday news forum at a restaurant along Scout Borromeo Street when the police arrived to read his Miranda rights to him, according to a report by GMA News. The same report also said lawyer Dino De Leon, who was also present at the forum, will serve as Lustre’s legal counsel moving forward. DARGON Law, where De Leon is a partner, later said in a statement that it is currently processing Lustre’s bail, which has been set at P48,000. “DARGON Law will steadfastly protect Mr. Lustre’s legal interests and constitutional rights. Mr. Lustre reserves all legal rights and remedies to file appropriate counter-charges and administrative complaints to vindicate his rights,” the law firm wrote. Notably, the warrant of arrest was issued by Branch 10 of Davao City’s Regional Trial Court. Lustre’s arrest comes just after Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte filed a cyber libel complaint against GMA Network’s journalists over a report about bribery claims against him and Vice President Sara Duterte. Must Read Paolo Duterte files cyber libel complaint vs GMA Network over Gracioso report In a video posted by ABS-CBN News , Lustre said he does not know who the complainant is. Lustre will remain under police custody until further court proceedings are made. – Rappler.com

title: Stonebwoy donates GHS100,000 to Black Challenge ahead of Amputee World Cup
body: Ghanaian dancehall artiste Stonebwoy has donated GHS100,000 to the Ghana Amputee Football National Team, the Black Challenge, ahead of their participation in the 2026 Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico. The award-winning musician visited the team’s training session at Mensah Sarbah Park on the University of Ghana campus to motivate and encourage the players ahead of the tournament before making the donation. “I’m supporting them with GHS100,000. This is a token from me and the Burna Boy Music Group. This is not much at all, but I know it will go a long way to support the group,” he said. Stonebwoy also called for increased financial support for the team as they prepare to represent Ghana on the global stage. “We need funds directed to the Amputee team so that they can continue to perform because these are people’s fathers, uncles and our own brothers, and they’re representing the nation,” he added. The musician further commended the President of the National Paralympic Committee of Ghana, Samson Deen, for his leadership and commitment to the team. “I want to say thank you to the President of NPC Ghana, President Samson Deen, a great man. He has carried a lot on his shoulders, and may God continue to open his wings and bless him so he can continue to make people happy,” Stonebwoy said. The Black Challenge have been drawn in Group D for the 2026 Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico, where they will compete against Angola, Iraq and Colombia. The team are expected to depart Ghana for Mexico in the coming days as preparations continue for the tournament.

title: 3 Tankers of Russian Diesel Headed for North America, Russian Deputy PM Says
body:
Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their way to North America, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Friday.
Novak, in a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, said the cargos were part of a deal to supply U.S. and world markets.
"The first three fuel tankers are already on their way to the eastern coast of the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the RDIF [Russian Direct Investment Fund]," Novak said.
Novak said Russian companies could supply 500,000 metric tons in October.
Under a deal announced this month by U.S. President Donald Trump, Russia agreed to supply ​diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. The Trump administration temporarily lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its ‌war on Ukraine.
The deal as announced by Trump provided for 300,000 metric tons in October and more later.
A Reuters exclusive story published earlier on Friday, quoting ship-tracking data, said the first Russian diesel was on board a tanker headed for New York.

title: Ukraine's Sine Engineering launches joint defense tech initiative with Finland
body:
A leading Ukrainian defense tech firm, Sine Engineering, launched a new joint initiative with Finland to develop, test, and produce dual-use technologies in the Nordic country as it steps up support for Ukraine.
The initiative will focus on resilient communications, navigation, and onboard autonomy, as Sine Engineering specializes in producing satellite-independent navigation software, enabling drones to fly without relying on GPS.
The company announced the new research and development initiative at the Ukrainian-Finnish Business Forum on Oct. 22, attended by President Volodymyr Zelensky and Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo in Kyiv.
The firm expects the Ukrainian and Finnish governments to support the initiative by including it in the new Ukraine-Finland Drone Deal signed on Sept. 23. The deal lets both countries share technology and expertise, collaborate on research and innovation, and jointly develop and manufacture drone technology.
"We look forward to the support of the governments of Ukraine and Finland in including our joint R&D initiative among the projects under the Drone Deal," said Andrii Chulyk, CEO and co-founder of Sine Engineering.
"We are confident that this initiative will strengthen the technological capabilities, defense, and resilience of Ukraine and Finland, while contributing to the security of Europe and our allies."
As the Kyiv Independent first reported in March, Sine Engineering was selected as the first project under the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, the result of last year’s "minerals deal" discussions between Kyiv and Washington.
The defense tech company produces technology for around 200 Ukrainian drone producers, including interceptor drone manufacturers. Its technologies can also be applied for civilian use.
The new initiative is an expansion of Sine Engineering’s operations in Finland, after the company opened an office in the Nordic country last year. The company said last year that it was looking to open R&D centers abroad to attract radio engineers in Europe to help address Ukraine’s shortage of specialists.
Finland has a long history of developing radio technologies, and Sine Engineering said it hopes to expand its Finnish team to 100 people by the end of the year, 80% of whom will be engineers.
Following the business forum on Oct. 22, Kyiv and Helsinki signed seven agreements worth a total of 330 million euros (over $336 million), including support for Kyiv's energy infrastructure and greater access to Finland's satellite networks.
The Finnish tech companies ICEYE and Nokia also signed a letter of intent with Ukraine's Defense Ministry, formalizing a partnership aimed at developing Ukraine's own satellite communications system amid disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink services.

body:
