title: Big Chill Between Turkey and Azerbaijan
body:
Relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan appear to have deteriorated sharply. A speech delivered at a party conference in which President Ilham Aliyev emphasised his country’s independence has been interpreted as an attack on Ankara. A ban on headscarves in Azerbaijani schools has met with sharp criticism in Turkey, and now Baku has imposed entry bans on 31 Turkish nationals.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“This can’t be just about headscarves. Clearly a major bone of contention between the two countries emerged even before the headscarf issue escalated. ... What the real problem is, we don’t actually know. Why do we not know? Because the scope, strength and nature of relations between the two countries are determined less by institutions than by the friendship between the two presidents. ... It’s odd that these two leaders – who we thought had the closest, most genuine and brotherly relationship among all leaders – have not uttered a single conciliatory word since the crisis began. Absolute silence. They haven’t even talked on the phone, let alone paid a visit.”
The pro-government Yeni Akit (Turkey) suspects that the ban on headscarves in Azerbaijan is driven by the autocratic president’s fear of losing power:
“Aliyev, who has revived the headscarf ban for no apparent reason and is willing to risk falling out with the Turkish people – who prayed for him during the Karabakh War – and with Turkey, which has supported him politically and militarily, is in reality driven by the fear that his own people might be influenced by the climate of freedom in Turkey. ... But as he commits these acts of tyranny he overlooks the fact that ‘no tyranny lasts forever’.”

title: US President Trump’s defeat turns into a domestic challenge
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 24 (MNA) – The growing public dissatisfaction in the United States regarding the continued conflict with the Islamic Republic of Iran has emerged as a significant challenge for the Donald Trump's administration.
Nowadays, there is a growing public dissatisfaction with the United States regarding the US war waged against Iran and this issue has been turned into a challenge, a challenge that, in addition to increasing economic pressure on American citizens, could also impact the political standing of the Republicans ahead of the congressional midterm elections. Recent polls indicate that a majority of Americans are unhappy with how the US President has handled this crisis, and skepticism has grown regarding Washington’s ability to achieve its stated objectives.
Within this framework, a Democratic Senator from Connecticut and member of the US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations Chris Murphy has criticized the Trump administration’s policies toward Iran, emphasizing that American people have no desire for this conflict to continue and that the costs to the nation are far from negligible. Murphy, a staunch critic of the Trump administration’s military policies, highlighted the financial burdens, the risks faced by American forces, and the security implications of these policies. Furthermore, he has called for an end to the conflict, asserting that Congress must take responsibility regarding the continuation of this course of action.
Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump's performance
Data from recent polls indicate that opposition to the handling of the conflict with Iran has spread to a significant segment of American society. According to a Pew Research Center poll, the results of which were released on October 8, 2026, 65 percent of Americans are dissatisfied with how Donald Trump has managed US military action against Iran, while only 33 percent approve of his performance. The survey, which included 5,062 American adults, was conducted between September 28 and October 4. The significance of these figures becomes even more apparent when compared to the results of a poll from March; at that time, 61 percent of respondents were dissatisfied with Trump’s handling of the situation, while 37 percent approved of his performance. Consequently, over the course of a few months, the level of dissatisfaction has risen, while support for the President’s performance has declined.
In general, US President Donald Trump's approval rating has tremendously been plummeted which is unique of its kind as compared with the previous presidents of the United States.
Furthermore, only 34 percent of Americans believe that the initial decision to use military force against Iran was the right one—a figure that represents a four-percentage-point decrease compared to March.
These findings suggest that the issue is not limited merely to disagreements over how government policies are implemented; rather, a segment of American society has also developed a more negative assessment of the very decision to employ military force.
Skepticism regarding realization of Washington’s goals
Another sign of public dissatisfaction is the growing skepticism regarding the Trump administration's ability to achieve its stated objectives. According to the same Pew Research Center poll, 52 percent of Americans have little or no confidence that the Trump administration will achieve its goals in the confrontation with Iran. In contrast, 24 percent stated that they have a great deal or a fair amount of confidence that these objectives will be realized.
On the other hand, a large segment of American society does not expect this crisis to end in the short term. According to the survey results, 47 percent of participants predict that U.S. military action against Iran will continue for more than another year, while 30 percent expect the situation to last between six months and a year. Consequently, approximately 77 percent of respondents anticipate that the conflict will persist for at least another six months.
These concerns arise against a backdrop where a prolonged conflict could impose greater financial and military costs on the U.S. government, further straining the nation’s resources. Consequently, the gap between the administration’s promises regarding the achievement of its objectives and public anxiety over the protracted crisis has become a focal point for criticism of the Trump administration’s policies.
Economic costs and concerns regarding American forces
Concerns regarding the economic consequences of a conflict also play a significant role in shaping public opposition. A survey by the Pew Research Center indicates that 73 percent of Americans are very or somewhat concerned about rising gasoline and fuel prices resulting from a conflict with Iran. Furthermore, 71 percent of respondents expressed concern about the injury or death of American troops. Additionally, 58 percent of participants stated that they are very or somewhat concerned about the deployment of U.S. ground forces to Iran.
These statistics indicate that the consequences of the crisis, as perceived by the American public, are not limited solely to military developments. Rising energy costs, the potential for the conflict to spread, and the risk of casualties among U.S. forces all factor into citizens' assessments of the administration's policy.
Under such circumstances, the continuation of the conflict could become a significant factor in U.S. domestic debates—especially if citizens feel that the costs incurred are disproportionate to the outcomes announced by the government.
Murphy’s warning regarding costs of continuing the conflict
Chris Murphy has also highlighted this same set of concerns in his criticisms. In a speech on the floor of the US Senate on September 24, he criticized Republicans for opposing a resolution to end the conflict, noting that public support for this policy has become very limited.
In this speech, Murphy stated that, according to the data he cited, only 18 percent of the American public supports this conflict; he urged Congress to heed the citizens' call to bring it to an end. He also warned of the security and economic repercussions of the crisis, as well as the risks facing American troops. Murphy argues that, in evaluating the outcomes of this policy, the U.S. government must consider not only the stated military objectives but also the costs imposed on American citizens, military personnel, and the nation's security interests.
Political consequences for Trump and the Republicans
Growing public dissatisfaction regarding a conflict with Iran could have significant political consequences for the Trump administration—especially with congressional midterm elections on the horizon, where the administration’s foreign policy performance could emerge as a key point of contention between Republicans and Democrats.
A decline in public support for government policies could pave the way for intensified criticism from opponents and the raising of more serious questions regarding the costs and outcomes of this conflict.
Notably, this erosion of support is not confined solely to Trump’s political adversaries. According to a Pew poll, his approval rating among Republicans and those who lean toward the party has fallen from 69 percent in March to 63 percent in October. While a majority within this group continues to support his performance, a six-percentage-point drop may signal growing reservations among a segment of his political base. Conversely, the negative view Democrats hold of Trump’s performance has remained virtually unchanged—a fact indicating that opposition to his policies remains widespread among his political opponents.
Generally speaking, polling data and criticisms from figures such as Chris Murphy indicate that the conflict with Iran has evolved into an issue that transcends mere US foreign policy. Economic costs, concerns regarding the safety of American troops, skepticism about the realization of stated objectives, and growing public opposition have intensified domestic pressure on the Trump administration.
In this regard, what Trump’s critics characterize as a failure to achieve stated goals could develop into a significant challenge within the realm of US domestic politics. Nevertheless, the extent to which this issue influences the outcome of the midterm elections will depend on future developments, the state of the economy, and how the administration manages the situation in the coming months.

title: US authorities repeatedly used SpaceX for foreign policy goals — Reuters
body:
LONDON, October 24. /TASS/. The White House has repeatedly requested SpaceX to switch on or off its satellite internet services globally to advance US foreign policy priorities, Reuters reported, citing sources.
The news agency noted that Kiev had previously complained about operational restrictions on the SpaceX satellite communication terminals used by the Ukrainian military. Although US officials denied imposing any restrictions, President Donald Trump stated on October 22 that Kiev’s access to the Starshield military communications network had been restored, without specifying who originally ordered the connection to be slowed down. Meanwhile, some US politicians, primarily Democrats, are demanding an investigation into why Starshield access for Kiev was restricted.
According to Reuters, the White House had utilized SpaceX services to advance its geopolitical agenda long before this incident. In 2023 and 2024, the Joe Biden administration requested the company to block pro-Iranian forces in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink terminals that US intelligence believed they had acquired.
Furthermore, in 2024, SpaceX submitted filings to the US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, stating that it collaborates closely with the government on export licensing and technology security to further US national security and foreign policy interests.
Citing two former officials, the agency reported that in 2022, following the start of Russia's special military operation, Biden administration officials asked SpaceX to expand the Ukrainian military's access to Starlink. That same autumn, the White House requested SpaceX to ensure internet availability in Iran amid local protests. While the US successfully smuggled Starlink terminals into Iran at the time, sources did not specify the exact number. The Trump administration took similar steps during its operations against the country in 2025 and 2026.
"The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy," the agency says.

title: Starlink and Starshield operating at speeds above 161 km/h – source
body:
A source at the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said this to Ukrinform.
"As of the morning of October 24, Ukraine's Defense Forces and Ministry of Defense specialists have observed that Starlink/Starshield has begun operating at speeds exceeding 161 km/h," the source said.
According to the source, the military continues to "monitor and conduct tests at higher speeds, determine the upper limits and establish the extent to which the operation of these communications systems has actually been restored."
President Volodymyr Zelensky reported on October 23 that speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield remained in effect.
U.S. President Donald Trump previously said that SpaceX owner Elon Musk had restored Starlink service for Ukraine.

title: AstraZeneca and Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi team up for $50 million clinical trials action plan
body: Global biopharmaceutical company AstraZeneca is to invest $50 million to carry out dozens of clinical trials in Abu Dhabi in a major partnership with one of the emirate's leading hospitals. The company is joining forces with Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi in a long-term drive to address pressing healthcare challenges, with the first studies expected to start before the end of the year. About 30 trials will be conducted in the emirate in the coming years, focusing on advancing treatment for patients with cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases. According to the UAE Ministry of Health and Prevention, cardiovascular disease is responsible for 34 per cent of all deaths in the country, highlighting the need to strengthen medical care. “The investment is around $50 million over the next few years," Iskra Reic, international executive vice president for AstraZeneca, told The National on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit this week. "We have already finalised the feasibility work for six studies and are planning to start the first by the end of this year.” Ms Reic said the initiative, which is being supported by Abu Dhabi's Department of Health, is poised to benefit patients and the wider medical community in the emirate. “The expansion of clinical research may allow more patients from here to be included in global clinical trials. It will expand and enhance the collection of data that is relevant to the local population and the local healthcare system. “Equally, it will allow the local research community and healthcare professionals to be more connected and to become part of the global clinical research network. At the end of the day, it helps the researchers and it helps the patients.” AstraZeneca also announced a global collaboration with Oracle. Its first programme, taking place in Abu Dhabi, will focus on hypertension care and clinical research with M42, using AI and real-world data to explore earlier diagnosis, clinical-trial recruitment and safety monitoring. “All the partnerships we have signed today are related to two main things: how we can combine clinical development and healthcare expertise with AI and the opportunities that technology offers,” Ms Reic said. “On one side, we want to improve patient outcomes. On the other, we want to support healthcare systems to become more sustainable and resilient.” She said the aim was to use available data and harness AI to identify diseases more quickly, enabling earlier intervention to improve patient care. “If the early detection of hypertension proves to work, we will be able to identify patients who are at risk of developing hypertension much earlier,” she said. “That means they will have an opportunity to receive treatment early and improve their outcomes. Both partnerships are very much focused on supporting local patients and the local healthcare system.” Investing in health Ms Reic said the UAE was an ideal partner for its projects due to its robust data collection, research network and the government's commitment to bolstering the health sector. “The UAE is one of very few countries presently suited for these partnerships,” Ms Reic said. “On one side, we have very well-connected medical records and Emirati genomic data. By using AI, that allows you to predict specific diseases. “When you add very engaged and fast regulators, and a knowledgeable and committed clinical research and academic network, you have almost the perfect ecosystem to revolutionise this area.” Earlier detection and treatment could improve outcomes for patients while making healthcare systems more financially sustainable, she said. “By treating patients too late, we are not helping patients, and we are not helping the healthcare system from a sustainability and financing perspective,” Ms Reic added. “If we intervene early and treat patients earlier, that will also help the healthcare system retain more funding for investment and innovation.” The pharmaceutical industry’s role has changed as AI, health data and other technologies have developed, she said. “The future is already here,” Ms Reic said. “Previously, from the pharmaceutical industry’s perspective, we looked at our business as developing and delivering medicine to patients. I would argue that today, and even more so in the future, that is not enough. “As a responsible, innovative pharmaceutical company, you need to transform care for patients. You need to look at every step of the patient pathway to see how you can reduce the barriers and intervene earlier.” She said collaboration between companies, governments, hospitals and research organisations was essential. “Every stakeholder in a healthcare system should act, and we should act together,” she said. “I don’t think any industry or organisation can change the healthcare system on its own. Bringing different industry players together with government and healthcare stakeholders actually makes a difference.”

title: Global Media Alliance and Japan Motors support Ghana Blind Union with 60 white canes
body: Global Media Alliance (GMA) and Japan Motors have donated 60 white canes to the Ghana Blind Union (GBU) to support the welfare and mobility of persons living with visual impairment. The initiative addresses accessibility challenges and empowers GBU members to navigate their daily environments with greater confidence and autonomy. The event commemorated International White Cane Day. The 2026 Corporate Run made the donation possible, earmarking 25% of all participant registration proceeds to support visually impaired persons. Global Media Alliance Chief Executive Officer Ernest Boateng expressed excitement about the initiative, highlighting the company’s long-standing commitment to inclusion and equal opportunity for all. “As members of Run Ghana, we have always supported the Ghana Blind Union, and we are very happy to continue this relationship. Inclusion is part of who we are as a company; we were among the first in Africa to introduce a blind news reader. “My team and I are passionate about running, and through the Corporate Run we want to extend that fun and privilege to persons with disabilities, including the visually impaired. Seeing the proceeds of the run go directly to members of the GBU is what makes it all worthwhile,” he said. Lakeside Estate Executive Director Salah Kweku Kalmoni was elated by the initiative, describing the donation as a show of solidarity with the union and its members. “It gives me great joy to be part of this support for the Ghana Blind Union. These white canes show solidarity with the union, and our relationship keeps growing stronger every year. “I can assure you that the GBU will always be dear to Japan Motors and Global Media Alliance, and we will keep running so that more people can move with confidence and independence,” he said. Receiving the canes on behalf of the union, Ghana Blind Union Executive Director Dr Peter Obeng-Asamoah expressed appreciation for the partnership’s consistency and its commitment to including the less privileged. “We are very excited to be associated with Global Media Alliance and Japan Motors. This tradition has been consistent, and they always think about including the less privileged in these social activities. “We stand firmly for inclusion and equal opportunity, and we are proud to see that Japan Motors and Global Media Alliance truly recognise and champion this vision,” he said. Over the years, the Corporate Run, organised by Global Media Alliance in partnership with Japan Motors, has evolved beyond a corporate fitness event into a platform that combines wellness with social impact. The white cane donation continued that tradition, showing how corporate partnerships can create lasting change and champion independence and equal opportunity for all.

title: Russian strikes injure seven people in Kharkiv region, including two children
body:
According to Ukrinform, Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, reported this on Telegram .
According to Syniehubov, a 12-year-old girl was injured in Kharkiv, while a 13-year-old boy and women aged 46 and 37 suffered acute stress reactions. In the village of Cherkaski Tyshky, part of the Tsyrkuny community, men aged 57 and 52 were injured. In the village of Blyzniuky, a 39-year-old woman suffered an acute stress reaction.
In addition, medical workers provided assistance to a nine-year-old girl who was injured in Izium on October 22.
Over the past day, Russian troops attacked Kharkiv's Slobidskyi and Osnovianskyi districts with drones. Across the region, they used six missiles, three guided aerial bombs, a Geran-2 drone, two Molniya drones, five FPV drones and 140 UAVs whose type is being determined.
In Kharkiv, two civilian enterprises, an apartment building and four private houses, seven cars, the circus building, an office, a gas station and a garage were damaged.
In the Bohodukhiv district, a private house and three cars were damaged in Zolochiv. In the Kupiansk district, houses, a car, an administrative building and a garage were damaged.
In the Izium district, private houses and outbuildings were damaged in Oskil, Dibrova and Izium. In the Kharkiv district, two private houses were damaged in Derhachi, while a vehicle service station and garages were damaged in Nova Vodolaha.
In the Lozova district, a civilian enterprise, eight private houses and two apartment buildings were damaged in Zlatopil, while a gas station and a car were damaged in Blyzniuky. In the Chuhuiv district, a car was damaged in Novyi Burluk and two private houses in Lyman.
Over the past day, the transit evacuation center in Lozova received 154 people.

title: Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
body:
FILE - Smoke rises after an attack by Houthi rebels on the city of Taiz, Yemen, on Oct. 21, 2015. (AP Photo/Abdulnasser Alseddik, File) Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP hide caption
Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.
The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.
Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.
"We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily," al-Shahid said in a phone interview.
Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.
The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.
Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."
Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents' access to wells
Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.
War-related damage to Taiz's aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.
By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.
As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents' access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.
The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.
As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.
The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food
Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.
Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.
Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.
These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.
"The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises," Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.
Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.
Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.
"We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food," he said in a phone interview.
Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.
While the Yemeni government still controls the center of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city.
Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south toward Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that won't be easy.
"Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters," said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.
Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to brief the media, but Yemen's foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group's tightening grip on the city.
The Houthis' fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials said.
Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians.
Abdel Gaber said he can hear loud explosions every day from fighting that is happening roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away. The family isn't returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety.
Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive.
"Staying in our home is inevitable — whether it be a matter of life or death," al-Shahid said.

title: Why sports insider Brian Windhorst’s career begins and ends with writing
body: Brian Windhorst has broken some of the biggest sports stories from the least glamorous places imaginable. Long before he became a renowned NBA insider and a household name among basketball fans globally, he learned that the news doesn’t wait for a convenient time or location. Over his 20-year career, Windhorst has taken urgent, league-shifting phone calls in chaotic airport terminals, public bathrooms, and cramped stadium broom closets. He even reported a massive NBA development from a hospital room while waiting for his wife, Maureen Ellen Fulton, to undergo a scheduled cesarean section. “It wasn’t going to be for an hour, so… you’re just killing time,” Windhorst shared to Rappler during a recent Manila visit. But somehow, that round-the-clock hustle is what a kid from Akron, Ohio wanted — Windhorst decided early on that a conventional life wasn’t going to cut it. Play Video Today, his globe-trotting career is defined by television appearances, the flash of cameras, and millions of social media followers. Yet, Windhorst insists that all of it — the television sets, the viral moments, and the multi-million-dollar sports spectacles — isn’t exactly complete without the quiet, grinding work of a writer. To him, sports journalism operates exactly like a ride at Disneyland: before visitors can climb aboard an attraction, there must be a movie. Before the movie, a character; and before that character ever comes to life, someone has to sit down at a keyboard. “The character doesn’t exist without the writer,” Windhorst said as The Hoop Collective visited the Philippines to launch NBA on Disney+’s 2026-2027 season. “It all comes from writing,” he said. “Everything that we do comes from writing. You can never stop writing. I will never stop writing, ever.” Finding LeBron Growing up near Cleveland, Windhorst’s future was once mapped out on an ordinary Saturday with a strict $10 budget. As a high schooler looking to escape his parents’ conventional nine-to-five routine, he would stretch that budget to cover bus fare, a movie ticket, and his favorite, now-discontinued Taco Bell item: the Chilito. He was just a local kid who wanted to get out, see the world, and chase something grander. “I wanted to be, at some level, extraordinary,” he said. Basketball offered him that exact path. While studying journalism at Kent State University, Windhorst fell in love with the specific rhythm of the NBA. The league’s 82-game regular season offered a perfect balance, providing frequent competition alongside unique opportunities to travel. But he’ll always remember covering high school basketball in Ohio, where he watched a 14-year-old LeBron James play his first high school game. Windhorst remembers a tall, lanky teenager with big feet who was still growing into his body. What stood out immediately was how smoothly James moved. “There’s a lot of tall, you know, teenagers — he was barely a teenager — are awkward,” Windhorst said.. “You know, they don’t move that well when they’re growing so tall. He moved so smooth.” James scored 15 points that night. Afterward, his coach told Windhorst that James was the best player he had ever coached — a sweeping assessment that the young reporter struggled to believe at the time. James, of course, became one of basketball’s greatest icons, and Windhorst’s coverage of him became a defining pillar of his own career. Windhorst readily acknowledges that he would not have reached the same professional heights without James. But the experience also taught him to look beyond the box score. Going for a scoop, going viral In 2003, Windhorst began covering the Cleveland Cavaliers for the Akron Beacon Journal . He moved to The Plain Dealer in 2008 before joining ESPN in 2010, bringing behind-the-scenes developments to a national audience. The relentless nature of his national role affected everyone around him, creating a landscape where work never truly stops. Windhorst recalls a time when Philadelphia 76ers coach Nick Nurse had to abandon a long-awaited round of golf midway through the course just to take an urgent call from James’ agent. “Sometimes that’s the nature of this job,” Windhorst noted. “It’s a job that doesn’t have nine-to-five hours.” Yet, despite the intense pressure to break news first, he insists that speed must never compromise accuracy. “Being wrong once is way worse than being right a hundred times in a row,” he said. One of Windhorst’s biggest career scoops arrived when Kyrie Irving suddenly demanded a trade away from the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2017. The news blindsided the basketball world, but as Windhorst points out, trade reporting rarely begins when a deal is officially announced. It begins months in advance by tracking minor shifts in behavior and recognizing when a situation no longer looks the way it did before. “The real value for me is: can you say what a team is going to do before they do it, or what they might do?” Sometimes, that deep reporting translates into unforgettable television. During an episode of ESPN’s First Take , Windhorst delivered a brilliant, dramatic analysis of the Utah Jazz’s future, using precise hand gestures to stress his prediction. He was 98% sure of an impending trade but couldn’t legally report it as confirmed yet, so he teased it cryptically. Within two hours, his prediction came true, and his dramatic delivery instantly became a viral internet meme. The sudden internet fame caught him off guard. “It sort of scares you about social media, in all honesty,” he admitted, noting that the viral moment didn’t replace the actual journalistic grinding required to get the information in the first place. The price of trust Another important thing in Windhorst’s line of work is trust. Maintaining deep league relationships means showing up to empty arenas, attending grueling training camps, and remaining present during ugly losing stretches. As he values trust, he would even prefer to miss a major breaking scoop entirely rather than burn a bridge for a fleeting headline. “No one story is worth damaging a relationship that maybe involves 5, 10, 15 years of building,” Windhorst said. “Time. Nobody ever wants to talk about time because they want stuff right away.” Windhorst deeply admires fellow ESPN journalist Michael Wilbon for the decades of respect he has earned from players, coaches, and owners alike by simply being fair to people. For Windhorst, that kind of legacy is the goal because the game itself is secondary to the people playing it. “Ultimately, the game is throwing a ball through a ring,” he said. “That’s all it is. It’s a child’s game. The player’s job is to provide the spectacle. My job is to tell the story.” And for him, that work will always begin with writing. – Rappler.com Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

title: The next president Ghana needs after this sham reset
body: We have been here before. Big slogans. Big promises. A government comes in shouting “Reset.” But what has been reset? Not the price of kenkey. Not the cedi. Not the attitude of those in power. Only loyalists’ bank accounts have been reset. The evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa exposed it all. GH¢49.72 million spent. GH¢5,000 given to a man who lost a shop he built for 10 years. A Foreign Minister telling American citizens, “We will forgive them.” Forgive them for what? For losing everything? That is not a reset. That is a sham. It is old wine, arrogant wine, in a new bottle. So Ghana’s next conversation cannot be about NDC vs NPP. It cannot be about who shouts loudest on the radio. The next election must be about CHARACTER. The next President to get it right for us must have three things this current lot does not have: 1. Good Character Over Good English We don’t need a President who can speak big grammar at the UN while insulting citizens at home. We need someone with good character. A person who understands that public office is not a chiefdom. A Ghanaian who lost his livelihood in South Africa is not a beggar to be forgiven, but a citizen to be restored. Good character means you tell us the truth the first time, not after the Minority exposes you. Good character means you don’t hide that a private businessman paid GH¢16 million for a state evacuation. Good character means you don’t call GH¢5,000 an achievement. 2. Courage to Choose Merit Over Loyalty The reason Ghana is not developing is not a lack of ideas. It is loyalty over merit. Both NPP and NDC do it. When in opposition, they cry about protocol. When in power, they break protocol even worse. They sack a competent director because he was appointed by the other party and replace him with a loyal youth organiser who cannot manage a district budget. The next President must be prepared to do what it takes: Keep the competent Ghanaian even if he wears the other party’s colours. Sack the incompetent loyalist even if he followed you in opposition for 8 years. If your child needs heart surgery, you will not choose the most loyal surgeon. You will choose the most competent one. Why then do we give the heart of Ghana to loyalists? 3. A Unifier, Not a Divider The reset we have seen is divisive. It is “us versus them.” If you complain about GH¢5,000, you are ungrateful. If you ask for an audit, you are unpatriotic. A country cannot develop when half the country is treated as enemies. The next President must bring us together as Ghanaians. Ewe, Akan, Dagomba, Ga, Frafra, we all suffer the same economic conditions. The next President must be a President for the returnee from South Africa, the nurse who wants to travel to Canada, the trader at Makola, and the farmer at Ejura. We are tired of leaders who forgive us. We want leaders who serve us. The sham reset will end, as all sham projects end. When it ends, Ghana will need more than a politician. Ghana needs a person of good character, prepared to do what it takes to get it right. Not for his party. For all of us.

title: Starlink, Starshield Speeds Exceed 161 km/h in Ukraine, MoD Says
body:
Satellite communication terminals operating under SpaceX’s commercial Starlink and defense-tailored Starshield systems inside Ukraine are functioning at velocities exceeding the previously enforced 161 km/h cap, a Ministry of Defense source told Kyiv Post on Saturday morning, Oct. 24.
According to defense specialists, Ukrainian Defense Forces began registering operational velocity parameters above 161 km/h (100 mph) early Saturday. The development suggests a progressive rollback of software or geographic constraints that had compromised domestic counter-drone interception networks over recent weeks.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“As of the morning of Oct. 24, the Defense Forces of Ukraine and specialists of the Ministry of Defense record that Starlink/Starshield has begun working at speeds greater than 161 km/h,” the defense ministry source stated.
Technical teams and military communications detachments are conducting diagnostic trials to determine whether service parameters have been restored unconditionally across Ukrainian combat airspace or whether secondary operational ceilings remain in place.
“The military continues to monitor and conduct verifications at higher speeds, determine upper limits, and ascertain the extent to which the operation of this communication has truly been restored,” the source added.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara later responded to journalists’ questions by stating that the Defense Ministry’s monitoring systems are detecting a resumption of Starlink/Starshield speeds.
“We are recording speeds of over 400 km/h, and the connection is stable. This is yet another example of how direct dialogue and the Ukrainian President’s firm stance at the highest level yield results.
And this result is, above all, important for our front lines, for our military personnel, for drone operations, logistics, and communications. The Ministry of Defense continues to monitor and track the operation of Starlink/Starshield,” Khmara added.
The reported speed restoration follows days of acute operational friction between Kyiv, Washington , and SpaceX over artificial limits placed on satellite-guided defense platforms.
President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed on Oct. 17 that satellite terminals deployed on domestic unmanned interceptors were disconnecting automatically whenever vehicles or platforms exceeded 161 km/h . Exceeding the threshold severed telemetry feeds and caused operators to lose control of unmanned aircraft in mid-flight.
The artificial cap severely impaired Ukraine’s tactical air defenses against high-speed aerial threats, specifically Russian turbine-propelled Shahed loitering munitions that cruise at velocities between 400 and 600 km/h (249-373 mph)
To confirm that the restriction was deliberate rather than an engineering anomaly, Ukrainian specialists transported Starlink-equipped vehicles into EU territory, where the terminals functioned uninterrupted at 180 km/h (112 mph).
The operational curbs also disrupted robotic uncrewed ground and aerial logistics delivering emergency medical kits, rations, and potable water to frontline infantry holding isolated positions under Russian fire.
The technological dispute triggered intense debate across Washington and European capitals, sparking conflicting accounts regarding the origin and oversight of the restrictions.
US President Donald Trump denied ordering operational curbs on Ukrainian satellite links, claiming that “everything is the same as it’s always been.” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio similarly pushed back against assertions by Ukrainian officials, stating that the White House had not mandated bandwidth or velocity caps on commercial terminals.
Rubio noted that Starshield remains a dedicated US military capability not currently authorized for Ukrainian deep strikes inside Russia.
However, reporting published by The Telegraph cited four sources familiar with the matter who stated that SpaceX founder Elon Musk proposed service limitations directly to Trump , who approved the initiative, enabling the Pentagon to restrict Starshield functionality.
Sources indicated Musk sought to avoid European consumer boycotts following civilian infrastructure strikes.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Rubio Says War Is About Donbas, Requires Diplomatic Compromise
body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the war between Russia and Ukraine is centered on the Donbas region, arguing that the conflict cannot be resolved militarily and will require mutual concessions at the negotiating table.
Speaking during a press conference on Thursday, Oct. 22, Rubio responded to questions regarding realistic diplomatic avenues to end the conflict following statements by Russian President Vladimir Putin expressing conditional openness to a tripartite summit involving the US, Ukraine, and Russia.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Rubio characterized the conflict as an impasse over a specific territorial area, asserting that Moscow has failed to capture the region by force while Kyiv legitimately refuses to surrender sovereign territory.
“People keep talking about it’s a war in Ukraine. That war is about Donbas . It’s about one region of the country,” Rubio said.
“At its core, it’s about 11 percent of one part of that country that Russia wants and cannot take militarily and that Ukraine is unwilling to give up. And they have good reasons why they don’t want to do that – for sovereignty and their own security long term.”
The secretary of state emphasized that US President Donald Trump has dedicated extensive administrative resources toward bridging the diplomatic gap between Kyiv and Moscow, noting that administration officials are working continuously to identify viable frameworks for negotiations.
Rubio maintained that an outright battlefield victory remains unachievable for either belligerent, insisting that an armistice must be brokered through diplomacy.
“And so the question is whether there’s some accommodation, that both sides will have to make some concessions in order to bring an end to the war,” Rubio explained.
“This war is not going to be solved militarily. This war is only going to end diplomatically. And the question is: Can you arrive at an outcome in which both sides receive something of benefit but also give concessions and bring this to an end?”
Acknowledging the logistical and political hurdles confronting prospective negotiations, Rubio stressed that direct consultations between the warring parties remain the sole avenue to test diplomatic solutions, positioning Washington as a neutral mediator.
“As hard as it is, it is impossible to do unless both sides are at the table talking, and we’re happy to play the mediating role in that regard,” Rubio stated.
“So that’s really what we’re trying to do – not claiming that just getting them in the room is going to solve this problem, but we have no chance to solve it if we can’t get them in the room.”
Rubio’s characterization of the conflict arrives as President Volodymyr Zelensky articulated Kyiv’s red lines regarding prospective peace frameworks.
In an interview with ABC News, Zelensky rejected proposals requiring territorial cessions , clarifying the exact proportion of Ukrainian sovereign territory currently under Russian occupation.
When asked whether Ukraine would consider relinquishing 25 percent of its sovereign territory to halt hostilities, Zelensky clarified that Russian forces currently occupy 19.3 percent of the country. He explained that reaching 25 percent would necessitate surrendering the entirety of the Donbas, an outcome Kyiv firmly rejects.
“When someone speaks about 25 percent, it implies that we would have to surrender the entire Donbas, and only then would the Russians control 25 percent. Right now, they control 19.3 percent,” Zelensky said.
While Zelensky affirmed that Ukraine remains open to freezing active combat operations along the existing line of contact to halt casualties, he stressed that Kyiv will never extend legal recognition to occupied lands as Russian sovereign territory.
Rubio’s remarks also coincide with ongoing efforts by US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to organize leader-level summitry.
US envoys have explored prospective host locations for tripartite consultations between Trump, Zelensky, and Putin, with potential venues including the United Arab Emirates , Saudi Arabia , or European host nations.
Witkoff traveled to Russia earlier in the week to assess the Kremlin’s willingness to engage in structured talks, while European leaders have debated designating a European envoy , such as Finnish President Alexander Stubb, to ensure continental security priorities are represented.

title: US warns citizens that Houthi attacks 'have potential to escalate rapidly'
body: The US has warned citizens against travelling to Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Qatar, Syria, Yemen and Israel. All of the advisories referred to the threat of "terrorism". Washington urged people to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia owing to threats including the "risk of drone and missile targeting of American interests by Iran and the Iranian-supported Houthis", as well as armed conflict and terrorism. "Do not travel to the Yemen border due to terrorism," it added said in the advisory for the kingdom. The US said the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area". A State Department official said after the announcement that the advisories were "not indicative of new capabilities from the Houthis, but reflect the strikes we have seen over recent days, including on the airport". That was a reference to attacks by the Iran-backed group on the Riyadh, Dammam, Najran and Jazan airports in recent weeks. The deadly strikes caused disruption to air travel. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport only partially reopened after it was closed this month and international services have not yet been fully restored. The latest Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the Eastern Province, killed two people and injured eight, Saudi Arabia's Civil Aviation Authority said on Wednesday. Fears are growing of a renewed escalation between the US and Iran. On Friday, US President Donald Trump said Washington may ⁠carry out another military operation against ​Iran if a deal was not reached. "We may do another little Epic Fury," Mr Trump told a rally in Florida yesterday, ⁠using the US military's term for its war on ​ Iran . ⁠ "If they're smart, they'll just say, 'Let's get down to business.' But, you know, I doubt they'll do that because perhaps they're not smart." Earlier this month, he said the US would not strike Iran before the November 3 midterm elections. Iranian officials have vowed to carry out an even more widespread response to any new attack than the strikes Tehran launched across the region after February 28. Cables, data centres and artificial intelligence sites could be attacked by Tehran , Iran's National Security Council chief Maj Gen Mohsen Rezaei told Iranian media this week. Meanwhile, US intelligence has found that Iranian plots to attack American diplomats and officials in the Middle East have reached "advanced stages", according to a memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio obtained by Axios . It said Tehran had "substantially increased" its efforts to attack US personnel and that "lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages both in the Middle East and certain other countries". Axios quoted US officials as saying the intelligence is one of the reasons the State Department has been withdrawing personnel from embassies across the region, amid mounting fears of a renewed conflict.

title: Nigeria’s Judiciary and Its Corruption Malady
body: By Mobolaji Sanusi “An impartial judiciary is essential to the administration of justice and the preservation of liberty.” — James Madison (1751-1836) Democracy without a credible judiciary is an invitation to a Hobbesian state of nature, where life is brutish, nasty, poor, and short. Like all human creations, state institutions established by human reasoning are not infallible and are susceptible to sometimes avoidable foibles. But when such imperfections become abysmally alarming, every right-thinking citizen should be deeply perturbed. That is the shameful state of the Bench in Nigeria today, which is continually acknowledged by very senior stakeholders in the legal profession and beyond. Conflict, which is an essential part of societal coexistence, is becoming increasingly difficult to resolve fairly through the instrumentality of the courts. This must have informed the country’s uninspiring, dismal ranking of 120th out of 143 countries in the 2025 World Justice Project Rule of Law Index. Given the exposed entrenched corruption on the Bench and in the legal profession generally, coupled with unchecked political interference and inadequate funding, the rating might even be worse by the time the 2026 ranking is released. Expectedly, the court is a reflection of the society we live in, and the depth of its rot raises a pertinent and fundamental question: Is there any facet of Nigerian life that is immune to the malady of corruption? Yours sincerely acknowledge that there are still honourable judges and other Nigerians who remain above board, but they are so few in number that their feeble voices of reason have been drowned by the tumultuous horde of corrupt plunderers of the public till. From the days of yore till the present, stakeholders within the legal system and observers outside the noble profession have been concerned and have consistently spoken out against the rot in that increasingly desecrated, fast diminishing profession in the country. Yet, the abysmal state of affairs in the judiciary and legal profession is not improving, and it continues to trouble reputable persons in the polity. It is therefore unsurprising that retired Justice Amina Adamu Augie has become the latest voice in that regard. She is in a better position to know the extent of endemic corruption in the legal profession as a former teacher of lawyers and a retired Justice of the nation’s apex court. She might not be completely insulated from the rot like other justices/judges and lawyers, but she has raised a justifiable alarm at the recently held 40th anniversary of the Nigerian Law School Class of 1986, where she decried high-level corruption within Nigeria’s judiciary and legal profession. She declared that corruption in the legal profession, wherever it exists — “on the Bench, at the Bar, or in the Registry — poisons everything by turning the one place where a citizen should find impartiality into one more market stall.” That damning description of the judiciary as a “market stall” should not be taken lightly, because of the significance of the judiciary and the legal profession towards resolving recurring societal disputes, both human and institutional. Until now, some Justices of the apex court have curiously deployed their valedictory sessions to expose the rot in the judiciary and the legal profession as a whole. Justice Musa Dattijo Muhammad, who retired as the second most senior Justice of the Supreme Court and Deputy Chairperson of the National Judicial Council, some time earlier noted the “witheringly scornful and monstrously critical” public perception of the judiciary, stemming from “court officials and judges easily being bribed by litigants to obviate delays and/or obtain favourable judgments.” Similarly, Justice Adefope-Okojie, JCA, at the point of her exit, asked what qualifies any person to bear the exalted title of ‘Honourable Justice’ if not to administer justice without fear or favour. She bemoaned the increasing degeneration of honourable traits in members of the Bench and the Bar. Justice Ejembi Eko, at his valedictory from the Supreme Court in 2022, expressed concerns about the tepid handling of corruption issues on the Bench by the NJC when he said: “With deference to the NJC, the punishment usually falls short of public expectation… When the punishment for an outstandingly bad and outrageous conduct is far too lenient, it encourages impunity and/or a repeat by others of such errant or atrocious misconduct.” So far, the effort of the NJC in this regard is work in progress. Afam Osigwe, the immediate past Nigerian Bar Association President, also earlier this year, during the National Association of Seadogs-organised Ralph Obiora Lecture that held in Enugu State, corroborated the rapacious corruption ravaging especially the Bench when he said: “The judiciary, once revered as the last hope of the common man, is increasingly perceived as a marketplace where justice is auctioned to the highest bidder.” Osigwe relied on a 2024 survey by the UNODC and the National Bureau of Statistics which revealed that approximately N721 billion in cash bribes was received by public officials in 2023, with judges named as top recipients. An ICPC survey also reportedly showed that N9.4 billion in bribes passed through the justice sector, with lawyers and litigants identified as primary bribe-givers between 2018 and 2020. This is alarmingly condemnable. Even the revered quintessential jurist of our time, Justice Kayode Eso, who passed on in November 2012, observed the rot in his book The Judiciary: The Shield of Justice, thus: “Corruption in the judiciary is a major problem that needs to be addressed. It is a problem that has been affecting the integrity and effectiveness of the judicial system… We need to take urgent steps to address corruption in the judiciary.” Again, the question arises: are the necessary steps being taken to address this problem when the judiciary unfortunately relies absolutely on the executive branch for its survival? It made for shameful optics when, not too long ago, the Chief Judge of the nation’s Federal High Court, Honourable Justice John Terhemba Tsoho, led fellow judges cap-in-hand to beg the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, for landed property and other perquisites. In my Yoruba culture, there’s a saying that “Ti enu ba je, oju a ti” — He who pays the piper dictates the tune. Following from this, it can be inferred that it will be difficult for the Bench to say a complete NO to the demands of their benefactor called Wike or anyone in the executive arm whenever the need arises. Too bad! No wonder it is widely believed that corruption in the judiciary will subsist for as long as we have a judiciary that “…must beg the executive for a courtroom roof, vehicles, judges’ entitlements and financial autonomy for the courts” — all of which should ordinarily be constitutional perquisites of office for Justices and Judges. The 2027 general elections are fast approaching and ours is a country where no politician contesting for positions accedes to defeat at the polls. Election losers in our clime always approach the Election Petition Tribunal on the flimsiest of excuses to contest their loss. Do we rely on “compromisable or tainted judicial officers” to move our democracy forward? This question under the prevailing circumstance is better left unanswered. Too bad! The country must get its act right if we truly desire a judiciary that is, in words and deeds, largely an impartial referee, not a player in the game. What we have now is largely a courtroom where the calm and neutral administration of the law yields to political interests and pecuniary inducements; a complete reflection of the times we all live in and shamelessly adore for parochial sentiments. On this note, l rest my case for this week. Ipoola Omisore Relocates ‘Ile-Ife Greats’ To Lagos “A room without books is like a body without a soul.” – Marcus Tallius Cicero (January 3, 106 BC—December 7, 43 BC). The date is October 30, 2026. On that day, Lagos will be agog with a momentous event meant to celebrate recorded reputable sons and daughters of the Yoruba cradle from the Source in Ile-Ife, Osun State. The convener of the event is none other than the elder statesman, accomplished advertising professional, educationist, author, and two-term former member of the House of Assembly of the Centre of Excellence, Hon. Ahmed Ipoola Omisore, who authored the book titled: “Great Ifes in History,” which will be launched on that day. The Royal Father of the Day is His Imperial Majesty, Oba Babatunde Enitan Ogunwusi, CFR, while the Principal Guest of Honour is His Excellency, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat—the incoming governor of Lagos state come May 29,2027, insha Allah. The Father-of-the-Day is Chief Oyekunle Alex-Duduyemi, while the book reviewer is the accomplished journalist, President Emeritus of the Nigerian Guild of Editors and Provost of the Nigerian Institute of Journalism, Mr. Gbenga Adefaye. Definitely, next Friday promises to be an interesting day at the Lagos Airport Hotel, Ikeja, venue for this promising event by Honourable Omisore. Trust me, yours sincerely will be present at the occasion to celebrate the day with invited guests…..Congratulations in advance Honourable Omisore… •Sanusi, former MD/CEO of Lagos State Signage and Advertisement Agency, is currently Managing Partner at AMS RELIABLE SOLICITORS. title: Rains to begin from Sunday: Met
body:
Weather conditions in the Sultanate of Oman are expected to be affected by a trough of a low-pressure system, leading to active thunderstorm formations over the Hajar Mountains and the adjacent areas, as well as parts of the coasts of Musandam Governorate, which may extend to the coastal areas of the Sea of Oman, starting from Sunday, October 25. The weather system is expected to continue for several days, according to the Oman Met Office. Low cloud formation and fog were observed late at night and early morning in parts of the Eastern and Central Governorates, Dhofar, and Al Buraimi. The weather forecaster at Oman Meteorology said rain of varying intensity is expected to lead to the flow of wadis on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. Speaking to Observer, he said, "We are going through the transition period to winter, and the atmosphere is not homogeneous. We have local cloud development in Al Hajar mountains, and in the upper area it is the winter situation. "Rain in Muscat is only a slight probability with a weak chance, as per the weather forecaster. "The circumstances are not ideal, and the system has no vertical extension. The system is mainly in the areas of Al Hajar, North Al Batinah, South Al Batinah, and Musandam," he explained. The weather system may lead to a decrease in horizontal visibility.
