title: Drones attack Russia's Tolyattikauchuk plant producing components for rocket fuel – media
body:
That is according to ASTRA , Ukrinform reports.
Local Telegram channels reported a drone attack and numerous explosions. They said that, according to preliminary information, the industrial area of Tolyatti had come under attack.
An ASTRA OSINT analyst examined video footage from the scene and concluded that the Tolyattikauchuk plant was on fire.
Local chat groups reported that the street where the facility is located had been closed off. Reports also emerged of possible damage to the nearby Tolyatti Thermal Power Plant. Residents complained of disruptions to electricity and water supplies.
Tolyattikauchuk has been part of the Tatneft group since 2019. The plant produces synthetic rubber, monomers, hydrocarbon fractions and gasoline additives. The synthetic rubber manufactured at the plant is also used to produce solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.
On June 12, 2026, Ukrainian forces also struck the Tolyattikauchuk facility in Russia's Samara region. A fire broke out on the plant's premises.

title: Digital Dominance and Neo-Imperialism
body: In Abuja, the Nigeria AI Collective, under the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, hosted the BUILD Conference from October 21 to 23, 2026, themed “Building Africa’s Shared Compute and AI Infrastructure”. Policymakers, students, researchers, journalists, innovators and investors gathered to discuss how Africa can build, share and govern the computing power its AI future depends on. It also reminded us how Africa can break the chain of digital imperialism. When Kwame Nkrumah published Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism, in 1965, the parades for independence had barely ended. New flags were flying, new anthems were being sung, but Ghana’s founding president warned that empire had not died. It had simply changed its accounting. If Nkrumah were alive today, he would recognise the method instantly. Only now it lives in the cloud. Classical imperialism was brutally direct: redirect local resources to the metropole, stifle domestic industry, lock colonies into unequal trade, and draw arbitrary borders. The Berlin Conference of 1884 did it with rulers and maps. Today it is done with terms of service, cloud subscriptions and training data. Consider the infrastructure that runs the modern world. Three American companies — Amazon, Microsoft and Google — control over 65 per cent of global cloud capacity, according to industry estimates. Africa, with 18 per cent of the world’s population, controls less than one per cent. That gap tells you who owns the foundational infrastructure of the digital economy, and who merely rents it. News organizations across the continent increasingly rely on global tech platforms (social media and search engines) to distribute content, which subjects them to external algorithms and rule-setting. This new face of neo-imperialism is not an abstraction. It is an extractive business model that threatens economic self-determination and is dismantling one of Africa’s most vital democratic pillars: its independent press. The assault has come in three waves. The first wave was distribution capture. Foreign tech conglomerates monopolised digital advertising, capturing over 80 per cent of local ad spend in key African markets, according to the Reuters Institute. Newsrooms that had survived military decrees and fuel scarcity suddenly found themselves dependent on algorithms in Menlo Park for their audience. When those platforms deprioritised news to maximise screen time, the floor collapsed. As CEO of the Newspaper Proprietors’ Association of Nigeria, I have sat with publishers who cut 40 per cent of their newsrooms in the last two years not because readers left, but because the platform that delivered readers changed its mind. The audience is still there. The business model is not. The second wave has been faster and more extractive. Generative AI has turned distribution capture into data colonialism. Decades of African journalism — investigations produced under military regimes, during fraught elections and public health crises, often at great personal risk — are being scrapped without licence, credit or compensation to train large language models in California. Those models then return our work in a form that kills the original: the zero-click summary. Why visit a Nigerian newspaper’s website when a chatbot synthesises its exclusive investigation into a single paragraph, offering no traffic, no attribution and no revenue to the newsroom that funded it? Worse, because African content constitutes under two per cent of global AI training data, according to several AI governance audits, these summaries routinely default to crude Western stereotypes. When AI fails to comprehend Africa, it invents Africa. It is erasure by statistics. Then comes the third wave, which should alarm everyone. Call it Stealth AI. This is no longer a chatbot hallucinating. It is an industrial factory of synthetic fakes: artificial reporters, deepfake audio of political candidates on election eve, autonomous bot swarms manufacturing consensus on WhatsApp and Facebook. Threat researchers recently exposed international firms that invented a French-Ghanaian investigative journalist wholesale, name, byline, face, to plant coordinated smear campaigns in West African media. More than 60 per cent of African journalists now say they struggle to distinguish genuine sources from synthetic fakes, according to surveys by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Research. That confusion is the point. It’s good to note that the The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (the Commission, FCCPC, has opened formal inquiries into this practice, but the scraping continues daily. But Stealth AI is only possible because of a deeper economic surrender. Africa is home to 1.5 billion people, 60 per cent under 25, speaking over 2,000 languages. Every day it generates billions of valuable data points — mobile money receipts, agricultural telemetry, Nollywood scripts, voice notes in Amharic. This is the raw material of artificial intelligence. Yet where is it processed? Northern Virginia. Where is it stored? Dublin and Singapore. Who owns and monetises the resulting models? Companies headquartered in San Francisco, Seattle and Hangzhou. We export raw data for free across platforms we do not own and subsea cables we do not control, only to import it back as an expensive finished product: a chatbot that stumbles over Hausa, a credit scoring model blind to informal markets, an educational tool unversed in Achebe. This is why the conversation in Abuja must move from declaration to dominance. Compute — the combination of reliable energy, data centre capacity, fibre and specialised processors — is the railway and seaport of this century. Digital sovereignty is impossible without energy sovereignty. Whoever controls compute and power controls commerce. What should that look like in practice? First, we need a fair compensation framework. Just as Australia and Canada forced tech platforms to bargain with publishers, Africa needs a continental AI and data bargaining code. If your model was trained on our archives, you must licence it and pay for it. When a news organisation invests money to create content, it must get a fair share from its consumption. And this cannot be glossed over: the press is an essential national and civic infrastructure. “Were it left to me” says Thomas Jefferson, a one time American President, “to decide whether we should have a government without newspapers or newspapers without a government, I should not hesitate a moment to prefer the latter”. At all times and through all ages, this national infrastructure must be jealously protected and defended. Second, a sovereign storage mandate. All public data, government archives and data generated with public funds must be stored on cloud infrastructure physically located in Africa and subject to African law. No sovereignty without location. Third, a concrete compute target. The African Union, through the African Continental Free Trade Area, should set and fund a goal: five per cent of global data centre capacity on African soil by 2030, powered by reliable energy. Ambitious, but not impossible — the continent already attracts over $2 billion annually in data centre investment; it now needs policy to direct and scale it. The question is whether Africa will be a tenant or a landlord in it. Adediran is Chief Executive Officer of the Newspaper Proprietors’ Association of Nigeria (NPAN).

title: Carrick cannot solve United’s problems with optimism alone
body: Michael Carrick insists Manchester United will soon be winners again and, as the club’s manager, he is refusing to panic. But after just one victory in seven Premier League matches, even his most loyal supporters must be wondering how much longer they will have to wait. Pressure intensified following the 4-1 loss to Como in the Champions League on Wednesday night. United have now gone six league games without a win since beating Ipswich Town. It is their poorest start to a top-flight campaign for 40 years and, while Carrick deserves enormous credit for rescuing their season last year, he cannot continue living on past achievements. What concerns me most is that United still appear uncertain about how they are supposed to play. Are they a possession-based team? Are they meant to press opponents aggressively high up the pitch? Or should they be using their considerable attacking talent to catch teams on the counterattack? Carrick has encouraged his players to press higher, using the attacking qualities of Bruno Fernandes, Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha and Marcus Rashford. The problem is that pressing only works when the whole team moves together. United’s defence and midfield have too often failed to provide the necessary support, leaving huge spaces for opponents to exploit. Cunha has struggled to convince as a central striker, while Rashford’s return has forced Carrick to rethink his attacking structure. Injuries to Benjamin Šeško and Amad have hardly helped. There have been some encouraging signs, not least the introduction of Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos in midfield against Leeds. Both have the energy to improve United’s balance, but individual improvements will mean little unless Carrick can establish a clear system. There are frustrations in the dressing room, too. I understand that players are not necessarily blaming Carrick for their disappointing performances, but questions have been raised about the club’s recruitment and long-term planning. INEOS, under Sir Jim Ratcliffe, remain unpopular with sections of the support, while the Glazer family continue to attract criticism. United have spent enormous sums over the years without building a team that consistently looks capable of challenging for major honours. The failure to turn promising positions into victories points to poor concentration, questionable game management and a defence that remains vulnerable. Carrick is optimistic. Of course he is. That is part of his job. But Manchester United do not lack expensive footballers or individual talent. They lack a recognisable identity. Carrick must decide exactly how he wants his team to play and find the right combination of players to carry out those instructions. Otherwise, another manager could find himself paying the price for years of muddled recruitment. Sunday’s home match against Bournemouth is another opportunity to begin putting things right. United’s supporters have heard enough promises. They want to see a team that knows what it is doing. Haaland keeps scoring while uncertainty hangs over City There are dark clouds hanging over Manchester City, but nobody seems to have told Erling Haaland. The Norwegian has already scored eight Premier League goals, leads the Golden Boot race and continues to terrorise defenders while the club faces one of the most uncertain periods in its recent history. An independent commission has found City guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules. City deny wrongdoing and have appealed the decision, leaving the eventual outcome and possible sanctions unresolved. The remarkable thing is that the controversy has done nothing to slow down Haaland or City’s extraordinary domestic form. Seven league matches, seven victories. That is an impressive achievement for Enzo Maresca, who has taken over from Pep Guardiola and demonstrated that City’s winning mentality remains firmly intact. Haaland has already reached 100 non-penalty Premier League goals in record time. His appetite for scoring appears as strong as ever, and the suggestion that he might struggle under a different tactical system has so far proved wide of the mark. But can City maintain this remarkable run with so much uncertainty surrounding the club? Maresca insists the controversy has brought his players and supporters closer together. That may well be true. Footballers are often at their most dangerous when they believe the world is against them. The bigger question is what happens if City’s appeal fails and serious sanctions follow. Nobody yet knows what the final consequences might be, but the implications could extend far beyond the football pitch. City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, has overseen an extraordinary transformation of the club and considerable investment in the surrounding Manchester community. How would the ownership react to severe punishment? What would it mean for future investment, recruitment and the club’s long-term ambitions? Those questions cannot yet be answered, but they are impossible to ignore. There are more immediate concerns for Maresca, too. Antoine Semenyo is facing a lengthy absence following the knee injury he suffered against Ipswich, potentially keeping him out for around two months. Haaland also left the Etihad Stadium with a foot problem, although I am told the injury is not considered serious. Maresca has suggested Phil Foden could provide an alternative through the middle, while Rayan Cherki is another possibility as a false nine. Summer signing Iliman Ndiaye has previous experience playing centrally, having scored 14 goals for Sheffield United during their promotion season of 2022-23. Jérémy Doku looks the natural replacement for Semenyo on the wing. City’s visit to Aston Villa on Saturday will be another examination of their strength in depth. For the moment, Haaland keeps scoring and City keep winning. But football has a habit of changing very quickly, and the greatest threat to their season might eventually come from events beyond Maresca’s control. Mateta interested in move to United My sources have revealed that Crystal Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta is eyeing a move to Manchester United in January. The Frenchman has shown little enthusiasm for committing his future to Palace, and the uncertainty surrounding his contract could force the club into a difficult decision when the transfer window opens. United’s need for a recognised centre-forward is obvious. Benjamin Šeško’s injury problems have left Michael Carrick short of options, with Matheus Cunha often asked to operate in a position that does not necessarily bring out his best qualities. Mateta would provide a different type of attacking presence: a powerful, experienced Premier League striker capable of holding the ball up and giving defenders a physical battle. The complication is his fitness. A hamstring injury has restricted him to just 92 minutes this season, and United would need assurances that he is ready to make an immediate impact. Palace must also consider whether they can afford to lose another important player during a difficult campaign. Nevertheless, Mateta’s interest in Old Trafford is one to watch as January approaches. Chelsea move to secure Acheampong Chelsea are preparing to offer highly rated defender Josh Acheampong a new contract, despite his existing agreement running until 2029. The youngster has featured in six of Chelsea’s opening seven Premier League matches and is attracting considerable interest. I am told Manchester United are among the clubs to have shown an interest, but Chelsea have no intention of making it easy for anybody to prise him away from Stamford Bridge. The club have already moved to secure the futures of important players, including Cole Palmer and Moisés Caicedo, and Acheampong is regarded as another valuable part of their long-term plans. For all the criticism Chelsea have received over their recruitment policy, keeping their most promising young players is every bit as important as buying expensive new ones. Ayari attracting Arsenal and Milan Brighton’s excellent start to the season is bringing a familiar problem. When their players perform well, Europe’s biggest clubs quickly begin watching. Midfielder Yasin Ayari is the latest to attract attention, and I understand Arsenal and AC Milan are monitoring the 23-year-old Sweden international. Ayari was another impressive performer in Brighton’s emphatic 5-0 victory over Crystal Palace, underlining why his reputation continues to grow. His energy, movement and ability to influence games from midfield make him an attractive prospect. Brighton also have an important contractual decision to consider. His present deal is approaching its final months, although the club are understood to have an option to extend it by another year. That option could strengthen Brighton’s negotiating position considerably. The club have built an impressive reputation for developing players and selling at the right price. Ayari could eventually become another example, although Brighton will be in no hurry to lose him. Sage’s attacking gamble is leaving Palace defenceless Pierre Sage is under enormous pressure at Crystal Palace, and after watching their humiliating 5-0 defeat against Brighton, it is not difficult to understand why. Quite frankly, some of Palace’s defending was embarrassing. They have conceded 17 goals in seven Premier League matches, the worst defensive record in the division, and there is little evidence that Sage has found a way to correct the problem. I would not lay all the blame at the manager’s door. Palace’s hierarchy failed to provide sufficient defensive reinforcements during the summer, particularly following the departure of Maxence Lacroix. Chairman Steve Parish and sporting director Matt Hobbs must accept their share of responsibility. But Sage’s tactics are also inviting trouble. He wants his team to press high and attack with numbers. That is admirable when it works, but Palace are leaving themselves hopelessly exposed when possession is lost. The wing-backs advance so far up the pitch that opponents are presented with acres of space behind them. Quinten Timber regularly pushes forward from midfield, leaving Adam Wharton with far too much ground to cover. One misplaced pass can leave three defenders and Wharton trying to contain an opposition counterattack. Under Oliver Glasner, Palace generally maintained better defensive protection, with one wing-back often remaining deeper when the other advanced. Sage appears determined to commit more players forward without providing the necessary cover. There is nothing wrong with attacking football. Supporters love it. But attacking without defensive organisation is not bravery. It is recklessness. The players also have to accept responsibility. There have been too many individual errors, too many occasions when opponents have been allowed to run unchallenged towards goal. The atmosphere among Palace supporters is changing rapidly. Palace face Newcastle on Sunday, and Sage urgently needs to restore some balance. He may want his side to entertain, but the first requirement of any successful team is to stop opponents scoring almost at will. Maddison gives Tottenham hope — but Chelsea will reveal the truth Tottenham supporters have waited a long time for something to cheer, and the return of James Maddison and Dejan Kulusevski has finally given them genuine hope. The reception for Kulusevski was particularly emotional as he returned to the matchday squad after 526 days out following his serious knee injury. But it was another of Tottenham’s long-term casualties who stole the show. Maddison produced a magnificent performance against Coventry, controlling large parts of the game and scoring a spectacular opening goal in Tottenham’s 3-1 victory. It was his first Premier League goal for 610 days, an extraordinary wait for a player of his ability. There was added significance in the fact that it came against Coventry, the club he supported as a boy and where his professional career began. Maddison has endured a miserable succession of injury problems, including a serious cruciate ligament injury and further setbacks. There must have been moments when he wondered whether he would ever return to his best. His goal was a wonderful reward for the determination required to fight his way back. One player does not make a team, but the return of two outstanding creative footballers can transform its possibilities. But I would caution against declaring Tottenham’s troubles over. Coventry were beaten, but Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday will present a much more demanding examination. How much patience will Marinakis give Glasner? Oliver Glasner enjoyed considerable success at Crystal Palace, but his move to Nottingham Forest has provided a reminder of just how quickly a manager’s fortunes can change. Forest have struggled badly, and Glasner has yet to find the formula that brought him so much praise at Selhurst Park. The failure to score at the City Ground since the final game of last season is particularly worrying. Glasner insists there are positives to take from his team’s performances. He believes the chances are being created and that the goals will eventually follow. He also remains convinced that his players possess the character to turn things around. I admire his optimism, but I wonder whether Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis shares it. Forest went through four managers last season, and Marinakis has hardly established a reputation for unlimited patience when results are disappointing. Glasner knew he was joining an ambitious club, but ambition brings expectations, and Forest’s supporters are entitled to demand better. There is an interesting contrast with his former club. Palace are struggling to replace Glasner’s defensive organisation, while the Austrian is struggling to reproduce the success he enjoyed there.

title: Russia hopes new UN chief election will rid Secretariat of Western dictate — MFA
body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Russia expects that the election of a new UN Secretary-General will rid the organization’s Secretariat of Western dictate and "backroom deals," Kirill Logvinov, Director of the Department for International Organizations at the Russian Foreign Ministry, said on the occasion of United Nations Day.
"Serious problems within the UN’s operations cannot be ignored. Every effort must be made to restore a spirit of collegiality to the organization’s work, ensure strict adherence to the principles of its Charter in their entirety and interconnectedness, adapt UN mechanisms to today’s polycentric realities, abandon backroom deals in favor of honest and mutually respectful dialogue, strengthen the voice of the Global South, and rid the Secretariat of Western dictate. In this regard, we place particular hope in the election of a new UN Secretary-General," the diplomat wrote on his Telegram channel.
Logvinov emphasized that the UN is currently experiencing a "profound systemic crisis." "There is a growing tendency toward the politicization of the Secretariat’s work, the bureaucratization of decision-making mechanisms, inefficient budget spending, interference in the internal affairs of states, and the promotion of a neoliberal agenda. It is evident that a number of states are driven by an unrestrained desire to use the UN not to seek collective solutions, but solely to push through their own narrow, self-serving interests. As a result, the organization’s prestige and effectiveness are suffering significantly," the diplomat noted.
"We will continue to strive in every possible way for the full restoration of the UN’s authority and standing, so that its constructive potential may be realized to the fullest," he stated.
The term of Antonio Guterres, who has led the UN since 2017, expires on December 31, 2026. Members of the Security Council will select a candidate to recommend for the top UN post, after which the General Assembly will hold a vote to officially elect the new UN Secretary-General. As Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov previously emphasized, Moscow does not express preferences regarding specific candidates, maintaining that the key requirement is for the candidate to meet the criteria of professionalism and impartiality. United Nations Day is marked on October 24.

title: Oleshky: The Kremlin’s Next Propaganda Spectacle?
body:
As reports emerge of a ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson region, beginning Oct. 29, understanding the Kremlin’s modus operandi is crucial.
The Kremlin will be seeking to repair the reputational damage caused by the humanitarian catastrophe in Oleshky and surrounding communities. As the technical details of the evacuation are being discussed, the global community is to expect a controlled press tour of the occupied part of the Kherson region.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Kremlin-funded media have already begun gaslighting and shifting responsibility for the crisis onto Ukraine and its military. On Oct. 7, Ukraine’s Security Service warned that Russia is launching information and psychological operations on the situation in temporarily occupied Oleshky.
“According to operational data, servicemen from one of the occupying units have been ordered to prepare a series of ‘compromising’ interviews with the residents of the occupied town. In these videos, local residents are required to accuse the Ukrainian Defense Forces of constant shelling and the blockade of the town; discredit the decisions of Ukraine’s military and political leadership; and express a positive attitude and gratitude towards the military of the aggressor state.”
Following these orders, one of the leading Kremlin propagandists, Margarita Simonyan, has shared a video of Oleshky residents accusing Ukrainian forces of carrying out the attacks.
In reality, the Ukrainian military has been trying to save Ukrainian civilians trapped in Russian-occupied Oleshky. For months, the 34th Separate Marine Brigade “Borysfen” has been delivering food and essential supplies by drone across the Dnipro River, as Russian forces block conventional humanitarian access. Russian forces have shot down humanitarian drones and confiscated supplies intended for starving civilians.
With the US now involved, Moscow can turn to a familiar strategy: orchestrated press tours for foreign journalists.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, the Kremlin has organized controlled press tours of occupied Ukrainian territory to promote its narratives. Journalists, bloggers, and influencers presented as independent foreign reporters interview preselected witnesses and film carefully arranged scenes, producing reports that support the Kremlin’s version of events. Russia organized visits to Mariupol in 2022 , followed by recurring tours of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant and other occupied Ukrainian cities .
The international community should be aware of the fact that these press tours are part of an organized international influence operation.
In a 2024 report, Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service established that Russian intelligence services used state agencies and Kremlin-linked organizations to recruit foreign journalists, bloggers, and influencers for visits to occupied Ukrainian territory, arranging and financing their trips. Some participants were paid to produce reports.
“The Kremlin’s key objective is to reshape the Western public’s anti-Russian attitudes and undermine support for Ukraine,” the report explains .
From the first months of the full-scale invasion, Russian authorities deployed large-scale information and psychological operations. Several campaigns launched in March 2022 established a pattern that would recur throughout the war: create or exploit a humanitarian catastrophe, deny responsibility, blame Ukraine, and present Russia as the rescuer.
In Mariupol, Russian forces destroyed bridges, damaged railways and trains, and blocked food deliveries and evacuation routes, creating conditions reminiscent of those now reported in Oleshky. Russian propaganda then falsely claimed that Ukrainian troops were preventing civilians from evacuating and using them as “human shields.”
Following a Russian airstrike on the Mariupol maternity hospital , Kremlin-controlled media claimed the attack had been staged by Ukraine and that injured pregnant women were actresses. The Russian Embassy in London amplified allegations that photographs of the victims were fake.
After a Russian airstrike destroyed the Mariupol Drama Theater, where hundreds of civilians had taken shelter, Russian propaganda claimed that Azov fighters had blown up the building themselves and held civilians hostage.
By June, Russian television was broadcasting a guided tour of the theater’s ruins, during which the guide blamed the destruction on “Ukrainian Nazis.” Occupation authorities announced plans to resume performances at the destroyed theater, reinforcing a narrative of normalization. Kremlin-controlled media always promote stories of reconstruction, reopened cultural institutions, and the restoration of ordinary life in a city devastated by the Russian siege.
In Kherson, Russian occupation forces arranged to bring people from Crimea and occupied Donbas to stage a demonstration supporting so-called “Kherson People’s Republic.” At the same time, they blocked humanitarian aid deliveries, creating a crisis so they could portray the occupiers as rescuers distributing food.
The weaponization of hunger has a long history in Soviet and Russian state practice, most notably Stalin’s Holodomor , the man-made famine that devastated Ukraine in 1932–1933.
On March 14, 2022, Russian media claimed that Ukrainian forces had committed mass killings near a railway in Popasna, Luhansk region, and used civilians as human shields. No photographic or video evidence was provided, and local residents did not confirm the allegations.
On March 28-31, Russia’s Ministry of Defense organized a press tour in occupied Donbas titled “Za Pravdu” (“For Truth”), for foreign journalists to document the alleged “atrocities of Ukrainian neo-Nazis.” A US State Department Global Engagement Center assessment documented another “Za Pravdu” tour on April 24, involving approximately 20 journalists from multiple countries. The report described these visits as “Potemkin Village Press Tours of the Donbas,” designed to present pro-Kremlin activists as independent foreign journalists.
On April 8, a missile strike on the Kramatorsk railway station killed more than 50 civilians waiting to evacuate. Russian propaganda blamed Ukraine, circulating several contradictory explanations: a deliberate Ukrainian provocation, an accidental strike, defective ammunition, or an attack on civilians supposedly considered disloyal to Kyiv. RIA Novosti published information about the explosion before the first eyewitness reports appeared.
Also in April, after the bodies of murdered Ukrainian civilians were discovered in Bucha, Russian authorities and propagandists claimed the massacre had been staged by Ukraine and Western media. Reuters published an investigation identifying Russian military units and personnel present in Bucha during the occupation.
The same month, the Russian Ministry of Defense claimed that Ukrainian psychological operations units were filming staged scenes of civilian deaths in Moshchun, near Kyiv, and conducting similar operations in Sumy and Konotop to blame Russia for atrocities.
In July 2022, the deaths of Ukrainian prisoners of war at Olenivka prison became the subject of another disinformation campaign. After an explosion killed Ukrainian POWs, Russian propaganda claimed that Ukrainian forces had deliberately attacked their own prisoners using American HIMARS rockets. Representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross were not granted access to investigate the site.
In September, after mass graves were discovered following the liberation of Izium, pro-Kremlin outlets again claimed that Ukraine had staged evidence of atrocities, this time with the assistance of controlled media.
The tactic is consistent and clear: when the Russian military commits atrocities, the Kremlin denies responsibility and blames Ukraine. Controlled press tours, selected witnesses, and staged or misleading reports help give these narratives an appearance of independent verification.
A ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump must provide Ukrainian civilians with food, medicine, and safe evacuation. It should not provide Moscow with an opportunity to rewrite history and win sympathies abroad. The responsibility for the humanitarian catastrophe must not be obscured by a Potemkin villages press tour.
Zarina Zabrisky is a US, Ukraine-based journalist and war correspondent for Byline Times. She has contributed to BBC News, Voice of America, Euromaidan Press, TVP World, The Sunday Post, and more; co-produced the award-winning documentary Under the Deadly Skies.

title: Ballistic missiles targeting Saudi cities intercepted
body:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Ansar Allah said it ​destroyed two ballistic ​missiles fired by the Iran-aligned group towards Taif and Yanbu on Saturday, as fighting between the sides continued. Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy ⁠city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah. About 10 ⁠minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed. The interceptions came two days after the Ansar Allah said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's defence ministry ‌in Riyadh, facilities belonging to oil ​giant Saudi Aramco ⁠in the Red Sea city of Yanbu and ​King Fahd International Airport in ‌Dammam, where Saudi authorities said two people were killed. Saudi authorities have not confirmed the ​reported attacks in Riyadh and Yanbu. Aramco told staff to evacuate its headquarters in the Gulf city of Dhahran, six people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters on Thursday. The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday it ‌intercepted drones over Riyadh and Medina, not far from Yanbu. ​On Wednesday, the Ansar Allah denied launching drones towards Medina after the coalition ​said ‌it ⁠had intercepted drones over the holy city and Saudi Arabia's Eastern region. The Ansar Allah warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi ​airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca ⁠and Medina, as ​they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

title: IRGC pounds PJAK training center
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 24 (MNA) – In a preemptive operation by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC), one of the most significant gathering and training centers of the terrorist group PJAK came under attack.
Following monitoring by the intelligence society and operational oversight of the activities of terrorists, one of the key centers of the gathering of hostile elements was identified, and necessary measures were taken against it.
In this operation, one of the most significant gathering centers of the terrorist group PJAK came under operational strike by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
The area where the operation took place is a strategic location for the separatist terrorist group. It is a site where many of their key meetings and training programs were held, and it consistently serves as a center for the movement and presence of these terrorist outlaws.

title: Trump Weighs 200% Tariffs on Ukraine and Russia, Doubts Impact
body:
US President Donald Trump suggested that imposing 200 percent import tariffs on Ukraine and Russia could theoretically compel both nations to conclude a peace settlement, but expressed skepticism that the measure would prove effective due to low bilateral trade volumes.
Speaking during a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Oct. 23, Trump asserted that his administration had previously halted international conflicts by threatening punitive commercial duties, before questioning whether trade leverage could alter the trajectory of the war between Moscow and Kyiv.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We ended five wars thanks to tariffs. I said, ‘If you continue to fight, we’re going to put a 200 percent tariff on you,’ and they stopped,” Trump told supporters.
“We should probably immediately do it with Ukraine and Russia. Never thought of it. But we don’t buy enough to do it to them, so it doesn’t work.”
Trump’s statements arrive amid ongoing debate over Washington’s economic tools to influence Moscow and Kyiv.
President Volodymyr Zelensky recently stated that the US president possesses ample statutory leverage to bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table , pointing to congressional sanctions measures awaiting presidential implementation.
“Trump could very easily bring Putin to the negotiating table, because he has the means to do so. The way he speaks about me – President Trump should speak about Putin in the same way,” Zelensky said in an interview on The Diary of a CEO podcast.
Zelensky highlighted that bipartisan sanctions approved by the US Congress remain at the White House’s disposal, while expressing frustration over the administration’s reluctance to enact mandatory statutory penalties.
“Sanctions are sitting on his desk. He didn’t vote for them – Congress voted for strong sanctions. He has the power to act,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian head of state also disputed arguments that domestic US fuel benchmarks depend on Russian energy exports.
While Trump has linked consumer fuel inflation to Ukrainian drone interdictions against Russian refineries and justified a bilateral commercial arrangement to facilitate Russian diesel sales, Zelensky maintained that US domestic prices are decoupled from Russian export volumes.
“I can tell you with 100 percent certainty that diesel prices do not depend on the volumes Russia sells,” Zelensky said, noting that American private companies actively export domestic energy resources without federal export prohibitions.
Trump’s tariff remarks in Florida follow his administration’s recent decision to suspend statutory sanctions and trade duties codified under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 .
On Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Graham Act to waive mandatory 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent secondary duties targeting global buyers of Russian hydrocarbons, just 48 hours before the measures were scheduled to take statutory effect.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the suspension as a 60-day paus e to analyze the broader economic fallout of tariffs on both the US and international economies, citing third-party partner dependencies such as India’s reliance on Russian crude.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers similarly asserted that immediate enforcement of the penalties would complicate ongoing diplomatic efforts to broker an armistice.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Air defense neutralizes 101 out of 126 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram .
According to the military, starting at 18:00 on Friday, October 23, the enemy attacked Ukraine with 126 Shahed-type attack UAVs (61 of them jet-powered), S8000 Bandеrol/Dan-T, Gerbera UAVs and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo, Bryansk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk, Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea, and the Sea of Azov.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on Saturday, October 24, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 101 Russian Shahed-type UAVs (50 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and UAVs of other types.
Hits were recorded at 14 locations, while downed targets (debris) fell at five locations.

title: Greek Tourism Faces New Challenges After Record-Breaking 2025
body: Greek tourism has entered a new phase of maturity, with record-breaking figures in 2025 confirming its position as one of the country’s strongest competitive advantages. However, a new study warns that Greece must translate continued growth into greater economic and social value without exhausting destinations, straining infrastructure or depleting the natural resources on which the industry depends. The study, Greek Tourism: Achievements, Challenges and Prospects , by the Institute of the Greek Tourism Confederation (INSETE), examines the sector beyond visitor arrivals and revenue. It assesses employment, business competitiveness, destination management, infrastructure, environmental sustainability and public acceptance. Its central conclusion is clear: the future of Greek tourism will depend not only on how many visitors arrive, but also on how the country manages growth and distributes its benefits. Record numbers and the real economic value of tourism Greek tourism reached historic highs in 2025. According to figures cited by INSETE, international arrivals excluding cruise passengers reached 37.98 million, rising to 43.3 million when cruise visitors were included. Revenue from inbound tourism, excluding cruises, reached €22.6 billion, an increase of 9.8% compared with 2024. Tourism directly accounted for 13% of Greece’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025, while its combined direct and indirect contribution approached 30%. Investment in the sector reached an estimated €5 billion. These figures demonstrate tourism’s importance beyond hotels and restaurants. Visitor spending supports a broad network of businesses and professions, spanning transport, retail, agriculture and food production, construction and cultural services. Tourism’s real economic value therefore depends not only on direct revenue, but also on how effectively the industry connects with the wider domestic economy. However, rising visitor numbers do not automatically translate into greater value for individual destinations. The average length of stay fell from 7.4 nights in 2019 to 6.1 nights in 2025, a decline of 17.2%. Uneven tourism distribution across Greece INSETE identifies the uneven geographical distribution of tourism as one of the sector’s most significant challenges. Eight of Greece’s 13 administrative regions account for just 10% of tourism revenue, while five islands attract 47% of international arrivals. Figures cited by INSETE from the Special Spatial Planning Framework for Tourism show that 90% of municipal units, covering 95% of Greece’s territory, have little or negligible tourism development. This imbalance suggests that Greece’s challenge is not simply the total number of visitors. Pressure concentrates in specific destinations and periods, while large parts of the country remain outside the main tourism flows. Seasonality also remains a structural weakness. The third quarter of 2025 accounted for 52.4% of international arrivals and 52.5% of tourism receipts, although these concentrations had declined compared with 2019. Greece therefore faces a twofold challenge. Popular destinations need better management of visitor flows, transport, waste and water resources. Meanwhile, less-developed destinations need investment, improved connectivity and tourism products capable of attracting visitors beyond the summer months. Destination Management and Marketing Organisations (DMMOs) could play a central role in this strategy. According to INSETE, their responsibilities should extend beyond promotion to include strategic planning, coordination among stakeholders, data analysis and management of tourism flows. Tourism depends on its workforce Tourism cannot sustain its growth without a sufficient supply of skilled workers. During the third quarter of 2025, employment in accommodation and food services reached 475,200 people, representing 10.8% of total employment in Greece. The study also records improvements in employment quality. The proportion of full-time workers rose from 82.1% in 2019 to 90.4% in 2025, while the sector achieved a balance between male and female employment. However, these improvements have not eliminated persistent labour shortages. In 2025, staffing gaps in Greek hotels accounted for 14% of available positions. Only 24% of hotel workers had graduated from tourism schools. Seasonal employment makes it harder for workers to establish stable careers, while digitalisation and artificial intelligence continue to change the skills employers require. INSETE argues that the answer must go beyond filling vacancies during peak periods. Greece needs to move from offering temporary jobs towards building long-term careers through training, continuous skills development and a longer tourism season. The quality of hospitality depends on the quality of employment and on workers’ ability to remain in the industry and progress professionally. Infrastructure remains a weak point in competitiveness Greece ranks 21st globally in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index, according to the study. This places the country 38 positions above its ranking for overall economic competitiveness. The result highlights the strength of Greece’s tourism product, but also the gap separating it from competitors such as Spain, France, Italy and Portugal. INSETE identifies infrastructure and governance as major areas of weakness. Tourism businesses invested an estimated €5 billion in 2025, including €2.8 billion in the hotel sector. However, private investment alone cannot compensate for deficiencies in public spaces and the networks that support the visitor experience. Delays in air transport, staffing shortages and outdated air navigation systems, weaknesses in road and rail connections, and the needs of maritime transport all affect access to destinations. Other priorities include water management, cleanliness, signage, accessibility and public cultural infrastructure. The lack of an internationally competitive convention centre for major conferences also limits Greece’s ability to attract high-spending visitors outside the summer season. Modern marinas and cruise ports represent further opportunities that remain underdeveloped. Taxation presents another challenge. Greece ranks fifth among seven competing countries for tourism tax competitiveness, according to the study. The issue concerns not only the level of taxation, but also businesses’ ability to reinvest and operate profitably beyond the peak season. Sustainability, public acceptance and artificial intelligence Environmental sustainability will play a decisive role in the industry’s future. According to INSETE, only 8% of Greek hotels hold sustainability certification, while 73% of tourism businesses have not set an emissions-reduction target for 2030. Climate change, coastal erosion and growing pressure on water resources require systematic planning and long-term investment. The establishment of the Special Spatial Planning Framework for Tourism provides a foundation for strategic planning after years of delays. Its effectiveness, however, will depend on implementation and the incorporation of its guidelines into local and specialised urban plans. Unregulated construction outside designated development zones, particularly on islands, continues to place pressure on landscapes, public utility networks and available land. Tourism’s relationship with local communities is equally important. The study finds that 82.4% of citizens view the sector’s economic contribution positively, although concerns about rents and the cost of living remain significant. INSETE notes that many factors influence housing prices and living costs, meaning tourism alone cannot explain these pressures. Nevertheless, addressing the industry’s negative effects is essential to maintaining public support over the long term. Technology adds another dimension to the challenge. Artificial intelligence is changing how travellers discover destinations, compare services and organise holidays. INSETE identifies the development of a national tourism data hub, digital upgrades for businesses and workforce training as strategic investment priorities. Expanding into markets such as China, India and Australia will also require better air connectivity and tailored promotional strategies. Protecting Greece’s tourism reputation Greece benefits from a strong international brand and highly positive visitor evaluations. The country scores 9.1 out of 10 for the visitor experience and records a destination recommendation index of 54. However, this reputational advantage is not inexhaustible. Maintaining it will require high-quality services, reliable infrastructure, protection of Greece’s natural and cultural heritage, and stronger links between tourism and local economies. The next phase of Greek tourism will therefore depend less on pursuing visitor records alone and more on creating sustainable growth that delivers lasting benefits for businesses, workers, communities and the wider economy. title: Greece-Cyprus Cable Slips Again as Nexans Eyes 2028 Restart and 2031 Completion
body: The Greece-Cyprus cable has suffered another setback. French cable maker Nexans now says production for the Great Sea Interconnector (GSI) may not restart until 2028, while Cyprus’s energy regulator has pushed the project’s expected completion back a full year, to January 2031. Nexans fills its factory with other work Nexans chief executive Julien Hueber told analysts during the company’s nine-month results presentation that the firm has secured an alternative project that will keep its cable plant busy until mid-2028, according to Kathimerini . “With or without the GSI, our forecasts do not change until 2028,” Hueber said. He explained that the extra time allows Nexans to pursue other Mediterranean projects for the period after mid-2028. Equally, if the GSI restarts, it gives time to complete the seabed surveys, preliminary engineering and financing so the work “can start from 2028”. Asked about surveys resuming and the €25 million payment Cyprus has yet to make, Hueber was cautious. “At this moment, discussions are under way at a political and diplomatic level and I will let the political processes unfold,” he said. Regulator: completion now January 2031 Meanwhile, in Nicosia, the head of the Cyprus Energy Regulatory Authority (CERA), Polys Lemonaris, told the House Energy Committee on 20 October that the original January 2030 target now looks like January 2031. He said the regulator had received a letter from Nexans, via the project promoter, referring to the new date. Lemonaris also warned that the €1.9 billion budget no longer looks realistic. “It is certain that it will be more than €1.9 billion,” he said, adding that the final figure depends on the remaining seabed surveys. So far, about 280km of cable has been laid out of a roughly 900km route between Crete and Cyprus, while a further 232km has been manufactured but not yet laid. About 60% of the seabed surveys are complete, and the remaining 40% would take around six months. Ownership questions after Meridiam deal French infrastructure investor Meridiam has acquired 66% of the company behind the project, while Greece’s Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO/ADMIE) keeps a minority stake and remains project promoter. However, CERA says it is still waiting for IPTO to answer questions it sent in August about ownership and management after Meridiam’s entry. Turkey and the Greece-Cyprus cable surveys The delay of the Greece-Cyprus cable also has a strong diplomatic dimension. In July 2024, Turkish warships shadowed a survey vessel off Kasos. The surveys later stalled, and reports say they will resume exactly where they stopped, at the edge of Greece’s six-nautical-mile territorial waters off the island. The French-flagged survey vessel Abeille Marengo left Naples on 23 October and is due in Heraklion on 27 October. Even so, it is awaiting a Greek NAVTEX, which reports expect in early November. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told Ta Nea that Ankara would not object if it received written notice with the survey coordinates. In response, Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis said Greece is “the only country from which authorisation will be requested”, although information could be shared without it being an authorisation procedure. Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides has said Cyprus will release its first €25 million contribution once a NAVTEX is issued for the surveys. title: Customs Speaks On Recruitment List Amid Controversy
body: The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) has accused some applicants protesting their exclusion from its 2024/2025 recruitment exercise of attempting to secure employment through unofficial channels. The accusation is coming amid the allegations of irregularities that have continued to trail the selection process. The service, however, has promised to reinstate applicants found to have been wrongly disqualified. The controversy centered on why some candidates whose names appeared on the successful candidates’ list were allegedly dropped. The NCS spokesperson, Abdullahi Maiwada, disclosed this in an interview with BBC Hausa. He explained that inclusion on the list did not guarantee automatic employment. He explained that candidates were required to pass further screening checks before they could proceed to training. Maiwada added that some applicants were disqualified after failing to meet the prescribed requirements. “Among those who are currently complaining, some attempted to use backdoor channels to gain entry, which is why they were removed,” the spokesman said. He, however, assured applicants who believed they had been unjustly excluded that their complaints would be investigated. “If we find that any candidate was removed erroneously, we will promptly reinstate them,” he said. The controversy followed allegations that some applicants whose names appeared on the list were screened out and replaced by individuals who did not participate in the recruitment exercise. In a statement, the NCS acknowledged receiving complaints from applicants who participated in the exercise but were subsequently excluded. The service said 397 applicants were disqualified during physical screening over issues relating to substance abuse, age, physical fitness and documentation. Maiwada said some candidates were found to have medical conditions, including Hepatitis B and high blood pressure, while others allegedly submitted fake credentials or exceeded the stipulated age limit. He explained that the list published after the examination stages was not the final guarantee of employment. Further checks, he noted, were necessary to establish candidates’ eligibility. “It is important to understand that being invited for screening does not mean you have automatically secured the job,” he said. According to him, the screening process included drug tests, age verification and medical assessments. He said candidates who failed to satisfy the requirements would be disqualified. He added that applicants who believed their exclusion was unjustified could submit formal complaints for investigation. The spokesperson also addressed reports that some candidates had resigned from their previous jobs after finding their names on the successful candidates’ list, only to be dropped during the subsequent screening. Maiwada said the service had warned applicants against leaving their existing employment before completing the recruitment process. “We warned them not to terminate their current employment because being invited to this stage does not guarantee a job,” he said. He added that applicants who intended to leave their jobs were advised to liaise with their employers and comply with the required notice arrangements. Maiwada further explained that candidates who passed the screening would still have to satisfy the requirements of the training programme before being commissioned as customs officers. He listed examinations, parade drills, firearms training and customs operational courses among the requirements recruits must successfully complete. However, Maiwada did not comment about an unverified list in circulation, where the recruitment is skewed in favour of a particular region. The recruitment exercise has also drawn the attention of the Federal Character Commission (FCC), which called for its suspension over alleged violations of federal character principles. Abdulwasiu Bawa-Allah, chairman of the FCC Financial Services Committee, said the commission was not invited to monitor the exercise. The development has raised questions about compliance with federal character requirements in the recruitment of personnel into federal agencies. However, Comptroller-General of Customs, Adewale Adeniyi, had defended the recruitment process in August, saying the allocation of successful candidates was equal across the 36 states of the federation. In July, the NCS announced 3,852 successful candidates from 573,680 applications for positions across three entry cadres: superintendent, inspectorate and customs assistant. The service subsequently invited successful candidates for physical screening and documentation at the Nigeria Customs Command and Staff College in Gwagwalada, Abuja, in September, after which some were invited for training. The latest controversy has put the recruitment exercise under renewed scrutiny. Applicants are seeking explanations for their exclusion amid the FCC concerns over the monitoring of the process. The NCS has maintained that candidates must meet all stipulated conditions before they can be employed. It promised to correct any errors established through its investigation of complaints.

title: Greece Electricity Exports Surge, Generating €475 Million Surplus
body: Greece increased its electricity exports by 70% in the first eight months of 2026, generating a €475 million trade surplus as imports fell by 27%, according to data from the Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO) and the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT). Despite rising electricity prices internationally and across the region amid the energy crisis, Greece has maintained a competitive advantage over neighbouring countries and expanded its electricity exports across Southeast Europe. IPTO data show that Greece recorded net electricity exports of 6.1 terawatt-hours (TWh) between January and August 2026. Imports fell by 27% year-on-year to 3.14 TWh, while exports rose by 70% to 9.24 TWh. IPTO Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Manos Manousakis told the Athens-Macedonian News Agency (AMNA) that Greece was strengthening its position as an electricity exporter in Southeast Europe. “Over the past three years, the electricity export balance has continued to expand, with exports in the first eight months of 2026 already exceeding the total electricity exports recorded last year,” Manousakis said. He attributed the growth to Greece’s national energy strategy, which promotes the use of abundant domestic renewable resources, particularly solar and wind power, alongside the systematic expansion of electricity infrastructure. Following the completion of the second interconnection with Bulgaria, IPTO is developing the new Greece-Cyprus energy corridor. It is also beginning work with Italy’s TERNA on a second undersea electricity interconnection with Italy, which will triple electricity exchange capacity in the coming years. Manousakis added that IPTO’s investment programme included strengthening existing interconnections with neighbouring countries along Greece’s northern borders, developing new connections in the Eastern Mediterranean and expanding the domestic high- and ultra-high-voltage transmission network. These projects aim to transport electricity reliably and safely to consumption centres in Greece and abroad. Electricity trade balance reverses into surplus Greece’s electricity trade balance has undergone a significant turnaround since 2019, when the country imported almost 10 TWh of electricity, equivalent to approximately 20% of its needs. That year, electricity imports exceeded €500 million in value, while exports totalled just €106.7 million, leaving Greece with a trade deficit of almost €400 million. According to ELSTAT, the electricity trade balance moved into surplus in 2024, reaching €121.5 million, before expanding to €261.8 million in 2025. Greece has already surpassed last year’s annual performance. During the first eight months of 2026, the electricity trade surplus reached €475 million, with imports valued at €391 million and exports at €866.8 million. The improvement represents a turnaround of more than €800 million compared with 2019, when Greece recorded a deficit of approximately €400 million. The surplus could increase further by the end of 2026. Battery storage helps reduce renewable energy curtailment Energy storage through batteries has emerged as a new factor in Greece’s electricity generation mix this year. Its importance is expected to grow as additional storage capacity comes online. According to an analysis by the Green Tank environmental think tank, batteries that began operating in April 2026 absorbed 121.8 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of electricity through August and delivered 106.4 GWh back to the grid. The batteries prevented 5% of total electricity curtailments during that period while reducing gas consumption for electricity generation by 1.2%. As Greece continues to expand renewable energy production, battery storage could play an increasingly important role in managing surplus electricity, reducing reliance on gas-fired generation and strengthening the country’s position in regional electricity markets. title: That AI Temptation
body:
I continue low-intensity work on Quamina ; among other things, it benefits my mental health. At the moment there’s this little voice at the back of my brain that keeps saying “This would be a great job for Claude.” So far I’m ignoring it, but the internal conversation is worth sharing.
Disclosure · I’m not a GenAI expert, have never relied on it for any substantial piece of work. However, I’ve seen plenty of PRs with LLM fingerprints, and I follow a whole lot of indie devs who are in it up to their elbows. It seems to me that a pretty clear picture emerges of what it can and can’t do, where the wins and losses are. This essay reflects that picture but maybe I’m just wrong, in which case I’ll confess my errors.
Negative externalities · For me (and I’m not alone), the biggest issue isn’t what GenAI can and can’t do, it’s the ethical and economic discomforts. This technology is being peddled by terrible people who are rich and whose goal is to get richer. It’s bought and deployed by terrible people who want to slash their payrolls by throwing thought workers onto the street. It facilitates the oncoming climate catastrophe and devalues human creative effort.
Notice that I said “ethical and economic”? That second issue is all about the bubble and how nobody knows what GenAI technology will really cost, post-explosive-decompression. It wouldn’t surprise me if we ended up in a future where most software devs are using beefy “desktop” computers running open-weight models; or else they’re using AWS/GCloud/Azure (but still open-weight). Or something completely different. Or we’ve learned that the cost of AI, as measured in mental fitness and organizational health, is simply too high.
The stage has been set; let’s talk about bits on the wire.
Quamina and JSON and … · At the moment Quamina does its super-fast-matching magic on JSON blobs. But it should be perfectly possible to work with any other data format that has nested fields and boolean/numeric/string values at the leaves. Oh, and arrays of the above. There’s no shortage of candidates: Thrift, Protobufs, Apache Avro, and CBOR come to mind immediately.
Quamina has the built-in notion of a “Flattener”, that turns input data into a sorted list of “Field” structures. For example, here’s a JSON blob:
The output of the flattener, what the matcher works on, would be something like this:
In Quamina, flattening eats more time than matching. It used to eat dramatically more time, but the JSON flattener has been heavily optimized by me and other contributors.
Maybe the most important optimization is maintaining a list of which fields are actually up for matching and skipping over the ones that aren’t. Obviously this means that the parser can’t be the typical thing that turns your JSON blob into a fully-serialized tree of structures and arrays in a one-shot call. In fact, you need a parser that’s a tokenizer and lets the calling code decide how to deal with each little piece of it, one at a time.
Protobufs · Someone out there asked Claude to build a Flattener for Protobufs. It seemed to partly work but was kind of buggy and I found the code hard to read. Hmm. Of course the usual GenAI “That was six months ago, it’s much better now” narrative applies.
CBOR · For those who don’t know, CBOR is JSON but binary, which is claimed to make it more compact and faster to process. It’s also got a richer type repertoire, but whenever I’ve run across it in the field, it’s basically being used as JSON-only-faster.
So, I’ve started working on a CBOR Flattener for Quamina.
The simplest thing that could possibly work · The default CBOR processor for Go , from Faye Amacker , looks very polished. But it’s not a tokenizer, it’s a “deserialize your whole blob in one call” thing. So the simplest thing would be to make that one call on each incoming blob, then run around the deserialized tree and compute the flattening. Ignore all that stuff about bypassing for efficiency. Because it might be plenty fast enough and that optimization would have been premature. After all, if you read Faye’s page linked above, they seem to be something of an optimization fanatic.
And you know what, I bet if I gave Claude the problem of turning CBOR into Fields, I’d get OK code back; tell it find a way to fuzz-test the process and it’d be surprising if it didn’t work.
Right at this moment in history, I could make a case for that being a good engineering decision. Code, in the LLM-pre-bubble-pop era, is cheap. Time is still expensive. This task has clear, clean success criteria, easy to point an agent at. The Simplest Thing That Could Possibly Work is a powerful design principle, one that I’ve forced down the throat of more than just one or two over-aspirational engineering team leads.
But I’m not gonna do that. I mean, there’s the nauseating state of current AI culture and finance. But also, I’m doing this for fun. Writing high-performance tokenizers is fun! [Really? -Ed.][Serious fun. -T.] I’ve started poking around inside Faye’s library, raised an issue , and I’m confident that there is plenty of code and tests in there that I can steal.
Testing · Quamina has 14K lines of test code and 47M of of test data. A high proportion of the tests amount to “Run the code against this JSON and require these results.” Obviously, now I want to run 100% of those tests with equivalent CBOR input. It seems to me that Claude could do a great job of automating plenty of this work, which I predict will be grinding, tedious, and not fun at all. On top of which I tend to be lax and forgiving about test-code quality.
My internal engineering-leader mind has no doubt, it’d tell the devs to automate the hell out of replicating the test suite and not be picky about how. But I bet that it’d burn a whole lot of tokens, which means routing money to bad people with bad goals. So once again, I’m not going to do it with LLMs.
Post-bubble, it might be somewhere between forgivable and praiseworthy. But not as I write this.
From: Dave Pawson (Oct 24 2026, at 00:28)
" the biggest issue isn’t what GenAI can and can’t do, it’s the ethical and economic discomforts. This technology is being peddled by terrible people who are rich and whose goal is to get richer."
I'm sure humanity has met this before with other 'stuff'. Can we learn from history?
That's without the slow takeup of websites blocking AI bots, which may impact growth.
I've found "this activity routes money to bad people" to be a game that's frustrating, futile, and drenched in (usually unintentional) hypocrisy.
For one, in Western-style capitalism it's almost a truism that all roads lead to bad people. If you follow the supply chain all the way back you will surely find someone -- probably several someones -- whose politics or morals or actions you find repugnant.
For two, avoiding the whipping boy du jour sometimes requires a pivot to another supplier which is no less reprehensible, if possibly less shunned by the zeitgeist.
If you choose not to partake altogether, it then can underline those areas of your life where you have chosen to compromise, either through ignorance or expedience or just being so dang EXHAUSTED by the effort of trying to lead a moral life here in 2026.
I'm not saying to go ahead and put dollars in the pockets of fascists and pedophiles and the worst dregs humanity can cough up, but it's easy to get that warm glow of self-righteousness when bypassing a certain problematic business, only to ignore the fact that mere existence in Western civilization is to feed the beast that eats our planet and our young.
Thanks for writing this, and writing in general on a blog with RSS. I do the same re: LLMs, and it’s always nice to be less lonely.
This is indeed a symptom of capitalism. Another one is making you think there’s no point in fighting it because there’s no other way and that the world is doomed to climate catastrophe so you just get yours right now without worrying about others.
Capitalism isn’t all that old in the context of history, and there are other ways to exist. Many big changes seemed impossible before they happened, and that people that fought them were wasting their time.
From: Len Bullard (Oct 30 2026, at 09:04)
From my perch and ignoring the political social hysteria, the advantages are undeniable and the code is good enough. My concerns are conversion pipelines and the stability of the governing standards over the rendering systems. Bit twiddling is largely a nuisance particularly when it arrives wrapped in social engineering. There is a point of view that if the code in MCCF enables a ten year old to build real time 3D for a web of freestanding worlds, thus learning basic concepts of math, music, video, audio and graphics production for low to no cost, it’s worth the risks. LLMs are practical from that point of view.
The opinions expressed here are my own, and no other party necessarily agrees with them.
A full disclosure of my professional interests is on the author page.

title: Greece Unveils New Housing Measures to Ease Rent Pressures
body: Greece is introducing a series of housing measures to increase the supply of available homes and ease pressure on rents, including subsidies for renovating vacant properties, tax incentives for long-term rentals and restrictions on new short-term rental registrations in areas facing housing shortages. The government also plans to launch a new €2 billion My Home III housing programme in January 2027 and expand social housing initiatives to help more households buy their own homes. Meanwhile, the government is expanding rent refunds due to reach thousands of eligible recipients on November 30. Further measures and special tax arrangements will follow next year through a comprehensive bill, which the government plans to submit to Parliament in November. Immediate measures to bring vacant homes back into use As the government rolls out the measures, tenants and property owners will need to assess which incentives best suit their circumstances. 1. Renovation subsidies covering up to 95% of costs A programme led by the Ministry of Social Cohesion and Family, with EU funding channelled through the Ministry of National Economy and Finance, will subsidise renovations and energy-efficiency improvements in older homes. On October 20, the government published the implementation guide for its Home Renovation initiative. The programme offers up to €36,000 for renovation work, with an additional €2,500 available for supporting services. Basic subsidy rates range from 70% to 80%, depending on the applicant’s income category. Eligible increases can raise the rates to 85% and 95%, respectively. Applications have not yet opened. Authorities will initially activate the platform for vacant properties before extending it to homes already used as primary residences. They will announce the application dates separately. Authorities have already issued 94,000 eligibility certificates, including 14,000 for vacant homes and 80,000 for owner-occupied properties. However, an eligibility certificate does not guarantee funding approval. Owners can either occupy renovated vacant homes themselves or rent them out as primary residences. The scheme aims to address long-term housing needs while easing pressure on the market. 2. Tax incentives for vacant homes returning to long-term rentals The government plans to extend until December 31, 2027, a tax exemption on rental income for the first 36 months of eligible long-term leases. The Ministry of National Economy and Finance measure covers eligible homes of up to 120 square metres, with an additional 20 square metres allowed for each dependent child of the tenant beyond the first two. Leases must run for at least three years. As a general rule, the property must have remained vacant or not served as a residence during the previous three tax years. Properties used exclusively for short-term rentals during the previous tax year can also qualify if their owners switch them to long-term rentals. A special provision allows leases of at least six consecutive months to doctors and nurses employed by the public sector, public-school teachers and uniformed personnel. The exemption does not automatically apply to every new lease and remains subject to specific eligibility and compliance requirements. The proposed extension forms part of the comprehensive tax bill awaiting parliamentary approval. 3. Restrictions on new Airbnb registrations in Athens and Thessaloniki The government will continue freezing new short-term rental registrations in designated areas of Athens and Thessaloniki throughout 2027. The restrictions cover three municipal districts in Athens and Thessaloniki’s First Municipal District. They aim to prevent more homes from shifting out of the long-term rental market and into short-term accommodation. The measure targets new registrations in these areas rather than imposing a blanket ban on existing short-term rental properties. New housing measures planned for 2027 4. New My Home III programme The government plans to launch the €2 billion My Home III programme in January 2027, offering low-interest housing loans through the Hellenic Development Bank. Announced eligibility limits include an upper age limit of 55 for applicants, a maximum property market value of €300,000 and loans of up to €230,000, covering as much as 90% of a property’s value. The programme will broaden income eligibility thresholds to accommodate more families with children. It will also allow larger homes for families with several children, helping more households purchase their own properties. 5. New social housing using public properties The government’s plans include 2,350 energy-efficient homes across four disused military camps, with a budget of €435 million. Authorities also aim to create approximately 450 homes by renovating public buildings. In parallel, the government is advancing a social housing partnership model and plans to make the first eight public properties available for development. These homes remain at the planning stage and have not yet been delivered. 6. Tax incentives for build-to-rent housing The government is planning tax incentives for build-to-rent developments, which involve constructing buildings specifically for long-term rental accommodation. Authorities have yet to specify the terms, the level of tax relief or the launch date. The initiative aims to add hundreds of homes to the long-term rental market. Further measures to support tenants and property owners 7. Rent refunds on November 30 The government will pay rent refunds on November 30 for eligible tenants who paid rent during the 2025 tax year. Doctors, nurses and teachers serving in regional areas will qualify for double the standard refund, providing additional financial relief to eligible households. 8. Lower rental income tax for property owners A new intermediate tax rate of 25% will apply to the portion of rental income between €12,000 and €24,000 for the 2026 tax year. The reduction aims to encourage owners to make more properties available for rent. Landlords may also pass some of their tax savings on to tenants by lowering the rents they charge. 9. Expanded ENFIA property tax exemptions from 2027 From 2027, the government will extend exemptions from Greece’s annual ENFIA property tax to more primary residences in small settlements. The measure covers settlements with up to 2,000 residents, rising to 2,200 residents in Western Macedonia. It excludes Attica, except for the Islands Regional Unit. Eligible applicants must be individuals with tax residence in Greece, and the full-ownership taxable value of their property must not exceed €400,000. The exemption does not automatically cover every property an owner holds. 10. Extended tax relief for renovations and construction The Finance Ministry’s proposed bill will extend several tax measures until the end of 2027. These include tax relief for eligible building improvement expenses, the suspension of VAT on new buildings and the suspension of capital gains tax on property transfers. While the VAT suspension remains in force, developers can apply for the relevant arrangements, and qualifying property transfers will attract a 3% transfer tax instead of VAT. 11. Higher property transfer tax for buyers from outside the EU and EEA From July 1, 2027, Greece plans to increase the property transfer tax from 3% to 15% for residential purchases by individuals who are not tax residents of EU or European Economic Area countries. The measure aims to curb large-scale property purchases by investors from regions including the Middle East and China. The key criterion is the buyer’s tax residence, not their nationality.
