title: “Don’t like it? Too bad”: third day of Constitutional Court hearings on opposition ban in Georgia
body: Georgia opposition ban case On 23 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the third day of hearings on a lawsuit filed by 88 MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that the parties have violated Article 23 of the constitution, which prohibits political parties whose objectives include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments cited in the lawsuit is the parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining the country’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The party is held responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia , when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the allegations. Hearings will resume on 26 October and continue throughout the week. The court must deliver its ruling by 24 June 2027. Proposed ban on five opposition parties in Georgia: what’s happening and why Georgia opposition party ban case: Day two of court proceedings Court begins hearing case to ban opposition parties in Georgia: first-day developments Key events and statements from third day of Constitutional Court hearings The day focused on motions submitted by Gakharia for Georgia, all of which were rejected by the court. No opposition motion has been granted during the three days of Constitutional Court proceedings in the case. Court rejects request to postpone hearings by a month Berdia Sichinava , representing Gakharia for Georgia, asked the court to postpone the hearing by one month. He argued that procedural rules allow that much time to prepare a response, but his party had only seven days from the announcement that hearings would begin. The United National Movement, Lelo and Coalition for Change joined the motion. Archil Gorduladze, chair of parliament’s legal affairs committee and one of the MPs who filed the lawsuit, argued that neither the procedural rules, the organic law nor the constitution stipulates that failure to submit a response prevents the court from hearing the case. The judges deliberated and unanimously rejected the motion. Court president Revaz Nadaraia said the request should have been submitted earlier, as proceedings had already been under way for three days. He added: “ If you don’t like it, you don’t like it. What can I do about that? ” Judge Eva Gotsiridze noted that the proceedings would take a long time, adding: “ You will have the month provided for in the procedural rules .” Request to recuse judge Sergo Metopishvili rejected Gakharia for Georgia’s legal team filed a motion seeking the recusal of judge Sergo Metopishvili. The full bench rejected this request too. Court rejects request to summon Bidzina Ivanishvili and Irakli Kobakhidze as witnesses Berdia Sichinava asked the court to summon senior Georgian Dream figures as witnesses, including the party’s founder and honorary chair, billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili ; Tbilisi mayor Kakha Kaladze ; prime minister Irakli Kobakhidze ; and current and former senior officials Archil Talakvadze, Mamuka Bakhtadze, Vakhtang Gomelauri and Grigol Liluashvili. He said their testimony was relevant to the criminal case against party leader Giorgi Gakharia . Criminal proceedings against Giorgi Gakharia, Georgia’s former prime minister and current leader of the For Georgia party, began on 12 November 2025 and relate to two separate incidents . Gakharia has left the country and is currently abroad. One case concerns events in 2019, when Gakharia was interior minister. He is accused of unilaterally deciding to set up a police post near the village of Chorchana, in the Georgian-Ossetian conflict zone, triggering a sharp escalation of tensions. Prosecutors say Tbilisi subsequently lost control of another section of its territory. The second case relates to the dispersal of a mass protest in Tbilisi on 20 June 2019. Police used force, including rubber bullets, without prior warning. Two people lost an eye and five others sustained serious injuries. Gakharia is accused of ordering the police operation in his capacity as interior minister. Berdia Sichinava said that under direct questioning, Ivanishvili, Kaladze and others would not be able to evade responsibility for the 2019 decision to establish a police checkpoint in the village of Chorchana. He also argued that the events of 20 June 2019 in Tbilisi could not be used as grounds for banning the party. “This is an issue on which society cannot reach a consensus,” Sichinava said, adding that “the protest was genuine, but the attempt to storm parliament was unacceptable”. In response, claimant Archil Gorduladze reminded the court that Giorgi Gakharia was currently wanted and argued that the evidence in the two criminal cases against him should not be considered by the Constitutional Court. The court rejected this motion too. Should state have right to ban political parties? Tbilisi street poll – Video Most respondents said that banning political parties was unacceptable in a country that claims to be a democracy. Georgian Dream’s position Before the hearing, claimant Archil Gorduladze, chair of parliament’s legal affairs committee, told journalists that the opposition’s statements “only strengthen the case filed with the Constitutional Court”. Asked about the opposition’s request to invite experts from the Venice Commission to take part in the proceedings, Gorduladze replied: “ The opposition apparently believes that a foreigner knows Georgia’s constitution better than the Constitutional Court judges .” Responding to criticism that a single lawsuit had been filed against all five parties, Gorduladze said: “They are all just the same National Movement. ” Tengiz Sharmanashvili, another Georgian Dream MP who filed the lawsuit, also told journalists that “the opponents want to drag things out”. He said he was concerned that the opposition was deliberately submitting motions in a form that made it impossible for the court to grant them. “ The opposition is collecting rejected motions for the Strasbourg court, and none of the five parties intends to engage seriously with the proceedings at the Constitutional Court, ” Sharmanashvili said. Outside the court Opera singer Paata Burchuladze , who was convicted over an attempt to seize the presidential administration on 4 October 2025, has sent a letter to the Constitutional Court offering to testify if the events of 4 October are discussed during the proceedings. Burchuladze argues that opposition parties are being unfairly accused of organising the events. “ I was the organiser of those events, and I alone ,” he said, urging the opposition to file a motion to have him summoned for questioning. Sopio Khorguani, an MP from the opposition party Gakharia for Georgia, told journalists that Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s statement that “the days of this opposition are numbered” was unacceptable. Khorguani described the remark as a direct instruction to the Constitutional Court on the verdict the government expects it to deliver. Another representative of the party, Giorgi Sharashidze, said that “ the whole process resembles a theatre of the absurd” . He said Gakharia for Georgia had been added to the lawsuit at the last minute, calling its inclusion “entirely artificial”. The claimant, he added, had still been unable to specify which article of the constitution the party had violated. News in Georgia

title: Annoh-Dompreh earns double honours for environmental advocacy
body: Minority Chief Whip and Nsawam-Adoagyiri MP, Frank Annoh-Dompreh, has received two awards for his advocacy on environmental sustainability and efforts to advance green legislation. He received the Green Societal Impact and Sustainability Ambassadorial Award and the ICESDA Green Capital Partnership Award at the third International Conference on ESG and Sustainable Development of Africa (ICESDA). The conference was held under the theme, “The Africa We Want: Driving Transformational Inclusive Green Growth Through ESG and Digitalisation.” Presenters recognised the MP’s efforts to bring community-level environmental concerns to Parliament and support legislative action on sustainability. They highlighted his advocacy at times when such issues attracted limited political attention. The Green Societal Impact and Sustainability Ambassadorial Award acknowledged his contribution to promoting environmental concerns through Parliament. He also received the ICESDA Green Capital Partnership Award at the ceremony. The recognition highlighted lawmakers’ role in connecting environmental challenges in their constituencies to national policymaking. Presenters also stressed the importance of considering environmental evidence when debating and passing legislation. The conference brought together stakeholders to examine how environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles, alongside digital technologies, could support Africa’s development. Discussions focused on inclusive green growth and the need for collaboration among policymakers, businesses and civil society organisations to balance economic development with environmental protection.

title: Russia, Ukraine Agree on Ceasefire in Embattled Oleshky, Plan New Peace Talks Next Month
body:
Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered through U.S. first lady Melania Trump, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said peace negotiators would meet next month for new talks.
The two sides said the ceasefire would go into effect on Oct. 27, allowing the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia and some to Ukraine,” Melania Trump said in a statement.
The first lady noted that her intervention allowed both Russia and Ukraine to assign teams to work on the technical terms of the process, including de-mining the heavily mined roads. “All parties have worked around the clock since that moment,” she said.
Amid a U.S. push to organize new talks aimed at ending the 4.5-year-old war, Zelensky said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A U.S. official later said the three countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland.
Zelensky said he hoped a meeting of the countries' leaders would follow.
Previous rounds of talks headed by the United ​States ​stalled in February ⁠with no significant progress towards ending the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War II. Russia continues to demand Ukraine cede all of the eastern Donbas ​region, including territory Russia has not occupied militarily, while Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds.
The latest peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by US President Donald Trump seen as favouring Russia.
A major source of friction was limitations placed on SpaceX's Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem with the system, he would straighten it out and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Another contentious point was Trump's announcement of a deal to allow Russia to provide diesel for the US and global markets, an agreement denounced by Ukraine and meant to keep prices down as the president's Republicans contest U.S. midterm elections.
On Friday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the first three tankers with Russian diesel were on their way to North America.
In the town of Oleshky, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, residents have reported that they faced a deepening food crisis.
"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," the White House said in a statement.
The chief of staff of Russian forces, Valery Gerasimov, said on the Defense Ministry's Telegram channel that Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time on Oct. 27 to allow for the humanitarian operation to start.
Ukraine's General Staff issued a statement agreeing to observe the ceasefire from the same time and pledging to "do everything possible to help Oleshky's residents." Ukraine says it has already used drones twice to send food into the town.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also said the ceasefire would go into effect on Oct. 27 and told Reuters the operation would involve demining roads to the town, deliveries of food and evacuations of civilians.
Both sides said Melania Trump played an important role in coordinating the agreement. The first lady has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.
"Oleshky is a frontline war city on the brink of disaster," she said in a statement.
"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water."
The White House said Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, had 1,700 to 2,000 residents remaining, down from 24,000 before the war.
Moscow and Kyiv both accuse each other of blocking supplies to the population of the town, which Ukrainian forces have been trying to retake.
Earlier, the Kremlin said that President Vladimir Putin had discussed the situation in Oleshky with U.S. President Donald Trump and told him that Russia’s human rights commissioner was working on humanitarian efforts there.
Putin also told Pope Leo in a phone call last Friday that he supported a Vatican initiative to help deliver supplies to civilians in Oleshky and was ready to cooperate on the matter. At the same time, he laid blame for the dire humanitarian situation in the town on Ukraine.
Zelensky's comments on resuming peace talks followed a meeting with U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway early this week and a subsequent meeting between Witkoff and Putin in St. Petersburg.
Zelensky said he spoke on Friday with Witkoff and U.S. envoy Jared Kushner. He said any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees for Ukraine and funding for 10 years to maintain the Ukrainian army.
"The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelensky told the Hudson Institute think tank via a video link. He said much would depend on Russia, noting that a similar meeting expected this month had not materialized.
Zelensky spoke of the importance of continued diplomatic efforts to reach a ceasefire and end the war, now in its fifth year, adding that Europe should also be involved in the talks.
Ukrainian officials said on Friday that speed restrictions on Starlink systems in Ukraine remained in place, despite Trump's previous statement that the services had been fully restored.
Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he had not spoken to Musk about the restrictions but would do so if required.
"If there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out," he said. The caps have been in place since Oct. 13.
Ukraine and Russia also swapped 270 servicemen each in a prisoner exchange on Friday, the Russian Defense Ministry said. Zelensky described the swap, the first since August, as a "very important result."
Ukraine's acting prosecutor, Anton Kovalskyi, writing on Telegram, said more than 19,000 Ukrainian civilians, including 762 children, had been killed since Russia launched its full-scale war more than four years ago.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,576,600 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
body:
Russia has lost 1,576,600 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 24.
The number includes 1,980 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,444 tanks, 25,600 armored combat vehicles, 166,501 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,565 artillery systems, 2,232 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,722 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,011 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: MOMO FinTech Lab backs young innovators in northern Ghana
body: Young innovators in northern Ghana are getting an opportunity to turn ideas into technology-driven solutions to local challenges, as MOMO FinTech steps up efforts to nurture talent beyond Accra and develop the next generation of financial technology entrepreneurs. Four top-performing teams from the northern zone have secured places at the National Demo Day in Accra, where they will be paired with mentors to refine their projects before presenting them to investors and other stakeholders. The initiative, known as the MOMO FinTech Lab, seeks to identify promising young innovators, equip them with practical skills and support them to develop solutions that can improve livelihoods in their communities. Speaking to the media after the hackathon in Tamale, the Chief Executive Officer of MOMO FinTech, Shaibu Haruna, said the initiative was introduced after the company observed that FinTech businesses were largely concentrated in Accra, despite the availability of talented young people across the country. He said the company wanted to create opportunities for young people to develop ideas that addressed local needs and had the potential to compete on the national and international stages. “We took it upon ourselves to say there are so many talented young men and women across the length and breadth of Ghana who have great ideas and who can be groomed to solve for their local needs,” he said. Mr Haruna disclosed that the competition had attracted more than 1,000 entries nationwide, with submissions from northern Ghana accounting for 14 per cent of the total. Participants in the northern zone spent four days working with experts to refine their ideas through practical testing, market research and technical guidance. He said the company was impressed by the effort participants had put into developing solutions aimed at tackling everyday problems and improving the livelihoods of ordinary people. The programme is also expected to open up opportunities for partnerships and investment to help promising innovators turn their ideas into practical, market-ready solutions. Mr Haruna added that selected participants would have opportunities to undertake internships with organisations to deepen their technical knowledge and gain practical work experience. He encouraged young people, particularly those in northern Ghana, to believe in their ideas, develop them carefully and take advantage of available opportunities to advance their innovations. “I encourage all young people who have ideas across the length and breadth of Ghana, especially in the northern sector of Ghana, to be bold about their ideas, to think through them, and then take advantage of some of these opportunities,” he said. Mr Haruna described the programme as a talent-development initiative that would require sustained support to help participants improve their ideas and build viable solutions. Contestants look ahead Meanwhile, members of the four selected teams said their qualification for the national showcase was an important milestone after days of competition and project development. The Team Lead of Team MoMoCovert, Lukman Seidu, said the competition had been demanding but expressed excitement about the team’s success. “It’s been a tough competition but we are excited that we have been able to make it out which means a lot to us,” he said.

title: Zelensky Ready to Freeze Front Line to Halt War, Rejects Land Cession
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine is prepared to freeze combat operations along existing front lines to bring a rapid end to the war , while rejecting territorial concessions and emphasizing that Kyiv will never legally recognize occupied regions as Russian sovereign land.
Speaking in an interview with ABC News broadcast, he addressed prospective diplomatic frameworks to halt ongoing hostilities.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Yes, we are ready to put an end to this war as quickly as possible... To freeze the front line,” Zelensky stated.
When asked by the interviewer whether Kyiv would agree to cede 25 percent of Ukrainian territory to achieve peace, Zelensky rejected the premise, clarifying the exact proportion of territory currently held by Russian forces.
“When someone speaks about 25 percent, it implies that we would have to surrender the entire Donbas , and only then would the Russians control 25 percent. Right now, they control 19.3 percent,” Zelensky explained.
The Ukrainian head of state stressed that while Ukraine is open to freezing the conflict along the active line of contact to stop the killing of civilians and soldiers, Kyiv maintains an unyielding red line on legal sovereignty: “We will never recognize the occupied territory as Russian.”
Zelensky also acknowledged that international interlocutors had advanced similar proposals in ongoing backchannel discussions.
Zelensky’s comments to ABC News follow an address to Washington’s Hudson Institute on Friday, Oct. 23, in which he warned that Ukraine still lacks concrete commitments from the US and European allies regarding how partners would respond to future Russian military aggression.
Addressing international security specialists, Zelensky argued that any lasting armistice must be anchored by three core pillars: an immediate ceasefire, binding allied defense commitments, and long-term funding to sustain a formidable Ukrainian military.
“We need not just peace. Peace which has to be fair and strong,” Zelensky told the Hudson Institute.
Zelensky proposed the formation of a European -led coalition of willing nations capable of deploying personnel inside Ukraine, backed by American strategic guarantees. However, he questioned what specific actions an American “backstop” would entail if Moscow launched renewed missile barrages or ground offensives.
“Who will react? Not only our army. Who and how? And till now we don’t have answers,” Zelensky observed.
The president emphasized that Ukraine’s primary deterrent against future aggression remains a well-equipped standing military requiring sustained foreign financial support for at least a decade.
“We need a big, big strong army, minimum ten years,” Zelensky said, explaining that Ukraine’s war-damaged domestic economy cannot independently sustain the necessary force structure without multi-year international financing.
Zelensky reiterated that while Kyiv continues to pursue formal NATO membership, bilateral US security guarantees modeled after NATO’s Article 5 and ratified by the US Congress could serve as an effective alternative.
He warned that purely declarative agreements would invite renewed assault, cautioning that “Russia will attack if they feel that they can, if they feel that you are weak.”
Zelensky disclosed that Ukrainian, American, and Russian negotiating delegations could convene for tripartite consultations in Abu Dhabi in early or mid-November, though the schedule remains contingent upon the Kremlin’s willingness to engage. The prospective meeting follows preliminary diplomatic contacts conducted in Oslo and Saint Petersburg.
“We are ready to meet any day, even tomorrow, but it all depends on the Russians,” Zelensky said, noting that Moscow derailed a planned October meeting by introducing procedural objections.
Zelensky maintained that an enforceable ceasefire must serve as the primary prerequisite before complex political settlements can advance, designating an armistice as “point number one.”
The diplomatic maneuvering unfolds as European capitals evaluate how to establish direct channels to the Kremlin to ensure European and Ukrainian interests are preserved in any settlement brokered by Washington.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia earlier in the week to discuss parameters for a prospective three-way summit involving Zelensky, US President Donald Trump , and Russian President Vladimir Putin .
In response, European leaders have debated appointing an envoy to represent European interests, with figures such as Finnish President Alexander Stubb attracting attention due to Finland’s border management experience and diplomatic communication lines with both Washington and Moscow.
Stubb participated alongside Zelensky and Witkoff in consultations in Oslo on Oct. 20, joined by European Commission presidential aide Björn Seibert.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Pres. Pezeshkian pays tribute at tomb of martyred Leader
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 24 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian paid tribute to the tomb of martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei on Friday morning.
During his daylong trip to the shrine city of Mashhad, Khorasan Razavi province, President Pezeshkian attended Dar al-Dhikr Portico to pay his homage to the resting place of martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei.
On February 28, the US and Israel jointly waged a war of aggression against Iran which led to the assassination of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, high-ranking military commanders and civilians.

title: Verdi’s Nabucco Opens a Big New Season in Heraklion
body: Verdi’s Nabucco will open the new season at the Cultural and Conference Centre of Heraklion in November, with 150 performers taking part in a co-production with North Macedonia’s National Opera. The four-act opera, with a libretto by Temistocle Solera, will be staged on 12, 13, 14 and 15 November at 7:30pm in the Andreas and Maria Kalokairinou Hall. Acclaimed soloists will join the orchestra, chorus and ballet of North Macedonia’s National Opera, together with the Heraklion Choral Ensemble. Renato Bonajuto directs, with a staging adaptation by Dejan Proshev. Greek conductor Myron Michailidis, the centre’s artistic director, will lead the performances. The story behind Nabucco Conductor Myron Michailidis at the Cultural and Conference Centre of Heraklion in 2024. Photo: Myron Michailidis, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons Solera’s libretto tells of the captivity of the Jews under the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar, or Nabucco, in 587 BC. His arrogance in demanding to be worshipped as a god leads to his fall and, finally, to his conversion. A hunger for power, devotion to God and a love tested by political and personal upheaval sit at the heart of the plot. Nabucco premiered at La Scala in Milan on 9 March 1842. It made Verdi’s name and turned him into a national symbol, because his music captured the spirit of mature Romanticism and the desire for a free and united Italy. Its best-known moment is “Va, pensiero” , the chorus of the Hebrew slaves. It became an emblem of patriotic longing and national awakening for Italians. A season of 34 productions in Crete However, Nabucco is just one of 34 productions and 70 events planned for the season, with 740 artists taking part. The programme spans opera, dance, tributes, recitals, festivals, symphonic and chamber music, traditional and Byzantine music, contemporary and choral music, and theatre. Highlights include Puccini’s Madama Butterfly, a tribute to the Greek composer Yannis Markopoulos and a recital by the award-winning Russian pianist Nikolai Lugansky. Presenting the programme, Michailidis said the centre is consolidating its position as an important cultural institution with national and international reach. He said it does so “by investing in major productions, important artistic collaborations, new works and, at the same time, in showcasing the artistic talent of Crete, which now takes part in many of our productions” . title: War update: 181 clashes on front lines over past day, heaviest fighting on Kostiantynivka axis
body:
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces stated this in a Facebook post .
The enemy launched 88 airstrikes, dropping 309 guided aerial bombs.
In addition, Russian invaders deployed 10,270 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,755 attacks on settlements and Ukrainian troop positions, including 45 using multiple launch rocket systems.
Settlements shelled by the enemy included Bezsalivka, Koreniok, Tovstodubove, Ulanove, Rohizne, Neskuchne, Bachivsk, Volfyne, Vovkivka, Kozache, Smolyne, Brusky, Novovasylivka, Sopych, Baranivka, Rivne, Smykarivka and Nova Huta in the Sumy region, as well as Mykhalchyna-Sloboda in the Chernihiv region. Tovstodubove was hit by an airstrike.
Ukrainian missile troops and artillery struck two areas where Russian personnel and military equipment were concentrated, three guns, a UAV control post and two other important Russian targets.
On the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk axes, Russian troops launched two airstrikes using six guided aerial bombs and carried out 47 attacks on Ukrainian troop positions and settlements.
On the Southern Slobozhanshchyna axis, Ukrainian units repelled five Russian attacks. The invaders attacked Ukrainian positions near Okhrimivka, Rybalchyne and Chuhunivka.
On the Kupiansk axis, Russian forces made five attempts to improve their positions, launching offensive operations toward Radkivka and Podoly.
Attempts to break through Ukrainian defenses were repelled on the Lyman axis, where Russian invaders launched three assaults toward Zarichne, Zakitne and Kolodiazi.
On the Sloviansk axis, the Russian army launched five attacks near Ozerne, Kryva Luka, Pyskunivka and Rai-Oleksandrivka.
Russian troops conducted no assault operations on the Kramatorsk axis.
On the Kostiantynivka axis, 23 Russian attacks were recorded. The invaders conducted offensive operations near Kostiantynivka and toward Druzhkivka, Novoselivka, Mykolaipillia, Novopavlivka, Toretske, Vilne and Rusyn Yar.
Russian troops launched 19 attacks on the Pokrovsk axis. The invaders attempted to advance toward Dobropillia, Sviatohorivka, Chernihivka, Myrne, Hulive, Serhiivka, Molodetske and Novopavlivka.
On the Oleksandrivka axis, the enemy launched one assault toward Myrne.
On the Huliaipole axis, Russian invaders attacked Ukrainian defenders' positions ten times, attempting to advance toward Uspenivka, Rizdvianka, Hirkе and Yehorivka.
On the Orikhiv axis, the enemy made two attempts to attack toward Pavlivka and Chervona Krynytsia.
Russian forces conducted no assault operations on the Dnipro River axis.
No signs of Russian forces forming offensive groupings were detected on the Volyn and Polissia axes.

title: Air defense down 616 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian regions — Defense Ministry
body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Russian air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 616 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian regions and the waters of the Azov and Black seas, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Over the past night (from 08:00 p.m. Moscow time on October 23 to 08:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 24), on-duty air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over the territories of the Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kirov, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Penza, Rostov, Ryazan, Samara, Saratov, Smolensk, Tambov, Tula, and Ulyanovsk regions, the Moscow region, the Republic of Crimea, the Republic of Tatarstan, and the Krasnodar Region, as well as over the waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea," the ministry said in a statement.

title: Manos Loizos Legacy: 89 Years On, Greece Still Sings His Songs
body: The Manos Loizos legacy reached a milestone this week, with the 89th anniversary on Thursday 22 October of the composer’s birth. The Greek Cypriot composer wrote the music for “Jamaica”, “Ola Se Thymizoun” and “Kalimera Ilie”. He died in Moscow in 1982, aged just 44. Even so, the Manos Loizos legacy endures, and his songs remain a fixture of Greek concerts, radio and family gatherings. He worked with lyricists Lefteris Papadopoulos and Manolis Rasoulis, and with singers including Haris Alexiou and Giorgos Dalaras. Where the Manos Loizos legacy began Haris Alexiou in concert at the Berlin University of the Arts, Berlin, on Saturday 21 October 2006. Photo: Inge Kanakaris-Wirtl, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5 Manos Loizos was born on 22 October 1937 in Alexandria, Egypt, according to his Wikipedia biography . His father, Andreas Loizou, came from the village of Agioi Vavatsinias in the Larnaca district of Cyprus. Despina Manaki, his mother, had roots in Rhodes. Some accounts instead place his birth in Cyprus, before the family moved to Egypt. At the age of seven, he began studying the violin. Initially he played as an amateur, then studied at the National Conservatory of Alexandria. Still, he never completed formal musical training, and biographers describe him as largely self-taught. After graduating from the Averofeio high school in 1955, he moved to Athens to study. He enrolled in pharmacy, then switched to economics and briefly studied painting. By 1960, he had left university. He then worked as a waiter, a graphic designer and a musician in small music clubs. In 1962, Mikis Theodorakis chose him to lead the choir for performances of “Omorfi Poli”. Later that year, he recorded his first single, a setting of words by Federico García Lorca sung by Giorgos Moutsios. Songs written with Lefteris Papadopoulos His closest creative partner was the lyricist Lefteris Papadopoulos, a personal friend. Much of the Manos Loizos legacy rests on this partnership. Together, they released “O Stathmos” in December 1968, the first album issued under the Minos label, with Giorgos Dalaras, Giannis Kalatzis and Litsa Diamanti singing. Additionally, the pair wrote “Thalassografies” in 1970 and “Na ’Hame Ti Na ’Hame” in 1972, whose lyrics the dictatorship’s censors cut. Their songs include “Jamaica”, “Ah Helidoni Mou”, “Den Tha Xanagapiso” and “O Koutalianos”. In 1979, he released “Ta Tragoudia Tis Haroulas”, sung entirely by Haris Alexiou with lyrics by Manolis Rasoulis and Pythagoras. Although critics attacked it at first, the album went on to reach platinum sales. It includes “Ola Se Thymizoun”, one of the biggest hits of her career. Her recordings form a key part of the Manos Loizos legacy. In 2024, Greek City Times reported that she paid tribute to Loizos on stage at a concert honouring the lyricist. He also worked with lyricists Fontas Ladis and Yannis Negrepontis. Similarly, singers Maria Farantouri, Vasilis Papakonstantinou and Dimitra Galani recorded his songs. His last album during his lifetime, “Gia Mia Mera Zois”, appeared in December 1980. Politics, censorship and arrest Loizos belonged to the Communist Party of Greece and spoke openly against the military dictatorship. He wrote both the music and the lyrics of “Che”, dedicated to Che Guevara. That stance remains part of the Manos Loizos legacy. When the colonels’ regime took power, he left for England in September 1967. He returned early the following year. In 1972, he helped found the Union of Greek Composers and Lyricists. The union campaigned against cassette piracy and censorship. On the night of 17 November 1973, during the Athens Polytechnic uprising, he was arrested at his home in Cholargos. Authorities held him for ten days. That same month, he was recording the album “Kalimera Ilie”, with lyrics by Dimitris Christodoulou. Haris Alexiou, Kostas Smokovitis and Aleka Aliberti sang on it. Later, in 1976, Giorgos Dalaras recorded “Ta Tragoudia Mas”, with lyrics by Fontas Ladis. The state broadcaster censored nine of its 11 songs. Political songs such as these shaped the Manos Loizos legacy. Greek City Times listed the album among the classics Greece still sings in August 2026. In 1978, Loizos became president of the composers’ union. Final months in Moscow In October 1981, he entered hospital in Athens with pericarditis and kidney failure. Following a stroke on 8 June 1982, he travelled to Moscow for treatment in August. There, he suffered a second stroke on 7 September and died ten days later, on 17 September 1982. He was buried at the First Cemetery of Athens on 25 September. The Manos Loizos legacy also includes his final album, “Grammata Stin Agapimeni”, released after his death in October 1983. It gathered his own recordings of poems by Turkish poet Nazim Hikmet, in Greek translations by Yannis Ritsos. In 1985, more than 50,000 people attended a memorial concert at the Athens Olympic Stadium. Dalaras, Alexiou, Kalatzis, Galani and Papakonstantinou performed there. Greek City Times has also profiled how Dalaras recorded with almost every major composer of his time, Loizos included. Greece’s music world marked 2007 as Manos Loizos Year, for 70 years since his birth and 25 since his death. Today, the Manos Loizos legacy lives on through new performers. They keep his melodies alive in concert halls and on the radio. title: Watchdog Finds Milos Hotel Should Never Have Got Permit
body: MILOS, October 2026 — The White Coast hotel on Milos should never have received a building permit, Greece’s National Transparency Authority has found, and it wants the permits revoked within two months. The watchdog carried out the investigation for the Ministry of Environment and Energy. Its findings were delivered to the main parties involved in the past few days, and the report is being forwarded to prosecutors to examine possible criminal liability. According to the report, the core problem is access. The White Coast site, owned by the company V Tourism, fronts only an unpaved farm road, as its own topographic plan states. Under planning law, a plot must front a formally recognised road before it can be built on. The authority said that “agricultural roads do not make plots buildable” . As a result, the Milos planning office should never have granted the project pre-approval, it found. Errors in the White Coast permit The volcanic coastline of Milos near Sarakiniko. Photo: dronepicr, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons Auditors also found that the permitted building ratio was set at 0.20 instead of the correct 0.18. That allowed 5,634 square metres of construction on the 28-stremma (2.8-hectare) site, instead of 5,070 square metres. Different ratios appeared on the topographic plan, the coverage diagram, the pre-approval and the technical report. In each case, the figures applied were those that favoured the developer, the report said. Additionally, the approved plans were never uploaded to the national e-permits system. This made it impossible to confirm that the plans cleared by the Central Council of Architecture matched those used to issue the permit. Inspectors who visited after pre-approval, but before the final permit, found that the north face of one building had already been built. The watchdog also said the architecture council’s approval lacked a properly reasoned opinion. Calls for revocation and a building freeze The authority wants disciplinary checks on Elisavet Chorianopoulou, who headed the Milos planning office at the time. She is now the South Aegean deputy regional governor for the environment. The report faults the office’s checks but does not accuse her of a crime. It also asked the Milos office to revoke the White Coast pre-approvals and permits, which would effectively declare the hotel unauthorised. According to English-language reports, 99 of its 271 planned beds are already operating. More broadly, the report said Milos is essentially unprotected, with no special planning limits even for its most valuable areas. It urged the ministry to extend the island’s suspension of works and new permits until a local urban plan is complete. A separate complaint that coastal plots had been extended onto public land was also examined. The watchdog concluded that the White Coast site is most likely private, although no land registry check was carried out. Earlier, the Council of State threw out an appeal by environmental groups against the hotel’s environmental licence, because it was filed too late. Greek City Times has reported on the White Coast expansion dispute and the suspension of building works on Milos . title: Maria Sakkari Chases One Last Ranking Boost in Tokyo
body: Maria Sakkari will close her 2026 season at the WTA 500 tournament in Tokyo, hoping to climb the rankings before the 2027 Australian Open seedings are set. The Greek player is entered in the event in the Japanese capital, which runs from 26 October to 1 November. It is her last chance to collect ranking points before her winter preparation begins. Sakkari heads to Japan on the back of a run to the quarterfinals of the Wuhan Open , where she picked up important wins and improved her position in the rankings. Why Tokyo matters for Maria Sakkari Maria Sakkari at the 2023 DC Open in Washington. Photo: Hameltion, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons In the WTA rankings published on 19 October, the 31-year-old was ranked world No. 31 with 1,706 points, just outside the top 30. Tokyo also matters for Melbourne. Her ranking when the Australian Open draw is made will decide whether she is among the 32 seeded players. A seeding would mean she cannot meet another seeded player in the first two rounds of the year’s first Grand Slam. Strong results in Tokyo could make her path through the opening rounds at Melbourne Park noticeably easier. Her 2026 season has had its highlights on home soil and beyond. In July she reached the final of the Athens Open, losing the title match to Barbora Krejcikova, and at the US Open she staged a comeback win in the opening week. Final preparations in Dubai Before the trip, Maria Sakkari has been in Dubai completing her preparation before travelling to Japan. In a post on Instagram, she wrote “Ready for the last battle” , signalling her focus on the final challenge of her year. Greek tennis fans in Australia will be watching closely, with Melbourne’s large Greek community traditionally among her loudest supporters at the Australian Open. title: Moonshot curbs hacking ability in new Kimi model as fears grow over AI-powered cyberattacks
body: Moonshot AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said on Saturday, October 24, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous AI could turbocharge hacking. Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model’s weights — files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems — by November 4. Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills. “We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability,” the company said. Governments, technology companies and security researchers are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks. Must Read Millions of hacking attempts as companies, governments rush to patch PHP flaws China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be used against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections. Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention. Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files are widely distributed, the original developer has less ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service. K3.1 Pro scored 81.0% on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5% for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The test involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model’s offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified. K3.1 Pro has a 1-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to three times the speed of the standard model. – Rappler.com

title: The Day History Stood Still: A Traveler’s Diary From Hiroshima
body: Standing in Hiroshima today left me truly speechless. I have visited many places in the course of my academic and professional life, from bustling capitals to quiet rural communities recovering from crisis, but standing in the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park this afternoon is an experience that sits quietly in my heart long after I walk away. I am here in Japan with the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) as part of a programme on state resilience, post-disaster recovery, and public governance. For weeks, we have been dissecting frameworks, resilience indices, reconstruction models, and governance structures that help societies bounce back from catastrophe. On paper, Hiroshima is the ultimate case study. However, being here in person hits you on a completely different, deeply human level. No report can capture it. The morning was cool and misty, the kind of weather that made the Motoyasu River look like glass. The park itself was immaculate, green, open, and serene. Students cycled past, elderly couples walked hand in hand, and tourists whispered. It was so deliberately peaceful that you almost forgot why it existed until you saw it: the Genbaku Dome. The Atomic Bomb Dome was not imposing. It was not grand. It was a ruin, left exactly as it was after 8:15 a.m. on August 6, 1945. The exposed steel ribs of its dome, the hollow windows, the crumbling brick, it stands in defiance of preservation. While the Americans wanted it demolished, the people of Hiroshima insisted it remain. Standing before it, I felt a deep, heavy silence fall around me, despite the crowd moving all around. It is the silence of 140,000 souls. It is the silence of a city that vanished in a flash of light brighter than the sun. Walking slowly to the Peace Memorial Museum shatters the comfortable distance of history, transforming the abstract date of August 6, 1945, when the atomic bomb was dropped, into an overwhelming confrontation with human loss and enduring resilience that echoes in your heart long after you leave. Inside, the air is different. You don’t see history. You feel it. They have chosen to tell the story not through numbers or military strategy, but through the ordinary: a child’s lunchbox, a small, blackened aluminium box with charred rice and peas still stuck inside. The owner, a first-year middle school student named Shigeru Orimen, never got to eat it. A wristwatch stopped at exactly 8:15. A little girl’s stained red dress. A tricycle that belonged to Shinichi Tetsutani, who was only three years old. He loved riding it; he died that night. Looking at these simple personal belongings, like a child’s lunchbox or a burned watch, you don’t think about politics, stats, or policies anymore. The language of governance, collateral damage, strategic necessity, and casualties loses all meaning. You think about families. You think about a mother packing lunch. You think about human lives that were getting ready for an ordinary Monday. It makes you feel the need to step outside for a moment. But what moved me to my core wasn’t just the history of sorrow; it was the story of what happened next. This is where Hiroshima becomes a profound lesson for every leader, every public servant, and every Nigerian who has experienced loss. In 1945, experts predicted that nothing would grow there for 75 years, that the soil was poisoned and the city was dead. Yet, by 1946, red canna lilies bloomed defiantly through the ashes. Taking that as a sign, the people of Hiroshima planted trees, rebuilt their homes, and cleared the rubble with their bare hands. They made a conscious, almost spiritual choice not to let bitterness define them. Refusing to build a city of revenge, they chose to build a city of peace. Instead of a memorial to anger, they created a global home for peace and hope, an act of leadership more profound than any policy document I have studied. An elderly hibakusha, an atomic bomb survivor in his late eighties who volunteers as a storyteller in the park, spoke to our group. He was seven when the bomb fell, and he lost his sister. He looked at us and said with a calm smile, “We hated the bomb, not the people.” I wrote that down immediately. Standing near the Children’s Peace Monument, surrounded by millions of colourful paper cranes sent by children from across the globe, I understood what he meant. The monument is dedicated to Sadako Sasaki, the 12-year-old girl who developed leukaemia from radiation and believed that folding 1,000 paper cranes would grant her wish to live. She died having folded over 1,300. Today, schools from Sokoto to São Paulo still send cranes here. I saw a fresh strand from Kenya just that morning. When I rang the Peace Bell, a large bell inscribed with a world map without borders, the sound did not just ring; it lingered. It travelled across the river and seemed to ask us all a question: What will you do with the peace you have? As a PhD candidate in Public Governance and Leadership, and as a Nigerian who has witnessed communities struggling to recover from conflict and disaster, I am taking home lessons that no lecture could ever teach. Resilience is not built on infrastructure alone. It is rooted in identity. Hiroshima rebuilt not just roads and houses, but a new identity for itself, transforming from victim to peacemaker. True resilience is demonstrated when a people decide who they want to become after a tragedy. Hope became a public policy. The city government made hope tangible. They preserved the Dome not to remember death, but to protect peace. They created spaces where the world must come and promise “never again.” Hope was institutionalised. Real strength lies not in how hard we fight, but in how deeply we care for each other and protect peace. This city forgave a world that had destroyed it, and in doing so, it gained moral authority over that same world. Buildings can be replaced, but hope is what truly rebuilds a society. Hiroshima is living proof that no matter how deep the trial or how total the loss, a people united in hope, and guided by visionary, compassionate leadership, can always rise again. Not just to return to what they were, but to become even greater. I left a paper crane there. I folded it poorly, but I folded it with Nigeria in my heart. Arigato, Hiroshima. Thank you for teaching me. Mahmud Muhammad is a PhD candidate in Public Governance and Leadership, currently on a study programme in Japan with JICA

title: US has spent $11b in taxpayer money to defend Israel in 3 yrs
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 24 (MNA) – Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi has said that the United States has, over the past three years, spent $11 billion in taxpayer money on missile defense for the Zionist regime.
In a post on his X account late on Friday, Iran’s top diplomat wrote, “The US has, over the past three years, spent $11 BILLION in taxpayer money on missile defense for Israel.”
It has fired more interceptors defending Israel than Israel has, he emphasized, noting, “This is not a symbolic relationship. It is a parasitic one.”

title: 2 Injured as Russian Strike Hits House in Kyiv
body:
A Russian aerial strike damaged a private residential home in Kyiv’s northern Obolonskyi district early Saturday morning, Oct. 24, injuring two people, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) reported .
According to municipal authorities, an air raid alert was declared across the capital at approximately 3:42 a.m. local time after the Ukrainian Air Force Command detected several adversary turbojet-powered strike drones maneuvering directly above the city.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Emergency responders, medical personnel, and specialized civil defense teams deployed to the impact zone in the Obolonskyi district to secure the perimeter, assist the victims, and inspect the structural integrity of neighboring residences. Officials confirmed that two civilians sustained injuries in the strike and were provided with immediate medical care.
The capital strike was part of an overnight air assault launched by Russian forces from 6:00 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 23, through Saturday morning.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force Command, Russian forces launched 126 strike and decoy unmanned aerial systems against Ukrainian territory. The incoming wave included 61 high-speed turbojet-powered Shahed variants, alongside S-8000 Banderol and Dan-T compact cruise systems, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoy platforms.
Munitions were staged and launched from multiple staging areas, including Shatalovo, Oryol, Bryansk, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk within Russia, as well as occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea .
The aerial assault was engaged by Ukrainian combat aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare forces, unmanned systems detachments, and mobile air defense fire teams.
As of 8:00 a.m. on Saturday, Ukrainian air defenses had intercepted or electronically suppressed 101 aerial targets nationwide, including 50 turbojet-powered Shahed loitering munitions. Air Force Command reported that kinetic impacts were registered across 14 distinct locations nationwide, while falling wreckage from intercepted targets was logged at five sites.
The strike on Kyiv’s residential sector follows a sequence of deadly Russian standoff bombardments directed against urban settlements in eastern Ukraine.
In the Donetsk region, Russian tactical aircraft released three FAB-250 high-explosive aerial bombs fitted with universal glide and correction modules (UMPK) against an urban residential sector of Kramatorsk on Friday, Oct. 23.
The Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office confirmed that the Friday strikes killed one civilian, wounded six others—including three young children – and damaged at least 27 private residences.
Among the six wounded in Kramatorsk were two women aged 45 and 54, a 47-year-old man, two girls aged 7 and 10, and their one-year-and-10-month-old brother. Medical personnel confirmed that the victims sustained blast trauma, traumatic brain injuries, acoustic concussions, and penetrating shrapnel wounds.
The bombardment in Kramatorsk on Friday followed strikes on the same municipality on Tuesday, Oct. 20, which killed four civilians, including three municipal heating workers executing emergency winterization repairs on the city’s district heating network.
An additional civilian was killed that day in a separate first-person view (FPV) drone attack, while at least six others sustained injuries alongside extensive damage to apartment buildings and educational institutions.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Swift response key to limiting environmental impact of UAE oil spill, experts say
body: Rapid containment of an oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is essential to limit potential damage to the UAE’s marine ecosystems, experts have warned after authorities confirmed the spill off its coast . The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirmed the spill on Friday after residents in Dubai and the Northern Emirates reported a strong fuel-like smell earlier this week. Rob Mortimer, chief executive of Dubai-based Fuelre4m, which supplies substances used to disperse oil slicks, said the initial priority should be “to keep it all together” using floating barriers known as booms, allowing as much as possible to be recovered from the sea surface. “It’s reasonably easy to do it while it’s all together,” he said. “Once it’s spreading and moving around, it’s more difficult. Even with the dispersant, you have to cover a greater distance … The longer you leave it, the more the oil gets dispersed.” Another early measure, Mr Mortimer said, is to use dispersants, substances that break oil into tiny droplets. Dispersants break oil into tiny droplets, making it easier for naturally occurring microorganisms to break it down into simpler compounds, including carbon dioxide, water, and other harmless products. However, using these substances requires careful assessment because some can harm marine organisms, including corals, fish, crustaceans and plankton. “You have got to look at how toxic these dispersants are themselves,” Mr Mortimer said. “Some of the chemicals that are used, they’re not very nice. You have to weigh up whether the treatment is better. Sometimes it’s quite marginal.” The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirms the UAE’s technical monitoring and environmental assessment system detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain’s beaches. Odors noticed in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain pose no health risks to residents. Teams… pic.twitter.com/KKIP45k1Dj — ‎وزارة التغير المناخي والبيئة (@MoCCaEUAE) October 22, 2026 When dealing with oil slicks, preventing pollution from reaching the coast is typically a top priority. If that happens, clean-up becomes harder, and habitats can suffer lasting harm. “Once it hits the shoreline, you have to do a lot of clean-up and remediation,” Mr Mortimer said. Clean-up operation Prof Richard Thompson, director of the Marine Institute at the University of Plymouth, said cleaning a wide, sandy beach would typically be a less complex task than dealing with a rocky shoreline. “If you have intertidal habitats with a large range of organisms, it’s going to make it more difficult to clean than if you can capture it [the oil] at the sea surface,” he said. “If it’s among rocks or mangroves or seagrass, it’s going to be very difficult to clean … Ideally what you’re trying to do is catch it before you get the encounters between the creatures and the oil.” The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has highlighted the trade-offs in using dispersants, including the benefits of removing oil from the sea surface and reducing the risk of shoreline contamination, weighed against potential effects on plankton and other organisms in the water column. “Part of the work of planning the response to potential oil spills is the difficult task of evaluating these trade-offs, which requires careful consideration of the resources and issues involved,” the agency said in an online briefing document. Mr Mortimer said Fuelre4m supplied vegetable-based substances intended to disperse oil and was seeking approval from UAE authorities to use them. The risks associated with some oil-spill treatment chemicals were highlighted after the Torrey Canyon tanker ran aground off south-west England in 1967 while transporting oil from Kuwait to Wales. Some of the chemicals used to disperse the resulting slick were reported to have been more toxic to marine life than the oil itself. Taking action Umm Al Quwain Municipality said on Friday it was working to contain the pollution and to reduce any harm to marine and coastal environments. The source of the oil has not been officially confirmed. This oil spill is the latest in a series of incidents that have raised concern about the “unprecedented” environmental effects of this year’s US-Iran war. In response to the spill, beaches and coastal areas in Umm Al Quwain were closed, while Sharjah’s Al Hamriya Beach was also shut. Inesaf Benzaki, campaigns lead at Greenpeace Mena, said timely containment was particularly important because the Gulf’s semi-enclosed geography limited the exchange of water with the open ocean, potentially allowing pollutants to persist. “We acknowledge the UAE authorities’ ongoing efforts to contain the reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain and address its immediate effects,” she said. “As these efforts continue, understanding the potential environmental impact will be important to protecting the area’s marine ecosystems.” Ms Benzaki said the coastline formed part of a wider marine environment where shallow coastal waters, mangroves, seagrass meadows and lagoons provided important habitats for marine life and supported coastal livelihoods. She warned that even after visible oil was removed, residues could remain in coastal sediments and sensitive habitats, prolonging the spill's effects. If oil reached the UAE coastline, it could “threaten sensitive marine and coastal ecosystems”, she said. Continued environmental monitoring and assessment would help establish the extent of any damage, identify areas requiring further attention and guide recovery measures, she added. Protecting these ecosystems matters not only for marine biodiversity but also for coastal communities that depend on healthy seas. Prof John Burt, director of New York University Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, previously warned that if oil reached the coastline, remediation could be expensive and a full recovery could take years. Millions of barrels of oil were released into the northern Arabian Gulf during the 1990-91 Gulf War. Prof Burt said submerged habitats, including coral reefs and seagrass beds, were not as severely affected in some areas because oil generally floats on the water’s surface. However, coastal areas in the northern Gulf that oil reached suffered considerable damage. Mangroves and mudflats used by feeding birds were among the affected habitats, while footage from the period showed birds covered in oil. The latest incident has renewed attention on the importance of rapid containment, careful selection of clean-up methods and sustained environmental monitoring to limit potential damage to the Gulf’s marine and coastal ecosystems.

title: Kazakhstan’s Recycling Problem Is Not Lack of Willingness
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. Editor’s note: The Astana Times continues a section featuring articles by our readers. As a platform that values diverse perspectives and meaningful conversations, we believe that this section provides space for readers to share their thoughts and insights on various topics that matter to them and the AT audience. Samat Tulepbayev. Photo credit: Samat Tulepbayev’s personal archive. Kazakhstan has entered 2026 with an ambitious new plan for dealing with its waste. The government’s Waste Management Concept for 2026–2030 calls for less landfill disposal, more recycling and better monitoring of where waste ultimately goes. The timing could hardly be better. In 2025, Kazakhstan collected 4.1 million tonnes of municipal waste — 7.7% more than the year before. The country is producing more waste, and the question is no longer whether recycling matters. It is whether the system makes recycling easy enough for ordinary people to participate. The central problem is surprisingly simple: Kazakhstan’s waste system still places too much responsibility on individual citizens and too little on the infrastructure surrounding them. I see this problem in Astana. At home, I separate plastic, paper and cans instead of throwing everything into one bin. But doing so is only the first step. I often have to take recyclable materials myself to private collection points. For someone already motivated to recycle, this is possible. For a family rushing to work, taking children to school and dealing with daily responsibilities, it becomes a lower priority. This is why telling people to “be more environmentally responsible” will never be enough. Kazakhstan is not starting from zero. Astana already operates a two-fraction collection system separating “dry” materials such as paper, plastic, glass and metal from “wet” waste such as food. The city has thousands of waste containers and collection sites. Nationally, progress is also visible: 1.5 million tonnes of municipal waste were sorted in 2025, 16.3% more than in 2024. Astana alone accounted for 377,000 tonnes of sorted waste. Yet sorting statistics tell only part of the story. Waste must be separated correctly, collected separately, transported without being mixed again and eventually reach a recycler that can use it. If any step in that chain fails, a carefully separated plastic bottle may ultimately have the same destination as ordinary household rubbish. A more effective waste system therefore has to make separation convenient, rewarding and accountable. Convenience comes first. Residents should encounter the same simple system wherever they live: clearly marked containers, consistent colours and straightforward instructions showing what belongs where. Collection schedules should ensure that separated waste remains separated throughout transportation. Organic waste deserves particular attention because food mixed with paper and other recyclables can contaminate material that might otherwise be reused. Kazakhstan’s Environmental Code already assigns local authorities responsibility for organizing environmentally safe municipal-waste systems, including separate collection. The challenge is turning that principle into an everyday routine people can trust. Incentives can reinforce that routine. Deposit-return systems for bottles and cans, discounts or rewards for recycling, and convenient collection points can give recyclable materials visible value. The objective is not to pay people simply for behaving responsibly. It is to design a system in which throwing valuable materials into a landfill becomes the least attractive option. Finally, accountability matters. Residents are less likely to spend time separating waste if they suspect everything is mixed together later. Municipalities and waste operators could publish simple data showing how much waste was collected separately, how much was actually recycled and how much went to landfill. Digital tracking, one of the priorities in Kazakhstan’s new waste strategy, could help make those flows more transparent. Kazakhstan’s new waste policy sets a target of reducing the amount of municipal waste sent to landfills by 10% from the 2025 level by 2030. Meeting targets like this will depend not only on new recycling plants or government strategies, but on millions of small decisions made every day in kitchens, apartment courtyards and workplaces. The important lesson extends far beyond Kazakhstan. Governments often treat recycling as a question of environmental awareness: educate people, run campaigns and hope for behaviour changes. But awareness works best when infrastructure makes the responsible choice the easy choice. People should not have to be environmental enthusiasts to recycle. A successful waste system is one in which an ordinary resident can separate a bottle, a cardboard box or food waste without giving the process much thought. That is when recycling stops being an individual effort and starts becoming normal urban infrastructure. The author is Samat Tulepbayev, a graduate student at the Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Public Policy.
