Streaming second (Litestream): one writer, cheap recovery, no cluster. Merge third (cr-sqlite, and parts of the local-first movement): many writers, eventual consistency. Each is correct for a different question, and most of the arguments are arguments between their users about which question is being asked.
And the money went to the platforms. rqlite, dqlite, and Litestream are open source and free. The projects that raised the capital or got acquired are the ones that turned replicated SQLite into a service with a bill. That is the usual fate of infrastructure ideas, and I do not mind it. But it is worth recording that the idea was open source for eight years before anyone sold it.
rqlite is still here. It does the same thing it did in 2014, a good deal better, and it is still the thing you reach for when you want a fault-tolerant relational database you can run yourself, understand fully, and not pay anyone for. Twelve years in, I am content with that position in the story.

title: Indian Pilot Flight Tests Major Su-30 Fighter Upgrade as Air Force Considers Deep Modernisation
body: Indian and Russian air force personnel have conducted joint combat exercises using Su-30SM2 fighter aircraft in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region as part of the wider Indra 2026 military exercise. According to Russia’s Ministry of Defence, the training focused on engaging small, low-flying targets and destroying aircraft carrying short- and medium-range aerial weapons. Crews also practised air combat manoeuvres at medium and low altitudes, strengthening operational coordination between the two countries’ air forces. The exercises come as India pursues an extensive modernisation programme for its Su-30MKI fleet under the Super Sukhoi initiative, with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) expected to play a central role. The programme has been reported to target an initial batch of 84 aircraft, with the potential for upgrades to be extended to more than 200 additional fighters. After developing the Su-30MKI to meet Indian requirements in the late 1990s and early 2000s, Russia developed a superior variant for its own fleet, the Su-30SM, and has since enhanced them to the Su-30SM2 standard, potentially providing a template for some of the upgrades that will be offered to India. This could include integration of AL-41F-1S engines that have been used on the Su-30SM2, providing a far superior flight performance, a longer range through improved fuel efficiency, and reduced operational costs and maintenance needs. The engines have comparable thrust levels and thrust to weight ratios to early fifth generation engines such as the F119 powering the F-22 fighter. The Su-30MKI has been by far the most successful Russian fighter type on foreign markets in the post-Soviet era, with comprehensive modernisation across the fleet expected to be a leading source of revenue for Russia’s defence sector. The integration of the AL-41F-1S can considerably improve availability rates for the large and high maintenance aircraft. It would also provide three dimensional thrust vectoring capabilities. The integration of new armaments, most notably the much improved R-77M air-to-air missile, is also expected. The modernisation of the Su-30 fleet is being planned as talks are ongoing for the sale of more advanced Su-57 fifth generation fighters, which would provide highly complementary capabilities to the Su-30. The perceived underperformance of the Indian Fighter fleet during operations against Pakistan in May 2025, with the loss of several fighters confirmed including at least one newly procured French Rafale, is considered a major factor stimulating interest in modernising the Su-30MKI. During a visit by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India from December 4, representatives of both countries reportedly discussed plans to upgrade the Su-30MKI fleet and the possibly of further expanding production. Indian industry was confirmed in August 2026 to be reviving production of the Su-30MKI, with the first deliveries expected to begin during the next financial year. A total of 222 Su-30MKI fighters had before this already been produced under licence agreement with Russia, with 50 more having been built in Russia and delivered to the Indian Air Force fully assembled.

title: Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing at training
body: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club’s second team train on Friday. The 40-year-old had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday prior to Bayern’s Champions League game against Arsenal. The former Manchester City and Belgium defender was subsequently on the touchline for the match on Wednesday. Reports in Germany say Kompany is in a stable condition in hospital. “Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during an FC Bayern reserve team training session on Friday,” said a statement from the Bundesliga club., external “The first-team head coach was watching the second string’s session. “Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations in hospital and will remain under medical care. “His coaching staff will oversee training and match activities until further notice.” Bayern’s next game is against Freiburg in the German top flight on Sunday. “Vincent Kompany’s health is our top priority. We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure his speedy recovery,” said Bayern sporting director Max Eberl. “Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, and all the time he needs. “His coaching team, in whom we have complete confidence, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery.” Aaron Danks, one of Kompany’s assistants, took the pre-match news conference for Bayern before the Arsenal game. German football journalist Taufig Khalil told BBC Radio 5 Live that Kompany had been “suffering with the virus for about a week”. He added: “The thing started last weekend on Saturday against Leipzig, and that’s the first time we saw Vincent Kompany [when] he didn’t look very well. “He didn’t do the press conference after, and Max Eberl told us that he’s suffering with a virus. “Everybody was really surprised that Vincent Kompany was standing there with his black jacket in the pouring rain of Munich on Wednesday night against Arsenal. Everybody expected Aaron Danks to be there. “The problem was that maybe you couldn’t bench Vincent Kompany, the game was too important for him. “Bayern Munich just told us that he’s in stable conditions. There was a helicopter involved in the whole thing, which landed on the training ground at Bayern Munich, but he was not brought into the hospital by helicopter. They brought him with a medical car and he will be now there.” ‘Get well soon, Vinny’ Kompany left his role as Burnley manager to take over at Bayern in May 2024, succeeding current England manager Thomas Tuchel. He had won the Championship with Burnley in 2022-23 and, despite the Clarets being relegated from the Premier League under him the following season, Kompany was appointed by the Bundesliga club. He has led Bayern to the German top-flight title in the past two seasons and reached the 2025-26 Champions League semi-finals before being beaten by eventual winners Paris St-Germain. Kompany spent 11 years at Manchester City as a player, winning four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and four League Cups. “Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and club legend, Vincent Kompany,” said City in a post on social media. “Get well soon, Vinny.” “Everyone here at Burnley FC sends our best wishes to Vincent and we wish him a speedy recovery,” said a Burnley statement.

title: Interest Rate Cut: Is Now Right Time to Take Loan?
body: Omolabake Fasogbon A cut in the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) monetary policy rate (MPR) usually raises hopes that loans will become cheaper for households and businesses. The expectation is understandable: when banks’ borrowing costs fall, customers may eventually benefit too. In September, the CBN cut its benchmark rate from 26.5 per cent to 23 per cent amid easing inflation and relative stability in the foreign exchange market. The move aimed to make credit more affordable. For a household planning a major purchase or a business hoping to expand, this may seem like the right time to borrow. But a rate cut does not mean banks will immediately reduce the interest charged on loans. Lower rates at the CBN do not always reach customers, and industry stakeholders have repeatedly questioned why borrowing costs remain high after monetary policy is eased. The CBN wants cheaper credit to encourage investment, production and job creation. It can also help reduce government financing costs and improve productivity. For households and business owners, the practical question is: should they borrow now or wait? Why Loans May Not Get Cheaper Banks consider more than the CBN’s benchmark rate when deciding what to charge customers. Their rates also reflect funding costs, operating expenses, the risk of non-payment, available cash, regulatory requirements and uncertainty in the economy. Another factor is the 45 per cent Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), which requires banks to keep a portion of deposits with the CBN rather than lend it out. Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, Dr Muda Yusuf, said the high ratio limits the share of deposits available for loans and raises the cost of providing financial services. Yusuf said lower MPRs failing to reduce borrowing costs had been a longstanding concern and pointed to weaknesses in Nigeria’s financial system, including limited financial access, fragmented credit markets, high lending risks and inadequate systems for assessing borrowers. Who Benefits First? Even when rates fall, not everyone benefits equally. Larger companies often have stronger financial records, better collateral, lower perceived risk and greater bargaining power. Yusuf said they are better placed to negotiate cheaper loans or refinance existing debts. Small and medium-sized businesses, despite their importance to the economy, face a tougher challenge. Many have limited assets to offer as security, fewer financing options and less power to negotiate with lenders. As a result, their borrowing costs may fall more slowly and by less. What Businesses Should Do Now While waiting for lower rates to reach borrowers, businesses can review their finances and borrowing plans. Finance expert Dr. Ozemoya Pedro, advised owners to assess existing loans and consider whether refinancing or renegotiating could reduce repayments. He cautioned against taking a loan simply because rates are falling. Businesses should calculate how much they need and compare complete offers from banks, fintech companies and development finance institutions. The advertised interest rate is only part of the cost; fees, repayment periods and other conditions matter too. Pedro also advised businesses to prepare financial statements, cash-flow records and tax documents before applying. Lenders will assess whether applicants can repay their debts. Any borrowed money, he said, should go towards activities that produce measurable returns. A loan is useful only when it supports real business growth. Households should apply the same discipline. Before borrowing, work out whether repayments fit income and essential expenses, compare the total cost of offers and avoid taking on debt simply in the hope that rates will fall later. Existing Loans, Savings and Investments The rate cut may create opportunities to restructure or refinance debts, but stronger borrowers are likely to have more room to negotiate. Yusuf said customers with floating-rate loans may qualify for lower rates, depending on the benchmark and the terms agreed with lenders. Fixed-rate loans generally retain their interest rates until maturity unless the borrower and lender agree to renegotiate or refinance. Savings and investments may also be affected. Lower MPRs can moderate returns on bank deposits and newly issued fixed-income products. Investors may consider spreading their money across assets, including shares and property, according to their goals and willingness to take risks. Yusuf said the cut signals a move towards less restrictive monetary conditions. This could help businesses plan with greater confidence, encourage investment and give borrowers an opening to renegotiate financing. However, the benefits depend on inflation continuing to ease, exchange-rate stability and confidence in economic policy. He called for further reforms to ensure lower MPRs translate more quickly into affordable loans. These include gradually reducing the CRR when conditions permit, improving credit information and lending efficiency, expanding financing for small businesses, and maintaining fiscal discipline so government borrowing does not crowd out private-sector credit. For households and businesses, a CBN rate cut may create an opportunity, but it does not guarantee cheap borrowing for everyone. Compare offers, understand the full repayment cost and borrow only when the money serves a clear purpose and repayments are affordable.

title: Benedict Oramah: Africa Must Build Its Own AI Models, Not Just Supply the Data
body: Former President of Afreximbank, Dr. Benedict Oramah, has urged Africa to build its own artificial intelligence models rather than remain a supplier of data to foreign technology firms, stressing the need for greater economic independence. In this interview with Nume Ekeghe on the sidelines of the just-concluded IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, he argues that Nigeria can leverage its cheap gas to power data centres, establish technology parks and attract investment, while calling for massive infrastructure financing, industrialisation and deeper continental trade to drive growth and create jobs Y ou have completed your tenure at Afreximbank and established Marob Strategies and Consulting, what services does Marob Strategies offer and what are your plans for it? I just completed my two terms of office at Afreximbank. You know the journey we embarked on, which I’ve been involved in for the past 30 years. Fragmentation as you know is the bane of the continent. Finishing at Afreximbank does not mean that the problem has been solved. As I moved on to other things, I kept focusing on the challenges that we had to solve, and there aren’t enough soldiers to attack that problem. Retreating when you still have energy would betray the commitment to the continent. I never saw my departure from Afreximbank as retirement because, thank God, I still have the energy and the faculties. It would be a disservice to the continent if the experience, contacts and capabilities acquired over time were lost overnight. Marob is the strategy firm we have established. I have always believed that one of Africa’s challenges is the proper articulation of strategy and its execution. That is what I created Marob to do. It is not primarily about making money, although we have to generate revenue to meet our obligations. Essentially, it is about continuing to develop strategic interventions that I believe the continent still needs, helping African institutions articulate their strategies, and mobilising the capabilities and resources required to execute them efficiently. I believe we can do even more for the continent through Marob because it gives me greater freedom to think and challenge conventional wisdom. Once we develop and test these ideas, we can take them back to Afreximbank, other African multilateral financial institutions, commercial banks and other organisations working across the continent. Your work with Dangote’s refinery and its subsequent share offering has attracted attention. What informed Afreximbank’s support for the project? We expected the reception because Dangote had built a brand, and we helped him build it. We are happy that Dangote became what it is and the refinery itself. It’s all credit to Alhaji Aliko Dangote’s perseverance and determination. For us at Afreximbank, when we were supporting him, a bank can only do so much. We began by doing principal financing, but we were looking for entrepreneurs. A bank has money, but a bank is not organised to do certain things. For a bank to be effective, you need entrepreneurs who are credible, trustworthy, who can envision, execute and strategise. Dangote embodies all of this, and that refinery, for me, was a no brainer to support. I recall that initially, our first facility to the refinery was almost a billion dollars. When we went to the board, I didn’t go there to argue about credit. My argument to them was that when we see this kind of thing in other parts of the world, we say these people are doing great things. This one is here. This is our project. I told them I didn’t think this is a matter of credit, but a matter of continental pride and continental survival. Since we started that relationship, Afreximbank has provided $18 billion. Most of it was to the refinery. I must also say it’s not just me. There was no way I was going to do it alone. The management, everybody, believed in it. It was like a mission, and I bought into it. When it got to this stage and we had to do the IPO and the private placement, I was very pleased that Alhaji recognised all of that and gave us the opportunity to participate in a big way. We worked with Afreximbank to underwrite about 25 per cent of the private placement and also about 24 to 25 per cent of the IPO. That was a significant opportunity, and I believe it shows Alhaji’s appreciation of the road we travelled together. Afreximbank always achieves smooth transition between presidents, unlike many African institutions where former leaders are pushed out. Why is continuity important? I think people who fight like that are small people, and people who doubt their competence. Why would you throw away a trove of wisdom that will make you stronger? I’ve done my own. I’m gone. But if I can contribute to making President Elombi successful, I think it would be stupid of President Elombi to tell me not to contribute because it’s him. I was in the bank from day one, so I know all the challenges. I was privileged to have worked very closely with all the presidents as an adviser and special assistant, handling very sensitive issues, research and strategy. That experience helped me later because there was hardly anything we went through that I didn’t know about or participate in resolving. As president, why would I throw that knowledge away? There were times when I had to go back to my predecessors for advice. I remember when we wanted to develop the idea of export trading companies. Rather than issue a request for proposals to find an expert, I told the team to bring in a former president of the bank because I knew his experience in export trading companies. He helped us undertake the study, and that work eventually led to the establishment of the African Trade and Distribution Company. If I had burnt that bridge, would I have been able to go back to him? Even if we paid him more, he might not have been willing to help us. That is how we approach continuity at Afreximbank. It is not just about presidents; it also applies to staff. Whenever we have a task that a former colleague can handle, we bring them in. It is not only because we want to support our colleagues, but because we know their capabilities and can identify who is best suited to do the job. So, I would be surprised if President Elombi discarded that experience. In fact, he has continued to involve me, and I have had to tell him that I also need to attend to other things. For us, it is about preserving institutional knowledge and using the experience of people who have helped build the bank to strengthen the work that continues. You earlier spoke about building a continental strategy and advisory firm. What problem are you trying to solve? The big picture for me is that we build a number one continental strategy and advisory firm, so that we no longer have a situation where our people run to someone else to do the things we can do. We are already rapidly going there because of the kind of mandates we are getting. I would rather find partnerships than tell a country, company or bank that comes to us that we are overstretched. Ultimately, we may become the nucleus of a federated advisory platform that brings credible advisory firms in different African countries under one umbrella, so that we can give our people the right advice. Your Pan-African approach to business is quite strong. Where does this conviction come from? Everybody in the banking business, including our governments and corporates has to regard themselves as economic freedom fighters. We are combatants for economic freedom. Those in banking and financial services are engaged in financial guerrilla warfare. Our sensibilities have been numbed by the so-called belief that things are good. We did not understand that there is still economic bondage. It is only now that we are beginning to break away from it. During the struggle for political independence, many of those who fought for it went into the bushes, fought with guns, were killed and were jailed. They were ready to sacrifice and pay the supreme price. That is why we can go around, carry flags and say we are a nation. But if you read the works of people such as Nkrumah and Nyerere, you recognise that this was just the beginning. Political independence gives you the platform to achieve the ultimate independence, which is economic independence. We were quickly sabotaged in pursuing this. There used to be a time when the issue was the struggle against neocolonialism. It quickly disappeared from the lexicon, so that we no longer remembered there was something to deal with. The fight we are in now is not going to be fought in trenches, but on factory floors, in technology incubation centres and so on. It is not going to be fought with brute force. It will be fought with ideas. Capital is key, not bullets. That capital includes human capital. Afreximbank supported several initiatives aimed at integrating African economies. What do these initiatives say about the continent’s ability to achieve economic independence? I’m very proud of what we did at Afreximbank during my time, and even before, under my predecessors. The first meeting of the Organisation of African Unity in May 1963 produced key decisions. The leaders asked the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa to conduct a study towards delivering a continental free trade area, an African Payments Union, a Pan-African trade fair, transit schemes and a strategy to break the technical attachment of currencies to foreign currencies. We didn’t know this until after we had done some of the things ourselves. In 2018, the AfCFTA was launched, and we supported the process. We were paying the salaries of quite a few people. Even the negotiations of protocols were supported by grants we provided. We launched the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), which the African Union adopted. We introduced the Pan-African Transit Guarantee Scheme, and we organised the Intra-African Trade Fair. We never saw that 1963 resolution. We only discovered it after we had asked a team to examine the African Union’s archives and identify decisions from many years ago that were still relevant but had not been implemented. When they came back and told me what they found, I asked, why did it take 60 years? The leaders knew that after independence, we had to move quickly to integrate our economies. At the AfCFTA signing, you said signing papers would not open borders. Why has implementation been difficult? We have really progressed. One of the surprises for me was when we came to Rwanda to open the papers for signing the AfCFTA. We thought 21 countries would sign, based on all the discussions. But as the books were opened, I think 45 countries signed that day. The problem is that we have been divided and fragmented into these atomistic units for so long. There are vested interests and so much fear of losing authority or power that people think will happen if they open up and start implementing what they signed. To be fair, I don’t expect everybody to be so open-minded. You just need a strong nucleus to get things moving. It is moving now. I think 24 countries have created their tariff schedules, which means they can implement the agreement. Non-tariff barriers remain the biggest problem. It took the Europeans almost 50 years to achieve what they achieved. It will take time, but I always knew that businesses would push the boundaries. People always said we had infrastructure problems and that was why we were not trading among ourselves. My view was, and remains, that Africa has infrastructure challenges, but the infrastructure deficit is a generalised challenge. The stock of infrastructure on the continent today can carry, depending on the year, between $1 trillion and $1.4 trillion of African trade. The question is, why is Africa’s share of that trade only between $170 billion and $200 billion? Why is it not $800 billion? The infrastructure stock can carry more than $1 trillion, yet our share is only 15 to 16 per cent. Why is it not 30 per cent? China’s share of our trade is higher than the trade we do among ourselves. The issue is trade information. We don’t know what is going on around Africa. Our traders and businesses trust Chinese, Europeans and Americans more than they trust the person next to them because they don’t know what is happening in neighbouring countries. We have factories in Ethiopia manufacturing leather products that import semi-processed leather from New Zealand at a higher cost than Burundi exports the same product to the world. We have many such absurdities. That’s one of the reasons we created trading companies, trade information platforms and the trade fair. How can Africa bridge its infrastructure gap when governments cannot provide all the required financing? I always knew there was no way governments could finance the infrastructure gap. To bring African infrastructure to world standards would require investment of about $100 billion a year. That is more than a trillion dollars over time. I asked my team to aggregate the budgets of all African countries, and I found that it would amount to about 60 per cent of their total budgets. You don’t need to be a rocket scientist to know that would not work. You need private capital. The only way is to demonstrate that there are businesses. Once businesses demonstrate the opportunity, private capital will finance infrastructure. People who invest in commercial infrastructure don’t need anybody to plead with them. The business case will attract them. What policies should Nigeria and other African countries adopt to create decent jobs? I don’t see anything other than a better economy that grows. Then you have to invest in human capital. There are jobs people are looking for people to fill, but they cannot find them because we have so many people who do not have the training and education to fill those jobs. The birth rate is very high, which is good, but we have to invest in human capital. We have to invest in quality education right from the first year in school and produce the right calibre of skills for the decent jobs we are talking about. I went to a company in Nigeria that does additive manufacturing. They wanted me to come and help them. Initially, I was skeptical, but when I saw what they were doing, I was surprised. It is 3D printing. You need skills in computer-aided design, material science and other areas. They have to go to India to get some of these skills. When you expand a refinery, you don’t necessarily double the number of jobs because some things can still be done by the people already there. But the refinery may start looking for skilled people and not find them. There may be thousands of jobs that it can only fill partially. I am the chairman of a number of companies, and I know the challenges we face. At our hospital and African centres of excellence, we sometimes struggle to find people with the appropriate skills. We prioritise quality service. It is not charity. The economy has to grow to create opportunities, but the system has to produce the quality of human capital that the growing economy needs, through formal and vocational education and relevant skills. I must also add good healthcare because healthcare is part of human development. We have to read the trends and create financing arrangements that support young people who want to start businesses. Some will fail and some will succeed, but the few that succeed may become the Google or SpaceX of the world. Except for a few countries, our educational systems are not producing the right kind of people. Our universities are not being funded to train people, and only a few have the capabilities. We also need vocational education because quite a lot of jobs will emerge from labour-intensive manufacturing. There will be repetitive jobs, technical jobs and jobs created by expanding manufacturing. These can be decent jobs. If somebody has good skills, they will get paid well and can set up their own company. How can African countries use artificial intelligence to drive industrialisation and economic growth? AI is a fact of life now. But we should make sure we don’t become those who are just applying models and using what other people have done. We should also generate our own models. One of the things additive manufacturing does is shorten production time. You don’t need to keep physical inventory. You keep the computer design and use it when needed. The waiting time for certain parts can sometimes be 15 months, but they can manufacture them in days. One of the things the Nigerian company is doing is manufacturing parts for the oil industry, where equipment is very old. Some of the parts no longer have designs, so they use infrared to examine them and create the designs. They told me that what used to take months to design now takes hours with AI. China is leading in AI because of its population. They are generating data all the time. In Africa, we should not allow ourselves to be feeders of the data that people use to build models. We should build our own. To do this, you need data centres. Data centres require huge power, and we haven’t even met the basic electricity demand. My attitude is that we can build technology parks where we concentrate energy and diversify sources, using solar, gas and whatever is available. We are working with people on an AI factory and technology park. Nigeria is in a good position because we have cheap gas. The country should make a decision to build technology parks and sell electricity at a price that attracts investment. You will see heavy investment, people who can do the civil works, people who can work in the data centres and people who bring equipment. Some investors don’t want to do the civil works. They want to set up their facilities and lease the infrastructure. What would you consider your major legacy at Afreximbank, and how is the bank performing under your successor? The legacy is the people you leave behind who continue the work, and the way they continue to think and do things. At Afreximbank, we amplified the mantra we work with: ‘If it is possible, it will be done; if it is impossible, it can be done.’ I believe we proved that we can be architects of our own future and not rely on anybody for anything. We were not driven by so-called international best practice. We focused on African best practice, rooted in our realities, ambitions and priorities. The idea of people coming to exploit us and saying they are helping us is something we quickly made sure was gone. Nobody can deal with us except on a win-win basis. You are gaining, we are gaining. We are not going to beg you. If you give us something, of course we will take it, but with dignity. You cannot give it to us and make us look like beggars. The way we do things in Afreximbank is that we have overlapping strategies. President Elombi is completing my second strategy, which ends this year. They have just completed their retreat, and they will launch a new five-year plan starting in January. Some of the things we started are multi-year endeavours. They don’t just stop. The fact that he is giving impetus to those things we worked on together is important. He was part of them, so I don’t see him suddenly repudiating what he was part of. That is not our culture in Afreximbank. We debate a lot. Everybody has a chance to bring their ideas when we conceive things. That’s why most people support whatever we commit to, and that’s why we execute them. It looks seamless because we debate things thoroughly and consider different views. Financially, so far, things are very good in my view. They are doing very well. In terms of development work, he has taken the course we set and is emphasising value addition and manufacturing. I don’t think the strategy he will announce will deviate violently from the direction of travel we had set for the continent. The Pan-African Transit Guarantee Scheme is being continued. The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System is becoming continental. The African Trade and Distribution Company has been established, and the Africa Energy Bank is expected to launch. The constitutional financing window will bring a new way of doing concessional financing. Some of the existing concessional financing arrangements make capital too dependent on governments. This window will provide concessional financing to the private sector. Take Nigeria for example, somebody wants to build a textile factory. He has to build his own power plant, water treatment plant and road to connect to the factory. When he brings the proposal, the infrastructure costs can account for 16 per cent of the project cost. If he had all these facilities, he would only need to seek financing for the actual project. His competitors in India, China, Malaysia and Indonesia have these facilities. He comes to you with a bloated project cost and is expected to compete in the global market. How can he compete? What we proposed with the constitutional financing window is to break the financing into two. Afreximbank would commercially finance the actual project, while the concessional window would finance the infrastructure that government ought to have provided. They would blend the financing to make it more patient, with a longer tenure. Then the entrepreneur can dream of competing with somebody else. That’s how we manufacture. That’s how growth will happen to create jobs.

title: UN secretary-general welcomes agreement on ceasefire in Alyoshki — office
body:
UN, October 24. /TASS/. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomes the agreement on the imminent start of a ceasefire in the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, his spokesman Stephane Dujarric said.
"The Secretary-General welcomes the announcement by the US First Lady Mrs. Melania Trump of a negotiated ceasefire to begin shortly in the town of Alyoshki, and commends the efforts of all who have contributed to that end," he said in a statement.
"He hopes that this and other steps will help to relieve the dire humanitarian situation in Oleshky and enable urgent provision of life-saving assistance, as well as the safe and voluntary evacuation of the town’s residents in a manner strictly compliant with
international humanitarian law. He hopes that such arrangements can be extended to other areas where civilians are suffering."
Earlier, Russia’s Chief of the General Staff, First Deputy Defense Minister, Army General Valery Gerasimov said that Russian troops would impose a ceasefire in the Kherson direction starting at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October·27 for the humanitarian operation.
The White House said on October 23 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in the Alyoshki area from October 29 to ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid and to prepare for the evacuation of civilians through a special safe corridor. An independent media organization from the United States will monitor and document the actions of Russian and Ukrainian groups on the ground throughout the entire process.

title: Umahi: South-east Voted Obi In 2023 Over Marginalisation, But Will Reward Tinubu in 2027
body: .Says Obi ‘can never be the best’ presidential material from region .Lagos-Calabar coastal highway cheaper than comparable Nigerian, international road projects .Accuses Landmark of ‘land-grabbing’ on Lagos beach, vow to take them to court .Hitech got coastal highway contract through legal direct procurement; Seyi Tinubu not on board Demola Ojo Nigeria’s Minister of Works, David Umahi, has said the South-east’s overwhelming support for Peter Obi in the 2023 presidential election was driven by anger over years of marginalisation, but predicted the region would respond differently in 2027 because of President Bola Tinubu’s treatment of the region. Umahi, who was emphatic that Obi failed to consult South-east leaders before his presidential bid, argued the region has other qualified political figures. The former governor of Ebonyi State also defended the cost of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, arguing that the project is cheaper than comparable road projects in Nigeria and internationally when its specifications and difficult terrain are taken into account. The minister who accused Landmark Africa of “land grabbing” on the Lagos beachfront, threatened legal action against its chief executive, Paul Onwuanibe, over claims surrounding the impact of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway on the business. Umahi, who defended the award of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway to Hitech Construction, also rejected claims that President Bola Tinubu’s son, Seyi Tinubu, sits on Hitech’s board, amid longstanding questions about the relationship between the President’s family and companies associated with the Chagoury Group. Speaking in an interview on Arise News Channel, Umahi described the South-east’s 2023 voting pattern as an “accident of history,” arguing that voters were expressing dissatisfaction with the region’s treatment under the previous administration. “In 2023, it was an accident of history,” Umahi said. “It was a demonstration of the anger of the people of South-east on how they were treated.” The Works Minister said the region had legitimate reasons to feel aggrieved at the time, citing what he described as inadequate federal appointments and infrastructure. “We’ve been marginalised in the past, but it’s no longer so,” he said. Umahi argued that Tinubu had changed the political equation through increased federal infrastructure and appointments for the South-east, predicting that voters would acknowledge that treatment when they return to the polls in 2027. “If in 2023 they demonstrated their anger, in 2027 they are going to demonstrate their joy on how the President has treated them,” he said. Umahi maintained that the South-east would “pay the President” for what he described as Tinubu’s commitment to the region, particularly through major infrastructure projects. He pointed to ongoing federal road projects and other investments as evidence that the region had received greater attention under the current administration. The minister also argued that the political environment had changed significantly since 2023, saying serving governors, former governors, traditional rulers and other influential figures across the Southeast were increasingly aligned with Tinubu. He said voters would be reluctant to abandon what he described as tangible infrastructure gains in favour of another political “gamble.” Umahi rejected suggestions that support for Tinubu amounted to a betrayal of the South-east or Peter Obi, arguing that the region’s political interests should not be tied permanently to one candidate. He also criticised social media supporters who insult South-east political leaders for backing Tinubu rather than Obi, saying such attacks were counterproductive. According to Umahi, ethnic and regional antagonism would not advance Obi’s political interests or those of the Southeast. The minister said the region’s long-term political interests required engagement and negotiation with other parts of Nigeria, particularly if the South-east hoped eventually to produce a president. He maintained that Tinubu’s record in the region would ultimately determine the 2027 vote rather than the voting pattern recorded four years earlier. Asked whether he believed Tinubu would defeat Obi in the South-east in 2027, Umahi was emphatic. “Why do you say I believe?” he responded. “That is what is going to happen!” Umahi said the South-east would not repeat its 2023 electoral choice because, in his assessment, the circumstances that produced that result had fundamentally changed. He said Obi “can never be the best” presidential material from the South-east, arguing that the former Anambra State governor failed to adequately consult political leaders in the region before his 2023 presidential bid. Umahi said his position was not driven by personal animosity towards Obi, but by his assessment of the political leadership available in the Southeast. “Peter Obi is not the best of our finest in South-east,” Umahi said. “He’s not the best, he can never be the best.” He argued that a presidential candidate seeking to represent the political aspirations of the South-east should first build consensus among governors and other political leaders in the region. “You cannot play politics in South-east without consulting people like us,” he said. Umahi said that if he were seeking the presidency himself, he would approach the process differently by consulting extensively with political stakeholders before presenting himself as a candidate. “If I were contesting, I would have consulted,” Umahi said, maintaining that a presidential ambition carrying the expectations of an entire region could not be pursued in isolation. He argued that Obi should have consulted South-east governors and other leaders before emerging as the region’s dominant presidential candidate in the 2023 election. Umahi also challenged the suggestion that Obi should automatically be regarded as the South-east’s strongest candidate for the presidency because of his performance in the last election. He said the region had other qualified political figures and argued that presidential politics required negotiation and engagement with other parts of the country rather than relying principally on regional enthusiasm. Umahi said he had “nothing personal” against Obi, stressing that different political circumstances required different qualities in a leader. The Works Minister also questioned arguments that the presidency should automatically return to Anambra State if the opportunity arose for the South-east to produce a president. He noted that Nigeria’s first President, Nnamdi Azikiwe, came from the area now constituting Anambra State and argued that other states in the South-east should also be considered. Umahi identified Ebonyi, Enugu, Abia and Imo as states that should have an opportunity in any future discussion about producing a president from the region. His comments came as he defended the growing support for President Tinubu among political leaders in the South-east ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Umahi argued that the South-east’s path to the presidency ultimately depended on political negotiation and integration with the rest of the country rather than treating support for a particular candidate as a test of loyalty to the region. He also rejected criticism of South-east political figures supporting Tinubu rather than Obi, saying it was wrong to portray them as betraying the region because of their political choices. The minister maintained that the South-east must negotiate and build alliances across Nigeria if it wants to produce a president, insisting that no single politician should be treated as the region’s only viable presidential option. He rejected criticism of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway’s cost, saying comparisons should be based on equivalent carriageways and engineering specifications rather than simply dividing the contract sum by the length of the road. “I deserve kudos for the cost of the coastal highway,” Umahi said as he compared the project with other major road developments. Using Section One of the highway as an example, the minister said the 47.47-kilometre stretch from Victoria Island to Eleko Village had a contract value of about N1.06 trillion, but argued that the figure had to be assessed against the number of carriageways and the extensive infrastructure included in the project. He said that when the cost was normalised to a standard two-lane carriageway, it amounted to approximately N7.3 billion to N7.5 billion per kilometre, or about $5.5 million at the exchange rate he used in his calculation. Umahi argued that the figure compared favourably with other major road projects, including the Bodo-Bonny Road, the East-West Road and coastal road projects elsewhere in West Africa. “You have to compare apple to apple,” he said, insisting that comparisons which ignored differences in road width, pavement type, bridges, drainage and terrain created a misleading impression of the project’s cost. The minister said the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway was being constructed with reinforced concrete pavement and would include solar lighting, underground drainage, two-metre walkways, crash barriers and a corridor reserved for a railway line. He also pointed to the extensive ground improvement required along the Lagos section, saying that approximately 30 kilometres involved the removal of unsuitable material to an average depth of about 10 metres, while the road level had to be raised by an average of about five metres. “You remove the pit, average of 10 metres, and then you fill it back,” Umahi said, describing the engineering work required before the pavement itself could be constructed. He said those features needed to be factored into any meaningful comparison of the project’s cost with conventional highways built on less challenging terrain. Umahi also cited the changing cost of construction materials, saying the price of concrete had increased significantly since the contract was awarded without a corresponding increase in the contract price. “When we started, concrete was N350,000 per cubic metre. Today, it is N460,000 per cubic metre,” he said. “The contract price has not changed.” The Works Minister compared the Coastal Highway with the Bodo-Bonny Road in Rivers State, as well as portions of the East-West Road, arguing that their costs demonstrated that the Lagos-Calabar project was not unusually expensive when assessed on equivalent engineering terms. His defence follows sustained public scrutiny of the project’s cost. Umahi has previously argued that the price approved for the Coastal Highway was lower than comparable projects and has repeatedly disputed calculations based on a simple cost-per-kilometre formula. In October 2025, he publicly challenged Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde to a debate after the governor questioned his explanation of the project’s cost. Umahi said international financiers had also scrutinised the project’s pricing before committing funding to it. He said Deutsche Bank, which led the financing for Section One, examined the project before the financing was syndicated and reached a favourable assessment of its pricing and construction quality. “They said the project was underpriced,” Umahi said, adding that the financing was subsequently “oversubscribed by $100 million.” Umahi has previously made the oversubscription claim publicly, saying international financial institutions regarded the project’s cost as competitive. He maintained that the cost of one section could not simply be extrapolated across the full 750-kilometre highway because terrain and engineering requirements vary significantly along the route. “There are no two sections that are the same,” Umahi said, arguing that bridges, soil conditions and other engineering requirements would ultimately determine the cost of individual sections. The minister insisted that when those factors were considered alongside the highway’s specifications, the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway represented value for money rather than the excessively priced project portrayed by its critics. Umahi also strongly disputed Onwuanibe’s account of the losses Landmark suffered following the federal government’s demolition of structures along the highway’s right of way. “He was land grabbing,” Umahi said, referring to Landmark’s occupation of portions of the beachfront affected by the project. The Works Minister challenged Onwuanibe to make public the company’s Certificate of Occupancy and other documents establishing its legal title to the affected land. “Let him publish his C of O,” Umahi said. He maintained that the federal government had deliberately adjusted the highway around Landmark’s permanent structures to prevent the destruction of its main facilities. “We saved his permanent structure,” Umahi said, arguing that what was removed consisted largely of “shanties” erected along the beachfront rather than Landmark’s principal permanent development. Umahi also rejected claims about the scale of Landmark’s financial losses, pointing to what he described as inconsistencies in figures publicly associated with the company. He said Onwuanibe had previously spoken of investments worth about $250 million but had more recently cited losses of about N42 billion arising from the demolition. The minister questioned the basis of those figures and said the government should not be portrayed as having arbitrarily destroyed a legitimate investment without regard for ownership or compensation rights. Umahi said smaller businesses and other affected occupants who were entitled to compensation had been identified and compensated by the government. He said the affected people were enumerated and payments made directly into their bank accounts, maintaining that the compensation process was transparent. The minister then warned that the continuing public claims surrounding Landmark could result in legal action. “If he doesn’t refrain from misleading the public, I may take him to court,” Umahi said. The dispute over Landmark became one of the earliest major controversies surrounding construction of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway after the federal government demolished parts of the Landmark Beach complex in April 2024 to clear the project’s right of way. Onwuanibe had publicly maintained that the demolition caused significant losses to the Landmark ecosystem and businesses operating within it, while the federal government consistently argued that the affected structures were within the highway’s legally established corridor. Umahi maintained that the government had gone out of its way to preserve Landmark’s principal investment, saying the highway was effectively divided around the permanent structure rather than demolishing it. He insisted that the disagreement should ultimately be resolved on the basis of documentary evidence establishing ownership of the beachfront land. Umahi confirmed that there was no public advertisement or open competitive bidding for the highway, but insisted the procurement method was lawful. When challenged if there was advertisement or public bidding, Umahi retorted, “But there was direct procurement. It’s within the law.” Asked specifically whether Seyi Tinubu was on Hitech’s board, Umahi responded: “He’s not.” The minister said the government had examined Hitech’s board as part of the pre-qualification process. “I’ve heard people that say, ‘Oh, Seyi Tinubu is on the board of Hitech’. We have the board of Hitech, because before we did pre-qualification,” he said. Umahi explained that federal procurement rules provide different routes for awarding contracts, including open tendering, restrictive tendering and direct procurement, with emergency procurement available under particular circumstances. “There are three kinds of procurement that are allowed,” he said. “There is a fourth one, which is emergency procurement.” Explaining the distinction, Umahi said open procurement involves public advertisement, while restrictive tendering allows government to invite companies considered to have the necessary expertise to pre-qualify and bid. “And so the third one is direct procurement,” he said. “Direct procurement is where there are no competitive bids. But it’s a specialised kind of procurement.” Umahi said the decision to use that method for Hitech was driven by the engineering challenges expected along the coastline, particularly the threat posed by Atlantic Ocean surges. “Our job was to construct road along the coast — coastal highway — and we knew that we were going to be confronted with the ocean surge,” he said. The minister cited the historical threat of coastal erosion to Victoria Island and the eventual development of Eko Atlantic as evidence of Hitech’s ability to undertake specialised coastal engineering. Umahi recalled that repeated interventions by expatriate contractors had failed to permanently resolve the threat to Victoria Island before Hitech became involved. “All over the years, the federal government would engage expatriates from Belgium, from France and all over the country,” he said. “Each time the flood came, there would be that kind of intervention. But it could not solve the problem of the VI.” He said Hitech initially resisted undertaking the coastal protection work because of the financial and technical risks involved. “The President called Hitech and said, ‘Please, can you invest to do this, to tame the Atlantic Ocean?’ They said, ‘No. You’re going to liquidate us. We won’t be able to do it.’” Umahi said the company eventually developed a solution involving massive concrete structures and geotextile materials to hold back the Atlantic. “They were almost liquidated until they came up with that method,” he said, referring to the coastal protection system. “And today we have a beauty to behold, the Eko Atlantic.” According to Umahi, that track record became central to the government’s justification for proposing Hitech for the Coastal Highway. “So when we knew that we were going to be confronted with this, we were going to look for that kind of technical expertise,” he said. “And that’s why we sent the name of Hitech.” He said the government presented Hitech’s Eko Atlantic work as evidence of its performance, technical capacity and capability to the Bureau of Public Procurement. “They put the Eko Atlantic as the attraction and the evidence of performance and capacity and capability to the BPP,” Umahi said. The BPP, he said, considered the proposal before allowing the government to proceed with direct procurement on a section-by-section basis. “BPP looked at it and said, ‘Yes, but procure this thing in sections,’” he said. Umahi said the government subsequently obtained a Certificate of No Objection before taking the procurement to the Federal Executive Council for approval. “Federal Executive Council approved: go ahead, direct procurement, but procure it in sections,” he said. Pressed on whether this amounted to confirmation that there had been no public bidding for the project, Umahi initially objected to the framing, insisting that the central question should be whether the procurement complied with Nigerian law. “You should ask me whether we conformed to the law of the federal government,” he said. When the interviewer ARISE News Anchor Ojy Okpe reiterated that there had been no advertisement or public bidding, Umahi ultimately confirmed the procurement method. He said, “It’s within the law.”

title: Tinubu Commends Leadership Philosophy of Army Chief, Says Nigerian Army Moving Away from Military Conservatism
body: .Defence minister assures ECOMOG veterans contributions to peacekeeping in Africa to be documented, preserved Linus Aleke in Abuja and Kemi Olaitan in Ibadan President Bola Tinubu has applauded the leadership philosophy of the Chief of Army Staff (COAS), Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, describing it as the foundation of a new Nigerian Army focused on professionalism, adaptability, combat readiness and resilience. Tinubu stated that the four pillars underpinning Shaibu’s command philosophy also guided the Army’s approach to training, equipment, combat operations and leadership. Also, the Minister of Defence, General Christopher Musa (rtd), has reaffirmed the federal government’s commitment to documenting and preserving the legacy and sacrifices of the Economic Community of West African States Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) in maintaining peace and security in West Africa. Also, the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Olufemi Oluyede, yesterday assured veterans of the Armed Forces of sustained welfare initiatives aimed at making their lives more comfortable after service, while calling for their greater participation in the national security architecture. The President described the doctrine as a significant departure from military conservatism, noting that the Army had shifted from static defence towards more mobile offensive operations under Shaibu’s leadership. Tinubu stated this in the foreword to a book titled, ‘The Shaibu Doctrine: Mission Command and the Remaking of Nigeria’s Army at War’, co-authored by Dr. Muhammed Sani Abubakar and Associate Professor Sunday Adejoh of the Nigerian Defence Academy (NDA). The President said the doctrine reflected the Armed Forces’ responsibility to secure Nigeria and create an environment in which democracy and development could thrive. “As Commander-in-Chief, I have charged our Armed Forces with one mission: to secure Nigeria so that democracy and development can thrive,” he said. He added that the ongoing reforms encompassed the adoption of technology, the indigenisation of military tools, improved personnel welfare and a renewed emphasis on military ethics. “These were not abstract reforms. They were choices made in the heat of battle, with lives on the line and the nation watching,” the President said. The book examines Shaibu’s leadership philosophy, particularly the role of Mission Command, troop welfare and decentralised decision-making in strengthening the Army’s operational effectiveness. Speaking about the motivation behind the publication, co-author Muhammed Sani Abubakar said his professional interactions with Shaibu began when the latter served as a brigade commander in Bama and continued during his tenure as Theatre Commander of Operation Hadin Kai. He said these experiences gave him insights into Shaibu’s approach to managing personnel and military resources while sustaining troop morale in demanding operational environments. Abubakar said he and Adejoh decided to document the philosophy systematically following Shaibu’s appointment as COAS, believing it offered lessons relevant to the Army’s evolving operational challenges. He explained that the philosophy was built around five pillars captured by the acronym PROSE: Professional Excellence, Robust Administration, Operational Readiness, Strategic Cooperation and Exemplary Leadership. At its core, he said, was a soldier-first culture that prioritised personnel welfare, morale, training, dignity and empowerment as the foundations of combat effectiveness. Abubakar described Mission Command as a leadership approach based on trust, initiative and the empowerment of subordinate commanders to make decisions within their respective areas of responsibility. Under this approach, he explained, senior commanders set operational objectives while allowing subordinate commanders to determine the best ways to achieve them, taking prevailing battlefield conditions into account. He said the central message was that effective leadership under challenging conditions required commanders to trust their subordinates, invest in personnel, align administration with operations, promote inter-agency cooperation and lead by example. The book is scheduled to be presented on 24 November 2026 at the Nigerian Army Resource Centre in Abuja. Meanwhile, the Minister of Defence gave the assurance when he received a delegation of ECOMOG veterans, led by Major General Ohifeme Ejimai (rtd), at the Ministry of Defence Headquarters in Abuja. According to a statement by the Minister of Defence’s Special Adviser on Media, Leah Katung-Babatunde, the delegation visited the minister to brief him on the group’s activities and ongoing initiatives. Speaking during the visit, General Musa acknowledged the significant human and financial resources Nigeria committed to ECOMOG, emphasising that personnel who paid the supreme price, particularly during peacekeeping missions in Liberia and Sierra Leone, would never be forgotten. He assured the delegation that ongoing efforts to document the remaining records, casualties and historical assets would be completed to ensure their proper preservation for posterity. Earlier in his remarks, Major General Ejimai (rtd) provided an update on the status of surviving Nigerian ECOMOG veterans, noting their readiness to continue contributing to national development and security. He urged the ministry to address existing gaps in documentation and consider establishing a dedicated remembrance day to honour the hundreds of Nigerian troops who lost their lives in the pursuit of peace and stability in West Africa. The Economic Community of West African States Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) was a regional peacekeeping and peace enforcement force established by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in 1990. Driven largely by Nigerian leadership and troops, ECOMOG played a decisive role in restoring constitutional order, protecting civilian populations and stabilising West Africa during complex regional crises. The CDS gave the assurance during his interactive session with veterans from the South-west region at Headquarters, 2 Division, Nigerian Army, Adekunle Fajuyi Cantonment, Ibadan, as part of his ongoing nationwide engagement with veterans. General Oluyede while addressing the veterans, appreciated them for their years of sacrifice in keeping the nation united and peaceful, saying “Your service and sacrifice will never be forgotten by the nation.” He noted that the federal government remains committed to improving the welfare of veterans in appreciation of their sacrifices, citing the recent increment in salaries of serving personnel and the consequential adjustment of veterans’ pensions as a demonstration of the Federal Government’s gratitude to the Armed Forces for their service to the nation. He added that issues arising from the consequential adjustment of pensions are being addressed. The CDS further outlined several initiatives being pursued by the Defence Headquarters to improve the welfare of both serving personnel and veterans which include his determination to dedicate at least one hospital in each geopolitical zone specifically to cater for the medical needs of veterans, in addition to existing healthcare arrangements. He informed the veterans that data collation is ongoing and necessary processes are at advanced stages towards actualisation. The CDS also disclosed ongoing efforts to establish a low-interest loan scheme for veterans to enable them engage in productive ventures and businesses after service. He explained the recently launched Defence Headquarters Online Shop in collaboration with Konga, noting that efforts are ongoing to expand the scheme to bring more major businesses on board to offer discounted goods and services to personnel and veterans. He called on veterans to continue to contribute their quota to peace and security in their respective communities and to sustain prayers for serving personnel as they strive to keep the nation peaceful and secure. During the interactive session, veterans raised pressing concerns and sought clarifications on issues affecting them, which were promptly addressed by the CDS. On hand to provide further clarifications were the Chief of Defence Administration, Rear Admiral Gideon Kachim; the Commandant, Nigerian Armed Forces Resettlement Centre, Air Vice Marshal NI Iloh; and the Chairman, Military Pensions Board, Major General JE Osifoh. Issues bordering on veterans’ entitlements, welfare programmes and other administrative matters were extensively discussed. The President of the Retired Army, Navy and Air Force Officers’ Association (RANAO), Major General HA Salihu (rtd), in his remarks, thanked the CDS for the engagement, urging veterans to continue to embrace dialogue in resolving issues of concern.

title: First Lady: Nigeria On Right Path To Total Economic Recovery and Sustainable Development
body: .Notes great improvement in investors confidence in nation’s economy .Inaugurates PBAT door-to-door campaign Hqs, says such campaign approach remains best avenue for true community engagement .Reiterates Tinubu govt’s commitment to youth empowerment Deji Elumoye and Juliet Akoje in Abuja Wife of the President, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, has declared that Nigeria is on the right path to total economic recovery and sustainable development emphasising that the confidence of investors in the nation’s economy has greatly improved. Speaking yesterday while inaugurating the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement Headquarters in Abuja, the First Lady stressed that the country’s economic recovery is looking up with both local and international investors having hope in Nigeria’s economy. She urged members of the Movement to not just go door-to-door but pass on the message of hope assured and shared prosperity. Her words, “The door-to-door campaign approach remains one of the most vital avenues for true community engagement, which gives us the privilege to listen to the heartfelt concerns of families, understand the aspirations of our young people, honour the wisdom of our elders, and learn directly from the women who serve as the resilient backbone of our homes and society as a whole. “As we embark on this noble mission, let us always remember that impactful outreach extends far beyond visiting doorsteps. Our message must consistently resonate hope, peace, unity and development, especially the impactful progress the Tinubu administration has made so far.” Mrs. Tinubu commended the leadership and members of the Movement for already traversing 14 states of the federation urging them to sustain the momentum as the APC presidential campaign formally kicks off. “To the members of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, I encourage you all to approach every community peacefully, engage every individual with respect and remember that every Nigerian deserves to be heard and valued, regardless of political affiliation. Let us win the hearts and votes through the strength of our message: Renewed Hope, True Federalism and Shared Prosperity.” In his remarks, Senate President, Senator Godswill Akpabio stated that the message to Nigerians is to have faith in the steady but assured improvement in the nation generally. “The message is that hope is here, hope has come and hope is alive.” Also speaking, Delta State Governor, Hon. Sheriff Oborevwori, was unequivocal in his declaration that the sub-nationals are having it much better under President Tinubu saying state revenues have improved in such a way that workers are not being owed salaries and contractors are being paid promptly. Convener of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, High Chief Government Ekpemupolo, in a speech read on his behalf by High Chief Matthew Tonlagha, assured that the movement will take the message to every nook and cranny of the nation to ensure victory for President Tinubu come January 2027. Also yesterday, the First Lady performed the Foundation laying ceremony of a state-of-the -art Renewed Hope Startup Hub in Wuye, Abuja. The hub is partnership between the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) and the Government of Japan through its Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA). Mrs. Tinubu described the hub as yet another important step towards technological advancement, youth empowerment and digital inclusion for youth across the nation. According to her, “The establishment of start-up hubs across the nation aligns with the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Tinubu, which prioritises youth empowerment through entrepreneurship, skills development and sustainable job creation, equipping young Nigerians to compete and thrive in the global economy. “To our young innovators, this start-up hub is yours. You can arrive here with a sketch and leave with a working prototype that takes you into the global market space. Let this hub be the home where your dreams are nurtured and scaled.” She commended the collaboration between the government of Japan and Nigeria which she noted with admiration that it birthed the startup hub and many other developmental projects and initiatives. “I want to acknowledge and express our appreciation to the Government of Japan, through the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), for providing the strategic grant that has made this intervention possible. This partnership highlights the mutual belief in the vast, untapped potential of Nigeria’s digital ecosystem and our vibrant youth population.” In his remarks, DG/CEO of NITDA, Mallam Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, noted that since 2021 the partnership between the organisation and JICA focused on strengthening Nigeria’s innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem through capacity building, knowledge transfer, infrastructure development and international collaboration. He said the proposed facility is intended to serve as a focal point for startup development, industry engagement and innovation ecosystem coordination that will strengthen access to infrastructure, technical expertise, mentorship and opportunities for collaboration between Nigerian innovators and international partners. “This partnership is an investment of approximately US$10.4 million depending on the conversion rate for the innovation hub. The project is also presented as part of a broader Japan–Nigeria start-up ecosystem support initiative involving complementary financing mechanisms.” On his part, Japanese Ambassador to Nigeria, Suzuki Hideo, promised that with the improved economic atmosphere in the country, Japan is pleased to continue to expand its partnerships with Nigeria especially in the areas of education and technology.

title: Victor Osimhen: Legacy of A Consistent Marksman
body: On a night charged with pure theatre, Victor Osimhen shattered records and silenced critics with a clinical strike in Galatasaray’s breath-taking 4-2 triumph over Lille. Returning to haunt his former club, the Nigerian talisman claimed his throne as his nation’s undisputed Champions League king. Then, standard-issue pleasantries were cast aside as a defiant Osimhen unleashed a fiery post-match storm against his detractors, Kunle Adewale reports. Nigerian international, Victor Osimhen cemented his legacy as Nigeria’s greatest UEFA Champions League marksman on Wednesday night, turning a highly anticipated return to his former stomping grounds into a historic masterclass. The Super Eagles forward struck Galatasaray’s decisive fourth goal in a thrilling 4-2 victory against LOSC Lille during the UEFA Champions League phase. On an evening thick with subplots, Osimhen did not just find his first European goal of the campaign; he completely rewrote the footballing record books for both his club and his country, before turning his sights on his critics in an explosive post-match declaration. The Night the Records Tumbled in France Heading into the match, Nigerian football portal Soccernet had framed the fixture as the perfect stage for Osimhen to open his European account for the season. Returning to Lille—the club that originally launched him into Europe’s elite consciousness—the script felt pre-written. Osimhen delivered flawlessly. According to data compiled by Afrik-Foot, Osimhen’s single strike on Wednesday evening shattered and re-established three distinct milestones: The King of Nigerian Champions League History With this goal, Osimhen moved to 17 total career goals in the UEFA Champions League. This feat establishes him as the outright highest-scoring Nigerian in the history of Europe’s premier club competition. He has now completely distanced himself from his compatriots; football icons, Obafemi Martins and Ademola Lookman sit a distant joint-second with nine goals each. Osimhen now holds nearly double the tally of his closest countrymen. For anyone to challenge his throne, they would need to score eight goals just to draw level—assuming the Galatasaray talisman never scores another. A Historic Nomad The strike also made Osimhen the first Nigerian footballer in history to score in the UEFA Champions League for three different clubs. His continental journey has seen him hit the back of the net for Lille, Napoli, and now Galatasaray, proving his elite adaptability across Europe’s top leagues. Galatasaray’s All-Time Foreign King in Europe Within the context of his current club, the numbers are equally staggering. Osimhen has now scored 14 goals in all European competitions for Galatasaray, overtaking Czech legend, Milan Baroš (12 goals) to become the club’s highest-scoring foreign player in European football history. The Continental Leaderboard Osimhen’s status among Europe’s elite is firmly backed by the numbers. Below is how he compares to Nigeria’s finest, alongside his next targets within Galatasaray’s historic ranks. With the Nigerian record safely secured, the striker’s next targets lie entirely within Galatasaray’s internal folklore. He currently possesses eight Champions League goals for the Turkish giants. Two more will pull him level with Burak Yılmaz, while five more will tie him with the legendary Hakan Sükür as the club’s greatest-ever Champions League scorer. “Nobody Can Teach Me How to Score” Despite walking away with the Man of the Match award and a pocketful of history, Osimhen was in no mood to celebrate quietly. Taking to the microphones after the final whistle, the Scudetto winner unleashed a fiery, defiant response to recent media criticisms aimed at his performances and Galatasaray’s recent form. Osimhen sits among the nation’s greatest forwards ? While raw statistics cannot completely settle an argument that includes the artistry of Nwankwo Kanu, the clinical precision of Rashidi Yekini, or the raw power of Daniel Amokachi, Osimhen’s consistency on football’s grandest club stage is nearly unparalleled in African history. Very few Nigerian players have ever scored on this platform with such ruthless regularity. At just 27 years old, he is entering his prime years with the international record firmly in his grasp and club records firmly in his sights. Next Stop: The Intercontinental Derby There is no time for Galatasaray or their record-breaking striker to rest on their laurels. The team must immediately pivot from the glamour of European nights back to the fierce realities of domestic football. On Monday night, Osimhen will lead the line for Galatasaray as they head into the ferocious atmosphere of the ‘Intercontinental Derby’ against bitter city rivals Fenerbahçe. It is a match where tactical notes are thrown out the window and local pride reigns supreme. If the critics thought Osimhen was fired up in France, Fenerbahçe will likely face a world-class striker determined to prove, once again, that nobody can teach him how to find the back of the net.

title: Zulum Targets End to Medical Tourism as Shettima Inaugurates 400-bed Teaching Hospital
body: Michael Olugbode in Abuja Borno State Governor, Babagana Zulum, has intensified efforts to curb medical tourism with the establishment of a 400-bed teaching hospital equipped with advanced diagnostic technology and specialist healthcare facilities in Maiduguri. Vice President Kashim Shettima yesterday inaugurated the Kashim Ibrahim University Teaching Hospital alongside other key projects delivered by the Zulum administration, in a move aimed at expanding access to quality healthcare and strengthening medical training in the North-east. The hospital, which combines specialist medical services with the training of healthcare professionals, is expected to reduce the need for patients in Borno and neighbouring communities to travel elsewhere for advanced diagnosis and treatment. Equipped with a 1.5-tesla magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner, a 160-slice computed tomography (CT) scanner, three conventional and two mobile X-ray machines, three 4D ultrasound machines, a fluoroscopy system and digital mammography equipment, the facility is designed to expand access to specialised medical services. Its infrastructure also includes 13 specialist departments covering diagnostic, medical, surgical, emergency, paediatric, internal medicine and physiotherapy services, among others. The project comprises a medical college complex, a students’ hostel, a 200-unit staff estate and an oxygen plant complex, providing supporting infrastructure for patient care, medical education and healthcare delivery. Beyond reducing the burden of seeking treatment outside the state, the hospital is expected to serve residents of neighbouring communities and people across the Lake Chad region, while improving access to specialist care for underserved populations. It is also expected to strengthen healthcare manpower development by providing training opportunities for doctors, nurses and allied health professionals, helping to address shortages that have constrained healthcare delivery in Borno and the wider North-east. Speaking at the inauguration, Shettima commended Zulum for investing in institutions capable of delivering lasting benefits to the state, particularly in healthcare and education. He said the value of public office should ultimately be measured by the institutions established, infrastructure delivered and lives improved, rather than the privileges associated with political positions. “We shall be judged by what survives our time in office, the offices we held, the aides who surrounded us, and the length of our convoys will have surrendered their importance. What will endure are the institutions we built, the roads we built and the lives we improved through service. That is the meaning of our gathering here in Maiduguri. That is why this occasion brings me such joy,” the Vice President said. Shettima said the hospital and the schools established by the state government reflected Zulum’s commitment to rebuilding Borno through investments that directly affect people’s lives. “According to Carl Sagan’s law of insignificance, 100 years from now, everyone you know or who knows you will be out of this world. This is why I do not doubt the vision of His Excellency Professor Babagana Umara Zulum; his passion for healthcare and education is expressed in the institution before us,” he said. He added that the teaching hospital and schools being established across Maiduguri and other parts of the state demonstrated the governor’s conviction that recovery must translate into tangible improvements in healthcare and access to education. “The ultra-modern Kashim Ibrahim University Teaching Hospital and the school that dotted our landscape in Maiduguri and across the state give substance to his belief that Borno recovery must reach the patient awaiting treatment and the child sitting in a place in the classroom,” Shettima said.
