title: U.S. Army activates Guam air and missile defense battalion, building on THAAD operations
body: The activation ceremony took place October 16 at Andersen Air Force Base. The unit falls under the 38th Air Defense Artillery Brigade and the 94th Army Air and Missile Defense Command. The battalion will support Guam’s defense and provide the Army’s contribution to the Guam Defense System. Its work includes maintaining readiness and integrating the equipment and procedures needed for a coordinated defense. “The Soldiers developed new procedures, relationships, and integration required to connect sensors, command and control systems, launchers, and interceptors to promote a unified defensive architecture,” said Lt. Col. Joshua Urness, the battalion commander. “It’s only fitting that 3-43 ADA now stands up the Army’s contribution to the strategic Guam Defense System.” Guam supports U.S. joint operations throughout the Indo-Pacific. Air and missile defenses protect the forces and infrastructure needed to sustain those missions. “Your vigilance will have strategic consequences,” said Col. Moseph Sauda, commander of the 38th Air Defense Artillery Brigade. “Your readiness will assist in shaping regional stability, and your professionalism will ensure millions living under the umbrella of peace that your discipline helps to maintain.” Task Force Talon established its air defense presence on Guam in 2013, operating the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system. THAAD is designed to intercept ballistic missiles during the later stages of flight. The task force worked with other military services and the Guam Army National Guard to maintain readiness. The shift to a battalion carries that experience into a permanent formation as the Army develops its integrated defenses. The battalion also retains the lineage of the 43rd Air Defense Artillery Regiment. Its predecessor was established in the Philippine Islands in 1916.

title: US lawmakers demand answers from Elon Musk over Ukraine Starlink restrictions
body:
U.S. Representative Gregory Meeks and Senator Peter Welch led four other lawmakers on Oct. 23 in demanding that Elon Musk answer questions about Ukrainian Starlink disruptions.
In a public letter , Democratic Senators and Representatives listed five questions concerning Starlink restrictions impacting Ukrainian forces, addressed to Musk. "As a publicly traded company, SpaceX has a legal obligation to disclose to shareholders and the public material events that could affect your business model," the lawmakers wrote in the letter. "The revelation that you personally wielded control over a foreign country’s military communications would require disclosure of elevated risks for corporate governance, geopolitical exposure, and potential adverse actions by foreign governments." The lawmakers gave Musk until October 31 to answer their questions.
The demand comes as Ukrainian forces continue to experience severe problems operating Starlink military systems. Since mid-October, Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk 's satellite internet system, Starlink, has been operating at limited capacity. With speed limit caps, Kyiv's ability to defend from deadly Russian jet-powered drones and coordinate strikes against Russian targets is hindered. "Just last month, more than 300 Ukrainian civilians were killed and 2,000 injured by Russian drone and missile strikes," the lawmakers wrote in their letter. "Ukraine has built an innovative network of drone systems to defend against the thousands of strikes launched each month by Russia. However, these life-saving systems often depend on Starlink’s military version, Starshield, for accurate communication and transmission of targeting data." Despite Ukrainian and U.S. officials apparently engaging in discussions to resolve the disruptions, nobody has publicly taken credit — or blame — for making or implementing the decision. However, the Trump administration officials continue pointing fingers firmly at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions, saying the president was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 160 kilometers (100 miles) an hour."
Trump said he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but might do so if the problems persisted.
"I have not spoken to him," Trump said. "I might have to, but I have not... I've heard it's fixed. If it's not, I will speak to him.... If there's a problem, I will get it straightened out." On Oct. 23, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that issues with Starlink continued to plague Ukrainian forces. "The speed restrictions for Starlink and Starshield are still in effect," Zelensky said. "The speed has not been restored. And the supply of interceptor missiles to protect against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed." On Oct. 23, U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal, also a Democrat, announced that he is opening a probe into the Starlink disruption. Blumenthal's investigation asks the Pentagon to clarify who ordered the restrictions and to provide information on the U.S. military's own reliance on Starlink.

title: Russia vows to continue to send aid to Cuba through UN World Food Programme
body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Russia will continue its support to Cuba through the United Nations’ World Food Programme (WFP) despite the logistical difficulties, Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov told Izvestia .
"There were delays in delivering aid to Cuba through the United Nations World Food Programme, but Russia has fulfilled its humanitarian duty to the people who are our friends. Since June, two shipments of sunflower oil with a total volume of just over 750 tons have been delivered to the island. We will definitely continue to support Havana through the UN WFP," the deputy minister noted.
Alimov also said that the humanitarian consequences of Cuba’s blockade go beyond politics. According to him, the US energy embargo remains an illegal and cynical practice that harms ordinary people.

title: Trypillia settlement discovered above Verteba Cave in Ternopil region
body:
Archaeologist Mykhailo Sokhatskyi, director of the Borshchiv Local History Museum, told this to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"A team of scientists from the S. I. Subbotin Institute of Geophysics of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, the Institute of Geophysics of the Polish Academy of Sciences, and Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv studied Trypillia sites using high-resolution magnetometry with unmanned aerial vehicles. This method makes it possible to detect underground objects and soil features by identifying changes in the magnetic field," Sokhatskyi said.
According to him, modern equipment enabled specialists to conduct a successful archaeological survey without excavation at three Trypillia settlements: one on the surface above Verteba Cave and others near the village of Hlybochok, covering an area of about 60 hectares.
"We were able to see the clear outlines of the remains of Trypillia houses and record a fairly accurate plan of these prehistoric settlements. For example, there turned out to be far more dwellings in Hlybochok than we had expected. We could see how people arranged their houses in accordance with the landscape, orienting them toward the sunny side," the archaeologist added.
The research findings are still being analyzed. However, the data obtained so far indicate that Trypillia settlements existed not only inside Verteba Cave but also above it.
"Verteba is unique because it is the only place where a Trypillia settlement existed underground. Moreover, it did so for a long time – about 750 years. We decided to find out whether people had also settled on the surface above it. We carried out small-scale exploratory excavations, digging test pits, and found that people had lived above the cave as well. Since large-scale excavations were not possible, we used equipment to 'see through' the ground above Verteba and discovered archaeological features in the form of dwellings. This means Verteba has taken on new significance. There is the underground Verteba, but there is also a cultural heritage site above ground. We will now determine its parameters – the extent of the settlement, its boundaries, where it was located and how it relates to the cave's karst sinkholes. Perhaps, there were other entrances to Verteba, or another cave nearby. The equipment allows us to see all this, so we are eagerly awaiting the final research results," Sokhatskyi said.
The research will provide an important basis for preparing the documentation needed to nominate two Trypillia culture sites – Verteba Cave and Hlybochok – for inclusion on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Photo credit: Borshchiv Regional Local History Museum

title: This is the fancy new F-16 Ukraine could get. It’s not what its pilots need most.
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine's air force has discussed the F-16 Block 70/72 with US manufacturer Lockheed Martin, which then gave President Zelenskyy a model of one The Block 70/72 is smarter and tougher than Ukraine's ex-European F-16 Block 15 Mid Life Updates, but that doesn't mean the newer model is a major priority The Ukrainian air force needs munitions more than it needs new airframes When Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., head of its aeronautics division, in Kyiv on 19 October, the talk was of Patriot interceptors and of repairing the Ukrainian air force's small but growing fleet of ex-European F-16 fighters inside the country. Lockheed designed the F-16 and still builds it. But the Lockheed officials may have had other things on their minds. They gave Zelenskyy a scale model of a new and improved F-16 variant in Ukrainian livery, according to a photo posted by the MilitaryNewsUA account. In late September, Ukraine's air force commander, Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko, and Lockheed discussed a possible move to newer F-16s. Now we have a clearer idea what those F-16s might look like—and what they might be capable of. The model Lockheed officials gave to Zelenskyy appears to be based on the Block 70/72 version of the classic supersonic fighter that Lockheed manufactures at its factory in Greenville, South Carolina. A model of the F-16 Block 70/72 fighter that Lockheed Martin representatives gifted to Volodymyr Zelenskyy during their personal meeting yesterday. pic.twitter.com/tprj5yuj2z — MilitaryNewsUA (@front_ukrainian) October 20, 2026 It's a world-class jet. But a pricey batch of factory-fresh Block 70/72s isn't actually at the top of the Ukrainian air force's wish list. Not as long as the air force's existing warplanes lack munitions. The Block 70/72 boasts a better radar, more fuel capacity, and a tougher airframe compared to older F-16 models, which have been flying since the late 1970s. The F-16 is still one of the most numerous fighter types in US Air Force service. Surplus 1980s-vintage F-16s from Denmark and the Netherlands make up the bulk of the Ukrainian air force's front-line fleet. Norway's six are still being refurbished, and Belgium's are coming. Whether Ukraine ever gets new F-16s is anyone's guess. Kyiv would need to pay around $100 million per copy, or find an ally to finance the purchase. Either could be a heavy lift. And to be sure, Ukraine has options as it rebuilds its battered air force. Sweden is donating 16 older Saab Gripens, the first due early next year, and Kyiv plans to buy 20 newer ones. Kyiv has negotiated to buy 16 Dassault Rafales from France, which may not arrive until 2028. Belgium has promised as many as 53 older F-16s, the last of them perhaps not until 2029. Ukrainian F-16s. Ukrainian air force photo. Welcome jets But new Block 70/72 F-16s would be welcome. The Block 70/72 builds on what already makes the F-16 great: its agility, flexibility, reliability, excellent electronic warfare systems, and compatibility with a wide array of munitions. Where the Block 15 Mid Life Update F-16s Ukraine currently flies have the older analog AN/APG-66(V2) radar, the Block 70/72 has a digital APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar. It can also carry overwing conformal fuel tanks for extra range. Perhaps most exciting for the Ukrainian air force, a newly made Block 70/72 is good for 12,000 hours of flight: enough for about 30 years at 400 flying hours a year. An aging Block 15 has a structural life of about 8,000 hours, and Ukraine's jets fly hard. Zelenskyy has said about half of them spend long stretches abroad for repairs, many at Sabena Aerospace Engineering in Belgium, a process that can take months. Ukraine F-16 Pilots Rationing Missiles as Russian Attacks Intensify | NEWSMAX2 Ukraine’s American-made F-16 fighter jets are defending the skies against Russian drones and cruise missiles — but a critical shortage of U.S.-made missiles is putting that mission at risk. In an… pic.twitter.com/WQgbasdks5 — Ukrainian Air Force (@KpsZSU) September 16, 2026 Newer F-16s require less maintenance. They can fly and fight more often. In that sense, 50 Block 70/72s are worth more than 50 Block 15s. But the availability of airframes isn't the biggest problem in the 107th Aviation Wing, the Ukrainian air force's sole F-16 unit. The wing is desperately low on air-to-air missiles. Its pilots often resort to gunning down Russian drones and cruise missiles with the F-16's built-in 20-mm cannon—a risky tactic given how close a fighter must get to its target to make use of its gun. While a few billion dollars' worth of fresh F-16s could keep the 107th Aviation Wing in fighting shape for decades to come, fresh airframes aren't actually the most urgent priority. Given a choice between getting new F-16s or getting substantial supplies of missiles for its old F-16s, the wing would surely opt for the latter. Explore further Belgium’s 10 F-16s bring Ukraine’s promised fleet to about 100 jets. Fewer than 40 are flying, as Russia’s jet drones run them ragged

title: Russia Pounds Kramatorsk With Aerial Bombs – 1 Killed, 6 Injured, Including 3 Children
body:
Russian forces dropped three powerful aerial bombs on a residential neighborhood in Kramatorsk, Donetsk region, on Friday, Oct. 23, killing one civilian and injuring six others, including three young children, Ukrainian prosecutors reported.
According to the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office , Russian aircraft struck the city, using three FAB-250 aerial bombs equipped with universal glide and correction modules (UMPK).
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The bombs hit a residential area, damaging at least 27 homes.
Among the six injured were two women, aged 45 and 54, a 47-year-old man, and three children – girls aged seven and 10 and their younger brother, just one year and 10 months old.
The victims suffered blast injuries, traumatic brain injuries, concussion and shrapnel wounds. All were receiving medical treatment, prosecutors said.
The latest bombing came just three days after Russian strikes on Kramatorsk on Oct. 20 killed four civilians, including three municipal heating workers preparing the city’s infrastructure for winter.
Another civilian was killed in an FPV drone strike that day. At least six people were injured, while apartment buildings, educational facilities and utility infrastructure sustained damage.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: In tight race for Ga. gov, Keisha Lance Bottoms has been outspent but still confident
body:
The GOP candidate Rick Jackson is a healthcare executive and billionaire.
In battleground Georgia, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms faces a massive cash disadvantage in the race to replace term-limited Brian Kemp as governor. But less than two weeks out from Election Day, she's confident in her chances.
"My opponent has put over $100 million of his own money in this race. And this race is still tied," Bottoms said in an interview with ABC News' Linsey Davis that aired Thursday.
Bottoms' Republican opponent in the race, Rick Jackson, is a healthcare executive and billionaire.
"I've said repeatedly over the course of this campaign: he has the money, but the people still have the power," Bottoms added.
A poll released Tuesday by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution shows this year's governor's race statistically tied, with 46% of likely voters supporting Jackson, and 45% saying they're backing Bottoms.
Georgia hasn't elected a Democrat for governor since 1998.
Jackson declined ABC News' request for an interview.
In a statement, Jackson campaign spokesperson Garrison Douglas said: "As Rick travels across the state, engaging with voters directly and answering their questions, our campaign has been running an historic ground game operation alongside our media strategy."
The statement added: "Rick Jackson is not letting up, refusing to be outworked by anyone, and is committed to sharing his story and vision with Georgians every day."
Bottoms spoke about her plans to address affordability, which she says she "didn't need a polling source to tell me."
In addition to suspending taxes on items like diapers and feminine hygiene products and funding an affordable housing trust fund for the state, Bottoms detailed a "grocery tax relief plan."
"It would give local governments the ability to suspend or end the grocery tax, because they are collected by local governments," Bottoms said.
Bottoms also said that as governor, she would stand up against the Trump administration's Immigrations and Customs Enforcement policies and cuts to federal agencies like the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Many of the attacks on Bottoms from her political opponents stem from her time as mayor of Atlanta.
Bottoms chose not to run for reelection in 2021 after a tumultuous first term in which she faced criticism over her handling of COVID-19 and city crime.
"Keisha Lance Bottoms had her chance to lead. The results were disastrous," Jackson said at a rally with President Trump in Dalton, Georgia last week.
"Bad mayors don't make good governors," Jackson told the crowd.
Bottoms places the blame for a rise in crime rates on the pandemic.
"Just before things shut down -- which, we didn't shut down very long in Georgia -- I was touting a reduction in crime in our city," Bottoms told ABC.
"Then there was the pandemic, and then the governor made the decision to reopen Georgia ... So, our numbers went up, and we started seeing the trend before many other cities saw it."
According to data analysis from the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, violent crime increased by 59% in Atlanta from 2019 to 2020, compared to an increase of 33% in other cities during that time period.
Bottoms also responded to criticism she's received for not seeking reelection during the difficult time for the city.
"I completed the four-year term that I was elected to serve," Bottoms said, calling the decision not to run again in 2021 "deeply personal."
"I had two kids in elementary school, one in middle school, one in high school ... And I was experiencing a number of health issues I'd never talked about publicly," said Bottoms.
"If I go to bed like my daddy did and I don't wake up, where do I want to spend these four years? And for me, it was wanting to be the best version of myself for my family. So that's very different than quitting," she added.
If elected in November, Bottoms would become the first Black woman governor in U.S. history.
She would also be the first woman and the first Black person elected governor in Georgia.
"My family goes back at least five generations in Georgia... I'm a descendant of slaves on both sides," Bottoms said, calling the potential milestone "much more personal" for her.

title: West indulges Kiev’s sense of impunity regarding Zaporozhye plant — Russian diplomat
body:
UN, October 24. /TASS/. The West’s patronage has deprived the Ukrainian regime’s mindset of criticism on the issue of nuclear safety and the Zaporozhye nuclear power station, Alexander Repkin, Russia’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, said.
"Unconditional protectionism from the West has normalized the absence of any critical line in Kiev’s mindset. External patronage is driving the Ukrainian regime deeper into the illusion of complete permissiveness. It is obvious that this cannot continue — the risks to nuclear safety and people’s lives have become critical. We call on the international community to stop ignoring Ukraine’s irresponsible actions and to unconditionally condemn any attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities," he told the UN General Assembly.
"The lack of a responsible approach on the part of individual countries is leading to a threatening situation around the Zaporozhye nuclear power plant and its satellite city Energodar."
He added that this summer attacks on the city’s and the plant’s infrastructure have become almost daily. "This is not just about creating threats to the nuclear safety of the Zaporozhye nuclear power plant, but also about Kiev’s targeted campaign to eliminate the plant’s staff, their family members, and local residents," he said.

title: Arab and Islamic countries call for resumption of traffic in Strait of Hormuz — statement
body:
CAIRO, October 24. /TASS/. Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey have called for an urgent and full resumption of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, they said in a joint statement of the foreign ministers after a meeting in Istanbul.
"We oppose any restrictions on civilian shipping and call for a swift resumption of safe and unimpeded passage of vessels through the Strait of Hormuz," the document says.
The foreign ministers added that the conflict between Iran and Israel with the United States, "must be resolved exclusively through diplomacy" and "in accordance with the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding." The ministers stated the "importance of preventing attacks on civilian infrastructure and civilians, including maritime vessels," and also called for "preventing further escalation" in the region.

title: Ukraine now fights two enemies. One is America
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); On 18 October, President Zelenskyy accused Donald Trump of trying to pressure Ukraine into capitulating to Russia. Asked by NBC whether Ukraine could win the war without the US, he answered : "Without United States support it's very difficult. But if United States will support Putin, it's historic mistake and big tragedy.... If the United States officially will take the side of Russia, if these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand." He said Ukraine hopes Trump will be on its side, or at least "in the middle," and that he will "change his decisions" on Russia, as "it's all mistakes, it will not help us, and it will not help United States." In an interview with NBC's Meet the Press, when asked whether Trump is still an ally of Ukraine, Zelenskyy said: "I hope so." Not a definitive yes, but a weak maybe. As diplomacy goes, statements do not come much stronger than this. What triggered them? Probably the sum of all things. We all remember Trump and Vance humiliating Zelenskyy in the White House on 28 February 2025. Trump told the Ukrainian President that he was "gambling with" a third world war. Zelenskyy was told to come back "when he is ready for peace". Most will also remember that the USA enacted the decision to halt its aid to Ukraine across two separate, sweeping actions taken during the first months of the second Trump administration in early 2025. Presently, it is only delivering military aid decided by former President Biden. Some might have forgotten that Trump called Zelenskyy a "dictator without elections," suggested Ukraine started the war, and pushed a "peace plan" whose original 28-point draft gave Russia terms more favorable than what Moscow sought at the 2022 Istanbul talks. After 640 days in office, Trump's disdain for Ukraine and admiration for Russia seem to grow by the day, and his kakistocracy—government by the least qualified—keeps undermining Ukraine's defense. In less than two weeks: 9 October: the administration imposed new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), an institution crucial for holding Putin and the Kremlin accountable for their atrocities in Ukraine. The same day, Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports, effectively helping fund Russia's wars. 10 October: Trump said of the elected president of a country fighting off Russia's full-scale invasion: "It's time for Ukraine to get a new president ." 11 October: Trump declared on Truth Social an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine that bound only Ukraine. Zelenskyy said it was "news to him." 14 October: SpaceX restricted Starshield , the classified, military-grade version of Starlink; Reuters reported on 15 October that the order came from the White House , undermining Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russian jet-powered drones and strike Russian forces in occupied territory. 15 October: the US suspended critical intelligence sharing for three days, Zelenskyy said on 18 October, leaving Ukraine without warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches against its citizens and energy infrastructure. 16 October: two days before they were due to take effect, Trump waived the sanctions , restrictions and tariffs on Russia required by the Graham Act, calling it in the US national interest, and put nearly all of the congressional sanctions package on hold. 18 October: the administration reportedly proposed that Europe resume buying Russian gas to help "entice Russia to end the war in Ukraine." Europe balked. 19 October: it emerged that the US is delaying Patriots procured by allies under NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), leaving Ukraine short of defenses against Russian ballistic missiles. Ukrainian officials say the shipment is stalled because Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not signed the transfer documents on his desk. 19 October: Trump said that "Xi Jinping has been very fair on Ukraine. He hasn't been very much involved. Same with Russia. They haven't been nearly what they could've been," ignoring that Russia is waging an unjust, unprovoked and genocidal war against Ukraine. The same day, Trump claimed Zelenskyy targets Russian refineries knowing the attacks are seriously hurting world diesel markets, including in the US, and that he "doesn't want to end this war , and probably never did." Talking to reporters outside the White House, Trump said Zelenskyy should get someone else to negotiate on Ukraine's behalf, and that he is willing to meet Putin and Xi to discuss the war, without the Ukrainian president. Kyiv fears Washington might decide Ukraine's future without it. 20 October: Vice President JD Vance said Ukraine should not join NATO and should stop striking Russian energy. He refused to call Ukraine a US "ally," downgrading it to a "partner": "We don't have a formal alliance... they're not in NATO... we're going to work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things, too." 21 October: after four and a half years of genocidal full-scale war and amid persistent Russian air strikes on Ukrainians, US special envoy Steve Witkoff praised Putin as a "humanitarian," echoing Trump's claim that Russia had restrained itself. The same day, Trump said the end of the war is closer than ever. He may step up efforts to coerce Ukraine into a deal by the end of 2026, The Atlantic reports, with Ukraine's prospects shaped by the US midterms and possible Trump-Putin-Xi talks in November. Less than two weeks, summarized. Explore further Europe now faces two strategic adversaries: Russia and the United States This is how Trump's administration talks about, and acts towards, the victim of an unjustified, unprovoked and horrendous war. Trump's USA (TUSA) is siding with autocracy against democracy and the rules-based world order. It talks about America's former allies in a similar manner: derogatory and disrespectful. None of the above is the word or deed of an ally. When one chooses to see the world as it is, Zelenskyy's statements become both necessary and important. This is not only about Ukraine's self-respect and survival. Once we acknowledge the realities—that Europe is in an undeclared war with Russia at a moment when the USA has chosen to become a strategic adversary —we stand better prepared to defend ourselves: to accept that our present security system does not work and new solutions are urgently needed, and that diplomacy alone does not work and military force is essential to protect freedom, democracy and international law. More than a year ago, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned that Europe is "not at war, but no longer at peace either" with Russia. Other heads of state have echoed him. NATO has since shifted from a peacetime alliance to one focused on urgent wartime readiness. Unfortunately, the process started years too late. By seeing the world as it is, European leaders might reach the long-overdue conclusion that Russia's wars in Ukraine and Europe can only be stopped by a demonstration of strength: an alliance willing and capable of using military force to stop Russia. The alliance Russia fears isn't NATO. It's a coalition that will actually fight . Explore further The alliance Russia fears isn’t NATO. It’s a coalition that will actually fight. European courage and action are urgently needed. Ukraine is exposed to a two-front war, defending itself against both Russia and TUSA, and their attacks are increasing in scale and scope. Both Moscow and Washington want to end the war this year and are ramping up their assaults on Ukraine accordingly. Irrespective of one's view of Ukraine, it is commonly understood that it is stopping Russia from advancing and increasing its border with NATO and the EU. Ukraine is defending European values and principles, ensuring the rest of us can continue living in something resembling peace. The consequences of its defeat would be truly devastating. There can be no European strategic autonomy without Ukraine. There can be no European security and stability without Ukraine. Europe can never become a Great Power without Ukraine. And neither Russia nor the USA want Europe to achieve any of the above. It is time to act according to the present-day realities and face down Europe's two strategic adversaries . In the worst case, Ukraine's destiny might be decided in November already. Hans Petter Midttun Hans Petter Midttun, independent analyst on hybrid warfare, Non-Resident Fellow at the Centre for Defense Strategies, board member of the Ukrainian Institute for Security and Law of the Sea, former Defense Attaché of Norway to Ukraine, and officer (R) of the Norwegian Armed Forces. title: Moonshot AI Releases Kimi K3.1 Pro: A 2.8T Total/104B Active Params (MoE) Model with 1M Context
body: Moonshot AI has just released Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in its K3.1 series. Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 3T-class open-weight* model with a 1-million-token context window. Moonshot team positions it against the strongest proprietary models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. For developers, it is cheaper API pricing than K3 and open weights yet not available. *open weights are expected to release in November 2026 . TL;DR Size: 2.8T total, 104B active parameters (MoE) , 1M-token context. Runs on: Kimi API today. For K3, Moonshot recommends supernodes of 64+ accelerators , with MXFP4 weights and MXFP8 activations. Not a single-GPU model. Performance: Near the proprietary frontier on terminal coding; behind it on scientific terminal tasks. Best: SWE-Marathon 51.7, ahead of every model in Kimi’s chart (self-reported). Worst: Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 at 38.1, versus 68.1 for GPT-6 Astra in Kimi’s chart. What is Kimi K3.1 Pro? Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with much larger post-training compute. Moonshot team ran joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains. To support this, the Moonshot team optimized the RL framework, long-context inference, sandbox infrastructure and rollout scheduling. The base K3 architecture uses Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes). It activates 16 of 896 experts through a Stable LatentMoE framework. The model accepts text, images and video through the API, per the quickstart docs . Moonshot team also shipped Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed . According to the official Moonshot blog, it runs 2 to 3x faster . How does Kimi K3.1 Pro perform on benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported by Moonshot at max reasoning effort, mostly with the Claude Code harness. Coding : On Terminal-Bench 4.0, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%. That is just behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4% in Kimi’s chart. On SWE-Marathon it leads at 51.7, ahead of Opus 5.5 at 46.3. On Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, an internal benchmark, it scores 61.2, up from K3’s 55.95. Science : Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 is the clear gap. K3.1 Pro scores 38.1, versus 68.1 for GPT-6 Astra and 63.3 for Opus 5.5 in Kimi’s chart. 3D and CAD : On BenchCAD with tools , K3.1 Pro scores 92.7. Opus 5.5 scores 96.2 and GPT-6 Astra 95.9. Without tools, K3.1 Pro scores 72.8, close to Opus 5.5 at 73.0. Finance : K3.1 Pro reports a state-of-the-art 64.4 on OfficeQA Pro v2. It scores 58.6 on Frontier Finance. On internal finance tests, it gains 7.2 points in modeling and 11.6 in research over K3. Hallucination : On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard, an internal stress test, claim-level hallucinations fell from 23.4% (K3) to 8.3%. That is roughly the 65% drop Moonshot cites. GPT-6 Astra still posts a lower 5.5% on the same test. window.addEventListener('message',function(e){if(e.data&&e.data.id==='mtp-k31'&&e.data.mtpH){var f=document.getElementById('mtp-k31-frame');if(f)f.style.height=e.data.mtpH+'px';}}); How does Kimi K3.1 Pro handle cyber risk? Moonshot removed cyber-related data from mid-training and RL for the open-weight release. On its internal xdev-bench-hard, an unfiltered checkpoint solved 90.5% at pass@3. The shipped K3.1 Pro solves 81.0%. Moonshot says it stays behind frontier proprietary models on offensive cyber tasks. How can developers access Kimi K3.1 Pro? The model is live on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code and the Kimi API . The API IDs are kimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed . The endpoint is OpenAI-compatible. Pricing for K3.1 Pro is $2.00 input and $10.00 output per million tokens. Cache hits cost $0.20. Highspeed costs $4.00 input and $20.00 output. K3 itself was priced at $3.00 and $15.00. Practical limits from the quickstart : Thinking mode is always on. Reasoning effort is low , high or max (default max ). Temperature 1.0 and top-p 0.95 are fixed. Output defaults to 131,072 tokens and can go up to 1,048,576. Access unlocks after a minimum $1 top-up. Vision input does not accept public image URLs. Use base64 or uploaded file IDs. How does it compare with competing models? window.addEventListener('message',function(e){if(e.data&&e.data.id==='mtp-k31c'&&e.data.mtpH){var f=document.getElementById('mtp-k31c-frame');if(f)f.style.height=e.data.mtpH+'px';}}); *Figure taken from Kimi’s comparison chart; not confirmed on the competitor’s own page. What are the limitations? Weights are not public yet, so self-hosting is not possible today. The 2.8T size points to multi-node, supernode-class serving. Science-heavy terminal work trails GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 by 25+ points. Several claimed wins come from internal benchmarks. For K3, Moonshot warned that dropping reasoning history in a harness destabilizes output . The K3.1 Pro docs also say to return the full assistant message. Key Takeaways Kimi K3.1 Pro: 2.8T total, 104B active, 1M context. Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 65.7%, 0.7 points behind Opus 5.5. Leads SWE-Marathon at 51.7; trails badly on Terminal-Bench Science (38.1). API costs $2/$10 per million tokens, cheaper than K3. Open weights are expected in November 2026. Check out the official tech blog , the API quickstart and the launch post on X . title: Moscow and New Delhi ready Modi’s visit to Russia — Indian ambassador
body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Moscow and New Delhi are preparing Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Russia and are determining the dates of the trip, Indian ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar said in an interview with TASS.
The previous summit took place in early December of last year. At that time, Russian President Vladimir Putin invited Modi to visit Russia in 2026. The embassy and the Russian Foreign Ministry are working to set the dates, and as soon as a preliminary agreement is reached, they will make the announcement, the diplomat said after the II Russian-Indian business forum Time.
Moscow and New Delhi will continue contacts in the coming weeks to prepare documents and agreements that can be signed at the end of the summit, when it takes place.
The II Time Russian-Indian Business Forum, geld in Kazan from October 15 to 16, was aimed at developing Russian·Indian trade and economic cooperation. Its participants discussed ways to implement joint initiatives, promising investment projects, and opportunities for technological and economic cooperation. TASS is the forum’s information partner.

title: Kiev not interested in resolving conflict via talks — BSW expert
body:
BERLIN, October 24. /TASS/. Sevim Dagdelen, a foreign policy expert for the BSW party, has described the current round of consultations in Oslo on resolving the conflict in Ukraine as a "glimmer of hope," but noted that Vladimir Zelensky’s position is hindering the achievement of results.
"It is becoming clear that Zelensky is not interested in resolving the conflict through negotiations. Europeans are taking on heavy blame precisely because they want to continue this war—until the last Ukrainian," Dagdelen said in an interview with the World News Monitor portal.
Speaking about the initiatives to resolve the Ukrainian conflict, in particular about the plan put forward by American economist Jeffrey Sachs, the politician supported his view about the key importance of Ukraine’s neutral status. At the same time, she emphasized that the West still lacks a real understanding of the security situation, as evidenced by NATO’s expansion. Dagdelen was skeptical about Ukraine’s possible accession to the European Union, since Kiev’s integration into the EU — which effectively positions itself as a replacement for the North Atlantic Alliance -- could create a "constant threat of war" for Europe.
Dagdelen is concerned about Western countries’ attempts to use a possible ceasefire merely as "Minsk·3" for yet another militarization of Ukraine. Nevertheless, she called the very fact of resuming the discussion of these pressing issues a positive factor.
A Ukrainian delegation and the US president’s special envoy Steve Witkoff met in Oslo on October 20. American leader’s son·in·law Jared Kushner (via video link), Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also took part. Later, Witkoff went to Russia for negotiations. A meeting with President Vladimir Putin, which took place in St. Petersburg on October 21, was primarily focused on a Ukrainian settlement and lasted about three hours.

title: Obuasi SHTS sex scandal: Second complainant alleges pressure to withdraw police case
body: Pressure is mounting on a second complainant in the alleged sexual abuse case involving the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Zakaria Abdulai, to withdraw her complaint, as police sources confirm that the first of two former rape complainants has withdrawn her case. The development has renewed concerns about the protection of the students involved in the case and whether they can pursue their complaints without intimidation or pressure to settle the matter outside court. Police sources at Bekwai confirmed to JoyNews that one of the two former complainants had withdrawn her complaint. The second complainant has reportedly said she is also facing pressure to abandon her case. The father of the second complainant had earlier alleged that a traditional ruler in the Obuasi area intervened and asked the family to settle the matter amicably. The claims have brought renewed attention to the role of community leaders and the need to ensure that complaints involving alleged sexual offences against students are handled through the appropriate legal and child-protection procedures. The Bekwai chief, Nana Yaw Anning II, confirmed receiving a delegation that approached him in August over the controversy involving the headmaster. He said four people visited him at home and explained that they wanted to discuss the case involving a student at Obuasi SHTS. “In August, while I was at home, I received a visit from four individuals, one of whom was my subject. They explained that their visit concerned a student at Obuasi Senior High Technical School. They said the headmaster’s actions had brought disgrace to the school,” he said. Nana Anning said he told the visitors that the matter was already under investigation and that he would give their appeal further consideration. “I told them that since the matter was already under investigation and they had come to plead on the matter, I would give it further consideration. They agreed and left. However, before leaving, they gave us 200 cedis to buy schnapps,” he said. The chief’s account confirms that a delegation approached him about the matter, but it does not, on its own, establish that he pressured the complainant or her family to withdraw a complaint. The Minister for Gender, Children and Social Protection, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, said her ministry was working with the Domestic Violence and Victim Support Unit (DOVVSU) of the Ghana Police Service and the Ghana Health Service to ensure that the appropriate procedures were followed in handling the students’ cases. “Our intervention is to go back to correct some of those things, and as to pressure being mounted on the girls not to report, I will give you information on that when we find the data speaking to that,” she said. Dr Lartey said the ministry was coordinating with the relevant agencies to ensure that the students received appropriate screening and support, with the consent of their parents or guardians where required. “But what I can tell you is that some of the protocols that needed to be followed, the ministry is working, especially with DOVVSU and the Ghana Health Service to ensure that they go back to, you know, report appropriately, get to follow the health protocols to ensure screening, get the consent of parents and guardians, so that we’ll be able to get the right protocols followed to ensure that the girls are safe,” she said.

title: FIFA approves normalisation committee for Nigeria
body: FIFA has moved to restore order in Nigerian football by approving the formation of a normalisation committee to take charge of the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) until a new executive leadership is elected. The decision, announced by the NFF on Thursday, follows a leadership crisis that left the federation facing uncertainty over its administration and electoral process. In a statement issued through its Communications Department, the NFF said the Bureau of the FIFA Council had approved the establishment of the committee, whose members will be appointed jointly by FIFA and the Confederation of African Football (CAF). A letter signed by FIFA Secretary-General Mattias Grafström and addressed to Dr Emmanuel Ikpeme outlined the committee’s mandate and the deadline for completing its work. “The normalisation committee shall consist of a suitable number of members, who will be appointed jointly by FIFA and CAF as soon as possible,” the letter stated. The committee will remain in office until it has completed its assigned responsibilities, but its tenure must end no later than May 31, 2027. “The period during which the normalisation committee shall perform its functions shall expire as soon as it has fulfilled all of its tasks, but by no later than 31 May 2027,” the letter added. Committee members barred from contesting FIFA has also ruled out the possibility of members of the interim body using their positions to secure places in the next NFF leadership. “None of the members of the normalisation committee will be eligible for the positions to be filled during the upcoming NFF elections under any circumstances,” it said. The restriction is intended to separate the committee’s temporary administrative responsibilities from the contest for elected positions in the federation. Until FIFA and CAF appoint the members, the NFF secretariat will continue to manage routine administrative duties and the day-to-day running of Nigerian football. Leadership crisis disrupts elections The intervention follows the resignation of NFF President Ibrahim Gusau, General Secretary Mohammed Sanusi and other members of the federation’s Executive Committee on August 27, 2026. Their departures came amid mounting criticism of Nigerian football following the country’s failure to qualify for the 2026 FIFA World Cup and the Super Falcons’ failure to qualify for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup. The mass resignations left the federation facing a leadership vacuum and disrupted preparations for executive committee elections scheduled for September 27. The normalisation committee is expected to provide temporary leadership while addressing the tasks assigned by FIFA and CAF and preparing the ground for fresh elections. Its appointment marks a significant intervention in the administration of Nigerian football, with the May 31, 2027 deadline providing a clear outer limit for the process.

title: Saudi Arabia not to host Intervision this year — TASS source
body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Saudi Arabia not to host the international music competition Intervision this year, a source told TASS.
"Due to a combination of circumstances, holding it in Saudi Arabia is not currently possible. According to our information, the competition is proposed to be held in 2027," the source said.
Back in early August, a source in Riyadh told TASS that the organization of the competition in 2026 was in doubt and there was no guarantee that the event would take place.
In May, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov expressed hope that escalation in the Middle East would not undermine the plans to organize the Intervision there. However, Saudi Arabia has not yet publicly announced the music competition and has not provided possible dates and the lineup of participants.
Intervision was a song contest organized by the International Organization of Television and Radio Broadcasting (OIRT), which existed from 1946 to 1993. It was held in the 1960s-1980s, following the same model as "Eurovision," a music award of the European Broadcasting Union, which broke away from OIRT. The contest involved not only socialist countries close to the USSR, but also Austria, Belgium, Spain, Canada, the Netherlands, Portugal, and Finland.
The Intervision was revived in 2025 in Moscow. Russia was represented by Honored Artist of the Russian Federation Yaroslav Dronov (Shaman). More than 20 countries, including all BRICS states, took part.

title: Ashie-Moore disputes report on alleged theft of businessman’s belongings
body: The Greater Accra Regional Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Emmanuel Nii Ashie-Moore, has rejected reports that the Attorney-General’s Department has recommended his prosecution for alleged stealing of a Singaporean businessman’s personal belongings. In a statement issued on October 23, Mr Ashie-Moore described the report as inaccurate, misleading and calculated to damage his reputation, particularly ahead of the NDC’s forthcoming internal elections. “I categorically reject the report published by JoyNews alleging that the Attorney-General’s Department has recommended my prosecution. I maintain that the report is inaccurate, misleading and calculated to tarnish my hard-earned reputation as the Greater Accra Regional Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), particularly ahead of the forthcoming internal party elections,” he said. His response follows a report on an advice from the Attorney-General’s Department indicating that investigators should charge him with stealing under Section 124 of the Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29). The report cited an investigation docket that included witness statements, CCTV footage from Fiesta Residences and a cybercrime analysis report. The recommendation, as reported, is not a conviction, and any criminal liability would have to be determined through the legal process. “I call on JoyNews to uphold the highest standards of responsible journalism by thoroughly verifying its claims, correcting any inaccuracies and ensuring that its platform is not used to unfairly damage reputations,” he said. The statement did not set out a detailed rebuttal of the specific evidence cited in the report or provide documents contradicting the reported advice from the Attorney-General’s Department. The case concerns allegations that Mr Ashie-Moore removed the luggage and personal belongings of Singaporean businessman Toh You Kang while the businessman was in police custody. The wider dispute between the two men also involves allegations connected to a purported US$800,000 payment for assistance in securing contracts with the Electricity Company of Ghana. Mr Ashie-Moore has previously denied receiving the money and rejected the allegations against him. title: Voices from the Arab Press: Iran, the Kurds, and the future of Arab power
body: Citizenship before maps of separationAn-Nahar, Lebanon, October 20The concern expressed by the leadership of Iraqi Kurdistan over the American withdrawal deserves careful consideration. It reveals that relations among the components of the Iraqi state still require guarantees from beyond its borders.I understand the reasons for this anxiety, given a long history of repression and broken promises. But the more important question is why a country cannot reassure some of its own citizens, leaving them to seek protection from a distant power whose priorities change with its interests.We see this in Lebanon, Iraq, Yemen, and elsewhere in our region, where national communities seek security through alliances with foreign powers. To me, this is a sign of the nation-state's incomplete development, and one we must recognize.Iraqi Kurds have achieved the most firmly established autonomous government among contemporary Kurdish communities. The 2005 constitution recognized the Kurdistan Region and its existing institutions, giving its people a parliament, government, and administrative structures within Iraq. These were substantial gains for a people who endured tragedies, including the Anfal campaign and the Halabja massacre. Yet the transition from autonomy to full independence collided with geography, economics, and the positions of neighboring countries and major powers.In September 2017, more than 92% of participants in the region's referendum voted for independence. The majority was overwhelming, but the desired state never materialized. Baghdad rejected the referendum, neighboring countries opposed it, and Washington withheld the support its organizers had anticipated. The region subsequently lost control of Kirkuk and other disputed territories. The lesson is clear: popular mobilization can produce an electoral result, but it cannot overturn the balance of power or independently create the conditions for statehood.In Syria, Kurdish forces established a de facto autonomous administration during the civil war, but it did not become a recognized independent state. In Turkey, the Kurdistan Workers' Party waged a prolonged armed struggle without achieving independence. Yet Turkish Kurds cannot be reduced to that organization; many have pursued political participation and elections. Kurdish movements themselves differ in their objectives, ranging from cultural rights and decentralization to autonomy and secession. Ignoring these distinctions distorts our understanding of diverse communities.The issue extends far beyond the Kurds. The Middle East is crowded with national, religious, and sectarian identities, some of whose members have suffered genuine injustices. In certain cases, memories of suffering have become permanent political projects, with leaders investing in fear and presenting separation as a ready-made solution. Regional or international powers then enter the picture, supplying weapons and promises while using these causes as bargaining chips. I believe the most dangerous illusion is that an external patron shares a community's aspirations as deeply as its own people do. Foreign powers have their calculations; they may leave, while the community remains among its neighbors.None of this means demanding silence from the oppressed or absolving central governments. Authorities that prohibit citizens from using their language, discriminate in employment or the courts, or bombard their cities inevitably drive people to seek alternatives.It is easy for rulers to proclaim national unity while governing as though the state belongs exclusively to their own group. Defending national unity must therefore begin with reforming government and guaranteeing rights. Citizenship is first an obligation of the state, before it becomes a demand placed upon its people.Switzerland offers a useful example. Four national languages and different religious and cultural traditions coexist within a federal state. French speakers were not required to abandon their language or imitate German-speaking regions. The distribution of powers, recognition of diversity, and political participation helped create a shared interest in remaining together. Switzerland is not a model that can be copied wholesale, but it demonstrates that respecting differences can strengthen a country, and that rigid centralization is not the only path to unity.In Canada, Quebec voters narrowly rejected sovereignty in a 1995 referendum, with 50.58% voting against it. Political disagreement continued, and separatists remained free to advocate their position without the province descending into civil war. What matters in these examples is the existence of institutions that permit disagreement and regulate it. Citizens who can challenge authority and seek legal remedies possess alternatives to retreating into communal loyalties. A state confident in its own fairness does not interpret every demand for cultural recognition as hostility.South Sudan offers a contrasting lesson. It gained independence in 2011, only to descend into civil war in 2013. Raising a new flag did not resolve struggles over power; divisions simply migrated inside the newly established state. This does not erase the injustices previously suffered by southerners, but it illustrates a painful truth: a community may succeed in separating while its leaders fail to build a functioning state. The practical question therefore extends beyond drawing borders to governing responsibly, holding officials accountable, and protecting minorities within those new borders.The struggle worth pursuing in our region is the creation of modern, just civic states that accommodate different identities without distributing rights according to them. Iraqi first, then Kurdish or Arab, Sunni or Shi'ite. Syrian first, then Kurdish, Alawite, or Druze. Lebanese first, then Christian or Muslim, Shi'ite, Sunni, or Druze. This is about the relationship between citizens and the state, not ranking people's worth or erasing their histories. It requires an independent judiciary, peaceful transfers of power, fair distribution of wealth, and enforceable constitutional guarantees. Without these conditions, citizenship becomes a beautiful slogan that people hear but never experience.We need citizens to feel that their futures depend on their abilities, their security is protected by law, and their dignity requires neither a sectarian intermediary nor a foreign embassy. We also need education that teaches children about one another's histories without accusations of betrayal or manufactured heroism. People learn coexistence in schools, workplaces, and neighborhoods, while politics destroys it by turning neighbors into suspects because of their names, religions, or languages. Nations achieve stability through justice before anything else. – Mohammed Al RumaihiEgypt, Saudi Arabia, and restoring the red linesAsharq Al-Awsat, UK, October 19Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's declaration concerning Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia marks a significant development in a crisis that has expanded beyond Yemen into a regional confrontation shaped by decades of Iranian attempts to overturn the established order.Egypt's position should come as no surprise. As a major Arab power, it cannot abandon its responsibility to defend Arab national security and its own direct interests. Egypt and Saudi Arabia form the backbone of any firm Arab position intended to protect the region's Arab interests.Egypt has approached Iran's regional expansion with considerable wisdom and patience, relying on diplomacy and time in the hope that Tehran would abandon its repeated efforts to encircle Arab decision-making centers and alter the balance of power within individual countries and across the region.Several years ago, I met el-Sisi and asked him about Egypt, its economy, and regional security. He told me: “The forces targeting Egypt are also targeting the region. These forces of evil include extremist organizations and regional states seeking to destabilize countries and overturn existing arrangements. “Our decision to confront these attacks and attempts is firm, and our determination is strong. As Arab countries, we must stand together to defend our national security and stability against attempts to divide our countries, plunge them into chaos, and exhaust their economies and opportunities for progress. “I am completely confident that, together with our brothers in the Gulf and other Arab countries, we can confront those targeting our countries, our region, and our role.” He emphasized that Egypt's relationship with Saudi Arabia was “deep and strategic, serving both countries and Arab national security.” “I say sincerely that our brothers in Saudi Arabia manage affairs with wisdom and firmness, and that is why I tell them we are always together.” He was equally emphatic that Saudi stability meant Egyptian stability, and vice versa.What struck me about that interview, published in Asharq Al-Awsat, was that El-Sisi deliberately avoided naming Iran, even though Tehran was clearly among the forces he described as seeking to destabilize the region. He wanted to preserve an opening for dialogue and give diplomacy every opportunity to moderate Iranian behavior, despite Tehran's continued violations of red lines on Arab territory.Saudi Arabia, likewise, demonstrated considerable patience toward Iranian intrusions, keeping diplomatic channels open both before and after the Beijing agreement. Yet Riyadh remained committed to fundamental principles: respect for the red lines established by international law and those imposed by genuine good-neighborly relations.Egyptian and Saudi policies consequently converged around supporting legitimate authorities in Palestine, Lebanon, and Yemen, while encouraging Iraq's government to restore the institutions of the state and reclaim Iraq's place within the Arab family.During major turning points in recent decades, Egyptian and Saudi determination have repeatedly converged. They stood together when Iraq's Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait, and again when Egyptians took to the streets amid fears that Muslim Brotherhood rule threatened their country's identity, stability, and regional role. Saudi Arabia acted on the conviction that its own security was inseparable from Egypt's, while Egypt understood that destabilizing Saudi Arabia would have catastrophic consequences for Egypt, the Gulf, the Arab and Islamic worlds, and the global economy.Regional coexistence requires respect for clear boundaries: internationally recognized borders, legitimate governments, and every state's right to choose its policies in accordance with established laws and norms. Encircling countries, penetrating their borders and security systems, and undermining their ability to make sovereign decisions are incompatible with those principles.The Houthi organization Ansar Allah has built its approach around violating virtually every red line, domestically and internationally. Its record extends from undermining Yemen's legitimate government and assassinating former president Ali Abdullah Saleh to holding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait hostage and carrying out the brutal bombardment of civilians at Riyadh Airport.Iran has similarly violated red lines on other countries' territory by establishing and arming militias, controlling their decisions, and assigning them regional missions designed to destabilize governments.Against this backdrop, el-Sisi's position sends a stern warning: Egypt is prepared to participate in defensive missions that help contain the region's destabilizing forces. The combined weight of Egypt and Saudi Arabia provides a foundation for mobilizing an Arab, Islamic, and international response capable of restoring these boundaries and preventing further attempts to overturn the regional order.The region is filled with the smell of a wider war and enveloped in uncertainty. Even the possible departure of a dangerous player named Benjamin Netanyahu would not necessarily mean a less aggressive Israel. Nor can we predict how US President Donald Trump might respond to an electoral setback for his party in the midterms. Iran's escalating behavior in the Strait of Hormuz could accelerate the arrival of still more dangerous confrontations. Tehran has changed neither its language nor its methods.An Arab official smiled at length when Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi claimed that his country had tried to persuade both Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to halt their escalation, but neither side had cooperated. Araghchi was particularly careful to insist that “the Houthis make their decisions independently.” That amusing assertion only deepened the Arab official's pessimism.– Ghassan CharbelCan Egypt pass the toughest test of political power?El Watan, Egypt, October 18In my view, the most important thing President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has said is that 2030 will mark the end of his presidency, that the decision is final and is not open to debate.This statement deserves serious consideration, without the usual applause or the automatic skepticism that greets almost everything. If the commitment is fulfilled, its significance will extend far beyond the president himself. Egypt has an opportunity to establish a principle essential to its future: that the end of a president's term should be a known date for which the state prepares and about which society can feel reassured. Countries need to know how responsibility will be transferred just as much as they need to know who bears it.I believe el-Sisi has an opportunity to shape one of the most important elements of his political legacy: leaving behind a state capable of functioning after his departure, institutions that understand their responsibilities, and a political system that produces people worthy of leadership. But this is where our own responsibility begins. Anyone who imagines that the public's role begins on election morning and ends with placing a ballot in the box reduces an enormous issue to a single moment.The ballot determines the outcome, but the quality of that choice is shaped over many years. It depends on public awareness; access to information; the ability to question, compare, and hold officials accountable; and the emergence of figures whose competence has been demonstrated through actual experience.We should not discover a presidential candidate for the first time when his photograph appears on a campaign poster. We should have seen him shoulder responsibility, explain his decisions, acknowledge mistakes, and propose solutions whose costs he understands before promising results. Egypt is too important to be entrusted to a gifted orator, a fleeting wave of popularity, or an organization that regards the presidency as a means of taking control of the state.Egypt has institutions, and I trust that they have an essential role in protecting the country from infiltration and undue influence. But genuine protection comes through clear rules, laws applied equally to everyone, oversight of political financing and conflicts of interest, and respect for the constitution and the will of the Egyptian people. Strong institutions reassure citizens that their country's future is safeguarded by a system of responsibility and accountability, and that any incoming president will govern within an established framework of rules and limits.That is why the remaining years until 2030 are just as important as the transfer of power itself. We need to see greater opportunities for qualified individuals, political parties offering practical and achievable programs, media organizations asking serious questions, and public officials judged by the results of their work. We must also learn that political disagreement does not make someone less patriotic, just as political support does not automatically establish competence.I see the president's declared position as an opportunity for a major advance in Egypt's political development. But realizing that opportunity requires preparations for the future to become visible action starting now. If that happens, 2030 could become a defining moment: a president completing his term and handing over responsibility, a public making an informed choice, and institutions guaranteeing the continuity of the state and respect for its rules.The greatest legacy a ruler can leave his country is a future that becomes more secure even in his absence. Egypt deserves confidence not only in whoever governs it, but also in the rules that will remain after the president leaves office. – John Al-MasriiSaudi Arabia and its historic roleAl Qabas, Kuwait, October 19I lived in Saudi Arabia for more than 10 years while serving as secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council. During that time, I came to appreciate the profound and historic significance of the kingdom – not only for its people, rulers, and neighbors, but for the security and stability of the Arab and Islamic worlds and, indeed, countries far beyond the region.Saudi Arabia, its land, and its people represent an essential pillar of stability for all who value a secure and dignified life. This is a reality recognized across continents.The kingdom is not merely the birthplace of Islam, the home of its holiest sites, and a land central to Arab history. It is also the guardian of those sacred places, fully conscious of the immense responsibilities entrusted to it and prepared to shoulder the burdens of protecting them, maintaining their significance, and ensuring that Muslims arriving from every part of the world can worship safely and comfortably. Fortunately, confidence among Muslims and others in the wisdom of Saudi leadership has continued to grow. The kingdom's rulers understand that their responsibilities extend beyond the physical protection of holy sites to preserving the historical and spiritual heritage of a religion whose reach spans Asia, Africa, and parts of Europe.What impressed me most was the Saudi state's readiness to fulfill these obligations with extraordinary dedication. I observed the preparations undertaken to receive pilgrims and visitors, with attention not only to effort but to tangible results.Roads leading to the holy sites, hotels, accommodation, shopping facilities, and essential services were developed to meet the needs of pilgrims performing Hajj and Umrah. Saudi officials and institutions devoted themselves to this continuing mission, making the comfort and safety of worshipers a central priority.As the kingdom succeeded in meeting these responsibilities, and its international reputation and standing rose, adversaries sought to undermine the prestige it had earned through its organization, hospitality, and commitment to ensuring visitors could return home safely.I performed Hajj twice. The first time was among senior invited guests, an exceptionally satisfying and enjoyable experience. The second was with friends, when we visited the holy sanctuary and Medina together. We still recall the beauty of that journey.King Khalid assumed the throne following the death of his half-brother, King Fahd. I have followed the Gulf Cooperation Council closely, including attending its summit meetings alongside King Khalid, who was deeply interested in its details and committed to strengthening its work. I maintained regular contact with his office to communicate developments within the council and secure his support. King Fahd was a monarch, leader, and initiator who sought to understand the council's progress in depth. He sometimes advised patience on particular issues, and encouraged collective agreement out of consideration for the circumstances of individual member states. There was no need to rush; what mattered was unity of purpose and firmness of position.Saudi kings have been statesmen attentive to regional events and global developments, capable of adapting to change, cultivating friendships, and drawing lessons from international affairs. They understood the art of accommodation without haste or unnecessary noise, keeping their doors open to Arabs, Muslims, and others, near and far.Saudi Arabia's spirit of brotherhood was demonstrated most powerfully during the catastrophe of Saddam Hussein's 1990 invasion and annexation of Kuwait. Saddam had opened the door to his own destruction, and history has recorded both the ugliness of his actions and our failure to adequately recognize the danger his recklessness posed to Kuwait. Saudi Arabia's response was unwavering. Under King Fahd's leadership, the kingdom committed itself fully to Kuwait's liberation, mobilizing its resources and determination to achieve that goal.I was close to King Fahd during those painful months. He was always eager to reassure the Kuwaiti community in Riyadh, and repeatedly asked me to tell Kuwaiti citizens that the day of their return was not far away, but that patience was necessary to complete the preparations that would guarantee liberation. It was a historic moment requiring careful planning and the conviction that the mission would succeed, alongside a willingness to accept whatever sacrifices might be necessary.Looking back, I recall the decisive Saudi role in launching the liberation effort and securing international support for an extraordinary collective mobilization. We Kuwaitis continue to take pride in Saudi Arabia's determination to confront aggression and restore our country to its people.The world witnessed that commitment with admiration, and history records how the Saudi-Kuwaiti partnership demonstrated the full depth of brotherhood between our nations. We and the generations that follow us will continue to admire the strength of Saudi resolve that opened the path to Kuwait's liberation. The kingdom will forever remain a steadfast and influential pillar in Kuwait's history.– Abdullah Bishara   ■Translated by Asaf Zilberfarb.
