title: In 1956, Moscow agreed to withdraw its troops from Budapest. One week later, it launched a 60,000-soldier operation to crush Hungary’s revolution.
body: Budapest residents burn images of Stalin and books in Russian. October 1956. On October 23, 1956, hundreds of thousands of Budapest residents took to the streets to demand political reforms, free elections, and the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Peaceful demonstrations quickly turned into an armed uprising. Within days, Hungary was on the verge of leaving the Soviet bloc. The Soviet leadership initially agreed to make concessions and withdraw troops from the capital, but then reversed course. On November 4, the Soviet army launched a large-scale military operation that crushed the uprising. Thousands of people died, and about 200,000 Hungarians left the country. Western governments condemned Moscow’s actions but stopped short of intervening. Why did Hungarians rise up against the communist regime? What made Khrushchev abandon compromise? Could the United States and Europe have helped the insurgents? And why, 70 years later, do the events of 1956 still provoke political disputes in Hungary? Historian Alexey Uvarov answers these and other questions about the uprising. What was happening in the world in the fall of 1956? By the mid-1950s, the Cold War had been underway for almost 10 years. After World War II, Europe split into two camps. The United States played the leading role in Western Europe, while communist regimes under Soviet control took power in Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany. In 1949, the United States and its allies formed NATO; in 1955, the Soviet Union and Eastern European countries established the Warsaw Pact. The confrontation extended beyond Europe. From 1950 to 1953, the United States and its allies fought in the Korean War against North Korea, which had Soviet and Chinese backing. By then, both superpowers had nuclear weapons and understood that a direct conflict between them could have catastrophic consequences. Tensions began to ease after Joseph Stalin’s death in 1953. The Korean War ended, and in 1955, the Soviet Union withdrew its troops from Austria, which became a neutral state. That same year, the leaders of the Soviet Union, the United States, Britain, and France met in Geneva for the first time in 10 years. Their rivalry continued, but both sides sought to avoid a direct confrontation. Soviet Premier Nikolai Bulganin, U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower, French Prime Minister Edgar Faure, and British Prime Minister Anthony Eden (left to right) in Geneva. July 19, 1955. Soviet policy was changing, too. Stalin’s death set off a power struggle in Moscow that Nikita Khrushchev won. In February 1956, at the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, he delivered a secret speech condemning Stalin’s cult of personality and mass repression. At the same time, the Soviet leadership began talking about the possibility of national paths to socialism. Across Eastern Europe, this prompted public debate about possible reforms and loosening Moscow’s political control. Dwight Eisenhower had been president of the United States since January 1953. His administration publicly advocated the “liberation” of Eastern Europe from communist rule, while the Washington-funded broadcaster Radio Free Europe encouraged anti-Soviet sentiment. In practice, however, White House policy was far more cautious. In June 1953, Soviet troops had crushed an uprising in East Germany , and the United States had not intervened. American leaders decided that attempting to liberate Eastern Europe by force could lead to nuclear war. They therefore sought to weaken Soviet influence primarily through peaceful means. The Suez Crisis erupted as events unfolded in Hungary. In late October 1956, Israel, Britain, and France launched a military operation against Egypt, whose president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, had nationalized the Suez Canal. The United States opposed its own allies’ actions, dividing the Western powers. The fall of 1956 was a time of contradictions. The Cold War continued, yet the superpowers were seeking to avoid confrontation and had resumed contacts broken off under Stalin. Changes underway in the Soviet Union were raising hopes for reform in Eastern Europe. But no one knew what the limits of those reforms might be or how far Soviet leaders were prepared to go in supporting them. What was Hungary like in the first half of the 20th century? Until 1918, Hungary was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, where it enjoyed considerable autonomy. The Kingdom of Hungary covered a much larger territory than modern Hungary, encompassing present-day Slovakia, Transylvania, and Croatia. After its defeat in World War I in 1918, Austria-Hungary disintegrated. Hungary became independent, and a republic was proclaimed in Budapest, but the new government could not hold on to power. In the spring of 1919, communists led by Béla Kun seized power. They proclaimed the Hungarian Soviet Republic, which lasted a few months. Communist rule brought political terror and ended in defeat by the Romanian army. After the communists fell, Miklós Horthy , a former admiral in the Austro-Hungarian navy, came to power. In 1920, Hungary became a kingdom again, but without a king. Horthy became regent and effectively ruled the country until 1944. His regime was conservative and authoritarian, though parliament and some political parties continued to exist. The country’s most pressing problem was the aftermath of the 1920 Treaty of Trianon : Hungary lost about two-thirds of its territory, and roughly a third of ethnic Hungarians found themselves outside its new borders. The desire to recover those territories largely shaped Horthy’s foreign policy. Hungary gradually drew closer to Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, whose support helped it regain some of the lost lands from 1938 to 1941. The price, however, was participation in World War II on Germany’s side. In 1941, Hungary entered the war against the Soviet Union, and in 1943 its army suffered catastrophic losses on the Eastern Front. Adolf Hitler and Miklós Horthy. March 21, 1944. Hungarian Jews arrive by train at the Auschwitz death camp in Nazi-occupied Poland. Summer 1944. In March 1944, Germany occupied Hungary, fearing that it would pull out of the war. With the active participation of the Hungarian authorities, more than 400,000 Jews were deported to Auschwitz within a few months. That fall, Horthy tried to negotiate an armistice with Germany’s enemies but was removed from power. The Nazis replaced him with Hungarian far-right politicians from the Arrow Cross Party . In February 1945, after a siege lasting almost two months, the Red Army took Budapest. The city had suffered extensive destruction, and Hungary was once again on the losing side of a world war. Its political future now depended largely on the Soviet Union, whose troops were stationed in the country. What happened in Hungary between 1945 and 1956? Did it become a copy of the Soviet Union? Hungary was treated as a defeated ally of Nazi Germany, so its reconstruction and political future depended on the victorious powers. Formally, the Allied Control Commission monitored compliance with the armistice, but Soviet representatives led by Marshal Kliment Voroshilov dominated the commission. Hungary also had to pay reparations, a substantial share of which was to go to the Soviet Union. Initially, the country retained a multiparty system. Free parliamentary elections were held in November 1945. The Smallholders’ Party won about 57% of the vote, while the communists received just 17%. With Moscow’s support, however, the communists kept their places in the coalition government and retained control of key security agencies. Their leader, Mátyás Rákosi , gradually eliminated political opponents using what he himself called “salami tactics”: Opposition parties were weakened piece by piece as their leaders were accused of conspiring and engaging in activities against the state. By the end of the 1940s, the communists had established complete control. In 1947, Soviet security services arrested Béla Kovács, a leader of the Smallholders’ Party, and Prime Minister Ferenc Nagy was forced to resign. In 1948, the communists absorbed the Social Democratic Party, and in 1949 a Soviet-style constitution was adopted. Hungary became a people’s republic, with one party holding a virtual monopoly on power. A harsh dictatorship took shape in the years that followed. Rákosi, who called himself Stalin’s best pupil, established a system of mass repression. Opposition figures, clergy, intellectuals, and even members of the Communist Party itself were arrested. In 1949, former Interior Minister László Rajk was executed on fabricated espionage charges. Cardinal József Mindszenty, the head of Hungary’s Catholic Church, was sentenced to life in prison. Tens of thousands of people were sent to prisons and camps, and many families were forcibly expelled from cities. Cardinal József Mindszenty (left). Fall 1956. At the same time, the authorities tried to restructure the economy along Soviet lines. Industry was nationalized, peasants were forced to join agricultural cooperatives, and resources went primarily toward the rapid expansion of heavy industry. The aim was to turn Hungary into an industrial hub for the Soviet bloc despite its limited raw material reserves. These policies led to falling living standards, shortages of consumer goods, and growing public discontent. By the early 1950s, Hungary’s political and economic system largely replicated that of the Soviet Union under Stalin. The communist regime lacked broad public support and survived mainly because of the Soviet military presence. After Stalin’s death, the discontent that had built up began to surface more forcefully. What happened in Hungary between Stalin’s death and the start of the uprising? In March 1953, Soviet leaders began reassessing their policies in Eastern Europe. Moscow understood that repression and economic hardship were fueling public discontent and decided to move away from Stalin’s approach to foreign policy. In June, Hungary’s leaders were summoned to the Kremlin, where Mátyás Rákosi faced sharp criticism. He was accused of mass repression, excessive industrialization, and ruining agriculture. Moscow demanded that Rákosi hand the prime minister’s post to Imre Nagy while remaining leader of the Communist Party. Nagy was a longtime party member who had spent many years in the Soviet Union. After World War II, he served as agriculture minister and oversaw a land reform that distributed large estates among peasants. On becoming prime minister in the summer of 1953, Nagy announced a “new course.” The authorities slowed industrialization, eased pressure on peasants, began releasing political prisoners, and gave greater priority to producing consumer goods. There was no talk yet of abandoning socialism or introducing a multiparty system, but the changes were substantial compared with previous policies. The reforms quickly made Nagy popular with the public. But Rákosi remained party leader and opposed these policies. The outcome of his struggle with Nagy depended largely on who prevailed in Moscow. In early 1955, Khrushchev strengthened his position, while Georgy Malenkov, who supported Nagy, lost his post as head of the Soviet government. This enabled Rákosi to oust his rival from power. In April 1955, Nagy was removed as prime minister and later expelled from the party. Socialist Hungary’s leaders tried to return to their previous policies, but it was too late: Reform-minded writers, journalists, and party officials continued to push for change. These movements gained momentum after the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party in February 1956, where Khrushchev condemned repression. Rákosi, who regarded himself as a follower of Stalin, became even more vulnerable. Public debate intensified in Budapest, particularly in the Petőfi Circle, a discussion group named after the poet Sándor Petőfi , which drew thousands of participants. In the summer of 1956, the Politburo decided to remove Rákosi but installed his closest associate, Ernő Gerő, as party leader. Most critics of the regime saw this as merely a symbolic concession that fell well short of what was needed. Tensions continued to mount. On October 6, the authorities allowed a ceremonial reburial of László Rajk, the party official executed in 1949 on fabricated charges. Tens of thousands attended, turning the ceremony into a mass demonstration against the Stalinist past. On October 13, Nagy was readmitted to the party. The leadership, however, still hesitated to undertake serious reforms. The situation in Hungary was full of contradictions. Moscow had first supported reforms, then allowed them to be rolled back, and then once again advocated change and began de-Stalinization. Yet the people responsible for repression and harsh policies remained in power in Hungary. Hungarians increasingly doubted that the communists could carry out the necessary reforms, and soon they decided to take to the streets. How and why did the uprising begin? Events in neighboring Poland provided the spark. In October 1956, Polish communists decided to restore Władysław Gomułka to the party leadership. He had been removed from power and imprisoned under Stalin. Moscow tried to prevent his return: On October 19, Khrushchev and other leaders hurried to Warsaw, and Soviet troops began advancing toward the city. After negotiations, however, the Kremlin accepted the appointment of Gomułka, who promised to preserve the alliance with the Soviet Union. In Hungary, these events raised hopes that similar changes could be achieved at home. On October 22, students at Budapest’s Polytechnic Institute drew up 16 demands for the authorities. They called for the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Hungary, Nagy’s return as prime minister, free elections, an end to censorship, and accountability for the country’s former leader, Rákosi. The students decided to hold a demonstration the following day in support of Poland’s reforms. The October 23 demonstration began peacefully but quickly grew into a mass protest. Workers and other Budapest residents joined the students; by evening, hundreds of thousands of people were in the streets. Some demonstrators gathered outside parliament, demanding Nagy’s return, while others toppled an enormous statue of Stalin. Gerő, the Communist Party’s first secretary, went on the radio and accused the protesters of nationalism and hostile actions against the socialist system. His speech only fueled the anger. The streets of Budapest during the uprising. Fall 1956. Meanwhile, thousands of people gathered outside the state radio building. They demanded that the students be allowed on air to read their 16 demands. The building was guarded by political police, and the demonstrators’ representatives, who had been allowed inside for talks, had still not come back hours later. Rumors spread through the crowd that they had been arrested or even killed. Tensions rose as demonstrators demanded the delegation’s release and tried to enter the building. State security officers used tear gas and then opened fire on the crowd, which included unarmed demonstrators. Some people were killed, and others were wounded. The authorities then lost control of the situation entirely. Protesters began arming themselves. Hungarian soldiers and police officers who refused to disperse the demonstration gave them some weapons; the protesters obtained others from warehouses and factories. Street fighting broke out around the radio building and continued through the night. Within hours, a peaceful demonstration had become an armed uprising. The bodies of slain insurgents in the bed of a truck in Budapest. Fall 1956. How did the Soviet leadership respond? Did Moscow immediately decide to crush the uprising by force? On the evening of October 23, as protests escalated into armed clashes, the Hungarian authorities asked Moscow for military assistance. Soviet leaders convened an emergency meeting at the Kremlin that night. Most supported sending in troops. Only Anastas Mikoyan opposed the move, believing that force would only deepen the crisis. The other Politburo members did not support him, however, and Soviet tanks entered Budapest on the morning of October 24. At the same time, Nagy was reappointed prime minister of Hungary in the hope that this would calm the protesters. Soviet tanks on the streets of Budapest. October 30, 1956. Insurgents in front of a Soviet tank in Budapest. November 1956. But sending in troops had the opposite effect: A local protest against the communist leadership became a national uprising against Soviet domination. Street fighting continued, and some Hungarian troops joined the insurgents. On October 25, demonstrators outside parliament came under fire on an even larger scale, and dozens of people were killed. The authorities were rapidly losing control of the country: Revolutionary committees sprang up in cities, and workers’ councils formed in factories. Soviet leaders again tried to find a political solution to the crisis. On October 28, Hungary’s new prime minister, Nagy, announced a ceasefire, recognized the uprising as a national democratic movement, and promised to disband the political police. Moscow, in turn, agreed to begin withdrawing troops from Budapest. Budapest residents watch as the families of Soviet diplomats and officers leave the city aboard a ship on the Danube. November 1956. Records of Soviet leadership meetings from October 28 to 31, 1956, reveal considerable hesitation. On October 28, for example, Soviet Prime Minister Nikolai Bulganin called a full-scale military operation a “reckless venture,” a view supported by Politburo member Lazar Kaganovich . That same day, Khrushchev himself advocated a political solution, saying, “All we’re doing is shooting.” On October 30, Foreign Minister Dmitry Shepilov even suggested that Moscow stop dictating terms to Eastern European countries. Soviet leaders changed course on October 31. They concluded that concessions had failed to halt the revolution: Communist Party rule in Hungary was rapidly crumbling, and Nagy’s government could no longer guarantee that the country would remain in the Soviet bloc. Meanwhile, the start of the British-French operation against Egypt reinforced Khrushchev’s fear that withdrawing from Budapest would be seen as a sign of weakness. Fear of criticism from the Soviet Communist Party’s conservative wing also played a role, as did confidence that the United States would stop short of military intervention. Khrushchev gave this explanation: If we leave Hungary, it will encourage the American, British, and French imperialists. They will see it as weakness on our part and press forward. We would be exposing the weakness of our position. Our party would not understand us. We would then be giving them Hungary on top of Egypt. We have no other choice. Moscow therefore abandoned compromise and decided to restore control over Hungary by force. How was the uprising crushed? How many people died? And what kind of regime emerged in Hungary? After deciding to intervene militarily on October 31, the Soviet Union began moving additional troops into Hungary. Dubbed Operation Whirlwind, the operation was led by Marshal Ivan Konev . About 60,000 Soviet troops took part in total. The plan called for seizing Budapest and other major cities simultaneously, disarming the Hungarian army, and taking control of key government institutions. Meanwhile, Soviet leaders continued to pretend they were willing to negotiate a peaceful settlement. On November 3, Hungarian and Soviet representatives discussed a troop withdrawal. That evening, however, the Hungarian delegation, led by Defense Minister Pál Maléter, was invited to a Soviet military base, where KGB officers arrested its members. At dawn on November 4, the Red Army launched its offensive. Prime Minister Nagy managed to broadcast a radio message announcing the invasion before taking refuge in the Yugoslav embassy. Moscow announced the formation of a new Hungarian government led by János Kádár. The Hungarian army was unable to mount organized resistance. Soviet troops quickly disarmed most of its units, leaving volunteer groups — mainly young workers and students — to do most of the fighting. Despite the Soviet Union’s overwhelming military superiority, street battles in Budapest continued for several days. The last major pockets of resistance were crushed by mid-November. Insurgents on the streets of Budapest. Late October 1956. About 2,500 to 2,700 Hungarians died in the fighting, and roughly 20,000 more were wounded. A total of 669 Soviet soldiers were killed in action or died of their wounds. Another 51 servicemen were missing, and about 1,500 were wounded. Resistance continued even after the fighting ended: Workers’ councils organized strikes, demanding the restoration of the country’s independence. With Soviet support, Kádár’s new government gradually suppressed these protests. Military defeat was followed by mass repression. Tens of thousands of people were convicted of taking part in the uprising, and about 230 were executed. More than 200,000 Hungarians left the country. Nagy, who had been promised safe passage from the Yugoslav embassy, was detained and taken to Romania. He was later returned to Hungary, where he was sentenced to death in a trial closed to the public. On June 16, 1958, Nagy was executed along with several associates. Budapest residents on the city’s streets during the uprising. Fall 1956. Kádár remained in power for more than 30 years. The early years of his rule brought brutal repression, but the regime gradually softened. A broad amnesty was announced in 1963, and in later years Hungarians gained more economic freedom and greater freedom in their private lives than people in many other Soviet-bloc countries. This system later became known as “goulash communism.” Political power, however, remained in the party’s hands, Soviet troops stayed in the country, and the events of 1956 were officially regarded as a “counterrevolution.” How did Western countries respond to the uprising? And why didn’t they help the Hungarians? The uprising caught the United States and its European allies off guard. American intelligence services had not expected a mass armed revolt against the communist regime, even though the Eisenhower administration advocated the “liberation” of Eastern Europe from Soviet domination. The American-funded broadcaster Radio Free Europe also encouraged anti-communist sentiment and called for resistance. Some Hungarians therefore expected the West to come to their aid if they rose up. But as events in East Germany in 1953 had already shown, the United States had no intention of liberating Soviet-bloc countries by military force. Washington understood that such a confrontation could escalate into nuclear war. When the Hungarian uprising began on October 23, 1956, the White House therefore ruled out direct intervention almost immediately. Instead, the Americans tried to find a diplomatic solution. Washington hoped that Hungary could become an independent, neutral state, following Austria’s example. Hungary would no longer be under Soviet control but would not join NATO either. On October 27, Secretary of State John Foster Dulles publicly said that Washington did not regard Eastern European states as potential military allies. American leaders hoped this would persuade Moscow to refrain from another military intervention. A demonstration in support of the Hungarian uprising in Paris. Fall 1956. The Suez Crisis complicated matters. As the uprising unfolded, Britain and France joined Israel in launching a military operation against Egypt, which the United States sharply condemned. Serious divisions emerged among the Western allies. The main reason Western governments refused to intervene militarily, however, was not the Suez Crisis but their unwillingness to risk a direct war with the Soviet Union. American policy thus proved contradictory: Washington publicly supported the liberation of Eastern European countries but had no intention of going to war for them. As a result, some Hungarian insurgents waited for Western help that never came. What form did Western support take, then? Although Western countries ruled out military intervention, they publicly supported the uprising and condemned Soviet actions. British Foreign Secretary Selwyn Lloyd told Parliament that the British government was following the Hungarians’ struggle for freedom with admiration. French Prime Minister Guy Mollet rejected Soviet accusations that fascists had organized the uprising. West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer called the Hungarian resistance an example of extraordinary heroism. Mass demonstrations in solidarity with Hungarians took place in European capitals. The U.N. Security Council began considering the situation in Hungary as early as October 28, and after the renewed Soviet invasion on November 4, Western countries demanded the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Moscow, however, used its veto to block a resolution to that effect. The issue was referred to the U.N. General Assembly, which voted on November 4 to condemn the Soviet intervention and demand a troop withdrawal. In January 1957, a special U.N. committee was established to investigate the events. Its report confirmed that the uprising had been a mass movement against Soviet domination, rather than a Western-organized coup. But General Assembly resolutions were not binding, and the United Nations could not compel Moscow to change its policy. Hungarian refugees board a U.S. military ship in Bremen. December 19, 1956. A child from a Hungarian refugee family waits to board a flight from West Germany to the United States. Flights on this route carried 10,000 people who fled Hungary after the uprising. December 17, 1956. The largest practical contribution was taking in refugees. After the uprising was crushed, more than 200,000 people — about 2% of the population — left Hungary. As many as 185,000 fled to neighboring neutral Austria, and about 20,000 more to Yugoslavia. Many crossed the border on foot without assistance. This was relatively easy because some of the border barriers between Hungary and Austria had been dismantled in the summer of 1956. The Austrian authorities set up temporary camps and provided refugees with food, shelter, and medical care. With support from the United Nations, the Red Cross, and other international organizations, refugees began resettling in other countries. The United States, Canada, Britain, West Germany, and other countries took in tens of thousands of Hungarians. In total, about 180,000 refugees later moved from Austria and Yugoslavia to countries around the world. How were the events of 1956 remembered in Hungary — and how are they remembered today? After the uprising was crushed, the communist authorities led by Kádár officially called it a “counterrevolution” organized by enemies of socialism. Participants were persecuted, and public discussion of the events was tightly controlled. Over time, the authorities preferred to keep silent about the subject, since memories of the Soviet invasion called the legitimacy of the Moscow-backed regime into question. Nevertheless, the memory of the uprising lived on among emigrants and opposition circles, particularly through the circulation of samizdat — publications distributed outside state censorship — in the 1970s and 1980s. The situation began to change in the second half of the 1980s, influenced by perestroika in the Soviet Union and reforms in Hungary itself. In 1988, Kádár was removed as party leader. In January 1989, Imre Pozsgay, a leader of Hungary’s Communist Party, publicly called the events of 1956 a popular uprising. A turning point came with the ceremonial reburial of Nagy and his associates on June 16, 1989, which drew about 250,000 people. A young opposition politician, Viktor Orbán, spoke at the ceremony, demanding the withdrawal of Soviet troops and free elections. On October 23, 1989, the anniversary of the uprising’s start, Hungary officially ceased to be a socialist republic. After the communist regime fell, the 1956 revolution became one of the symbols of Hungary’s new democracy. In 1990, October 23 was declared a national holiday. Gradually, however, political groups developed different interpretations of the uprising’s legacy. Liberal politicians more often emphasized the struggle for democracy and political freedoms, while national conservatives stressed resistance to foreign domination and the defense of national independence. Nagy himself also became a subject of dispute: He had led the revolutionary government and been executed, but he had also risen through the communist movement and initially advocated reforming socialism rather than abolishing it. A demonstrator in Budapest on the anniversary of the uprising’s start holds a sign reading “Russians, go home!” October 23, 2022. Under Orbán, who headed the government from 2010 to 2026, the government’s official commemoration of 1956 increasingly emphasized national independence. Orbán repeatedly compared the Hungarians’ struggle against Moscow in 1956 to Budapest’s contemporary disputes with the European Union. In late 2018, a monument to Nagy was removed from a square near parliament and later installed elsewhere. The decision drew criticism from the opposition. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the memory of the uprising became the subject of fresh disputes: Orbán’s opponents pointed to the contradiction between his reverence for those who fought the Soviet invasion and his warm relations with Putin’s Russia. In September 2024, an adviser to Orbán said that if Russia invaded, Hungary should not follow Ukraine’s example of armed resistance, because the 1956 uprising had ended in tragedy. The remark prompted another wave of criticism. Orbán was forced to distance himself publicly from his adviser’s words, calling them a mistake. The Hungarian uprising was one of the Cold War’s most dramatic events. It showed how sweeping the demands for change inspired by de-Stalinization could become, and how little change Soviet leaders were willing to allow. When Hungary’s place in the Soviet bloc came under threat, Moscow chose military intervention over political compromise. Despite their public support for the Hungarians, Western countries stopped short of a direct confrontation with the Soviet Union, limiting their response to diplomatic protests and aid for refugees. The uprising was crushed, but its memory survived and, three decades later, played an important role in the fall of the communist regime. Yet the history of 1956 has not become a national symbol everyone agrees on: Politicians still interpret the uprising’s goals and lessons differently. Hungarians continue to debate what freedom, independence, and resistance to outside pressure mean today. title: Graduates must be willing to start small to build careers – Ridge Royal MD
body: The Managing Director of Ridge Royal Hotel in Cape Coast, Sheila Adjetey-Anum, has urged graduates to be willing to start from entry-level positions and build their careers through hard work, practical experience and continuous learning. She said the expectation among some graduates to secure managerial positions and earn high salaries immediately after leaving school was a mindset that needed to change. Speaking in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the iNTTA Expo at Ridge Royal Hotel on Thursday, October 22, she cited her own career progression as an example of the importance of starting small. “I started as a housekeeping attendant and all that, with a degree. Yes, with a degree,” she said. Ms Adjetey-Anum, who said she had worked in the industry for about 20 years, explained that she had progressed from an entry-level position to become the managing director of Ridge Royal Hotel, having previously managed several hotels. She said graduates must be prepared to demonstrate their capabilities and prove their value to employers rather than focus solely on their academic qualifications. “Everybody thinks after the degree, I should start with 5,000 (Cedis). I should start as a manager. But what are you bringing to the table?” she asked. She stressed that career progression required a combination of education and work experience, adding that employees should be willing to learn and grow through the opportunities available to them. “You need education plus work experience to be able to earn as much as you want,” she said. Ms Adjetey-Anum also encouraged young people to exercise patience, manage their finances and give themselves time to achieve their career ambitions. “Hard work always pays. They say smart work these days, but also hard work pays,” she said. Her comments came on the sidelines of the iNTTA Expo in Cape Coast, which brought together tourism and hospitality stakeholders, businesses and investors to explore investment opportunities and discuss strategies for growing Ghana’s tourism sector. The expo’s second day, held on Thursday, October 22, was themed “From Vision to Transactions” and featured discussions on investment opportunities in tourism, hospitality, energy infrastructure, agribusiness and health tourism.

title: Ukraine thwarts attempt to hospitalize Alyoshki residents — Russian envoy
body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. An attempt to evacuate patients in need of highly qualified care from the besieged Alyoshki in the Kherson Region has failed because of Ukrainian shelling, said Rodion Miroshnik, Ambassador-at-Large of the Russian Foreign Ministry for Crimes of the Kiev Regime.
"Two days ago another attempt was made to evacuate patients in need of highly qualified medical care from Alyoshki to the district hospital in Skadovsk. The road was cleared by Russian field engineers after nighttime remote mining by Ukrainian drones. But resumed Ukrainian shelling prevented people from being taken out," Miroshnik wrote on Max messenger.
He added that the ambulances turned back to Alyoshki.

title: Russia steps up election influence efforts in final stretch of midterms
body:
A pedestrian looks at his smartphone on an embankment with the Kremlin in the background in central Moscow on Oct. 8, 2026. Researchers who track online influence operations say Kremlin-backed groups are renewing tactics they've used to sow distrust and discord in previous elections in the U.S. and around the world. Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Russian operatives are pumping out fabricated claims about Democratic candidates, AI-manipulated videos of celebrities and fake posts impersonating real news outlets in an effort to influence American voters in the final run-up to Election Day.
Researchers who track online influence operations and lawmakers who've been briefed by the intelligence community say Kremlin-backed groups are renewing familiar tactics they've used to sow distrust and discord in previous elections in the U.S. and around the world.
"It's a carnival out there," Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut , the ranking member on the House intelligence committee, told reporters this week. "They're throwing everything out there to generate a sense of chaos and anarchy."
The goal is to exacerbate divisions, erode confidence in democracy and, crucially, undermine U.S. support for Ukraine.
"At the end of the day, the main issue for Russia is and has to be Ukraine," said Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, who has tracked foreign propaganda campaigns for years.
Linvill says the Russian playbook is consistent. A false claim or divisive narrative is seeded on social media or on a fake website posing as a news organization or think tank. It's spread by state media, automated fake accounts or, increasingly, paid influencers, in the hopes that it gets seen and repeated by real people.
"In the same way that marketing companies will pay an influencer to disseminate, you know, 'Nike's a great shoe,' the Russians do it with false information and made-up lies," he said. "They use influencers that know their audience, that are part of that audience, and they know how to give that audience a message that they want to hear," Linvill said.
A Russian operation put that playbook to work this week to spread a baseless accusation against a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate.
Linvill and several other research groups attributed them to Russian operators the research community has dubbed Storm-1516 . It's known for staging fake videos with actors and laundering their claims through influencer accounts with large followings.
Two fraudulent videos targeting the Senate candidate were posted on Tuesday on X by an account created last month that had few followers. The account's X profile said it was based in the U.S. but the social media platform publicly flagged it as possibly using a proxy such as a virtual private network, which could disguise its location.
The videos were likely created using artificial intelligence, according to Graphika, a research company that analyzes online communities. Linvill said a hallmark of Storm-1516 videos is the use of real actors whose faces are swapped using AI to look like someone else.
The post was immediately shared by a network of 15 accounts Linvill flagged as bots. About 12 hours later, one of the videos was shared in new posts by three X accounts with large followings, which researchers said have previously amplified other narratives attributed to Storm-1516. One of them has solicited paid partnerships on X. Soon other X accounts began resharing the large accounts' posts in replies to politicians and journalists.
One of the two fake videos racked up roughly 857,000 views within 24 hours, according to an analysis by Alethea, a threat intelligence company. By late on Wednesday, the account that first posted the videos and one of the large accounts that reshared the claim had been suspended by X, and the two other large accounts that amplified it had taken down their posts.
In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Storm-1516 posted fraudulent videos making similar unfounded accusations against Democratic vice presidential nominee Tim Walz and purporting to show ballots for President Trump being torn up .
Linvill says the operation tries to glom on to narratives that are already circulating among Americans. "It is hard to persuade anybody of anything, ever," he said. "But what you can do is reinforce beliefs."
This election cycle, Russian operations have also spread messages about Democrats turning away from supporting Israel and fabricated news reports accusing Democratic candidates of corruption.
"I increasingly have come to think of Russia as essentially a dark money PAC," said Lisa Kaplan, who founded Alethea. "You know they're going to be running advertisements. You want to understand what's out there. You want to understand if they're actually effective in moving people in one direction or another."
Intelligence officials have long said Russia has favored Trump and targeted Democrats in its efforts to erode support for Ukraine in the U.S.
On Wednesday, Himes and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate intelligence committee, told reporters they'd seen a recent classified intelligence report on foreign election meddling showing Russia opposes candidates of either party who have backed Ukraine.
Himes stressed that while Russia and other foreign countries have sought to influence voters, there has been no indication that they have been able to interfere with the actual mechanics of voting.
"Nothing out there suggests that there is either the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment," Himes said.
The same Russian operations now active in the U.S. midterms have also targeted elections this year in France, Germany and elsewhere. They've used AI-generated audio and impersonated politicians, celebrities and media outlets, Graphika said in a new report on Friday.
"They have run this playbook in half a dozen other countries in the past six months throughout Europe. We're just the next in line," Linvill said. "They attack with these same themes. Anything that's going to make a candidate seem degenerate, seem corrupt, seem incapable."
Kaplan of Alethea says this focus on polarizing issues in the final stretch of the election is less about shaping voter's views and more about inflaming anger or fear to affect turnout.
"In these final posts in the lead up to the election, it's really more about evoking that emotion," she said.
Researchers tracking Storm-1516 and other groups say they expect more false claims and fake videos to come, and for these operations to focus on voting and ballot processing in the period immediately surrounding Election Day.
NPR's Eric McDaniel contributed to this report.

title: Kremlin-seized German company Metro AG transfers 1 billion rubles to Russian military without approval
body:
Almost one month after being placed under the Kremlin's control, German wholesale food retailer Metro AG announced on Oct. 23 that its Russian subsidiary had donated 1 billion rubles (11.1 million euros/ $12.4 million) to support Russian forces without the company's approval.
On Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree placing the Russian subsidiary of Metro AG under the Kremlin's control.
Metro AG responded on Oct. 23, saying it did not approve the donations.
"The decision by Metro Russia to donate to the Russian organization “All-Russia People's Front” was neither coordinated with Metro AG nor authorized or approved by Metro AG," the company said in a press release . "Since Metro Russia was placed under forced temporary administration as of September 28, Metro AG no longer has operational control over Metro Russia and has no influence over its operational decisions."
The Russian-controlled Metro transferred money to Russia's "People's Front. All for Victory!" fund. The funds "will be used to purchase equipment needed by soldiers on the front lines," according to a press release from the Russian company.
Metro AG is one of the world’s largest retailers, specializing in food wholesale and food distribution to restaurants and hotels. Metro AG first entered the Russian market in 2001 and operated 91 wholesale stores, employing around 9,000 employees in the country.
Moscow has seized Russian subsidiaries of Western companies throughout the war.
On Sept. 17, Putin signed a decree confiscating the assets of several international companies, including Nestle and Auchan . Other companies placed under Russian government management include Bati Logistics, FM Logistics, and Le Monlid LLC.
According to Deutsche Welle, other foreign companies taken over by the Kremlin in Russia have been used to donate to the "People's Front" fund.
In 2026, the fund received 1.5 billion rubles from Poland's Can-Pack, 1 billion rubles from the Dutch firm Akzo Nobel, and 600 million rubles from Denmark's Rockwool after all companies were placed under Russian control.

Xbox’s first chief operating officer (COO) is leaving after the new role was created just a few months ago. Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today, according to an internal Xbox memo seen by The Verge . Chiang has been at Microsoft for 21 years, serving as the head of Minecraft before being promoted to Xbox chief operating officer in July.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced Chiang’s departure in a surprisingly short memo today. “Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I’m grateful for her years of service and wish her well,” said Sharma. As Chiang is departing today, her immediate responsibilities are being split up between other Xbox leaders for now, and Sharma notes that “we’ll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalized.”
That sounds like the COO position isn’t going away after just a few months, but it’s not clear why Chiang is departing after such a short stint in the role. At the time of Chiang’s promotion, Sharma described the new COO role as a first for Xbox, “with end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services.” The role was created as part of Xbox’s big “reset.”
Chiang reported directly to Sharma and was promoted to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”
Chiang departs amid rumors that Xbox is preparing more layoffs this month, in November, and in January. The sudden and short memo from Sharma, coupled with Chiang’s responsibilities being assigned to other Xbox leaders, makes it seem like this wasn’t a resignation.
I asked Microsoft to comment on Chiang’s departure, and the company refused to discuss the circumstances of her exit. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters,” says Kari Perez, Xbox vice president of communications. “We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

title: Incremental Computation Graphs
body:
How to compute and invalidate computation graphs
I learned this as part of my work on Yabu . There I need to work recompile, regenerate code and type-check at interactive speeds.
You have two main things in the algorithm:
For example, in the case of Yabu an input would be the function definition. Let’s say you already have an image and you redefine a function.
The source string of this function would become an input and then from there you have defined several pure computations.
For example we can have a parse function, it depends on the source input and returns the AST of the source. Because this is a pure function, if the input hasn’t changed we can just return the memoized AST without having to re-parse it.
Now this gets interesting once you start composing computations, this looks very similar to regular functions calls except these internally keep track of which computations you are calling. Creating a runtime-graph of dependent computations. We’ll use this graph later to invalidate computations once inputs change.
NOTE: This is not a correct compile function for Yabu, because you are only checking if this function typechecks against the rest of the functions not if the rest of the functions typecheck against this function. We are also skipping around some complications around the staging system.
You can check the real algorithm at Yabu Incremental Typesystem
Here parse , typecheck and compile are all computations. These create a runtime graph where we see that compile <source> depends on typecheck , which will in turn probably depend on parse and it will probably depend on another computation type-signature for all of the functions the AST calls.
Now if f_1 changes type signature, automatically the typecheck of this function will get invalidated! This invalidation is key to make the Yabu typechecker very fast for interactive use even in large programs.
Each memoization entry stores several things:
For each dependency we track also what was the changed-at revision of the dependency when we depended on it.
So let’s see an example, we just redefined some-func as above and we call (compile "<source>") , this is a new source so there is no memoization for this, we execute the computation function. We call typecheck , since this is a new source this doesn’t exist either, that depends on parse which also doesn’t exist, that creates one memoization entry:
We then check type-signature for + with is (-> (int int) int) with a :verified-at and :changed-at of R1 (this is stdlib, so it was populated at the start of the session). Since R1 is less than R7 , it may be outdated and we need to check the dependencies of (type-signature +) . That depends on the source of + which also has a revision of R1 . Since the revision of the memoization and the revision of its dependency are equal we consider it fresh and we update the :verified-at for (type-signature +) to the current revision of R7 .
The typecheck passes so we memoize that as well and create an entry like
It’s important here to note when we consider something fresh:
You always need to walk the dependency chain until you bottom out at the inputs or you have already validated the subtree this revision.
During the walk as you come up the recursion you update all :verified-at to current-revision so any other computation in this revision short-circuits.
Next time, if we reevaluate typecheck over the same source we’ll recurse through the graph, arrive at the same input, check that it hasn’t changed, go upwards the computation tree, updated :validated-at and skip typechecking and compiling altogether.

title: Swiss government acknowledges failings in F-35 purchase and agrees procurement reforms
body: Parliament has approved a supplementary credit of CHF394 million. The Federal Council’s latest response does not settle the final number of aircraft Switzerland will acquire. The government accepted six parliamentary oversight recommendations in full and one in part. Its response was adopted on October 21 and published on October 23, following the oversight committee’s September 8 report on F-35A pricing. The Federal Council acknowledged that Armasuisse’s legal department had played too limited a role in the fighter purchase . It said the team lacked the resources and specialized expertise required for a procurement project of that scale and complexity. The legal department has since been expanded and now acts as a center of expertise for procurement projects. The government considers that recommendation largely implemented. But the council rejected the impression that only the former project manager had read the contracts in full. It said the former head of armaments and other Armasuisse employees had examined the complete documents. Former Defence Minister Viola Amherd and officials in the ministry’s general secretariat also reviewed the clauses relevant to fixed pricing in depth. The government said some employees who had read the contracts were not interviewed by the oversight committee. The defense ministry will examine whether negotiating mandates for major, complex purchases should require approval from departmental leadership or the Federal Council. The government also wants parliament more closely involved and is considering internal peer reviews for particularly risky acquisitions. Risk management must use project-specific, quantitative assessments to make contingency calculations more transparent. The accepted recommendations include closer attention to inflation and the calculation of risk allowances. The ministry disclosed the fighter evaluation criteria to parliament’s security policy committees on October 1. Those committees had already received access to the Letters of Offer and Acceptance covering the purchase. Source: swissinfo.ch .

title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1703: White House announces ceasefire for occupied Oleshky, where residents face starvation and blocked escape routes

Ukraine promised to sell surplus weapons abroad 12 months ago. Its arms makers now ask why a fee of up to 30% still blocks the deals. Starlink helped Ukraine pull off Operation Vivaldi. Now Starlink could help Russia take the ground back . The operation retook 277 square kilometers north of Lyman. The drones that now hold that line lose their Starshield link above about 160 km/h. Military Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles . OSINT projects reported that a strike hit the Proton plant in Orel, a facility whose electronic components are used in several Russian weapons systems. Drone strike sinks cargo ship near Romania, killing Ukrainian sailor. Romanian President blames Russia . The Khoryv capsized about 13 nautical miles off Romania’s coast, with nine crew members rescued and three still missing. The incident adds to a wave of attacks threatening Black Sea shipping and Ukraine’s export routes. Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones . Ukrainian pilots are already using the 20-mm ammunition to intercept jet-powered attack drones, as Russia deploys faster targets that challenge Ukraine’s air defenses. Ukraine wants partners’ Patriot interceptors now. Europe can hand them over only with US approval, Ukraine’s president says . Ukraine is contracting about 1,000 Patriot missiles that will take years to arrive, so it wants partners’ stocks today. Russia’s tax service runs on two key data centers. Drones went after one of them overnight, along with a chemical plant that supplies explosives makers . The data center in Gorodets stores state registers, including tax records, and opened in 2015 with Russia’s current prime minister on hand. Phones down, water off, a factory roof broken open: Russian-occupied Luhansk counts the damage after another night of drones . Ukrainian monitoring channels pointed to strikes on communications, and pro-Russian local channels filled in the rest of the morning’s picture. Russia kept sneaking troops through gas pipes behind Ukrainian lines. Now Ukraine has gone more than 15 km underground to do the same to Russia . More than 30 Russian soldiers were captured and Russian losses topped 100, the Khartiia Corps reported. Ukrainian OSINT analyst: Russia’s Yandex data center in Sasovo burned out inside, though its roof shows almost no significant holes . Yandex hasn’t said whether the AI supercomputers there were damaged. Intelligence and technology A modem from a Russian drone led reporters to its Chinese maker—which invoiced 500 for Russia’s drone plant . Posing as a Russian military supplier, journalists got a $2.87 million invoice, three bank accounts, and no pushback on military use. Russia may stage sabotage in Eastern Europe, but wants Kyiv blamed, Ukraine’s Intelligence warns . The agency says Moscow aims to weaken European support for Kyiv by making Russian attacks appear to be the work of Ukraine’s military. The money starts as bags of cash in a Moscow market and ends up clean in China, leaked files show . The firm, co-owned by the bank behind Russia’s defense industry, hides where the money starts before it reaches foreign banks. The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays . Ukraine’s military Starlink terminals still lose connection above about 160 km/h, nine days after the limit took effect, and Kyiv has no official explanation of who imposed it. Russia’s Doppelgänger operation used fake Ukrainian channels to spread disinformation. Hacked files show who ran it . The campaign targeted Ukraine’s military and political leadership, including with a fake about war widows receiving a can of stewed meat as compensation. International 40,000 tons of Russian diesel are bound for New York—due four days after Americans vote . The tanker loaded at a Baltic port Ukrainian drones struck in March. Trump wants cheaper diesel before the midterms. Russia’s attacks on Black Sea shipping raise risk of global famine, German FM warns . As Russian strikes increasingly threaten civilian vessels and Ukrainian grain exports, Germany’s foreign minister warned that shipping disruptions could leave vulnerable countries without essential food and fertilizers. Austria expels Russian Embassy and OSCE diplomats over suspected spying. Vienna remains a Russian spy hub . Austrian security authorities raised suspicions of espionage involving four Russian diplomats, prompting Vienna to declare them persona non grata. Russian Geran drone crashes in Moldova near homes and energy facility: Chisinau expels Russian diplomat . President Maia Sandu condemned the latest incursion as Russia’s war on Ukraine increasingly threatens neighboring Moldova. Finland gives Ukraine 10 diesel locomotives that keep trains running when Russian strikes cut the power . The engines come free from Finland’s state railway, part of a visit that also brought winter energy money and new defense, housing, and satellite deals for Kyiv. NATO’s weapons-buying agency opens dedicated door for Ukraine, non-member, letting it buy arms through its contracts and its firms bid for tenders . The agreement, signed by Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara, gives Ukraine a single entry point into 45 weapons programs. Humanitarian and social impact Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces . A truce announced by Melania Trump is due to take effect October 29, opening the way for humanitarian supplies and evacuations if Russia and Ukraine implement the agreement. Ukraine frees 270 from Russian captivity in “historic” prisoner swap, including 5 Olenivka survivors and American teacher Stephen Hubbard . The latest exchange returned 261 military personnel and nine civilians. Some had been held since 2018, while many others were captured during the defense of Mariupol in 2022. Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution . A captive soldier’s wife says that whenever families find a relative, Russia moves them to another prison and contact is lost again. Political and legal developments 45 seconds of voting in the Lviv Oblast Council sparked a new dispute with Poland: Warsaw says Kyiv promised the UPA year decision will not take effect . Poland is Ukraine’s main hub for Western aid, and every new fight over the two nations’ WWII past erodes the trust that role rests on. Russia keeps hitting Ukraine’s arms plants. Now private developers can dig them space underground—and sell or rent it to them . The state budget has paid to keep war-damaged arms plants running. The new model brings private money into the digging. Zelenskyy names three postwar security guarantees for Ukraine. Even Russia needs one of them, he says . He names NATO membership, direct US guarantees, and a European Coalition of the Willing as the paths under discussion. Trump cannot get Putin to halt strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, so he blames Ukraine instead, Zelenskyy says . Before that, US officials had cut Kyiv off from US intelligence and lowered a speed cap on Starlink to pressure Ukraine. Read our previous daily review here .

title: Trade unions banned from marching in Paris on agreed route — radio
body:
PARIS, October 24. /TASS/. The Paris police prefecture has banned trade unions from holding a procession along the agreed route from Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation in the east of the city, radio station France Info quoted a source as saying.
According to it, the trade unions were offered an alternative route from Porte d'Italie to Porte de Vincennes on the outskirts of the capital. The trade unions plan to challenge the decision in the State Council -- the highest judicial instance for administrative cases.
Previously Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said that the ministry would deploy around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes across the country on October 24. In many cities, prefects banned protests altogether. In Paris, only a trade union march against the decline in the people’s purchasing power was permitted.
On October 17, mass demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the decline in the purchasing power rolled through Paris and France. According to the organizers’ estimates, 800,000 people participated, while the police put the figure at 550,000, or twice as many as it expected. In some cities the protests deteriorated into riots and clashes with the police. Nunez vowed to continue to prosecute all participants in the ransacking and looting.

title: Putin claims Russia is ready for new talks with Ukraine, calls occupied land historical Russia
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia is ready to resume three-way talks with Ukraine and the US, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed in an interview with Pavel Zarubin of state broadcaster VGTRK, published on 22 October. He said they should settle security for both countries after a final peace deal, not a brief pause. Putin spoke a day after he hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would accept freezing the war along the front line. In May, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov named Ukraine’s withdrawal from Donbas and Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts as the only condition for peace. Any new round would start from that gap: Kyiv offers to stop where the armies stand, while Moscow’s last stated terms demanded more land. Talks in November Putin stated that Moscow and Washington had agreed Russia was ready to resume trilateral contacts. He added that he generally agreed with a US point that European security architecture should also be discussed. On 21 October, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov stated that the sides had settled on mid-November, with Abu Dhabi as the likely venue. "Historical Russia" In a 21 October Fox News interview , asked about a freeze leaving Ukraine 75% or more of its land, Zelenskyy answered: “Yes, right now, we have to freeze.” Explore further Trump cannot get Putin to halt strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, so he blames Ukraine instead, Zelenskyy says Asked about the land Ukraine would give up, Putin replied that the occupied regions were not Ukraine’s but "historical Russia." He claimed their residents had voted for independence and then to join Russia, and called any talk of territorial losses inappropriate. Putin linked Russia’s readiness to negotiate to Ukrainians being a people very close to Russians. He claimed the latest genetic studies show they are one people. Independent outlet Meduza noted it is unclear which studies he meant. Putin’s 12 July 2021 essay on the historical unity of Russians and Ukrainians made the same case, which Ukraine’s national memory institute rebutted . He closed that answer by asserting Russia would achieve all the goals of what the Kremlin calls its special military operation. He made a similar vow on 17 December 2025.
