title: On The Brink Of Epic Fury Round Two?
body: U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack suggested on Friday that the U.S. could strike Iran as early as this weekend. His statement caps a week of growing speculation about whether America and Israel could resume major attacks on the Islamic Republic. “Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely,” Barrack told online commentator Mario Nawfal when asked to explain the end game of efforts to seek a diplomatic resolution. “The president is very clear. He’s open and available and accessible to a deal. And we’ve been at the table for months and months and months… the nuclear proliferation and where we go with the enrichment and all those things are, are details, the punctuation in the chapter that needs to be finished.” BREAKING: AMB. TOM BARRACK WARNS U.S. STRIKE COULD HAPPEN THIS WEEKEND I asked Trump's Special Envoy, Tom Barrack: “Could there be a strike on this this weekend? His answer was direct: "Absolutely.” Amb. Barrack laid out exactly where things stand with Iran right now.… pic.twitter.com/upe7UlgGvb — Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) October 23, 2026 Asked about Barrack’s comments regarding the potential timing of a strike on Iran, President Donald Trump told reporters that the ambassador “is a powerful man, I guess. If that’s the case, I don’t know anything about it.” Q: Your ambassador to Türkiye said that "absolutely" there could be a strike on Iran this weekend. Trump: He is a powerful man, I guess. I don't know anything about it. pic.twitter.com/uDAqSYUocJ — Clash Report (@clashreport) October 23, 2026 Speculation about a return to hostilities was sparked earlier this week after heavy activity of fighter aircraft was reported over Iraq. Israeli Fighter Jets Simulate Possible ATTACK on Iran Over Iraq Around 10 Israeli fighter jets reportedly flew through Syrian airspace into Iraq tonight, conducting simulated attack runs. Similar flights have occurred for DAYS as Iran remains on HIGH ALERT over a possible… pic.twitter.com/nK0c24vFP2 — Ryan Rozbiani (@RyanRozbiani) October 19, 2026 On Wednesday, Axios reported that dozens of Israeli fighters flew through Syrian and Iraqi airspace toward the border with Iran on Monday as part of a “power projection” exercise. The sorties, extending some 800 miles away from Israel proper, were launched after U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise trip to Israel earlier this week to meet with that country’s Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, reportedly to discuss new plans to attack Iran . “Israel notified the U.S. in advance and described the operation as a training exercise [on Monday] intended for ‘power projection’ and aimed at deterring Iran from launching attacks against Israel ahead of the elections [in that country],” according to Axios . “Dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft” were involved. One of the IAF’s KC-707s seen refueling an F-15. (IAF) After the Axios story came out, there were unconfirmed reports of additional major Israeli military air activity on Wednesday night. Intense IAF fighter jet activity is now being reported over Iraq, especially on the border with Iran. Meanwhile, continuous takeoffs are taking place from the Ramon, Nevatim, and Ovda airbases. https://t.co/c35xIbtAAu — MoloMonitor (@MoloWarMonitor) October 21, 2026 The last known Israeli strikes on Iran came in June. The U.S. military officially concluded major combat operations against the Islamic Republic in May, but tit-for-tat strikes have continued since then as part of an ongoing blockade of Iranian ports. For its part, Iran has continued to launch strikes on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which continues to have major impacts on global energy markets despite U.S. efforts to safeguard the flow of tanker ships out of the Persian Gulf. As TWZ editor-in-chief Tyler Rogoway pointed out on X Wednesday evening, the commotion over Iraq was likely practice runs and would be part of the prelude to any major new air operation targeting Iran. Conducting sorties relatively close to the Iranian border would also offer opportunities to gain valuable intelligence about the current state and disposition of that country’s air defenses. “Dry runs are important for such a large integrated operation,” Rogoway noted. “They can be scaled as the operation gets closer. Getting a large part of the intended force up and in position can really help with the chances of mission success if the actual order to execute is given. So many moving parts to align. Not great to find out any weak spots on night one of a new offensive.” “Stimulating Iran’s air defenses is critical,” he added. “By Iran operating as if a full scale attack could be coming, their air defenses can be detected, categorized and geolocated. This is absolutely critical prior to a major air operation. Surveilling them during times of lower alert does not provide the same fidelity of actionable intelligence. Knowing where those threats are and how they are operating can mean the difference of life and death and/or will help standoff munitions make their way to their targets as those defenses can be suppressed, destroyed, or avoided entirely via careful mission planning.” Couple things on the large scale tactical aircraft activity over the Middle East tonight: I don't have any info on this operation or if it truly has gone kinetic, but here is likely what is happening if not: 1.) Dry runs are important for such a large integrated operation. They… — Tyler Rogoway (@Aviation_Intel) October 21, 2026 “U.S. officials said the Israelis knew that Iran’s air defense systems would detect the sortie[s on Monday],” Axios ’ report also noted. “Some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Iran.” TWZ cannot confirm this; however pushing Iran to react would not fit with the goals of a major exercise like this. There have been other signs that a major new round of U.S. and/or Israeli strikes on Iran might be looming on the horizon. Fox News reported earlier this week that the Nimitz class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt and the rest of its carrier strike group, as well as the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group carrying the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), were heading to the Middle East, citing unnamed U.S. officials. “The ships will arrive in the Middle East by the end of November,” the officials said, according t o a post on X from Fox ’s Jennifer Griffin on Tuesday. “These new deployments will add about 10,000 sailors and Marines to the Middle East.” Per @Liz_Friden The U.S. is sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, two U.S. officials confirm to Fox News. The ships will arrive in the Middle East by the end of November, the officials said. These new… — Jennifer Griffin (@JenGriffinFNC) October 20, 2026 There have been indications of increased U.S. military air activity in the Middle East recently, as well. Observers have called particular significant influx of aerial refueling tankers to bases in the region, as well as in Europe, which would be critical to any new major air campaign . US Tanker Fleet Update 21/OCT/2026 #IranWar‌ Overall numbers across CENTCOM and Europe have now stabilised back to the levels they were at back at the start of September, around 190-195. There are a few tankers dotted around at other sites temporarily (Glasgow Prestwick and… pic.twitter.com/taKi8op7Tv — DefenceGeek (@DefenceGeek) October 21, 2026 In addition, there are claims that Russia is evacuating its scientists from the Bushehr Nuclear Power plant and other Russians ahead of a potential new round of strikes. TWZ cannot independently verify this. BREAKING: Russian airforce TU-134 used to evacuate high ranking personnel has just left Iran with its transponder off rumoured to be picking up Russian scientists from Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant. We saw similar evacuation flights before US strikes on Iran in February… pic.twitter.com/dFLvQvesNk — WarMonitor (@WarMonitor3) October 23, 2026 The New York Times reported on Wednesday that the U.S. and Israeli militaries had “developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections,” citing U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations. Authorities in Washington and Jerusalem appear to be planning “a short but intensive operation” that would last between three and five days, the newspaper added. “The targets would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Some officials say one more big round of attacks could push Iran’s economy over the brink and force the country to make diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict.” Separately on Wednesday, NBC News also reported that the Pentagon and U.S. State Department were relocating personnel from bases and diplomatic facilities in the Middle East, amid the possibility of new strikes on Iran, as well as broader regional security concerns. The State Department subsequently pushed back on that report, saying that non-emergency U.S. government employees and dependents had only been directed to leave Saudi Arabia in response to attacks from Iranian-backed Houthi militants in Yemen. This is inaccurate. The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only. Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on… https://t.co/yNrCwDcfIg — Tommy Pigott (@statedeptspox) October 21, 2026 A high-ranking Israel Defense Forces (IDF) official we spoke with said a new war with Iran is not a foregone conclusion. “I would describe the situation as increasingly tense, with a real risk of renewed escalation,” the IDF official told us. “However, I would be cautious about concluding that another war is inevitable or that its timing can be reliably predicted.” “The recent IAF [Israeli Air Force] activity is significant, as are the reported military preparations and the increasingly confrontational rhetoric from both Washington and Jerusalem,” he added. “But military readiness, deterrence, and operational planning do not necessarily mean that a final political decision to launch another campaign has been made.” An Israeli Air Force (IAF) F-15I. (IAF) IAF “We do not see any indications of a need to strike Iran before the election,” IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir also said during a recent closed-door meeting, according to Israeli media reports . At the same time, “if we determine that a strike on Iran is necessary, we will carry it out.” “Iran is once again attempting to develop a nuclear bomb,” Israeli Prime Minister Netanyua also warned again this week, according to The Jerusalem Post . “My directive to the IDF, the Mossad, and the defense establishment… [is] to overthrow the regime in Iran.” The IDF official who spoke also raised questions about the potential efficacy of any new major air campaign against Iran. “Both Trump and Netanyahu have previously described the results of earlier rounds of fighting as a decisive, even total, victory, emphasizing the damage inflicted on Iran’s ballistic missile capabilities, its production and supply chains, and its nuclear infrastructure,” the official noted. “This raises an obvious question: If the results were as decisive as they claimed, what has changed to make another confrontation necessary now?” “I believe we must recognize the limitations of trying to defeat a country like Iran through targeted killings and stand-off kinetic strikes alone,” he added. “Such operations can destroy infrastructure, eliminate key personnel, disrupt production, and delay military programs. They can impose significant costs on an adversary. But they do not necessarily eliminate the adversary’s strategic ambitions, prevent the regeneration of capabilities, or produce a durable political outcome.” U.S. President Trump’s repeated threats to launch strikes on a very hardened Iranian facility known as Pickaxe Mountain have raised similar questions. The Pickaxe Mountain site is believed to be tied to Iran’s nuclear program, but is also arguably the hardest-to-reach target in the country , and has gone untouched in previous U.S. and Israeli operations. A satellite image showing vehicle activity at one of the tunnel entrances to the Pickaxe Mountain site on June 21, 2026. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor CBS News reported last week that the White House and Pentagon “have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb [MOAB] to hit military sites in Iran,” including Pickaxe Mountain, “if ordered by President Trump.” However, the 22,000-pound-class MOAB, also designated the GBU-43/B, is not a deep-penetrating munition, and it was not immediately clear from that story how the weapon might be employed. The bomb is also only known to be currently cleared for employment via C-130-type aircraft . It has only been used in combat once, in Afghanistan in 2017 , where the skies above were entirely permissive. You can read more about the targeting challenges specific to Pickaxe Mountain, and what options the U.S. military might have for halting, or at least degrading activity there, in a previous TWZ feature here . MOAB’s use case would be limited against sites like Pickaxe Mountain. While its unique overpressure effects could harm any personnel openly exposed inside tunnel systems, it is unlikely to destroy or even heavily damage the hardened facilities themselves. It could cause damage to external support infrastructure and act as a psychological weapon in its own right, but it is not a bunker buster in any way. Not what this weapon is really used for. Psychological effect, maybe https://t.co/hDWSXYKexr — Tyler Rogoway (@Aviation_Intel) October 15, 2026 The puzzling leak about the MOAB may be part of the administration’s effort to use the media to try and compel Iran to negotiate. This has been a glaring pattern throughout the ebb and flow of this conflict and a common tactic used by the Trump administration. Talking threatening plans against Iran here. They are always planning and have a slew of options. The leaks and sources are by and large fully aware what their marching orders are. It’s coordinated. A lever this admin pulls non stop right on cue. — Tyler Rogoway (@Aviation_Intel) October 15, 2026 For its part, Iran is operating on the assumption that a U.S.-Israeli attack is a “certainty,” The Jerusalem Post reported on Wednesday, citing Iran’s Fars News Agency , a quasi-state media outlet affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). “The report, which cited a senior Iranian security official, added that Iran will consider U.S. politicians legitimate targets if such an attack involves the assassination of Iranian officials.” The IRGC has also threatened to launch expanded retaliatory attacks on targets across the Middle East in response to any new waves of strikes. As we noted earlier in this story, Iran continues to actively attack commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz. The official Iranian IRNA news agency reported that the IRGC Navy claimed that it recently struck four ships transferring oil cargoes in the northern Persian Gulf, while three other vessels suffered damage after striking mines west of the Strait of Hormuz. While TWZ cannot independently verify those claims, the Ambrey maritime security firm said that the number of vessels damaged during Strait of Hormuz transits has “increased sharply” this month. “During the two weeks from 3 to 16 October, the number rose to 11 and 13 vessels per week, respectively, compared with an average of three to four per week in the preceding weeks,” Ambrey senior analyst Daniel Mueller noted today in the company’s latest security assessment . “This increase coincided with an expansion of Iranian operations aimed at restricting transits deemed unauthorized, while the US continued to facilitate transits along the Omani coastline.” On Oct. 9, “the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) threatened to pursue and target vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian authorisation throughout the wider Gulf region,” Mueller added. “During October, incidents attributed to Iran involved merchant vessels off Qatar, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Saudi Arabia and Sohar, Oman. Between 8 and 16 October, six merchant vessels – five tankers and one gas carrier – were damaged outside of the Strait of Hormuz. Additionally, a tanker was damaged offshore Iraq on 20 October.” Ambrey Reports emerging earlier this week from The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post do say that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have returned to prewar levels thanks to U.S. efforts to safeguard tankers out of the region. “Middle East oil flows, including shipments through Hormuz and alternative routes across the region, averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week through Oct. 18, surpassing prewar levels of 23.3 million,” according to the Journal , citing ship tracker Kpler. “Preliminary figures show Hormuz oil flows, including offshore transfers in the Gulf of Oman, came to around 14 million barrels a day on average for the same period, or 82% of prewar levels.” From the @WSJ : “Persian Gulf oil exports have surpassed prewar levels, as an improvised shipping system under U.S. protection is helping tankers move oil through one of Iran’s fiercest waves of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.” https://t.co/SJo2jlUfew — Javier Blas (@JavierBlas) October 21, 2026 However, global energy oil markets continue to be under immense strain as a result of the ongoing fallout from the conflict with Iran, thanks in no small part to surging insurance costs for shipping companies. This has been further exacerbated now by Yemen’s Houthis expanding their attacks on oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including a recent strike near the Shaybah oilfield . The Houthis are also exerting their own pressure shipping passing through the Bab Al Mandab Strait, a critical chokepoint that links the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. A Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government has been embroiled in an on-again-off-again conflict with the Houthis since 2014. Fighting with the Iranian-supported Yemeni militants in and around the Red Sea was inflamed last year as a by-product of Israel’s 12 Day War with Iran. The Houthis also retaliated with missile and drone attacks in support of Iran in the wake of U.S. and Israel launching their major operations against the regime in Tehran in February. The U.S. government and the Houthis have been observing a tenuous ceasefire since May 2025 . This has continued despite the Yemeni miltants now imposing a blockade on the Bab Al Mandab Strait, and a new campaign of strikes on Saudi ships in the southern part of the Red Sea, as well as targeting critical energy terminals on that body of water and Saudi refineries. Iranian proxies have also struck the vital East-West pipeline that carries oil to the Red Sea to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. That line has reportedly since reopened after being shut down following a long-range drone attack. The two sides have also been fighing battles across much of Yemen and the conflict between the two parties is ongoing. “On Wednesday, two people were killed and two others injured by debris from intercepted drones near a processing plant at the Shaybah field, one of the biggest oilfields in Saudi Arabia,” The National noted . “Operations at the Shaybah field and its processing facilities remain unaffected, but the attack rattled markets again amid concerns about potential disruption to Saudi supply just as the Kingdom has largely restored its exports via the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.” As a result, the per-barrel price of Brent crude has jumped to more than $114 as of Friday morning, according to OilPrice.com , the highest that it has been since May during intensified fighting between the U.S. and Iran. In addition, Saudi Aramco has told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely, Reuters reported , citing six people with knowledge of the matter. The move came a day after two people were killed in an attack on a nearby airport. The order marked the ​first time Aramco had asked staff to evacuate its headquarters since the start of the Iran war, Reuters added. The Houthis “caused extensive damage ⁠to the company’s headquarters earlier this month when they struck the building, with fire spreading across several floors,” the outlet explained. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have spurred Britain to commit to providing “defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets,” Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement . “These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis. The UK will provide an RAF A400M to support the movement of defense materiel within Saudi Arabia, alongside UK military advisers to support Saudi staff officers.” “The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable,” Streeting said. Sunset photo of Saudi Aramco’s headquarters. (Saudi Aramco) brigido alcayde As we noted earlier in this story, the U.S. is continuing its naval blockade of Iranian ports. U.S. Central Command said Thursday on X that its renewed naval blockade of Iranian ports, now in its 100th day, “has helped prevent Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil and constrained the IRGC’s ability to fund proxy militias, criminal networks, and terrorism. There have been no exports or imports to Iran by sea except for the humanitarian aid U.S. forces have allowed.” Today marks 100 days since CENTCOM forces resumed America's steel wall naval blockade against Iran. This effort has helped prevent Iran from exporting at least $25 billion worth of crude oil and constrained the IRGC's ability to fund proxy militias, criminal networks, and… pic.twitter.com/DwiamYBdHY — U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) October 22, 2026 Regardless of the reasons for taking action against Iran, the IDF official suggested a new round of kinetic strikes might not achieve the desired effects. “Both Trump and Netanyahu have previously described the results of earlier rounds of fighting as a decisive, even total, victory, emphasizing the damage inflicted on Iran’s ballistic missile capabilities, its production and supply chains, and its nuclear infrastructure,” the official noted. “This raises an obvious question: If the results were as decisive as they claimed, what has changed to make another confrontation necessary now?” “I believe we must recognize the limitations of trying to defeat a country like Iran through targeted killings and stand-off kinetic strikes alone,” he added. “Such operations can destroy infrastructure, eliminate key personnel, disrupt production, and delay military programs. They can impose significant costs on an adversary. But they do not necessarily eliminate the adversary’s strategic ambitions, prevent the regeneration of capabilities, or produce a durable political outcome.” For its part, Iran is operating on the assumption that a U.S.-Israeli attack is a “certainty,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)-affiliated Fars News Agency reported, according to the Jerusalem Post . “The report, which cited a senior Iranian security official, added that Iran will consider U.S. politicians legitimate targets if such an attack involves the assassination of Iranian officials,” the publication added. The IRGC also announced that it was preparing to unveil a new weapon, which it dubbed the “Father of All Bombs,” in response to U.S. threats to use the most powerful conventional bomb in the American arsenal against Iran’s nuclear facilities, the Jerusalem Post also reported . Officials, however, declined to offer any details about what kind of weapon it is, its power, whether it is operational or when it will be shown to the public, the Post noted. In addition to the strategic and tactical issues in the region, the IDF official we spoke with raised concerns that “domestic political considerations may influence the rhetoric and decisions” of Prime Minister Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump. Israel is holding nationwide parliamentary elections on October 27 that could have significant domestic political ramifications . The same is true of mid-term elections in the United States in November. “I cannot know their precise calculations, but the possibility that political incentives could affect decisions with such enormous strategic consequences should not be dismissed,” the IDF official cautioned. “With Israel’s elections approaching, I sincerely hope that Netanyahu will not make a decision with far-reaching consequences for the country’s security based, even partly, on immediate political considerations. The stakes are simply too high for military action to become a means of reshaping a domestic political narrative.” Israeli Prime Minister and Likud Party leader Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters during an election campaign event in a restaurant in Hatikva Market ahead of Israel’s general elections on October 27, 2026. (Photo by Amir Levy/Getty Images) Amir Levy In a phone call with Trump recorded live on Monday and posted on his X account, Netanyahu thanked the American leader for his election endorsement and suggested future operations against Iran. “Donald, we have a job to finish [in Iran]…and we’ll finish it together,” the Israeli leader told Trump. “We’ll finish it, and no one else will do it.” בשיחה עם ידידי הנשיא טראמפ לאחר שהודיע על תמיכתו בי בבחירות. יחד אנחנו הולכים להסיר את האיום האיראני לתמיד! צאו להצביע מחל! pic.twitter.com/GuPEAPn0Tc — Benjamin Netanyahu – בנימין נתניהו (@netanyahu) October 19, 2026 As for Trump, the President has previously said the war with Iran will end “immediately after the election” and has reportedly told aides he expects to resume strikes on the Islamic Republic after the midterms. Domestic U.S. polls show the ongoing conflict continues to be deeply unpopular with voters , who are also eager to see it concluded . Speaking to reporters Thursday afternoon, Trump acknowledged that the Iran war could have a negative impact on Republican hopes for the midterms. “Well in one way, they love it because I’m doing what should have been done by other presidents, and another way maybe they don’t,” Trump said. “It’s — there’s a price to pay, which I knew immediately when I did it, but we can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon. I mean, in one way, people probably don’t love it, but many people, many great patriots, really love it. This should have been done a long time ago by other presidents. The Iran War, and we’ve knocked the hell out of them, and we may do it a little bit further. “ Q: How do you feel the Iran war impacted the midterm races? Trump: In one way, they love it. In another way, maybe they don't. There's a price to pay. pic.twitter.com/qtkE9M2vSQ — Clash Report (@clashreport) October 22, 2026 Later on Thursday, the American president said that: “We’re gonna have Iran finished very soon, one way or the other. It’s almost insignificant to me which way.” U.S. President Donald Trump on Iran: "We're gonna have Iran finished very soon. one way or the other. It's almost insignificant to me which way. It's going to be done very soon, and your gasoline prices and your oil is going to come tumbling down." pic.twitter.com/vIGviqe8gi — Open Source Intel (@Osint613) October 23, 2026 While indicators are pointing to the U.S. and Israel at the very least in the very late stages of planning for new strikes against Iran, even if that doesn’t happen, the Middle East will remain a top concern. The ongoing threats to shipping and the escalating fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia are having increasingly dire impacts on gas prices, which is spiking inflation, and causing heavy pressure on the global economy. title: Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles

The strike comes amid Ukraine’s broader campaign to target Russian military production facilities and other infrastructure supporting Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Ukrainian strikes on such facilities aim to weaken Russia’s ability to manufacture and maintain the weapons it uses in its invasion. The plant reportedly supplies electronic components for Iskander-M ballistic missiles, which Russia regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities, as well as other weapons systems, including the Pantsir-S1 air defense system. The strike could disrupt production supporting Russia’s war effort. Photos show extensive damage to the building. Information about casualties remains unclear. Reports say a Ukrainian missile strike hit the Proton electronics plant in Russia’s Oryol on 23 October. The facility reportedly produces components for Iskander-M ballistic missiles used in attacks on Ukrainian cities, as well as other Russian weapons systems. Exilenova+… pic.twitter.com/nbqGPJ8EJj — Euromaidan Press (@EuromaidanPress) October 23, 2026 Plant reportedly produces components for Russian weapons Proton JSC manufactures semiconductor devices, LEDs, and electronic components for industrial and specialized equipment. According to Exilenova+, the plant’s products are used in the production of Iskander-M ballistic missiles, S-71 Kover missiles, and the Pantsir-S1 air defense system. Exilenova+ reported that the plant was struck by Storm Shadow cruise missiles. The weapon type has not been independently confirmed, and the extent of damage to the facility remains unknown. Russian authorities confirm strike on factory Oryol Oblast Governor Andrey Klychkov announced a missile threat in the region before reporting that missiles had struck a factory in Oryol’s Sovetsky District, according to Liga.net. Residents reported explosions, a fire in one part of the city, and columns of smoke rising over Oryol, according to local reports cited by OSINT projects Exilenova+, Supernova, and Astra. title: Yet two other supertankers hit mines in Hormuz: IRGC
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 24 (MNA) – The IRGC has reported that two non-compliant supertankers were disabled after striking naval mines off the southern coast of the Strait of Hormuz, leading the crews to abandon the vessels.
According to the Public Relations office of the IRGC Navy, early Friday, two offending supertankers—which were attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz via an unauthorized southern route—struck naval mines. The resulting explosions and intense fires incapacitated their engine rooms, bringing the vessels to a complete halt.
Together, these tankers were carrying over 4.5 million barrels of crude oil, the IRGC Navy saidm adding that following the mine strikes off the southern coast of the Strait of Hormuz, the vessels were left behind by their crews.

title: Russian envoy calls OSCE trench through which Moscow heard in Europe
body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. The OSCE is a "forward outpost" that cannot be abandoned, since it is through it that Europeans hear Russia’s position, permanent representative to the organization Dmitry Polyansky said in an interview with News.ru .
"I think that if we were to withdraw from the OSCE, many of our enemies would be very pleased about it. We are like a thorn in their side in this organization," he said. "They have to listen to us and put up with the fact that others are also listening to us, that our statements are quoted in the media and the blogosphere.
"The OSCE remains one of the few available channels for conveying Russia’s position. After all, most other channels in Europe through which we can communicate our position have long been blocked; European citizens are, in fact, in an information blockade. Many people hear us from Vienna, and we do everything we can to help them hear us.
"In this sense, the OSCE is a kind of forward outpost, which, in my view, we must not surrender under any circumstances."

OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday , OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.”
OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September , after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies , or swarm obscure websites . On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.
Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache:
Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.
OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”
In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects .

title: Trump doubles down on Amy Acton criticism as Ramaswamy ad controversy swirls
body:
"It's a mother speaking badly against Amy Acton," Trump said.
President Donald Trump on Friday continued to defend a highly controversial ad from Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton's estranged mother -- who Acton says stood by the man who was criminally charged with sexually abusing her as a child.
As he left the White House Friday morning, Trump repeatedly dismissed questions from reporters about the specific allegations of Acton's sexual abuse, asserting at multiple points that the ad has "nothing to do" with Acton's stepfather, who was criminally charged and pleaded not guilty.
Her stepfather, who died in 2004, fled the state with her mother before trial and never appeared before a judge, according to court records and an interview given by Acton's mother.
"It's a mother speaking badly against Amy Acton. And, to me, it's very easy," Trump said when asked about the ad, which features Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, saying that her daughter has lied about her past and her struggles growing up.
Acton has been public about her experience with abuse and openly spoken about her tumultuous relationship with her mother, whom she says she has not spoken to since she was 12 years old. Acton alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12.
Pressed on the fact that Acton has been estranged from her mother for decades, Trump said he did not care and insisted that the ad was fair game.
“I don't care,” Trump said. “If it were my mother speaking badly about me, you'd be making it the number one story on the news."
Trump also referred to Acton’s mother as a "smart woman" and said that he did not "know anything about" the stepfather.
“This has nothing to do with a stepfather or anything else," Trump said. "This has to do with the fact that a woman got out, the mother of a person running for governor of one of the greatest states, where I set records and said that she's a liar."
Trump defended the ad on Thursday afternoon as well , writing on social media that the ad was "powerful" and that he himself would run such an ad.
Several key Republicans have blasted the ad with Ohio's Republican Gov. Mike DeWine saying on Thursday that the ad is "deeply, deeply troubling" and that Ramaswamy's campaign should cease airing it.
Iowa Republican Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson also condemned the ad and said to ABC News Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl that "they should take the ad down" -- just hours before she shared the stage with Trump at a campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa, Thursday night.
Trump spoke about the ad during the rally, saying that he advised Ramaswamy to "ride with it."
“When I first saw it, I said, ‘Wow, that means Vivek easily will win the race,’” Trump recalled of the controversial ad, later adding "I said, 'you got to ride with it.'"
Acton has criticized the ad, calling it "horrible and hideous" during a campaign event on Wednesday, adding that the ad is "despicable" and "an exploitative thing to do."
Ramaswamy addressed the ad during a rally on Friday, saying it "had nothing to do with childhood abuse," according to audio provided by Cleveland ABC affiliate WEWS.
ABC News' Diana Paulsen and Sarah Beth Hensley contributed to this report.

title: Spiking ambulance response times spur calls for real-time tracking
body: 911 EMERGENCY: An ambulance in New York City now takes an average of 13 minutes to reach someone in life-threatening distress. That response time has risen five years straight and is up 41.2% from a decade ago, a city comptroller’s report revealed earlier this month . According to this year’s Mayor’s Management Report, which came out in September, ambulance response times to life-threatening emergencies shot up by almost 16% between fiscal year 2025 and fiscal year 2026 — the sharpest increase this decade. A core part of the issue is that calling 911 does not necessarily mean an ambulance will be immediately dispatched. Callers are put in dispatch queues. If a higher-priority call comes through, the ambulance might be rerouted. And all of this happens behind the scenes — which means those experiencing medical emergencies have no idea when help will actually arrive. Council member Joann Ariola, chair of the Fire and Emergency Management Committee, proposed a bill in August that would require the city to send New Yorkers broad notifications when the emergency response system is overloaded. Now, the Queens Republican is pushing for these notifications to be completely personalized. “The idea is that I would be able to track my ambulance in real time, just like you’re able to do for your bus, or your train, or your rideshare car,” she told Playbook. If patients know how far away help is, they can make an informed decision to forgo an ambulance and instead pursue other means of transportation to a hospital, she said. That would also alleviate pressure on the already overloaded EMS system and potentially get callers the care they need faster. The idea has support from a council member across the political aisle. “We get live texts about everything under the sun, but for some reason, in our current system, we don’t get alerts about this,” Democratic Council member Harvey Epstein said. “If I’m waiting for an ambulance because my kid broke their leg, and I learn that it’s going to be half an hour, it’s smarter for me to just hop in a cab anyway.” Ariola said she met with top FDNY officials — including Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore, Chief of Department John Esposito and Chief of EMS Paul Miano — ahead of Tuesday’s hearing to discuss the idea. All of them, she said, appeared more receptive to specific text alerts than to the broad notification system proposed in her initial bill. Amanda Farinacci, an FDNY spokesperson, said the department is “considering and exploring all options that will help us respond to emergency medical calls quickly and keep New Yorkers informed.” "We are exploring all our options, this included,” she said, referring to the live text-update model. Ariola said she’s submitted the new version of the bill and is waiting to hear back from the legislative affairs committee. The solution proposed by she and Epstein would address the public-facing side of the problem, offering relief to callers in emergency situations. The root cause of the issue, though, is retaining EMS employees — a challenge officials and union leaders say stems from low pay for a high-stress job. “This is not fixing the broken system,” Ariola said. “We are in a state of emergency right now. It’s a systemic problem with EMS because they cannot retain their members, because it’s not a career.” Entry-level pay for emergency medical technicians is less than that of sanitation workers, firefighters, correction officers and police officers. Since 2019, about 4,300 EMTs and paramedics have left their titles, many for better-paying jobs elsewhere in the department. Last fiscal year, 58% of departing EMTs became firefighters. The union representing emergency medical workers is negotiating a contract that lapsed in 2022, and it’s seeking pay parity with firefighters. But the comptroller’s report found that parity alone would raise EMS salary-related expenses by $184 million a year, a 66% jump. “The City can reverse this dangerous trend by ensuring members of EMS are treated as equals to members of fire operations, and by providing EMS personnel with pay and benefit parity comparable to their firefighter counterparts,” Local 3621 President Vincent Variale and Local 2507 President Michael Greco said in a joint statement. “These actions would not only treat our EMS workforce respectfully and properly; they would save the lives of New Yorkers in peril.” Response times to life-threatening emergencies saw the sharpest year-to-year increase of the decade between the last two fiscal years, a timeframe that straddles the Mamdani administration and the administration of former Mayor Eric Adams. “This is something that each mayor inherited, but the new administration, it is now absolutely their issue,” Ariola said. “I’m hoping this is the administration that finally solves the retention problem. And the only way to solve that problem is to pay EMTs their worth and also recognize them as uniformed workers.” The mayor’s office declined to comment on Ariola’s new proposal and referred to a comment from the fire department. “The Department is currently engaged in a challenging period of increasing response times. We know this is unacceptable and we are working tirelessly to reverse this trend,” Farinacci said. “We will continue to take steps to improve response times and keep New Yorkers safe, including improving coordination with hospitals, enhancing efficiency in high-volume areas, and increased operational visibility to help return units to service quickly." — Molly Reinmann FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL A SUBURBAN ALARM: Suburban voters across the country are turning against President Donald Trump, according to a poll that amounts to a major warning sign for the GOP this election season. The results of the National Suburban Poll by the National Center for Suburban Studies at Hofstra University paint a bleak picture for Trump and his party. “Numbers that are concerning Republicans throughout the country become even more so when they show up in suburbs, which for years have been the ‘swing’ voting bloc that determines national and many statewide elections,” said Larry Levy, the center’s dean. “When a party’s or candidate’s numbers are weak in the suburbs, as we’ve found in many instances for Republicans, the situation goes from concerning to alarming.” The survey found 33% of suburban voters approve of the president’s job performance. His approval rating in swing suburban House seats isn’t much better: 35%. Just over a quarter of suburban voters nationally — 26% — are satisfied with the direction of the country. Suburban voters by a margin of 50% to 42% prefer Democrats over Republicans in the generic Congressional ballot question. The GOP, though, is in a statistical tie with Democrats in suburban swing seats. In those districts, Democrats lead Republicans 47% to 44%. Taken together, the numbers highlight the challenge Republicans face this year, especially in deep blue New York, home to several swing House districts in the New York City suburbs. The most competitive race is in the Hudson Valley, where GOP Rep. Mike Lawler is fending off a challenge from Democratic opponent Cait Conley. The survey included 1,500 people nationwide and was conducted in late September. It oversampled suburban residents who live in swing House districts. — Nick Reisman SARATOGA FRESH: To get an idea of how much national headwinds might apply to the New York State Senate, look to Saratoga County. Plenty of indicators suggest two factors will heavily influence the outcome: Voters are angry at Republicans and willing to oppose well-tenured incumbents. That could be a double-barreled problem for Sen. Jim Tedisco, who’s running in a district where Donald Trump lost by 8 points two years ago. The Republican is now the dean of the state Legislature by a large margin: Tedisco came to Albany in 1983, the first year of Mario Cuomo’s time as governor. Only four other members who might be in office next year served in 1999. “Jim Tedisco’s been in office for over 40 years, almost as long as I’ve been alive,” said Sarah Rogerson, Tedisco’s Democratic challenger. “People are ready for some fresh voices.” Even if current assumptions about the electorate’s mood prove true, Republicans remain optimistic they won’t apply to New York. The GOP believes 2026 will be a repeat of 2022, when a lack of enthusiasm for the top of the ticket meant a good year for Democrats nationwide bypassed the Empire State. “If there’s going to be a blue wave across the country, it’s probably going to miss New York, and it’s largely because of how deeply unpopular Kathy Hochul is,” Senate Republican Campaign Committee Chair George Borrello said. Nobody’s predicting Republicans will retake the majority in a chamber where Democrats had a 41-22 edge this year. The main question now is whether Democrats can pull off a two-thirds supermajority of 42 or more members, a feat accomplished in 2020 and 2022 but not 2024. READ MORE in POLITICO Pro from Bill Mahoney. FROM CITY HALL BILL SIGNING TIME: Mayor Zohran Mamdani will sign two bills passed by the City Council that come with significant transit and housing policy ramifications, his office confirmed today. The first measure Mamdani plans to put his John Hancock on will abolish New York City’s horse carriage industry . The second will give nonprofit groups and local land trusts first dibs on buying distressed residential properties in their communities, with the idea that those regulations will protect affordable housing stock. Mamdani had already voiced support for both pieces of legislation before the Council passed them yesterday. But his office hadn’t until today confirmed he would sign the bills, as opposed to letting them lapse into law. Mamdani’s office did not immediately provide a date for when he plans to sign the bills. The issue of signing bills came to the fore this week when the New York Post noted that Mamdani has only inked one bill since taking office. Ultimately, as long as the mayor doesn’t veto a bill, there’s no practical difference between whether he signs it or lets it lapse, as it becomes law regardless. — Chris Sommerfeldt IN OTHER NEWS — IN THE SCHOOLS: New York City is considering closing a Harlem high school due to underenrollment, the first in what could be a growing number of school mergers and closures amid public school enrollment declines. ( Chalkbeat ) — HOCHUL: The governor’s vision for New York is largely shaped by her upbringing in a small Rust Belt city in western New York and her family’s slow climb up the socioeconomic ladder. ( New York Times ) — CORNELL 7: Attorney General Letitia James is asking a court to dismiss a request to remove her from the investigation into the alleged sexual assault at Cornell University due to impartiality concerns. ( Times Union ) Missed this morning’s New York Playbook? We forgive you. Read it here .

title: Palestinian resistance coalition hails West Bank operation
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 24 (MNA) – A coalition of Gaza-based Palestinian resistance groups has praised a retaliatory shooting operation in the southern West Bank city of al-Khalil that left two Israeli soldiers dead and three others wounded.
The Popular Resistance Committees (PRC), in a statement issued on Friday, praised the operation in al-Khalil, portraying it as a direct response to the horrendous crimes committed by Israeli authorities, the Israeli military, and extremist Jewish settlers across the occupied Palestinian territories.
Accoridng to the Press TV, the coalition stressed that the Zionist regime’s ongoing crimes would neither ensure the security of the occupying entity nor break the will of the Palestinian people.
The resistance coalition further noted that the retaliatory shooting dealt a heavy blow to Israel’s security, military and intelligence apparatus.
The Hamas resistance group called the shooting “heroic,” but did not claim responsibility for it.
For its part, the Lebanese Hezbollah resistance movement hailed as heroic the shooting operation in al-Khalil, stressing that it is a “natural and legitimate response to Israeli enemy’s ongoing crimes, including killings, genocide, destruction, and attacks on holy sites.”
Israeli media outlets identified the slain soldiers as Staff Seargent Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, from Ashkelon, and Sergeant Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, from Hod Hasharon. Roytman was reportedly a squad commander.
The Israeli army alleged that the two Palestinians fatally shot in the incident were planning a larger attack against settlers on Route 35. They realised, however, that they would not be able to reach the highway and decided to open fire on the temporary checkpoint instead.
The two were named as Mohammad Jaaba and Firas Jaaba, 27-year-old residents of al-Khalil. They were members of the same family, though as of late Friday morning their exact relationship remained unclear.
The men purportedly arrived by car at around 7:30 a.m. local time (0430 GMT) at a temporary checkpoint set up by Israeli troops at the exit to al-Khalil.
They got out of the car on a side street, armed with an assault rifle and a pistol, and allegedly opened fire on the checkpoint, using the buildings as cover.
Footage from the incident showed a prolonged gunfight between the Palestinian men and Israeli troops. According to the Israeli military, it lasted more than 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a situation assessment with the regime’s security chiefs in the aftermath of the retaliatory shooting operation, and ordered preparations for a full lockdown across the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu said he was joined by the Israeli military's chief of staff Eyal Zamir, war minister Israel Katz, David Zini, the director of Israel's internal spy agency, Shin Bet, top military adviser Shmuel Ben Ezra, and head of the Israeli army’s central command Avi Bluth.
In the wake of the West Bank shooting operation, Israel’s so-called security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for the Palestinian Authority (PA) to be dismantled.
“We have to act before it’s too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarized, and its infrastructure wiped out completely,” Ben-Gvir said.
The remarks came despite the fact that there was no indication of any PA involvement in the incident.
Israeli finance minister Bezalel Smotrich separately wrote, “There’s no avoiding a large-scale military action in Judea and Samaria [the West Bank] to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, gather weapons and eliminate fighters.”
A United Nations report published in July said more than 900 Palestinians had been injured in Israeli settler attacks in the occupied West Bank since the start of the year, while 76 Palestinians had been killed by Israeli forces or settlers, or died of their injuries, over the same period.

title: RDIF CEO lauds Melania Trump’s role in resolving humanitarian crisis in Alyoshki
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian president’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries and CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) Kirill Dmitriev has commended US First Lady Melania Trump and her team’s role in the organization of the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region.

title: Kadena Implements Curfew, Alcohol Restrictions for Junior Troops After Japanese Civilian Dies
body: The top Air Force commander on the Japanese island of Okinawa has clamped down alcohol and issued a curfew for junior enlisted Airmen and Guardians at Kadena Air Base for the next month. The order came roughly two weeks after a U.S. Marine was arrested for allegedly robbing and murdering a Japanese woman on the island. Brig. Gen. John B. Gallemore, commander of the 18th Wing at Kadena, issued the Oct. 22 memo, ordering the “Curtailment of Liberty and the Consumption of Alcohol,” according to a memo posted on the popular unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page. A PACAF spokesperson confirmed the memo’s authenticity. The order went into effect Oct. 22 and will last “throughout the 30-day period of reflection,” concluding on Nov. 8, according to the memo: All personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4 are not to consume alcohol. Off-base liberty between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. local time is curtailed for all personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4. Possession of alcohol is banned in all dormitories within Kadena Air Base, to include dormitory common areas. During the period, “commanders at all levels are authorized to conduct unannounced, systematic health and welfare inspections of dormitory rooms to ensure compliance of this order,” the memo states. The memo follows an Oct. 6 memo from United States Forces Japan that ordered similar liberty restrictions and personal conduct training as part of a “period of reflection” following the Marine’s arrest in connection with the alleged murder of an Okinawan woman in Naha. Japanese police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, on Oct. 4 for allegedly killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi and stealing her wallet, Marine Corps Times reported . “Incidents like this demand we pause for reflection,” Benjamin T. Watson, area coordinator for U.S. Forces Japan, wrote in the memo. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will continue to ensure full cooperation with Japanese authorities throughout the investigation.” Watson added that serving on Okinawa “comes with responsibility.” “We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home,” Watson wrote. “Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region.” The USFJ memo prohibited alcohol consumption for 48 hours from Oct. 7-9 but stopped short of restricting consumption during the 30-day period of reflection. In a statement, PACAF Gallemore’s Oct. 22 memo contains extra restrictions. “The 18th Wing continually assesses measures to reinforce good order and discipline and maintain positive relationships with our host community,” the PACAF statement read. “As part of the ongoing 30-day period of reflection on Okinawa, Japan, [Gallemore] determined that additional preventive measures were appropriate to reinforce expectations for responsible conduct among service members.” Periods of reflection and associated restrictions have been used by commanders on Okinawa in the past to reinforce discipline after violent, criminal incidents involving U.S. personnel and Japanese residents. In 2024, USFJ prohibited all American troops in the country from publicly consuming alcohol from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. every day after a string of alleged sexual assaults. In 2017, the command prohibited all drinking and cut off-base liberty for troops on Okinawa after a fatal car crash involving a drunk Marine. In 2010, then-Brig. Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach—now the Chief of Staff— instituted a brief period of reflection restricting alcohol and off-base liberty at Kadena after a string of alcohol-related arrests. In 2008, commanders imposed the measure to calm an uproar in the surrounding community over allegations that a Marine raped a 14-year-old girl on the island, The Guardian reported . Kadena is the closest U.S. air base to Taiwan , making it a strategically vital location should China ever launch an invasion. The post Kadena Implements Curfew, Alcohol Restrictions for Junior Troops After Japanese Civilian Dies appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Turkey says renewed attack on Iran would expand conflict, diplomacy only way forward
body: Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan cautioned on Friday against any renewed attack on Iran, saying such a move would exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict there, adding that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to end the war.Fidan met his counterparts from Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Germany, France, Britain, and Italy in Istanbul to discuss developments in the Iran war, attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthis, and Russia's war in Ukraine.It was the first collective meeting between the countries, comprising the Regional Four (R4) and EU 3 (E3), alongside Italy."We are all in agreement that a new attack on Iran would expand the war in the region," Fidan told a press conference after the meeting. "A military intervention on Iran is not in any way a solution. Nobody approves this at the moment," he added.French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said after Friday's meetings that renewed escalation between Iran and the United States would only have losers and raise oil prices.The comments followed a New York Times report on Wednesday that the US and Israeli militaries had drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm congressional election next month. Citing US officials, it said likely targets would include Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and its missile and drone arsenal.Trump says US would not launch attack before midtermsUS President Donald Trump said earlier this month that the US would not launch an attack on Iran before the midterms, as Washington and Tehran were having "productive" talks about ending their six-month-old war. On Friday, he said the US could end the war quickly but questioned whether Washington should seek a swift conclusion or allow the conflict to gradually wind down.NATO member Turkey has been in close contact with Washington, Tehran and regional mediators to seek an end to the war. It has repeatedly called for attacks to stop and warned against the regional expansion of the conflict.Fidan also said the countries meeting on Friday had discussed possible parameters to ensure the war in Iran does not expand further, but did not elaborate.Following Friday's meetings, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany, France, and Britain were ready to negotiate with Iran to rule out its acquisition of nuclear weapons, while calling for support for Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

title: 40,000 tons of Russian diesel are bound for New York—due four days after Americans vote
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A Malta-flagged tanker carrying Russian diesel is heading for New York after the fuel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Reuters reported in an exclusive on 23 October, citing LSEG shipping data. Two weeks earlier, the US Treasury temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel. The tanker is due in the US on 7 November, four days after Americans vote in the midterms. So the first US-bound cargo cannot reach American pumps before the election. Energy analysts also doubt the deal will lower diesel prices meaningfully. US fuel prices rose mainly because the war with Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Trump, however, has blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries. Loaded on the day Moscow promised The medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes took on 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel at the Baltic port of Primorsk on 22 October, shipping data showed. In March, Ukraine’s General Staff said its drones hit the Transneft oil terminal at that same port. A day before the loading, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak announced that the first tanker would sail for the US on 22 October. He pledged more shipments and said Russia would meet US needs within its capabilities. Explore further Russia resumes diesel exports to Türkiye, Brazil, after Trump lifts sanctions on fuel supplies, boosting Moscow’s war revenue – Reuters From a pledge to a partial lift On 9 October, Trump wrote that Russia would immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace.” Another 500,000 tons would follow in November, then 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Moscow had banned diesel exports on 8 July, after Ukrainian drone strikes shut down refineries and caused fuel shortages inside Russia. The Russian government stated on 10 October that it had partially lifted the ban, clearing 500,000 tons for the world market at this stage. Russian diesel shipments to Türkiye and Brazil have since resumed , boosting Moscow’s war revenue. Trump has made other moves to cut diesel prices before the vote, Reuters reported. He waived parts of a new sanctions law against Russia. He also threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more fuel from their emergency reserves. title: Attention people who think UB is fine
body:
After my post on undefined behavior in C some people insisted that itâs demonstrably fine, we know what the code will do, and at worst weâll get a segfault.
(sorry. This is C++, but the equivalent C code produces exactly the same assembly output)
Ruh roh. Exploding chocolate! The function explode() will be executed, even though it was never called!
Some people insisted that dereferencing a null pointer is fine . Itâll just try to access address zero! And these people supposedly know what happens when you try: if nothing is mapped there, youâll get a segfault.
Letâs say we change std::unreachable() to int* ptr = nullptr; *ptr = 99; in the previous example. Now we get this :
Curious, eh? First it writes zero, not 99, to memory address zero. Then it crashes the program using an invalid instruction. The number 99 never appears in the generated program. But the null pointer write does. Presumably the null pointer write is done in order to improve debugger error messages.
Ok, so what happens if we add ptr += 10 . Thatâs UB for three reasons:
Wow. Now it did what someone naively would expect, taking the code at face value. Lucky.
Why did GCC (and clang, by the way) not detect that *(ptr + 10) = 99 is equally UB as *ptr = 99 , and do the same thing?
Wrong question. No compiler is obligated to âdetectâ UB at all. Looks to me like GCC and clang, if we want to anthropomorphize them, saw âoh, null pointer dereference? Well that canât happen, so Iâll stop emitting instructions for this function, to save on the binary sizeâ. Because of the halting problem , it cannot in the general case know if the code will ever be executed.

title: Memory is slow, Disk is fast
body:
Big O notation is a lie. Well, okay, it's a simplification that lies by omission.
Can O(ân) scale better than O(log n)? Can a disk-based algorithm outperform an in-RAM data structure? Yes, and yes.
Scaled to 2 billion nodes, the AVL binary tree needs 144 GiB of RAM. DiskArray keeps its data on 8 NVMe drives and uses 264 MiB of RAM, but it's still faster at everything.
Part 1 showed that computers are getting wider, not faster, and that PCIe bandwidth is outpacing DRAM bandwidth.
Part 2 showed that streaming from disk can beat streaming from the page cache.
Part 2.5 showed that with the right hardware and software, streaming from disk can beat a buffer in DRAM. So far I've shown how a sequential read from NVMe is fast, which is a cool trick but not controversial enough.
I'm getting worried people still aren't getting the point.
The point is that our intuitions about computer performance are all wrong.
So this time we're going to show how an on-disk data structure doing random reads and writes to disk is faster than an in-RAM data structure. To make it worse, computer science textbook Big O notation says the on-disk algorithm is going to scale worse than the in-RAM algorithm.
Same old used box as Part 2.5 : a 24-core Xeon Platinum 8260 with 35.75 MiB of L3 and 192 GiB of DDR4, and 8 Samsung PM983 NVMe drives over NVMe-oF on four 100 Gb InfiniBand links.
Keep a sorted set of 8-byte keys, and support four transactions on it:
That's the core of a database index, an order book, a leaderboard, a time-series store.
Let's walk through the algorithm selection by first principles and childlike wonder.
The simplest solution is an array of keys, kept in order.
search(key) is a binary search. Look at the middle, throw away the half the key can't be in, and repeat. 16 keys take 3 or 4 hops. A billion takes about 30. O(log n).
at(i) doesn't search at all. The i-th smallest key is just array[i] , at a fixed offset from the start. One access. O(1). You can't beat that.
To insert, you have to make room. Everything after the new key moves over one slot to open a gap, then the new key goes in the gap.
Delete is the same in reverse. Take the key out, then everything after it moves over to close the gap.
Either way, on average, half the array moves, every single time. It's a memmove , about the most efficient thing a CPU can do with memory, but it's still O(n). At 4M nodes, every insert moves about 16 MiB. At a billion nodes it would be 4 GiB per insert. The array also has to be one contiguous block, so growing it means allocating a bigger one and copying everything over.
The textbook fix for "insert moves everything" is the linked list.
Each node holds a key and a pointer to the next node. To insert, you change two pointers. Nothing moves.
But to insert 21 you first have to find where 21 goes, and the only way to find anything in a linked list is to start at the head and follow the pointers one at a time. Search is O(n). at(i) is O(n). Insert and delete are O(1) once you're in the right place, and O(n) to get there.
Adding a node is cheap, but finding where to insert it is really expensive. So this doesn't solve our problem.
Use the pointers to branch out instead of to line up, and you get a binary search tree.
Smaller keys go left, bigger keys go right. Search walks down from the top, throwing away half the tree at each step, just like binary search on the sorted array. Insert walks down the same way and hangs the new node off the bottom, just like the linked list. Nothing moves. Keep a count of the nodes under each node and at(i) is a walk down too.
On paper it's the best of both: log n for everything.
In practice a plain binary tree has a problem. Its shape depends on the order you insert things. Insert keys in sorted order and every new node goes to the right of the last one. It would perform like a linked list.
The AVL tree fixes this: after each insert or delete it checks the heights of the two sides and, if they're off by more than one, rotates a few nodes to rebalance. The tree stays about logâ n deep no matter what.
But this isn't free; there is overhead to implement the tree. Every node is its own allocation with a key, two pointers, a balance factor, and a count. That's a lot of bookkeeping for an 8-byte key: 72 bytes of RAM per key, where the sorted array needs 8. The biggest sorted array I ran, 4M nodes, is 32 MiB of RAM. The same 4M nodes in the AVL tree take 288 MiB. At 2G nodes the AVL tree used 144 GiB of RAM.
Let's look at how things scale and compare that to Big O predictions.
At first glance, it looks like Big O gets the ranking right. The sorted array's performance for insert and delete falls off a cliff while the search and at() performance degrades more slowly. The AVL tree performance degrades slowly as predicted.
The AVL tree solves the insert and delete problem but costs a lot of overhead that shows up in search and at() performance as well as extra RAM. The sorted array has a lot going for it: everything is in order, in one place, with no pointers to chase and no overhead. Its only problem is that an insert has to move half the array. Let's try a more brute-force solution to insert and delete.
If we cut the array into pieces we could contain the areas affected by inserts and deletes. Our DiskArray data structure splits the sorted keys into small extents. A small index says which extent holds which range of keys. To insert, find the extent with the index, then do a sorted-array insert inside that one extent. You only ever move part of the extent, never the whole list.
Then, because we're making a point, we can put the extents on disk too. That way we only need the index in RAM with a small buffer pool to handle the IO for in-flight and active extents.
A textbook answer for this kind of structure depends on your assumptions. Extent size is a variable parameter. It could be as bad as O(ân) for insert and delete if we scale the extents with n. However, in practice, given the hardware constraints, I sized the extents to what the disks want and fixed them: 512-key extents because that's one 4 KiB disk block, 4096-entry directory blocks so a split only ever shifts a few tens of KiB. Most of the time an insert is effectively one 4 KiB read, one 4 KiB write, and a log n search of the index in RAM. But occasionally it has to edit a directory block. The extent, directory, and even I/O introduce constants that are significant factors in the math for the realistic scales we'll be working in.
Full Disclosure: if you look at the code you'll notice the top-level index that points to directory blocks is growing with n. I planned to make that split into blocks as well, extents all the way up the tree. But I didn't get around to it. So technically there is a corner case that is O(n). With my current settings a second tier would kick in at around 8G nodes. So in practice the O(n) means that, on average once every couple hundred thousand inserts, a directory block splits and the top level has to memmove() up to about 1.4 MiB and rebuild its count tree. That's noise next to the drive I/O. If I did add a recursive index tree as planned, then I think we're officially just a B-tree variant and are for sure O(log n).
To simplify, I'm just going to say as an algorithm it scales as bad as O(ân) and as good as O(log n). If that's not a reasonable argument, I'm sorry. I majored in Electrical Engineering, not Computer Science, so I don't know the theory as well as I do the reality.
Big O says AVL wins or at least ties. In-RAM vs On-Disk says AVL wins.
I want to compare DiskArray to AVL in DRAM not L3. 512K nodes Ã 72 B is ~36 MiB which is the L3 size. So we'll compare up to 512K nodes and more than 512K nodes in separate graphs.
AVL wins everything here: about 10x faster on search at 2K nodes, still almost 2x at 512K. Every pointer hop is a cache hit, and cache hits are cheap. DiskArray is flat at around 2M searches/s, because it's paying for machinery it doesn't need yet: queues, workers, a buffer pool. Its data still fits in the 24 MiB buffer pool, so the drives aren't even being read.
Nevertheless, even in cache, AVL performance is scaling down fast. Search goes from 19.6M/s at 2K nodes to 4.0M/s at 512K, about 5x slower.
Now let's compare them as we scale past 512K nodes:
From 16M nodes up, the disk-based structure beats the in-RAM tree at everything, all the way to where AVL ran out of RAM at 2G nodes. DiskArray kept going to 64G.
Let's compare what happens during an insert() at 2G nodes.
This doesn't help at first glance. In fact it makes it look like DiskArray is doing way more work.
It depends what you count, and every way of counting it is interesting.
Two definitions run through all of this. Used is the bytes an algorithm deliberately reads, plus the bytes it deliberately writes. Moved is what the hardware actually transfers: DRAM and the L3/L2 caches move in 64-byte cache lines, so reading 8 bytes moves 64, and the drives move 4 KiB blocks. The drive traffic is measured. The rest is estimated from the data layouts.
Inserts per second, times the data moved and used per insert, gives us the bandwidths. At 2G nodes:
DiskArray moves more data per insert than AVL, and it's faster on both counts. It moves the overhead faster: 5.1 GiB/s of traffic against AVL's 1.8, 2.9x. And it moves the data it actually needs faster: 2.1 GiB/s against 312 MiB/s, 6.9x. More bytes, moved faster, every way you count them.
Every AVL insert waits on about 62 reads, one after another, and uses 1 KiB of the 5.8 KiB those reads drag in. That's 312 MiB/s of useful work. Higher bandwidth DRAM wouldn't help, because DRAM latency hasn't moved in 20 years.
DiskArray is short of bandwidth. Its CPU work is about 0.3 Âµs per insert. The drives are the limit: from 32M to 1G nodes they hold at ~5.5 GiB/s, ~720K inserts/s. More drives, or faster ones, and it goes faster, until that 0.3 Âµs of CPU catches up at around 3M inserts/s.
A drive round trip is about 87 Âµs. If DiskArray did one insert at a time, every insert would wait that long, twice, and it would manage a few thousand inserts/s. It does 670K. Here's how:
DiskArray keeps 2048 transactions in flight, in two halves of 1024. One core does all the algorithm work and queuing; 28 io_uring workers just talk to the drives.
Big O counts steps. It assumes every step costs the same. They don't, not even close.
A billion L1 cache hits take about a second. A billion DRAM misses take a minute and a half, and a billion NVMe reads take a day. Big O counts every one of those as one step. Also, when you parallelize, the timescale comes back down to earth. So Big O notation is very limited in its predictive power in practice. It defines the shape of the performance curve but not it's slope or magnitude.
Let us observe the relative scaling performance these algorithms actually experience from 512K to 2G nodes.
We can see AVL is scales much worse than Diskarrary even though Big O would make us think the opposite is true.
I started at Intel doing flash memory out of college. In the early days of the technology, you could use very simple equations to predict the characteristics of a cell. At some point, the cells shrank to where the number of electrons in a cell was something that had to be quantified and thought about. Now, the equations have to start taking quantum effects into consideration.
Big O in its most reductive form isn't going to tell you how things are going to perform in practical scales. It didn't have to. But as the performance characteristics of various elements of the system continue to diverge and become extreme I don't think the single n term O() is useful anymore. I think it's time to start treating these equations and simulations more seriously and add in more nuanced effects.
Notice the curves aren't smooth log n curves. They have step functions where each step is something outgrowing hardware.
Big O can't see any of these yet they have a huge impact on the practical scales we're dealing with.
Nobody uses an AVL tree for this. Here's what happens with the structures you'd actually reach for:
First, everything doing one transaction at a time, like AVL:
The better structures beat DiskArray, but not by as much as you'd think. B+tree ties it on search and beats it by 1.35x on insert. NextArray, DiskArray's own design kept in RAM, is 1.4x on search and 1.9x on insert.
ART is the fastest at search and insert, about 3x and 5x, but its at() is the worst here: ART has no rank, so finding the i-th key means walking. So it's not a great example.
Still the best RAM structures aren't beating it by an order of magnitude.
ART and AVL have too much overhead to scale beyond 2G on this hardware. Both cost about 72 bytes per 8-byte key, 146 and 144 GiB at 2G nodes, and the box only has 192 GiB (188 GiB usable). The next doubling would have needed nearly 300 GiB. B+tree and NextArray, at 17-21 bytes per key, made it to 8G. DiskArray, at about 0.1 bytes of RAM per key, went to 64G and could have kept going.
Because DiskArray is pipelined it could have an advantage over the RAM structures. So we'll pipeline them the same way, and pull all the tricks we can try with prefetching and optimizing code paths.
This is a different league. The pipelined structures beat DiskArray by 3-6x across the board, on the same single core. Pipelining NextArray took search from 1.52M/s to 6.45M/s and insert from 1.29M/s to 4.02M/s. B+tree went from 1.13M to 5.03M searches/s. The one thing it doesn't speed up is NextArray's at(), which was already a short walk of a small count tree: one at a time it's faster up to about 256M nodes, and past that the pipelined version only pulls slightly ahead. Still not an order of magnitude.
Plain NextArray does one transaction at a time, like AVL. Each level of the index is a cache miss, and each miss waits on the one before it. The pipelined version is the same data structure, the same single thread, but it handles transactions in groups of 32:
A core can only keep about a dozen misses in flight, so it's not 32x, but it's 4x on search.
NextArray was built for this. Every transaction follows the same short path: a few levels of a flat, sorted index, then one contiguous extent. That's easy to batch and easy to prefetch. A tree of individually allocated nodes isn't, because you can't know where the next node is until you've loaded this one.
If this looks familiar, it should. It's DiskArray's pipeline, pointed at RAM instead of at the drives:
RAM stands for Random Access Memory, but it's not really random access anymore. It's a block device with 64-byte blocks and 80-90 ns of latency, and you have to use it like one.
To get even reasonable performance out of either memory or storage, you need to treat them as parallelized asynchronous block devices that feed the caches.
