title: General Atomics partners with Spirit Defense on FQ-42 uncrewed fighter production
body: The partnership follows the Air Force’s June award of an FQ-42 production contract to GA-ASI. The company said bringing in Spirit Defense would strengthen production resilience and reduce the risk of single points of failure. “We’ve established our proven design, development, and manufacturing capability for the FQ-42,” said GA-ASI President David R. Alexander. “With Spirit Defense we add capacity, which is exactly the kind of production resilience our U.S. Air Force customer is looking for with its CCA ramp-up.” Spirit Defense will contribute engineering and manufacturing expertise from design through production. The announcement did not specify production targets or a delivery timetable for its work. GA-ASI has been the sole manufacturer of its aircraft since its founding in 1992. Its portfolio includes the MQ-9A Reaper, MQ-1C Gray Eagle, MQ-20 Avenger and MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian. “We’re proud to bring deep manufacturing expertise and proven capabilities to this important program,” said Spirit Defense President and CEO Keith Schrader. “Our team understands the responsibility that comes with supporting critical national defense programs, and we’re ready to deliver for our customer and the warfighter.” Developed with the Air Force, the FQ-42 is a purpose-built uncrewed fighter in the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. Its modular design allows new mission systems and autonomy software to be integrated rapidly. GA-ASI said the software architecture underpinning that work had been demonstrated in live flight tests on multiple airframes. It provides the foundation for human-machine teaming in complex combat scenarios. The company is separately discussing its Gambit family of modular combat aircraft with international militaries. Those aircraft draw on development of the FQ-42, XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station and MQ-20 Avenger. Gambit variants are designed for roles including electronic warfare, suppression and destruction of enemy air defenses, and stand-off precision strike. GA-ASI said customers could participate in manufacturing and integrate their own sensors, weapons and other combat technologies.

title: Oryol Region governor refutes reports about dozens of casualties after Ukraine’s attack
body:
ORYOL, October 23. /TASS/. Governor of the Oryol Region Andrey Klychkov has refuted media reports about dozens of casualties after Ukraine’s missile attack on an enterprise in the city of Oryol, slamming them as enemy propaganda.
"Once again, I urge you to trust only official information. Regrettably, social media is rife with false reports of non-existent heavy damage, dozens of casualties, massive debris, chemical contamination, and so on. This is the work of enemy propaganda, aimed at sowing panic," he wrote on messaging app Max.
Eight people were injured after Ukraine’s missile attack on an enterprise in Oryol on October 23. Most of them received minor injuries. Clear-up operations are underway.

title: Defense Watch: LWCLU Award, Dutch FMS, UGVs in UKR, Drone U, Vectis Overseas
body:
LWCLU Award. RTX’s Raytheon said on Oct. 19 that its Javelin Joint Venture (JJV) with Lockheed Martin has received a $215 million production contract for the missile’s Lightweight Command Launch Units (LWCLU). Raytheon noted the award comes five months after the first LWCLUs were delivered to the Army, adding the new capability is “30 percent smaller and 25 percent lighter, while doubling target detection and recognition, compared to the current Block I Command Launch Unit.” “This contract reflects the strong partnership between industry and the Army to sustain and advance the Javelin system,” Jenna Hunt Frazier, JJV president and Javelin program director at Raytheon, said in a statement. “By modernizing our factory and strengthening our production line, we’re ensuring soldiers receive a lighter, more capable launcher that improves operational readiness across the force.”
Ukraine Priority. Restarting U.S. military aid to Ukraine to fight Russia will be a priority for Democrats, if they retake control of Congress in the coming elections. “If Democrats regain the majority in the House of Representatives in the next Congress, and I have the privilege to serve once again as chair of the committee, providing support for Ukraine and its defense of democracy will be one of my priorities,” Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), wrote in an editorial last month in the New Haven Register . DeLauro is the ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee and said she traveled with HAC Chairman Tom Cole (R-Okla.) to Ukraine this summer. “In total, Europe has provided some $235 billion in aid, roughly $100 billion more than the United States has to date,” she wrote in the editorial. “Defending Ukraine should be a partnership of democratic countries — the United States and Europe — against the belligerence of Russian expansionism…The F-35s protecting European airspace are propelled by engines made in Connecticut, while the [H-60] Seahawks and Black Hawks patrolling European coasts are assembled here as well. We cannot in good conscience continue to withhold desperately needed support for an American ally fighting for its independence against such brutal and senseless aggression.”
Netherlands FMS. The State Department said on Oct. 19 it has approved a potential $294 million foreign military sale with the Netherlands for Common Infrared Countermeasure (CIRCM) systems. The deal includes 16 of the Northrop Grumman-built CIRCM laser-based aircraft protection systems along with 38 AN/APR-39E(V)2 Radar Warning Receivers. “The proposed sale will modernize the Netherlands’ armed forces, expand its capability to strengthen homeland defense, and deter regional threats. This enhanced capability will contribute to the Netherlands’ military goals of updating capability while further enhancing interoperability with the United States and other allies,” the State Department said in a statement. The U.S. Army awarded Northrop Grumman a nearly $5 billion production contract for CIRCM in September.
UGVs in Ukraine. Forterra’s Lancer autonomous ground vehicle, based on the Polaris RANGER XP 1500 and powered by its AutoDrive software, has completed nearly 1,500 missions and 88 casualty evacuation operations in Ukraine, according to Physical AI firm Ouster. The Lancer platform, which first started arriving in Ukraine in October 2025, utilizes Ouster’s Rev7 OS1 digital lidar “at the core of its sensor fusion perception stack.” “Lancers are operating in high danger zones where persistent drone surveillance makes crewed vehicles high value targets and creates unnecessary risk for personnel. Instead, uncrewed Lancer systems deliver essential supplies and evacuate wounded soldiers without undue risk to additional personnel,” Ouster said. “Ouster’s sensors enable 360-degree situational awareness for autonomous ground vehicles operating in complex and unpredictable environments.”
Drone Payloads. Perennial Autonomous recently announced it’s partnered with McAlester Army Ammunition Plant (MCAAP) for the weapons manufacturing facility to build, load and delivery payloads for the company’s drone platforms, including the Merops interceptors, Hornet mid-range strike drones and Bumblebee quadcopters. “This combines MCAAP’s best-in-class explosives manufacturing capabilities with Perennial Autonomy’s advanced autonomy and guidance systems, enabling its drones to carry reliable and lethal ordnance into contested environments across the world. The partnership also supports the Army Materiel Command’s push to modernize the organic industrial base, adapting production lines built for traditional munitions to the demands of modern drone warfare,” Perennial Autonomy said in a statement. “For Perennial Autonomy, the partnership secures something increasingly scarce in the drone industry: a reliable domestic source of combat-ready ordnance at scale. As demand grows worldwide for the Merops, Hornet and Bumblebee platforms, a secure munitions pipeline through MCAAP means shorter delivery timelines and a resilient U.S. supply chain, both critical as production ramps up to meet warfighter demand.”
Ukraine Space Help. Two Finnish companies, satellite manufacturer and operator ICEYE, and telecommunications giant Nokia, have signed a Letter of Intent with Ukraine’s Defense Ministry to explore enabling sovereign satellite communication for the country’s defense needs. “Through this Letter of Intent, together with Ukraine and ICEYE, we will explore how trusted, sovereign satellite communications can strengthen Ukraine’s resilience and give it control over the connectivity it depends on,” Mikko Hautala, chief geopolitical & government relations officer, and chairman of Nokia Defense, said in a statement. ICEYE and Nokia earlier this month partnered to offer customers broadband network connectivity from low Earth orbit. The Letter of Intent with Ukraine after the country reported its access to SpaceX’s military version of Starlink had been restricted.
Regional Freighter. Natilus, which is developing the 3.8 ton, optionally-piloted KONA regional freighter aircraft, has received $3.5 million in research, development, test and evaluation funding from the Defense Department’s Operation Energy-Innovation Directorate and the Air Force Energy, Installation and Environment office to accelerate development of the blended-wing body aircraft toward full-scale flight testing and a U.S. joint force demonstration. “In a fuel-constrained environment like the Pacific, efficiency translates directly into operational flexibility,” Jim Hartle, an Air Force official for Operational Energy, Safety and Occupational Health, said in a statement. “KONA provides an opportunity to evaluate how a commercially developed aircraft can contribute to distributed logistics while generating the data needed to inform future requirements.”
Counter-Drone “U.” The Univ. of North Dakota last week said it and the Northern Plains Unmanned Aircraft Systems Test Site at Grand Forks, N.D., signed a memorandum of understanding with the Joint Interagency Task Force (JIATF)-401 to “help identify promising counter-drone technologies for further evaluation and development.” Army Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross, the JIATF-401 director, stated, “This partnership brings together world-class research and operational testing expertise to help us identify what works, accelerate promising technologies, and deliver effective counter-drone capabilities to our warfighters.”
C-UAS Testing and Scoring. The Tactien Group, an advisory firm focused on aviation, unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) and counter-UAS, last week disclosed it has developed a software platform that scores any vendors’ drone detection sensors and system to aid customers in knowing what C-UAS solutions to acquire and use. As part of CAST, Tactien uses drones in different scenarios to “red team” against vendors’ sensors installed at a customer’s site and then puts the data into the software to score how well each sensor performed in each flight against key performance indicators and then provides recommendations on which sensors to use and where. Tactien has begun to use CAST with commercial customers and will work to get the platform on the Pentagon’s C-UAS Marketplace, Nate Ernst, the firm’s founder and president, told Defense Daily . The Department of Homeland Security, and state and local law enforcement agencies are also interested, he said.
Vectis Releasability. As Lockheed Martin develops Vectis, its expected future entry into the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program, the unmanned aircraft is being designed with “releasability” in mind, meaning it can easily be exported to America’s allies, Jim Taiclet, the company’s chairman, president and CEO, said last week. “We’re going to try to make sure that it’s releasable immediately to our allies,” he said Oct. 22 during the company’s third quarter earnings call. “In other words, it will be designed in a way that the U.S. and or the international allies that qualify can buy it instead of having to do something for a U.S. only releasability standard and then hope we can get clearance to sell it overseas later.”
…Design Focus. Vectis is being designed and developed for both air-to-air combat and air-to-ground missions such as strikes against integrated air and missile defense systems, Taiclet said. Vectis will work with manned aircraft through manned and unmanned teaming, he said. The company is eyeing offering Vectis for the Air Force’s second increment of the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program that’s expected to arise within two years, Taiclet said. “Increment 2 we anticipate will have, again larger payload, larger range, and larger survivability requirement that will go with that” versus Increment 1, he added. The Air Force is currently flight testing CCAs from Anduril Industries and General Atomics in Increment 1.
AM for Tomahawk. Nikon AM last week said it received a $23.5 million contract under the Defense Department’s Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program to deliver and use multiple units of its two-meter z-height SLM Solutions laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing (AM) systems to manufacture prototypes of Tomahawk Land Attack Missile mid-bodies. Nikon AM said the work will be done at its technology center in Long Beach, Calif., adding the contract is to “scale critical production capacity.”
Carrier Controls MQ-25. The Navy said an underway aircraft carrier for the first time controlled an MQ-25A test aircraft located at Boeing’s Mascoutah, Ill., facility using a Proliferated Low Earth Orbit (pLEO) satellite. During a preliminary sea trial, the Unmanned Air Warfare Center (UAWC) aboard the USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) used its MD-5C Ground Control Station to connect with the aircraft via the satellite network. This was one in a series of build-up exercises the Navy is conducting to validate procedures, networks and interfaces for the future carrier-based unmanned aircraft tanker.
Drone Batteries. Global Ordnance Holdings said on Oct. 20 it has signed an agreement with Sparkz aimed at building and selling 210,000 battery packs for drones beginning in early 2027. “The agreement establishes the first fully domestic manufacturing for high-performance drone batteries as the U.S. Department of War directs more attention and funding to domestic drone technologies,” Global Ordnance said in a statement. “Sparkz will manufacture and supply batteries, while Global Ordnance will lead sales and distribution through its defense market relationships and distribution network. The high-energy-density batteries will be configurable to meet the power output and operational requirements of different unmanned systems.” The firms expect to achieve full manufacturing capacity by the second quarter of 2027.
DDG-91. The Arleigh Burke -class guided missile destroyer USS Pinckney (DDG-91) started the second phase of its upgrade process under the Destroyer Modernization 2.0 (DDG MOD 2.0) program in a Depot Modernization Period (DMP) at the General Dynamics NASSCO shipyard in San Diego. The Navy said this period marks the first installation of both the SPY-6(V)4 radar and High Efficiency Super-Capacity (HESC) air conditioning plants. When the work is finished, DDG-91 will rejoin the fleet “equipped with the most comprehensive multi-spectral integrated sensor suite designed to maintain maritime superiority for decades to come,” Capt. Tim Moore, program manager, DDG MOD 2.0, said in a statement. The Pinckney previously finished its first 1.5 DMP availability in 2024 as the first warship to receive the SLQ-32(V)7 Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program (SEWIP) and sponson modifications. The new HESC plans are needed to support the electrical and thermal needs of the radar and Aegis Combat Systems Baseline 10 on the destroyer.
Elbit AUVs. Israel’s Elbit Systems on Oct. 20 announced it completed the acquisition of the Canada-based International Submarine Engineering Ltd. (ISE) that specialized in autonomous underwater and remotely operated systems. The company said the purchase price was not material to Elbit. The 50-year-old ISE is headquartered in the Vancouver area and has delivered over 250 underwater vehicles to customers in over 20 countries. The company said adding ISE’s autonomous technologies aims to expand Elbit Systems’ capabilities in underwater Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR), Mine Counter Measures (MCM) and Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW), further strengthening the Company’s end-to-end maritime offering.
SubSea Craft USA. British maritime technology firm SubSea Craft appointed Matthew Zirkle as Chief Executive Officer of its SubSea Craft USA division as it looks to expand work in and with the U.S. In this new role, Zirkle will lead the company’s U.S. operations, with the company announcement saying he will focus on accelerating growth, strengthening partnerships across government and industry and expanding its ability to deliver maritime capabilities to customers. Zirkle is a retired rear admiral in the U.S. Navy who last served as chief of staff, U.S. Naval Forces Europe and Africa in August 2018. Previously, he also served as commander, submarines, NATO and director of Innovation for the Navy Reserve. Following his Navy career, Zirkle served as president of Defense Maritime Solutions for three years, regional director of maritime industrial base with the Navy at Serco, and president of the U.S. division of Rivencore Global Solutions.
MQ-8C Testers. The Army and Navy repurposed MQ-8C Fire Scout unmanned helicopters divested from the Navy into a second life as “dynamic test assets” for the U.S. Army within 14 months, the Navy said Oct. 22. The Office of the Chief of Naval Operations (OPNAV N98) directed that the Navy start divesting of Fire Scouts in February 2024, with final sundown scheduled by the end of fiscal year 2026, but in November 2024 the Multi-Mission Tactical UAS Program Office (PMA-266) got a request to evaluate if the MQ-8Cs could serve as a captive carry testbed for the U.S. Army Redstone Test Center (RTC) at Redstone Arsenal, Ala., to test Army sensor packages. By December 2024, teams started evaluating the MQ-8C and its systems and in January 2025 RTC submitted the formal request to OPNAV N98 for four MQ-8Cs, two Mobile Mission Control Systems, spare engines and support equipment for standup at Redstone Arsenal. OPNAV N98 approved the request in May 2025 and by July 2026 all of the aircraft and most of the equipment were delivered to Alabama. The final related equipment arrived at Redstone Arsenal in July 2026 and in August RTC completed ground testing and launched flight tests in Dugway Proving Ground, Utah, and at Redstone Arsenal to start building pilot confidence and build maintenance experience. The Navy said the whole effort saved the Army over $70 million in procurement costs alone.
Bluebottle Payloads. Australia’s Ocius on Oct. 21 announced the payloads of its two diesel-hybrid renewable powered Bluebottle Hybrid Uncrewed Surface Vessels (USVs) participating in this month’s U.S. Navy-led Maritime Big Play Pacific exercise as part of AUKUS Pillar II. In the first Bluebottle Hybrid participation in a U.S. Navy exercise, the company said they will carry ThayerMahan’s Outpost acoustic intelligence payloads and its TransparenSea processing software, which will allow them to detect and track undersea threats in an integrated suite of maritime capabilities. These hybrid vehicles supplement the USV’s renewable energy sources with a diesel generator, allowing persistent operations in low-light environments, high-latitude winters, and supporting payloads with higher power needs. Ocius billed the exercise as using “realistic operational scenarios spanning anti-submarine warfare, maritime strike and seabed operations, allowing defense, science and industry teams to test emerging technologies in operationally relevant conditions.”
Boeing CCA Participation. Boeing’s Wichita, Kansas-based Spirit Defense is to help build the airframe for the General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI) FQ-42 entrant in the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) engineering and manufacturing development (EMD) phase, according to GA-ASI. The FQ-42 is competing in EMD against the FQ-44 by Anduril Industries. Spirit Defense is to aid GA-ASI “to scale CCA production faster, while strengthening production resilience, and reducing the risk of single points of failure,” according to GA-ASI.
Army C-UAS Award. L3Harris Technologies last Friday said the Army has awarded the company a potential $60 million, three-year, Phase 2 contract to advance development of a long-range, maneuverable interceptor to counter small and medium-size UAS and traditional short-range air defense threats. The award was made under the Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation & Missile Center Xtended Ranged Counter-small UAS program. L3Harris said it will deliver a fully integrated interceptor for “flight performance testing.” Work is being done by the company’s Missile Solutions segment. “This design combines innovative propulsion with advanced seeker technologies to provide a highly capable, modular and cost-effective solution deployable from existing launch platforms,” Scott Alexander, president of propulsion systems at Missile Solutions, said in a statement.
…SOCOM C-UAS Awards. U.S. Special Operations Command (SOCOM) recently awarded one-year contracts to three companies for small form-factor C-UAS interceptors for use by dismounted, small unit maneuver forces. The ANCHOR Other Transaction Agreements were made to Askari Defense, $1.7 million, Mara Solutions, Inc., $1.5 million, and Tyco.AI, $894,788. SOCOM last week told Defense Daily that test, evaluation and operational assessment of the prototype interceptors are planned for fiscal year 2027. The small, high-speed, man-portable, lightweight interceptors are expected to engage small drone threats within 1 kilometer.
New GDIT Chief. General Dynamics last Friday said that Amy Johnson has been appointed as president of GD Information Technology, effective Nov. 3. Johnson is a 27-year veteran of GD Mission Systems, which along with the IT business, makes up the company’s $13.5 billion Technologies segment. GDIT had been led by Amy Gilliand, who abruptly departed the company earlier this month ( Defense Daily , Oct. 2). Paul Nedzbala has been serving as the acting president of GDIT since Gilliland’s departure. Johnson has held “increasingly senior roles in engineering, engineering management and business leadership across cybersecurity, defense electronics, space and intelligence systems, most recently as vice president and general manager for Space, Cyber and Intelligence,” GD said.

title: Senate Democrat Probes Tether Payments to Ex-White House Crypto Adviser’s Firm
body:
Tether is facing fresh scrutiny in the Senate over millions of dollars that reportedly flowed to a firm co-owned by Bo Hines while he helped shape U.S. stablecoin law at the White House.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino a letter Thursday demanding records of the company’s dealings with Hines and Nxum, the consulting firm he co-founded. Blumenthal gave Tether until Nov. 3 to respond.
Hines was executive director of President Donald Trump’s Presidential Council of Advisers for Digital Assets and a key architect of the GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025. He left the White House on Aug. 9, 2025, and Tether named him CEO of its new U.S. division the following month.
Blumenthal’s letter builds on an Oct. 14 Wall Street Journal investigation . The Journal reported that Nxum has earned $6.3 million from a deal Tether struck in May 2025. Tether agreed to pay a marketing firm, Notorious, $415,000 a month, and the firm passed most of the first payment to a wallet used by Nxum, where it was split three ways. Later payments went directly to Nxum after Hines left government. Hines kept his one-third stake in Nxum while serving in the White House, the Journal reported.
The Journal also reported that Hines urged lawmakers to double the law’s compliance window from 18 to 36 months, a change that chiefly benefited Tether. Messages it reviewed showed Hines sharing talking points about Republican holdouts with his Nxum partners. After a call from Ardoino, Hines’ father and Nxum co-owner, Todd Hines, wrote: “They want us to obliterate these members that are fighting crypto.”
A Nxum representative told the Journal that Hines wasn’t involved in the Tether deal while in government and “did not receive any Tether-derived funds during that period.”
“Tether is aware of the allegations reported in The Wall Street Journal that form the basis of Senator Blumenthal’s letter,” Tether today said in a statement. “External counsel previously conducted an in-depth internal investigation into the matter, which found no evidence of wrongdoing.”
Blumenthal wrote that the payment structure suggests Tether “was likely well aware of the illegality and impropriety” of paying a sitting official, and that the arrangement “implicates federal ethics, anticorruption, and lobbying laws.” He also asked about a Nxum pitch deck, reported by the Journal , saying Tether would buy a 25% stake in the firm for $56 million.
It’s Blumenthal’s second Tether-linked letter this month. On Oct. 8, he asked Cantor Fitzgerald , Tether’s reserve custodian and a 5% shareholder chaired by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s son, for records on that relationship.
That letter followed a report from his staff finding that most Iran-linked wallets used USDT. Tether responded by citing about $550 million in Iran-linked freezes , including $344 million in April.
Lutnick defended Tether at his confirmation hearing last year, and Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden pressed him in April over a reported Tether loan to a trust for his children.

title: Can Serbia’s student protesters stop Aleksandar Vučić from becoming prime minister? The country’s longtime leader has called an early election to extend his hold on power.
body: An opposition rally in Belgrade. October 22, 2026 Just over a month ago, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić addressed the nation on television. He lamented the difficult circumstances but said that, despite everything, the country had “managed to preserve stability.” To ensure that Serbia could continue “to develop and maintain its internal unity in the face of external threats,” Vučić announced that he would dissolve parliament and call early elections for October 25, 2026. He resigned shortly afterward. Vučić needs the election to stay in power: His presidential term would have expired soon. But he may not succeed. His main rival is the “Student List — Students Win” movement, which formally emerged a month ago but became known around the world during mass protests across Serbia in 2024. We explain why Vučić called the election now, what the main parties are campaigning on, and who is most likely to win. Why Serbia’s election matters Aleksandar Vučić joined the Serbian Radical Party as a young man and became known as an ardent Serbian nationalist. He became prime minister in 2014 and was elected president three years later. With the backing of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), Vučić built a regime that political scientists abroad describe as authoritarian. As early as 2019, the U.S. nonprofit Freedom House downgraded Serbia’s status from free to partly free. That same year, the European Parliament said Vučić and the SNS were blocking parliamentary debate on bills they opposed, accusing their critics of betraying the country, and suppressing independent media. Five years later, Freedom House said the ruling party was undermining political rights and civil liberties and putting pressure on independent media and civil society organizations. In 2024, V-Dem, an independent Swedish research institute that studies democracy worldwide, called Serbia an “electoral autocracy.” This year, the German think tank Bertelsmann Stiftung classified it as a moderate autocracy, citing the concentration of power in Vučić’s hands. Other indicators also show the problems facing Serbian democracy. Between 2014 and 2026, the country fell from 54th to 104th place in the annual press freedom index compiled by the international organization Reporters Without Borders. Transparency International ranked Serbia 78th in its Corruption Perceptions Index in 2014 and 116th in 2025. A survey conducted last year by Transparency Serbia found that 22% of respondents considered corruption the country’s biggest problem — the highest share in a quarter century. All this makes the coming election especially consequential. It will determine whether Serbia continues on the authoritarian course it has followed over the past decade and a half under Vučić and the SNS, or gets a chance to democratize if the Student List, the main opposition group, wins. How the electoral system works Serbia is a parliamentary republic. Parliament, officially known as the National Assembly, elects the government and holds it accountable. The constitution limits the president’s powers: He commands the armed forces, signs laws, and nominates a prime minister for parliament’s approval. He can also dissolve the Assembly — for example, if it fails to approve a government within 90 days. But the president cannot dismiss the government or hold other positions while in office. Vučić disregarded the latter rule: From his first election as president until May 2023, he also led the ruling party. The Assembly has a single chamber with 250 members. Under the constitution, elections are held every four years, but early elections have effectively become the norm since 2000. Only the 2012 and 2020 elections took place on schedule. Voters cast ballots for party lists; there are no single-member districts. Parties must clear a 3% threshold to enter parliament, but this requirement does not apply to ethnic minority parties. The current Assembly includes parties representing Hungarians, Bosniaks, Croats, Albanians, and even Russians. If the ruling party or coalition needs a few more votes to secure a parliamentary majority, ethnic minority lawmakers can wield disproportionate influence. The previous parliamentary election, held on December 17, 2023, was marred by serious irregularities, including the so-called Bulgarian train ballot-swapping scheme, busing in voters from Republika Srpska , and vote-buying . These practices helped the SNS win nearly 47% of the vote and a parliamentary majority, while the opposition Serbia Against Violence coalition had to settle for 23.7% and 65 seats. The vote-rigging triggered mass protests, but they had petered out by the end of December 2023. New grievances soon emerged. In July 2024, thousands took to the streets against a project to extract lithium at the Jadar mine in western Serbia. Events in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city, prompted a far larger response. On November 1, 2024, a canopy at the city’s railway station collapsed , killing 16 people, including children. The irony was that renovations at the station had been completed just four months before the disaster. Two Chinese state-owned companies had carried out the work under a contract awarded by the Serbian authorities without competitive bidding. Officials initially denied any responsibility. Pro-government media and Goran Vesić, the construction, transport, and infrastructure minister, repeatedly said that the station canopy had not been part of the renovation. The Transport Ministry refused journalists’ requests for financial documents relating to the work. All this raised suspicions of corruption and sparked large protests in Novi Sad and other cities. Many students joined and became the protests’ main driving force. The largest demonstration, on March 15, 2025, drew up to 325,000 people — an enormous number in a country with a population of just over 6.5 million. In addition to calling for the release of documents relating to the station’s renovation and for increased spending on higher education, protesters demanded the government’s resignation and early elections. The government could hardly ignore the protests. Vesić resigned in November 2024 and was behind bars a few weeks later. He and 12 other officials faced charges , but these were later dropped for lack of evidence. Prime Minister Miloš Vučević resigned in January 2025. Vučić, meanwhile, suggested that unnamed foreign powers were instigating the protests. Pro-government media accused protesters of betraying their country and committing crimes and called for their arrest and lengthy prison sentences. Police treated demonstrators harshly. Participants in a mass demonstration in Belgrade in March 2025 said a sound cannon had been used against them. During protests in Valjevo in August, police beat 25 demonstrators with batons. In Belgrade, police arrested , beat, and humiliated 15 protesters and threatened women with sexual violence. Why did Vučić call the election now? Protesters have been demanding new elections for the past two years, but Vučić did not dissolve parliament to accommodate them. He has his own reasons. His second presidential term was due to expire in May 2027, and Serbia’s constitution bars him from running again. But Vučić does not want to relinquish power. He is well positioned to hold on to it. He has the backing of the SNS, which has come to dominate Serbian politics over the past decade and a half. The party enjoys substantial political advantages through its access to state institutions and directly or indirectly controls all the country’s major television channels . These advantages helped it secure a decisive victory in the 2023 election. On October 25, it hopes to repeat that success and preserve the current regime. Aleksandar Vučić at a rally of his supporters. Belgrade. October 22, 2026 Under these circumstances, Vučić’s calculation is clear: He wants to move from the presidency to the prime minister’s office. That post would give him considerable powers. Under the constitution, the prime minister determines domestic and foreign policy, can introduce bills in parliament, oversees the state administration, appoints and dismisses ministers, and can even initiate the dissolution of parliament. The election date is no accident. First, Vučić has sought to deny the students time to build a stronger political organization. Their movement is not even a party, and it has yet to establish an extensive network of local branches to mobilize voters. Second, the election was scheduled for the earliest date legally possible after parliament’s dissolution: 46 days later. That gives the students as little time as possible to campaign, while Vučić and the SNS have been promoting themselves for months. Serbia will elect a new president in December, and Vučić will try to install a loyalist. One possibility is Ana Brnabić, the Assembly’s speaker and now acting president. She has already proved her loyalty to Vučić: During her years as prime minister, she effectively ceded all real authority to the president. Another candidate is Miloš Vučević, the SNS leader and a close Vučić ally, who ranks second on the party’s electoral list. The main contenders and their platforms A total of 18 parties and coalitions, including those representing ethnic minorities, will contest the October 25 election. But the main battle will be between the Aleksandar Vučić — United Serbia coalition and the opposition Student List. The pro-government camp The dominant party on the government side is the Serbian Progressive Party, founded in 2008 after a split in the Radical Party. The SNS espouses nationalist, conservative, and populist views, while its economic positions lean toward neoliberalism. With around 800,000 members in 2020 — 13% of Serbia’s population — it is Europe’s largest party by membership. It is running as part of the Aleksandar Vučić — United Serbia coalition, but its partners carry little weight. The SNS platform rests on several key tenets. These include defending Serbia’s territorial integrity — meaning refusing to recognize Kosovo’s independence — and supporting Serbs living abroad; steady economic development and efforts to combat corruption; social justice; and joining the EU while cooperating with Russia, the United States, and China. There is one problem with the platform published on the party’s official website, however: It dates from 2011 and has not been updated since. In the current campaign, the ruling party and Vučić are focusing primarily on recent economic successes. Serbia’s GDP has indeed grown steadily in recent years. According to the World Bank , it rose by 3.9% in 2024 and 2% in 2025, while the International Monetary Fund forecasts growth of 3.3% this year. Serbia has also been actively attracting foreign investment, which reached 5.2 billion euros in 2024 and nearly 3.5 billion in 2025. This September, Vučić proudly said Serbia accounted for 62% of all foreign direct investment in the Western Balkans . To sustain growth, the authorities are banking on large projects that can double as publicity opportunities. Work has recently picked up, for example, on the Belgrade metro, a project first launched in the 1990s. Chinese companies are now involved, and Vučić said with great fanfare that two enormous tunnel-boring machines were due to arrive in the capital in October — just in time for the election. For now, however, the spectacle of their arrival has had to be postponed: Technical problems have left the machines stuck in the Romanian port of Constanța. But nothing is stopping the ruling party from constantly talking about Expo 2027, the world’s fair that Belgrade will host. Vučić frequently visits the construction site and says the “historic” exhibition is moving the capital and the country as a whole “forward.” The exhibition was also one of the official reasons given for calling the early election: Vučić said the vote needed to be timed so that afterward the country could focus on preparing for Expo. The authorities also emphasize the need for stability. Serbia went through a turbulent period in the 1990s , and the authorities now use fears of a return to that era to argue that people should vote for the SNS. In their view, the main threat to stability comes, naturally, from the protesting students, who they say receive foreign funding and want to organize a “color revolution” in Serbia. SNS lawmaker Biljana Pantić said the choice in this election was clear : On one side are the SNS and Vučić, who put “care for citizens, stability, and Serbia’s continued development” first; on the other are those “who have no concrete platform or results and have reduced their politics to hatred, violence, and attacks on everything Aleksandar Vučić does or says.” The opposition The students, who form the backbone of the protests, hold a wide range of views, and their ranks include both nationalists and liberals. Nevertheless, they have managed to stay united by avoiding contentious issues such as European integration, relations with Russia, and Kosovo’s independence. On September 9, 2026, the day parliament was dissolved, they announced the formation of their own political movement, Student List — Students Win. In just a few days, the students collected the required number of voter signatures to run in the election and submitted their candidate list to the Electoral Commission, which unanimously approved their inclusion on the ballot on September 15. The list contains 250 parliamentary candidates. None are students; instead, they include scholars, university professors, experts, and athletes. At the top is cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, a professor at the University of Novi Sad, although the students stress that they are not looking for “a new leader around whom another personality cult could form.” The movement’s election platform is called the ” Student Plan ” and consists of 11 points grouped into three sections. The first, “Serbia or the Mafia,” calls for stronger efforts to fight corruption, barring from public office officials who have broken the law and have ties to the mafia, and guaranteeing media freedom. Belgrade. October 21, 2026 The second section, titled “Knowledge Is Power,” calls for adapting the education system to modern needs, introducing competitive selection for teaching positions, and subsidizing startups and innovation. The third section, “Serbia Grows With Us,” addresses social and economic issues. Among other things, it proposes providing housing for young families and essential workers, and improving health care by standardizing medication prices nationwide and modernizing hospitals, particularly in rural areas. The other parties Among the other contenders, two coalitions — Stability Factor and European Serbia — have a chance of clearing the 3% threshold, according to a poll conducted by Serbian market research agency Factor Plus and published on September 21. Stability Factor, led by Ivica Dačić , brings together the Socialist Party and partners such as the Social Democrats and the Greens. The coalition presents itself as an alliance of the patriotic left and intends to work with the SNS and Vučić. It is going through a difficult period, however, facing criticism for cooperating with the regime. On August 31, the Socialist Party expelled its vice president, Branko Ružić, for supporting the protesting students. Two members of its main council and several regional party leaders then left in protest. European Serbia, meanwhile, consists of pro-European parties and has a detailed plan to dismantle the regime built by the SNS within 100 days and begin building a “European Serbia.” The coalition did not join forces with the students but is willing to cooperate with them after the election. How the campaign unfolded Although the official campaign began on September 9, Vučić and the SNS effectively started much earlier. The SNS put its own spin on the student movement’s main slogan, “Students Win!” For several months, enormous billboards reading “Serbia Wins!” could be seen across the country. Government-controlled TV channels heavily promote Vučić. An analysis by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation found that he appeared on various channels 129 times in August — an average of four times a day. He appeared in his capacity as head of state, meaning he did not pay for the airtime. Vučić has used other methods as well. In September 2026, the government set aside money for one-time payments of 160 to 300 euros to pensioners. Vučić also promised to raise public-sector salaries by 8% and social workers’ salaries by 12% — but only starting in December, after the election. The students have no such resources, so they have to rely on social media and direct campaigning. They have set up booths in various Serbian cities where people can talk to candidates and learn about their platform. The students are also going door to door , trying to persuade voters to support the Student List. Meanwhile, opposition supporters face direct pressure and restrictions from the authorities. Universities are firing professors sympathetic to the protesters, while television gives the opposition half as much airtime as pro-government parties and portrays it negatively. CRTA, an independent Serbian election-monitoring organization, says opposition candidates, observers, and activists face surveillance, insults, intimidation, and even physical attacks. Who will win? It is difficult to gauge support ahead of the election: Opinion polls vary widely. According to Factor Plus, 48.7% of voters are prepared to vote for the SNS and its coalition partners, and 37.1% for the Student List. European Serbia, at 3.6%, and the Socialist Party-led coalition, at 4.9%, also cleared the 3% threshold in the poll. But opposition politicians accuse the agency of bias and of working for the SNS, whose support it consistently overstates. On September 30, Đorđe Vukadinović, editor in chief of the independent political science journal Nova srpska politička misao (New Serbian Political Thought), put support for the students at 44.4% and for the pro-government coalition at 41.7%. He did not explain the basis for those estimates. On October 15, political analyst Mirko Dautović suggested that support for the students had risen above 50% over the preceding month, but he too cited no specific poll. Serbia faces a fierce electoral contest, but observers say tensions could persist afterward. First, there is no guarantee that Vučić would willingly step back if he lost — he could declare the results invalid. But that would risk a repeat of Slobodan Milošević’s fate: In the fall of 2000, he too refused to acknowledge defeat, only to be forced to give in after 10 days of mass protests. Belgrade. October 18, 2026 Second, the students are determined and make no secret of the bleak future awaiting Vučić if they win: He will be put on trial. In September, a student-made video appeared online showing Vučić in various settings, followed by a figure mopping a prison floor. The video achieved its aim — it infuriated the Serbian authorities. Even setting Vučić’s fate aside, a student victory would leave the movement facing the question of what to do next. Once their common opponent is gone, their disagreements over Kosovo, European integration, and relations with Russia and China — which they have set aside for now — will surface. Maintaining a consensus will be very difficult. And winning an election alone will not be enough to eradicate corruption. As the example of 2000 shows, democrats coming to power does not necessarily mean a victory for democracy. What the election means for Russians living in Serbia After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Serbia declined to impose sanctions on Russia while also taking in tens of thousands of Russians. By December 2024, the Serbian authorities had issued 67,000 temporary residence permits. Estimates put the number of Russians in Serbia at 55,000 to 62,000 at the end of 2025, with more than 80% living in Belgrade . Most are young: People ages 24 to 39 account for 55%. And 66% of the Russians who have relocated to Serbia have a university education. Temporary residence does not, of course, give Russians the right to vote, but Serbian politics is of little interest to them. A survey by the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy found that 72.8% of Russians who had moved to Serbia did not want to take part in political or civic activities. They were far more concerned about their personal safety and economic well-being. The government’s approach to Russians who have relocated appears unlikely to change if the pro-government coalition wins. The Serbian authorities, for example, have repeatedly said they have no plans to revise the existing visa-free travel agreement with Russia. If the Student List wins, its policy toward Russian emigrants is impossible to predict at this point: The students have carefully avoided commenting on Russia or on Russians who have moved to Serbia. title: Zelensky says Ukraine’s speed restrictions remain on Starlink and its military version, Starshield, despite Trump’s assurances
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed restrictions on Starlink satellite communications terminals and their military version, Starshield, remain in place in Ukraine. He spoke in a video address to the Hudson Institute in Washington, Interfax-Ukraine reported. “The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there. The speed has not been restored. And the delivery of interceptors to protect us against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed. We’re waiting for interceptors that were already agreed on. But they are still not coming. Hope that everything is on the way. And this is a real problem for us, because the Russians attack us almost every day. Russia attacks us massively. So that’s where things stand today,” Zelensky said. He added that this was happening as Ukraine continues its “quite successful operations on the front,” and said the Starlink and Starshield restrictions had complicated the situation. “But our front line is still holding, and we are doing our best to keep our logistics working, and we continue defending ourselves,” he said. On October 14, Ukrainian military personnel reported encountering restrictions on Starlink satellite communications terminals — specifically, their military version, Starshield. The connection cut out when drones exceeded 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour). This came amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump. Two days later, Trump said he had not ordered Starshield service in Ukraine to be restricted and did not know who could have done so. However, The Telegraph , citing four sources, reported that Musk had approached Trump with a proposal to restrict Starlink speeds in Ukraine. The Wall Street Journal later reported that Musk had ordered Starshield service in Ukraine to be restricted. The Wall Street Journal also reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift the restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine. Trump later said Musk had lifted the restrictions. Ukraine’s military Starlink service How Ukraine’s military uses Starlink — and what would happen if the Trump administration cut off its satellite communications entirely Ukrainian troops lost Starlink access for a day. title: Show HN: Audio Splitter – Split long MP3 files at silence in the browser
body:
Split long MP3 recordings by silence — audio processing happens in your browser.
Downloading multiple clips? Your browser may ask once for permission.
The tool scans your file for quiet passages (silence below −40 dB lasting at least one second) and cuts in the middle of each quiet gap. Clips shorter than three seconds are kept together with their neighbors.
In your browser, using the Web Audio API. There is no account and no server-side step for your audio.
To keep every MP3 frame untouched, each clip keeps a few extra frames before its split point — up to about a quarter second. The frames themselves are never re-encoded.

title: Show HN: Translate Human Speech into Birdsong
body:
This site turns human voice into a birdsong!
This site turns human voice into birdsong. It's inspired by windytan's Blackbird experiment
A voice is a stack of harmonics over a fundamental pitch. The converter shifts that fundamental down to near 0 Hz, low-pass filters it to isolate it, and then uses FM demodulation to track its instantaneous frequency. AM demodulation on the same signal gives the amplitude envelope. The original harmonics are thrown away. The output is a freshly synthesized tone six times higher, shaped by the tracked pitch and envelope.
That is why it reproduces melody, rhythm and inflection so well but not words: only F0 and loudness survive, not the formants that make phonemes. Windytan's original ran on a Perl/SoX/csdr pipeline. This version ports the same DSP to an AudioWorklet, with extra pitch, timbre and trill controls.
"Voice range" is the most important value, change it to fit your low and high vocals. The "auto" button will try to guess it from the media file.
Hitting "Randomize" is very fun. You can checkbox which values you want randomized or kept.
The best input is exaggerated spoken word, poetry, or slow song acapellas. Try and make it rhythmic, like a bird song!
The conversion works best with clean vocals and no background noise. But you can try adjusting the Equalizer curve to try and focus audio range.
It can do birds with a clean voice: small singing birds, but also some bigger ones like pigeon, cuckoo, owl. It cannot do ducks' croak or crows' caw, they would need a different approach.

title: Investors are starting to find opportunities in the battered bond market
body:
Even after another bond market rout Friday, investors are turning their attention toward Treasurys, anticipating that yields may be topping out.
The benchmark 10-year note spent the day flirting with the psychologically important 5% level as oil prices surged and a fresh consumer survey showed that inflation expectations remain a good distance above the Federal Reserve's 2% goal.
Still, some market participants see reason for hope in a market bludgeoned this year over worries about rising prices, tensions in the Middle East and stiff competition from artificial intelligence hyperscalers flooding the market with debt.
Bank of America's Michael Hartnett in a client note declared "The Price is Right" on the battered Treasury market, which he noted has seen its worst long-run return in the past 100 years.
The investment strategist noted in his weekly money-flow summary that the "secular contrarian [trade] would be adding bonds," drawing a parallel to similar long-run negative returns for stocks and commodities that later proved to be good entry points
Despite the negative returns and soaring yields this year, investors are putting money into fixed income and government debt in particular.
Treasurys saw $5.4 billion in inflows over the past week, part of $12.1 billion overall into the bond market, according to data compiled by BofA. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, a $47.3 billion fund that offers exposure to long-dated government debt, has seen $1.14 billion in fresh investor cash over the past month.
One reason for investor enthusiasm is the simple belief that the Treasury sell-off has exhausted itself, with the market pricing in the various risks to the market and now at least ready to stabilize.
Thursday's trading saw the 10-year yield crater a massive 19 basis points, or 0.19 percentage point.
Nicholas Colas, co-founder of DataTrek Research, calculated the gain as a "3 standard deviation move," or well outside the expected trading range for the flagship Treasury security for the day. Given current conditions, including another sanguine reading on unemployment claims Thursday, Colas wrote in his daily market note that the trade "catalyst was not a sudden change in the market's view on the U.S. economy."
"Our read is that the Treasury market is taking the equity and corporate debt market's collective angst about AI-related CapEx funding as a sign incremental issuance will slow," he added. "With less of this paper coming to market, Treasuries face less competition for capital."
Historically, stocks and bonds generally move opposite each other. As risk appetite grows, investors generally eschew the safety of bonds, and vice versa.
That hasn't been the trend lately, as Friday's slide in the stock market coincided with an aggressive sell-off in bonds, a trade largely driven by fears of escalating oil prices hitting both asset classes.
However, Colas said history suggests the correlation again will return, making a stocks/bonds mix still "a reasonable approach, recent painful history notwithstanding."
Moreover, he called the Thursday plunge in yields "an important signal."
"The fever of higher rates may not have entirely broken," he said, "but [Thursday] was a solid step in the right direction."

title: Marine sniper veteran visits Ukraine to meet man behind 2,069-meter shot
body: Colby Barrett went to scout sniper school because that’s where his Marines were headed. Years later, that training took him to a front-line unit in northern Ukraine to shoot alongside one of the war’s most accomplished marksmen. Barrett was commissioned through Navy ROTC in 2000 and spent four years leading infantry and scout sniper Marines from 2000 to 2004. When most of his platoon headed to sniper school, he went with them. It was a “pretty unusual” move for a Marine officer, he told Military Times. The Marine Corps has since trained its final scout snipers and moved sniper training into reconnaissance and Raider units under Force Design 2030. After the Marines, Barrett built a business, sold it and started farming. When a friend asked him to join an aid convoy to Ukraine, he had four kids in school and a harvest underway. His first answer was no. That night, he read about pastors killed and churches destroyed by Russian forces. As a Christian, he wondered how he’d missed it. He made the trip, then kept going back. Now, despite declaring that he is “not a filmmaker,” Barrett has produced two series on the war in Ukraine: A Faith Under Siege and Faith in War . Within that series is Safe Ground , the story of a Green Beret who removes landmines in Ukraine . During those trips, Barrett heard about a sniper with the call sign of Lektor , a special forces sniper from the Department of Active Measures with Ukraine’s Defence Intelligence, who, in December 2024, hit a moving Russian soldier at 2,069 meters using a single .338 Lapua Magnum round from a Sako TRG M10. He fired standing in a trench, nearly level with his target, and hit on the first shot. Lektor is still running missions and only reluctantly agreed to press, Barrett said. Soon, however, Barrett’s time with Lektor will become a short documentary. Barrett’s crew spent a morning on the range with his unit testing whether American M118 ammunition could match its costly hand-loaded rounds. Lektor said there was “practically no difference,” so the unit stuck with the M118 it already had. “I was struck by just his humility,” Barrett said. Lektor, a former gamekeeper, waved off the praise. “Honestly, I don’t consider myself a super expert,” he told Barrett’s crew in an interview translated from Ukrainian. “This is my job for the duration of the war.” Before the shot, his team had spent two weeks on the zero line watching for a Russian assault, under orders not to fire. When the situation changed and the team was set to move, Lektor asked for one more chance. “So I simply begged the commander: give us a day or two for free hunting,” he said. He spotted a soldier whose gear set him apart from ordinary infantry. The man was walking a tree line at a steady pace and a workable angle. As Lektor prepared to fire, his partner called a wind correction in the wrong direction. “I managed to shout: recalculate, something’s wrong,” Lektor said. They fixed it in seconds while the target was still moving. Barrett pointed to the longest confirmed .338 Lapua kill — British Cpl. Craig Harrison’s 2,475-meter shot in Afghanistan in 2009 — which came after several sighting rounds. Shots like that, he said, are “really more like competition shooting.” Lektor is skeptical of the rankings for the same reason. “Two shots maximum: if you didn’t hit, that’s it,” he said. “That’s how you should compare.” Within half an hour of the shot, drones were overhead. “The only thing that saved us was that the enemy didn’t expect a shot from such a distance,” Lektor said. The Russians shelled an area about 500 meters out. His team waited a full day in a dugout before slipping out. Now, thermal cameras hunt for heat. “After a shot, a simple suppressor can give you away, because it’s hot, it glows,” Lektor said. Early in the war, Lektor said, the walk to a firing position was about a kilometer. He now walks eight. Barrett asked him whether snipers were even relevant anymore. Lektor admitted the role is “a little outdated” but not finished. “Snipers, in my opinion, are the neurosurgeons,” he said. A sniper team can watch a sector almost continuously, he explained. “Drones have to return to recharge, they get shot down.” Near Bakhmut, Lektor’s team killed a Russian sniper. A neighboring unit then told them he was the fifth one killed at that position. “They have absolutely no regard for the lives of their own men,” Lektor said. Barrett sees Ukraine’s regard for its own people as an advantage, along with its speed in adapting to new technology. Russia, he said, treats the war like a meat grinder: “If I just put so much meat into it, that it breaks the grinder, then we’ll win.” Lektor’s son enlisted first, and the two have served together most of the war. “He’s my child, I have to be there,” Lektor said. Once, while Lektor was hospitalized with wounds, his son was fighting with another team in Chasiv Yar. He was the only one of four men in his group to come out unharmed. On his own team, Lektor keeps one rule. “I [am] the first to go in and the last to come out,” he said. “That’s our unwritten rule.”

title: Scalpers offer Apple iPhone Duo buyers hundreds extra outside Beijing launch
body:
The iPhone Duo has an eye-popping price tag, but initial interest in Apple 's first foldable phone in China appears solid.
On the day of the global launch on Friday, scalpers like Alex Wang stood outside the flagship store in Beijing 's popular shopping area, Sanlitun, offering to pay customers an extra 3,000 Chinese yuan ($448) to buy their newly purchased phones on the spot.
"I feel the Duo can be sold with a higher price for half a month," he told CNBC while watching the lines of Duo customers who had pre-booked their phones. "The main reason is the tight supply."
Though foldables are still a niche product globally, China's market is the single largest, according to Counterpoint Research.
Apple fan Mary Tong, who was first in a line of about 100 people at the Sanlitun store, showed up at 6 a.m. to pick up her foldable device.
"Apple has been the laggard," she said. "I think many Chinese do prefer foldable phones."
Huawei is promoting its own AI assistant XiaoYi to boost the Chinese smartphone maker's competitiveness against Apple and other homegrown rivals. Huawei, which already has a broad lineup of foldable phones, launched a new trifold called the Mate XT2 that is priced at about $3,000 on Sept. 7, two days before Apple's Duo announcement.
China's Xiaomi unveiled its own pricey foldable, the 18 Fold, around the same time.
Even before the Beijing Apple store's regular opening hours, customers without a reservation showed up to test their luck to get their hands on the new phone. Apple had said the Duo would not be available for walk-in purchase on launch day in mainland China and would be "limited" in other countries. Each online purchase was restricted to two phones.
Zhang Zheng said he had tried to order one on the site but was discouraged by the delivery timeline, which stretched to January 2027. He said he still wants to buy one.
"I think it will be useful for work and it's cool to look at," he said.
While there was buzz about the device itself, expectations for Apple Intelligence were negligible. The company said a version of the AI system is set for beta testing this month for the mainland China market and will include features like live translation, Clean Up in photos, and writing tools.
On Oct. 14, Beijing approved Alibaba AI models for use in Duo and other Apple devices as part of the U.S. tech giant's pending AI rollout in the country. Apple received Chinese regulatory clearance over the summer.
Chinese official media cited ex-CEO Tim Cook on a recent China trip as saying Apple's revamped Siri AI would not be available in the country yet.
Duo customer John Zhao said he had tried Apple Intelligence while working overseas, and it was "nice but not beyond imagination." He expects the Chinese version to be less exciting.

title: First three tankers with Russia diesel heading toward Atlantic East Coast — deputy PM
body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia has already dispatched the first three tankers with diesel fuel to the Atlantic East Coast, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said.
"The first three tankers with fuel are already on their way to the Atlantic East Coast, with serious support from the RDIF (Russian Direct Investment Fund - TASS)," he told reporters.
Novak told TASS earlier that Russia is lifting its ban on diesel exports ahead of schedule and is ready to supply 300,000 tons of diesel in October, increasing the volume to 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in December. Monthly supplies could subsequently reach 3 million tons.
He also said that Russia and the United States are completing the process of signing contracts for diesel fuel supplies. The first tanker with 40,000 tons of Russian diesel fuel reportedly sailed off for the United States on October 22.

title: Vercel moved to kill static credentials. Then developers spotted its own deployment token.
body: Vercel wants to eliminate long-lived API keys from its ecosystem, and it is giving Marketplace vendors until January 2027 to comply or risk being delisted, a push that lands as a run of credential-stealing supply chain attacks — including a recent npm worm that scraped tokens straight out of CI pipelines — keeps proving how much damage a single leaked secret can do. Vercel’s own GitHub Actions deployment workflow still relies on the kind of persistent credential the company now wants gone. Developers have already pointed out a complication, though: Vercel’s own GitHub Actions deployment workflow still relies on the kind of persistent credential the company now wants gone. In a Thursday announcement , Vercel CTO Malte Ubl says the company surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported what Vercel considers secure authentication methods, and it is now pushing OpenID Connect (OIDC) and short-lived, identity-based tokens as the alternative to static API keys that can stay valid indefinitely. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch amplifies the message on X, writing that it is “time to kill ‘static credentials’” and arguing that while attacks and breaches can still happen, stolen credentials should behave more like “self-destructing keys” that expire before an attacker can keep using them. Vercel’s deployment double standard Developer and senior software engineer at Fanatics, Yordis Prieto sharpens that point, writing in reply that Vercel had “invented” OIDC federation yet still left him leaning on “a long-lived access token” in his CI pipeline, and he presses the company to drop the token requirement from GitHub CI while criticizing its non-expiring token option. Vercel’s GitHub Actions deployment guide still instructs developers to authenticate deployments with a VERCEL_TOKEN secret, and in Thursday’s announcement Ubl says the company is extending OIDC support across its API and CLI to retire long-lived tokens from deployment workflows, which for now leaves Vercel asking Marketplace vendors to adopt a standard its own deployment tooling has not fully implemented. By November 30, Marketplace integrations that fall short of Vercel’s authentication requirements will carry a “Not secure” warning on their listing, and the company has not published its survey methodology, named the companies it surveyed, or disclosed how many existing Marketplace partners will have to change their authentication systems. Short-lived tokens for agents As AI agents gain access to more external services, credential management is becoming a greater consideration for agent harnesses. One way to reduce the risks of persistent access keys is to use short-lived, just-in-time credentials that expire rather than leaving agents with ongoing access. As AI agents gain access to more external services, credential management is becoming a greater consideration for agent harnesses. Vercel’s Connect service addresses part of that problem by letting applications and agents request scoped credentials at runtime using their deployment identity rather than storing secrets in application environments. Connect also handles token exchange and renewal. An October 15 update added enterprise-managed authorization in public beta, allowing administrators to control access to supported services through identity providers such as Okta. Connect still allows static keys Even so, Vercel Connect still supports static API keys for providers that lack OAuth or another identity-based option, and its documentation describes storing those credentials centrally and pulling them at runtime, while the underlying keys can still live indefinitely. The company also introduced GitHub OIDC authentication for its Container Registry in late September, though that work does nothing to remove the VERCEL_TOKEN requirement from its documented GitHub Actions deployment flow. OIDC across Vercel’s own tooling For now, Vercel faces the same job it is handing its Marketplace vendors: replacing long-lived credentials across infrastructure it already runs, and until OIDC support reaches workflows like GitHub Actions deployments, developers will keep needing the very tokens Vercel is urging the rest of the industry to give up. …until OIDC support reaches workflows like GitHub Actions deployments, developers will keep needing the very tokens Vercel is urging the rest of the industry to give up.
