title: Kazakh Director Daulet Zhumabayev on New Film Kesu and Pursuing a Career in Hollywood
body: Kazakh director Daulet Zhumabayev hopes to bring his new action film, Kesu , featuring South Korean actors, to South Korean theaters. The film was released in Kazakhstan on October 15. It follows a Kazakh taekwondo practitioner and a South Korean champion as they travel to Seoul in search of their missing mentor. The film is Zhumabayev’s second feature, following the sports drama Arlan: The Final Round . Zhumabayev focuses on mainstream genre films and sees international collaboration as an opportunity to reach audiences beyond Kazakhstan. His debut feature became available on Amazon Prime Video, although he does not consider a streaming release equivalent to breaking into the American market. In an interview with The Times of Central Asia , Zhumabayev discussed working with South Korean actors, the prospects for international film production, his experience studying abroad, and why Kazakhstan may find it difficult to replicate Korean cinema’s success in Hollywood. TCA: Your new film, Kesu , features both Kazakh and South Korean actors. Did you have to change your directing approach when working with an international cast? Daulet Zhumabayev: No, I worked with everyone the same way. I don’t really have a fully developed directing system yet. I have my own methods for trying to communicate to actors what I want to achieve. I’ve taken some things from Judith Weston’s book Directing Actors , others from the Stanislavski method, and still others I’ve come up with intuitively. I gave both groups of actors the same kind of direction, and everyone understood perfectly well what I wanted from them. TCA: How did you build relationships between the Kazakh and Korean members of the film crew? Zhumabayev: That’s very important. And I’m extremely grateful to our lead actor, Asylkhan Tolepov, for the way he supported his Korean co-star, Ben (Joo Woo Geon). From the very beginning, we tried to create a particular atmosphere. When the Korean actors arrived in Kazakhstan, we didn’t just put them up in a hotel and provide meals. We welcomed them as real guests. We took them to Shymbulak, treated them to beshbarmak, and introduced them to our traditions. We wanted them to experience Kazakh hospitality and never feel like outsiders here, not even for a second. That immediately set the tone for our relationship. They could see that we treated them warmly and sincerely, that we cared not only about getting good performances from them but also about making their stay in Kazakhstan comfortable. And I think that probably motivated them to give their best on set as well. TCA: Did you make any allowances for the foreign actors during filming? Zhumabayev: None whatsoever. I expected complete dedication from them. They trained in the gym, learned Kazakh, and prepared for difficult scenes. We treated them as guests, but we worked as one team, with everyone having their own responsibilities. They’re very respectful and attentive. After filming ended, they all sent me warm messages thanking me for working together. They said they’d felt comfortable working with me and had learned a lot themselves. As a director, that was very gratifying. TCA: Were the Korean actors paid more? Zhumabayev: I wouldn’t want to divide actors by nationality or compare their fees. I’ll just say that we didn’t invite the most famous Korean performers. If we’d decided to cast stars from popular Korean dramas with huge audiences, the budget would have been completely different. We had some money, of course, but nowhere near enough to afford Korean superstars. TCA: Did you notice any cultural differences when communicating with the Korean actors? Zhumabayev: Of course there were differences, and it took the Koreans some time to get used to the way we communicate. Ben, for example, is a very sensitive, delicate person. But Asylkhan and I have a slightly different way of interacting. We’re constantly teasing each other, joking around. We might walk up to someone, slap them on the shoulder, and say something in our usual rough-and-ready, guy-to-guy manner. At first, Ben felt a little uncomfortable. He didn’t always understand that we were just joking and that it was completely good-natured. But eventually he got used to it, settled in, and communication became much easier. TCA: Did you notice anything distinctive about the South Korean school of acting? Zhumabayev: Before filming Kesu , I watched a lot of Korean movies. But honestly, I’m not enough of an expert on Korean cinema to analyze the characteristics of their acting tradition and offer you any observations right now. For me, an actor’s nationality or citizenship doesn’t matter. What matters is how convincing they are in a particular role. And I was very impressed with our Korean actors, especially Jang Hae-Jun, who plays Son. I liked him immediately. He has a very interesting appearance, a distinctive physical presence. Then he came onto the set, and in his very first scene, he gave this incredibly deep, piercing look. As a director, I was astonished. I immediately realized what a strong actor he was. It turned out he had serious theater training. Jang Hae-Jun graduated from a very prestigious theater school in South Korea, something on the level of Juilliard in New York. Although he’s better known in Korea as a stage actor and appears in films relatively rarely, he was incredibly easy to work with. He understood my direction precisely and immediately grasped what needed to be done. I think all my actors, both Korean and Kazakh, did an excellent job in their roles. TCA: When will Kesu be released in South Korea? Zhumabayev: We’re going to have a proper theatrical release in South Korea, but it’s difficult to say yet how wide it will be. That depends on the distributor. We might get a wide release, or it might be more limited. But I’ve already shown the film to representatives of the Korean film industry. We have preliminary agreements, and they like the film. It’s generating interest. In a couple of weeks, I’m planning to fly to Seoul, where distributors are waiting to watch the film and discuss the terms of its release. TCA: What are the prospects for cooperation between Kazakhstan and South Korea in filmmaking? Zhumabayev: I think the prospects are very good. South Korean filmmakers have already started coming to Kazakhstan quite actively. Of course, we need to distinguish between co-productions and Korean films that simply happen to be shot in Kazakhstan. Those are different things. For example, director Ruslan Pak shot a Korean project in Kazakhstan. It was his second film made in cooperation with South Korea. But this time, the entire production was Korean; filming simply took place in Kazakhstan. Other Korean film crews have also come to Kazakhstan for various projects. These are fully foreign productions. They bring their crews and equipment and organize shoots here. TCA: What attracts South Korean filmmakers to Kazakhstan? Zhumabayev: First and foremost, the scenery. You can’t imagine how interesting Kazakhstan has become to foreigners, including Koreans. They had a very popular show in which a guy traveled around our country. If I’m not mistaken, it’s called I Live Alone . There were two episodes devoted to traveling around Kazakhstan, showing attractions in Almaty – Shymbulak, Kok-Tobe, the Green Bazaar – and places nearby, such as the Kolsai Lakes. When the Korean actors arrived in Kazakhstan, they immediately started asking, “Can we go to Kolsai? Are we going to Kolsai?” They wanted to see it with their own eyes. And they knew about more than just Kolsai; they were familiar with other attractions too. Kazakhstan turned out to be a very appealing destination for them. TCA: You studied in Switzerland and the United States. Would you like to work in Hollywood? Zhumabayev: Yes, that’s my goal. And it’s entirely possible. I’m very inspired, for example, by two Belgian directors of Arab descent who work as a duo: Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah. They made Black (2015), a modern interpretation of Romeo and Juliet . But instead of medieval Verona, the story takes place in disadvantaged neighborhoods of Brussels. Instead of the feuding Montagues and Capulets, there are two street gangs, one Moroccan and one Congolese. A young man and woman from different gangs fall in love and find themselves on opposite sides of a criminal conflict. The film attracted attention at international festivals, and the directors were subsequently invited to work in America. They started with television projects and then got the opportunity to direct major Hollywood films, including Bad Boys for Life . For me, that’s a very interesting example of how directors from Europe managed to break into Hollywood and establish themselves there. TCA: Are you primarily interested in mainstream, commercial cinema? Zhumabayev: Yes, I’m talking about mainstream cinema. I can’t really discuss auteur filmmaking from the perspective of someone who makes those kinds of films himself. I don’t even know whether I’d be capable of making a film like that. And to be honest, it doesn’t interest me all that much. Of course, I watch the classics: Kurosawa, Bergman, Hitchcock, and other great directors. I have to know their films because I’m a director myself. But I don’t particularly want to immerse myself in, say, Estonian cinema of the 1960s. I’m drawn to a different kind of cinema: audience-oriented, genre-driven films that can engage a broad public. TCA: Which directors do you feel particularly close to? Zhumabayev: Probably David Ayer. He directed Fury with Brad Pitt and Street Kings with Keanu Reeves. I really connect with the way he handles genre, characters, and storytelling. And my all-time favorite film is Gus Van Sant’s Good Will Hunting . A wonderful movie. TCA: Your debut film, Arlan , became available on Amazon Prime Video. Can that be considered a breakthrough into the American market? Zhumabayev: Yes, Arlan was released on Amazon Prime Video. Other Kazakh films had appeared there before it. But I wouldn’t overestimate the significance of simply getting a film onto a streaming platform. Being on Amazon doesn’t mean you’ve conquered the American market. There’s an enormous gap between having a film available on a platform and achieving real success with audiences. TCA: What would it take for a Kazakh film to appeal to mainstream American audiences? Zhumabayev: I think it’s possible if you make stories about America. If we’re talking about the mainstream American market, of course. But to make a good film for Americans, you need to understand American audiences: their culture, interests, and habits. And you need to tell stories they can relate to. TCA: So American audiences aren’t interested in Kazakh stories? Zhumabayev: No. Just as they’re not particularly interested in French or Belgian stories, or stories from anywhere else. You have to understand how focused American audiences are on their own country. Let me give you an example. Remember the war in Georgia in 2008? In English, Georgia is both the name of a country and the name of an American state. Now imagine an American from the state of Georgia seeing a news report: “There is a war in Georgia.” He goes outside, looks around, and says, “I go outside, there is no war outside. What the hell is going on?” The guy doesn’t even realize they’re talking about another country! Of course, that’s an exaggerated example, but it illustrates how difficult it is for foreign cinema to break through to mainstream American audiences. TCA: But South Korea’s Parasite won Oscars in 2020 for both Best International Feature Film and Best Picture. Doesn’t that demonstrate that a distinctly national story can succeed on the global market? Zhumabayev: Of course it does. But let’s look at how long it took the Korean film industry to achieve that success. When did the Korean Wave begin? Back in the 1990s. How many films have been made since then? How many wonderful directors have emerged? Park Chan-wook, Bong Joon-ho, and many others. And it wasn’t until 2020 that Parasite won the top Oscar. In other words, that success was built on decades of development across an entire industry. You can’t just make one good film and expect Hollywood to immediately open its doors to you. Besides, by the time Parasite triumphed, Korean pop culture had already conquered America. People were listening to BTS and watching Korean dramas. TCA: But even after Korean culture’s success abroad, stereotypes about other countries persist. For example, is Kazakhstan still associated with Borat ? Zhumabayev: Exactly. If we’re talking about mainstream American audiences, we have to understand how difficult it is to change their perceptions of another country. How many years have we been fighting the image of Kazakhstan created by Borat ? We fought and fought, and then Sacha Baron Cohen released another promotional video for his new film, appearing as Borat again. And that’s it. America once again remembers Kazakhstan in exactly that way. TCA: Were you personally hurt by jokes about Kazakhstan after Borat came out? Zhumabayev: Of course I was. I happened to be in America when Borat was at the height of its popularity, and it was very unpleasant. I remember there would come a moment in class when everyone had to introduce themselves, say their name and where they were from. And I’d already be feeling tense because I knew that as soon as I said “Kazakhstan,” someone would inevitably chuckle. Things were different at school in Switzerland. There were about twenty of us from Kazakhstan studying there, and nobody really dared to make jokes about us. But at the American university, I was the only Kazakh student in my group. And every time, I had to go through that awkward experience. I never hid where I came from. I never said I was from another country. I’m proud to be Kazakhstani. But even so, I’d tense up inside whenever I had to say the word “Kazakhstan.” TCA: How old were you at the time? Zhumabayev: About twenty. At that age, you take these things especially hard. TCA: Did that experience change your desire to work in the U.S.? Zhumabayev: No. Back then, I wasn’t even thinking about becoming a director. Now I believe that breaking into the American market is difficult, but possible. Take our own Aisultan Seitov, who has directed music videos for American stars like J. Cole and 21 Savage, and now has a new project with A$AP Rocky. I think he has excellent prospects of establishing himself in Hollywood in the future, perhaps getting a television series or another major project. TCA: Apart from the Belgian duo, are there other examples of directors who have successfully moved from their national film industries into Hollywood? Zhumabayev: Yes, I believe that path is possible for me. But that’s not the only example. Take Russian director Ilya Naishuller. He started out as a musician, made a famous music video, and then made his feature debut with Hardcore Henry , a film shot almost entirely from a first-person perspective. After that, he started working in Hollywood. He directed Nobody with Bob Odenkirk – a great film, by the way. Last year, his action comedy Heads of State , starring Idris Elba and John Cena, came out. That’s already a major American project for Amazon. There’s another example of a director who managed to break into the international market. I find his career fascinating to follow. TCA: Kazakhstan is also hosting international productions involving major stars. Filming recently wrapped on a project involving Jackie Chan. How important is that for the local film industry? Zhumabayev: Yes, I think that’s a major precedent. Our guys managed to reach him and negotiate a collaboration. From what I’ve heard, the negotiations went on for several years, almost three years. Can you imagine how much effort it took to establish contact and turn it into an actual project? I have enormous respect for them. Jackie Chan is a legend! There’s a wonderful expression in English: larger than life . Someone who has long since transcended the boundaries of his own profession. And the very fact that Kazakh filmmakers managed to reach an agreement with him is already a huge step. I hope that one day I’ll also get to make films with major stars that audiences around the world will find interesting.

title: Iran threatens to sever Gulf internet cables in retaliation if US, Israel renew attacks
body: Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections."If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.The official warned Washington not to "play with fire," and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited, as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.Iran expects war to resume soonThe plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's ​leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centers and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region."Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.Cable cuts could slow down internet, disrupt global networksMultiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic traveling between regions, Mauldin said.Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

title: TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 roundtables: Go deeper on the challenges founders are solving right now
body:
TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 is coming to SoWa Power Station in Boston on November 4, bringing founders, investors, and operators together for a full day of candid conversations, practical sessions, live pitching, networking, and smaller roundtables built for deeper discussion.
The roundtables are where attendees can get especially specific. Bring your questions, share what you are seeing in your own company, and join experts and fellow founders tackling many of the same challenges, from enterprise sales and vertical strategy to AI, lean teams, and building a category that does not exist yet.
Save 25% on your ticket today , and bring a colleague along for free with our limited BOGO deal .
Alexandra Ames , founder and chief event strategist at Blueprint Lab , looks at how early-stage companies can use events strategically before they have the budget or headcount for a dedicated events team. Expect a practical conversation about choosing the right opportunities, defining what success looks like, and making limited resources work harder.
Chirag Shah , partner at Define Ventures , explores what happens when the market with the biggest potential is also one of the hardest to enter. Founders navigating regulated industries, complex buyers, or specialized customers can compare notes on making that first major vertical bet.
Shishir Tewari , head of enterprise data engineering at Procore Technologies , gets into one of enterprise AI’s most persistent challenges: trust. The discussion will examine how knowledge graphs and GraphRAG can give AI systems stronger context and help founders build products that work more reliably in real-world organizations.
Merve Kitapci , managing partner and CGO of ADIN.AI , breaks down what it takes to win major enterprise customers early. From long buying cycles and multiple stakeholders to the credibility that comes with landing the right logo, this is a tactical conversation for founders selling into large organizations before they have a large sales team behind them.
Andy Tang , partner at Draper Associates , leads a conversation for founders building something that does not fit neatly into an existing category. How do you explain it, sell it, and get investors to understand the opportunity when the market still needs vocabulary for what you are creating?
Linden Tibbets , CEO and founder of IFTTT , explores how smaller teams can use AI to increase their speed and output without simply adding headcount. For founders thinking about hiring, efficiency, and how to structure an AI-enabled company, the discussion gets directly into what lean teams may be able to do differently now.
The value of these sessions is not just hearing how someone else approached a problem. It is the chance to ask the question that matters to your company, compare experiences with the people around the table, and leave with ideas you can put to work.
And the roundtables are only one part of the day. Across the Build and Impact Stages, Founder Summit will also tackle product-market fit, hiring, founder leadership, fundraising, pitching, and what it takes to build and scale companies outside the Bay Area.
Attendees can hear founder perspectives from leaders , such as Toast co-founder Steve Fredette, then see founders put their stories to the test during the live “So You Think You Can Pitch?” competition. A Networking Lounge with Braindate and a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares create additional time to connect throughout the day.

The United States’ National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has developed a revolutionary new battery that could power the country’s return to the moon while potentially also revolutionizing the way that we power electric vehicles here on Earth. The new technology can function at extremely cold temperatures, opening new possibilities for powering lunar rovers and tools, and could eventually make batteries for terrestrial applications safer, more versatile, and more efficient.
“The technology could eventually power lunar rovers, scientific instruments, and emergency equipment used by astronauts under NASA’s Artemis program,” states a recent report from Interesting Engineering. “However, the batteries remain small laboratory prototypes and have not yet been demonstrated in space,” the article goes on to note.
During thermal vacuum testing conducted as part of NASA’s Solid Power for Extreme Environment Adaptability and Resilience in Space (SPEARS) project , the new ‘freeze-proof’ solid-state battery has successfully endured temperatures as low as 274 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 170 degrees Celsius). In addition to surviving these superlow temperatures without damage, the prototype batteries proved operational (although at a reduced performance level) in temperatures as low as 112 degrees Fahrenheit below zero minus 80 degrees Celsius), with more optimal levels of performance in the extremely impressive range of negative 76 to positive 176 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 60 to 80 degrees Celsius).
These findings are a big win for the SPEARS project, which is charged with developing batteries that can survive the extremely harsh lunar environment without a constant source of heat to keep them from freezing and thereby becoming damaged. On the South Pole of the moon, where the United States aims to go, temperatures can drop as low as 328 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 200 degrees Celsius).
Traditional lithium-ion battery models are no match for such harsh conditions. Typically, lithium-ion batteries pass lithium ions from electrode to electrode through liquid electrolytes. Solid-state batteries are therefore a far more promising technology for extreme cold, as they don’t carry the same risk of freezing in the cold and performing poorly in the heat.
Plus, the liquid electrolytes used in typical lithium-ion batteries are highly flammable and are becoming an increasingly serious fire hazard around the world. “Plain and simple, solid electrolytes provide a safer and more stable environment for lithium ions to move through, enabling faster charging,” Popular Mechanics wrote late last year in an article about emerging electric vehicle (EV) battery technologies.
While the EV industry doesn’t need batteries that can withstand temperatures in the hundreds of degrees below zero (at least not until Elon Musk colonizes Mars ), NASA’s incredible breakthroughs in solid-state battery technologies could provide critical science and technology to the sector. The SPEARS project’s findings “could eventually translate into commercial terrestrial applications,” according to recent reporting from HotHardware. “Space-rated solid-state tech could very well enhance the safety, temperature tolerance, and efficiency of Earth-bound electronics, including EVs, commercial drones, cell phones, and grid-scale energy storage systems operating in extreme climates. For EVs specifically, this battery breakthrough could, in theory, lead to longer ranges in colder climates and/or during frigid winter months.”
Moreover, SPEARS is not the only project bringing together NASA’s astronautic aims with the country’s broader energy development goals. NASA has also partnered with the United States Department of Energy to develop next-generation nuclear energy technologies to power a new era of deep space exploration. “We are entering the ‘Nuclear NASA-era,’ which represents a major transformation for space exploration,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said earlier this month . “Nuclear power will allow us to go farther, operate longer, and field more capable spacecraft and instruments than ever before. The work we’re doing today is laying the foundation for the fission-powered spacecraft of tomorrow and opening an entirely new frontier for exploration and discovery.”

title: Show HN: Fine-tune an embedding model on your own search logs
body:
Embedding projects are live on ReOpenly: fine-tune an embedding model on your own data, and we host it for you to call with the OpenAI SDK. Tuning helps search find the right passage: Google Cloud measured up to 41% better search results (12% on average) on public tests, and NVIDIA found 10% more right passages in the top 10 on its own docs. In RAG, better search means a better answer, because the model only sees what search finds.
Does your app search a big database, or run RAG, and the results are still bad? Your embedding model may be too generic: it finds passages that look similar to the question, not the ones that answer it. Your own searches know the difference, and an embedding project turns them into training data.
New accounts start with a free balance . Before you train anything:
Train only after you have reviewed some searches. Before you switch, compare the tuned model with the base model on searches you kept aside for testing.
The same three steps, and that comparison, run from code in the ReOpenly cookbook : one Python script and one command each, and a notebook with all four. It uses the public base model, embedding requests are billed like any API call, and nothing in it starts training.
You pick the type when you create the project, and it never changes. An embedding project has:
Most RAG setups start on a general model: OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small or -large through an API, or an open model such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (207 million downloads on Hugging Face in the last 30 days), bge-m3 or nomic-embed-text. Two things set an embedding project apart:
Qwen3-Embedding-4B (an embedding project base)
Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (an embedding project base)
These are the base models' public MTEB results, run by their makers with the benchmark's open code; we recomputed them from its public results on October 19, 2026. They are not our measurement. We serve both Qwen3 bases with up to 512 tokens per input, and what a tuned model gains on your data is yours to measure.
Import them. Upload a CSV or JSONL file with anchor (the question), positive (a passage that answers it) and optional negative (a near miss) columns. Check how the columns map, and confirm. The rows are added in the background.
Save them while you test. In the Playground's Search, build an index from a dataset, run a search, and save a result you mark as a training pair.
Collect them from real searches. After your app ranks its results, your server sends the query and the results it showed (up to 20, in order) to the dataset's Search feedback endpoint. ReOpenly stores that text, no vectors. It never connects to your index and never charges for reporting. Each search waits in an inbox. Mark the results that answer the query as Positive, and the highest-ranked result you did not keep becomes the hard negative: the near miss. One click adds that training example to your dataset, tagged retrieval_feedback . Nothing becomes training data until you review it, and a score never picks a label.
Why your own searches? An embedding call only holds text, not which result answered the query. Your users' searches, and the results that really helped, are the best training data for a search model.
Start a run on a dataset, or on a tag such as retrieval_feedback . About a tenth of the examples are kept aside to check the training, in whole groups that share no text with the rest, so the model never trains on them. You choose the settings within the limits the project shows: the batch size (the rest of a batch counts as wrong answers, so a bigger batch is a harder lesson), the learning rate, an instruction put before every query, the vector size, the longest input, and more.
Before you start, you see the split and the most the run can cost. You pay only for GPU training time, so a run that never starts training is free. The run keeps the version of the model (a checkpoint) that did best on the examples kept aside. That score picks the version; it does not measure how well the model searches, so compare models in the Playground before you switch.
When the run succeeds, host the model under a name you choose. It answers the OpenAI embeddings API at your project's base URL, so to switch you change the base_url and the model name:
from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="https://reopenly.com/api/projects/<owner>/<project>/openai/v1", api_key="<your key>") vectors = client.embeddings.create( model="docs-retriever", input=["How long do refunds take to arrive?"], extra_body={"input_type": "query"}, )
Send input_type query for questions and document for passages. Then embed your documents again with the new model, because vectors from different models cannot be compared. You can also download the trained adapter (the small add-on the training produced), with a checksum for every file.
These are other teams' results on their own data, not ReOpenly's. Each tuned an embedding model on examples from its field and measured search quality before and after.
text embedding models, public retrieval benchmarks
a 1B embedding model on its own documentation
Recall@10 0.630 â 0.693 (+10.0%); NDCG@10 +10.9%
gte-large on FinanceBench, trained on queries an LLM wrote from the documents
Recall@10: the share of the right passages found in the top 10 (Recall@60: the top 60). NDCG@10 also counts its rank.
Your gain will depend on your data, your queries and your base model. Databricks says so too: on two other datasets its gains were small or none, because "finetuning works best when retrieval is a clear bottleneck".
free; up to 20 results per search, 60 requests a minute per dataset
billed as embedding requests, like the API
you pay only for GPU training time; you see the most it can cost before you start
up to 512 tokens per input (a model trained on longer inputs accepts up to its training length, at most 2,048); up to 64 inputs and 32,768 tokens per request
reported searches are kept until you ask us to erase them; you can edit or delete your training pairs
A fine-tuned model is not always better on every query. Start with the base model, collect real searches, and compare the two on searches you kept aside before you switch.
Create an account : new accounts start with a free balance. The quickstart for embeddings shows a whole project from the API. Search feedback lists every field and limit, and Dataset imports lists the file formats.
Which search in your product would you train first?

title: UK-France deepen nuclear defence ties in first joint exercise
body:
For the first time, RAF Typhoon fighters have taken part in a French nuclear air exercise, flying alongside French Rafale in a show of allied strength.
Exercise “Rummy” marks a major step forward in UK-France defence cooperation under the Northwood Declaration.
This partnership is vital to protecting the UK and deterring threats in an increasingly complex security environment.
The UK’s defences are being strengthened as RAF Typhoon fighters join French Rafale jets in a French nuclear exercise for the first time.
Exercise “Rummy” saw British and French forces operate side by side over the Mediterranean, demonstrating the readiness and capability that help deter threats and keep the UK safe.
Launching from Saint-Dizier Air Base in France, French Rafale simulated a nuclear strike mission, escorted by RAF Typhoons.
Conducted under robust safety and security arrangements, the exercise did not involve nuclear weapons. The exercise focused on improving how our forces work together, ensuring that if the UK faces a serious threat, our military can respond quickly and effectively alongside our closest European ally.
This exercise shows the UK’s commitment to standing united against any threat, strengthening deterrence and protecting peace and security alongside European Allies to protect national security. As close NATO Allies and European nuclear powers, the UK and France play a vital role in the security of the Euro-Atlantic region.
The exercise complements the work the UK is doing to invest £63 billion over the next four years to strengthen the UK’s nuclear deterrent, funding Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS submarines, a new warhead and other vital nuclear work. The UK will also buy 12 F-35A aircraft and join NATO’s nuclear mission, delivering a more European NATO and reinforcing the UK’s contribution to collective defence.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said:
This exercise marks a new chapter in the defence nuclear relationship between the United Kingdom and France.
As Europe’s nuclear powers, we have a shared responsibility to contribute to the security and stability of the Euro-Atlantic region. This exercise demonstrates the depth of our partnership, the credibility of our deterrents and our determination to stand together in the face of emerging threats.
In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt: the UK and France remain united in our commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations.
Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans Catherine Vautrin said:
Having independent nuclear forces does not exclude coordination. Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom keeps deepening: on Tuesday night, UK Typhoons participated for the very first time to a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafales.
Through coordination, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the Alliance and to the peace and stability of the Euro Atlantic area.
Exercise “Rummy” represents a key milestone in the UK-France nuclear partnership and the programme of cooperation agreed under the Northwood Declaration.
Demonstrating the commitment of both nations to jointly deter common threats, the exercise showcases the depth of their bilateral nuclear defence relationship and proves that British and French forces are ready and able to operate together to protect shared interests and contribute to collective security in a period of heightened global instability.
The UK and France are close defence allies, underpinned by the refreshed Lancaster House Agreement between our two nations, expanding our joint deployable force, boosting our nuclear cooperation and developing the next generation of high-tech weapons.
Notes to Editors:
Operation Rummy took place from 20-21 October 2026.
Both the UK and France and retain sovereign, independent nuclear forces and national decision making.

title: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
body:
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that aims to reduce mortgage costs as rising interest rates and inflation make homeownership less affordable .
The order , titled "Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People," directs federal agencies to proactively cancel mortgage insurance on eligible future loans and expand a program to make refinancing cheaper, among other actions.
In an X post on Thursday , Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Pulte said "millions of Americans will save thousands and thousands of dollars."
But it's difficult to know the future consumer impact without more details, according to Keith Gumbinger, vice president of mortgage website HSH.
Trump's executive order comes less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections , with rising costs and housing affordability a major concern among voters. It builds on previous orders to restrict Wall Street firms from buying single-family homes, among other actions.
Homeownership has become less affordable in recent years. In 2025, the monthly payment for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage on a median-priced home was roughly 33% of the median family's income, up from 26% in 2022, according to the Federal Reserve's latest Survey of Consumer Finances published in early October.
Whether you're a current homeowner or future buyer, here are some of the key things to know about the new executive order.
Conventional loans — mortgages not insured or backed by U.S. government programs — typically require private mortgage insurance, or PMI, when a down payment is less than 20% of the home's purchase price. By contrast, Federal Housing Administration mortgages require mortgage insurance on all loans.
Trump's executive order directs the FHFA to create a pilot program that cancels eligible borrowers' mortgage insurance "proactively" once their home equity reaches a certain threshold, according to the White House. This would apply to mortgages originated after the pilot program launches.
Currently, conventional loan borrowers can generally remove PMI once their loan balance is below 80% of the purchase price or once they have reached 20% equity, according to Fannie Mae. Once your balance reaches 80% of the original value, you can ask your loan servicer if you're eligible to remove PMI, or they may remove it automatically when your balance reaches 78% of the original value.
In a statement Thursday , Seth Appleton, president of U.S. mortgage insurers, an industry trade organization, said: "We commend the President's focus on lowering costs for future homeowners, and the private mortgage insurance industry is proud to already be delivering on that goal."
Typically, the cost of PMI can be 0.2% to 2% of the loan annually , but varies based on your down payment size, credit score, amount borrowed and other factors, according to Fannie Mae.
For example, if you purchased a $600,000 home with a 10% down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 7.3%, your monthly mortgage insurance could be $351, according to a private mortgage calculator from Freddie Mac.
"Most mortgages ... are carrying PMI at this point in time, especially with the way home prices have been and down payments being as small as they've been in recent years," Gumbinger said.
During the second quarter of 2026, the median home down payment was 13.7% of the home's purchase price, or $27,100, according to a September report from Realtor.com.
Trump's executive order also aims to reduce mortgage refinancing costs by making permanent the FHFA's pilot program that waives the lender's title insurance policy and allows "cost-friendly alternatives," according to the White House.
"I don't know that it's necessarily a game-changer in terms of the cost of housing, which is dictated by home price and mortgage rates at the moment," Gumbinger said. "But you know, every little bit certainly helps."
As of Oct. 23, mortgage interest rates for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages were 7.32%, according to Freddie Mac, and refinance demand was down 59% in mid-October, compared with the same week the previous year.
Originally planned through November 2027, the FHFA pilot was "limited in scope," for refinances with a loan-to-value ratio below 80%, in a handful of states, former FHFA director Sandra Thompson said during a congressional hearing in April 2024.
Thompson estimated that consumers could save $500 to $1,500 in closing costs for loans sold under the pilot program.
Making the program permanent could save borrowers because the lender's title insurance policy, which is usually required for new loans and refinances, "has always been fairly pricey," Gumbinger said.
The lender's fees related to title and title insurance generally make up the largest share of mortgage closing costs , according to a 2025 Urban Institute report.

title: FURTHER MODIFYING THE SCOPE OF PRODUCTS OF CANADA SUBJECT TO THE ADDITIONAL DUTIES IMPOSED TO OFFSET CANADIAN DISCRIMINATION AGAINST THE COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES WITH RESPECT TO MOTOR VEHICLES
body: Presidential Actions Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA A PROCLAMATION 1. In Proclamation 11048 of July 20, 2026 (Imposing Additional Duties To Offset Canadian Discrimination Against the Commerce of the United States With Respect to Motor Vehicles), I found as a fact that Canada is discriminating in fact against the commerce of the United States through Canada’s motor vehicle tariff scheme; that this discrimination places the commerce of the United States at a disadvantage compared to the commerce of other countries; and that Canada’s imposition is unreasonable, is not equally enforced upon the like articles of every foreign country, and places a burden on the commerce of the United States. To offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce from Canada’s discrimination or unreasonable and unequal imposition on U.S. auto and auto parts exports, I imposed under section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1338) (section 338) additional ad valorem duties, effective August 19, 2026, on certain products of Canada. 2. In Proclamation 11056 of August 18, 2026 (Temporary Suspension of Additional Duties To Offset Canadian Discrimination Against the Commerce of the United States With Respect to Alcoholic Beverages, Dairy, and Motor Vehicles), I temporarily suspended for 3 days the effective date of the additional ad valorem duties imposed under Proclamation 11048 after Canada expressed a commitment to remove the discrimination or unreasonable and unequal imposition at issue in Proclamation 11048. 3. On August 21, 2026, Canada reneged on its commitment, ceased negotiating in good faith, and did not remove the discrimination or unreasonable and unequal imposition at issue in Proclamation 11048. 4. Accordingly, at 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 22, 2026, the 3-day suspension imposed by Proclamation 11056 lapsed, and the additional ad valorem duties imposed under Proclamation 11048 became effective. 5. In Proclamation 11065 of September 8, 2026 (Modifying the Scope of Products of Canada Subject to the Additional Duties Imposed To Offset Canadian Discrimination Against the Commerce of the United States With Respect to Motor Vehicles), I modified the duties imposed under Proclamation 11048 after receiving certain information, opinions, and recommendations from senior executive branch officials to continue offsetting the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce and better serve the public interest. 6. I have received certain additional information, opinions, and recommendations from senior executive branch officials on the status of the circumstances involved in Proclamation 11048 and the effect of the additional ad valorem duties imposed in Proclamation 11048, as amended, including how effectively those duties are offsetting the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce. According to senior executive branch officials, although the additional ad valorem duties imposed in Proclamation 11048, as amended, offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, modifying the scope of products subject to the additional ad valorem duties imposed in Proclamation 11048, as amended, would still offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce and better serve the public interest. In my senior executive branch officials’ opinion, modifying the scope of products subject to the additional ad valorem duties imposed in Proclamation 11048, as amended, is required by the public interests and is consistent with the interests of the United States. 7. After considering the information, opinions, and recommendations that have been provided to me by senior executive branch officials, among other relevant information and considerations, I determine that the public interests require modifying the scope of products subject to the additional ad valorem duties imposed in Proclamation 11048, as amended. 8. In my judgment, the modification in this proclamation will offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, is consistent with the public interests and the interests of the United States, is required by the public interests, and will better serve the public interest. 9. Section 338 authorizes the President, if he determines it will serve the public interest, to offset any burden or disadvantage placed on the commerce of the United States by an unequal imposition or discrimination by a foreign country by specifying and declaring additional duties not to exceed 50 percent ad valorem (or its equivalent) and not to take effect earlier than 30 days after the President’s proclamation finding that a foreign country is imposing an unreasonable charge, exaction, regulation, or limitation that is not equally enforced on the like articles of every foreign country, or discriminates in fact against U.S. commerce in a way that places the commerce of the United States at a disadvantage compared to the commerce of any foreign country. Section 338 also authorizes the President to suspend, revoke, supplement, or amend any proclamation under section 338 whenever the President deems that the public interests require such action. Further, section 338 authorizes the President to exclude from importation articles of the foreign country if the foreign country maintains or increases the discrimination against the commerce of the United States and the President deems the exclusion to be consistent with the public interests and the interests of the United States. 10. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the President to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, including the removal, modification, continuance, or imposition of any rate of duty or other import restriction. NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, including section 338; section 301 of title 3, United States Code; and section 604, do hereby proclaim as follows: (1) Except as otherwise provided in this proclamation, certain products of Canada, as set forth in Annex I, Part A to this proclamation, imported into the United States shall no longer be subject to the additional ad valorem duty of 50 percent imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11048, as amended. In addition, certain products of Canada, as set forth in Annex I, Part B to this proclamation, imported into the United States shall be subject to the additional ad valorem duty of 50 percent imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11048, as amended. The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11048, as amended, and as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1862). These changes shall be effective with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on October 30, 2026. (2) The HTSUS is modified as provided in Annex II to this proclamation, effective with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on October 30, 2026, and the modifications shall continue in effect unless this action is expressly suspended, revoked, supplemented, amended, or terminated. (3) The head of each executive department and agency (agency) is authorized to and shall take all appropriate measures within the agency’s authority to implement this proclamation. The head of each agency may, consistent with applicable law, including section 301 of title 3, United States Code, redelegate the authority to take such appropriate measures within the agency. (4) The Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Commerce, and the United States Trade Representative, is authorized to issue such rules, regulations, guidance, instructions, or determinations as may be necessary to implement this proclamation and is authorized to take any necessary measures to administer this proclamation. (5) The Commissioner of CBP, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Commerce, the United States Trade Representative, the Chairman of the United States International Trade Commission, and any other senior executive branch official the Commissioner of CBP deems appropriate, shall determine whether any additional modifications to the HTSUS are necessary to effectuate this proclamation and shall make such modifications to the HTSUS through notice in the Federal Register , including any technical or ministerial correction to the annexes to this proclamation. (6) For any rule or regulation the Commissioner of CBP makes to implement this proclamation, the Commissioner of CBP shall, to the extent required by law, obtain the approval of the President or the United States Trade Representative. The United States Trade Representative is delegated the President’s approval authority in 19 U.S.C. 1338(h). (7) Any provision of previous proclamations and Executive Orders that is inconsistent with this proclamation is superseded to the extent of such inconsistency. (8) If any provision of this proclamation or the application of any provision to any individual or circumstance is held to be invalid, the remainder of this proclamation and the application of its provisions to any other individuals or circumstances shall not be affected. IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this twenty-third day of October, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first. Annex I Annex II DONALD J. title: Musk's SpaceX is still restricting Starlink in Ukraine and the toll is rising
body:
SpaceX 's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a national security expert said Friday.
"Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters," wrote Denys Sienik, Ukraine's deputy ambassador to the U.S., in a Friday post on X .
"Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives," Sienik said. "Unfortunately, as of today, nothing has changed. We continue to wait."
Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said.
Despite recent comments from President Donald Trump that indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade.
"They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike , told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on."
"Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are."
Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel.
"While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google.
Elon Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear.
Democratic lawmakers have since called for an investigation into Musk and the Starshield throttling. A group of bipartisan lawmakers penned a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday urging the agency to "act expeditiously to expand its Starshield arrangements and ensure uninterrupted satellite communications support for Ukraine."
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump spoke to Musk by phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals. Trump said Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back."
But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored.
"I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him."
Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service.
Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."
On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed a letter of intent with Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release.
"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."
-- CNBC's Eamon Javers and Lora Kolodny contributed reporting to this story.

title: Air defense soldiers who shoot down 5 incoming threats could get a new skill badge
body: Air defense artillery soldiers who successfully engage at least five hostile targets in a combat zone could get a new skill badge, Task & Purpose has confirmed. Details of the new badge were included in a copy of an Army PowerPoint slide that was circulated on social media. An Army official said the information included on the slide was “pre-decisional” but confirmed that the badge was in the works. Based on the Army slide, soldiers would need to have five or more “successful hostile engagements in an operational environment” to earn it. Eligibility could apply to soldiers as far back as 2022. “The Army is currently staffing the establishment of a new Air Defense Artillery badge to recognize soldiers’ tactical and technical mastery. Design, eligibility criteria, and implementation guidance are currently under review and will be formally published to all commands once finalized,” Maj. Travis Shaw, an Army spokesman, said in a statement. Top Stories This Week News Airman dies in rappelling demonstration at Navy football game By Nicholas Slayton News Hegseth’s plan to restore Confederate memorial at Arlington expected to cost taxpayers $9 million By Austin Campbell News Marine Corps establishes its first medium-range missile battalion By Nicholas Slayton The Army slide showed that the badge’s proposed gold wreath design is inspired by the Army Air Corps’ “flying ace” history, which were monikers given to World War II pilots who intercepted enemy aircraft in combat . In recent years, the Army has referred to a handful of soldiers who have shot down five or more enemy drones as “aces.” A 10th Mountain Division infantry soldier even became known as the “Ace of Syria” after his fifth one-way attack drone kill while he was deployed to a forward operating base in northeastern Syria. Skill badges are official military decorations that soldiers wear on their uniform to recognize a specific technical or tactical achievement. The Army breaks its skill badges up into six groups based on their precedence and how they are worn on service and dress uniforms. The slide indicates that the badge could be classified as a “Group 4” special skill badge, which is the same category as parachutist, military freefall parachutist, air assault, diver badges, and space badges, according to Army uniform regulations . The post Air defense soldiers who shoot down 5 incoming threats could get a new skill badge appeared first on Task & Purpose .

title: Fewer Overdoses May Explain US Death Decline
body: “Researchers found that naloxone use did not increase relative to the number of overdoses as deaths have fallen since 2023, suggesting that other factors may be driving the national decline in overdose deaths… Comparing trends before and after May 2023, researchers found that nonfatal drug overdoses were 20.9% below levels projected from earlier trends, while opioid-related overdoses were 32.7% below projections. Naloxone administrations also fell, dropping 21.3% below projected levels. Because fewer overdoses would naturally mean fewer people needing naloxone, the researchers also examined how often the medication was administered relative to the declining number of overdoses. They found that naloxone was being used at nearly the same rate as before the decline. Use by bystanders, including friends and family members, however, was 28.6% lower than expected based on earlier trends, even after accounting for the decline in overdoses. Barnett said the findings suggest that fewer overdoses overall — possibly because of changes in the illicit drug supply or how people use opioids — may be helping drive the decline in deaths rather than more people being revived with the medication.” From Brown University . The post Fewer Overdoses May Explain US Death Decline appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Drone strike sinks cargo ship near Romania, killing Ukrainian sailor. Romanian President blames Russia
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A Russian drone strike sank the Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv in the Black Sea near Romania’s port of Constanța on 23 October, killing a Ukrainian sailor and leaving three crew members missing. Nine others were rescued, Digi24 reported. The sinking comes amid a surge in attacks on commercial shipping near Romania and Bulgaria, threatening civilian crews and routes used to transport Ukrainian agricultural exports. As Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian ports and shipping, the Danube corridor and nearby waters have become increasingly important to Ukraine’s maritime trade. Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia for the attack, describing it as part of Moscow’s escalation of the war against Ukraine and its attacks on NATO’s eastern flank, Reuters reported . Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry confirmed to Radio Svoboda that a Ukrainian citizen was among those killed. Ukrainian sailor killed, three crew members missing The Khoryv sent a distress signal at around 10 a.m. local time, about 13 nautical miles (24 kilometers) east of Constanța, just outside Romania’s territorial waters, Digi24 reported . The vessel caught fire, sustained major damage, and capsized, with only a small part of its hull remaining visible above the water. Romania’s naval authority said 13 crew members were aboard: 10 Ukrainians and three Azerbaijanis. Rescue teams recovered nine sailors alive and one body, while three crew members remained missing, Reuters reported. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said the vessel had been traveling from a Turkish port and confirmed that the Ukrainian Embassy in Romania had received information from Romanian authorities about one Ukrainian sailor’s death. Four Ukrainian survivors, including the captain, were taken to a hospital, while two others did not require medical assistance. Attacks threaten Black Sea shipping The sinking comes amid a surge in attacks on commercial vessels off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. At least seven cargo ships have been hit over the past two weeks, with around 30 sailors reported dead or missing, according to Reuters. The vessels targeted in recent incidents were either anchored near or heading toward the Sulina Canal, which connects the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal has become a key export route for Ukraine, one of the world’s largest exporters of grain and vegetable oils. Ukraine has increasingly relied on Danube ports and routes through Romanian territorial waters as Russia attacks its own Black Sea ports. Strikes on commercial vessels threaten crews and risk disrupting Ukrainian agricultural exports to international markets. Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships traveling to or from Ukraine. Moscow has described its strikes on vessels as retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian or Russia-linked ships. Explore further Russia’s attacks on Black Sea shipping raise risk of global famine, German FM warns NATO plans stronger Black Sea surveillance NATO said on 20 October it would send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones to the Black Sea following the attacks on commercial shipping, according to Reuters. The alliance has not specified which capabilities it will deploy. Romania, Ukraine, and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial vessels. The latest sinking adds urgency to those calls as attacks increasingly affect shipping near NATO territory. The latest incident highlights the growing risks to commercial shipping as Russia’s war against Ukraine increasingly affects maritime traffic beyond Ukraine’s own coastline.
