title: AFOSI Seeks Enlisted Airmen to Train as Special Agents
body: The Air Force Office of Special Investigations is looking for a few good Airmen to swap jobs and become special agents. No, they won’t get the 007 James Bond code—but they could learn to conduct counterintelligence and investigate procurement fraud and major crimes, OSI spokesperson Trevor Saylor told Air & Space Forces Magazine. The office is looking to recruit agents from backgrounds other than law enforcement—it’s seeking Airmen with less than 11 years in service, with some exceptions, and is calling for applicants from other job fields in part because other areas of expertise can prove valuable in the unique types of investigations OSI conducts. “A maintainer may understand an issue involving an aircraft or weapons system, while a contracting or acquisitions professional may recognize a process or irregularity relevant to a fraud investigation,” Special Agent Jennifer Holland, an OSI recruiter, said in a recent release . “Intelligence professionals may bring experience analyzing adversaries, identifying patterns and working with sensitive information.” As threats to the Department of the Air Force cross traditional boundaries between criminal investigations, counterintelligence, cyber activity, and technology protection, that range of experience has become more relevant, Holland said. Special Agent Isaiah Moore, Air Force Office of Special Investigations Detachment 422 investigator, scans a subject’s fingerprints into the Live Scan Management System at Altus Air Force Base, Okla. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Kari Degraffenreed Current threats and demands placed on OSI have “placed a renewed focus on defending the homeland, strengthening deterrence, protecting critical capabilities and preserving military advantages to generate combat power,” according to the release. Skills such as foreign language proficiency, cybersecurity expertise and advanced computing skills are helpful, but not required or all that is needed. “We’re looking for Airmen capable of exercising independent judgment, communicating with people from different backgrounds, managing competing priorities and documenting investigative activity with precision,” Holland said. The requirements include: Technical sergeants who exceed the 11-year limit may be considered on a case-by-case basis and should pursue a time-in-service waiver through their local AFOSI detachment before applying. First-term Airmen must also meet applicable retraining window requirements. First-term Airmen assigned within the continental United States who are serving four-year enlistments may generally apply from the first duty day of the month in which they complete 35 months of their current enlistment through the last duty day of their 43rd month. For Airmen serving six-year enlistments, the corresponding window is from the 59th through the 67th month. First-term Airmen assigned outside the continental United States generally must apply between 12 and 15 months before their date eligible to return from overseas. They must also enter their 35th month of service, or 59th month for six-year enlistees, on or before that date. Applicants on a current Control Roster or with a current Unfavorable Information File are not eligible. Applicants must be worldwide qualified and have a current passing fitness assessment without exemptions or a profile. OSI does not require enlisted applicants to have a college degree. Air Force Special Agent Michelle Jones, 2nd Field Investigations Squadron, Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, left, along with Special Agents Angela Velazquez-Colon, center, and Kenneth Reed, right, Department of the Air Force Office of Special Investigations Detachment 223, conduct a fingerprint lifting technique known as “cyanoacrylate fuming” at Tyndall Air Force Base, Fla. (Air Force) Diverse Experience Traditionally, law enforcement, cyber defense, healthcare, and logistics Airmen have had success translating their skills into the special agent role, Saylor wrote. The recruitment effort isn’t from any shortage or operational gaps, Saylor said. Instead, it is part of an ongoing effort to maintain a “highly credible, robust force” of agents. “We remain fully postured and staffed to meet all operational requirements,” Saylor wrote in an email. OSI isn’t targeting a specific job field, and the application process is open to all Airmen who meet the criteria. The office evaluates using the “Whole Airman” concept, Saylor wrote. The concept focuses on evaluating Airmen as well-rounded individuals across their military and personal lives, using tools such as Enlisted Performance Reports and special duty selections, with an emphasis on leadership, job performance, self-improvement, base/community involvement, and well-being aspects tied to Airman fitness. If an Airman submits their application package correctly and follows the USAF Personnel Center windows to secure a release from their current job, their AFSC Career Field Manager will be the final authority to approve or deny their request to move to special agent selection and training. Application Steps: Apply online , complete documentation, and secure your commander’s recommendation. AFOSI requests your career-field release, though approval is not guaranteed. Approved applicants undergo suitability screening at their local unit. Candidates complete interviews and background investigations before final selection. The application process takes about three to six months. A U.S. Air Force Office of Special Investigations special agent reviews investigative files during a staged photo at Seymour Johnson Air Force Base, N.C. (Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Holly Leonard) If selected, the Airman then gets a short-term Assignment Limitation Code while they go through vetting and onboarding for special agent training, Saylor wrote. Newly retrained Airmen-turned-agents will train at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Ga., to learn the fundamentals of federal criminal investigations before completing OSI-specific training. They’ll then be put into specialties such as counterintelligence, procurement fraud, and major criminal investigative roles once they join their units, Saylor wrote. Then there’s cyber. “For roles in AFOSI’s cyber defense positions, AFOSI vectors Agents who show promise in the field into the specialized cyber fields upon the completion of probation,” Saylor wrote. Most agents will begin their 15-month probationary period working felony-level criminal investigations and counterintelligence operations. While some may specialize in certain areas, all special agents are expected to work interchangeably in a variety of missions and types of investigations. Special Agents often travel more than many in the Air Force as part of their job and sometimes work high-stress cases that involve violent crime, fraud, and national security threats. To mitigate burnout, Saylor wrote that OSI proactively supports personnel through a structured career progression plan and uses embedded wellness resources. “Upon completing an initial probationary period of approximately 15 months focused on general criminal and counterintelligence work, agents have the opportunity to transition into specialized investigative sections,” Saylor wrote. “This structural pathway provides variety in their assignments and a deliberate break from the initial high-tempo investigative grind.” OSI also has its own embedded chaplain corps and psychologists to provide ready access to mental health support, he wrote. The post AFOSI Seeks Enlisted Airmen to Train as Special Agents appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Probable Dengue Cases Drop Sharply in Brazil
body: “Brazil reports a drop of approximately 70% in probable cases of dengue in 2026, compared to the same period in 2025. As of September 26, 470.5 thousand probable cases were counted in the country, up from 1.5 million in the same period of the previous year. There was also a reduction in the chikungunya and Zika records. 67,902 cases of chikungunya were counted, 43% less than the 118,885 recorded in 2025. For Zika, there were 2,141 cases, 35% below 3,724 cases recorded in the same period a year earlier.” From Ministério da Saúde . The post Probable Dengue Cases Drop Sharply in Brazil appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Prime Editing Used in a Patient for First Time
body: “A powerful gene-editing technique has been used to edit DNA directly in a person’s body — the first known instance of such a treatment. The milestone treatment is part of a clinical trial of prime editing, a technique that can alter DNA with more precision than standard CRISPR–Cas9 methods can. In this case, prime editing was used to treat a condition called Wilson’s disease by rewriting DNA in liver cells, to erase a mutation that prevents them from eliminating excess copper. Prime Medicine, a biotechnology company in Cambridge, Massachusetts, announced that it had treated the first person in its trial earlier this month. It expects to announce the first results from the study next year.” From Nature . The post Prime Editing Used in a Patient for First Time appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Child Labor in Brazil Fell From 2024 to 2025
body: “Brazil had 1.499 million children and adolescents engaged in child labor in 2025, representing 4 percent of the population aged 5 to 17. The data come from the National Household Sample Survey (PNAD), released on Friday (Oct. 16) by Brazil’s statistics bureau IBGE. The survey also shows that child labor declined by 9.2 percent from 2024, when 1.65 million children and adolescents aged 5 to 17 were engaged in child labor, representing 4.3 percent of that age group’s population.” From Agência Brasil . The post Child Labor in Brazil Fell From 2024 to 2025 appeared first on Human Progress .

title: US military needs ‘urgent revolutionary institutional change’ to prepare for modern war, Petraeus says
body: Unmanned systems now inflict more than 90% of Russia’s casualties on the front lines in Ukraine, yet no NATO military, including America’s, has begun the overhaul that kind of war demands, Ret. Army Gen. David Petraeus said Oct. 16, weeks after the Pentagon announced a new command for autonomous warfare. The extent of the drone war is underestimated, with Ukraine and Russia each using roughly 10,000 drones a day, the former CIA director and onetime commander of U.S. Central Command said, speaking at an American Primary Aluminum Association event in Washington. “This is an unmanned systems war,” Petraeus said . “Tanks aren’t survivable there anymore.” For Ukraine, drones and unmanned weapons have become central to how the country has leveraged a smaller, outgunned force against a much larger, better-financed adversary for almost five years. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ordered the creation of a new Unmanned Systems Forces military branch in 2024, and the Defense Ministry has said time and again that developing more autonomous weapons is a top priority. But for the rest of the world, Petraeus said, the fighting in Ukraine is a window into the future and a warning about the dangers of being underprepared for the battles to come. “Really, no NATO country and not even the United States is undertaking yet the urgent revolutionary institutional change that should be taken based on what we see in Ukraine, which is the future of war,” he said. The U.S. needs a new concept of warfare that runs through force structure, training, procurement, personnel policy and bases, the general said, replacing much of the legacy, heavily manned equipment with unmanned systems that are cheaper and far more numerous. “What’s going to happen is we’ll see the introduction of autonomous systems really for the first time in warfare,” Petraeus said. Washington is making “some commendable steps” toward developing these weapons, according to Petraeus, including establishing a new Autonomous Warfare Command that requires each military branch to stand up its own component command. “But my hope is that they will not just create an unmanned systems force in terms of force structure, but that they will also spur the initiation of true institutional change,” Petraeus said. That includes how the U.S. buys weapons, Petraeus said, calling for “very, very substantial manufacturing capacity but not necessarily producing all the time.” “You want it to be able to make software changes every week, hardware changes every few weeks, which is what’s going on in Ukraine because the enemy continues to evolve and Russia’s been innovating very substantially as well,” he said. Ukraine will produce as many as 20 million unmanned systems this year, Zelenskyy said in a July speech , with a shortage of trained operators and the acquisition of some weapons components — including optics, gimbals, brushless motors and fiber-optic cable — becoming the domestic industry’s production bottleneck. The general also rejected the idea that the U.S. war with Iran has hurt Washington’s ability to help Kyiv, though he acknowledged the U.S. has used “a fair number of missile interceptors,” which “makes it more difficult to share those with others around the world.” The war has consumed between one-half and two-thirds of the U.S. inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors, according to a Congressional Budget Office estimate released in September. “We can help the Ukrainians in any way in which we decide to assist them,” Petraeus said. “These are policy decisions.”

Washington is making “some commendable steps” toward developing these weapons, according to Petraeus, including establishing a new Autonomous Warfare Command that requires each military branch to stand up its own component command. “But my hope is that they will not just create an unmanned systems force in terms of force structure, but that they will also spur the initiation of true institutional change,” Petraeus said. That includes how the U.S. buys weapons, Petraeus said, calling for “very, very substantial manufacturing capacity but not necessarily producing all the time.” “You want it to be able to make software changes every week, hardware changes every few weeks, which is what’s going on in Ukraine because the enemy continues to evolve and Russia’s been innovating very substantially as well,” he said. Ukraine will produce as many as 20 million unmanned systems this year, Zelenskyy said in a July speech , with a shortage of trained operators and the acquisition of some weapons components — including optics, gimbals, brushless motors and fiber-optic cable — becoming the domestic industry’s production bottleneck. The general also rejected the idea that the U.S. war with Iran has hurt Washington’s ability to help Kyiv, though he acknowledged the U.S. has used “a fair number of missile interceptors,” which “makes it more difficult to share those with others around the world.” The war has consumed between one-half and two-thirds of the U.S. inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors, according to a Congressional Budget Office estimate released in September. “We can help the Ukrainians in any way in which we decide to assist them,” Petraeus said. “These are policy decisions.”

title: US military needs ‘urgent revolutionary institutional change’ to prepare for modern war, Petraeus says
body: Unmanned systems now inflict more than 90% of Russia’s casualties on the front lines in Ukraine, yet no NATO military, including America’s, has begun the overhaul that kind of war demands, Ret. Army Gen. David Petraeus said Oct. 16, weeks after the Pentagon announced a new command for autonomous warfare. title: Sewage Overflows Into the Tidal Thames Drop Sharply
body: “The first annual Tideway Benefits Report has revealed significant improvement in river health following the opening of the super sewer in 2025. Storm overflows to the tidal Thames have been successfully reduced by 86%, compared to pre-Tideway levels, as the operation of this significant asset is transferred to Thames Water from Tideway, the company set up to deliver the project. The findings mark a new chapter for the River Thames and signals that London’s principal waterway, which was once declared biologically dead in the late 1950s, is firmly on the road to recovery.” From Thames Water . title: Bangladesh’s climate migrants are arriving in cities unprepared to protect them
body: In 2024, disasters displaced 2.4 million people within Bangladesh even as the International Monetary Fund predicts that rising seas could eliminate more than one-seventh of Bangladesh’s land area and nearly one-third of its food production by 2050. As environmental pressures drive people from their homes, researchers are examining the risks migrants face in the secondary cities where they relocate and whether these cities are equipped to accommodate growing numbers of climate-displaced people. To cope with increasing climate-related pressures, migration is often viewed as an adaptive strategy because moving away from areas exposed to hazards such as flooding, cyclones, river erosion and sea-level rise can help people reduce their exposure to climate risks and seek safer housing and more stable livelihoods. In these circumstances, urban informal settlements are often among the first destinations for displaced people. Yet, in Bangladesh, these settlements are risky in nature because of the structural formation, and the residents are exposed to various hazards. This raises a broader question: Are the cities receiving climate migrants equipped to support a safer, more stable future or leaving them more exposed? A new study published in Climate and Development on climate migrants living in informal settlements in southwestern Bangladesh examines what happens to migrants after relocation to secondary settlements. The study findings suggest that moving away from regions affected by climate hazards does not necessarily mean moving toward safety, particularly when urban planning and social protection systems fail to account for their needs. title: SpaceX Filing Gives Elon Musk the Final Word on Tesla Merger He Says He’s Staying Out Of
body:
Elon Musk recused himself from the SpaceX-Tesla merger talks. His company’s SEC filing suggests that doesn’t mean much.
SpaceX’s October 22 10-Q disclosed that any potential combination with Tesla “would be subject to further approval by our special committee, our board of directors and our controlling shareholder.” Musk controls roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power. He is the controlling shareholder.
Both companies formed special committees on October 20 to evaluate a proposed deal analysts estimate could create a combined entity worth around $3.5 trillion. Musk described staying out of the talks as “an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation.” The filing language suggests he’ll have the last word anyway.
Elon Musk explains where a SpaceX–Tesla merger stands:
“I mean, this is definitely kind of a question where I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield. But so I have to be thoughtful about what I say here."
"I think so both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees… https://t.co/10Hc1mrbfk pic.twitter.com/LYwYW0y14u
— Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) October 20, 2026
He’s also already been in the conversation. Reuters reported that Musk’s public endorsement of the deal earlier this month created a “mess” for the independent process, with insiders saying it complicated the special committees’ ability to negotiate at arm’s length.
Critics are pointing to Tesla’s 2016 SolarCity acquisition—another conflicted transaction that cleared Delaware courts—as the closest governance precedent. SpaceX’s own investor disclosures have flagged Musk’s overlapping interests as a material risk.
Tesla shareholders must clear a 50%-of-all-outstanding-shares threshold—not a simpler majority of votes cast—a standard Musk himself called “quite a high hurdle.” REX Financial estimates the merged company would give him roughly 57% of combined voting power.

title: DUNE Project Aims to Unite Legacy and Cloud Tools in Air Ops Centers
body: After decades of building isolated, vendor-locked systems to run the Air Operations Centers that serve as the Air Force’s “combat brains,” the program office tasked with creating the next-generation AOC is working to fold those systems into a new cloud-based system. Col. Brian Viola , the newly appointed commander of Kessel Run, the government-led, vendor-managed program office underneath the portfolio acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview that his team is standardizing how cloud-based applications and software updates to AOCs get accessed worldwide in real time. Starting this spring, Kessel Run launched the Dynamic Unified Net-enabled Environment, or DUNE, which merges cloud and on-premises capabilities for AOC operators, commanders, and their customers—the rest of the operational Air Force. “Evolving the architectural foundation is vital because the information our warfighters rely on depends on the integrity, speed, and agility of the underlying domain,” Viola said. “We are rapidly entering the era of software-defined warfare, where tactical superiority belongs to the force that can iterate, secure and deploy code faster than the adversary can adapt.” Essentially, DUNE standardizes how legacy and current software communicates across the Air Operations Center’s systems. It’s unclear whether the DUNE acronym is a nod to the popular book, film and TV franchise of the same name. But the Air Force has a history of using sci-fi-inspired names and acronyms—Kessel Run itself is named after a Star Wars reference. Speaking the Same Language Currently, Viola said, AOC operators must choose between using real-time, cloud-based tools or sticking with the often aged, legacy hardware they have on hand. “The ability to rapidly integrate new mission capabilities, enable distributed command and control, and incorporate new technologies depends on the architecture beneath them,” he said. DUNE is an overarching project that builds on Kessel Run’s Applications Transformation project, or AppTX, which the service introduced to conduct large-scale migrations of legacy software apps to the cloud. Companies such as Parsons, General Dynamics Information Technology, and Astrion compete for taskings through AppTX. DUNE focuses on the issue of Data Definition Language, which has gained prominence with the recent push to rush artificial intelligence into systems across the Pentagon. DDL is a kind of programming language that can create, modify, or delete database structures without modifying the data itself—it allows legacy infrastructure and software “talk” with new software and applications, breaking down silos and stovepipes. Without it, Viola said, “you’re going to have to work with what you have”—an Airman in an AOC will only be able to draw from a tool or solution they have in their local network, on site near the tactical edge, without access to the cloud. “We don’t want to necessarily have every AOC be a snowflake that we have to go, ‘this is tailored for you now, AOC 1, and this is tailored for the 613th [AOC], this is tailored for the 607th [AOC],” Viola said. Tailoring the solutions by AOC is “sucking away from the innovation we really want to get after,” he said. Project DUNE aims to get the continuous delivery of cloud-based capabilities and applications down to an on-premises solution, he said. Solutions won’t be as “elastic” as the cloud, but they will be a resilient capability that users can rely on, he said. Beyond DUNE, Viola said next steps include building the “Revolutionary AOC” with industry partners. The effort will involve operators, mission partners, engineers and acquisition teams working together in operational scenarios to identify gaps and improve the system architecture. Work on DUNE and recent pushes in the PAE C3BM and Kessel Run specifically predate Viola’s tenure. Air & Space Forces Magazine reported in February that Kessel Run was launching its “next generation” AOC effort, which seeks to integrate AI, machine learning, data fusion, and cloud-based software into the centers. The Air Force has 21 AOCs across the force and sees these operational hubs as weapons systems in their own right, calling them AN/USQ-163 Falconers. In 2022, the Air Force awarded SAIC a $374 million contract through mid-2027 to sustain and modernize its AOCs. The current Falconer system is in Increment 10.1, with a 10.2 (aka Block 20) upgrade in progress. The post DUNE Project Aims to Unite Legacy and Cloud Tools in Air Ops Centers appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

Remember Popcorn Time , the app that served as an easy-to-use front end for streaming torrents of movies and TV shows? Development of the MPAA’s least-favorite app of the 2010s has been abandoned for years , but the “Netflix of Piracy” software is still installed on millions of devices that are just waiting to join a bot army. Researchers at Eye Security found the updater for a Popcorn Time fork called “Time4Popcorn” still running on tons of Windows, macOS, and Android devices located around the world, phoning home to now-abandoned web domains over unencrypted HTTP and running an outdated, insecure version of Chrome.
Eye Security’s Niels Teusink says the updater could have been used to install and run basically any kind of software with full privileges, easily enabling someone to create a botnet just by taking over one of the domains, using a man-in-the-middle attack to target specific devices, or perform surveillance by identifying the machines running the software.
Their solution was to register one of the domains and use it to send their own update that instructed the updater to disable itself. Despite ethical concerns about the fix, the researchers say their only alternative “was to do nothing,” pointing out, “The update process wasn’t doing anything functional anyway, it was only creating risk for users.”
Eye Security said on Windows devices, their update “simply stops and disables the service via the Service Control Manager” without deleting any files or anything else. On macOS, it uses a shell script to execute a command that blocks the update process from starting. They didn’t address the software on Android devices, where installing the update would still require actual user interaction first.
They had to tweak their update after it was uploaded to VirusTotal, causing security programs to flag it as malware and block it while leaving the vulnerable updater running. It’s unclear exactly how many devices were at risk, but Eye Security says it “sent out over 2 million update downloads” by March, when they stopped sending the update and transferred the domains they used to the Shadowserver Foundation , a web security non-profit.

Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model called Dessa that’s trained “from scratch on nothing but human conversation,” and to show off the model, Block shared chats it has had with humans that can occasionally be a little awkward and uncanny.
Take this one , for example, shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam. The conversation between the model and the speaker does have a mostly natural back and forth (though for some reason, the model initially mistakes the speaker for somebody named “Ronaldo”).
Here’s a video of Dessa playing a guessing game over voice:
The Dessa website features a few other examples, like a back-and-forth about Christopher Nolan’s films (including Dessa going on an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s Superman films), a person telling Dessa about taking it on a surprise trip to Paris (to which Dessa, as the website describes, “then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude”), and a conversation between OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1 voice model and Dessa (where Dessa comes across as more natural). You can hear clips from some of those conversations in this video .
On the website, the Dessa team says that Dessa is a “true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech,” and it can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max “or better.” As for why they made it, the team gives the three reasons “curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety,” and provided some more detail:
Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.
Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing.
AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it.
The Dessa team says it will be giving “a small group of AI safety researchers” early access to the model.

title: The Pentagon's guidelines for "responsible AI" aren't always followed, report shows
body:
Three of the Pentagon projects surveyed by GAO included weapons for counter-camouflage (upper image) and target recognition (lower images). Government Accountability Office/GAO hide caption
The Pentagon is building weapons and projects with artificial intelligence capabilities that officials say don't always closely adhere to the agency's own guidelines for AI, according to a congressional watchdog report published in October.
AI researchers and international organizations have long advocated for strict regulation of AI when used in weapons that could become unpredictable or function with little human control, arguing that those tools could endanger the lives of soldiers and civilians and risk quickly escalating wars. But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has repeatedly dismissed previous caution of AI tools and encouraged rapid autonomous innovation at the Pentagon.
The Pentagon issued a memo in January saying the department would become "an 'AI-first' warfighting force across all components, from front to back." Last month, Hegseth announced a new warfare command focused on autonomous weapon development, including drones.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth arrives on stage for a discussion during an annual Army meeting on October 14, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America hide caption
The watchdog report, published by the U.S. Government Accountability Office on Oct. 14, grants a rare look inside how those kinds of projects are being developed.
The GAO surveyed 10 officials involved with building 10 weapons and tools for the Pentagon that use AI to automatically identify targets on the battlefield, process surveillance and improve tactical decision making, and other tasks. The projects are among more than 300 being built with AI in the Pentagon.
When responding to the GAO survey, six of the 10 officials said their teams had "identified risk(s)" with using the projects "in an operational environment."
To address some of those sorts of risks, in 2021, the Pentagon sent a memo outlining six basic tenets to ensure that weapons built with AI are created responsibly. Those six guidelines mainly stress the importance of Pentagon-wide oversight, verification and "real-time monitoring" of the technology, and cooperation with allies "to advance global norms grounded in shared values."
Alissa Czyz, who directed the GAO review, said the tenets evolved from earlier ethical principles, and while they weren't rules, they were understood to be important by people involved with building AI tools at the Pentagon.
"It's a memo, right, at the end of the day, so it's not a department instruction," said Czyz. "It's something that the department has signaled that should be implemented."
Most of the people involved with making the 10 weapons and projects reviewed by GAO had taken "at least initial steps" to follow the six tenets outlined in the memo, according to the report, and some of the projects were in early stages, Czyz clarified.
But some of the responses indicated officials weren't always closely following the guidelines.
Four officials told the GAO that requirements for the weapons and projects they were working on weren't "aligned with Responsible AI tenets." And three of the 10 officials told the GAO they "don't know" if the projects will be continuously monitored after they're deployed, though the six tenets encourage monitoring.
Officials told the GAO that more access to expertise about the agency's guidelines or staff who know about them would increase their ability to incorporate AI responsibly. But the group that helps manage education on the Pentagon's guidelines, the Department of the Responsible AI Division, is understaffed. Although the group was authorized to hire 10 people in 2023, as of February, only three of those positions were filled and the Pentagon "is unlikely to fill vacant positions or increase staffing," the report states.
"That's a very small number of folks tasked with a large responsibility of responsible AI throughout the department," said Czyz.
The GAO issued two recommendations: The Pentagon should more clearly outline the responsibilities and meeting schedules of the office charged with overseeing AI regulation, and address understaffing. Although the Pentagon agreed with those recommendations, as of Oct. 22, the agency had not implemented those changes, a GAO representative confirmed to NPR.
NPR asked the Pentagon when it planned to make those changes, but did not receive a response.
When delivering a speech at SpaceX in January, Hegseth indicated he believed AI development at the Pentagon should not be slowed by those sorts of steps.
"Our enterprise currently operates on staffing and committee cycles measured in months and years, and that's unacceptable," said Hegseth. "Military AI is going to be a race for the foreseeable future where the risks to U.S. national security of moving too slowly outweigh the impacts of imperfect alignment."
NPR would like to hear from more people who work with federal agencies or AI companies and have information to share about how agencies are using AI. You can email the reporter of this article, Chiara Eisner, at ceisner@npr.org or contact her on Signal here , username ceis.78.

title: Chinese naval hospital ship concludes West African tour
body: The Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) hospital ship Auspicious Ark docked in Conakry, Guinea, on 3 October and departed on 10 October after a seven-day goodwill visit, the first stop by a Chinese naval hospital ship in that country. The call was part of Mission Harmony-2026, the twelfth edition of a PLAN medical diplomacy programme that began in 2010. Guinean government and military officials, the Chinese ambassador to Guinea, the defence attache, embassy staff, local residents and representatives of overseas Chinese communities and businesses met the ship at the Port of Conakry on arrival. A separate mobile team visited the China-Guinea Friendship Hospital for academic exchanges and a military camp for consultations and treatment, while Chinese and Guinean service members played a friendly basketball match. Guinea’s prime minister, Amadou Oury Bah, toured the ship and attended a deck reception during the visit, according to Xinhua. A farewell ceremony was held at the port when the ship left on 10 October, with senior Guinean defence and foreign affairs officials among those seeing it off. The Guinea stop followed two earlier West African calls on the same deployment. The ship spent seven days in Nouakchott, Mauritania, in mid-September, where medical teams handled more than 1,600 consultations in a single day and delivered a baby for a woman with a high-risk pregnancy. It then sailed to Dakar, Senegal, arriving 25 September for its first-ever visit to that country. Over the week in Dakar the crew logged 6,060 patient visits, performed 29 surgeries and ran 61 health checkups, with shore teams adding 350 further consultations and two rounds of health training for 150 people. Auspicious Ark left Qingdao, in eastern China’s Shandong Province, on 22 July to begin the voyage, its first overseas mission. The deployment is scheduled to run more than 200 days and will take the ship through multiple African and South Asian ports before it returns home. The vessel is a Type 920 hospital ship, the third in a class that also includes Peace Ark and Silk Road Ark, and entered service with the PLAN’s North Sea Fleet in 2025. At roughly 10,000 tonnes, it carries 18 clinical departments and five auxiliary diagnostic units, giving it the ability to run more than 60 types of medical examinations, treatments and procedures across general surgery, orthopaedics, obstetrics and gynaecology, and ophthalmology, among other specialties. Eight onboard operating rooms allow simultaneous surgeries, and an embarked helicopter extends the ship’s reach for medical evacuation. The roughly 100-strong medical team aboard is drawn mainly from the PLA Northern Theatre Command Navy, with additional staff from the Naval Medical University. Peace Ark carried out the first ten Mission Harmony deployments and has, according to Chinese state media, called at 49 countries and treated more than 370,000 patients since 2010. Silk Road Ark ran the eleventh mission, which concluded in April this year. Auspicious Ark’s current voyage extends that pattern to a third hull and a longer operating tempo, letting the PLAN keep one hospital ship available for routine fleet duties while another is at sea on a Mission Harmony tour. The ship’s value lies less in any single procedure than in the platform itself: a self-contained surgical and diagnostic facility that can begin treating patients within hours of tying up, without relying on a host nation’s hospital infrastructure. That capability sits inside a wider pattern of PLAN activity along the West African coast and the broader African littoral. In July 2024 the 43rd Escort Group called at Lagos, Nigeria, Pointe-Noire in the Republic of Congo, and ports in Ghana and Gabon. In July 2026 Ivory Coast’s navy commissioned two Chinese-donated patrol vessels at the Plateau Naval Base in Abidjan. And in 2025 the PLAN formally rotated its presence at the Project 141 overseas support base in Doraleh, Djibouti , with the 48th Naval Escort Group taking over operational duties there. None of these activities are formally linked, and a hospital ship visit carries none of the operational weight of a support base or a patrol vessel transfer. But taken together they describe a steadily expanding routine of Chinese naval contact across African ports, mixing humanitarian outreach, equipment transfers and basing arrangements. Analysts tracking China’s maritime posture in Africa generally read hospital ship tours as the softer end of that spectrum, building familiarity with ports and officials that can pay off later in access or goodwill, even when no military logistics are directly at stake. Guinea’s Overseas Chinese Association chairman, Chen Renbing, said the visit marked “a new level in the friendship between Guinea and China,” a comment that fits the diplomatic framing Beijing has placed on the mission. China’s defence ministry has described Mission Harmony-2026 as intended to deepen cooperation and contribute to what it calls a maritime community with a shared future, alongside its Global Security Initiative.

title: Air Force Considering Air-to-Air Role for Bombers amid Fighter Procurement Constraints
body: The Air Force’s future strategy for fighting wars could include arming bombers with air-to-air strike capabilities, the service said in a new report to Congress. The report, titled “Long-Term USAF Fighter Force Structure” and submitted to lawmakers Oct. 16, said that “developing air-to-air capabilities on bombers” is being considered as a way to expand the service’s combat capabilities. In the report, which was briefed to reporters Oct. 20 and obtained by Air & Space Forces Magazine, the Air Force estimates it will need 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035 to meet the demands of the National Defense Strategy at moderate risk, with about 40 percent of its fighter fleet consisting of F-35A Joint Strike Fighters. That’s up from the 1,288 combat-coded fighters the service has today. The Air Force is working on ways to procure as many Lockheed Martin F-35As, Boeing F-15EX Eagle IIs, and Boeing F-47 sixth-generation fighters as possible, the report said. However, the report acknowledges that hitting its fighter procurement targets may not be achievable due to “fiscal realities and industrial production limitations.” Other recapitalization options could include acquiring an entirely new fighter, relying more on semi-autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft—and giving air-to-air roles and capabilities to bombers, the report said. Air Force fighters have long carried out air-to-ground strikes, but bombers have not traditionally performed air-to-air missions. However, with the Air Force’s fleet constrained by slow procurement of new fighters and the retirement of aging ones, the service has been looking for new ways to accomplish its missions. Former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin signaled an openness to the B-21 Raider stealth bomber carrying out a greater role in the service’s air dominance plans in an October 2024 discussion with reporters in Washington. At the time, the Air Force had put its F-47 program—then called Next-Generation Air Dominance—on hold amid concerns about its potential costs. The Air Force was reviewing its approach to air superiority to try to figure out ways to get the job done, potentially without the plane that would become the F-47. When asked if the air superiority review could lead to a more prominent role for the B-21, Allvin said “We have not taken that off the table.” A year later, in September 2025, sources told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the Air Force was studying whether a large flying wing-type stealth aircraft—potentially based on a B-21—armed with dozens of air-to-air missiles could be an element of its future air superiority force. In its latest report, the Air Force wrote that it is “committed to the full modernization and recapitalization of its legacy fighter fleet, while placing an enormous effort into our newest fighter, the F-47.” CCAs are also rapidly advancing and likely to at least meet, if not beat, the program’s schedule, the report said. But the Air Force said CCAs aren’t yet ready to change how the service plans for its future fighter fleet, though that day will come. “There is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters,” Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, told reporters Oct. 20. The report also said it will be “essential” to modernize its current cadre of older F-15s and F-16s into a fleet of “advanced fourth-generation capability” jets—planes that do not have stealth capabilities but can still operate in highly contested environments, often with the aid of advanced sensors and electronic warfare weapons. But it would take more than a decade of investments in the Air Force’s current depot infrastructure to modernize enough jets to increase the Air Force’s aircraft availability, the report said, calling that approach “insufficient, as it perpetuates reliance on a fleet averaging 30+ years in age.” Aside from upgrading existing fighters, the service could also buy new advanced fourth-gen jets like the F-15EX and, potentially, a new version of Lockheed Martin’s F-16 Fighting Falcon, dubbed the F-16G. Tabor said the service has not yet made any decision on buying new F-16s, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.” In its report, the Air Force said it has to pursue a two-track strategy of modernizing existing aircraft to meet immediate operational requirements, while recapitalizing its legacy fighters at the same time. The post Air Force Considering Air-to-Air Role for Bombers amid Fighter Procurement Constraints appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Corruption is voters' top issue ahead of midterm election, CNBC survey shows
body:
Voters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final CNBC All-America Economic Survey before the Nov. 3 midterm election.
The finding follows a monthslong messaging effort by Democrats to link widespread economic dissatisfaction with what they allege is rampant corruption by President Donald Trump and his Republican allies.
CNBC's survey of 1,000 registered U.S. voters found 36% of respondents pointing to government corruption as one of the most important issues facing the country right now. The cost of food and groceries came second with 34%, followed by protecting democracy and the price of gas, which garnered 23% each.
The nationwide poll, which gauged attitudes about the economy, Trump, Congress, artificial intelligence, the Iran war and more, was conducted Oct. 14-18. It was co-led by Democratic pollster Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Public Opinion Strategies, and carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.
To be sure, the question asking voters to name their top concerns lists several economy- and cost-related topics separately, subdividing an issue that might otherwise rank higher if lumped into a single category.
But the results nevertheless align with other recent polls showing corruption has shot to the top of voters' list of pressing worries.
A Fox News poll published last week found 60% of registered voters are extremely concerned about government corruption, surpassing concerns about inflation and high prices. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released Sunday found some two-thirds of respondents think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, up 10 percentage points since September 2025. Gallup recently found perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. have hit multi-decade highs. And an August poll from Reuters/Ipsos found nearly 7 in 10 Americans believe Trump's businesses influence his presidential decisions.
Republicans have also tried to seize on growing anti-corruption sentiment. The Trump administration has launched a task force led by Vice President JD Vance aimed at cracking down on fraud, while the president frequently accuses his Democratic enemies of crookery.
"I just want to say that from day one of my administration, we've waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum," Trump said Tuesday while unveiling a new reward program for whistleblowers.
But with Republicans in charge of the federal government — and as high costs linked to Trump's tariffs and the Iran war have put the GOP on defense — Democrats have been able to cast blame more directly.
"Americans have spent well over $100 BILLION extra on gas because Trump chose to go to war with Iran," Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said Wednesday on X . "His ego-fueled decisions cost you thousands."
Their arguments often spotlight Trump , attempting to draw a contrast between Americans' widely felt financial struggles with the president's surging net worth , his family's lucrative business dealings and his focus on pricey construction projects .
Other Democratic candidates have widened the scope of the message, delivering a pitch that the system itself is broken.
"The problem is that the people's elected representatives don't represent the people. They represent the donors and special interests," Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said in an April campaign video. "Corruption is why things don't work for ordinary people."
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has hammered the claim that Republicans have betrayed their vow to bring down costs.
"The wealthy and well-connected are cashing in. What are Republicans doing to lower costs for everyone else? Absolutely nothing," Jeffries wrote Friday .
Democrats' push appears to be resonating with voters, even as large swaths remain skeptical of both parties.
Respondents to the CNBC survey gave Democrats a 4-point edge over Republicans, 35% to 31%, when asked which party would do a better job dealing with government corruption.
But that gap grew to 17 points in Democrats' favor among voters who said corruption was their most important issue.
And independents, by a 15-point margin, said Democrats would address corruption better than Republicans – though 41% of those respondents think neither party would do a good job.
The apparent rise in concern about corruption is welcome news to critics of the president who have long lamented that Americans have become numb to scandal in the Trump era.
That shift is taking place because voters are feeling the impact of inflation and connecting it to what they see in Washington, said Brian Lemek, executive of the Democrat-backing political action committee Defend the Vote, in an interview.
"It's the only thing people are talking about right now," said Lemek, whose group briefed candidates on the issue in June.
Voters are "looking at the reality that their costs are high" and "making the connection between this corrupt and broken system and their high costs," he said.
Additionally, survey respondents overwhelmingly opposed the idea of elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, personally owning or trading stocks in individual companies that have contracts with the federal government. That should not be allowed, 93% of voters said in the poll.
A similar proportion – 89% – said that companies owned, or invested in, by a sitting president's immediate family members should not be allowed to receive contracts from the federal government.
"This definitely ties back to the corruption issues that we've been talking about," said Alicia Simmons of Hart Research Associates.

title: Meta shares are down 9% this week. Here's why Mike Khouw is buying now
body:
Size is a relative matter. The standard Manhattan apartment would seem almost claustrophobic compared to the vast expanses offered by suburban living. A similar dynamic is playing out in the market.
Mega-cap companies are generally defined as those with market capitalizations exceeding $200 billion. Of course, the largest companies are another order of magnitude larger than that. For example, Meta, which reported stellar earnings this week, has a current market capitalization of $1.65 trillion.
But concerns about its AI buildout expenses wiped $135 billion from its market cap in just four sessions, or put another way, roughly the value on and entire Uber. Market cap is one way to understand how big these companies are, but another is by examining the size of their operations, and their opportunities.
Meta's personal AI agent is designed to be more of an active digital assistant than a conventional conversational chatbot. Muse can open browsers, fill out forms, send emails, schedule appointments, book travel, and (potentially) even make purchases.
To understand how large an economic opportunity this represents for the company, consider what something like that might be worth. $5 per month per user? (Not in subscription fees necessarily, mind you, just monetizable economic value). That seems a bit low for something so powerful. $10/month? Quite realistically. Then consider the size of Meta's ecosystem's daily active user base across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. That number is truly "mega": 3.6 billion, supposedly counting each person only once. If we assume that each of those individuals has and uses a global phone - 5.86 billion unique people on the planet do - that means Meta interacts at least once with 61.4% of them each day.
If Muse is worth $120/year and reaches just 1% of Meta's Daily Active People, that's $4.3 billion/year. If it's worth half that amount, but reaches 20% of their daily actives, that's $43.2 billion/year. The first number seems absurdly low as a back-of-the-napkin figure, but the $135 billion valuation loss in less than a week is offset by $20 billion in revenue (the company trades at just under 7x revenue). If Muse can generate $30 billion in revenues, it is a megacap company in its own right!
So why has the company sold off if everything is so rosy? A massive $25 billion lawsuit in New Mexico, a potential PR headache related to a deal struck between the company and its founder to resolve potential tax liabilities associated with a possible billionaire's tax in California that preserves his voting rights, and, of course, concerns about debt, on the balance sheet and off, to finance the enormous investment that the company is making (and expanding) in AI, and AI jitters generally. But at 20x FY earnings, and less than 17x FY2027 estimated earnings, the company is now pricing a lot of that in. Those headaches create headwinds, but the underlying story provides support.
I like selling December strangles here, specifically the 580/745 strangle, for which one would collect about $21.30/share as of today's closing prices. The trade makes profits virtually anywhere between the 1-year highs and lows - and it's pretty much right in the middle of that range now.

title: Carta and NewView partner, hoping to entice more startups to let employees sell shares early
body:
Startups are staying private longer, leaving employees, who typically take a portion of their compensation as stock they can’t sell, with little hope of early liquidity.
An increasing number of late-stage startups are recognizing this and offering tender offers to employees. These are transactions that allow employees (and, often, early investors) to sell a portion of their shares for a predetermined price to an approved investor.
To simplify the tender process, NewView Capital, which specializes in secondary deals along with typical venture investments, recently partnered with Carta. The collaboration combines NewView’s secondhand deal-structuring experience with Carta’s equity platform. Ravi Viswanathan, founder and managing partner of NewView, pitches this as a way to help startups launch and manage liquidity programs more seamlessly.
“The hope is that this partnership will make it easier for CEOs and companies to think about tenders,” he said. He wants founders to think about giving employees early liquidity as a “win-win-win” for workers, companies, and investors alike.
A growing number of startups seem to agree. Over the past three years, tender offers increased threefold for Series C and later-stage startups, according to a recent study from NewView and Carta. Plus, the startups that do choose tender offers are no longer just the most valuable private companies, like OpenAI, Databricks, or Anduril, according to Viswanathan.
He pointed to marketing customization startup Hightouch, a NewView portfolio company, which held a tender offer at a $1.3 billion valuation last year.
However, Carta and NewView also found that the overall share of startups launching these offerings remains relatively small, with just 44 executed in the first half of 2026 across their dataset. So Viswanathan wants to encourage other startups to consider tender offers, calling them excellent retention tools and morale boosters.
A decade ago, being a unicorn was enough to attract talent, Viswanathan said, but with so many billion-dollar companies around today, that status may not be as much of a draw now. Offering a tender, he said, “is an opportunity to say you will also get liquidity in your journey with us.”
Some of the companies that recently held tender offers include AI customer support startup Decagon , self-driving tech developer Wayve , and AI voice generator ElevenLabs , which executed two such offerings in less than a year.
“The companies are staying private for 12 to 15 years. That’s not changing,” Viswanathan said. “In that interim, so that we don’t have this talent drain from high-quality venture-backed companies into their public counterparts, we need to make sure that there is liquidity for the employees.”

title: Trump denies his envoy’s statement about potential strike on Iran this weekend
body:
WASHINGTON, October 23. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump disavowed statements by US Ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack about the possibility of a strike on Iran this weekend.
Journalists asked the US leader to comment on the statement upon his arrival in Florida. "That was my ambassador?" Trump asked the reporters skeptically. "He's a pretty powerful man, I guess," the president added sarcastically. "Well, if that's the case, I don't know anything about it," he emphasized.
Earlier, when asked by blogger Mario Nawfal if a strike on Iran was possible this weekend, Barrack said: "Absolutely." He added, however, that the goal would not be "regime change.".

title: Moscow court orders four critics to pay Russian billionaire Oleg Deripaska 40 million rubles in defamation case
body: Moscow’s Tagansky District Court has ruled partly in Oleg Deripaska’s favor in his defamation lawsuit against Anti-Corruption Foundation investigators Maria Pevchikh and Sergey Yezhov, former Popular Politics host Irina Alleman, and human rights activist Olga Romanova, the businessman’s lawyer, Alexey Melnikov, told Interfax. Melnikov said the court found that the information the defendants had circulated was false and defamatory. The court also ordered the defendants to pay 40 million rubles in compensation. Deripaska had sought 1 billion rubles from Pevchikh, Yezhov, Alleman, and Romanova. In his lawsuit, Deripaska alleged that for several years, “the defendants have been waging a large-scale campaign against him to tarnish his honor and good name.” The lawsuit stemmed from a video titled “Organized Crime, Officials, Girls: The Criminal Biography of Oleg Deripaska” on the Navalny Live YouTube channel. The video’s description calls Deripaska “an oligarch for whom crime has always been the norm.” Oleg Deripaska has repeatedly sued the Anti-Corruption Foundation. In August 2022, he filed a lawsuit against Alexey Navalny, Maria Pevchikh, Georgy Alburov, and The Insider over an investigation into Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. In October 2022, Moscow’s Zelenogradsky District Court ruled in Deripaska’s favor. He had previously sued over an investigation by Navalny’s team into his yacht vacation with Sergey Prikhodko, then a Russian deputy prime minister, and escort agency employee Nastya Rybka. title: Screening Linked to Fewer CRC Deaths in Basque Adults 50–69
body: “This population-based cohort study in the Basque Country, Spain, examines whether an organized fecal immunochemical test–based screening program was associated with lower colorectal cancer mortality rates from 2004 to 2024… In this cohort study of 438 134 total all-cause deaths among approximately 2.2 million individuals from 2004 to 2024, biennial FIT-based screening was associated with a 50% decline in age-standardized CRC mortality among adults aged 50 to 69 years, with a significant trend inflection observed 3 years after program initiation.” From National Center for Biotechnology Information . title: Fusion Startup Says It Made Gold From Mercury
body: “A San Francisco startup says it has pulled off the alchemist’s oldest dream: turning mercury into real, stable gold. Marathon Fusion says it did it in September with fusion neutrons, at ten times a record CERN set in 2025. Here’s the trick. Deuterium-tritium fusion fires out fast neutrons. When one slams into mercury-198, it knocks a neutron loose, leaving mercury-197. That’s unstable, and over a few days it decays into gold-197, the only stable form of gold. Marathon posted a gamma-ray readout showing mercury-197’s fingerprint, the gold on its way. But here’s the catch. The company hasn’t said how much gold it made, and nobody outside has checked the data. For scale, CERN’s collider made about 29 trillionths of a gram of gold in four years. Ten times tiny is still tiny. The real goal is scale. Marathon’s 2025 paper, still not peer reviewed, says a big fusion plant could make tonnes of gold a year, roughly doubling its revenue.” From Interesting Engineering . The post Fusion Startup Says It Made Gold From Mercury appeared first on Human Progress .

title: College campuses have (largely) gone silent. Can practicing small talk and phone-free spaces change that?
body:
Charlie Harker had high hopes for college.
Before starting her freshman year in 2023, the Lebanon, Ohio, resident had planned to meet people through clubs or at the dorms. She'd expected there would be an open, vibrant atmosphere ripe for making friends. She'd quickly find her people.
"And then I got to school," says the 21-year-old senior at the University of Cincinnati. "I didn't know anyone on my floor. No one had their door open. No one would really talk to you." That fun and peer-filled campus life she'd been promised by both family and pop culture turned out to be, at least to some extent, a relic of the past.
Harker's college experience is fairly common these days. From 2003 to 2025, 20-to 24-year-olds' socializing and communicating in the U.S dropped 52%, from an average of 64 minutes per day in their leisure time to an average of just over 30 minutes per day. Over the same period, 15-to 19-year-olds' leisure time socializing dropped 32% to 38 minutes, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics .
Students these days view school as more "transactional" than in the past, says Steven Rogelberg , Chancellor's professor of organizational science, management and psychology at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. "You go there, you take your classes, and then you leave."
That's a problem for a variety of reasons. If they're not meeting in class or stopping each other in the hallways, young people may be missing out on developing both friendships and social skills , which are critical for long-term life and career success. Making small talk , for instance, can help forge both personal and professional relationships down the line, says Kristie Patten , dean of NYU's Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development.
Also essential: building confidence, which can come both from successfully navigating social situations and making painful mistakes. Without that practice, both campus and life can become more insular and sterile.
"Parents and school systems, and maybe even legislators, are going to have to deal with this if we want a future where we have kids and adults who understand how to be social with one another," says Lance Garrison , dean of the College of Professional Psychology at The Chicago School.
"The trajectory we are on right now is one toward increasing isolation, increasing loneliness, increasing anxiety ."
Some students and schools are tackling their campus antisocial problems head-on. CNBC Make It spoke with 15 students, educators and mental health experts to see how we got here — and where we might be going.
Today's college students were already at a disadvantage, socially speaking, well before stepping foot on campus.
Not only were they forced to isolate during middle school or high school because of the pandemic, many are also finding fewer spaces to meet in real life, as malls and movie theaters — traditional meeting grounds for young people — have shuttered in recent years. "A lot of them never had to build those muscles of how do you socialize in person," says Chicago-based therapist Andrew Fishman .
For some teenagers, that inability to connect meant new norms. "I think a lot of people just got used to not hanging out with people after school," says Harker about high school.
For others, it's made approaching people that much scarier. The less you have a chance to talk to someone new, says Garrison, "the more anxious you are going to be about engaging in those types of activities."
On campus, that could also mean high rates of loneliness . When asked how often they feel or felt lonely in college in a CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll conducted in August 2026, a quarter of 18-to 34-year-olds said "always" or "often," versus just 14% of 35-to 64-year-olds. The modeled error estimate for this survey was plus or minus 3.0 percentage points.
When they finally reach the hallowed halls of their universities, many students are constantly connected to a device. Often, they are heads down in screens or engrossed in whatever's happening in their headphones.
Before class, 19-year-old Karla Berrueto, a junior in standing at the University of Houston, reports: "No one really talks to each other." Twenty-one-year-old Jean Antoine, a senior at Loyola Marymount University, offers a similar appraisal. At the dining hall, it's "more of people with AirPods and watching YouTube sitting alone" than talking, he says.
Even when people go out of their way to connect offline, they're frequently stymied. Franco Geldart, a 20-year-old sophomore at Northeastern University, joined a cooking club his freshman year. He found striking up conversations with people a bit awkward. Often, "I was sitting [there] for an hour and I didn't speak with a single person," he says.
Most of the students CNBC Make It spoke with attended up to a handful of parties per year. Some described them as events you attend with friends and leave, rather than fluid opportunities to engage with new people.
Asked how often they initiate or initiated conversations with people at school they didn't know, 31% of Gen Z said "rarely" or "never," according to the CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll, versus 26% of Millennials and 22% of Gen X.
Another new element of today's campus is the plethora of online platforms on which one can be called out for doing … anything, really, making even the most mundane decisions terrifying.
Yik Yak and Fizz are anonymous digital message boards. Fizz alone is live at more than 800 U.S. college campuses, according to its website . Many schools also have dedicated Barstool Sports Instagram pages, often affiliated with the popular sports blog but unaffiliated with the schools. All three may contain posts making fun of individual students' behavior.
Harker remembers going to a football game her freshman year and losing the friend she came with. She felt paralyzed, scared of trying to befriend people who'd reject her and even more terrified of getting photographed sitting at the game by herself.
"If I just sat there alone," she says she thought, "would I get on the Barstool page?" What would the social repercussions of that be?
Yik Yak, Fizz and Barstool Sports did not respond to CNBC Make It's request for comment.
To be clear, young people are still forging connections on campus. They are figuring it out. Some are even experiencing similar levels of social fluidity as prior generations.
And some see what's been happening on campus and taking action.
Geldart is working on an application for a new club at Northeastern this year called Wildcard. It would partner with existing clubs and do one-off drop-ins in which members from each club would be randomly paired up for a project.
"It's just to get people talking," he says.
At New York University, students have spearheaded a campus-wide initiative called NYU IRL , centered on connecting in the age of technology. With the help of a coalition of deans, faculty, staff and grad students, NYU IRL projects include phone-free spaces, a phone breakup challenge with Catherine Price , author of "How to Break Up With Your Phone," and a video series about how to make small talk. More than 1,000 students have signed up for the phone breakup challenge alone.
For her part, Harker found someone she knew at the football game where she'd lost her friend and the two became each other's go-to game date. She joined a sorority and now lives in a house with a number of her friends.
Harker's working on creating more opportunities for people to meet. She remembers attending one house party her freshman year, for example. "It was the best experience I ever had," she says. It was an easy, casual way to get to know people. Harker and her roommates are now trying to replicate that experience.
"We have this thing," she says, "we're going to bring back house parties."

title: Brent crude oil tops $116, a six-month high, as tensions swell in the Middle East
body:
Brent crude oil rose to a six-month high on Friday, as investors increasingly expect the U.S. to resume strikes on Iran in the coming weeks.
Brent futures gained 3.1% to close at $116.72 a barrel, the highest settlement for the international benchmark since April 29. U.S. West Texas Intermediate added 3.8% to settle at $103.27 a barrel.
Iran's army chief, meanwhile, said the country's military is fully prepared for "asymmetric warfare" after strengthening its capabilities, according to the state media agency Tasnim .
Brent added 6.2% for the week, the third consecutive week of gains. WTI advanced 2% for the week.
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. was not negotiating with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon." His cryptic remarks came as U.S. officials told The New York Times that the U.S. and Israel have plans for fresh strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
Iran-allied Houthi militants have continued to strike Saudi Arabia.The U.S. State Department has ordered all non-essential personnel to leave Saudi Arabia due to the strikes.
A drone attack targeting the Shaybah oil field Wednesday in the Eastern Region left two people dead and two injured, according to Saudi state media. At least two people were killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday.
Oil giant Saudi Aramco have told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely following a series of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Reuters reported .

title: AI-Designed Virus Used to Treat a Patient’s Infection
body: “For the first time, scientists say they have used viruses designed by artificial intelligence to treat a human patient. Researchers announced on Tuesday that they had administered the virus, known as a phage, to a patient suffering from a deadly bacterial infection. Phages attack bacteria, and the hope is that this one will kill the microbes causing the infection. Radical Numerics, the start-up that created the viruses, posted a technical report about them on its website. But the company declined to provide information about the patient or the doctors running the trial, citing confidentiality requirements. The report has not been peer reviewed or published in a scientific journal. Company officials said the trial had been authorized by the Food and Drug Administration.” From New York Times . L3Harris said it offers greater range, speed and operational flexibility than current systems but did not release performance figures. Compatibility with existing launchers The contract supports the Xtended Range Counter-sUAS Missile program at the Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation & Missile Center. L3Harris is developing the weapon for compatibility with existing U.S. military platforms to simplify integration. “We are leveraging L3Harris’ deep technical expertise across propulsion, guidance and advanced manufacturing to deliver a next-generation interceptor that meets the Army’s evolving mission requirements,” said Scott Alexander, president of Propulsion Systems within L3Harris’ Missile Solutions business. “This design combines innovative propulsion with advanced seeker technologies to provide a highly capable, modular and cost-effective solution deployable from existing launch platforms.” Ramjet technology supports longer range L3Harris said its approach to air-breathing ramjet engines would improve fuel efficiency and extend engagement range. The interceptor combines propulsion and seeker technologies in a modular design. The announcement did not identify compatible launchers or give a flight-test timetable. It also provided no unit-cost estimate or date for operational deployment.

title: Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war has redrawn global energy markets
body:
Before the Iran war, Qatar was one of the biggest natural gas exporters in the world. After only eight months, the Gulf state is now buying supplies from its principal competitor — the United States.
QatarEnergy struck a deal Thursday with U.S. exporter Cheniere Energy to buy 4 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, annually through 2054. The purchase price is indexed to the U.S. Henry Hub price plus a fixed fee. Deliveries are expected to begin in the 2030s.
"We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century," Cheniere CEO Jack Fusco said in a statement.
The gas that Doha will buy is less than 1% of the global LNG trade of more than 400 million metric tons. But "in terms of an individual deal, this is about as big as you see in the U.S," said Alex Munton, director of global gas and LNG at Rapidan Energy in Houston.
The deal signals how the Iran war is reshaping global energy markets to the benefit of U.S. companies, cementing the dominance of American LNG exporters. Shares of Cheniere and Venture Global , the other independent U.S. player, have gained 26% and 40%, respectively, since the start of the war.
Qatar was second only to the U.S. in LNG exports before the war. But shipments have since collapsed in the eight months since Iran bombed its key production facility at Ras Laffan. The attack badly damaged two production lines, taking out about 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity.
It will take about three years to repair the damage at Ras Laffan, Qatar's energy minister, Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, has said. The Persian Gulf state has declared force majeure — citing unexpected, uncontrollable events preventing contracts from being honored — every month since the March attack.
"It did give us a big blow, if you will, for our production capability for the next few years," Al-Kaabi said in an interview on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in September. Qatar is exporting "very little" LNG right now because "we can't export through the Hormuz Strait," he said. "Very sparingly, some ships are crossing the straits but a very small amount, it's not something that would even be measurable in a percentage point," the energy minister said.
And it is far from clear what security conditions in Hormuz will look like when the repairs are done at Ras Laffan. The decades-long contract with Cheniere indicates that Qatar sees a risk that freedom of navigation will never return to Hormuz as Iran keeps attacking tankers, Munton said.
It is harder to find ways to get around Hormuz in the case of LNG because it is fundamentally a waterborne product, the analyst said.
"It's liquefied so it can be put on a ship and that requires access to seaborne routes," Munton said. "They've got to access the Strait of Hormuz. There's no other way of getting LNG to market. They're just stuck."
With its production badly damaged and Hormuz blocked off, QatarEnergy is expanding its LNG trading business through the Cheniere deal, Munton said.
It secured a $3 billion loan earlier this month from Chinese banks that could allow it to secure more U.S. LNG to honor its international delivery commitments, said Manav Gupta, a UBS analyst, in a note to clients Thursday.
Venture Global, for example, is in advanced talks with QatarEnergy to supply 3 million metric tons annually, unnamed sources told Reuters .
With the Qatar deal, Cheniere is disproving the bears' case that it will struggle to secure incremental sales which would in turn constrain capacity expansion, Gupta said. UBS has a stock price target of $340 on Cheniere, implying 18% upside from Thursday's close.
Wall Street is broadly bullish on both Cheniere and Venture Global. Nearly 90% of equity analysts who cover Cheniere rate it a buy, with an average price target of $314, implying about 9% upside from Thursday's close.
Nearly 60% of analysts recommend Venture Global as a buy with the rest rating it a hold. The average price target of $17 would amount to some 35% upside from Thursday's close.
"The U.S. once again is being called on by buyers to diversify supply," Munton said. "So much is under construction in the U.S. that you get to the point where now the U.S. is becoming disproportionately big in terms of global [LNG] market share."
