title: Malaria Has Fallen Sharply on Bioko Island
body: “Bioko island, off mainland Equatorial Guinea, has managed to sharply reduce malaria infections and deaths. Bioko, roughly half the size of Rhode Island, has used familiar tools: indoor spraying, mosquito nets and keeping control of the larvae population. Its success, however, has depended on something less easily replicated: two decades of painstaking data collection, sustained funding and workers going door to door to win residents’ trust. Now the tiny, oil-rich country wants to bring that approach to its mainland and eliminate malaria altogether.” From Associated Press . The post Malaria Has Fallen Sharply on Bioko Island appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Turkish Amazon armoured vehicles spotted in Libya
body: Video footage circulating online shows dozens of Turkish-made BMC AMAZON 4×4 armored vehicles in service withLibyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF) that controls eastern Libya. The LAAF released a video of the event on 17 October showing about 90 vehicles that looked identical to the improved version of the Amazon made by the Turkish company BMC other than they had the initials ANS embossed on their front where BMC is usually written, raising the possibility they were assembled under license, similar to two different unmarked armoured vehicles supplied to Libyan forces in 2020. Libya remains split between the Government of National Unity in Tripoli and the eastern authorities aligned with Khalifa Haftar. Turkish equipment has historically flowed to the Tripoli side, which makes the western government the likelier customer. That is an inference, not a confirmed fact. The AMAZON is the smallest vehicle in BMC Otomotiv’s armored family. BMC first showed it publicly at the Eurosatory exhibition in Paris in 2016. It carries up to seven people and uses a V-shaped hull, which deflects mine and roadside bomb blasts away from the crew compartment. Unveiled in 2023, the improved version of the Amazon has only previously been seen in service in Syria, with the original version being in service in Qatar and Turkmenistan. BMC says the vehicle reaches 120 km/h (75 mph) and travels about 800 km (500 miles) on one tank of fuel. Those are manufacturer figures. The remote-controlled weapon station, or RCWS, is a common option. It usually carries a 7.62 mm or 12.7 mm machine gun that the crew aims and fires from inside, using cameras and a screen. The gunner stays under armor, which matters in patrol and checkpoint work where exposure is the main risk. The parade also included several 4×4 armoured vehicles that looked like the Jordanian-made Al-Wahsh fitted with remotely operated weapon stations for anti-tank guided missiles, a combination not previously seen in Libya. The launchers looked similar to the ones developed by the Jordanian company Jadara for its Terminator missile, which looks like the RK-3 used with the Ukrainian Corsar laser beam-riding system. The LAAF also displayed jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that looked identical to the Belarusian Mirotvorets (peacemaker) alongside two trailer-mounted pneumatic launchers. Turkey’s footprint in Libya Türkiye has been a main military partner of Tripoli since 2019, when the two governments signed a security agreement alongside a maritime memorandum covering Eastern Mediterranean borders. Ankara later sent advisers, drones and armored vehicles. In 2022 the two sides signed protocols on Libyan Air Force capability and pilot training. In 2025 the Government of National Unity and the Turkish defense ministry agreed to upgrade the readiness and technical capacity of Libyan army personnel. Turkish armored vehicles have a track record there. In May 2019 forces aligned with the then-government in Tripoli published photos of more than a dozen BMC Kirpi II mine-protected vehicles unloading at Tripoli port. The Kirpi is a larger 4×4 mine-resistant ambush-protected, or MRAP, vehicle. The delivery came while a UN arms embargo was in force, and the eastern-based Libyan National Army responded by announcing a naval blockade of western ports. The Kirpi did not earn universal praise. A Military Africa report from 2020 described Libyan National Army tests on captured Kirpi vehicles and called their performance poor. Turkey also reportedly deployed M60 main battle tanks to Libya in 2020. The supplied background also lists a lone Akinci armed drone seen in Libya in 2024 and a 2022 Libyan order for the Hürkuş-C light combat aircraft. The legal and political frame Turkey’s military presence now has a firm legal footing. Reporting from Türkiye Today says the Turkish parliament approved a 24-month extension of the Turkish Armed Forces mission in Libya on 22 Dec 2025, with the new term starting in January 2026. That runs the mandate to roughly early 2028. The mission mainly covers training and advice. The motion cited the lack of elections in Libya and the need to protect a fragile ceasefire. A steady flow of Turkish-made vehicles fits that pattern, because training missions generate demand for the equipment being taught. Apparently, Turkish suppliers moving from heavy armor toward lighter vehicles for internal security. That suits policing, border and checkpoint work better than front-line combat. It also keeps Turkish hardware in Libyan hands at a time when Ankara’s advisers are embedded with those same forces.

title: Russia’s attacks on Black Sea shipping raise risk of global famine, German FM warns
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned that disruptions to global shipping routes could trigger famine in vulnerable countries, citing Russian attacks on Black Sea shipping as part of the wider threat to international food supplies. Russia has increasingly targeted civilian shipping in the Black Sea as part of its campaign against Ukraine’s maritime trade, striking cargo vessels, port infrastructure, and ships transporting agricultural goods. The attacks threaten Ukraine’s ability to export grain to global markets, raise risks for international shipping companies, and jeopardize food supplies in countries that rely on Ukrainian agricultural exports. Speaking ahead of a meeting of foreign ministers in Istanbul on Friday, 23 October, Wadephul said attacks and threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Black Sea were disrupting trade in food and fertilizers, DW reported . The impact extends far beyond the conflict zones, threatening countries that depend on imported wheat and agricultural inputs. Wadephul said fertilizer shortages could threaten basic agricultural production in poorer countries, where access to imported food and farming supplies is already limited. He also pointed to Türkiye, the world’s largest wheat-processing country, as vulnerable to disruptions in the supply of grain. Russian attacks disrupt Ukraine’s grain exports Russia has intensified attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports and civilian cargo ships, disrupting a maritime corridor that carries most of the country’s agricultural exports. In July, Russian strikes brought traffic through the corridor close to a standstill during the harvest season, leaving grain with fewer routes to international markets. The attacks have also hit foreign-flagged vessels carrying or preparing to load Ukrainian grain. On 16 October, Euromaidan Press reported that Russian attacks had sunk merchant ships and damaged others in the Black Sea region, with seafarers missing. The campaign has increased risks for shipping companies and reduced the routes available for Ukrainian exports. Ukraine is a major supplier of wheat and other agricultural commodities to global markets, including countries in the Middle East and Africa. Disruptions to its exports can tighten global supplies and push prices higher, adding pressure on countries that depend on imported grain. Wadephul made the remarks ahead of a meeting of foreign ministers in Istanbul, where he said countries must send a signal that they will not accept Iran or Yemen’s Houthi militia holding global trade hostage. He called for an end to indiscriminate attacks on shipping and neighboring countries, warning that prolonged insecurity puts vulnerable populations at greater risk of hunger. His remarks place Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian shipping within a wider pattern of threats to key maritime trade routes, with consequences for food security far beyond the regions directly affected. title: Dessa: the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built
body:
We believe voice is the most natural way to interact with intelligence, so we created Dessa, the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built. Talking with it feels like talking with a person…full of emotion, nuance, pauses, and a natural cadence.
Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous.
We trained Dessa from scratch on nothing but human conversation. Sounds! No text, no pretrained models. It learned to hold a real-time conversation simply by listening. As far as we know, Dessa is the world’s first AI you can have a realistic live conversation with that was trained only from human speech.
Dessa advances the frontier of deep learning models and creates a different category with entirely new and interesting behaviors for researchers to discover. How efficiently do they learn language and facts compared to text? How efficiently can they learn new languages? What sorts of In-context learning can they perform?
Every clip below is a live recording of a person talking to Dessa. Nobody steers it. Dessa picks what to say, when to say it and how, down to its own voice and personality. Subtitles were added afterward.
It laughs the moment something’s funny, mid-sentence, the way people do. Other models wait for you to finish, then laugh on cue. Ask it to speak up and it gets louder. Nobody taught it that.
The person blanks on a movie title. Dessa finishes the sentence. It also knows a surprising amount, considering every fact it has come from raw sound.
A surprise. Dessa gasps “oh my god” under its breath, then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude.
In this demo, Dessa is talking with GPT-Live-1, a third-party AI model. Both voices are AI-generated. The developer of GPT-Live-1 is not affiliated with Block and has not reviewed or endorsed Dessa.
More recordings will be shared on X soon.
Audio in, audio out. Dessa is a true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech. It’s full-duplex, so it listens and talks at the same time, like you do. It learned from real conversation, so it knows when to cut in and when to backchannel (“yeah!”, “got it!”, “ooh”) to show it’s with you. Inference runs faster than real time, so there’s no awkward wait. And it runs locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better.
It natively hears and speaks emotion, sarcasm, laughter, a frustrated sigh, a voice cracking with sadness. Run speech through text and all of that is gone, which is why most voice AI feels stilted, slow and, worst of all, annoying.
LLMs need an insane amount of text. Dessa learned language from hundreds of times fewer words (in fairness, LLMs also have to learn C++ and whatever the hell Angular is).
And it had to learn far more than language. Accents, pauses, breathing, sarcasm, humor, inflection, emotion, when to cut in: every one changes what someone means. Say “I didn’t say she stole my CUDA code” out loud, stressing a different word each time. Same words, different meaning every time.
Speech never repeats. Say a sentence twice, exactly the same way, and the data still comes out different. Text is identical no matter who types it. And a single spoken word takes thousands of times more bytes than the same word in text. People learn to talk so easily that we forget how hard it is. For a machine with no text to lean on, it’s brutal.
But, we figured it out. And we figured out how to train Dessa on only one NVIDIA GB200 NVL72.
Three reasons: curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety. Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.
Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing.
AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it.
We’re a (very) small AI research lab at Block, founded by former members of Dessa, the Toronto deep learning startup. We’ve built deep learning models since 2012 and generative speech models for over eight years. We chase frontier problems others ignore, and we report directly to Jack Dorsey, Block’s cofounder, Chairman and Block Head.
A model that learned to talk from sound alone is new territory, and we want outside eyes on it. We’re giving a small group of AI safety researchers early access to find the risks we haven’t anticipated. If that’s you, get in touch .
In this demo, Dessa is talking with GPT-Live-1, a third-party AI model. Both voices are AI-generated. The developer of GPT-Live-1 is not affiliated with Block and has not reviewed or endorsed Dessa.

title: Op-Ed: Nicaragua mining – the golden bridgehead threatening US national security
body: (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, Nicholas Vafeas) In the wake of Daniel Ortega’s July declaration , formalizing the end of competitive elections, Western commentary focused almost entirely on the death of Nicaraguan democracy. From one geopolitical perspective, this is catastrophic. From another, it creates something of an oasis of mineral opportunity. But from a national defense perspective, it represents something far more immediate: the formal establishment of a sovereign, state-backed resource bridgehead inside the Western Hemisphere. For much of the last century, the Western Hemisphere has operated under a geopolitical reality that placed the United States as the dominant power, and countries that strayed too far outside its political and economic orbit discovered fairly quickly that Washington has a long reach. China has spent the better part of two decades testing the boundaries of that reality, and Nicaragua presents a textbook case. The critical minerals debate has become obsessed with pure geology, but mineral security is not determined by geology alone. It is determined by who controls access to that geology, under what political conditions, and for how long. Managua’s new institutional framework completely flips that calculation on its head. By removing competitive elections from the equation, long-term political continuity (and foreign state access) suddenly becomes much easier to price. China has already accumulated an extraordinary mineral footprint in the country, and it’s not difficult to understand the attraction. Nicaragua sits on the highly prospective Central American volcanic arc, home to high-grade epithermal gold systems like the 50km La India district, with an estimated Net Present Value of $1.4 billion. (For perspective, Japan’s Hishikari mine, one of the world’s richest epithermal deposits, occupies only a few kilometres of strike). But it’s worth remembering why gold holds value. In national defense terms, it is far more than commercial bullion. Physical gold extracted within an isolated autocracy represents off-grid, sanctions-proof war liquidity. A direct financial mechanism to keep the Ortega regime afloat and insulated from Western economic pressure. Whats more, epithermal gold systems rarely produce gold in isolation. They carry critical defense co-metals like antimony, tellurium, and silver. All materials essential for infrared sensors, night-vision optics, and military munition fuses. Recognising this potential, by early 2026, Chinese state-aligned firms had reportedly been granted mining concessions covering more than one million hectares, equivalent to roughly 8.5% of Nicaragua’s territory . The expansion has been remarkably rapid, with Chinese firms moving from a limited presence only a few years ago to becoming some of the largest holders of mineral rights in the country. To put it plainly, controlling 8.5% of a Central American state carries a massive physical, logistical, and intelligence footprint. Mining concessions bring heavy earth-moving equipment, surface survey rights, dual-use airstrips, heavy telecommunications infrastructure, and potential deepwater logistics flanking both the Caribbean and Pacific coasts. Positioned barely 1,000 miles from the U.S. border and sitting directly alongside the Panama Canal, this embeds a state-backed adversary presence firmly inside USSOUTHCOM’s primary Area of Responsibility. This is not a hypothetical Chinese resource strategy waiting to happen, but a lived reality. Political risk does not disappear, it changes ownership. In general terms, mining investors and private equity firms are typically wary of political instability, because elections introduce what financial models can never fully price: political discontinuity. Concessions agreed under one administration can suddenly find themselves under scrutiny by the next. Ortega’s decision changes that, effectively handing China a golden key. If the current political system remains intact, Chinese companies holding mineral concessions no longer need to consider the possibility of an opposition government coming to power in 2026, 2031, or beyond. Of course, that does not make Nicaragua politically low-risk. Quite the opposite actually, since it creates a highly asymmetric risk environment. For Western companies dependent on transparent institutions, independent courts, ESG mandates, and Western finance, the jurisdiction becomes unworkable. But for Chinese firms trading capital for regime survival, policy continuity becomes unusually strong. As seen across Africa and elsewhere, China’s advantage has never simply been that Chinese companies are willing to tolerate more risk. Rather, Chinese firms can sometimes operate in political environments where the risks facing Western investors are fundamentally different from those facing them. And Nicaragua is quickly becoming an extreme example. It’s an asymmetry that is rooted in capital architecture. Western mining firms answer to public stock markets and quarterly profit targets, making 30-year political risks nearly impossible to justify to a corporate board. Chinese state-owned companies answer to five-year state plans. Because they aren’t chasing short-term stock returns, they can ride out local political chaos to lock in decades of control over vital resources. Nicaragua doesn’t need to become the next Congo There is a temptation to judge Nicaragua’s strategic importance by slapping mineral labels on it. But in reality, it almost doesn’t matter. Nicaragua does not need to become another Democratic Republic of Congo, Indonesia, or Chile to matter to China. Chinese resource security is built through portfolios. Those familiar with the game of Monopoly will know that winning is not simply about owning the best property. It’s about owning ALL the property to restrict everyone else’s movement. That is optionality. In military circles, there is a brilliant term for this: “Anti-Access/Area Denial”, which basically involves preventing an adversary force from deploying, and then restricting its freedom from any further action. In much the same way, uncontested control over large swathes of Nicaragua’s geology gives China extraordinary optionality while executing a pre-emptive resource lockout. If an Indo-Pacific crisis severs Asian critical mineral supply chains, the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency and Western defense primes would naturally look to near-shore resources in the Western Hemisphere. By buying up “Nicaragua Street,” Beijing makes sure that when Western defense strategists look to secure their own backyard, the prospective geology is already locked down under 30-year state-backed concessions. This mineral footprint connects directly to broader strategy. Since Managua severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan and signed a Free Trade Agreement with Beijing in 2024, diplomatic recognition, trade, infrastructure, and mining have moved as a unified system. Viewed together, mineral access is both a beneficiary of that political relationship and the economic anchor that solidifies it. Because Nicaragua is increasingly isolated from Western institutions, Chinese capital becomes the regime’s primary lifeline. It is a beautifully crafted feedback loop. The further Managua moves from democratic governance, the harder Western investment becomes. The harder Western investment becomes, the more valuable Chinese capital becomes. And as that capital becomes economically embedded (backed by sanctions-proof gold reserves) Nicaragua becomes increasingly capable of withstanding Western diplomatic and economic pressure. The western hemisphere matters This exposes the core flaw in Western critical mineral strategy. If critical minerals are increasingly treated as a matter of economic and national security, analysis can no longer stop at resource geology and processing plants. It has to extend into the political systems, physical footprints, and sovereign relationships that dictate whether that resource can actually be secured in a crisis. China has understood this. By converting political alignment into physical, long-term territorial control in Central America, China has rewritten the rules of hemispheric defense, leaving Western strategists trying to play a market game on a board where the key spaces have already been taken. Nicholas Vafeas is the founder and director of BluMelt Mineral Consulting Limited, an independent consultancy specialising in geological assurance, critical mineral intelligence and investment de-risking.

title: AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan.
body: Welcome to another edition of Road to KubeCon ! We’re tracking movements in the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem as we count down to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 November 9–12 in Salt Lake City. Half of our column this week focuses on untangling Kubernetes as we add the demands of agentic AI: automating pod-restart troubleshooting, syncing communication between the scheduler and autoscaler, and maturing how we distribute inference across a cloud-native stack. The other half goes deeper into what we need to look at closely in Kubernetes environments: What context’s missing, what slips through the gaps in metrics, and whether the AI agents you already use are really worth their salt as SREs. Let’s get into it. HPE on automating pod restarts in AI development As more enterprises turn to Kubernetes for large-scale AI and machine learning jobs, they’re hitting a common obstacle: pod restarts. This is something that HPE has noticed as customers utilize its HPE Private Cloud AI (PCAI) to host long-running AI/ML workloads on inherently ephemeral container-based infrastructure like Kubernetes. Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments. According to HPE system software engineer Guoping Jia , Kubernetes provides some troubleshooting commands out of the box, but it still requires extensive manual investigation. “This operational workflow does not scale effectively in PCAI’s large-cluster environment,” writes Jia on the HPE blog . His solution involves smarter automation for troubleshooting, using an open-source Kubernetes troubleshooting tool, k8s-pod-restart-info-collector , to automatically gather details and send diagnostic information straight to a Slack channel. It’s one helpful strategy to improve usability for Kubernetes operators. Will the scheduler and autoscaler unite? There’s been a lot of talk recently about how Kubernetes is evolving to meet AI’s new demands. This week, AWS senior software development managers Sajjan Gundapuneedi and Neelendra Bhandari weighed in with this blog post on how AI is reshaping Kubernetes autoscaling. The core problem they highlight is friction between the scheduler, which places pods on existing nodes, and the autoscaler, which adds new ones, when managing GPU accelerators on Kubernetes. Often the two sides aren’t on the same page, leaving pods pending and pricey GPUs sitting idle. Capacity reservations, device topology, and GPU sharing complicate things further. “A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it.” “A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it,” the authors write. “Inference is what makes this pressing rather than academic, since bursty serving and agentic workloads have no patience for a cold node.” To them, solutions are already taking shape: dynamic resource allocation (DRA)-aware autoscalers, workload-aware scheduling , and a companion mechanism, provisioning requests , to bridge the two sides. Still, they expect the autoscaler to grow into “a more scheduler-aware partner.” Deeper integration is underway, too. A public proposal in the SIG-Autoscaling group sketches APIs that would let the two loops talk directly, so the scheduler could see capacity that could be provisioned, express placement preferences across it, and request it explicitly. Distributed AI inference grows up with llm-d v1.0 release On Tuesday, at PyTorch Conference North America , the CNCF sandbox project llm-d reached v1.0 . The project now bridges AI application developers in the PyTorch ecosystem and the production cloud-native stack. Carlos Costa , co-founder and lead maintainer of llm-d, and a distinguished engineer on IBM’s hybrid cloud platform for AI, says the v1.0 release signals maturity. “This is the moment open source AI serving crosses from experimental projects into dependable infrastructure you can build on,” Costa tells The New Stack . Whereas earlier versions focused on proving state-of-the-art performance, v1.0 is about sustaining that performance in production, he adds. llm-d has already seen plenty of use at Tesla , AWS, Oracle , Google, and beyond. Costa adds that a recent IBM Research demonstration found that an agent factory exploring quantum error correction hardware ran at 11.5x lower inference cost on open models with llm-d than on an all-proprietary configuration. “This demonstration shows where llm-d really shines: agentic workloads,” he says, adding that it absorbs bursty agentic traffic and, in IBM’s test, pushed cache reuse to about 98%. From building models to operating frontier intelligence at scale For a taste of the type of discussion to expect at KubeCon NA, let’s briefly visit the East. Chris Aniszczyk , CTO at CNCF, set the stage very well at last month’s KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026 in Shanghai, in the talk Operating Frontier Intelligence at Scale with Xiao Zhang. As he puts it, it’s not just about models anymore. It’s about putting them all to work. “AI is essentially moving from just purely about building the greatest models [to] how do we actually make this run at scale, stitch it all together and run in different types of environments,” says Aniszczyk. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince recently declared that bot traffic, driven by AI agents, has passed human traffic online for the first time. Aniszczyk says that shift is putting tremendous pressure on systems, pointing to recent GitHub outages . As inference becomes the predominant workload, everything shifts. “It’s the craziest kind of technology change that I’ve seen probably in my career.” This shift is causing all sorts of side problems, he notes, from building new infrastructure to building more data centers to ensuring enough power is available. “It’s the craziest kind of technology change that I’ve seen probably in my career,” says Aniszczyk. Still, he’s an optimist, framing it as a fun problem and challenge for the cloud-native community to tackle together. Promoting your AI agent to the SRE role Plenty of AI site reliability engineer (SRE) platforms are emerging. But according to Roy Libman , CPO, Radar ( Skyhook.io ), your next SRE hire might be right under your fingertips: the AI coding agent you already use. The trick is giving it the right context. “The coding agent your engineers use, whether that’s Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, can already investigate a Kubernetes cluster,” writes Libman on the CNCF blog . “What it usually lacks is context: what’s failing right now, and what changed before it broke.” In his benchmark of 50 injected faults on a live cluster, Claude Code, given read-only context through MCP tools, diagnosed slightly more accurately than with shell and kubectl access. The bigger difference was speed: with context, it reached a correct diagnosis within two minutes on 86% of faults, versus 60% with a shell. It’s an interesting sign that context is king for diagnosing complex errors, and that you might not need to shell (pun intended) out for another AI subscription just to triage issues. Industry take: what goes undetected in Kubernetes A previous Road to KubeCon asked what’s still missing with OTel and Prometheus. Well, one gap is state that isn’t a time series, like slowlog entries, client lists, and access control list (ACL) changes, shares Kristiyan Ivanov , former engineering manager at Redis , current contributor to Valkey , and founding CTO of BetterDB . “These get lost between scrapes,” he tells The New Stack . “Metrics count, but they don’t explain.” Metrics count, but they don’t explain.” According to Ivanov, much goes undetected in Kubernetes because Valkey and Redis keep evidence in in-memory buffers, which Prometheus reduces to lengths and counters. “Kubernetes makes this even worse in several ways,” he says, noting that pod restarts, failovers, and ephemeral pod IPs worsen tracking. “Almost everything in the ecosystem is an INFO scraper,” he says. “Missing across the board: durable history across restarts and failovers, attribution to a service or ACL user, an audit trail of ACL and config changes, and aggregation across shards.” Emerging approaches are helping cloud operators see these gaps. He points to improvements in Valkey’s detection capabilities and OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation to enable granular tracing. But eBPF can’t see evictions, ACL denials, or configuration changes, he says. Those require engine-level collection. As Kubernetes evolves, so do the demands on the teams running it. Presenting sponsor HPE helps teams address that complexity with software spanning virtualization, cloud management, observability, and automation. Half can’t measure AI agents effectively Eighty-seven percent of respondents say monitoring AI is a priority, yet over half admit they can’t effectively measure AI quality, like LLM response quality, or control AI costs, found Splunk State of Observability 2026 , which surveyed 2,050 ITOps and engineering professionals and was released Oct. 20. The report also found 83% are concerned about the unintended consequences of AI agents. This tracks with agentic AI’s tendency to take unexpected actions and create bursty traffic patterns, both of which are driving major infrastructure changes. “Most companies will soon have far more agents at work than people,” said Jeetu Patel, president and chief product officer at Cisco, in the press release . Monitoring AI is also driving more collaboration between observability and security teams, according to 81% of respondents. More updates from the cloud-native universe The excitement around cloud native never sleeps. Here are a few more community, project, and vendor updates from the past week or so. Congratulations to Anish Bista , the first Golden Kubestronaut from Nepal ! Kubernetes v1.38.0 is targeted for release on Wednesday, December 16. Per the release schedule , Kubernetes 1.34 hits end of life October 27. Fairwinds shares lessons from running n8n in production on Amazon EKS . Broadcom’s AAI v26 adds cost tracking and Kubernetes support; see EMA’s impact brief . Splunk now lets teams remotely configure OpenTelemetry Collectors on Kubernetes. New Relic shipped v4.8.2 of its Kubernetes integration with dependency updates. One more stop on the Road to KubeCon Road to KubeCon is an eight-part series presented by HPE. Before you go, explore how HPE Software helps IT teams do more with less complexity. This series is almost over — only one edition remains. We’ll be here next week to round things off with a special sign-off for Road to KubeCon. In the meantime, you can catch up on previous editions in the Road to KubeCon archive . Bill Doerrfeld, the writer of this series, is open to community pitches. Feel free to share interesting takes, new releases, or tips on the best dive bar in Salt Lake City. He accepts direct messages on LinkedIn , or you can reach him through his personal contact page . The post AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan. appeared first on The New Stack .

title: Environmental officials fear new wave of harassment if Flavio Bolsonaro wins in Brazil
body: Federal civil servants in environmental and Indigenous affairs fear a resurgence of the intimidation and institutional harassment they faced under the administration of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro (2019-2022) if his son, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, wins the presidency in Brazil. The candidate has announced that he will eliminate “environmental hurdles” so rural landowners can do “whatever they want on their land.” “We literally have a target in the middle of our forehead,” Tânia Maria de Souza, president of the federal environmental civil servants’ association, Ascema, told Mongabay. “It’s déjà vu.” The Bolsonaro administration brought a relentless series of actions against the environment and Indigenous rights. Bolsonaro refused to demarcate any Indigenous territories, fulfilling his 2018 campaign pledge, while deforestation and violence against Indigenous groups and public servants escalated alongside measures to open Indigenous lands to mining and agribusiness in clear violation of the Federal Constitution. “It was traumatic,”Alexandre Bahia Gontijo, former director of Ascema and former president of Asibama-DF, which represents IBAMA civil servants in the Federal District, said of the Bolsonaro administration. “Everyone is extremely apprehensive.” Activists call Flávio’s agenda “the return of the cattle herd,” referencing a 2020 statement by then-Environment Minister Ricardo Salles that the COVID-19 pandemic was an opportunity to “let the cattle herd run through” by changing environmental rules and regulations without drawing scrutiny from the National Congress and the press. Former Environment Minister Ricardo Salles left, with former President Jair Bolsonaro (right). Image courtesy of Marcos Corrêa/PR. Flávio finished first in the opening round…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: From Toast to Bessemer: Who founders will hear from at TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026
body:
Building a startup means making decisions before you have all the answers.
When should you scale? How do you know you really have product-market fit? What does it take to land enterprise customers? How do you build the right team? And when you finally get in front of an investor, how do you make sure your pitch earns another conversation?
On November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston, TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 will bring together founders, investors, and operators who have tackled those questions from different sides of the table.
Hosted by TechCrunch in partnership with Fidelity Private Shares, the full-day event goes beyond fundraising and AI to explore the realities of finding customers, building teams, sharpening a pitch, developing founder leadership, and scaling companies both inside and outside traditional startup hubs. Save 25% on your ticket today , and bring a colleague along for free with our limited BOGO deal .
Boston founders do not have to look far for an example of what can happen when a startup finds its market and continues evolving with its customers.
Steve Fredette , president, co-founder, and director of Toast , takes the Impact Stage for “Building a Company That Keeps Reinventing Itself.”
Toast’s story offers founders a compelling case study in identifying a customer problem, finding product-market fit, winning customers, and ultimately scaling a Boston startup into a public company.
But reaching scale does not mean the work is finished. Fredette’s conversation will look at what it takes to continue evolving a company as customer expectations, technology, and the market change around it, while staying connected to the needs that helped create the business in the first place.
Growth can be exciting. Growing too early can be expensive.
Kent Bennett , partner at Bessemer Venture Partners , will lead “Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale,” focusing on one of the most important questions an early-stage founder can answer: Are customers actually telling you that you are ready to grow?
The session will give founders a chance to think more critically about the signals that matter before adding headcount, increasing spend, or accelerating go-to-market efforts.
It is a useful counterpoint to startup culture’s constant pressure to move faster. Sometimes the smartest next move is making sure the foundation is actually there.
That same tension takes center stage with Rudina Seseri , founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures .
In “When to Scale and When to Hit the Brakes,” Seseri will explore how founders can distinguish between the moments that call for acceleration and the moments when restraint may protect the business.
Founders are constantly making trade-offs between growth and discipline. Knowing when not to scale can be just as consequential as knowing when to go all in.
AI is reshaping how new companies think about products, operations, and teams, but adding AI to an existing process is different from building a company around it from the start.
Lior Div , CEO and co-founder of 7AI , will tackle that distinction in “Built for AI From Day One.”
For founders building in the current technology environment, the conversation provides an opportunity to think beyond AI as a feature and toward how it can influence the architecture and operating model of an entire company.
The startup world does not begin and end in Silicon Valley.
Chase Garbarino , CEO and co-founder of HqO , will take the Impact Stage for “The Boston Founder Playbook,” examining what it means to build and scale a company from Boston.
For founders across New England and the broader East Coast ecosystem, the conversation offers a particularly relevant perspective on talent, customers, capital, and community outside the Bay Area.
Combined with Fredette’s Toast story, it also gives this year’s Summit a strong local through line: Ambitious companies can be built in Boston, and founders here do not need to copy Silicon Valley to do it.
A pitch does not have to close the deal. It has to make someone want the next conversation.
Dave Balter , venture partner at True Ventures and CEO of Edisyl , will explore that idea in “Your Pitch Has to Earn the Next Conversation.”
For founders accustomed to explaining their companies every day, the session is a reminder that knowing your business and communicating its story are two different skills.
Later in the afternoon, attendees will see that theory put into practice.
Catch the full list of Founders Summit speakers here .
At “So You Think You Can Pitch?,” founders will put their stories to the test live on the Build Stage.
Balter will be joined by Chirag Shah , partner at Define Ventures , and Simran Suri , principal at Maveron , as startups make their cases in front of an investor judging panel.
For attendees, it is an opportunity to watch what happens when founders have limited time to make an idea connect, and to hear how investors react in real time.
It is one of the most interactive parts of the Founder Summit program and a chance to learn from both the pitches that land and the ones that leave questions unanswered.
The rest of the program stretches across many of the decisions founders are facing right now.
Hunter Worland of NEA will explore why distribution may become a startup’s next competitive advantage. Vineet Edupuganti , co-founder and CEO of Cogent Security , will discuss building 10x teams. Tina Tosukhowong of TDK Ventures will examine the hidden signals that can identify category winners.
Fidelity Private Shares will also bring its perspective to conversations about fundraising trends with Kristen Craft and enterprise relationships with Evan Schnidman .
Together, the agenda creates a day that is not just about raising the next round or chasing the latest AI trend but is also about building the company.
TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 takes place November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston.
The day brings together candid founder conversations, practical sessions, smaller roundtables, live pitching, networking, and a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares.

title: Chinese AI model Kimi K3.1 Pro is closing in on Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5
body:
Moonshot AI's new reasoning model Kimi K3.1 Pro lands at number four on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, just 3 points behind the top proprietary models.
Chinese AI company Moonshot AI has released Kimi K3.1 Pro , a post-trained version of its predecessor Kimi K3 with significantly more post-training compute. The model scores 55 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , an 11-point jump over K3 that lands it in fourth place.
Only Claude Opus 5.5 (58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (56), and Muse Wonder Full (56) rank higher, according to Artificial Analysis . If Moonshot releases the model weights as planned by November 4, 2026, K3.1 Pro would become the highest-scoring open-weights model available. That would shrink the gap between open and proprietary models from 12 to just 3 points, assuming nothing else changes by then. Ad
Alongside K3.1 Pro, Moonshot is shipping a variant called K3.1 Pro Highspeed that runs two to three times faster, according to the company. Both are available now through Kimi.ai , Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and the Kimi API . Ad
K3.1 Pro's strongest improvements show up in agentic tasks. On the GDPval-AA benchmark, it reaches 1,846 Elo according to Artificial Analysis, 312 points above K3. That puts it just behind Claude Opus 5.5 (1,866) and Muse Wonder Full (1,857). On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Moonshot reports 65.7 percent, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2 percent) and barely behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4 percent). K3 managed only 13 percent on the same test.
Hallucination rates dropped sharply too. On Moonshot's internal Kimi Hallu Bench Hard, claim-level hallucinations fell from 23.4 percent with K3 to 8.3 percent, according to the company. Moonshot says this is a stress test, not a measure of general error rates. GPT-6 Astra hits 5.5 percent on the same benchmark, so it still has an edge. Ad
On internal finance benchmarks, K3.1 Pro gained 7.2 points on Financial Modeling and 11.6 points on Financial Research. For general office tasks, the model tops all tested models on OfficeQA Pro v2, according to Moonshot.
Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro benchmark table. All results with reasoning effort set to "max." Ad
K3.1 Pro works directly with game engines like Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, handling both quick fixes and full project builds, according to Moonshot. On the BenchCAD benchmark, it scores 92.7 percent with tools, close to Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2 percent) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9 percent). Without tools, it hits 72.8 percent, nearly matching Claude Opus 5.5 (73.0 percent). Ad
Moonshot says the model is strongest at parametric modeling of mechanical parts, architectural models, and configurable products. It can write and run scripts for Blender and CAD software without MCP connectors. The company also launched a feature called "3D Make" on Kimi.com that lets users preview, edit, and export 3D models.
K3.1 Pro keeps the same dimensions as K3, with 2.8 trillion total parameters and 104 billion active ones. The context window spans one million tokens, and the model handles both text and images. According to Artificial Analysis, it sits at the top of the Pareto frontier. No model with a comparable parameter count scores higher on the Intelligence Index.
Token prices drop by 33 percent. Input costs $2 per million tokens (down from $3), output costs $10 (down from $15), and cache hits cost $0.20 (down from $0.30). Each Intelligence Index task costs $1.98, almost identical to K3 ($2.00), since the model generates 14 percent more output tokens.
Moonshot devotes an entire section of its technical blog post to cybersecurity. The company says it observed that vulnerability research capabilities kept growing as post-training scaled up, because cyber-related content was embedded in the general mid-training corpus and related tasks were part of the RL environment mix.
For the open-weights release, Moonshot stripped cyber-related data from both training phases. On its internal xdev-bench-hard, which reproduces recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software like the Linux kernel, Node.js, and JavaScriptCore, the uncleaned version solves 90.5 percent of tasks. After data cleaning, K3.1 Pro solves 81.0 percent. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reaches 85.7 percent on the same test, while Kimi K3 scored 33.3 percent.
Moonshot says no open-weights model should push the absolute frontier of offensive cyber capabilities. At the same time, the company wants to gradually raise what open models can do, since they also serve defensive purposes like auditing legacy systems. Anthropic previously showed that even GLM-5.3, which scores 45 on the AA Index, can write exploits at near-Claude Mythos levels .

title: Ether ETFs Are Having Their Worst Month of 2026. Who Buys Once Bitmine Stops?
body: Ether’s (ETH) demand this year has largely come from two places: spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and Bitmine Immersion Technologies (BMNR), the company building an ether treasury. In October, both are pulling back at once. No month this year has seen spot ether ETFs lose as much as October , with $1.2 billion in net outflows so far. Investors pulled money on all but two trading days through Oct. 2 2 . Bitmine, meanwhile, is about 6 6,000 ETH short of its goal of owning 5% of all ether , by our count from its latest holdings update . At the company’s current pace, it hits its target late next month. Ether bulls often parse their outlooks through adoption headlines, like JPMorgan bringing its deposit token to Ethereum this week. Adoption builds the network, but it only lifts the price when someone buys the coin. Presently, the question is who absorbs the roughly 20,000 new ETH the network issues every week once Bitmine stops. This issue of Bits + Bips measures how much of that supply Bitmine has been taking, why no other ether treasury can take over, and what ETF flows would need to look like for ether to hold up into year-end. Spot ether ETFs swung from $2.7 billion of net inflows in August and September to $1.2 billion of net outflows in October through Oct. 22. Source: SoSoValue; Farside. Bitmine’s Buying Has Already Slowed Bitmine is finishing its accumulation at a fraction of the pace it started with. The company has bought ether every week since June 30, 2025. In April and May it bought more than 100,000 ETH in a single week four times. In each of the last two weeks it bought about 12,500. It now holds 6.04 million ETH, or 4.9% of Ethereum ‘s circulating token supply, and its cash has fallen by about $30 million a week with no new capital raise in its last three updates. “We’re done stacking,” Bitmine Chair Tom Lee said earlier this month in a message to investors . Bitmine’s 5% ether target is “a hard cap,” Lee said at the Token2049 conference, adding, “We’re not gonna be accumulating past 5%.” One caveat on timing: 5% of ether’s supply is a moving target. Supply grows by about 87,000 ETH a month , so the finish line moves out by roughly 4,300 ETH a month, by our count. Additionally, Ethereum’s issuance is subject to change, and not fixed at roughly 20,000 new ETH per week. The network uses a fee-burning mechanism that dynamically adjusts to user demand. At times of high use, like in 2023, this mechanism burns more tokens than are created to pay the validators that secure the network, actually turning Ethereum’s token economy deflationary. That said, ether token inflation has stayed relatively stable this year, in part due to a migration of user activity onto Layer-2 networks, which has left mainnet gas fees too low to burn off the newly issued coins. ETF Money Moves in Billions The ETFs have been the larger and less predictable buyer this year. Net inflows reached $1.85 billion in August and another $832 million in September, then reversed in October. The funds now hold roughly 6.2 million ETH, about the same as Bitmine, from their combined net assets of $14.6 billion . However, the two buyers move at very different speeds. October’s outflows have averaged about $357 million a week . Bitmine’s recent purchases come to about $30 million a week at its own reported prices . The ETF swing is about 12 times larger. In the rest of the issue, subscribers get: How much of ether’s new supply Bitmine has been absorbing , and why part of the hand-off has already happened Why no other ether treasury can step in , judged by what their shares trade at against their coins What is driving October’s ETF outflows The weekly ETF number that would cover ether’s new supply after Bitmine stops , plus bull, base and bear ranges for ETH into year-end Already a subscriber? title: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI'
body:
American Express is cutting thousands of employees as the leading credit card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more of its internal processes.
Amex is eliminating 5% of its global workforce and taking a $336 million restructuring charge, CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts Friday on the company's third-quarter earnings call. The firm had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025.
Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI."
"You don't want to automate processes that are not optimally structured," Le Caillec said. "So what we're doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years."
The Amex announcement reflects a broader trend across financial services, where banks are working to replace repetitive roles with AI automation. On Thursday, Barclays confirmed plans to trim 5,000 jobs — also roughly 5% of its staff — in another tech-driven cost initiative. The moves come even as the sector is enjoying robust profits from growing consumer spending and resilient credit.
During the analyst call, Squeri said the charge was to improve the company's efficiency.
"We've got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become [a] more agile and efficient organization," Squeri said.
Squeri devoted a 10-minute section of his prepared remarks to his views on AI, focusing mainly on how it will be used to personalize experiences and offers for Amex cardholders.
While the CEO emphasized the need to meet customers' desires to use AI, including agents, he added that Amex is "not going to let assistants run rogue through our system."
"We need to protect our customers [and] merchants, and we're only going to allow agents to access our systems that are either approved through API or MCP channels," he said, citing two ways to securely connect outside platforms with Amex systems.
Amex posted quarterly results that topped Wall Street profit expectations. Adjusted earnings per share were $4.68, beating the $4.48 average estimate of analysts, according to LSEG.
The company raised its full-year earnings guidance to a range of $18.30 to $18.60 per share, on an unadjusted basis, up from its previous target of $17.30 to $17.90.
That metric was helped by proceeds from Amex's sale of its stake in Global Business Travel Group , part of which went into the restructuring plan, Le Caillec said.
Total revenue rose 9% to $20.06 billion, coming in slightly below Wall Street's $20.12 billion LSEG forecast. Executives attributed part of the spending drag to recent exits from small business co-brand partnerships.
Shares of the card company fell roughly 4% in afternoon trading.

title: Zelensky Says Starlink Caps Persist as Kyiv Eyes November Talks With Russia, US
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Starlink and Starshield restrictions remain in place, disrupting drone operations, while delays in agreed US interceptor missile deliveries continue to further strain Ukraine’s defense ahead of winter.
Zelensky made the remarks in a speech at the Hudson Institute on Friday, Oct. 23, excerpts of which he shared in a statement on Telegram. Around the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed he had no idea who ordered Starlink limitations on Ukraine and that he heard “ it’s fixed. ”
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“[SpaceX CEO] Elon Musk is a very good person. He is not going to do anything wrong regarding Ukraine,” Trump claimed . “He is a fair person.”
The dispute over Ukraine’s satellite access has dragged on since Oct. 13-14, when Starlink’s operating parameters in Ukraine were first altered. Since then, the White House and Musk have each denied responsibility, while pointing to the other.
Musk claimed Starshield is controlled by the US military, including Trump himself, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisted SpaceX, as a private company, makes Starlink’s operating decisions.
Despite constraints, Zelensky said Ukraine’s frontline is holding. The operations have so far been fairly successful, though the restrictions have made the fighting harder.
“This is a real problem, because the Russians attack us almost every day,” he continued.
During his speech, Zelensky also said that he and his team had spoken with senior US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, about the outcome of their recent meetings in Oslo and St. Petersburg earlier this week.
Steps on how to advance diplomacy next month were on the agenda as well.
“We are ready to meet any day, even tomorrow. But everything depends on the Russians,” Zelensky said, noting that a trilateral meeting had also been on the agenda in October, but fell through after Moscow “came up with yet another reason not to meet.”
So far, the Kremlin has rebuffed every proposal for a direct meeting with Ukrainian authorities, particularly with Zelensky himself.
Zelensky argued that progress remains unlikely without Washington’s direct involvement and pressure on the Kremlin, while urging the US to keep the issue a priority at all levels.
Ukraine’s goal, he said, remains to move beyond technical-level negotiations to a meeting of leaders, since the most important issues can only be settled through direct discussions.
The Kremlin, for its part, rejected an energy ceasefire with Kyiv, arguing that Moscow wants a broader peace agreement instead.
Kremlin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday, Oct. 21, that a full settlement of the war would be impossible without the participation of Ukrainian officials, signaling a shift from Moscow’s earlier position.
Russian President Vladimir Putin reportedly proposed a trilateral summit with his US and Chinese counterparts on Monday, Oct. 19 to discuss a settlement in Ukraine, excluding Kyiv from the meeting.

title: SEC Flags AI 'Super Intelligence' and Tokenization as Systemic Market Risks
body:
The SEC's Division of Examinations dropped its FY2027 priorities on Thursday, and buried in the eight-point list it included "super intelligence and other advanced technologies that may affect market operations, compliance, fraud prevention, and investor protection” as part of its official examination playbook.
The broader technology bullet groups AI under a category called "emerging technologies," which also signals the Division's intent to scrutinize how AI tools affect compliance programs and fraud detection across registrants.
That's a shift in scope—prior editions focused on AI as a business tool advisers were adopting; the 2027 language positions it as a systemic market variable.
Tokenization got its own bullet under market infrastructure. The Division listed "risks associated with evolving market infrastructure, including Treasury clearing reforms, tokenization, and related developments" as a priority area.
For brokers, investment advisers, and transfer agents already building out tokenized product lines under the Atkins-era regulatory thaw, that line means their compliance programs will now draw examiner attention—not just policy attention.
Director Keith Cassidy framed the priorities as an adaptive posture. "Our approach enables us to adapt to changing market conditions, identify developing risk patterns, respond to emerging threats, and anticipate areas where investors and the markets may be vulnerable," he said in the SEC’s release.
The Division explicitly noted the list isn't exhaustive—examiners retain discretion to review anything touching federal securities law compliance across the full registrant base.
The FY2026 exam priorities, released in November 2025, were notable for dropping crypto as a standalone focus area for the first time since 2021—a signal, at the time, that the Paul Atkins SEC was pulling back from the Gary Gensler-era enforcement posture.
The 2027 document doesn't restore that section, but it does fold AI risk and tokenization into the list, covering the two technology trends that have most shaped capital markets activity in the past year.
The Division's examination program now covers more than 34,000 registrants, including investment advisers, investment companies, broker-dealers, clearing agencies, and transfer agents.

title: U.S. dropping some Canada tariffs, Susan Collins says as trade war looms over Maine Senate race
body:
The White House on Friday said it would drop tariffs on some Canadian goods , but replace them with other products from the major U.S. trade partner.
The move was revealed after Sen. Susan Collins , R-Maine, took credit for pushing the Trump administration to issue tariff exemptions on several categories of Canadian imports she says are "crucial" for her state's industries.
But Collins' announcement, which The Wall Street Journal first reported, did not mention that while tariffs would be removed for some Canadian products, new ones would be added to the list of goods subject to steep U.S. duties. The White House announced the new tariffs less than an hour after Collins touted the new exemptions to the tariffs, which are unpopular in the state where she's fighting for reelection.
President Donald Trump earlier Friday signed a proclamation "removing certain products" from the list of items that he slapped 50% tariffs on over the summer using a 96-year-old trade law.
But he is "replacing those products with certain valves, carpets, waste products, and others," according to a White House fact sheet detailing the proclamation.
The changes are being made to "further refine the scope of the tariffs on certain Canadian products," according to the fact sheet, which does not mention Maine.
The new additions and removals from the list of goods covered by the "Section 338" tariffs will take effect Oct. 30, four days before the Nov. 3 U.S. election, the fact sheet said.
Asked what Collins had agreed to in her conversations pushing Trump administration officials for lower tariffs on products affecting her state, her spokeswoman Phoebe Keller told CNBC that the senator "requested exemptions for products that are important to Maine and will continue to do so."
Before the fact sheet was made public, Collins' office sent a press release crediting the senator with securing the new tariff exemptions on "nine categories of products crucial for Maine's agricultural industries."
That announcement came as voters have already started casting ballots in the pivotal Maine Senate race , where Trump's unpopular tariffs have been a top issue.
Collins' Democratic opponent, fifth-generation Maine logger Troy Jackson, quickly pushed back, insisting Collins deserves blame for enabling Trump's tariff policies.
"Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire," Jackson said in a statement.
Trump has slapped heavy tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods during his second term as president as he has escalated a trade war against the top U.S. economic partner. Many of those tariffs have put considerable strain on businesses in Maine , which imports far more products from Canada than from any other country.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC in a statement Friday afternoon that Trump's latest tariff proclamation is part of his efforts to "address Canada's discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce."
"The President is taking action in response to Canada's continued discrimination against and additional retaliation targeting U.S. commerce, with the goal of protecting American farmers, manufacturers, and workers," said Middleton. "This administration will continue to use every available tool to restore reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships and safeguard the economic prosperity and national security of the American people."
Collins has previously touted her efforts to push back on the president's protectionist trade policies. In the first televised debate between Collins and Jackson on Oct. 6, the GOP incumbent took credit for removing some items from Trump's list of tariffs on Canadian goods, including road salt.
Jackson fired back, "What about everything else? We can't eat road salt."
In her press release Friday, Collins said she has asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "for tariff relief" for the Maine-centric products, stressing the "burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families."
"I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally and largest trading partner," she said.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau , Mexico is the largest U.S. trading partner.
The products being exempted from the Section 338 tariffs include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and packing bags, refrigeration equipment, multiple forms of machinery and seaweed and algae products, according to Collins.

title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: AI Drives A Varied Lineup Of Large Financings
body: Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board . This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here . It was another interesting week for AI-related startup funding, with a number of large rounds and quirky companies. The largest financings went to Tenstorrent , a developer of AI processors and systems, and AI lab Flapping Airplanes . The quirkiest round, meanwhile, was undoubtedly a $200 million financing for Warhound , which wants to breed elite military dogs. A number of big rounds in areas including biotech, space tech and physical AI rounded out the list. 1. Tenstorrent , $1.5B, AI infrastructure: Santa Clara, California-based Tenstorrent, a developer of AI processors and systems, secured $1.5 billion in Series E funding. Trace Capital and Innovation X led the round, which set a $6.2 billion valuation for the 10-year-old company. 2. Flapping Airplanes , $1B, foundational AI: Flapping Airplanes, an AI lab with a focus on developing models that cost less to train and run, closed on $1 billion in Series A funding led by Lux Capital and Index Ventures . The round comes less than 10 months after the year-old San Francisco startup raised a $180 million seed financing. 3. ASI , $325M, AI for critical infrastructure: ASI, a developer of AI technology for securing and operating critical infrastructure in areas such as aviation, transportation and defense, picked up $325 million in Series C financing. Spark Capital led the round, which set a $3 billion valuation for the Boston-based company. 4. Xona , $250M, space tech: Xona, a startup developing a next-generation version of GPS, raised $250 million in Series D funding led by Future Ventures . The round sets a $2.4 billion valuation for the Burlingame, California-based company. 5. Pathos AI , $237M, biotech: Pathos AI, a startup applying AI to drug development, completed a $237 million Series E financing at a post-money valuation around $3 billion. Bristol-Myers Squibb led the financing for the New York-headquartered company. 6. Warp Sciences , $215M, AI, robotics and life sciences: Warp Sciences, a startup applying AI and robotics to help develop new medicines faster, raised a $215M Series A round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners . 7. (tied) Whop , $200M, online business marketplace: Whop, a platform that helps entrepreneurs build and run online businesses, secured $200 million in Series D funding led by Sequoia Capital and Shopify Ventures . The round set a $5.1 billion valuation for the New York-based company. 7. (tied) Star Therapeutics , $200M, biotech: South San Francisco, California-based drug developer Star Therapeutics says it raised $200 million in new financing led by OrbiMed and Janus Henderson Investors . The investment follows Incyte ’s July acquisition of Vega Therapeutics , a subsidiary of Star, in a deal valued at up to $2 billion. 7. (tied) Warhound , $200M, military dogs: Warhound, a startup that wants to breed working dogs for U.S. military forces and emergency responders, launched from stealth with $200 million in seed funding from a long list of backers including Sequoia Capital and 8VC 1 . The startup, co-founded by AnduriI ndustries founder Palmer Luckey , plans to equip the dogs with Anduril technology. 10. Arda Industries , $160M, AI manufacturing software: Arda Industries, a developer of AI-powered software for manufacturing engineering, closed on $160 million in Series A funding at a $1.5 billion valuation, co-led by Altimeter Capital , Accel and Khosla Ventures . The San Francisco-based startup also announced a previously undisclosed $72 million seed financing. title: First lady Melania Trump says she brokered 'temporary' ceasefire in Ukrainian town
body:
It's unclear exactly how long the ceasefire is set to last.
First lady Melania Trump announced on Friday that she had secured a localized "temporary" ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which will begin Oct. 29.
A statement from the first lady’s office said that the temporary ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city was agreed to by both countries to "allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway."
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water,” the first lady said in a statement, adding that without her intervention, "the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."
Asked about the ceasefire and whether his wife would be part of trilateral peace talks, President Donald Trump said "it's not the worst idea I've ever heard."
"What she wants to do is save children, and that's her focus. And both sides are cooperating with her, so she's doing a very good job," Trump said Friday morning as he departed the White House.
It's unclear exactly how long the ceasefire is set to last in the town where about 1,700-2,000 residents remain of an estimated 24,000 before the war, according to the first lady's office.
The Russian military is currently coordinating the timing of a ceasefire in the Oleshky area, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Friday. Peskov also confirmed that Melania Trump played a coordinating role in reaching a ceasefire agreement in Oleshky.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said in a social media post on Friday that it will carry out the ceasefire orders.
A temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine also happened in May 2025 during the 80th anniversary commemoration of V Day, which celebrates the victory of the Soviet Union over Nazi Germany in 1945.
This ceasefire comes amid the Trump administration's larger efforts to engage peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, who have been at war since February 2022.
In recent weeks, the president waived a raft of sanctions on Moscow and again blamed Kyiv for the lack of progress in U.S.-sponsored peace talks, even suggesting that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should be replaced as the nation's leader.
Earlier this week, President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that the U.S. had received "nothing" for its support of Ukraine.
Melania Trump said in a statement that residents who want to evacuate "to their preferred destination" will receive support from civilian, non-military leaders in both countries.
"I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," she said.
Melania Trump added that she had also gotten assurances that an unnamed "impartial American media organization" will be able to accompany Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground amid the ceasefire. ABC News has reached out to the White House for additional details.
The first lady’s office said that she became involved in brokering the agreement during a private discussion at her Fostering the Future event at the U.N. General Assembly last month.
Melania Trump has worked to bring awareness to the children impacted by the Russian-Ukraine war as the yearslong conflict drags on. Last year, she said she has an "open channel of communication" Russian President Vladimir Putin on the matter.
The first lady said she had written a letter to Putin stating it was time to protect the children impacted by the war, which was Trump hand-delivered to Putin. The Russian president responded, "signaling a willingness to engage with me directly and outlining details regarding the Ukrainian children residing in Russia," Melania Trump said last year.

title: Lebanese people want Israel ties, stronger government to oust Hezbollah, AMCD head says
body: The Lebanese people want “full diplomatic ties” with Israel and to enjoy the benefits of tourism and trade with their neighboring state, but both Hezbollah and a government unwilling to confront the Iran-backed group are disregarding this wish, the co-chair of the American Mideast Coalition for Democracy (AMCD), John Hajjar, told The Jerusalem Post.Hajjar, who visited Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, and Haifa several years ago, said he grew up hearing stories from his Lebanese grandparents about Jewish holidaymakers who would visit the Lebanese mountains for rest and relaxation when his grandmother was young.He said Israel and Lebanon had much to offer each other's citizens, but that Lebanon's 1955 Boycott Law, which criminalizes social and business ties with Israel, had created unnecessary barriers between the two neighboring countries.The law was originally intended to prevent trade and financial dealings with Israel as part of the Arab League's efforts to economically isolate the Jewish state, but has since been used to prevent even the most basic forms of communication, benefiting Hezbollah and Hamas, Hajjar said on Thursday.When the law was first introduced, Article 7 stipulated that violations could be punished with three to 10 years of temporary hard labor, alongside financial fines, asset seizures, and product confiscation.However, Hajjar said, members of the Lebanese diaspora have since faced sentences of up to 15 years in absentia simply for expressing the view that Lebanon would benefit from pursuing peace with its neighbor.More recently, there were efforts to have Lebanon's Ambassador to Washington, Nada Hamadeh Moawad, prosecuted over her message of support to Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter, whose son was severely wounded in a terrorist attack.The Lebanese people demand peace“The Lebanese people demand peace. They want to grow their economy. Lebanon's infrastructure is in shambles. Lebanon is still a beautiful place, and a lot of economic activity still goes on. It could be so much better if there were strong ties with Israel,” Hajjar said.“It would be mutually beneficial for both Lebanese and Israelis if peace is established,” he continued.Earlier last week, Hajjar and his co-chair, Tom Harb, wrote an open letter urging Washington to use its influence with Lebanon to push for the repeal of 1955 Boycott Law, which would allow religious groups in Lebanon to visit the many holy sites in Jerusalem. They also called on the US to sanction members of the Lebanese judiciary involved in prosecuting violations of the law.“You see it in poll after poll among the Lebanese. They're trying to break the wall of silence imposed by Hezbollah and other terrorist organizations. I believe the day is fast approaching when people will finally break free and say, 'That's it. We're not going to tolerate these laws that forbid us from speaking with Israelis, and we want full diplomatic ties,” Hajjar said.Nostalgic for the years he said Lebanon was the “Paris of the Middle East,” Hajjar shared it had been disheartening to see a country he felt so connected with struggle to bear the weight of sectarian violence, terrorism, and wars.He said that, given Lebanon's own experience with Palestinian terrorism, many Lebanese could empathize with Israel following the October 7 attacks even as the war touched their own country following Hezbollah's attacks a day after the invasion.“I think the Lebanese diaspora in the United States understands the persecution of minorities, and they feel a natural affinity to the State of Israel and what Israelis have endured, because the Lebanese themselves have endured the same things in Lebanon for hundreds of years,” he said.“The horrible terrorist acts of October 7 happened to the Lebanese in 1976 in Damour and Aishiyeh, another Christian village, which the Palestinians savagely attacked. I think a lot of Lebanese [therefore] understand the suffering and feel a natural affinity for Israeli citizens,” he explained.Palestinian armed groups, including Fatah and other PLO-aligned factions, attacked the predominantly Christian town of Damour in January 1976, killing hundreds of people and forcing its inhabitants to flee.In October that year, Palestinian factions, including Fatah and As-Sa'iqa, then attacked the southern Christian village of Aishiyeh, killing dozens of civilians and displacing its population.Displaced Palestinians who were housed at the Tal al-Za'atar refugee camp east of Beirut were then resettled in Damour, while Aishiyeh was used as a PLO base. In total, more than 600 people were killed in both attacks.Asked how to deal with Hezbollah, particularly as AMCD advocates sanctions that critics argue could push Beirut closer to Tehran, Hajjar said Lebanon's government needed to end the “double game” of promising to disarm Hezbollah while simultaneously disregarding that promise.Hajjar calls for stronger government capable of getting rid of HezbollahSofter in his stance on Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Hajjar didn't mince words on corruption in Beirut. He argued Lebanon Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri has grown rich while pushing the boycott laws that deny opportunity to Lebanon's struggling economy.“It's time for him to go and if President [Joseph] Aoun and Salem can't get Hezbollah disarmed, then it's time for them to go, too,” he said.Hajjar added that while the Lebanese people were often seen as eternally patient with a government unable to fulfill its promises, that patience was waning, as was their willingness to remain “captive by Hezbollah.”“Hezbollah has, despite its claims to the contrary, carried out wave after wave of assassinations against prominent Lebanese officials,” Hajjar warned. “It has infiltrated every segment of the government and civil society.”“It has operatives throughout the country, even in Druze and Christian areas; the Lebanese have strong reasons to be very fearful. They also lack strong political leaders, and that is a direct result of the fact that those who have been outspoken and principled have paid with their lives,” he said, acknowledging how hard it has been for the Lebanese to push for any kind of change.Asked about the war with Israel and the collateral damage that has wreaked havoc across multiple sects in southern Lebanon, Hajjar blamed the Lebanese government, saying that some people were too emotionally affected by the tragic losses to see its culpability.“Some people have paid with their lives, unfortunately, because the Lebanese government is really a failed state. When you don't have a government that can protect its people and is strong enough to negotiate peace, the consequences can be very disastrous, and that's what has happened,” he shared.“I understand why Israel is conducting this war against Hezbollah, and I just wish the Lebanese government would realize that it has a common enemy in Hezbollah and other terrorist groups,” Hajjar said.“Until all those terrorist organizations are defeated and held accountable, either paying the ultimate price or serving long prison terms, then you're going to have more of this,” Hajjar warned.“Hopefully, justice will be served, and the Lebanese government will stand up and look out for the interests of the Lebanese, not terrorists and foreigners who don't even hold Lebanese citizenship and are not patriotic Lebanese.”
