title: Critics call for halt to road construction in Mexico’s Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve
body: MEXICO CITY — In early October, Mexico’s environment ministry published a statement about minimizing infrastructure development inside the Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve, a protected area on the Caribbean coast. But environmental groups say road construction continues to move forward there, threatening mangroves, cenote sinkholes, and dunes. The courts should address a lawsuit filed by local communities to halt the road construction and repair ecological damage, they said. They added that while the statement by the ministry, formally the Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat), is hopeful, it doesn’t provide the same legal guarantees as a court ruling. “We want certainty for the communities that, first, the project is canceled, and second, that they repair the damage already done,” Viridiana Maldonado, co-coordinator with Territorios Diversos para la Vida, an environmental NGO that supports Indigenous peoples defending the environment, told Mongabay. “Because a good part of the project is already built, the damage is done. They cut down mangroves, they cut down forest, they interrupted hydrological flows.” The Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve covers more than 528,000 hectares (1.3 million acres) of mangroves, rainforests, and dunes in the southern state of Quintana Roo. It received UNESCO World Heritage status in 1987 and provides extensive habitat to jaguars (Panthera onca), Central American tapirs (Tapirus bairdii), and hundreds of migratory birds, among other species. The reserve also has 47 community-based tourism initiatives and 140 permits for tourism and recreational activities, according to Semarnat. title: Touchscreen MacBook: Will Apple's upcoming event contradict Steve Jobs?
body: Apple 's “pro and tell” event will take place next week, and a significant upgrade to the MacBook line-up is likely to be announced – potentially going against something that Steve Jobs once said. News outlets have reported that the technology giant will introduce a MacBook that uses an organic light-emitting diode (OLED) display with a touchscreen option. It would be the first MacBook to contain a touchscreen, and the expected debut starkly contrasts with Apple-cofounder Mr Jobs 's stance on portable computer touchscreens. “We've done tonnes of user testing on this, and it turns out it doesn't work,” the late Apple chief executive said in 2010 during a product launch event, discussing why trackpads worked well with laptops and touchscreens didn't. “Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical, and it gives a great demo but after a short period of time, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off. It doesn't work, it's ergonomically terrible.” Apple's current MacBook line-up uses mini-LED displays. But there is a lengthy list of products that have made debuts years after Apple, and even Mr Jobs, dismissed their concepts. Those products include video-capable iPods, stylus pens, larger iPhones and medium-sized iPads. “Asus, Lenovo, HP, and Dell have already helped bring OLED screens to premium notebooks, but Apple’s entry could be a turning point,” said David Naranjo, associate director for technology market analysis firm Counterpoint Research. He also pointed out that Apple's expertise in establishing dominance in supply chains could help it significantly, and even help other companies. “Not unlike smartphones, when Apple adopts OLED, it boosts manufacturing capacity, improves yields, and lowers panel costs, making OLED more affordable for a wider range of products,” he explained. Mr Naranjo said that he believed a 14-inch MacBook with an OLED display, based on the price of materials, might cost between $2,799 and $2,999. “This higher price would cover the cost of advanced tandem OLED technology, possible touchscreen features, and ongoing memory expenses,” he said. But he cautioned that although Apple's products tend to exceed expectations, new MacBooks are arriving at a time when overall PC sales are starting to slow, giving the California technology company an additional hurdle to overcome. View on Threads According to Bloomberg, Apple will also be changing the MacBook Pro's name to MacBook Ultra. As has been the case with the company's events in recent years, some are expecting new iMac and iPad models with simple upgrades consisting of faster semiconductors, improved displays and slightly tweaked designs. Regardless of what transpires at the event on Wednesday, it will cap the busiest Apple product introduction seasons in recent years. In September, the company announced the keenly awaited foldable iPhone Duo. Weeks later, it introduced a new device, HomeView , which incorporates AI, Siri and the company's iOS to allow people to interact with various products in their home. It also announced the Apple TV 4K, the first significant upgrade to the product in several years.

title: Russia’s Khachanov falls to Bublik in quarterfinals at 2026 Almaty Open tennis tournament
body:
ALMATY, October 23. /TASS/. Russia’s Karen Khachanov failed to reach the semifinals stage at the 2026 Almaty Open tennis tournament after he fell in to Alexander Bublik from Kazakhstan on Friday.
In the match that lasted for 2 hours and 27 minutes, the 5th-seeded Russian, who is playing under a neutral status at the tournament, lost to his 3rd-seeded opponent from Kazakhstan 4-6; 7-6 (7-5); 7-6 (7-5).
Bublik is now set to clash in the semifinals of the tournament on his home soil against Russia’s top-ranked tennis player Daniil Medvedev, who earlier in the day outplayed France’s Terence Atmane in straight sets 6-4; 6-4.
A seven-time ATP champion, Khachanov, 30, is currently the 25th-ranked player in the world. His best performance in the Grand Slam series was when he reached the semifinal rounds at the 2022, 2026 US Open and the 2023 Australian Open.
The Russian player also took home the silver medal in men’s singles at the 2020 Summer Olympic Games in Tokyo. He also won the 2021 Davis Cup as part of the Russian national team.
The 2026 Almaty Open is the ATP 250 class tournament played on indoor hardcourts on October 19-25 and it offers $1.075 million in prize money. Russia’s Daniil Medvedev is the tournament’s reigning champion.
On February 28, 2022, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) issued recommendations to international sports federations to bar athletes from Russia and Belarus from taking part in international tournaments, citing Moscow's special military operation in Ukraine as the reason.
Following the IOC's recommendations in late February 2022, the majority of global sports federations moved to exclude athletes from Russia and Belarus from all international sports tournaments.
The International Tennis Federation (ITF) ruled on March 1, 2022, to suspend the membership of the Russian and Belarusian national tennis federations while also canceling all previously scheduled tennis tournaments in the two countries.
On March 14, 2022, the ITF also confirmed its prohibition on the Russian and Belarusian national tennis teams from participating in the 2022 Davis Cup and the 2022 Billie Jean King Cup.

My colleague John Higgins considered Soundcore’s Space One some of the best budget noise-canceling headphones you could buy when they launched in 2023 — and their successor has only improved upon their winning formula, albeit with a $30 price increase. The Space 2 builds on the original with improved active noise cancellation, particularly when it comes to the low-frequency sounds associated with trains and airplane engines. title: Meduza’s sources say prosecution of popular Russian Communist was planned before his election defeat
body: Moscow’s Basmanny District Court has ordered Oleg Mikhailov, a former State Duma deputy and former head of the Communist Party’s Komi branch, held in pretrial detention. He is charged with justifying terrorism over a post supporting imprisoned political scientist Boris Kagarlitsky and faces up to seven years in prison. Mikhailov built one of the Communist Party’s strongest regional branches, brought together people with different political views, took part in environmental protests, and challenged the republic’s authorities. During his State Duma election campaign, he was also one of the few Communist candidates to campaign for peace. Yet after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, Mikhailov repeatedly voted for repressive laws. Warning : This article contains profanity. Meduza previously reported that the presidential administration was urging the Communist Party’s leadership not to nominate strong regional candidates who had defeated United Russia candidates in single-member districts in the previous election. Among them was Mikhailov, a Communist from the Komi Republic. The Communist Party partly complied, but its Komi branch leader ran anyway, both in his district and on the federal party list. His original position on the list offered him no prospect of winning a seat. A Communist Party source told Meduza that the party leadership provided almost no funding for Mikhailov’s district campaign. After his nomination, the source said, Mikhailov and the party began receiving “hints” from the Kremlin: If he did not withdraw, he would face a criminal investigation. Meduza has learned, however, that the authorities planned to launch an investigation regardless, and that the Federal Security Service (FSB) began examining Mikhailov’s social media accounts as early as 2024. “I told him: Go on vacation after the election, to whatever country you can, and maybe stay a little longer. He agreed to take a vacation, but he ruled out emigrating. He wanted to stay in Russia,” an acquaintance of the former deputy told Meduza, requesting anonymity. Mikhailov failed to win reelection to the State Duma in September 2026. On October 21, he was detained at Moscow’s Domodedovo Airport as he returned from vacation. Mikhailov was born in 1987 in Pechora, a district seat in Komi. After studying biology at Syktyvkar State University, he went to graduate school, earned a doctorate, and worked at Komi’s Institute of Biology. He joined the Communist Party in 2007 while still a student and became an activist. At the time, the party’s Komi branch attracted little attention compared with branches in other regions that had prominent local politicians . “You could’ve called the Komi regional party committee a retirees’ club. They were an opposition group — not very active, but honest,” Pavel Andreyev, founder of the Revolt Center and an acquaintance of Mikhailov’s, told Meduza. “At first, he came across as pretty off-putting — this guy with no sense of fashion, like he’d stepped out of Soviet times. But the older crowd liked that.” An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s who spoke to Meduza anonymously said he “steadily worked his way up through the party”: He’d help [the branch leadership] with one thing, lend a hand with another. They promoted him for obvious reasons: He did the things [the branch leadership] didn’t have enough people to do, and [the party leaders] also felt it was time to retire. And before he knew it, Oleg had become a Syktyvkar city council member, then head of the regional party committee and a member of the regional legislature. As head of the committee, Mikhailov actively supported protests against the construction of a landfill at Shiyes railway station. The station is in the Arkhangelsk region, practically on the Komi border, and much closer to Syktyvkar than to Arkhangelsk. Mikhailov laid out his position on Shiyes in 2019: There’s no middle ground on Shiyes: You’re either for it or against it. If you’re for it, you’re an accomplice to the garbage occupiers; if you’re against it, you’re a normal person. There’s no third option. Another deputy once said to me, “Maybe you should go work in the Arkhangelsk region? It’s their problem, after all.” That tells you something about a deputy who doesn’t understand that administrative and national borders are drawn by people, while nature has no borders. It’s all one ecosystem: Pollution will flow into the Vychegda and Northern Dvina [rivers], then into the White and Barents seas, and we’ll pollute half of Europe. Oleg Mikhailov at a rally against the construction of a landfill at Shiyes. Syktyvkar, April 7, 2019 Oleg Mikhailov tries to enter Komi’s government building to deliver a copy of the resolution from the rally against the construction of a landfill at Shiyes to Sergey Gaplikov. The door was locked. April 7, 2019 Syktyvkar residents march against the construction of a landfill at Shiyes railway station in a protest organized by the Communist Party’s regional branch. April 7, 2019 Speaking to Meduza that same year, Mikhailov called the landfill’s construction “a political issue, rather than an environmental one.” He spoke with considerable emotion in that interview: The federal government treats Russia’s regions and the people who live in them unfairly. What are we, second-class citizens? Is that why you’re building a dump here? How about we put a dump in your backyard? We’re a region that sends out huge amounts of resources — 151 billion rubles in taxes last year. We send you money, resources, and even our talent. The best of everything goes to Moscow! And we get Moscow’s garbage. At the time, Mikhailov organized Syktyvkar’s largest protest in several years: The Communists said at least 1,800 people attended. The republic’s authorities authorized the rally at the local “Hyde Park,” a designated protest area , but it turned into a march and continued in the city’s main square. During the Shiyes protests, the Communist Party’s Komi branch built ties with environmental activists and the Komi national movement. Mikhailov told Meduza that he was half Komi himself and supported compulsory Komi-language instruction in the republic’s schools. It had become voluntary shortly before, in January 2018. “In places like Vorkuta or Inta, nonindigenous residents openly say, ‘What do we need this language for?’ But if you live here, if you’re staying rather than waiting to move away, then respect the traditions of the local people. If I move to any European country and want to live there, I have to learn the language,” Mikhailov told Meduza indignantly. In 2019, the Communist Party’s Komi branch actively supported Komi national activists in elections to the interregional civic organization Komi Voityr . For the Communists, that campaign was something of a warm-up for the 2020 elections for the republic’s leader and its State Council . By then, residents saw the Communist Party as the main force for political protest. Hi, I’m Yulia. I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia. I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true. Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting. An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said he had “an ability to build electoral alliances with people of different views.” Previous secretaries of the Communist Party’s regional committee had focused solely on the party and its voters, the acquaintance told Meduza, while Mikhailov worked with “the whole range of civic activists — environmentalists, housing activists, human rights advocates, liberals, and patriots.” “This guy, who basically never picked fights, hoovered up opposition-minded people and pulled them into his orbit. But the activists didn’t roll over for him. They just understood that Oleg was a reasonable person they could work things out with,” Mikhailov’s acquaintance said. Opposition to the Kremlin’s appointee, Komi leader Sergey Gaplikov , and his team of “outsiders” was central to the Communists’ 2020 State Council campaign. Gaplikov had had no connection to Komi before his appointment. Mikhailov spoke about him to Meduza in 2019: Before Gaplikov, the leaders had at least built their careers here. He’s a complete outsider. The State Council meets seven to nine times a year, and the republic’s head shows up exactly once a year, to deliver his report. [During rallies,] people stand on the steps of the republic’s government building, shouting, “Gaplikov must go!” — and he couldn’t care less. The main thing is that everyone who’s more or less politically active understands that these people are just passing through, here for a stint. They’ll leave anyway. The Communists did well in the republic’s State Council election, winning 14.8% of the vote — nearly twice their share in the previous election, in 2015. Four Communist Party candidates won seats in Komi’s parliament: three through the party list and one in a single-member district. United Russia received 28% of the vote. Shortly before the election, the republic did get a new leader: Another “outsider,” Vladimir Uiba , replaced Gaplikov. Mikhailov was barred from running for Komi’s top job after the republic’s election commission ruled that he had failed to collect the required endorsements from municipal officials. Uiba proved a poor choice for the job. The new leader clashed with local residents and with Mikhailov himself. At a State Council meeting in April 2021, Mikhailov told the republic’s head that Uiba had “even run his campaign like a complete coward, picking outright spoiler candidates as his opponents.” Uiba responded by calling Mikhailov a “horse” and threatening to “beat the shit out of” him. Vladimir Putin during a video meeting with Vladimir Uiba. August 31, 2020 This confrontation only cemented Mikhailov’s position as Komi’s leading opposition politician — and possibly its most popular politician overall. He regularly traveled around the region and met with residents. In the 2021 State Duma election, he won his single-member district, while the Communist Party received 26.9% of the vote in Komi, according to official figures. United Russia had one of its lowest vote shares nationwide in Komi that year: 29.4%, compared with 49% across Russia. After Mikhailov moved to the federal parliament, libertarian Viktor Vorobyov took over his State Council seat and his position as the party’s caucus leader there. In the State Duma, Mikhailov did not vote for the 2022 laws recognizing the independence of the self-proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk people’s republics, or for the law imposing penalties for “discrediting the army.” Nevertheless, the European Union, the United States, and Canada sanctioned him for allegedly supporting the latter law. Mikhailov did support other measures, including the November 2022 ban on “LGBT propaganda,” the November 2024 ban on adoptions by people in countries that allow “sex changes ,” and the July 2025 law allowing the FSB to establish its own pretrial detention centers. Meanwhile, the Communist Party’s Komi branch continued to oppose Uiba, who remained in office until November 2024 despite his unpopularity. He was replaced by Rostislav Goldstein, the former head of the Jewish Autonomous Region. Goldstein had close ties to Komi: He had run businesses in the republic, served in its State Council, and then represented the region in the federal parliament. An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said that, unlike Uiba, Goldstein and his team initially “tried to reach an understanding” with the Communists. “At least an agreement not to fight dirty with each other,” the acquaintance told Meduza. Gradually, however, relations between the republic’s authorities and the Communist Party branch began to deteriorate, he said. “Goldstein is a pretty tough guy. He also wanted to show the federal leadership that he’d brought everyone to heel in a region known for protest and dealt with the Communist Party problem,” a source close to the presidential administration’s domestic politics team told Meduza. The confrontation between Goldstein and the republic’s Communists culminated in Mikhailov being barred from the 2025 election for regional leader. As before, the official reason was his alleged failure to collect the required endorsements from municipal officials. Ahead of the 2026 parliamentary election, Komi’s authorities deliberately worked to keep the “troublesome deputy” out of the State Duma, a political consultant who works with the presidential administration’s domestic politics team told Meduza. To that end, the consultant said, they fielded Stanislav Kochev , who had fought in the war against Ukraine, in the single-member district. “A veteran can’t lose — anything goes to make sure he wins,” the consultant said. Oleg Mikhailov at a protest against the blocking of social media in Ukhta. April 4, 2026 Mikhailov, meanwhile, campaigned on the slogan “For peace,” a rarity among Communist Party candidates. Officially, he lost the State Duma election, but the vote tallies from in-person polling stations where observers were present indicate otherwise . In electronic voting, the United Russia candidate received 2.5 times as many votes as Mikhailov. An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said the politician’s arrest could make it harder for the Communist Party’s Komi branch to function and would probably turn it into a typical, largely inactive party branch. “Yeah, he probably could’ve done more. But he could’ve done jack shit, like most politicians,” the acquaintance said of Mikhailov’s work. The acquaintance still considers Mikhailov one of Komi’s most popular political figures: “His [Telegram] channel is called ‘Voice of the Republic.’ I think that’s how residents see him — as the voice of the people.” Russia’s State Duma election Gerrymandering à la russe: To preserve United Russia’s supermajority, the Kremlin is pressuring Communists to sideline their strongest candidates in September’s elections Russia’s State Duma election delivered record turnout and a landslide for United Russia. Kremlin insiders say the results were achieved ‘through very dirty means.’ At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter . Andrey Pertsev

title: Initia halts blockchain after exploit reportedly drains over $2.6M
body:
The blockchain suspended its layer-1 network and rollups after security researchers identified unauthorized token minting and millions in assets transferred to Ethereum.
Initia halted its layer-1 blockchain and rollups after blockchain sleuths reported an exploit that allowed an attacker to mint tokens without authorization and drain more than $2.6 million in crypto assets.
The network was halted at 3:41 p.m. UTC on Friday following a security incident, Initia said in a post on X. The team said it was working with security researchers, validators and exchanges to determine the full extent of the impact.
Blockchain security researcher Spreek first flagged the exploit on Friday, reporting that an attacker had minted tokens without authorization and converted approximately $2.6 million into other assets, with additional funds still being moved.
DeFi platform D2 Finance later reported that the attacker exploited a vulnerability to mint 2 million AUSD tokens without sufficient backing. The attacker then used cross-chain transfers to withdraw approximately 1.4 million AUSD, 105 Ether (ETH) and 1.08 million USDC (USDC) to Ethereum.
The stolen assets were subsequently consolidated into an Ethereum wallet holding approximately 1,135.5 ETH, worth $2.73 million, according to D2 Finance. The firm attributed the exploit to a vulnerability in a Move function that allowed the attacker to create unbacked tokens and exchange them for assets on Ethereum.
Initia is a layer-1 blockchain designed to support a network of interconnected rollups, known as Minitias. Its native token, INIT, briefly fell to around $0.115 on Friday before rebounding above $0.15, according to CoinGecko data . The token was trading near $0.1496 at the time of writing, an increase of about 14% over the previous 24 hours.
Initia has not publicly confirmed the estimated losses or the precise cause of the exploit, and the extent of the impact on users and the timeline for restoring network operations remain unclear. Cointelegraph was unable to contact Initia for additional comment through its official X account.

title: Austria expels Russian Embassy and OSCE diplomats over suspected spying. Vienna remains a Russian spy hub
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Austria has ordered four Russian diplomats to leave the country over suspected espionage, declaring them persona non grata following findings by Austrian security authorities, Austrian media outlet Heute reported on 23 October. The expulsions come as European countries step up efforts to counter suspected Russian intelligence operations amid Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Three of the diplomats worked at the Russian Embassy in Vienna, while the fourth served in Russia’s delegation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which is headquartered in Vienna. Austria’s Foreign Ministry said the four had engaged in “activities incompatible with their diplomatic status,” a term usually used for spying, Reuters reported . It did not disclose details of the alleged activities or the intelligence findings behind the decision. The three embassy diplomats were declared persona non grata under Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. The fourth, who worked on military security and arms control at Russia’s OSCE delegation, was also ordered to leave Austria. Vienna remains a hub for Russian intelligence The latest expulsions bring the number of Russian diplomats Austria has expelled since 2020 to 18, according to Reuters. In May 2026, Austria expelled three Russian Embassy employees suspected of using antennas on diplomatic buildings to intercept satellite internet data transmitted by international organizations based in Vienna. Vienna’s concentration of international organizations, including the OSCE and United Nations agencies, has made it a key location for intelligence activity. A 2024 report by The Wall Street Journal, described Vienna as a major Russian spy hub for operations targeting Western countries, including surveillance of arms supplies to Ukraine. title: USTR Proposes Extending China Ship Port Fee Suspension Through January 2027
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
A cargo ship full of shipping containers is seen at the port of Oakland, California, U.S., August 4, 2025. REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo
The Trump administration is proposing to extend its suspension of port fees targeting China-linked vessels for another two months, pushing their potential return into January 2027 as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of global shipbuilding.
The proposal, outlined in a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication October 26, would extend the existing one-year suspension through January 9, 2027. The current pause is set to expire November 9.
The extension would provide another reprieve for shipping companies facing potentially significant fees on Chinese-owned, Chinese-operated and Chinese-built vessels calling at U.S. ports, as well as certain foreign-built vehicle carriers.
“The United States is continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices at issue in the investigation,” USTR said in the notice.
Under the proposal, the measures would remain suspended from November 10, 2026, through January 9, 2027. During that period, shipping companies would not incur liability for port fees under Annexes I, II and III of the original Section 301 action. The suspension would also continue to cover certain duties on ship-to-shore cranes and cargo-handling equipment.
The proposed extension comes nearly a year after President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to suspend the port fees as part of a broader trade agreement reached in South Korea.
Washington began collecting the fees on October 14, 2025, but suspended them on November 10, meaning the measures were in effect for less than four weeks. China also suspended its retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels.
The original measures emerged from a Section 301 investigation launched during the Biden administration following a 2024 petition by the United Steelworkers and other labor organizations. The investigation concluded that China’s industrial policies and subsidies distorted global competition and undermined U.S. commerce.
The resulting port fees became a central part of the Trump administration’s strategy to counter China’s maritime dominance and encourage investment in American shipbuilding.
The latest proposal comes despite mounting pressure from some lawmakers and maritime labor groups to bring the fees back.
In June, Senators Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) urged the administration to immediately reinstate the measures , arguing that their suspension undermined efforts to rebuild the U.S. commercial shipbuilding industry.
“Section 301 port fees are critical to revitalizing U.S. shipbuilding,” the senators wrote in a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
The lawmakers pointed to China’s growing share of global shipbuilding, noting that Chinese yards now account for more than half of global commercial vessel production, compared with just 0.1% for the United States.
They also questioned whether Washington had secured meaningful concessions from Beijing in exchange for suspending the fees and how the administration intended to fund its proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund without the revenue.
Maritime labor unions have similarly criticized the suspension, arguing that it weakens one of the few measures specifically designed to counter China’s state-supported shipbuilding industry.
Shipping companies, meanwhile, have welcomed the reprieve.
The original fees threatened to impose substantial costs on carriers and disrupt established shipping networks. During the brief period the measures were active, U.S. carrier Matson reported incurring $6.4 million in reciprocal Chinese port fees, while China’s state-owned COSCO faced an estimated $1.5 billion in annual U.S. charges.
Andy Abbott, CEO of ACL, told gCaptain that any port fees would impact its growing US export business, and customers are concerned ACL.
“ACL’s unique ships were mistakenly classified by USTR as vehicle carriers even though only 1% of its cargo is automobiles,” explained Abbott. “Our largest US container and heavy machinery customers were panicking that we would redeploy our ships out of the US trade to the booming China trade. This development allows us to continue serving the US market with the fastest transit times from the US East Coast to Europe.”
The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and World Shipping Council both welcomed last year’s suspension, warning that the competing U.S. and Chinese measures risked increasing transportation costs and disrupting global trade.
The proposed extension also comes as the administration considers a much broader port fee system under its Maritime Action Plan , unveiled earlier this year.
Unlike the China-specific Section 301 measures, the plan envisions fees on all foreign-built commercial vessels calling at U.S. ports, with proceeds supporting domestic shipbuilding through a proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund.
The plan outlined potential fees ranging from 1 cent to 25 cents per kilogram of imported cargo, which the administration estimated could generate as much as $1.5 trillion over 10 years at the upper end.
ICS has warned that such broad-based charges could significantly increase shipping costs and disrupt global trade, even as it supports efforts to expand U.S. shipbuilding capacity.
The proposals underscore the competing pressures facing the administration as it seeks to revive American shipyards without imposing additional costs on U.S. importers, exporters and consumers.
For now, the latest USTR proposal would leave the China-specific port fee measures on hold for another two months, while negotiations continue.
USTR has opened a public comment period on the extension, with submissions due by 5 p.m. Eastern Time on October 30. Comments can be filed through the USTR public comment portal under docket USTR-2026-0694.
The extension has not yet been finalized. The notice also does not address whether China will extend its own suspension of retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels.

title: European and Middle Eastern foreign ministers urge restraint at Istanbul talks
body: Regional and European powers on Friday urged parties to war in the Middle East to avoid further military escalation, amid fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran and continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthi rebels. “Military intervention is not a solution, and nobody approves this at the moment,” Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told journalists in Istanbul after a meeting with counterparts from across the region and Europe. Foreign ministers from the UK, France, Germany and Italy met with counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt at a hotel alongside the Bosphorus strait on Friday afternoon, in the first meeting of its kind between all the ministers. The countries represented had agreed to “give the message to all parties” that diplomacy needed to prevail over more war, Mr Fidan said. “A repeated attack on Iran could spread the war and conflict in the region further,” said Mr Fidan, who maintains dialogue with both the US and Iran. “On the other hand, the opening of the Strait of Hormuz is needed, and the attacks on Saudi Arabia shall also stop.” A new escalation between Tehran and Washington “would create nothing but losers”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told journalists after the talks on Friday. Ministers from the eight countries discussed the “urgent need” for diplomacy to resolve regional challenges, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement. Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar briefed his counterparts on Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions and prevent a resumption of hostilities, it added. Ministers discussed the “parameters” for preventing the conflict from spreading across the Middle East, Mr Fidan said, declining to elaborate. The US and Israel have reportedly discussed launching a new major military operation against Iran, potentially involving strikes on missile and nuclear sites as well as oil installations, although US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that he would not strike again before the US midterm elections on November 3. Iranian officials have vowed an even more widespread response to any new attack than the strikes Tehran launched across the region after US-Israeli military operations began on February 28. Cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities could all be attacked by Tehran , Iran's National Security Council chief Maj Gen Mohsen Rezaei told Iranian media this week. The US continues to impose a military blockade on Iran’s seaports, while Tehran regularly attacks ships that attempt to navigate the Strait of Hormuz without its authorisation. 'Constructive discussions' After “very constructive discussions”, the eight countries around the table had decided to meet regularly, “to address issues related to a lasting resolution of the Iranian regime’s actions”, Mr Barrot said. They are also seeking to ensure freedom of navigation in Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Black Sea, where suspected Russian drone attacks have struck ships near Bulgaria and Romania in recent weeks, raising fears of another chokepoint on global maritime transport. A ceasefire and peace agreement in Ukraine were also needed “as soon as possible”, Mr Fidan added. Attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia were also a central agenda item, and Mr Fidan said he had discussed them in a meeting with the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Egypt before the talks with their European counterparts. Three of those nations – Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey – signed a collective defence pact in August, and Islamabad and Ankara have vowed to defend Saudi Arabia. Turkish officials have made it clear they draw a line at offensive actions against the Houthis in Yemen, whose fatal attacks on Saudi Arabia have prompted the kingdom to cancel major events and furthered the turmoil in global energy markets. Saudi Arabia confirmed Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan’s attendance at the Istanbul meetings but did not provide details. Mr Dar held a bilateral meeting with Mr Farhan, in which he expressed Pakistan’s “full support” for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, according to a post on X from Islamabad's Foreign Ministry. The talks in Istanbul also come against a backdrop of growing unrest in Europe, partly over a cost-of-living crisis exacerbated by rising fuel prices resulting from the Middle East war. France has been buffeted by weeks of protests that began around education but which have expanded to encompass demands over the high cost of living, while Italians have taken to the streets over soaring fuel prices and living costs. Mr Barrot underlined efforts to secure energy supplies during President Emmanuel Macron's tour of the Gulf this week, which included a surprise stop in Saudi Arabia. France has also confirmed it was sending military capabilities to protect the key Yanbu oil export terminal in western Saudi Arabia. Violations of freedom of navigation, whether in the Black Sea or Gulf region, have “extremely concrete consequences for us”, Mr Barrot said. “They significantly drive up transportation costs, which ultimately leads to inflation – that is, rising prices – and thus a reduction in the purchasing power of French citizens.”

title: Ohio could decide control of the Senate. Its rural voters might decide the winner
body:
Chris Gibbs, a cattle farmer in rural Ohio, says he's been in a deficit for almost three years. Keren Carrión/NPR hide caption
At the weekday farmers market in Athens, Ohio, colorful vegetables are on display for patrons to purchase, community members interact with each other and vendors and one another. It feels like most people in attendance know one another on some personal level.
For a small town like Athens, the farmers market is a gathering place.
"Our Saturday markets have been fully at capacity," said Paige Walters, the Athens farmers market promotions manager.
Athens, Ohio is home to Ohio University. The city is, like many college towns, pretty liberal. But that's not the case in most of the Appalachian communities in the region.
Walters noticed that this year, for the first time in a while, the Athens County Republican Party has set up a table at the market.
"I think that does speak to the political climate right now – that it's pretty competitive," she said.
Despite its past as a swing state, Ohio is now considered to be reliably Republican. This election is a little different. With toss-up races for governor and U.S. Senate, Democrats have a chance to win statewide.
But if Democrats want to win, they have to capture voters who voted for Republicans in the past. That includes the rural Ohio voter base, which historically leans conservative.
While rural voters nationwide have voted red in the past (they backed Trump in 2024 by 40 points), recent polling has shown his approval rating in rural America dropping dramatically amid high inflation, tariffs and the war in Iran.
Democrats are trying to gain ground in the unexpected areas. That's especially true in the competitive Senate match up between Sen. Jon Husted, the Republican nominee, and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown as both candidates invest in outreach to rural parts of the state.
"There's a lot of people in rural Ohio that are not happy, whether it's gas prices, diesel prices, the tariffs, the war," Matthew White of Athens told NPR at the farmers market.
Multicolored bell peppers, onions and squash line the table at the Cowdery Farms booth. While the weekday market usually has slower foot traffic, farmer Larry Cowdery sold a good amount of produce.
He owns a small vegetable farm along the Ohio River in Long Bottom. There are two big concerns at the top of Cowdrey's mind. The first is the cost of healthcare.
"The big, big issue that we run into is since we're self-employed, we have to find health insurance somewhere," he told NPR. "It's going to be much more expensive next year."
Healthcare premiums on the Affordable Care Act marketplace are expected to increase by roughly 15% in Ohio , in part because of the expiration of federal subsidies. Republicans, including Husted, voted to eliminate the subsidies under the Trump-backed "One Big Beautiful Bill." As a result of sticker shock, Ohio saw the biggest drop — tied with Oklahoma for the most in the nation — in the number of people enrolled in the marketplace last year, with a nearly 33% decline in enrollment.
Cowdery's second concern is the survival of his multigenerational family farm. It's becoming too expensive to run. He said the cost of electricity and gasoline is a big factor. Plus, he relies on fertilizer to grow his vegetables.
"I'm not convinced we're even going to be able to get fertilizer next year," Cowdery said.
That's because of the war in Iran. Most of the nitrogen used in fertilizer travels through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping channel in the Middle East controlled by Iran. Travel through the Strait has been volatile.
As a result of the healthcare and business hardships, Cowdery isn't keen on voting Republican this year. He added that he hasn't been happy with the Republican-led Ohio legislature for the last few years and he doesn't like Husted, either.
"I don't trust Jon Husted at all. I think he's a crook," Cowdery said.
Dean Ferrell is at the farmers market chatting with people and milling around the market. The 62-year-old man, a lifelong resident of Athens, said the cost of gas, utilities and groceries have become burdensome. He has had to cut back on buying certain foods because he can't afford it.
"I mean, who would ever thought you'd be paying ten bucks a pound for ground beef? That used to be filet mignon prices, not ground beef," he said.
Ferrell tried to look on the upside of his financial reality. Since he's older, Ferrell said he doesn't eat as much as he used to, so he can save some money that way. He added that he wishes politicians could spend "a week or two living like I do."
"Their attitude would be a lot different. I mean, I gotta save money wherever I can, buy reduced and on sale items," Ferrell said. "There's very few things that I pay full price for. You got to, to survive."
Ferrell considers himself to be an independent. While he hasn't decided who to vote for the Senate, Ferrell said he is leaning toward Husted. He doesn't like the direction the Democratic party is headed.
"The far left has basically hijacked the Democrat Party," he said.
On a crisp fall day in rural central Ohio, farmer Chris Gibbs climbs into his John Deere utility terrain vehicle, setting out to survey his land.
"It started in 1983 on our own with $2,500, a pickup truck and a two-year-old daughter," Gibbs said with a chuckle. "So we built that up to 560 acres."
Gibbs, a first generation farmer in Shelby County, grows corn, soybeans, alfalfa hay and has a few dozen cows.
Farming is a tough industry at the best of times. Farms are at the behest of market fluctuations, domestic policy, international relations and mother nature. Tack on high fuel and fertilizer prices, along with Trump's tariffs and the cost of production exceeds the profit.
Sitting in his huge combine that used to harvest corn and soybeans, Gibbs said the diesel fuel to run the machinery has increased 50% under the Trump administration and the war in Iran. He fills up the combine about seven times during the harvest season.
"I think about 150 gallons at $7 is $1,000, and that'll run a day and a half," Gibbs said. "That'd be $7,000 worth of diesel fuel."
Politically, farmers tend to vote Republican. Gibbs was one of those Republicans at one point. In a past life, he was the chair of the Shelby County Republicans. He voted for Trump in 2016.
"I'm looking at certainly, buyer's remorse," Gibbs said about voting for Trump.
Gibbs couldn't stand behind Trump's character, his persona on the global stage or the punitive tariffs he said hurt "United States of America's soft underbelly," referring to agriculture. He moved away from Trump in 2018.
Now, in 2026, Gibbs is the chair of the Ohio Democratic Party Rural Caucus and he wants to send Democrat Sherrod Brown back to the Senate.
Brown, Gibbs argued, has the experience necessary to represent rural Ohioans at the federal level.
"We're going to get Sherrod Brown across the line. I have complete confidence in that," Gibbs said.
At a Republican Party event in Guysville, Melissa Jant said she doesn't want a career politician representing her in Congress and that's exactly how she views Brown.
"I absolutely do not want Sherrod Brown back in there. He was there for 30 years. We saw the policies that he put in place. He ran the country down. He ran Ohio down. We just need new blood in there," she told NPR.
VANDALIA, OHIO - OCTOBER 03: U.S. President Donald Trump (R) is joined by Sen Jon Husted, R-Ohio, on stage with President Trump in Vandalia, Ohio on Oct. 3, 2026. Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images hide caption
VANDALIA, OHIO - OCTOBER 03: U.S. President Donald Trump (R) is joined by Sen Jon Husted, R-Ohio, on stage with President Trump in Vandalia, Ohio on Oct. 3, 2026. Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images hide caption
President Trump spoke near Dayton recently, throwing his support behind Republican Sen. Jon Husted. His stop is part of a series of rallies to support Republicans heading into the midterm elections.
Her displeasure toward Brown isn't just because he is a Democrat. Some voters view him as the establishment, despite not being a lawmaker anymore.
Jimmy Williams of Monroe County feels similarly. He said Brown was voted out and shouldn't try and head back to his old stomping grounds. Instead, Williams views Husted as the anti-establishment candidate, despite the fact that he is a sitting senator.
"He's a first-term senator there, and he hasn't even been in there long enough to do everything that they're saying on television," Williams said about ads aimed at Husted. "And people need to be smart enough to look through that."
Bob Rouch, of Washington County told NPR he is optimistic that Ohio will stay Republican. He believes Trump has done a lot of good for the county and "it's Ohio's responsibility to keep up with that." If Democrats win control, Rouch thinks they won't doing anything aside from target Trump.
"We're going to have these damn investigations, these attempted impeachments and all the baloney that we went through," he said, referring to the last time Democrats controlled Congress while Trump was president.
Williams argued preserving Republican control of Congress is the goal right now.
The audio version of this story incorrectly says that if the incumbent, Jon Husted, wins in November, he will serve his first full term in the U.S Senate. Husted was appointed to the Senate seat vacated by JD Vance last year, and whoever wins this year's election will serve out the remainder of Vance's term, through 2028.

title: Air Force unit halts rappelling, ropes training after airman dies during public demonstration
body: Less than a week after an airman died from injuries sustained during a rappelling incident , the service member’s special operations unit has suspended all rappel and ropes training events and demonstrations. On Saturday, Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas, fell from a football stadium’s rafters during a rappelling demonstration before a game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the U.S. Naval Academy. During UTSA’s annual Salute to Armed Forces & Veterans game, videos show Patterson wearing combat fatigues and rappelling down to midfield from the Alamodome’s rafters before falling onto the field at full speed, feet first. Subsequent videos show medical personnel assisting the airman on the field before transporting him to a local hospital. Later Saturday night, Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, which houses the 6th Combat Training Squadron, announced Patterson had died at the hospital from the injuries sustained during the demonstration. Members of the 6th Combat Training Squadron are trained in rappelling from heights of 100 feet or more. The football stadium’s rafters are around 170 feet above the stadium floor. “Tech Sgt Patterson’s squadron, 6th Combat Training Squadron, has paused all rappel and ropes training events and demonstrations until further notice,” an Air Force Warfare Center spokesperson told Military Times. The spokesperson declined to comment on when the suspension began and who enacted it. The comment did not include when the office expects the events and demonstrations to continue. Rappelling and ropes are a large aspect of the Tactical Air Control Party’s skill base, with familiarization training designed to give service members basic information and techniques needed to conduct live operations, according to an Air Force description . Patterson was from Fort Stewart, Georgia, and served in the Air Force for 15 years. His decorations include the Air and Space Commendation Medal with three oak leaf clusters, as well as the Army Commendation Medal, Air and Space Achievement Medal and Army Achievement Medal, each with one oak leaf cluster. He was named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the headquarters level in 2022. The incident is currently under investigation, according to a release at the time of identification.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is above average in intelligence, but somewhat expensive when comparing to other models of similar price. It's also notably slow and somewhat verbose. The model supports text and image input, outputs text, and has a 1M tokens context window.
Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 46 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it above average among comparable models (median: 38). When evaluating the Intelligence Index, it generated 110M tokens, which is somewhat verbose in comparison to the median of 71M.

At 31 tokens per second, Kimi K3.1 Pro is notably slow (83).

title: Record Tanker Rates Threaten to Push U.S. Oil Exports to Asia to Seven-Year Low
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
By Yongchang Chin and Nathan Risser (Bloomberg) –US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million.
Asian refinery orders for US crude for delivery in November tumbled roughly 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels this month sequentially, according to traders who asked for anonymity because they weren’t authorized to publicly comment. If that pace of orders holds through the end of this month, it would mark a seven-year low, based on ship-tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa.
The tanker rate along the US Gulf Coast-to-China route has more than tripled since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February to almost $60 million as of Thursday, according to Baltic Exchange figures. Earlier in the month, it touched $79.6 million, an unprecedented ruction in a market where rates averaged less than $8 million in the half decade before the conflict.
As it stands, leasing the largest class of crude carriers for the 30-day voyage is equivalent to half the cost of building a brand-new vessel. Those eye-watering rates doesn’t include the cost of the oil itself, which is trading around $100 a barrel.
Cost to Ship US Oil to Asia Has Never Been Higher
“The main story right now in the market is freight rates,” Randy Hawkins, Valero Energy Inc.’s head of oil trading, said during as conference call with analysts.
Tanker rates are so inflated that refiners are effectively spending $30 to $35 to haul each barrel of crude from the Gulf Coast to Asia, or as much as seven times what they shelled out last year, Hawkins said.
IEA: Gulf Oil Shipping Costs Top $37 Per Barrel, Five Times Pre-War Levels
To be sure, the end of the November trading cycle isn’t a hard deadline, which leaves some leeway for traders to snap up last-minutes cargoes. At least one market participant who asked to remain anonymous said Asia-bound US cargoes for November may recover to as much as 40 million barrels in post-cycle trades.
Vortexa, however, is skeptical that such a turnaround is imminent.
“We don’t currently see evidence of a near-term surge that would push those volumes significantly higher,” said Rohit Rathod, a senior Vortexa analyst.
The drop in Asian demand appears to be rippling across US crude pricing.
Export-bound Permian Basin oil was trading for 25 cents above the benchmark futures contract at the Magellan East Houston hub as of Wednesday, down from more than $3 six weeks earlier, according to Link Data Services.
Medium sour export grade Mars, which is pumped from deepwater wells in the Gulf of Mexico and is similar to Middle Eastern crude, has seen its premium to futures plunge to $6 from $17.50 in late March.
US Oil Exports Surged to Record High This Year | The US sent over 6 million barrels of oil abroad each day in late April as war curtailed flows from the Middle East Valero’s Hawkins said one factor hindering global tanker availability has been the increased use of smaller vessels to pick up crude in the Persian Gulf that are less likely to be hit by Iranian fire in Strait of Hormuz. Once they’ve traversed the waterway, their cargoes are transferred to larger vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman.
“The inefficient process of this ship-to-ship transferring that they’re doing of crude oil in the Gulf of Oman is really tying up global shipping and to require more tankers to move the same amount of oil,” Hawkins said. Insurance rates and high fuel costs also are driving up freight costs, he added.
“The primary factor remains high freight costs, which continue to squeeze arbitrage economics for long-haul routes,” Vortexa’s Rathod said. “The incentive for Asian buyers to source from the US Gulf Coast has diminished.”

title: “Endless Forms Most Beautiful and Most Wonderful”: Ruliobiology and the Theoretical Foundations of Biological Form
body:
Biology is (as Charles Darwin put it a century and a half ago) full of “endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful”. But just where do such forms fundamentally come from? And is there any kind of general theory one can make of them? Darwin seemed to imagine that natural selection alone would (like “the fixed law of gravity”) inevitably lead to such forms. But it’s never been clear just why that would be so. Or how one might in fact set about constructing a theory of such things. But from work I’ve done in the past couple of years , I think we begin to see some possibilities. And that’s what I’m going to be talking about here.
The starting point is what we can call “ruliobiology”. We can think of ruliobiology as a metamodel of biology: an abstract framework not intended to provide a specific model of any particular biological system, but rather intended to capture the essence of certain core features of what’s fundamentally going on in biology. Ruliobiology is ultimately about what happens in systems based on simple rules subject to adaptive evolution—and we can explore it using the general methods and concepts of ruliology .
And what we’ll discover here is that a remarkable range of what we might consider to be “quintessentially biological” phenomena already show up in ruliobiology. And indeed ruliobiology seems to give us a way to see that, yes, in some sense Darwin’s supposition was correct: there is a certain theoretically-derivable inevitability to the generation of “endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful”.
One of the ingredients that’s needed is indeed Darwin’s idea of natural selection—and the process of adaptive evolution associated with it. But another crucial ingredient is what we can think of as the central phenomenon of ruliology: computational irreducibility . Computational irreducibility is what makes even simple underlying rules very often lead to behavior that is in effect irreducibly complex. And in effect it supplies the “raw material” for ruliobiology—on which adaptive evolution can act. It is then the interplay of adaptive evolution with computational irreducibility that leads to the core phenomena of ruliobiology.
Darwin seems to have imagined that there might be “laws of biology” analogous to laws of physics (like “the fixed law of gravity”). And here indeed we’ll see that there are “laws of ruliobiology”—though they are different in character from laws of physics. For traditional laws of physics tend to concern themselves with aspects of physical behavior that are computationally reducible , and that can be described, say, with mathematical formulas. Ruliobiology—and, I believe, biology—have computational irreducibility at their core. So, for example, whereas in physics one can discuss a phenomenon just as something happening “here and now”, in ruliobiology—and biology—there is an inevitable dependence on history, and on the computationally irreducible process that led us to here and now.
In the past one might have imagined that this would mean there could be nothing general one could say about ruliobiology—or biology—and that everything would have to be attributed just to “accidents of history”. But by thinking about the ruliad and about spaces of all possible rules we discover that there are in fact general things that can be said. One approach is to make use of the concept of the rulial ensemble : the set of rules that are reached by adaptive evolution with some computationally simple fitness function. And the key point is that while the details change with different fitness functions (and different classes of underlying rules), certain emergent features do not—and can therefore be seen as general to ruliobiology.
As is often the case, the introduction of the new methodology of ruliobiology lets us start addressing new kinds of questions—that in many cases one had never even thought to ask before. Ruliobiology is ultimately a rich and vast domain—and here I’ll only begin to scratch its surface. But from what we see here I think it’s already clear that ruliobiology can finally provide the basis for broad theoretical thinking in biology—with the potential to transform how one approaches many important issues in biology.
The basic setup in ruliobiology involves looking at “rulioorganisms” that “grow” according to simple fixed rules—with the rules being determined by an overarching process of adaptive evolution. Here I’ll be using rules based on symmetric 5-color cellular automata , grown from “seeds” consisting of a single cell:
The rules (shown on the right) can be thought of as corresponding to the genotype of the rulioorganism; the pattern (shown on the left) obtained by following these rules can be thought of as the phenotype of the rulioorganism. The rules are progressively updated by a process of adaptive evolution—with successive steps of this evolution involving random mutations that change the outcomes for particular rule cases:
The mutations are preserved if they increase (or at least leave constant) a fitness function; otherwise—in an analog of natural selection—they’re rejected. The particular fitness function we’ll mostly use here is “lifetime”, defined as the number of steps for which a phenotype pattern survives before dying out. (We take infinite patterns to have zero fitness.) With this setup we can plot (as red dots) the fitness values obtained by a sequence of mutations:
We see that many mutations decrease fitness—which means they’re not preserved. But every so often there’s a “breakthrough” that increases fitness. And looking at the rulioorganisms corresponding to these breakthroughs we see—a bit like in the fossil record—that they involve a sequence of “discoveries” that build on one another to progressively increase the fitness:
It’s immediately striking how “biological” these patterns look—with lots of complexity, but also identifiable patches of regularity reminiscent of the structures like organs that we see in biology.
The particular rulioorganisms in the picture above are the result of a particular sequence of random mutations. As we will soon see, other sequences of random mutations will lead to quite different rulioorganisms. But despite their detailed differences, what we’ll find is that there are features of these rulioorganisms—and their evolution—that are widely shared, and in effect represent the core phenomena of ruliobiology.
What can rulioorganisms be like? Here are a few examples:
The resonance with Darwin’s “endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful” is certainly striking. Each of these rulioorganisms was ultimately evolved with the same simple objective of “living as long as possible”. But what we see is that the rulioorganisms achieve this objective in a remarkable diversity of different ways. Notably, not a single one of these ways is “simple”, in the sense that one can readily give a simple “mechanical” description of how it works. And at some level all of them “just happen to work”, in the sense that they represent frozen pieces of computational irreducibility that turn out to achieve the objective—even though one can’t see that this will be the case except in effect by explicitly running them and observing what happens.
So how did these rulioorganisms evolve? Here are some examples of the sequences of breakthroughs that were involved, in all cases starting from the trivial “null” rule:
The details are different in each case. But there’s an important common theme. In the course of the adaptive evolution, some “innovation” is invented (like “use triangular regions of purple”), and then, as the adaptive evolution proceeds, this innovation is progressively (and often “creatively”) elaborated.
Look at a biological organism at different scales and you’ll see different things. Indeed, it seems as if in biology there’s—quite ubiquitously—“novelty” at every scale. When biological organisms were first examined under microscopes it was a big surprise how much unseen structure was discovered. And with essentially every new level of microscopy that’s introduced, yet more—often very different—new structures seem to be revealed.
Nesting and the idea of fractals captures the notion of having smaller copies of the same structure at different scales. But what we’re talking about here is something very different: we’re talking in effect about having a whole hierarchy of novelty, where fundamentally different things are happening at each scale. It’s something that’s been hinted at—particularly in biological contexts—for centuries. But so far as I know, it’s not something that’s ever explicitly been given a name. Here I’ll refer to the phenomenon as polyplexy. (As we’ll discuss below, it’s a different phenomenon from what one sees in something like the Mandelbrot set .)
So do we see polyplexy in ruliobiology? The answer is yes, quite ubiquitously so. Consider for example this rulioorganism:
What we probably first notice is its complicated overall shape:
Next we might notice its areas of purple—and the random-looking “connective tissue” between them. But let’s zoom in a bit, say near the lowest part of the pattern:
There are areas of purple alright. But they’re laced with (irregularly placed) vertical stripes. And we can now see that the connective tissue isn’t really random: there’s actually all sorts of structure in it. Zooming in a little more (and showing only the left half of the pattern) we start to see a whole variety of specific highly ordered structures dotted around:
At a still smaller scale we begin to see how those structures are embedded in the larger pattern:
And zooming all the way down to “ruliological atoms” we can finally identify some of the “lowest level structures” in our rulioorganism:
We can think of such structures as corresponding to patches of computational reducibility. But sometimes—even at the lowest level—there’s just too much immediate computational irreducibility for us to be able to discern any kind of “describable structure”:
Looking at our rulioorganism as a whole, we see that—like a typical biological organism—it contains many small structures that are basically repeated in different places
though often in slightly different forms:
Biological organisms are typically viewed as having a hierarchy of types of parts (from organ systems to organs to tissues to cells to organelles, etc.) And one might have imagined that cellular automata of the kind we’re using here—with their simple, uniform underlying discrete structure—would never be able to exhibit any such hierarchy. But in fact we find that our rulioorganisms are full of hierarchy—usually with visibly different kinds of structures on different scales:
Another feature of rulioorganisms is that their different parts are often differentiated from each other. In the end, the parts must all “work together” to achieve the fitness objective that’s been defined. But in general, many of them will in some sense “do different things”—much like different parts of biological organisms.
(It’s useful to contrast this with what happens in something like the Mandelbrot set , where there’s plenty of visual diversity, but where at every coordinate position and every zoom level one’s just seeing geometric distortions of a single object, with the distortions defined essentially by the digit sequences of the coordinates.)
We saw above various examples of rulioorganisms. But what is the space of all possible rulioorganisms like? I’ve argued elsewhere that any “rulial ensemble” of what we now call rulioorganisms selected according to any computationally simple fitness function will have certain overall features in common. But to be specific here, let’s start by considering (symmetric) rules selected purely on the basis of lifetime, and let’s look at the rulioorganisms we get after 1000 steps of adaptive evolution (here with the lifetime in each case indicated):
As we’ll discuss later , our process of adaptive evolution is fundamentally open ended, and by continuing it we can expect to find rulioorganisms with longer lifetimes. But for now, let’s just impose the criterion that the lifetime after 1000 steps of adaptive evolution has to be above 500:
There is a certain sameness to the overall appearance of these rulioorganisms—perhaps much as there is a certain sameness to the overall appearance of a great many species of biological organisms. But the distribution of possible forms of rulioorganisms is broad, and selecting for “visual impact” (measured, say, on the basis of width and compression size) one gets some more exotic examples, including many quite unexpected forms:
(Later we’ll discuss the convergent evolution that we can see here.) It’s perhaps notable that among rulioorganisms one typically finds that “visually exotic” ones arise at the level of a fraction of a percent—perhaps not so different from the level of visually exotic fish or other species typically on display in aquariums, etc. (And, yes, the fact that one can even imagine saying something scientific about a topic like this is remarkable, and a sign of the fresh and different paradigm that ruliobiology introduces.)
One might have assumed—in a natural selection kind of way—that to get exotic forms one would need an exotic environment, and exotic fitness function. But what we’ve seen here suggests that exotic forms can actually arise—albeit rarely—without an exotic fitness function, in effect just as examples of “surprises” that can inevitably be created by computational irreducibility.

Remember that here we are selecting only for lifetime. So any extreme values of other attributes are in a sense just “side effects”. And what we’re seeing is that “extreme side effects” appear to be a ubiquitous phenomenon in ruliobiology.
In traditional evolutionary biology, there tends to be an assumption that organisms with extreme traits arise because of selection associated specifically with those traits. So let’s say we’re looking at maximum width as a trait. Adaptive evolution using width as a fitness function yields for example these “fittest rulioorganisms”:
And what we see is that the widths achieved in this way are somewhat larger than the ones we got just as side effects, but not dramatically so. In other words, explicit adaptive evolution for a particular trait doesn’t seem to be getting us much more extreme values of that trait than we would get just by looking for this trait as a side effect. In essence, at least when it comes to extremes, the intrinsic “element of surprise” that exists in ruliobiology (and that ultimately results from computational irreducibility) is essentially just as strong an effect as specific adaptation.

But what about finding a general way to characterize the overall shapes of rulioorganisms? It’s not an easy problem, mathematically or otherwise. And in ordinary biology even simple analogs of it have proved challenging. Occasionally— as in the case of mollusc shells —there’s a continuous range of shapes, say determined by a growth parameter in a differential equation . But more often one ends up just with a taxonomy—in which classes of forms are named, often by analogy with everyday objects, as for example in the case of leaf shapes :
