We’ve talked about the outer boundaries of rulioorganisms. But what about their internal structure—their anatomy? Something that’s remarkable is how many general features of this structure are similar to what we see in biological organisms. At the simplest level, we can think of rulioorganisms as consisting of regions of tissue interspersed with “voids”—shown here as white:
There’s a lot of diversity in the overall “topology” of the “tissue”:
And there are several very different types of “tissue”. Sometimes there are patches of pure periodicity:
Sometimes there are patterns with pure nesting:
Sometimes there are regions of typical class 3 cellular automaton behavior enclosed within boundaries:
And, yes, what might at first here seem like uniform diamond-shaped patterns are actually full of class 3 behavior:
But perhaps the single most striking feature of most rulioorganisms is the presence of repeated modular structures that seem somehow “functionally separated”—in a way that’s reminiscent of organs, organelles, etc. in actual biology:
Sometimes these structures are delimited by highly regular “skeletal” elements:
But often the boundaries show considerable randomness:
And in fact there are often whole regions of randomness
One can think of these regions of randomness as representing a kind of “connective tissue” between organ-like structures. And what’s remarkable is that this mirrors what one sees in actual biology. In some sense we can see this as a case where ruliobiology—on purely abstract computational grounds—can in effect “derive” an important, though typically unspoken, feature of biology: the presence of distinct “connective tissue” that separates organized structures, but is itself seemingly quite random.
(By the way, at a medical level, the randomness of connective tissue can be seen as an important part of what makes surgery possible—because it’s this randomness that allows connective tissue to be rearranged, yet still achieve its function.)
Biological organisms tend to operate only as integrated wholes; their parts typically don’t usefully work in isolation. And so it also is with rulioorganisms. For example, imagine a patch in the pattern corresponding to a rulioorganism. Now ask what happens if we take the configuration at the top of that patch, and run it in isolation. Typically what we find is that in isolation the part behaves very differently from how it does in the whole:
There is, in effect, widespread bulk orchestration in which everything is orchestrated to work together, with parts on their own not doing what they do in the whole.
We can think of rulioorganisms as being “frozen pieces of computational irreducibility” that “just turn out” to optimize certain fitness objectives. And from this point of view, the fact that a rulioorganism forms an “integrated whole” where “everything matters” can be thought of as reflecting underlying computational irreducibility. Just as you can’t reduce computational effort by jumping ahead and skipping everything in between, you also can’t reduce it by considering only a limited patch of underlying cells and ignoring everything else. Or, put another way, there’s an irreducible need to include the context of the whole rulioorganism to get the parts to behave as they do in the whole rulioorganism: there’s no systematic shortcut one can take.
There’s something else as well: in ruliobiology—just like in biology—adaptive evolution ultimately operates on whole rulioorganisms. And this means that not only do the parts of a rulioorganism build up to determine the behavior of the whole rulioorganism, so also—because it’s what adaptive evolution operates on—the whole rulioorganism in a sense determines the forms of its parts. One way to describe it is to say that the parts define the mechanism that builds up the whole, while the fitness of the whole defines what one can think of as a purpose for it.
This interplay between parts and whole—and purpose and mechanism—seems to be something very characteristic of what we see in biology. But now, in ruliobiology, we can see its fundamental origins: it’s all about the presence of computational irreducibility and its interplay with the computational boundedness of fitness functions of the kind used in adaptive evolution.
We’ve seen many examples of remarkable forms produced by adaptive evolution—here for 1000 steps:
But what happens if we just keep going with our adaptive evolution? Do we continue to get “even fitter”, and perhaps even more remarkable forms? Here’s what happens if we go another 1000 steps in this particular case:
The increase in fitness has “kept going”, here achieving a final fitness (i.e. length) of 1445—nearly 2.5 times the 580 achieved after 1000 steps. Can we go even further? With a fixed number of discrete elements in the rule (i.e. ruliogenome), we’ll eventually “hit the edge of rule space”. But if, for example, we not only change the rule, but also change the size of the initial conditions , we’ll get an indefinitely large number of cases—and we can expect that we’ll have entirely open-ended evolution, that can eventually reach arbitrarily large fitness. In other words, with this setup, there’ll normally never be a “final best rulioorganism”; in effect, there’s always something better to be found somewhere in the ruliad.
The example above illustrates a typical phenomenon: that as the process of adaptive evolution goes on, it’s continually “reusing ideas” (like here of having large patches of purple)—but progressively refactoring and embellishing them.
Occasionally in the “ruliological fossil record” one will see a kind of alternation between rather different boundary forms—even as many of the same features are maintained inside:
Here’s another example that again illustrates “reuse of ideas”, but “refactored” into a sequence of forms that—if one didn’t know their “ruliogenetic” connection—might seem rather hard to relate:
In the evolution of life on Earth a repeated phenomenon that’s observed is that some feature of organisms—like eyes or wings—arises independently multiple times, by different routes. The same kind of convergent evolution also happens in ruliobiology. For example, here are four different ways “green pincers” can arise:
The main features of at least the pincer part of the final morphology are the same each time. But the way this morphology was reached is different. There are in effect multiple different “origin stories”, all converging on the final feature of green pincers.
Here’s another example, now of generating patterns with overall diamond-like boundary shapes:
And here again the paths of evolution are different—even though they “converge” to give the same overall final boundary shapes.
(What we’re looking at here is approximate convergence, to qualitatively similar forms. It’s worth noting that in a discrete rule space there will always be adaptive evolution paths that lead to exact convergence—and indeed we looked at this previously in much smaller rule spaces using multiway systems .)
When we adaptively evolve on the basis of a particular fitness function, what other traits will our rulioorganisms also end up having? In other words, what are the “side effects” of particular adaptive evolution? For example, if we evolve to maximize lifetime (as we’ve been doing here), then does this mean that we’ll inevitably produce rulioorganisms that also have some other—perhaps seemingly unrelated—identifiable feature?
As a very simple example, we can ask what maximizing lifetime (i.e. length) implies for the widths of patterns. Do patterns that are longer also tend to be wider? Or do they tend instead to be narrower? Running 100,000 cases of adaptive evolution (each for 1000 steps) we see that there is in fact a general trend for longer lifetimes to be associated with greater widths—or, in other words, for maximizing lifetime to have as a side effect an increase in width:
If we instead explicitly maximize width, we see that the widths we get can sometimes be larger than the ones that arose purely as side effects:
But the effect is not all that dramatic. And so—in a phenomenon that’s important in thinking about explanation in biology in general–if we just see a rulioorganism with a large width we can’t reasonable conclude that it’s that way because of direct selection for width; its large width could just be a side effect of selection for something else.
And in general lots of things can arise as side effects. Indeed, we can ask about any trait that we can systematically measure, and how it is affected by adaptive evolution for any other trait. Or, a little more formally: if we do adaptive evolution with some computationally bounded fitness function, how will this affect some other computationally bounded function that we can measure? Sometimes there may be obvious connections between such functions (typically associated with the basic forms of the rules for rulioorganisms). But the difficult issue is to understand the inevitable non-obvious connections, say associated with the structure of ruliobiological space, and with relations between different pockets of computational reducibility.
If a rulioorganism ends up having one trait, does that make it more—or less—likely that it’ll end up having some particular other trait too? One might imagine that perhaps one could develop some kind of “algebra of traits” that would describe what can occur with what. And when it comes to extreme traits, one might imagine a “theory of monsters” that would tell one, for example, what science-fiction-style chimeras can plausibly arise from adaptive evolution, and what cannot.
As a first example, let’s consider rulioorganisms generated as usual by adaptive evolution with lifetime as a fitness function. Now we ask how many red cells and how many green cells such rulioorganisms contain:
We see there are outliers with many red cells, and ones with many green cells. But—at least in this sample—there aren’t any “red-green chimeras”, with large numbers of both red and green cells.
What about yellow and green, though? As so often in the ruliological world, there’s a surprise: a rulioorganism with both many yellow and many green cells:
One might think it would have something like a simple pattern of stripes. But no. It’s contained class 3 behavior that happens to have both lots of yellow and lots of green:
And, yes, it’s a feature of the open-endedness of ruliobiological evolution that one doesn’t get traditional forms of “Pareto frontiers” with tradeoffs between traits. Instead, as in this example, there can be outliers that “open-endedly” in essence “win on all counts”.
But insofar as what we consider “traits” correspond to computationally bounded properties of rulioorganisms, we can think of correlations between traits as being associated with maps of connections between pockets of computational reducibility in ruliobiological space. At some level it’s inevitable that such connections must exist, defining what amount to laws about the forms of rulioorganisms. But the phenomenon of computational irreducibility implies that in general there will be no immediate way to know what such laws will be. And in effect there will be no choice but to do what amounts to experimental ruliobiology to try to find them.
Even when the final forms of evolutionarily related organisms look completely different, it is typical in biology for their early stages of development to nevertheless look very similar. So what’s the story for rulioorganisms?

The essential point is that—at least in this example—only a subset of rule cases are used in early development, and while these remain constant, so does early development. In some sense, one can think of conserved behavior as reflecting the notion that adaptive evolution is “coming up with an idea and then sticking to it”. Different paths of adaptive evolution “come up with different ideas”. But along one path one can imagine that ideas are somehow typically conserved, and progressively built on.
Eventually one may hope to have a general characterization (and perhaps theory) of this “progression of ideas”. But, for now, that is something for the future.

But let’s say we know the color fractions for a rulioorganism. Typically there are lots of rulioorganisms with very nearly identical color fractions:
And if we look at successively more predecessors of these, we see they quickly diverge in color fraction space:
In other words, knowing just a coarse feature like color fractions is not enough to be able to successfully “retrodict” what happened in the process of evolution; one needs more detail. Or, put another way, there’s no simple “law of motion” for ruliobiological evolution, that talks only about color fractions.
The basic goal of ruliobiology is to capture certain essential features of life. But in operating as it does at a very foundational level it has the potential to capture not only life as it is here and now on Earth, but also life as it can be, in generality. And in this sense we can think of ruliobiology as providing a new theoretical basis for astrobiology—that lets us discuss in a systematic way what characteristics potential instances of something like life might have elsewhere in the universe.
In formulating ruliobiology we already assume certain core features of what we think of as life, in particular the “code=data” phenomenon (presumably implemented through self-reproduction) of having an underlying rule where the results of running that rule affect the subsequent form of the rule. Elsewhere I have argued that with this adaptive evolution setup, computationally simple fitness functions inevitably pick out a certain rulial ensemble of possible rules, that lead to rulioorganisms that share certain important general features.
Here we’ve looked in more detail at rulioorganisms obtained with a specific setup. But—particularly in view of our results about rulial ensembles—we can expect that many, if not most, aspects of what we’ve seen will actually be quite general to rulioorganisms of any type.
And this means that we can have some confidence that our results will be relevant for astrobiology, as well as, for example, for understanding previous and alternate forms of life on Earth. So what do we learn from ruliobiology for astrobiology?
Perhaps the most immediately actionable result is an essentially visual one: we’ve seen that rulioorganisms tend to have certain characteristic visual features—essentially manifestations of mechanoidal behavior in which structured, modular parts are visible within overall complexity. And we can anticipate that these kinds of forms are also what one should expect in astrobiology.
Another central result in ruliobiology is that there’s a great diversity of forms for rulioorganisms—and again we can anticipate that this will carry over to astrobiology. And, in a sense, we must expect the unexpected: we must expect to see exotic forms that lie far out in distributions we might try to construct.
No doubt some of these features will apply not only to overall morphology (as one might see with a microscope in a physical specimen), but also to molecular-scale structures and processes.
But the key point is that ruliobiology—and the concept of the rulial ensemble—leads one to conclude that there are definite signatures of extended processes of adaptive evolution. In other words, just by looking at features of what comes out, one can get confidence that there was a long, arduous and computationally irreducible process of adaptive evolution underneath, that one can think of in its computational essence as being like what happens in the evolutionary development of biological life as we’re familiar with it.
Almost exactly 100 years before I was born, Charles Darwin ended his Origin of Species with
It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us. These laws, taken in the largest sense, being Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance which is almost implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and direct action of the external conditions of life, and from use and disuse; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved forms. Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death, the most exalted object which we are capable of conceiving, namely, the production of the higher animals, directly follows. There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
So what can we now add, with ruliobiology, to what Darwin said? For a start, Darwin seemed to imagine that—like the law of gravity—there would be a fundamental law that causes “endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful [to be] evolved”. We’ve never before had any kind of general or formal way to talk about biological form. But now, with ruliobiology, we do. And we can confirm that—as Darwin suspected—there are indeed general principles at work that lead to diverse and complex forms. But those general principles need something beyond what Darwin knew, or imagined: they need ideas that are fundamentally computational, and ruliological.
In what he wrote, Darwin in effect asserted that the appearance of forms such as those of “higher animals” would “directly follow” from the “war of nature” and the mechanism of natural selection. But despite often strident claims to the contrary over the past century and a half there’s never been a clear picture of how this would work. Yes, one can see that natural selection can lead to adaptive evolution. And one might imagine that the complexity of the ecological environment would somehow be imprinted on the forms of organisms and lead to the kind of diversity and complexity we see. But there’s been no formal theory that shows us this.
And what ruliobiology now suggests is that actually there’s a quite different driving force at work: the phenomenon of computational irreducibility. And indeed the picture that emerges is that the core features of biological form are instead in many ways just frozen fragments of computational irreducibility, in effect assembled and selected by adaptive evolution. The complexity—and diversity—that we see in biology is, more than anything, a reflection of intrinsic, fundamental computational features of a system that, in Darwin’s words, shows growth, reproduction, inheritance and variability. And this is something very robust; it doesn’t depend on the details of the system, so that even without knowing all those details, we can start building a rich and broad theoretical framework. Which is what ruliobiology aims to do.
In the course of this piece, we’ve seen a whole variety of phenomena associated with ruliobiology—many of them reflected in features of biology and biological form that had rarely, if ever, even been systematically discussed before. There is much to do in ruliobiology, and we are still at the very beginning—surveying as an analog of natural history the world of rulioorganisms, and starting to see some general principles emerging. Over time we can expect to see a whole formal tower of theory develop, eventually in scope perhaps within striking distance of physics, but very different in character—and with computational irreducibility, rather than computational reducibility, at its core.
Darwin took pains to emphasize his perception of the “grandeur” of his view of life. But for us, there is, in a sense, still much greater grandeur. For through ruliobiology we can now see just what kind of computational process is needed to build up the kind of richness we see in biological form. There’s computation going on throughout the physical universe—all ultimately encapsulated in the ruliad that represents the entangled limit of all possible computational processes. But ruliobiology—and presumably biology—corresponds to a certain coherent slice of the ruliad, in effect picked out by adaptive evolution. And to reach life as we know it we now realize that we need an immense and irreducible tower of computation. Indeed, we might even say that as living organisms we are the product of the largest coherent tower of computation that we know or can currently imagine.
Darwin spoke of the richness of life as being the result of “laws acting around us”. A century and a half later I believe ruliobiology begins to fill in the essence of what those laws might be. It also opens up a vast new domain of theoretical science—a different theoretical basis for a science of biology. I’m excited to have been able to take some first steps in ruliobiology here. But there is much still to investigate and discover, and I shall look forward to seeing ruliobiology develop, and move towards taking its place among the major theoretical frameworks of science.

“ Foundations of Biological Evolution: More Results & More Surprises ” (2024)
“ What’s Special about Life? Bulk Orchestration and the Rulial Ensemble in Biology and Beyond ” (2025)
“ Towards a Computational Formalization for Foundations of Medicine ” (2025)

title: Restaurant holding !Fest to open first Piana Vyshnia location in Germany in Dec
body:
Restaurant holding !Fest is preparing to open the first location of its Piana Vyshnia (Drunken Cherry) chain in Germany in December, the holding's CEO and co-owner Andriy Khudo said.

"We are preparing to open the first Piana Vyshnia location in Germany... It is at 5 Rathausstraße, next to the TV tower, where lots of people walk around. And, of course, there are many Ukrainians in Germany, and in Berlin in particular, these days. Future customers come up to the door and try to open it by pulling the handle... So it is already a little 'tired'... But winter will come, and we plan to open our first business in Germany in December 2026, and the handle will work!" he said on LinkedIn.

The first Piana Vyshnia location opened in Lviv's Rynok Square in 2015. The chain currently has more than 70 locations in Ukraine and abroad, including in the United Kingdom, France, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Moldova.

title: PrivatBank launches Open Banking for retail and small business users
body:
PrivatBank has launched an open banking service in its Privat24 app for individual customers and in the web version of Privat24 for Business for individual entrepreneurs, the financial institution's press service reported.
"For individuals, this will change the experience of using financial apps, since all accounts and personal finances will be brought together in one Privat24 app. For individual entrepreneurs, it offers an opportunity to simplify the tracking of operating expenses in Privat24 for Business," said Dmytro Musienko, a member of PrivatBank's management board responsible for retail banking.
With the service, users can, with their consent, add accounts from other banks, view balances and transaction histories, top up cards and make transfers. Individual entrepreneurs using Privat24 for Business can monitor transactions on their business accounts at other banks and make payments.
Currently, individual customers can link accounts from Universal Bank, including monobank, as well as FUIB, A-Bank and Globus Bank, to Privat24. In Privat24 for Business, users can link accounts from Universal Bank, including monobank.
The bank said the list of participating institutions would gradually expand as they integrate with open banking technology.
As reported, National Bank of Ukraine Resolution No. 80, which provides for authorized third-party service providers to access customer account information only with the customers' consent, took effect on August 1, 2025.
For the following 12 months, the regulator did not impose enforcement measures for violations of requirements concerning continuous access to accounts and the configuration of dedicated interfaces.
PrivatBank is Ukraine's largest bank. According to the National Bank of Ukraine, the financial institution's total assets stood at UAH 983.82 billion as of September 1, 2026, accounting for 22.8% of the banking sector's total assets.
At the end of the first half of 2026, the bank had 18 million active individual customers, 13.7 million Privat24 users and 950,000 business customers.

title: How a Special Forces veteran with cancer finally got this photo with Chris Pratt
body: Chris Cathers looks a little nervous in the photograph, which, say the people who knew him, was not typical for the former Green Beret and veterans advocate. Robert Vaughn met Cathers when the two were young soldiers suffering together through the Army’s Special Forces selection course at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. They both became Green Berets, and through 30 years of friendship that included war and cancer, Vaughn said he never knew Cathers to be scared of much. Cathers spent his career in Special Forces and, later, as a CIA ground officer, deploying to the post-9/11 wars. Off-duty, he was a fearless prankster who once tricked Vaughn into holding fireworks while Vaughn was recovering from knee surgery. “He said he needed me to hold one,” Vaughn said, who was walking with crutches. “He lights it, and it had a short fuse, and he yells, ‘Run!’ I was like, ‘you motherfucker.’” But though fearless when pranking Army buddies, Cathers looks anxious in the photo. Perhaps because the man next to him, giving a ‘you da man’ finger point and putting his arm around Cathers, is Chris Pratt, the actor who has made a career in the last decade making military fare like “Zero Dark Thirty” and Amazon’s “The Terminal List.” Cathers might be nervous because, having blown a previous chance to get a photo with Pratt, this moment would be his last. After a multi-year battle with cancer, Cathers died in February in North Carolina. A fatal diagnosis leads to a new mission In 2018, Cathers received a terminal cancer diagnosis and was told he should expect six months to live. The news drove him to alcohol and a suicide attempt, but he fought through the turmoil For him it was alcohol,” Vaughn said. “But he got clean and sober, basically.” In 2022, he asked Vaughn and a third friend from Green Beret selection, Ron Griffin, to come by his house to talk about something by the fire pit. “We thought this was gonna be some bad news, ya know,” Vaughn recalls. “That’s when he said he wanted to start Brothers Keeper.” Under the mantra, “Connection is prevention,” Cathers launched the Brothers Keeper Veteran Foundation , whose goal is to connect veterans in mental crisis with survivors like him who have been there. The foundation became the focus of his final years. One vet the foundation works closely with is Christian Brunetti, a former Army Psychological Operations soldier turned Hollywood stuntman and filmmaker, struggling with his own mental health. Left, Christian Brunetti, right, Chris Cathers, on the set of the second season of “The Terminal List.” Photo courtesy of Amazon Studios. With shared backgrounds in Army special operations, Brunetti and Cathers became friends, as Brunetti picked up work on Amazon Studio’s “The Terminal List,” starring Pratt. Cathers loved the show and Pratt, in particular, Brunetti said. In 2025, as his cancer worsened, he called Brunetti. “He knew he was dying,” Brunetti said. “He literally called me up and said, ‘Hey, I don’t know if I’ll be around next year. I know you’re working. I’d love to just come see you.’” A missed photo and immediate regrets Brunetti enlisted the show’s David DiGilio. “And as soon as Dave DiGilio and everybody heard Chris’s story, they’re like, ‘We want him to come to the [filming of the] finale.’” Catchers joined Brunetti in Toronto for the final days of shooting the second season of “The Terminal List.” Cathers made fast friends on the crew, which included 17 veterans. “He said, ‘I’m coming as your friend. I’m not even going to take a single picture,’” Brunetti recalls. “‘I don’t want to get you in trouble.’ I was like, ‘You’re not going to get me in trouble. You’re fine.’ But he was paranoid about getting me in trouble.” The two found Pratt after the final scene. “They start talking,” Brunetti recalled. “They have a quick 10, 15 minute conversation. They’re laughing, and Chris turns to Cathers and says, ‘Hey, man, you want to take a picture?’ And Cathers froze.” News Airman dies in rappelling demonstration at Navy football game By Nicholas Slayton News Hegseth’s plan to restore Confederate memorial at Arlington expected to cost taxpayers $9 million By Austin Campbell News Marine Corps establishes its first medium-range missile battalion By Nicholas Slayton Pratt, in an interview with Task & Purpose ahead of the season two debut of “The Terminal List,” recalled their first meeting. “I think everyone had been told, like, ‘Hey, listen, we’re not doing photos, no one’s doing photos,’” Pratt said. “I was like, ‘Are you kidding, of course we’re gonna take a picture.’ What kind of an asshole would be like, ‘I can’t believe he asked me for a picture.’” “He goes, ‘No, man, I’m good,” Brunetti said. “And I just die laughing because I know, immediately, what was going on in his head, because he wanted to take a picture.” With that, the two left. “Chris kind of gave him a hug and said, ‘Well, it was nice to meet you,’ and walked on,” Brunetti said. “And Cathers, as soon as he walks off, he goes, ‘What did I just say?’” Brunetti teased his friend relentlessly in the coming days. But within a week, the two would have another chance at the August 2025 premiere party for an earlier season in New York. In a boozy ballroom filled with other special ops vets involved in the production, Catheres grabbed Pratt as Sarah Schmiedeknecht, Brothers Keeper’s executive director, snapped a picture. Pratt gave him the pointed finger. Chris Cathers and Chris Pratt at the August 2025 premiere of “Terminal List: Dark Wolf” in New York. Photo courtesy of Sarah Schmiedeknecht. Cathers passed away six months later in February. Vaughn now runs Brothers Keeper, raising funds and looking for outreach opportunities. Though he runs the operation, he says the non-profit will never name another formal CEO. “Chris will always be the CEO,” he said. At the core of the foundation, said Vaughn, is connecting an active network of veterans in various stages of recovery and treatment. The foundation breaks its programs into three phases: survive, stabilize, and thrive. That begins, he said, with connecting vets to each other. “It’s a brotherhood, and you want to feel that camaraderie again,” said Vaughn. “They want to connect to that feeling, and it’s gone.” The “survive” stage, he said, is the most urgent. “It’s the most dangerous time,” Vaughn said. “They have such a short window. Usually the suicide idiation comes with some kind of substance abuse, and you might have a window of an hour.” The foundation runs clinical programs, from group sessions connecting veterans, to programs for caregivers and family, to financial literacy classes. “Sometimes you go back on the wagon or fall off the wagon and have to get back on,” he said. “Sometimes those categories go back and forth.” The post How a Special Forces veteran with cancer finally got this photo with Chris Pratt appeared first on Task & Purpose .

title: Amazon communities lose water as mining and deforestation reshape rivers
body: “People think that because we live in the forest we have plenty of water, but this is the reality,” Erick Tijé, an Indigenous Harakmbut resident of the southern Peruvian Amazon, says in a tone of disappointment, pointing to the murky water flowing down the Inambari River. That river isn’t what it was five years ago, when fishing and life along its banks were very different for residents of the Arazaire Indigenous community. Illegal mining stole their water, only to return it to them polluted. Today, they have to buy the water they drink. On the other side of the Peruvian border, in the Colombian Amazon, Lázaro Ibañez, an elder of the Coreguaje people who live in the Jácome Indigenous Reserve, blames cattle ranching and climate change for reducing water availability around their territory. “The cattle have been destroying everything, and now all you can see is pastureland; there are hardly any trees left,” he says, having witnessed how deforestation to create grazing for cattle has gone hand in hand with the drying up of their water sources. Inhabitants of parts of the world’s greatest rainforest face a paradox: they’re surrounded by water, but can’t use it. For Indigenous peoples, it’s also the loss of the spirits that guard their water sources, driven away by the advance of logging and cattle ranching. title: The flight nurses of the Pacific who saved thousands of Marines
body: As U.S. Marines desperately crawled, ran and slipped toward the entrenched Japanese on Iwo Jima in February 1945, U.S. Naval and Marine planners were met with another pressing issue: how to get the wounded out of the exposed, shifting black volcanic sand and off an island little more than four miles long. On March 6, 1945, the Navy found its solution in Jane Kendeigh and her 11 fellow flight nurses. For the first time in the war, the U.S. Navy began deploying combat nurses to an active battlefield. With only six weeks of training, these nurses began to instantly triage and evacuate wounded Marines, working in frigid, unpressurized aircraft amid constant enemy assaults. Oftentimes called “mom” by their wounded comrades, these 12 women evacuated 2,393 men on 125 flights — more than 13% of everyone evacuated from Iwo Jima — and continued their bloody, lifesaving work in what was to become the largest Allied amphibious landing in the Pacific theater and the final island battle of the Pacific, Okinawa. Author and professor at Hunter College, City University of New York, Leah Garrett, sat down with Military Times to discuss her latest work, The Flight Nurses’ War: The American Women Who Saved Thousands of Lives at Iwo Jima and Okinawa , as well as the conditions these women worked under and how researching her latest book left her with one of “the most moving moments of my life.” Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity. Military Times: When one thinks of Iwo Jima, images come to mind of the blackened sand, brutal conditions and Mount Suribachi, but never women. How did the story of these 12 women come to your attention? Leah Garrett: When I was writing my last book, I kept hearing these rumors that there had been women at Iwo Jima, and I thought there was no way that there were women at Iwo Jima. I reached out to the Navy, and I got military clearance and worked with an archivist there. He had written a bit about it, but there had never been a book about it — the full story of who these women were and what they were doing there. Once I started to search about it, I found out that there had indeed been these 12 Navy flight nurses who had landed at Iwo Jima under fire, and in the worst kind of nightmare anyone can imagine, and flew out these men. Part of the reason that no one had done their stories is that these women themselves … I don’t think they realized how extraordinary it was what they had done. I started to reach out to the families of those 12 flight nurses, and discovered that every historian wants to discover — there was a massive amount of material. Most of the story was actually in these well-cared-for boxes in basements and garages, and so the way I wrote the story was I worked with the military archivists, but then I flew around the country and met with the families themselves, interviewed the children, and went through the boxes and found just all this extraordinary first-person material: photographs, letters, memoirs. This concrete Japanese shelter on Iwo suffered a direct artillery hit, but the standing portions were used as aid stations for wounded Marines. (U.S. Marine Corps) Before we get into the nurses themselves, can you talk about the creation of flight nurses? All of the flight nurses signed up to join the military after the attack on Pearl Harbor. For each of them, that was the watershed moment when they said, “I need to serve.” There’s this one woman named Mary O’Connor who goes to Washington and says, “Look, we want you to set up a flight nurses program.” The reason that they wanted to set it up is that the Army had women in combat positions who were nurses, but the Navy didn’t. As we get into 1945, the final two battles in the Pacific were really far more horrific than anyone expected them to be in the Navy, particularly at Iwo Jima. The Japanese were targeting the medical corps as well, so there was a massive attrition rate, and they did not have enough people there to take care of the men. And also, Iwo Jima is really complicated because you can’t set up field hospitals in Iwo Jima because of the landscape; it’s just too exposed. So then the question becomes: “Well, how do we get these men out?” What happens is all these different nurses are serving in the Navy at different military hospitals, Navy hospitals around the country, and their supervisors reach out to the best one or two of each group and say, “Look, would you be interested in overseas service?” Nobody knows what it will be, but these women say yes. O’Connor gets hundreds of applications. She picks the top 24 that seem the best to her — basically smart, very capable, very brave women. So these 24 women are then sent out to Alameda, California, to do … this very intense six-week training. The cream de la creme of the 24 were then flown to Guam, and once they’re in Guam, they’re going to be given their assignment. This had never been done before. The Navy had never put women in combat positions under direct fire, and it was a very incredibly dangerous thing to do. I mean, what if they’re killed? What if they’re captured? What if they’re used for propaganda? Like, there’s so much that could have gone wrong, and I think, much to everyone’s surprise, probably including some of the women, they were so effective in getting those men out. A wounded Marine receives blood plasma in a shell hole where an aid station has been established. (U.S. Marine Corps) On March 6, 1945, Jane Kendeigh became the first Navy flight nurse to appear on an active Pacific battlefield. Ultimately, she and 11 other nurses evacuated 2,393 men from Iwo Jima. That’s an incredible statistic, but does any story in particular stand out to you? One of the crazy aspects of this story is that when you’re in an aircraft flying from Iwo Jima to Guam, there are no doctors on these flights. They fly over there with their corpsman and then a pilot, maybe a navigator. And when they get to Iwo Jima, it’s active fire. Every time they’re supposed to be landing, there’s supposed to be a lull. There’s no lull because it’s such a horrific battle. They can’t turn around. They have to land. And when they land, they all talked about this visceral aspect of it. The smell of death. The sulfur smell. That the airstrip is shaking. And again, because there are no field hospitals there, they walk over to scores of extremely wounded Marines who are just lying there on stretchers on the ground in terrible, terrible shape. It’s absolute chaos that they have to face, and then they’re on the aircraft, and they’re by themselves. One of them said, “I can’t even phone anyone to ask what I should do. I’m in the middle of the Pacific. There are these men who are dying or near death all around me, and I have to figure out what to do.” All of it was this learning curve on the plane. It’s freezing cold. There’s no air pressure. One of the stories that moved me so much — it’s actually one of the more famous stories — but I think one of the most moving ones is about Kendeigh’s first flight. She’s actually not supposed to go on the first flight. There’s this photo a Navy photographer takes of Jane, where she gets off the plane, and she walks over to a Marine, Sgt. Bill Wyckoff, lying there. He’s got bandages all over his face. Wyckoff later said it was like an angel took my hand. He’s lying there near death, and he hears this woman whispering in his ear, “It’s going to be okay.” Albeit brief, what kind of relationship did these Marines and nurses forge? The men called them mom. They would say, “Mom, can you come here?” “Mom, can you put on your lipstick?” “Can I watch you put on your lipstick like my mom used to do?” When the book was published, I insisted the font color on the cover be that lipstick red. The women always said, “We were treated with the greatest respect by these men.” They never dealt with any hassling, no sexualization, none of that. It was just pure respect and love that they received and gave back. Wounded Marines are being shipped out aboard a plane at the Yontap Airstrip on the first day of the assault on Okinawa. (HUM Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) One of my colleagues likes to talk about “research rapture.” What was the process like researching for The Flight Nurses’ War ? The families were incredible because I think that they were so glad somebody was finally telling these amazing stories of their role. And I had so many extraordinary moments. Part of the way that the unpacking of the boxes would work was that I would be with the children as we unpacked the boxes, so it was this extremely moving and rich moment that the kids would remember: “Oh wait, like there’s a shell necklace from Guam,” and then they would tell the story of how the mom got it when she was there. I talk about this moment a lot in the book, and I always get very seriously teary when I talk about it. Another one of the flight nurses, Mary Leahy Hudnall, came from Massachusetts. She didn’t particularly want to go on planes. She joined the Navy because she thought that she would be on a ship. There you go. She ends up on these flights, and in one instance they’re putting these men on the aircraft who are mortally wounded, right? There’s no doctor; it’s just them and the corpsman. One of the Marines on her flight out of Iwo Jima, who she knows is very, very, very wounded. He’s probably not going to make it, and he insists that she take a vial of sand from Iwo Jima that he took. She says, “No, you’re going to be fine, you’re going to be fine,” but he keeps saying, “No, can you please take this. I need you to take it because you need to tell the story of what we went through.” So she takes the vial of sand, and then he unfortunately passes away. She gives that vial of sand to her daughter, and then when I’m in Canada visiting with her daughter, we find that vial of sand in one of the boxes. I got to hold it, and it was honestly one of the most moving moments of my life. I took a picture of it and put it in the book because, as a historian, it’s my imperative to tell his story. I’m not only telling the story of the nurses, but I’m equally telling the story of the wounded men under their care whose stories need to be told.

The families were incredible because I think that they were so glad somebody was finally telling these amazing stories of their role. And I had so many extraordinary moments. Part of the way that the unpacking of the boxes would work was that I would be with the children as we unpacked the boxes, so it was this extremely moving and rich moment that the kids would remember: “Oh wait, like there’s a shell necklace from Guam,” and then they would tell the story of how the mom got it when she was there. I talk about this moment a lot in the book, and I always get very seriously teary when I talk about it. Another one of the flight nurses, Mary Leahy Hudnall, came from Massachusetts. She didn’t particularly want to go on planes. She joined the Navy because she thought that she would be on a ship. There you go. She ends up on these flights, and in one instance they’re putting these men on the aircraft who are mortally wounded, right? There’s no doctor; it’s just them and the corpsman. One of the Marines on her flight out of Iwo Jima, who she knows is very, very, very wounded. He’s probably not going to make it, and he insists that she take a vial of sand from Iwo Jima that he took. She says, “No, you’re going to be fine, you’re going to be fine,” but he keeps saying, “No, can you please take this. I need you to take it because you need to tell the story of what we went through.” So she takes the vial of sand, and then he unfortunately passes away. She gives that vial of sand to her daughter, and then when I’m in Canada visiting with her daughter, we find that vial of sand in one of the boxes. I got to hold it, and it was honestly one of the most moving moments of my life. I took a picture of it and put it in the book because, as a historian, it’s my imperative to tell his story. I’m not only telling the story of the nurses, but I’m equally telling the story of the wounded men under their care whose stories need to be told.

title: Building the Autonomous Warfare Command – DRPM UxS
body:
SUBJECT: Building the Autonomous Warfare Command
In 1928, Secretary of War Dwight Davis ordered the Army to experiment with a unified mechanized force: tanks, armored trucks, and motorized infantry fighting as one. It was soon disbanded. Mechanization was broken up to support existing branches as add-ons. It took the German blitzkrieg of 1940 to force the creation of the U.S. Armored Force.
We face an equally urgent revolution. Low-cost drones have changed the character, speed and economics of war. Rather than repeat 1928, Secretary Hegseth chose the maximal path. He established Project Agincourt to change how we fight. Agincourt has two missions.
First, stand up a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM) by October 1, 2027, with the authority its commander needs to drive the largest institutional change since the interwar years. Second, continue the mission of the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM-UxS) while pioneering a new acquisition model that pairs autonomous and robotics companies directly with operational forces at the edge. The goal is not a particular drone. It is a system built to adapt at scale.
This is not change at the margin. Since the Cold War, American power projection has rested on a small number of sophisticated, expensive weapons. That model has been disrupted. The U.S. can build a new generational advantage by adapting at the edge faster than adversaries by leveraging two strengths: our lead in superintelligence, and an unmatched NCO corps. Urgency does not excuse imprecision.
We will work analytically with the Joint Staff, the Services and, above all, the operational units that will serve as our incubators. Evidence will decide outcomes. Competitions, exercises and combat performance will determine which systems scale and which are cut. The power of the purse demands strict stewardship. To flip the cost exchange, every auditable dollar we spend should reduce cost-per-kill or risk-to-force.
We have set a hard test for ourselves. These new systems will not be declared ready on paper. Combatant commanders must be able to wield them in combat. The new model must strengthen the Services while empowering each theater build its own mix. The ideal Pacific portfolio is not right for Europe. This work will demand professional courage. We must challenge the obsolete processes, platforms and spending habits that have built up over decades. As Chairman Caine asks, “If not us, who? If not now, when?”
We are on the clock. In service of AUTOWARCOM, Agincourt must quickly remove the barriers that constrain the initiative of our service members by fusing operations and development. We will not replace one bureaucracy with another. One measure of success will be the time it takes for an operational problem to receive a fielded solution evaluated for scale. If we get this right, we will do more than establish a new command. AUTOWARCOM will institutionalize a mission-based system whose main product is adaptation, building a next-generation development model for sustained American military advantage.

title: Ukrainian customs automates processing of intl express mail
body:
Ukraine's State Customs Service has introduced a mechanism for the automatic customs clearance of imported and exported international postal and express shipments without physically presenting them to customs authorities and without the involvement of customs officials.
According to a statement posted by the agency on its Telegram channel on Thursday, the new system is designed to speed up the processing of large volumes of parcels and optimize logistics processes, particularly under martial law. The mechanism combines an automated risk management system, including the use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, with the processing of advance information by customs specialists. Additional criteria and stricter requirements have been established for automatic clearance.
Clearance decisions are made automatically after electronic data are submitted. This allows customs officers to focus on analyzing information and handling cases that require additional checks or professional intervention.
The State Customs Service added that the new approach was developed and implemented with the participation of the Kyiv and Lviv customs offices. In particular, Kyiv customs specialists submitted proposals on organizing the processes, while the first cases of automatic shipment clearance have already been recorded in the area of responsibility of the Lviv customs office.
As reported, on October 15, the Verkhovna Rada, on its third attempt, adopted at second reading and in its entirety bill No. 16051-1 amending the Tax Code regarding VAT taxation of e-commerce transactions. The amendments abolish the exemption from tax for international postal shipments valued at up to EUR 150.
Implementation of the law, together with amendments to the Customs Code adopted on the same day under bill No. 15460, is a condition for Ukraine to receive the next tranche of approximately $0.7 billion under its program with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the second tranche of EUR 3.7 billion in macro-financial assistance from the European Union under a EUR 90 billion loan to support Ukraine. Under the updated memorandum with the IMF, Ukraine was required to adopt this law by July 2026. The original deadline had been the end of March, alongside other tax provisions, but this structural benchmark was not met.
The law provides for special VAT rules for distance sales of goods, excluding excisable goods, imported in international postal and express shipments addressed to individuals and valued at up to EUR 150. Electronic interface operators or their intermediaries are designated as responsible for calculating and paying the tax.
At the same time, the VAT exemption remains in place for small noncommercial consignments valued at up to EUR 45, sent free of charge between individuals, as well as for goods in unaccompanied baggage valued at up to EUR 150 and goods intended for security and defense purposes, including energy equipment and goods for the defense forces.
During consideration of the legislation, Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko said the provisions would begin to apply on July 1, 2027, following the technical implementation of automated tax payments by international online marketplaces.

title: General Staff: We expect humanitarian access for people in Oleshky will be guaranteed
body:
The Ukrainian Armed Forces (AFU) will ensure the implementation of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief's decisions to carry out a humanitarian mission in the occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region, according to a statement from the AFU General Staff.

"The relevant orders will be communicated to the troops in accordance with established procedures," the General Staff said on its Telegram channel on Friday.

The General Staff said Ukrainian units have previously carried out missions on multiple occasions to deliver humanitarian supplies via drones to residents of Oleshky and surrounding villages.

"We expect that humanitarian access for the people of Oleshky will be guaranteed," the statement reads.

title: War claims lives of 2,960 civilians this year, incl 87 children – acting prosecutor general
body:
The deaths of 19,349 Ukrainian civilians have been confirmed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, including 762 children, Ukraine's acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalsky said on Facebook on Friday.
According to him, more than 55,000 people have been wounded. More than 19,000 Ukrainian children have been forcibly displaced by the aggressor state.
Since the beginning of 2026, some 2,960 civilian deaths have been confirmed, including 87 children. Another 16,316 civilians were wounded, including 668 children, which accounts for nearly 30% of the total number of wounded civilians recorded throughout the entire period of full-scale armed aggression.
"In 2026, 84 individuals were sentenced for committing war crimes. Among those convicted this year are 54 Russian military personnel, including eight commanders. Another 261 individuals have been notified of suspicion… In total, over 266,000 war crimes have been registered in Ukraine. A total of 317 people have been convicted," Kovalsky said, noting that the scale of Russia's aggression cannot be measured by the number of criminal cases.
He reported on a meeting with Ukrainian and international partners who are assisting in bringing the perpetrators to justice and discussed joint efforts for further work with them.
"It is important to me that accountability for these crimes not be postponed until the end of the war. We must simultaneously document new crimes, bring already investigated cases to trial, and ensure that those who are currently beyond the reach of Ukrainian justice can be held accountable. This is a task that will take years," the acting Prosecutor General said.
The meeting was also attended by coordinators and representatives of the Advisory Group on the Most Serious International Crimes (ACA) – Clint Williamson (ICJI), Wayne Jordash (GRC), Claudio Pala (EUAM), Tinna Goletiani (PravoJustice4EU), Serhiy Drozach (IDLO), as well as experts from Global Rights Compliance, Project Expedite Justice, Justice Rapid Response, Truth Hounds, the Ukrainian Legal Advisory Group, and The Reckoning Project.
Kovalsky said uniform standards for investigating torture, unlawful deprivation of liberty, deportation, and forced displacement have already been implemented, a model indictment regarding attacks on the civilian population has been developed, and this week, joint guidelines on investigating sexual violence related to armed conflict came into effect.
"The next step is the implementation of the Strategy for the Prosecution of International Crimes for 2026-2028. Our priorities also include creating a Registry of Victims of War Crimes, establishing clear criteria for prioritizing criminal proceedings, introducing digital tools for analyzing large volumes of evidence, and developing a support system for victims and witnesses," he said.

title: Ukraine joins NSPA partnership to speed military purchases and open tenders to its defence industry
body: The Security Cooperation Support Partnership allows the agency to handle Ukrainian requests through existing contracts or new tenders. Ukraine’s defense ministry said the arrangement could shorten procurement times and improve purchasing terms. NSPA can pool Ukraine’s requirements with those of other countries to negotiate better prices. Purchases can be funded by Ukraine’s state budget, international partners or both. The agency can adapt its procedures to Ukrainian needs and use an emergency response procurement mechanism. Ukraine could potentially draw on capabilities across NSPA’s 45 partnerships, covering acquisition, maintenance and support throughout an equipment’s service life. New opportunities for Ukrainian suppliers Ukrainian companies can register in NSPA’s supplier database, submit proposals and compete alongside foreign manufacturers. Successful bidders can sign contracts directly with the agency. “The Ukrainian defence industry is developing rapidly, increasing its production capacity and creating new solutions. We want our partners to access this experience and these technologies, and for Ukrainian manufacturers to gain new opportunities for cooperation,” said Deputy Defense Minister Anna Gvozdiar. The North Atlantic Council approved NSPA’s authority to issue solicitations and sign contracts with Ukrainian industry in April 2026. Ukraine’s participation agreement was announced on October 14 at an industry event in Kyiv. Around 150 Ukrainian defense industry representatives attended the event. Officials explained registration, bidding procedures and the requirements companies must meet to become suppliers. Partnership builds on existing support Established in 2025, the partnership now comprises Belgium, Luxembourg, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom, NATO Headquarters and Ukraine. It provides a structured framework for sustained procurement support. NSPA has mobilized around €400 million through the Ukraine Comprehensive Assistance Package Trust Fund for medical supplies, fuel, infrastructure and cybersecurity. The IT Capability Coalition has contributed another €219 million to modernize Ukraine’s digital defense capabilities.

title: Are you ready for retirement? Because it's not just a question of having enough money
body: Many people I speak to could stop working tomorrow if they chose to. The income from employment stopped being the obstacle some time ago. And yet many keep going. Sometimes, that's because they love what they do, and there's nothing wrong with that. More often, when we talk it through, something else is holding them in place. They lack clarity and aren't sure what the next stage looks like, or who they'll be once the job title goes. That hesitation deserves attention. Work gives far more than just an income . It gives your week a shape, puts people around you, makes you feel useful and hands you real problems to solve. Most of us don't notice how much we rely on that until it's gone. Other people have the opposite problem. Their retirement date arrives because they've had enough. Sometimes it comes suddenly, after a particularly hard year. Sometimes it builds over years of deadlines and long days, until their patience finally runs out. They leave to get away from something, which is a perfectly good reason to go, of course. I've seen capable, financially secure people leave this way with everything in order on paper. Then they find themselves unsure what to do with a Tuesday morning. Some stay too long and others leave too fast, but both are wrestling with the same question. Am I ready for what comes next? Readiness comes down to whether you've built something to step towards. Everything a career gave you can come from somewhere else, provided you set it up. Structure can come from any standing commitment you take seriously. A fixed morning with a coach or trainer, a residential programme at a university you've long admired, a weekly lesson towards your pilot's licence, or a protected day each week with the grandchildren all give the diary its shape back. Connection takes more effort than it did at work, where clients and colleagues filled your diary without you lifting a finger. A club where you see the same faces each week, a regular dinner with former colleagues and clients who've become friends, or a sailing syndicate can fill that gap. So can more unhurried time with family, who'll be glad to see more of you. Purpose is often the hardest to replace. Many executive leaders draw their sense of worth from being the one others call when it matters. That can carry forward through a non-executive role, chairing a charity or an endowment , advising founders in your field, or taking an active hand in how your family's wealth is governed and given away. These roles nearly always come through your existing network. That makes them far easier to secure while your title still opens doors than after you've left. Stimulation matters too. Your work has kept you addressing genuinely hard problems for decades. Serious study can do the same, whether that's a master's in a subject you set aside at 20, learning a language well enough to argue in it, or mastering an instrument, a craft or a sport. It works best when it keeps stretching you and puts you among peers. None of this falls into place overnight. It takes some trial and error, and the people who settle best tend to start years before their last day. So, if you've been putting off a date you could have afforded some time ago, it may be worth asking what you'd be stepping towards, and starting to build it now.
