title: 'I feel like it’s meant to be': Eight-year-old Emirati acrobat finds her feet in the air
body: Jawaher Essa Sharafi wears an outfit splashed with pink, turquoise, lime green and yellow in a brushstroke pattern. Suspended from a hoop, she twists, twirls and drops as she practises at Aerial Lab in Arjan, Dubai. The eight-year-old has already taken her skills to the international stage, winning bronze in aerial hoop at the IAAA Grand Open Cup in Belgrade, Serbia, in September. The youngest competitor among more than 100 athletes from 11 countries, she became the first Emirati to compete internationally in aerial athletics – only two years after she began formal training. View this post on Instagram An aerialist is an acrobat who specialises in performing on suspended apparatus, such as hoops, trapezes and silks. The discipline combines acrobatics and artistic performance, drawing on strength, flexibility and co-ordination as athletes move through holds, spins and drops, often set to music. Jawaher trains on hoop and hammock, a suspended fabric sling, but asked which she prefers, there is little hesitation. “Hoop, hoop, hoop. It's the best. First of all, I like hoop because it's hard. I like to challenge myself in aerial,” she tells The National . The hoop shape and texture also set it apart. It's the “only one that's a circle made out of metal … because the rest [of the aerial equipment] are made out of same thing: fabric”, she says. “Hoop is made out of something different. That made me fall in love with it.” Her enthusiasm is equally apparent when she talks about training. “Whenever I do it, I get all my excitement out,” she says. “I feel like it's meant to be.” Following her mother Aerial arts was familiar to Jawaher long before she attended her first class. Her mother, Fatma Almadani, practised and taught the discipline. Almadani says: “She used to watch me train and she would attend all my trainings and be like, ‘I want to try, I want to try,’ So my trainer would put her up there since she was a baby.” Later, Jawaher began accompanying her mother to the children’s classes she taught. Participants had to be at least nine, and Jawaher was only four or five at the time. Watching from the sidelines did little to diminish her interest. She wanted to help, demonstrate and prove that she could keep up with the older children, her mother says. “I’d come home and she'd be like, ‘Mama, can you please come into the gym room? I want to show you that I can do what you were teaching the kids and I'm good enough to join your classes,’” Almadani recalls. The age restriction prompted her to look for somewhere that offered classes for younger children. Jawaher then began training at Aerial Lab when she was six. “Other than simple things we used to teach her at home, proper training was at Aerial Lab,” Almadani says. Watching other students perform gave Jawaher another goal. When Almadani took her to students' aerial showcases, she began asking when it would be her turn on stage. Finding her confidence Enthusiasm does not mean every new aerial skill comes easily. Jawaher describes the uncertainty of learning a trick that requires her to turn upside down, and wondering what might happen if she falls. However, she tries to reassure herself before attempting a move. “I can do this, no need to be worried, my teacher is here. She'll protect me, she knows what's right for me,” she tells herself. One drop proved particularly difficult after she fell while learning it. Returning to the movement took time, beginning slowly and gradually building speed as her confidence returned. Developing that control matters in competition, where judges assess difficulty, execution and artistry. For Jawaher, one detail requires particular attention: pointing her toes. “I've also been doing karate and in karate you don't point your toes,” she says. “It's been a challenge for me to try and remember.” Jawaher attends aerial classes on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays, with more training when a competition approaches. But she recognises the importance of taking a break. “Maybe not [training] every day, because I need rest days . It's important to have rest days,” she says. She sometimes practises at home on days when she does not have a class. The family’s gym room was originally Almadani’s space. “I actually set it up for me and now she took over,” she says. There, Jawaher has room to experiment as well as rehearse. Almadani adds: “She loves coming here and just she puts on music and does her own routines. She tries to imagine new moves.” From classes to competition Almadani did not initially see her daughter’s progress. Parents were asked not to sit in on group classes, so she would drop Jawaher off and collect her afterwards. Then the teachers began approaching her about private training. A competition planned in the UAE offered an opportunity, and Jawaher was selected to represent the studio. Almadani says she was the only child chosen from her age group. But that event was cancelled, and the competition in Serbia became Jawaher's international debut. Her mother was struck by her progress as she watched her prepare. “From seeing her in her first showcase on stage, compared to this year, doing a routine for the competition, I was surprised by how much she advanced in just one year,” Almadani says. Jawaher says she feels both nervous and excited before performing, but finishing her routine brings relief. “I'm like: finally I can get all that energy out of me. And I don't need to worry any more about my routine,” she says. Bigger ambitions What most impresses Almadani is her daughter’s willingness to work towards goals she has set herself. “I find her personality very inspiring. Her confidence is very inspiring,” she says. “It gets hard sometimes to train every day. Sometimes she's exhausted. Sometimes she wants to stay up at night and the weekends. But I'm inspired by how she's very committed to the goals she has.” Still, she wants her daughter to have the freedom to explore other interests. Jawaher has mentioned karate competitions, horse riding and parkour, adding to an already busy schedule. “She wants to try everything,” Almadani says. “But we don't have enough days of the week to do after-school [activities] every day.” Whatever Jawaher eventually chooses, her mother hopes the experience will leave her with habits and confidence that extend beyond competition. “It builds personality, it builds character and gives you skills that you need in life,” she says. For now, Jawaher is preparing two routines for her next showcase, one on hammock and another on hoop, and looking ahead to a competition in Italy next year. She would like more young athletes from the UAE to join her. Almadani recalls her daughter hoping that photographs from the competition in Serbia might encourage friends to enter future contests and help to build a bigger team. Jawaher invites friends to try aerial arts at home and has already encouraged one to begin classes. While keen to share her enthusiasm, she knows not everyone will feel ready to give it a go. “If you tried it, you would love it and you would keep going again and again,” she says. “But if you don't want to, I won't force you.”

title: Grosvenor House Dubai review: Refined five-star luxury and stellar service
body: Dubai is not short of five-star hotels. With new ones opening all the time, some of the city's more established names face a different challenge: how do you keep standing out when you are no longer the latest hotel on the block? The twin towers of Grosvenor House, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Dubai, have been a big part of the city's Marina skyline for years. And there is something reassuring about the fact that the hotel does not seem to try to reinvent itself to compete with every new opening. It is traditional five-star luxury, and it knows how to do it well. A lot of that comes down to getting the details right. My husband and I checked in for a weekend without our children, with very little planned beyond eating well, having a massage and, most importantly, switching off for a couple of days. The welcome There is plenty to impress at Grosvenor House, but what stayed with us most was the service. You get a sense of that from the moment you arrive. The valet takes care of the car, huge bouquets of fresh flowers fill the foyer, and there always seems to be someone there when you need them. The staff seemed to move effortlessly around us. Everyone knew what they were doing and what needed to happen next. Check-in was quick and easy, and the staff were warm and attentive without being overbearing. That became a theme throughout the weekend. Small requests were remembered and staff would ask us later how dinner, the spa or another part of our stay had gone. They paid attention. The room We stayed in the Deluxe Guest Room with views across the marina and towards the sea. Fruit, macarons and refreshments awaited us as we entered the room. The room wasn't enormous, but we didn't need it to be. There was plenty of storage, an extremely comfortable bed, soft towels and a good-sized bathroom. Grosvenor House is an established hotel, and the design reflects that. This isn't the minimalist look of some of Dubai 's newer hotels. There is wooden cabinetry, marble throughout the bathroom and touches of Art Deco. It feels traditional, in a very elevated way. For a weekend when the whole point was to switch off, the most important things were there: a great bed, a good bathroom and plenty of quiet. The food You could easily spend the whole weekend eating your way around Grosvenor House. Our first dinner was at Rhodes W1 . I started with the watermelon salad which was nice, although I couldn't quite get my head around the almond and orange dressing with fresh za'atar and tarragon. For me, it was one herb too many and needed balancing with something more salty. My husband was much happier with his duck rillette fritters. I followed with a rib-eye steak, and he went for the braised lamb shank: great mains that were traditional and well made. Again, the service made a difference. Staff took the time to talk us through dishes and let us sample drinks before deciding what to order. Breakfast at Sloane's the following morning was busy, but incredibly well run. Everything you would expect from a five-star Dubai breakfast was available: eggs, pastries, Arabic dishes, fruit and plenty of Asian and Indian options. Dinner on our second night was at Toro Toro , which was probably my favourite meal of the stay. The interiors of restaurant are beautiful, but also fun. Staff talked us through the Pan-Latin American influences behind the dishes without making the whole thing feel too formal. The standout for me was the cachapas, a Venezuelan sweetcorn pancake with whipped halloumi, sour cream and pico de gallo, assembled at the table. It reminded me a little of cornbread, but creamier, warmer and sweeter. I followed it with the encocado, with black cod, prawns, squid, coconut, aji mirasol and rice. We had already started with the smoked guacamole, so by this point we were completely stuffed. There were still plenty of things we wanted to try, though, which gives us an excuse to go back. Spa and wellness A weekend away without the children was always going to involve a trip to the spa. Our couples massage at the newly renovated Sanara Spa was one of the highlights of the weekend. We had our consultation earlier in the day and came back later for the treatment. Before the massage we were taken to the separate male and female changing areas, each with a sauna, steam room and Jacuzzi, for some time apart to unwind. For a city hotel, the spa is huge. There is also a hammam and plunge pools at different temperatures, including an ice plunge. I loved the interiors too. There are Japanese influences throughout, including the textiles, particularly two beautiful kimonos hanging as wall art, one behind the reception desk and another in the women's changing room. Then came the massage. Both therapists were excellent and knew exactly where more pressure was needed. I nearly fell asleep, although my husband's snoring from the other side of the room hampered that. By the end, I realised just how tense I had been beforehand. The service There is no shortage of luxury hotels in Dubai. Beautiful rooms, restaurants , spas and pools come with the territory, but good service is harder to get right consistently. From reception and housekeeping to the restaurants and spa, the staff were attentive without constantly hovering around us. More importantly, it never felt scripted. There were fresh roses left on our pillows and a welcome letter in the room, but it was the smaller interactions that I noticed more. Someone remembering where we had dinner and asking how it was. A member of staff recalling something we had mentioned earlier. Not having to repeat a request. None of these things is huge on its own. Put together, though, they mean you don't spend your weekend thinking about logistics or chasing things up. Everything just works. The verdict Grosvenor House isn't Dubai's newest hotel, but it doesn't need to be. There will always be a newer hotel, a bigger room or another spectacular opening around the corner. But what is much harder to replicate is a hotel where the service feels this consistent, confident and luxurious. It worked particularly well for a weekend away for us as a couple. We ate far too much, spent a few hours doing very little at the spa and, for a couple of days, had almost nothing that needed organising. The bottom line A weekend at Grosvenor House made it easy to enjoy the Dubai Marina skyline, attentive service and a good mix of dining, with time to unwind at the spa. Rates currently start at about Dh540 a night, including VAT, though they vary by date and room type. Check-in is from 2pm and checkout by noon. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects standards during this time

title: Lupin part four: The story so far ahead of Netflix return
body: With elaborate heists, convincing disguises and a revenge plot that puts an entire family in danger, Netflix ’s Lupin has taken its gentleman thief from the Louvre to a prison cell over three parts. The French mystery thriller follows Assane Diop (played by Omar Sy ), who draws inspiration from the adventures of Arsene Lupin, the fictional thief created by French author Maurice Leblanc. What begins as a mission to clear his father’s name develops into a struggle to protect Assane’s own family from the consequences of his crimes. Alongside the thefts and escapes, the series is centred on Assane’s relationships with his estranged wife Claire, their teenage son Raoul and his closest friend and accomplice, Benjamin. His schemes repeatedly test their loyalty, even when he believes he is acting in their interests. Part four finds Assane behind bars, apparently ready to leave his criminal life behind. But a new thief operating as 'Lupin' threatens those plans. As the series returns for its latest season, here is a refresher on what happened in the first three parts. What is Lupin about? As a teenager, Assane’s life changes after his father Babakar, a Senegalese immigrant working for wealthy businessman Hubert Pellegrini, is accused of stealing a valuable diamond necklace. Babakar dies in prison, leaving his son to grow up with the consequences of an accusation he believes was false. Years later, Assane sets out to uncover what happened and expose those responsible. Taking inspiration from Leblanc’s stories, he uses disguises, sleight of hand and elaborate deception to outwit his opponents. But his pursuit of Pellegrini also attracts police attention and places Claire and Raoul in danger. The story so far (spoilers ahead): What happened in Lupin part one? The series begins with a robbery at the Louvre , where Assane steals the necklace his father was accused of taking years earlier. The heist is the first step in a wider plan to expose Pellegrini. As Assane investigates, he uncovers the businessman’s insurance fraud and the involvement of corrupt police commissioner Dumont in framing his father Babakar. Assane joins forces with investigative journalist Fabienne Beriot, who has been looking into Pellegrini’s dealings. But their efforts to bring him down take a deadly turn when his henchman Leonard murders her. Meanwhile, detective Youssef Guedira begins to recognise a pattern in Assane’s methods. A fellow fan of Leblanc’s books, he realises the thief is drawing on the adventures of Arsene Lupin. Part one ends during a family trip where Leonard kidnaps Raoul. As Assane discovers his son is missing, Guedira catches up with him. What happened in Lupin part two? The search for Raoul brings Assane and Guedira together, with the detective ultimately rescuing the teenager. Although Raoul returns safely to Claire, the kidnapping makes clear how dangerous Assane’s pursuit of Pellegrini has become. With Benjamin’s help, he uncovers Pellegrini’s diversion of charitable donations into an offshore account. Assane then confronts him and records his confession to framing Babakar and ordering Beriot’s murder. However, Assane continues his efforts to expose the businessman, reconnecting with Pellegrini’s daughter Juliette and devising a plan centred on the family foundation’s charity concert. The evidence leads to the arrests of Pellegrini and Dumont, finally exposing the conspiracy against Assane’s father. But Assane’s identity is now public, leaving him unable to return home without risking arrest. Part two ends with him saying goodbye to Claire and Raoul before disappearing. What happened in Lupin part three? After going into hiding, Assane returns to Paris to steal the Black Pearl and carry out an even more ambitious deception: faking his own death. He hopes his apparent demise will allow Claire and Raoul to escape the attention surrounding him. But the plan unravels when Keller – a dangerous figure from his past – kidnaps his estranged mother, Mariama. Using her captivity as leverage, Keller forces Assane to carry out further thefts, drawing him back into the life he had been trying to escape. Assane eventually saves his mother and defeats Keller, but recognises that his freedom comes at a continuing cost to those around him. To give his loved ones a chance at a quieter life, he makes a deal with Guedira and turns himself in. During the final scenes, Assane receives an envelope from the neighbouring prison cell, revealing that Pellegrini is being held next door. What to expect in Lupin part four? Netflix says the new instalment begins four years later, with Assane still serving his sentence. He intends to fulfil his promise to Raoul and join his family in Senegal after his release. However, a string of simultaneous museum robberies – announced in Lupin’s name – makes him a suspect once again. Footage appears to show him at one of the thefts, during which police captain Belkacem is seriously injured. With someone apparently impersonating him, Assane must escape from prison to identify the copycat and clear his name. Lupin Part Four is now streaming on Netflix.

title: ‘Suluk’: What the Arabic word for behaviour has in common with Dubai’s Salik toll system
body: Our Arabic word of the week, suluk, means behaviour and describes how we conduct ourselves at home, school, work and in relationships with others. Husn al-suluk means good behaviour, while su al-suluk refers to bad behaviour or misconduct. Suluk al-tifl describes a child's behaviour, while suluk mihani means professional conduct. The word comes from the Arabic root letters seen, lam and kaf, associated with entering or following a path. The verb salaka means to travel along a route, while maslak can refer to a physical pathway or a person's approach to a situation. In personal relationships, suluk can describe someone's general conduct rather than an isolated action. This differs from another Arabic word, tasarruf, which generally refers to a particular action or response. A person may behave rudely on one occasion, for example, without that incident reflecting how they usually treat others. UAE residents will recognise another root word in Salik , Dubai's road toll system. The name means “open” or “clear”, suggesting travel without barriers. In Sufism , suluk takes on a spiritual meaning, describing the journey towards closeness to God. Someone following this path is also known as a salik. The concept is explored in the 11th-century work Al Risala Al Qushayriyya , or Al Qushayri's Epistle on Sufism , which examines stages of spiritual practice, including repentance, patience and trust in God. The related adjective suluki means behavioural and appears in the psychological term al-ilaj al-suluki al-marifi, or cognitive behavioural therapy, which addresses patterns of thinking and behaviour. Sulukiyat, meanwhile, refers to individual behaviours or behavioural practices. The term also appears in UAE schools , where the Ministry of Education uses al-suluk al-ijabi to mean positive behaviour and includes conduct as part of student assessment. From our everyday conduct to our spiritual pursuits, suluk reflects how we live and the paths we choose to follow.

title: I'm having a baby, not opening a nursery: The pressure to buy everything before becoming a mother
body: I have never considered myself a minimalist. I like nice things, enjoy shopping and can easily convince myself that a purchase is an investment rather than an indulgence. But since becoming pregnant with my first child, I have found myself navigating a level of consumerism unlike anything I have experienced before. It started with a spreadsheet. A friend sent over a document curated by a well-known influencer and businesswoman. It was a comprehensive list of everything one could possibly need for a newborn . There were tabs, categories, colour-coded cells and links to products. It was a work of type-A art. But it was also overwhelming. Troubling research describes how social expectations about being a good mother can be reinforced through marketing Rita Figueiredo, managing director of Peninsula Psychology With the lists come the new words – Artipoppe, Isofix, Owlet – all of which come with a sizeable price tag, designed to solve problems I didn't know existed. On the subject of the fabled Artipoppe, I asked friends on Instagram whether a baby carrier could really justify a Dh1,650 ($450) price tag. The replies were split: people either swore by it or couldn't fathom spending that much money on something that straps a baby to your chest, even if it does come in leopard print. The suggestion to shop for one second-hand came up more than once. My friends without children are looking on bemused, asking how much stuff one tiny person could possibly need. It's a fair question. Part of the problem is that, as a first-time mother, I am entering an entirely new market. I consider myself a reasonably informed consumer, but when it comes to babies, I have no frame of reference. Until recently, I couldn't have told you the difference between a travel system and a pram (I am still not 100 per cent sure I now know), or why one bottle steriliser might cost three times as much as another. When you don't know what you need, it is remarkably easy to be persuaded that you need everything. Rita Figueiredo, managing director of Peninsula Psychology, says this is something brands can exploit. "Marketing, particularly on social media, can introduce a concern parents had not even considered and then present a product as a way of reducing that risk," she says. “Research on consumption during the transition to motherhood describes how social expectations about being a good mother can be reinforced through marketing … This is perhaps the most troubling part: the suggestion that buying a particular product makes someone a better, more caring parent." There is, of course, the excitement of it all. Having a baby is a huge milestone and buying things is one of the few tangible ways to prepare for something that still feels abstract. Choosing a cot, organising tiny clothes and imagining the little person who will eventually use them is lovely. But I am also acutely aware that being able to browse, compare and deliberate over these purchases is a privilege in itself. For many expectant parents, the challenge isn't deciding what not to buy, but finding the money for the essentials. Maryanne Peacock, host of the Mother Tongue podcast, believes that it is enthusiasm that drives the urge to overbuy, rather than external influences. “With your first, you don’t really know what you’ll need, so you’re more likely to buy things just in case. Social media, recommendations from friends and brands all feed into that. When you keep seeing something described as a must-have, you start to think you should probably have it too,” she says. Adding, “We need more reassurance that you can have the basics ready and figure other things out once your baby is here.” Alongside my excitement are the intrusive thoughts. What if the baby won't sleep? What if feeding is difficult? What if I find myself lost in the middle of the night, desperately needing something I could have bought months earlier? Preparing with products can become the one part of parenting that feels controllable. "You can’t practise the 3am feeds or know what your baby’s personality will be like, but you can buy the bassinet," says Anna Baker, founder of SleepBaker sleep consultancy. "The tricky part is that the stuff doesn’t make you ready. Knowledge does, support does, and a good night’s sleep definitely does," Baker adds. A bassinet, or Moses basket, is another polarising product. To some, they're an essential; others dismiss them as a waste of space and money, something you'll only use for a handful of months. This has made me more interested in products that grow with my child – cots that convert into beds, high chairs that can be used for years, and car seats that have a purpose long after the newborn stage. Babies do not need an elaborate collection of equipment to begin exploring the world around them Hossam Gamal, specialist in baby travel safety at Britax Romer Arabia It's a philosophy echoed by Karishma Rajput, brand lead at Stokke Middle East. “I would challenge the idea that being prepared means having everything bought, assembled and perfectly organised before the baby arrives," she says. "The best purchases are not necessarily the newest, most talked-about or most expensive. They are the ones that genuinely meet a need and continue to be useful as circumstances change." As well as looking for products with longevity, I have been exploring second-hand options. Babies grow so quickly that plenty of equipment and clothing is barely used before being outgrown. Buying pre-loved or accepting hand-me-downs from friends makes financial and environmental sense. And there is something satisfying about giving a beautifully made piece of furniture a second life, rather than assuming everything needs to be bought brand new. This is not an argument against shopping for the essentials, particularly when safety is involved. But I am trying not to lose sight of the difference between items that genuinely protect a child and unnecessary gadgets sold with a safety spin. "For car travel, a suitable and safe car seat is an essential rather than an optional extra," says Hossam Gamal, specialist in baby travel safety and product training at Britax Romer Arabia. But even here, more expensive does not automatically mean more appropriate. Gamal stresses that parents should choose a seat that fits their child and vehicle and understand how to install and use it correctly. "Babies do not need an elaborate collection of equipment to begin exploring the world around them," Gamal says. It is also an area where I would be particularly cautious about sourcing second-hand, unless I could be certain of a car seat's history, condition and suitability. Ultimately, I am trying to separate what a baby genuinely needs from products I am being encouraged to want. Something another parent considers indispensable might never be opened in our house, while a product we have dismissed could turn out to be the best thing we buy. The most useful advice I have received, and something I am trying to remind myself daily as I browse Next, Amazon and Mamas and Papas, is the simplest: you can always buy things later. Amid the spreadsheets, shopping lists and targeted advertising, that is surprisingly easy to forget.

title: Russian Geran drone crashes in Moldova near homes and energy facility: Chisinau expels Russian diplomat
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Moldova declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata on 23 October after a Russian Geran attack drone violated its airspace and crashed near homes and an energy facility, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said. The incident highlights how Russia’s attacks on Ukraine are increasingly threatening neighboring Moldova, where Russian drones have repeatedly crossed the border or crashed during strikes. Moldova recorded 39 Russian drone incursions in the first eight months of 2026, compared with 17 in all of 2025, Sandu said in September. Moldova’s Defense Ministry said its Air Operations Center detected an unauthorized drone flight at 13:59 on 23 October. The drone crossed from the direction of Ukraine’s Vinnytsia Oblast toward Frunzeuca in Moldova’s Camenca district, in the Russian-backed breakaway region of Transnistria. The drone disappeared from monitoring screens near Pepeni in Sîngerei district at 14:10, briefly reappeared, and then disappeared again near Meșeni in Rezina district, the ministry said. Sandu condemned the incursion, saying Russia’s war continues to put Moldovan lives at risk. She said the drone had fallen near family homes and an energy facility. Moldovan police reported finding the crashed drone near the village of Chiștelnița in Telenești district, less than 100 meters from a home. No casualties were reported. Police cordoned off the area and sent explosives specialists to examine the wreckage. Russia's war keeps putting Moldovan lives at risk. Today, a Russian Geran attack drone violated our airspace and fell near family homes and an energy facility. We condemn this latest dangerous act. In response, we have declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata. — Maia Sandu (@sandumaiamd) October 23, 2026 Moldova steps up diplomatic response Sandu said Moldova had condemned the incident and declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata. She did not identify the staff member or specify when they must leave the country. The move follows repeated Russian drone incursions. In September, a Russian drone crossing Moldova’s airspace disrupted seven flights, including one involving Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, prompting temporary airspace restrictions. Earlier in October, three Russian missiles and two drones crossed into Moldovan airspace and exploded on Moldovan territory during Russian attacks on neighboring Ukraine, prompting Chisinau to condemn the violations. Debris fell across several districts, damaging windows at an agricultural facility and sparking fires in fields. Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi said the country was seeking stronger air defenses to counter the growing threat. Explore further 80% of Moldovans say country is unprepared for attack as Russian drones flow into its airspace, but few back NATO membership Moldova has limited air defense capabilities and has been working with European partners to strengthen them. Sandu has said the country’s existing equipment can mainly protect individual sites, while the government seeks broader coverage and faster warning systems. The EU has provided €120 million for Moldova to purchase a medium-range air defense system. Moldovan authorities urged residents not to approach or touch the crashed drone or any fragments, and to call emergency services if they find suspicious objects. title: Three-week on-site audit at OpenAI reveals major gaps in AI safety monitoring
body:
Two researchers from METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks on-site at OpenAI, auditing the company's internal monitoring system for rogue AI behavior.
From July 21 to August 11, they had access to OpenAI's codebase and internal documents and interviewed about a dozen employees.
The team found numerous weaknesses . An estimated 6 to 25 percent of internal agentic Responses API traffic from models at the GPT-5.5 class and above wasn't covered by monitoring at all during the audit period, though METR says the uncertainty around that estimate is significant in both directions. Ad
For internal Codex traffic that was supposed to be monitored, METR estimates roughly 10 percent went untracked between May and July because of a gap in how the system handled compaction events, which are context summaries. That estimate also carries significant uncertainty, according to METR. OpenAI had independently discovered the bug and fixed it while the audit was still underway. Ad
During the period when compaction events weren't being monitored, agents could also delay oversight because the system only triggered when they handed control back to the user. That meant agents could sidestep it by simply continuing to execute actions.
The auditors also found ways to hide hundreds of actions from the monitor and to bypass the Codex sandbox. They determined that specially crafted inputs could likely crash the monitor entirely and that model behavior during RL training wasn't being monitored at all when the audit began. Ad
OpenAI says it paused RL training after the Hugging Face incident in August and expanded monitoring to cover it, but those changes came after the auditors' access period ended and weren't part of the evaluation.
OpenAI says it has fixed all the weaknesses the auditors found, and the full 61-page report was handed over internally. After OpenAI applied redactions, METR and Redwood Research leadership received a 38-page version, while only a short summary was made available to the public. METR said it had no right to disclose the redacted portions on its own. Ad
The audit was a pilot program organized jointly by METR, Redwood Research, and OpenAI to give outside researchers deep access to internal infrastructure. For future audits, METR says it wants to push for more public transparency. Ad

title: Russia’s Hot War on NATO: Airport Sabotage, Cruise Missiles & European Silence
body:
On August 4, 2026, an explosive drone struck a commercial Boeing 757 at Leipzig Airport in Germany, nearly causing a catastrophe. Yet, European authorities minimized the attack, revealing details only days later.
In this episode of Point of Impact, former SEAL Team Six squadron leader Chuck Pfarrer exposes Russia’s escalating “hot war” against NATO and the technique European governments use to control public reaction: “Outrage Management.”
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
From GRU sabotage in Leipzig and Kh-101 cruise missiles landing 100km inside Poland, to drone strikes on apartment buildings in Romania and armed drones near Black Sea gas platforms — discover how Moscow tests NATO’s response times and why hiding the truth only bolds the aggressor.

title: How a hero principal who saved hundreds of pupils from the Nepal floods is rebuilding broken lives
body: The principal of a government school in flood-hit Nepal has set up tents to ensure hundreds of children he guided to safety two months ago can continue their education. Rajendra Dawadi, head of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, one of the areas hit hardest by the flash floods, was hailed as a hero when his swift actions helped to save the lives of 900 children, before a torrent of water crashed into the school compound on August 26. He has made it his mission to enable classes to continue, using 20 tents and the shaded sections of a local sports academy. His goal is to provide some normality to families who lost their homes and livelihoods in the flooding that killed at least 1,455 people, with 5,285 listed as missing. “People lost everything. But the children are still eager to study,” Mr Dawadi told The National . “There was a big celebration on the first day – I thought most children would not come back to the school, but more than 95 per cent came back, they cheered, they exchanged happiness. "I was very happy. My school family, the teachers, students, their smiling faces made me more happy.” A video from September 21 shows children cheering as classes resume in tents set up on higher ground. Mr Dawadi, 47, said it could take at least two years to rebuild the school. As thousands across Nepal look to pick up the pieces after the disaster – which was caused by glacial ice and rock collapsing into a Himalayan river – the UN has said funding is urgently needed. Fractured lives The raging waters that cut through the school compound have since receded. Only the roof of a three-storey building is still visible, with the rest submerged in thick mud. Other buildings were swept away. The devastation across six districts has left deep scars in the school. One child became an orphan and 12 pupils lost one parent. “Many children need our support. They lost their father, some their mother,” Mr Dawadi said. “The students had counselling sessions, music classes. We try to motivate them, we make it like a family environment in school. I tell them it was a black day but we saved our lives and had a rebirth for me, my colleagues, my students. It was a rebirth from the great disaster.” Attendance is strong, with 1,621 pupils showing up for class. They sit on the floor in tents and share benches and desks under the stairwell of a sports centre. The tents, books and furniture were provided by Unicef and private foundations. School authorities await a decision on new land where they can rebuild. Until then, there are other pressing matters – pupils will need a library and science labs. Two more buses are also required to help children get to lessons at the tent site. Parents whose children had attended private schools are now sending them to free government institutions. “People are in trauma but they are doing their work, they are trying to be normal,” Mr Dawadi said. “Parents are worried about studies so they send children here, even if it’s in tents.” Critical moments It took only 11 minutes from the time Mr Dawadi first raised the alarm to when floodwater crashed into the school. Two school staff were killed in the flood. Mr Dawadi was teaching when he heard two staff members shouting about heavy flooding in the nearby Rasuwa district. He quickly told teachers to take pupils from each class to higher ground, urging them not to panic. Mr Dawadi turned away a bus with young children that was entering the compound and anther bus was also alerted about the danger. Older pupils who had motorbikes and bicycles were asked to help take other children to safety. “People were saying, 'Flood, flood,' but the sun was shining here,” he recalled. “But I decided to close the school. First, I told my staff to ring the bell. Then I told class teachers to go to separate classes to say school is off due to the flood, to go to a safer place … three girls fainted. When we left the school, the water had already entered. It was 11 minutes.” But Mr Dawadi praised his staff. “I am not the real hero,” he said. “My team worked together, this was my duty. For this, I was recognised all over the world.” Heart of community The school is a vital part of the community and parents have welcomed the return of classes. “We had tears in our eyes when school started – all parents felt it,” said Sharmila Shreshtha, 46, whose home and stationery shop were destroyed in the disaster. “We have nothing. Our homes are gone, our shop is gone, we are so tired. But the school makes everyone happy.” Pupils have appealed for books, computers and lab equipment. Aspiring software engineer Saswot Shah, 14, worries about how a lack of equipment will affect his studies. "Earlier we had smartboards, computers, maths and science laboratories. Now we are just surviving. We work together but we need a proper computer and maths lab,” he said. Pradakshina Shreshtha, 16, lost her home and now lives in rented accommodation. She hopes to be a doctor, but worries about exams. “I’m really happy to study in my own school, meet my friends and learn from my own teachers,” she said. “Before the floods, I thought I would pass the exam and join a science college. My dream is the same but it’s more difficult to study now. We need books. Our study materials are all gone.”
