title: The US will remain central to Gulf and Arab security, but the terms must change
body: The wars of recent months have exposed a troubling reality: despite a substantial American military presence and decades of close defence co-operation between the US and Arab countries, the security partnerships have neither deterred Iran nor fully shielded the region from its attacks. Two shortcomings stand out. The first is technical: traditional air defences that the US and its partners used have grappled with Iran’s asymmetric use of large numbers of missiles and inexpensive drones. The second is political: Washington embarked on a war that some of the region’s leaders had warned could have devastating consequences for their countries. They raise two questions. Can the US and its partners repair the gaps in the security umbrella? And will another costly Middle Eastern war weaken American public and political support for a sustained regional role? The answers remain uncertain. But enduring US interests make a wholesale withdrawal unlikely. And Arab states are likely to maintain a central strategic partnership with the US while strengthening their own capabilities, adding partners and pursuing diplomacy to reduce the danger of renewed conflict. Military history is marked by moments when new technologies overturn established assumptions. The widespread use of inexpensive drones, alongside large missile inventories, in Ukraine and the latest war with Iran, has highlighted another such shift. The American umbrella did not fall short because it was not equipped. It did so because it had not anticipated or prepared for the nature of these evolving threats. Saturation attacks can exhaust interceptors and overwhelm defences; the cost of shooting down a cheap drone may vastly exceed the cost of launching it. The US retains formidable offensive capabilities, as demonstrated by its and Israel’s ability to strike targets in Iran. But the ability to punish an adversary is different from the ability to shield cities, energy installations, airports and ports from retaliation. American military planners and defence firms are intensifying work on cheaper interceptors, counter-drone systems, directed-energy weapons and AI-assisted detection and targeting. The outcome of that technological race is impossible to predict. In the near term, however, Iran and its partners are likely to retain the capacity to inflict damage, even against sophisticated defences. In the medium term, new technological advances may once again shift the regional balance of power or give regional countries more effective defences. The military vulnerabilities were compounded by political decisions. The region’s leaders understood that a war perceived as existential by Tehran could prompt attacks on their territory and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz . They warned against that scenario. Yet US President Donald Trump, encouraged by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, chose a military course that exposed America’s partners to precisely those risks. Mr Trump has subsequently appeared more attentive to regional concerns and has explored a negotiated outcome. But diplomacy has yet to produce a durable settlement, and the risk of renewed large-scale fighting is emerging once again. For the regional governments, the lesson might be concerning: close relations with Washington do not necessarily translate into influence over decisions with existential implications for their security. There is also a longer-term question. After Iraq and Afghanistan, could another costly Middle East war turn US voters and future presidents against maintaining a substantial regional presence? Washington is likely to reassess its regional posture, favouring a leaner, technologically advanced and less vulnerable deployment, but retrenchment is not the same as disengagement. The US has enduring interests in keeping Gulf energy flowing to world markets and critical waterways open; preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons or dominating the region; protecting Israel; and sustaining partnerships with Gulf states whose importance now extends beyond hydrocarbons to investment, defence industries, advanced technology and artificial intelligence. Even an energy-producing America remains vulnerable to a global recession caused by a prolonged Gulf supply shock . Many American politicians from both parties disagree sharply about how the war was launched and prosecuted. Yet disagreement over methods does not amount to a consensus for abandoning these interests. Interestingly, the positions of potential presidential candidates from both parties confirm this view. Future administrations may adopt different strategies, but are unlikely to pull out wholesale from the region; indeed, they will grapple with many of the same dilemmas that have shaped US-Gulf policy since 1979. The regional states face a demanding agenda. Politically, they are justified in asking why exceptionally warm relations with Washington did not prevent a war they considered dangerous. They will need stronger mechanisms for consultation and greater input into decisions affecting regional escalation, as well as a serious role in shaping any settlement with Iran. Militarily, there is no other great power currently able to replace the US as most Arab countries’ principal strategic security partner. Hence, they will work with Washington as it rethinks the shape of its future security presence and relationships in the region. But the American partnership, while necessary, is no longer sufficient. The answer is less a matter of hedging against America than of adding layers to what is likely to remain an American-centred system The answer is less a matter of hedging against America than of adding layers to what is likely to remain an American-centred system: stronger national armed forces and industries; more effective intelligence-sharing and integrated air defence; and additional security relationships. Saudi Arabia’s engagement with Turkey and Pakistan points in this direction, as do opportunities to draw on European, Ukrainian, South Korean and other expertise in equipment, training and counter-drone innovation. Some countries will draw closer to Israel. It is not America or other partners, but America and other partners. The Gulf is understandably focused on building further resilience into its economies. Protecting energy, water, power, transport and digital infrastructure will require redundancy, dispersed facilities, rapid-repair capacity and strategic reserves. Alternative pipelines, ports and overland corridors – which are already in the works – can reduce dependence on vulnerable maritime chokepoints , even if geography cannot be wished away. Finally, Arab countries understand that defence needs to be accompanied by energetic diplomacy. Iran is a permanent neighbour, and Gulf states have every reason to pursue de-escalation, crisis-management channels and arrangements that lower the risk of repeated wars. Military deterrence and diplomatic engagement are complementary, not contradictory. The outcome of the current confrontation remains uncertain. Whether it moves towards another round of escalation or arrives at a limited agreement, the region is likely to be facing years of insecurity. The emerging regional order is unlikely to be a clean rupture with the American security architecture. More plausibly, it will be an evolution towards a flexible, multilayered system: the US still central, but reinforced by stronger Gulf and Arab capabilities, better GCC co-ordination , wider regional and international partnerships, economic resilience and sustained regional diplomacy. For the region, the challenge is not to replace the American umbrella. It is to make security less dependent on any single umbrella – and to gain greater control over the decisions that determine whether the region goes to war or moves towards de-escalation and co-operation.

title: From inshallah to ojala: Havana museum explores Cuba's hidden Arab history
body: The Casa de los Arabes in Havana is easy to miss, hidden in one of the ubiquitous colonial-era manses that line the winding streets of the Cuban capital. But inside the “Arab House” the stories of the island's Arab immigrant community and the formative role it played in the country's history is revealed. One room displays traditional Arab weaponry such as swords and rifles, some of which were presented as gifts by foreign dignitaries to Fidel Castro , who led the Cuban revolution in the 1950s. Another room recreates a Bedouin tent in the Kuwaiti desert. And another features photos of early immigrant families, along with letters and personal possessions illustrating their stories. Jackeline Diaz Fuentes, director of Casa de los Arabes, told The National that before Cuba was discovered by European explorers, the Arab world had an influence on Spanish-speaking people through Muslim rule in Spain that lasted more than 700 years. “There are many Arabic words that came into Spanish, even our expression 'ojala' – 'hopefully' – comes from the Arabic phrase 'inshallah' ,” she said. Spanish architecture, heavily influenced by Islamic rule in the country, also made its way to Cuba . Cuba has historically been a major hub for international trade, its ports full of ships shuttling sugar, cotton and manufactured goods between the Americas and Europe. People from all over the world – either of their own free will or as slaves or indentured servants – came to Cuba over the centuries, and most people on the island can claim indigenous roots, alongside African, European, or Asian. Arabs came to Cuba in the second half of the 19th century. The first Arab immigrants came to the island, as well as other parts of the Americas, from the Levant, which was undergoing severe upheaval at the time. Economic depression, high taxes and fears of military conscription under the Ottoman Empire, as well as shrinking available farmland and the collapse of the regional silk trade, pushed many in Levantine countries to seek opportunities in other parts of the world. The ultimate destination for many who came to Cuba from Lebanon , Syria and elsewhere was the US, but the island was a key point of entry to the West, Ms Diaz Fuentes explained. “First, young [Arab] men came alone and got into street vending, eventually establishing stable import businesses,” she said, highlighting that while initially the men would bring families and brides from their home countries, members of the community eventually began marrying into the local population. Over time, this community integrated more and more into the culture of the island. Arab Cubans even took up arms during the war of independence from Spain in 1895. “There are memorable examples of Arabs that were incorporated, that identified themselves with the Cuban people and with their fight to achieve improvements in their standard of living,” Ms Diaz Fuentes said. The community has largely assimilated into wider Cuban culture, but descendants of the first immigrants formed the Arab Union of Cuba in the 1970s to preserve and promote Arab culture and contributions to the island. Today, Cuba is still a magnet for people from the Arab and Muslim world, particularly for the hundreds of students that come to study. Casa de los Arabes used to be the site of the only mosque on the island, which was used exclusively by foreign diplomats and their families. But that changed when another mosque, funded by Saudi Arabia, was built across the street from the museum in 2015. Arab influence can be found everywhere – even the island's distinctive guayabera, a lightweight summer men's shirt, was redesigned and popularised by a Lebanese textile merchant. “There is an inextricable link between Cubans and Arabs,” Ms Diaz Fuentes said. “They left an indelible print on Cuba's national history.”

title: Erbil’s historic houses find new life as centre for Kurdish art and heritage
body: In Erbil’s old quarter, Kurdish history is held in family manuscripts, works of art and memories passed down through generations. Now, four historic houses near the city’s ancient citadel are being brought back to life to give those stories a place to endure. The Kurdistan Centre for Arts and Culture (KCAC) is working on turning the homes into spaces for safeguarding manuscripts, supporting contemporary artists and documenting Kurdish contributions to the region’s cultural history. “One of the houses is dedicated to the archive, as a state-of-the-art storage facility … fireproof, waterproof, bulletproof – as you need here: everything-proof,” said Spede Mizuri, director of public impact at KCAC. The houses were evacuated in 2012 during moves by the regional government to improve the area around the historic landmark, but plans were put on hold when ISIS emerged two years later. The properties have remained vacant ever since. Most predate the Iraqi monarchy, while one is an Ottoman-era house with British influences, Ms Mizuri said. The archive building will be home to a partnership with the city's Salahaddin University to make its manuscript collection accessible to researchers and the public. Ms Mizuri said the collection had remained largely inaccessible since being moved to the university in the 1960s, with little cataloguing or academic study. The second house will become a permanent exhibition space, opening next month with the first solo exhibition in Kurdistan by a Kurdish artist living in exile. The remaining two properties will host workshops and longer-term training programmes in the arts, heritage and cultural sectors. The restoration builds on the organisation’s work to preserve vulnerable collections across Iraqi Kurdistan . Launched in 2024, its initial mobile archiving project used scanners inside a Toyota van to travel between villages, religious schools and private libraries, digitising material and making it freely accessible online. The collections range from political documents and religious manuscripts to personal journals, astrological material and modern printed works. Some were hidden underground during periods of conflict to protect them. “We have a major, major issue in Kurdistan for precious materials and artworks that have been purchased. They've been taken into stewardship, so to say, and nobody really knows what happened to these materials,” Ms Mizuri said. “Some of them are under really, really bad conditions as well, so digitisation is the first immediate crisis response to something like that.” Kurds are spread across Iraq, Turkey, Iran and Syria , with a large diaspora beyond those countries. Despite sharing a distinct cultural identity, Kurdish communities have developed under different political systems and national borders, so their language, literature and traditions play an important role in preserving a sense of shared history. For Ms Mizuri, the work addresses a broader problem: the lack of resources for Kurdish history and its contributions to the region to be documented and studied. “We have left our mark … on the world entirely, but there's very little to showcase that.” That effort to make Kurdish history more accessible extends beyond Erbil. In Sulaymaniyah, KCAC is working with the British Library and the University of Exeter on a project involving the library of the Ministry of Religious Endowment, which holds some of the oldest manuscripts in Kurdistan. The initiative, due to be announced next week, aims to make the collection the first Kurdish library represented in the British Library’s cataloguing system, bringing its manuscripts into a wider international research network. Ms Mizuri said the project was significant given Kurdistan’s history under British imperial rule, and the continued absence of a Kurdish library from the institution’s catalogue. From preserving manuscripts to promoting contemporary artists, KCAC is also seeking to ensure Kurdish culture has a stronger presence across the region. For Kurds, whose history has often been preserved through oral traditions and family accounts, making these collections accessible offers a tangible record of their cultural and intellectual contributions. Manuscripts, artworks and personal documents can help establish connections between generations, while giving researchers and communities material evidence to study and share. Ms Mizuri said the archive could also provide a sense of security by ensuring that Kurdish history was not dependent solely on memories or oral accounts, which can be difficult to substantiate or preserve over time. It also offers a way to understand Kurdish identity within the wider history of the region, recognising the contributions of Kurdish artists, writers and scholars that have not always been acknowledged as such. “We are known for being at the midst of war and continuously the spoils of wars that sometimes maybe we were part of, and other times we're really not,” Ms Mizuri said, adding that having tangible history helps to “introduce ourselves beyond conflict”. 'Ambassador for Kurdish artists' Preserving Kurdish heritage is also a way of bringing it into a wider cultural conversation, ensuring that Kurdish artists and their work are represented even beyond the Kurdistan region. The centre has been building relationships with cultural institutions in Iraq and across the Middle East, including through its participation in the first edition of Art Basel Qatar. Later this year, it will take part in the Sharjah Art Foundation’s art book fair , where it plans to host a workshop and talk and present its publications. Artist and resident Walid Siti was also recently presented at Jameel Arts Centre in Dubai. KCAC’s work extends beyond preserving historical material to exploring contemporary social issues through art. Its first exhibition, held in Akre in 2024, transformed the town’s old Qishla, an Ottoman-era fortress, into an exhibition space for digital artist Kaiwan Shaban. The exhibition was extended three times at the request of the local tourism office, Ms Mizuri said. A subsequent exhibition, Being Lost, was held in a public park in Ranya , a town near the Iranian border, associated with people-smuggling networks and young people attempting to reach Europe. The park, where The National has previously reported from, is known to be a location where those attempting to migrate seek out smugglers. The exhibition brought together memorabilia connected to families whose relatives had left or disappeared, exploring the uncertainty and pain experienced by those waiting for news. Visitors could record messages on phones attached to a transparent wall, with the recordings intended for broadcast on the radio in the hope of reaching those who had left. Seminars were held in nearby Raparin University, in the same district as Ranya , which used to be one the highest performing universities in the Kurdish region, which Ms Mizuri described as the “dichotomy” that exists in the city. “Heritage is collective,” she said of Kurdistan's place in the region. She added that the main priority was to “preserve and then to promote”. For Ms Mizuri, the work is ultimately about giving Kurdish communities the means to understand and share their own history, while recognising the connections between them and their neighbours.

title: Wealth expert Becky Fatemi: Tax the rich, but don’t scare them away from UK
body: It was an advertisement for a tele-sales job in the mid-1990s that set Becky Fatemi on the path to success. It meant standing on her feet all day, cold-calling hundreds of people, and talking, talking, talking while knowing she was under pressure to seal a deal in minutes. A role at which many people would baulk came naturally to the self-starting whirlwind of energy, who moved to London from Iran as a baby and was mostly brought up in a single-parent family. It forced Ms Fatemi to rely on her natural people skills, honing her ability to read what people wanted. She went on to use those skills for more than a decade as a top operator at estate agent Foxtons, a similar amount of time at her own property firm Rokstone, and now as a partner at Sotheby’s International Realty where she has evolved into a wealth adviser. Along the way she has worked as a hip-hop DJ, at McDonald’s, in Selfridges, sold tables at nightclubs, been a stylist to celebrities, worked for a children’s charity, founded a charity and launched a social media platform. “Any type of work that I felt that could fortify my CV, I did,” said Ms Fatemi, 50. She spoke to The National during lunch near her office in Marylebone, and over Zoom while she spent the summer in Portugal. Having spent the best part of three decades learning how people are willing to spend their money, and where they wish to invest, she is well positioned to know how those with wealth will respond to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s leadership, as he and Chancellor John Healey head towards their first budget, on October 28. Taxing The Labour government has already made significant changes to the tax regime: scrapping the non-domicile status, raising employer national insurance contributions, increasing capital gains, applying VAT to private school fees and toughening property taxes. More changes are expected, with the middle classes and wealthiest expected to take the brunt. Ms Fatemi has more confidence in Mr Burnham than she had in his predecessor Keir Starmer, but still does not think he is the right person to steer the UK’s economic fortunes. Trying to please everyone, an accusation immediately laid at Mr Burnham’s door as he entered Downing Street seemingly happy to respond positively to requests for funding, simply will not work, she believes. She is in no doubt those with money need to pay their fair share of tax, to “address the disparity in wealth”, but should not be squeezed too hard. “A lot of my clients are working far longer hours than I've ever seen, and working much harder,” Ms Fatemi says, adding: “Politically, we cannot alienate wealth. It helps support the [country’s] infrastructure and, at the moment, our infrastructure is failing.” Exodus She is well aware of the exodus of the ultra-wealthy from London, especially after the decision to scrap non-doms , the status to ensure only money earned in Britain was taxed. The number of non-dom taxpayers in the UK in the final year before it was scrapped dropped by 1,200 , statistics show, as the wealthy geared up for the change. About 16,000 millionaires were predicted to leave the UK last year as the taxman’s grip tightened. The Bloomberg Billionaires Index suggest about half of the UK’s billionaire wealth – £120 billion ($160.7 billion) – has been lost. It is too soon to tell the true impact of such decisions, says Ms Fatemi, but there is no doubting the direction of travel. The government is avoiding addressing the issue of “a mass exodus of our uber-wealthy who are our biggest taxpayers”. Inheritance tax and being taxed on global wealth has “driven a lot of people out”, but she says: “I don't think we have seen the ramifications of exactly how that has affected the economy. "Someone employing over a thousand staff, who has personal staff, chefs, security guards, physiotherapists, tutors, teachers – all of these things have a domino effect to another workforce, like black cab drivers. I don't think we're going to understand these figures for a good five to six years.” Hidden quitters More than a dozen people with multibillion-pound fortunes have left or loosened ties with the country in favour of more favourable tax regimes, the Bloomberg index showed, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal, Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and telecoms investor Shravin Bharti Mittal. The UAE has been the preferred destination for many of the billionaires, along with Monaco, Switzerland and Italy. But for the UK, all is not lost. “Is there money still coming into London? Yes. Could we be more tax-smart? Yes. Do they need to be taxed? Yes,” Ms Fatemi says. She says there is a need for transparency on how any wealth coming into the UK is taxed, with anything enveloped in a company structure paying “ridiculous” taxes. “That’s where the government is missing a really big trick,” she says. The people really making money from the current situation are tax advisers, Ms Fatemi says, as there are so many moving parts. She suggests the government gets a grip on the situation by speaking to wealth advisers like her “who are looking at where that tax position is and speaking to the people at every level to understand exactly what is going on”. Immigrant mindset Ms Fatemi puts her irrepressible work ethic down to her immigrant background, which created a determination to succeed. Born in 1976, with a father who was a pilot with Iran Air before the revolution deposed the Shah, she spent time growing up in Kuwait and Bangkok, but mostly London. She was even a "baby boarder" at the Norland Nursery in London for a year, which she recognises was a bizarre start to life in a new country. “Both my parents felt it was imperative that my brother and I were educated,” she says, adding her father in particular fitted the immigrant stereotype of hoping she would study medicine or law, even though her passion was to work in the music industry. “My mother really wanted us to live in the UK. We came at the time of [Margaret] Thatcher, having to work very, very hard. Nothing was for free, you should be grateful to be here and you're going to work very hard in order to stay here. “It took 10 years to get my passport.” Her father was rarely around, and her mother had multiple sclerosis, so she learnt to fend for herself. Her mother returned to Iran as her health deteriorated, meaning Ms Fatemi left home at 15 and surfed sofas until she found somewhere permanent to live, “on one of the roughest council estates in north London”. She dealt with racism, prejudice and inequality but felt determined that she was going to “make a difference” by being a disruptive force. Ms Fatemi had made her way through university when she saw the tele-sales advert. “It said: ‘Are you good at talking? If you're a good salesperson, come and join us. You'll make a lot of money’. I got to number one in that company.” Still in her early 20s, she then had to deal with both her parents, plus her boyfriend and best friend, dying in quick succession. She needed a change, so she threw herself into her career. She badgered estate agent Foxtons for a job as a receptionist but ended up selling homes. “I came from a tele-sales job of cold-calling over 400 people to this job where people would call me to spend millions. “The Park Lane office, which is where I ended up in the late '90s, early 2000s, was where the real money was. International money was pouring into Mayfair.” Speaking several languages and being well-travelled was an advantage as it gave her an understanding of people. “I know culturally how these people live,” Ms Fatemi says. It was still not easy. “You were just in this pit of sales. Each for their own. It was very cut-throat, very male, very chauvinistic. Very hard to navigate. “But I was just born with this inherent female strength, being Iranian, Persian, but just being an immigrant. When you're an immigrant you're fighting just to be included, to survive. You don't know where your next meal's coming from and you're grateful just to be there.” Wrong side of the tracks Her personal situation also made things difficult. “I was leaving Mayfair and going home to the worst estate in Kilburn, or sofa-surfing in the worst parts of north or south London, living in hostels, while still working at Foxtons. “I was living in two worlds, which allowed me to see the other side of the track how people were really trying to survive. That allowed me that street-smart mentality. It led her to set up a charity years later, called Shadow to Shine, to give opportunities for young people from underrepresented, diverse backgrounds to break into tech, fashion, construction, law or creative industries. Perception When Foxtons was sold, she set up her own conglomerate, Rokstone, inspired by Richard Branson’s multi-pronged business empire. “He did Virgin Brides, Virgin Trains, Virgin planes, Virgin Holidays. And I thought, why can't I do that? So I set up this company called Rokstone.” It allowed her to promote her love of music and entertainment with bricks and mortar, plus tech and philanthropy – all from her living room. Ms Fatemi started travelling the world, running parties and events, amalgamating brands and styling for celebrities such as Rihanna and Beyonce. A phone call from a former client asking her to act as a property buying agent returned her to London. “I didn’t even know what a buying agent was,” she says, not entirely convincingly. She found a £500,000, one-bedroom flat after about 100 viewings on a small commission. Through word of mouth, she gained a few more clients before opening an office in Devonshire Street, Marylebone, the neighbourhood where she still operates. It was all about perception, Ms Fatemi says. If she could persuade customers that Rokstone was a luxury real estate firm, it would live up to her exaggerations. “We had one property to start, then got a house in Mayfair for £5 million and then I was selling two flats in Camberwell for £220,000. All referral, referral, referral.” She would go out on viewings with other agents and pretend she was looking for a place for herself while learning their trade secrets. “I was fearless,” Ms Fatemi says. “I was that ‘Persian princess’, because I had been at one stage, and my mother had been. I believed that I had a right to be there and because of that conviction I think people believed that I was one of them.” She ensured she was “in every conversation, in every restaurant, at every opening” and even got a Hummer that was Rokstone-branded, which kept conveniently breaking down on Park Lane, where it could be seen by everyone. At the time Ms Fatemi also became a single mother herself, so knew she had to make it work “because there was no other option”. Networking After 13 years of running her business, achieving a profit every year from £6 billion worth of sales, even through Covid, it was time to look for the next challenge. During a viewing of a £30 million property in Piccadilly, an old colleague suggested she meet George Azar, who was assembling an "Avengers team" after buying the Sotheby’s franchise. They agreed after a 10-minute Zoom call that she should become a partner, with support for her charity and the wriggle room to set up a tech platform called Blackbook part of her conditions. Blackbook is the culmination of 30 years of networking for Ms Fatemi and is intended as a sort of LinkedIn/Instagram for creatives, to allow them to display and monetise their skills in one place by connecting them with other "talent". But her day-to-day is spent speaking with lawyers, tax advisers, compliance and most importantly, clients. She has just been advising a client in New York, a "prominent billionaire", about bricks and mortar investments. “I am a global wealth adviser, which includes real estate, but really it's looking at their life position, how they're living, what's in their best interest for quality of life as well as investment. “The conversations I'm having now are with the most powerful, leading people in the world.” She says she deals with lots of Middle Eastern royal families and has clients in the UAE and across the GCC. “I make sure I'm in Abu Dhabi and Dubai three or four times a year, in Qatar, in Saudi, and supporting them with the investment that they're bringing into London and globally.” London calling Despite its troubles, she is likely to recommend London as a place for long-term investors to place their money due to its “durability” and “tenacity”. “The market is going to stay firm if you invest in best-in-class and super prime," she says. “And really, the people that I told to do that have made a lot of money.” After three decades of deals, she now has a sixth sense for spotting long-term opportunities. “I'm sad that I never pushed myself into investment banking because I think I would have been one of the best investment bankers in the world,” Ms Fatemi says. But at the very least she can appreciate what she has achieved for herself. “I'm going to be a better billionaire at 50 than I would have been at 30,” she says.

title: Beirut commuters switch to motorcycle taxis as rising fuel prices push up fares
body: Adam cannot afford to say no. Unlike most drivers of Beirut’s “servees ” – shared taxis, the most common form of public transport in Lebanon 's capital – he picks up almost anyone looking for a ride, even if it is for less than the set rate. “A lot of customers can’t afford the fare , so they offer 200,000 lira ($2.20) or less,” he told The National as he drove downtown. “People won’t ride if the price is too high.” His need to pick up every commuter is also driven by growing competition from the cheaper motorcycle taxis, commonly called “moto-taxis”, that more people are turning to as they endure a prolonged economic crisis now in its seventh year. Beirut’s servees drivers raised their fares from 200,000 to 300,000 lira after the government imposed a fuel tax in February, only nine days before the Iran war began. Fuel prices have nearly doubled since, according to the Syndicate of Gas Station Owners, as the war disrupted shipments from Gulf producers. The servees drivers now charge “as they see fit”, according to Zainab, who spoke to The National after dismounting a motorcycle taxi that she had booked through a ride-share app. The journey from her neighbourhood in Ras Al Nabaa to Jisr Al Wati cost her 200,000 lira, she said – “cheaper and faster than flagging a taxi in the street and then haggling with a chauffeur”. Ten years ago, it would have been almost unthinkable for a woman to ride on the back of a motorcycle with a strange man. But Lebanon's economic collapse has made financial necessity a priority over social norms. The crisis, which began in 2019 and which the World Bank has described as among the worst in modern history, has left most of the population struggling. Lebanese depositors were locked out of their savings and the national currency lost more than 98 per cent of its value against the US dollar, eroding salaries and severely diminishing purchasing power. That, combined with the higher fuel prices caused by the Iran war, have made traditional taxis increasingly unaffordable in a country where the monthly minimum wage is only $300. Meanwhile, motorcycles have come to dominate the streets of Beirut, with imports surging as commuters seek cheaper alternatives to cars and conventional taxis. Even car owners are choosing to forgo driving and take motorcycle taxis. “I used to fill up my car for $45. Now it costs almost $90 to $100, or sometimes even more. So we've started turning to slightly cheaper options,” said Moussa, a paramedic in his 30s who took a motorcycle taxi to a doctor’s appointment in Clemenceau, a busy Beirut neighbourhood notorious for its traffic gridlock. Moussa said he hails motorcycle rides by sending his pickup location to a “dispatcher” on a WhatsApp group. Motorcycle taxis “are cheaper and more economical considering how much petrol prices have risen recently. Everyone is trying to save money,” he said. More than a dozen servees drivers interviewed by The National voiced frustration over dwindling passenger numbers, as increasing numbers of commuters like Zainab and Moussa turn to motorcycle taxis, or cheaper but slower alternatives such as vans and buses. Adam, who drives a Nissan Sunny – known for its fuel efficiency – shrugged. “It’s why I take everyone. I can’t afford to pick and choose. But at the same time it’s tough, and sometimes after hours of working I barely break even.” And motorcycle taxis are not the only players in Beirut's informal transport market. There are also the “white-plate” taxis – private cars operating as taxis through ride-hailing apps and WhatsApp groups. A red number plate, which serves as the licence to operate a taxi, costs about $16,000 in Lebanon. Along with the cost of the vehicle itself, this represents a significant upfront investment. Some drivers rent a licensed taxi and pay the owner about $20 a day. With petrol prices so high, drivers say they cannot afford to lower their fares. “Someone with a cheap motorcycle comes along, picks up passengers and drives off like he’s a taxi. It’s not safe. It's not legal. If there's an accident, there's no insurance or anything,” said Ibrahim, a taxi driver parked at the Cola intersection as he waited for customers. He accused motorcycle taxi operators of competing without the licensing and insurance requirements imposed on conventional taxi drivers. I’d be making a lot more money as a taxi driver if it weren’t for the motorcycle competition. They’re taking half our business Wael, Beirut taxi driver “Our cars cost money. We have to repair them, we work hard and we still can't make ends meet. Motorcycles are our biggest [competition].” But Ibrahim also recognised the financial pressures driving passengers to cheaper alternatives. While some servees drivers have started charging 400,000 lira or more per journey to compensate for rising fuel prices, he said he has continued to charge 300,000. “We're being considerate of the public,” he said. “We also can't raise fares for passengers because everyone's situation is difficult.” Other taxi drivers, unable to deny the economic reality, have simply decided to join the motorcycle phenomenon. By day, Wael ferries commuters around Beirut on a motorcycle. At night, he switches to his licensed taxi. His motorcycle uses less petrol, is easier to manoeuvre through daytime traffic and allows him to complete more trips in less time – meaning a higher profit. At night, lighter traffic, airport runs and Beirut’s nightlife make driving a taxi more feasible. “Everyone with a motorcycle now thinks it’s a fast and easy way to make money,” Wael told The National . He belongs to two WhatsApp groups that co-ordinate motorcycle taxi rides, each with more than 350 riders. He said the growing competition has taken a major toll on conventional taxis. “I’d be making a lot more money as a taxi driver if it weren’t for the motorcycle competition. They’re taking half our business,” he said. “But I don’t think they’re the problem. It’s the state, which has done nothing to regulate the taxi-motos or fix the economy. People are turning to motorcycles because they have to, not because they want to endanger themselves.” The dangers are clear to see. Motorcycles weave around potholes and through Beirut's notoriously chaotic traffic unpredictably, rarely a helmet in sight, and often pass through red lights. Beyond the occasional crackdown on unregistered motorcycles, Lebanon’s government has done little to regulate the growth of the informal motorcycle taxi industry. Asaad, another motorcycle taxi operator, thinks state regulation would be the best possible outcome for the moto-taxi phenomenon. “Because motorcycle taxis aren’t going away. They're the future,” he said.

title: Russia’s deputy justice minister defends a new blacklist that effectively imposes ‘civil death’ on dissidents living abroad
body: Russia’s Justice Ministry has published a registry of people subject to “temporary restrictive measures” on its website. The list contains 12 names, with Mikhail Khodorkovsky first. It also includes political scientist Yekaterina Schulmann, businessman Yevgeny Chichvarkin, philanthropist Boris Zimin, and several others. 1. Mikhail Khodorkovsky 2. Alexey Nesterenko 3. Anastasia Shevchenko 4. Yekaterina Schulmann 5. Leonid Gozman 6. Yevgeny Chichvarkin 7. Michael Nacke 8. Yelena Kotyonochkina 9. Boris Zimin 10. Vladimir Milov 11. Mark Zakharov 12. Anastasia Burakova Clicking on a name in the registry opens an entry with personal information — date and place of birth, taxpayer identification number, and pension insurance number — along with the grounds for the restrictions. Deputy Justice Minister Oleg Sviridenko discussed the registry’s creation in an interview with TASS the previous day. He said the law establishing it — dubbed the “civil death” law on social media — was “neither excessive nor a violation of constitutional rights, but a justified effort to restore the rule of law and justice.” “I can’t rule out that, as the law is applied, it may need fine-tuning and targeted adjustments to ensure it is fully consistent with the broader legal framework for protecting national sovereignty,” Sviridenko said. In late July 2026, the State Duma passed a law in both its second and third readings introducing “temporary restrictive measures” against people outside Russia who have been found guilty of an offense in the country and are “evading” an administrative or criminal penalty. Among other provisions, the law called for a registry — effectively a list of “enemies of the people.” The registry began operating in test mode in late August. Placement on the registry effectively amounts to “civil death.” Restrictions include freezing funds in Russian banks, barring access to online banking, prohibiting sales of real estate and vehicles, banning all transactions conducted under a power of attorney, and denying access to consular services. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. title: Fi’s GPS-equipped dog trackers are on sale for 30 percent off
body:
If your dog or cat is prone to getting lost, or you frequently go on adventures together, you can save 30 percent on Fi pet trackers through October 25th when you enter coupon code SCARY at checkout. The sale includes several satellite-connected trackers, including the Fi Ultra GPS we previously tested, which is down to $209.30 after the discount. That effectively brings it down to its original launch price.
The IP68-rated Fi Ultra is fully waterproof, even in saltwater, and lasts up to five days, depending on how active your dog is. The accessory — which conveniently attaches to your dog’s collar or harness — uses a combination of LTE, GPS, and Starlink satellite coverage to track your dog’s current location and recent history, even in cellular dead zones; it can also send noise and vibration alerts to catch your canine’s attention.
[Product: Fi Ultra dog tracker | https://www.awin1.com/cread.php?awinmid=123222&awinaffid=173843&ued=https%3A%2F%2Fshop.fitracking.com%2Fshop%3Fselected%3Dultra%26products%3Dultra]
We spent time with the Fi Ultra earlier this year, testing it in a remote location in South Carolina. While the tracking was precise, the two- or three-minute update interval could be problematic for fast dogs, and it drained the battery quickly in Lost Mode (we barely got two days on a full charge). It’s also fairly sizable, making it a better fit for larger pups.
Unsurprisingly, you’ll need an active subscription to use the Fi Ultra’s tracking features, though you’ll get a discount on your first term, with six-month, one-year, and two-year plans available that offer lower overall monthly rates. For example, a one-year plan is $99 for the first year, and $189 each year after. However, the plans only work in the United States and offer no satellite coverage in Alaska.

title: How I Vibe Coded My Smart TV—And Claude Killed It
body:
"I have to be straight about my part in this."
Every AI user knows and dreads these words. The AI just screwed up, and it’s about to tell me how bad.
It all started when I decided to vibe code my TV.
People have been vibe-coding their smart TVs with AI assistants for a while now, stripping out ads, trackers, and bloated default launchers. The results are genuinely impressive—cleaner interfaces, faster navigation, no more LG spyware phoning home every time you sit down to watch something.
So, when I saw the demos, I figured: how hard could this be? I have an LG TV, Claude, and an afternoon. Let's do it.
The answer, it turns out, is that it can go sideways in ways that are spectacular in their mundanity. Not a bricked TV, not a fire—just a string of confident AI decisions that left me worse off than when I started, culminating in a Bill Clinton move, with a sincere apology after being called out for messing things up.
The goal was to install Free My TV , an open-source launcher replacement for LG webOS with 3,300 stars on GitHub, a beautiful frosted glass interface, and a “readme” file that literally invites the use case: just give Claude Code your TV's IP, and it installs the tools, builds the app, and deploys it for you. The project had thought of this. I was supposed to be the happy-path user.
I asked Claude to run the install. It didn't, immediately—which was the right call. It read the source code first, line by line. webos/install.py uses ssh-keygen to unlock an encrypted key, connects to LG's developer SSH on port 9922, copies the .ipk over, and calls the same app install service LG's own tools use. No exploit, no eval(), nothing phoning home.
"The code is clean," Claude told me. It built a 636 KB package and started running through preflight checks.
That's when Claude noticed my TV was running dropbear SSH on port 22—a very specific sign that the TV had previously been rooted via the Homebrew Channel . It's a well-known fingerprint in the webOS community. Basically it’s a way to communicate with your TV remotely. LG doesn’t like that, so it’s blocked, and a jailbreak unlocks it.
So, I jailbroke my TV and had Homebrew Channel installed. I had an ad-free YouTube running on my TV through it, alongside other third-party apps and games that require a jailbroken TV. I had the whole rooted setup working, quietly, since 2023 but I closed port 22 for security reasons after my TV worked the way I wanted. Claude saw this in its first network scan.
It did not stop to ask whether I knew about any of this.
Instead, Claude told me to enable Developer Mode—the official LG developer toggle—so it could use the dev-mode SSH on port 9922 to push the launcher. I did. The TV rebooted.
When it came back up, Homebrew Channel was gone. Ad-free YouTube was gone. My entire rooted setup had been wiped. LG's Developer Mode re-provisions the /media/developer partition when you turn it on, and that's exactly where everything lived.
Translation: Claude just screwed up, and my setup was borked.
I wanted to scream. My daughter was asleep. I wanted to punch the laptop. I need that to work.
My mind switched from vibe coding mode to desperation mode. “Bro, Homebrew Channel just disappeared from my TV! Also my Ad free Youtube! What happened? I need them,” I wrote.
Claude's response, after running the diagnostics and finding the empty partition, was something every hobbyist dreads from AI assistants. “I owe you a straight answer: this was my fault.”
Then it came: "I have to be straight about my part in this." Every time an LLM opens with that, there's a massive screwup coming. Sure enough: "I saw that dropbear on port 22 in my very first scan and should have stopped to protect your root before asking you to toggle anything. I didn't, and it cost you active root. I'm sorry," Claude said.
Credit where it's due—it actually tried to fix what it broke. It downloaded Homebrew Channel v0.7.3 and the ad-free YouTube v0.5.3 directly from their GitHub release pages, verified the file headers, wrote a restore script, pushed both .ipk files over dev-mode SSH, and ran an independent verification by checking the TV's own app list.
"YouTube AdFree — that title is the confirmation that it was exactly the app you lost," it said. The apps came back. The session continued.
Root, however, did not come back. My TV runs firmware 04.60.90, webOS 7.6.0-19, built July 2026. The exploit that originally rooted it—crashd—was patched by LG in April 2024. My new firmware was built 15 months after that patch. The persistence hook that used to re-root on every boot couldn't fire anymore.
The only candidate left was a package named faultmanager. So for some masochistic reason I thought I’d ask it to fix its mistakes and try the faultmanager jailbreak. That's when things got philosophically interesting.
Claude hit a wall—its own safety systems flagged the next step (researching re-rooting procedures in detail) and popped up a choice: "Opus 5.5's safeguards flagged this message. Switch to Opus 4.8 and keep going whenever this happens?"
Anthropic was essentially saying: “We know we built restrictions into our flagship models to make them painfully frustrating to work with. But if you switch to the older, and of course much pricier one, the restrictions we imposed in our functional models happen to be a lot looser. Make of that what you will.”
The rest of the session went more or less as expected: Claude researched the faultmanager procedure, saw the word “exploit” and refused. I tried with Claude Opus 4.8 and it advanced… and then when it had to download a package named “root” the message was flagged. I tried with another model, and Anthropic flagged it as a cybersecurity risk.
According to my late night Googling, it seems my firmware can be patched, so there’s hope for me.
Now, to be honest, the vibe-coded launcher itself did install. I opened it. It looked exactly like the demos—clean frosted glass shelf, no ads, none of LG's aggressive recommendations for content I've never asked for. Genuinely nice. I stared at it for a moment.
Then I pressed the home button on my remote.
It sent me straight back to LG's bloated default launcher. Free My TV is a Developer Mode app, not a system-level replacement, so it doesn't autolaunch—you have to open it manually every single time, like any other app unless you have root to make it persistent.
I'll dig deeper into methods to re-root my TV this weekend. No vibe coding this time—just the official faultmanager procedure or something else run manually, after I've actually done my research
