title: Oleshky Evacuation: Russia Announces Kherson Frontline ‘Silence Regime’
body:
Chief of the Russian General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced Moscow will halt fire along the Kherson frontline in what it described as a “silence regime” to allow a humanitarian operation in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, starting Oct. 27.
Gerasimov set the announced date two days earlier than the date previously agreed upon with the White House , noting that it would take effect at 4 a.m. Moscow time.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“To ensure the safety of people and the delivery of socially important cargo, engineering reconnaissance will be organized and safe movement of a humanitarian convoy into the settlement of Oleshky in Kherson region will be ensured,” Gerasimov said, according to Interfax-Russia on Friday, Oct. 23.
Asked about the duration of the humanitarian operation, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov declined to provide a specific timeline.
However, according to Russian state-owned media TASS , he said that the operation would “naturally” take “at least several days.”
Although Ukraine has confirmed the White House-brokered arrangement, it has yet to comment on Moscow’s earlier start date.
The Kremlin’s decision to declare a ceasefire raises immediate concerns of possible sabotage among Ukrainian media, given Moscow’s pattern of breaking previous ceasefires, particularly those it declares itself.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, who led the talks with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, earlier confirmed that the ceasefire would take place on Oct. 29.
He outlined three key components of the deal. “First, a silence regime will be ensured; second, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky; third, free movement of civilians from Oleshky will be ensured,” Lubinets said , according to Ukrainska Pravda .
However, he did not provide additional details on how long each stage would take, nor how much aid would be delivered. No details were given on the evacuation routes either.
Lubinets also urged the public and media to be careful when sharing information about the mission. “The whole world now knows about Oleshky,” he said, promising to keep Ukrainians informed and show the results of the operation.
Davyd Arakhamia, who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, said that the operation to unblock Oleshky and its surroundings would begin soon.
He described the agreement as a result of a long process involving many people at different political levels, singling out Pope Leo XIV and Melania Trump for their roles.
At the time of the report, neither Kyiv nor Washington has explained why Moscow announced a start date earlier than the one agreed upon.
Oleshky, located in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River, about 5 km (3 miles) southeast of the city of Kherson, has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Ukrainian officials and European leaders have long been aware of the crisis in Oleshky and have worked for months to secure a safe evacuation and restore food supplies, which have not reached the city since May 26.
Beyond food, the town’s residents barely have any drinking water or medicine.
According to Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, Oleshky’s only pharmacy has also reportedly run out of essential medications months ago, while overall medical care has been significantly complicated due to power cuts and lack of fuel as the city remains isolated.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said .
In a statement on Sept. 16, Lubinets said that the residents had started escaping on foot independently across mined fields and under threat of constant Russian drone attacks, simply because they saw no other way out. At the time, he also said Russia had failed to uphold previously agreed arrangements for a humanitarian mission.
“They see no other way to escape this hell,” Lubinets said, adding that his office had received 176 appeals regarding the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, and had already verified at least 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
On Monday, Oct. 19, Lubinets confirmed that Kyiv and Moscow were in daily contact over a possible evacuation , noting that the Russian side had taken up all proposals previously submitted by Ukraine.
“I cannot disclose many details, but I will say this: In my view, we have made significant progress,” he said.
Ukrainian authorities estimate that about 6,000 people, including some 200 children, remain across Oleshky and the surrounding settlements.
According to European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno, who declared a hunger strike on Tuesday, Oct. 20, in protest over the starvation of civilians in Oleshky, roughly 1,700 people remain in the city from a prewar population of 24,000, including 47 children.
However, neither figure could be independently verified, particularly because Russian occupation authorities narrowly restrict access to information from the area.
Earlier on Friday, the White House announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to temporarily halt military activity in Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare civilian evacuations, starting Oct. 29.
It was not specified how long the truce would last or how many people are expected to be evacuated.
According to Washington’s statement , non-military representatives from Ukraine and Russia would visit residents at home to assess their needs.
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” said US First Lady Melania Trump.
The Associated Press previously reported that neither the Ukrainian nor the Russian government immediately commented.
Pope Leo XIV held a telephone discussion with Putin on Oct. 16, in what marked the second phone call between the two, following their first conversation on June 4, 2025 that also focused on the war in Ukraine.
The pope had expressed his deep concern about the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, urging the Russian president to agree to an immediate ceasefire and allow the delivery of food and medical assistance to the city.
He also called for a safe evacuation of the civilians.
While the Kremlin backed Vatican’s initiative and agreed to cooperate, it again pinned the blame for the crisis on Ukraine, despite Kyiv’s repeated appeals to Russian authorities and international partners to secure humanitarian access to the town.
The pontiff then spoke to President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 19, reiterating his earlier request for a humanitarian ceasefire . He expressed hope for a cooperation between Kyiv and Moscow which would allow for the desperately needed food and medical supplies to reach trapped civilians.
“We are working to help our people there. We are preparing decisions,” Zelensky said , confirming the conversation.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
body:
Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome. Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder . The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result. This post uses Wordle , a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting. In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models . All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository . Solution overview The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect. Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word , and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) adapter on the policy model. Three design points matter for what follows: The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function. The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring. The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5, and never making a valid guess pays -1.5. A small shaping term rewards good strategy within each tier. Supported models and AWS Regions MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter: Base model AWS Regions Amazon Nova 2 Lite US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) GPT-OSS-20B US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) Gemma 4 31B (instruction-tuned) US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) Qwen 3.6 27B US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) We chose GPT-OSS-20B because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list. Pricing You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model: Prefill: input tokens the policy model processes. These accumulate in a multi-turn task, because every turn re-reads the history. Sample: tokens the policy model generates, including reasoning tokens. Train: tokens processed in the backward pass that updates the LoRA adapter. The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339: Dimension Tokens Price per 1M Cost Prefill 491,616,806 $0.12 $58.99 Sample 159,737,098 $0.30 $47.92 Train 643,308,554 $0.36 $231.59 Total 1,294,662,458 $338.50 The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. DescribeJob reports the token counts under BillableTokenUsage . See Amazon SageMaker AI pricing for current rates. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, you need the following. See also the MTRL prerequisites . Python 3.10 or later, uv, Node 20 or later, and the AgentCore CLI ( npm install -g @aws/agentcore ). See Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for installation and the IAM permissions the CLI needs. botocore 1.43.37 or later, on the machine that launches the job. This is the first version that includes the AgentRFT CreateJob operation. Two AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, described in Step 1. An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the same Region as the agent. The training job must also run in that Region, because CreateJob rejects a cross-Region runtime ARN. Step 1: Create the IAM roles MTRL uses two roles, and one of them has a trust policy that the general SageMaker AI documentation doesn’t mention. Agent runtime role. agentcore deploy creates this role for you. It trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and needs the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, which lets the agent call the policy model and report rewards. The CDK stack in the sample repository attaches this policy automatically. Training job role. You create this one. It must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession , and it needs the AmazonSageMakerJobFullAccess managed policy. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Service": "job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com"}, "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"] }] } Note: The trust principal is job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com , not sagemaker.amazonaws.com . With the generic principal, CreateJob fails with “Could not assume role,” and the message names the correct principal only after retries. Step 2: Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Clone the sample repository , set your account and Region in Wordle/agentcore/ aws-targets.json , and deploy: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle cd sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle/Wordle agentcore validate agentcore deploy The CLI builds the agent’s dependencies for the runtime’s Linux ARM64 platform, creates the execution role with AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess attached, and deploys through AWS CloudFormation. We recommend it over uploading a code package on the console, where it’s common to get the roughly 700 MB of compiled dependencies or the policy attachment wrong. Note the runtime ARN in the output for the training job. Figure 2: The Wordle agent runtime in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console with status Ready The runtime reads two environment variables from agentcore.json . REASONING_EFFORT=low sets reasoning_effort on every request to the policy model. In our evaluation jobs, low effort used 63 to 83 percent fewer sample tokens per game than medium. REASONING_PROMPT_HINT=true also adds “Reasoning: low” to the system prompt, which is how gpt-oss reads the setting in its Harmony chat format. Neither variable gives the model any hint about the secret word. Figure 3: Runtime environment variables showing REASONING_EFFORT set to low The agent is one file, main.py . Simplified, its entrypoint looks like the following. For your own task, you change the task parsing, the tools, and the reward: app = BedrockAgentCoreApp() @app.entrypoint # outermost: starts the HTTP server AgentCore invokes @sagemaker_rft_handler # reports the returned reward to SageMaker AI def handle_rollout(payload): prompt, answer = parse_task(payload["prompt"]) game = WordleGame(answer) @tool def guess_word(guess: str) -> str: """Submit a 5-letter Wordle guess and get feedback.""" return game.guess(guess) agent = Agent(model=build_model(), system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT, tools=[guess_word]) agent(prompt) return {"reward": game.final_reward()} Important: The sagemaker_rft_handler decorator does not start an HTTP server by itself. Wrap it with BedrockAgentCoreApp and @app.entrypoint , with the entrypoint decorator outermost. Without this, every invocation times out after 30 seconds. Step 3: Verify the runtime Before spending GPU time, confirm the whole chain works with a payload shaped like the one the training service sends. The repository includes one as Wordle/ payload.json : { "prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"beach\", \"id\": \"smoke-test\"}", "metadata": { "jobArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-1:111122223333:job/AgentRFT/smoke-test", "rolloutId": "r1" } } The fake job ARN is expected to fail, and the way it fails is the proof. Put your own account ID into it first: for a job ARN in another account, the service returns a 403 before it checks whether the job exists, which looks like a broken IAM setup. From the Wordle directory, run: ACCOUNT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text) sed "s/111122223333/$ACCOUNT/" payload.json > /tmp/payload.json aws bedrock-agentcore invoke-agent-runtime \ --agent-runtime-arn
\ --runtime-session-id smoke-test-$(date +%s)000000000000000 \ --payload fileb:///tmp/payload.json /dev/stdout In the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch logs, you see the agent parse the prompt, authenticate to the Job Runtime endpoint, and receive a 400 error reading “Could not find job.” That failure confirms that parsing, authentication, and error reporting work. The command itself prints {“reward”: -1.5}, because the agent never reached the policy model. A 403 reading “not authorized to access this resource” means the job ARN still names another account. A 30-second timeout instead means the HTTP server is not starting (see the Important note in Step 2). Step 4: Prepare the dataset The MTRL dataset has no target responses, transcripts, or labels. Each row is one task for the agent to attempt. Here are the first three rows of the training file: {"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"riser\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0000\"}"} {"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"swoon\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0001\"}"} {"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"dirty\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0002\"}"} The service reads the prompt column (or the first column) and passes the string to your agent verbatim, without parsing it. We made the string a small JSON object with three fields: prompt: the instruction the agent shows the policy model, identical on every row. answer: the secret word. Only the environment and the reward function use it. The policy model never sees it. id: a row ID for tracing a rollout in the logs back to its source row. The sample repository’s make_dataset.py draws 640 training words (five full batches of 128) and 128 validation words from the answer list with no overlap, so the validation solve rate measures generalization. The service also accepts Apache Parquet, JSON arrays, and CSV. Upload both files to Amazon S3: uv run python make_dataset.py aws s3 cp training-data.jsonl s3://
/wordle-mtrl/train/ aws s3 cp validation-data.jsonl s3://
/wordle-mtrl/validation/ Because the service never inspects the prompt string, a production task can pack a full message list, tool configuration, or reward specification into it. See the MTRL documentation for examples, including how to protect sensitive content in the string. Step 5: Launch the training job The launcher uses the MultiTurnRLTrainer class from the sagemaker-train SDK. Point it at the runtime ARN from Step 2, the role from Step 1, the datasets from Step 4, and an MLflow app for metrics. The MLflow app is required, so if you don’t have one, create it first with aws sagemaker create-mlflow-app : uv run python run_mtrl_training.py \ --model openai-reasoning-gpt-oss-20b \ --agent-runtime-arn
\ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::
:role/
\ --train-dataset s3://
/wordle-mtrl/train/training-data.jsonl \ --val-dataset s3://
/wordle-mtrl/validation/validation-data.jsonl \ --s3-output-path s3://
/wordle-mtrl/output/ \ --mlflow-app-arn arn:aws:sagemaker:
:
:mlflow-app/
The launcher overrides three hyperparameters and leaves every other one at the gpt-oss-20b default. It sets sampling_max_tokens to 8192, the service maximum, because at the default of 4096 gpt-oss often ran out of tokens while reasoning, before its first tool call. It sets max_epochs to 20 and max_steps to 100: 640 rows at the default global_batch_size of 128 is 5 steps per epoch, and with the default group_size of 8, each step plays 1,024 games. The job moves through Starting, Downloading, and Pending before reaching Training. After it’s training, your AgentCore runtime begins receiving rollout invocations. Important: Don’t redeploy the agent while a job is running. Redeploying restarts the runtime, in-flight rollouts see no sampling requests, and the service fails the entire job. Step 6: Monitor training in MLflow The service logs reward, token, and turn statistics at every step and runs validation every val_every steps. The metric to watch is val/reward/pass_at_1 , the fraction of held-out words solved. Every solve scores at least 1.01, so it clears the service’s success_threshold of 1.0 and pass@1 counts it. The following chart is built from this run’s MLflow history: Figure 4: Training curves for the 100-step run, with mean reward per game on the left and validation solve rate on the right Training reward climbs to about +0.57 within 15 steps and holds there. Validation reward stays lower, mostly because of temperature 1.0 versus 0 rather than overfitting (see Step 7). The validation solve rate jumps from 2 to 31 percent in the first 10 steps, then moves between 35 and 48 percent. With 128 words, those swings are mostly noise. We did not test whether more steps help at serving settings. The runtime’s OpenTelemetry traces in CloudWatch record every model turn and tool call. Here is one game the trained model played during an evaluation job (medium effort, temperature 1.0), with the reasoning trimmed. The secret word was PASTE: [model] Reasoning: [...] "CRANE" has 5 distinct letters: C,R,A,N,E. [...] We'll guess "CRANE". Tool call: guess_word(guess="CRANE") [tool] Guess 1/6: CRANE -> C=gray, R=gray, A=yellow, N=gray, E=green Current Knowledge: - Correct Position (Green): _ _ _ _ E - In Word, Wrong Position (Yellow): 'A' (at least 1) - Not in Word (Gray): C, N, R - Guesses Remaining: 5 [model] Reasoning: [...] "ALIVE": ends with E, includes A. Letters not C,N,R. Tool call: guess_word(guess="ALIVE") [tool] Guess 2/6: ALIVE -> A=yellow, L=gray, I=gray, V=gray, E=green [model] Reasoning: [...] So positions not 1 or 3 for A. Positions left: 2,4 for A. [...] We might guess "HASTE"? [...] Tool call: guess_word(guess="HASTE") [tool] Guess 3/6: HASTE -> H=gray, A=green, S=green, T=green, E=green [model] Reasoning: We have the word: _ASTE. [...] "PASTE" is a word. PASTE fits. Also "WASTE" also fits [...] Choose "PASTE" maybe. Tool call: guess_word(guess="PASTE") [tool] Guess 4/6: PASTE --- all green. Correct, you solved it! A trained-model rollout from the AgentCore runtime traces. The model keeps green letters in place, never reuses a gray letter, and uses each yellow letter to rule out positions, though nothing in the training data showed it how. Step 7: Evaluate the trained model at serving settings When the job completes, its page in SageMaker AI Studio shows the status and the model package group that holds the trained model. DescribeJob , with JobCategory set to AgentRFT , returns the output model package ARN and the billable token counts. Figure 5: The completed training job in SageMaker AI Studio on the Jobs, Training, Multi-turn RL tab An evaluation job ( JobCategory set to AgentRFTEvaluation ) plays your evaluation prompts through the same AgentCore runtime and reward, on the base model or the trained package, and logs eval/reward/pass_at_1 to MLflow. Unlike training validation, you can set the temperature. The repository’s launcher runs evaluations back to back, because the default quota allows one evaluation job at a time ( you can request an increase ): uv run python run_mtrl_eval.py --runs base:1.0 trained:1.0 \ --model-package-arn
\ --agent-runtime-arn
\ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::
:role/
\ --dataset s3://
/wordle-mtrl/validation/validation-data.jsonl \ --s3-output-path s3://
/wordle-mtrl/eval/ \ --mlflow-app-arn arn:aws:sagemaker:
:
:mlflow-app/
Figure 6: Reasoning effort and sampling temperature at each stage, where the training job fixes validation at temperature 0 and the deployed effort while evaluation jobs let you choose Each 128-word evaluation took four to seven minutes. Reasoning effort comes from the agent’s environment variables, so to change it you edit REASONING_EFFORT , redeploy, and evaluate. We evaluated both models at low and medium effort and at temperature 0 and 1.0: Figure 7: Base model versus trained model under four decoding settings, with solve rate on the left and mean reward per game on the right The gray segment of each bar is the base model and the blue segment is the gain from training. The low-effort, temperature-0 pair is the training job’s validation at steps 0 and 100. The medium-effort, temperature-1.0 trained result is the mean of two runs (80 and 88 percent). At temperature 0, both models often end the game without a solve, at either effort. With sampling on, medium effort adds 15 points for the trained model and 46 for the base model. The adapter adds 14–54 points in every setting, so what training taught transfers across settings. The training job’s own validation curve in MLflow told a different story: it peaked at 48 percent at step 90 and ended at 37 percent, scored at temperature 0. The hyperparameters reference recommends temperature 0 for evaluation because greedy decoding makes curves deterministic and comparable across runs. We report temperature 1.0 because that’s how we serve the model. At medium effort and temperature 1.0, the trained model solves 84 percent of held-out words, up from 61 percent for the base model. Tip: Evaluate at the settings you will serve at. The training curve says this adapter ends at 37 percent. At serving settings it solves 84 percent. The evaluation jobs that show this cost about $1.20 in tokens and took about an hour. Step 8: Clean up Training and evaluation jobs stop billing when they complete, but the AgentCore runtime, its IAM role, the MLflow app, and the S3 objects persist. From the project directory: # 1. Agent runtime and its execution role. remove all resets the project config; # the next deploy sees the empty state and tears down the deployed resources. cd sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle/Wordle agentcore remove all agentcore deploy # 2. MLflow app aws sagemaker delete-mlflow-app --arn arn:aws:sagemaker:
:
:mlflow-app/
# 3. Datasets, job output, and evaluation output aws s3 rm s3://
/wordle-mtrl/ --recursive Because agentcore remove all rewrites the files under agentcore/ , run git checkout -- agentcore/ if you want to redeploy later. Deleting the AgentCore-Wordle-default CloudFormation stack removes the same resources and leaves the files alone. The training job role and the model packages are not billed. Deep dive: Designing the reward Our reward needed one revision, and the mistake is a common one. The first design summed the per-guess scoring from the wordle-lora-rl project over the whole game. That scoring works there because each guess is an independent training sample. Summed into one reward per game, it produced two inversions we found only by reading traces: A lost game paid positive reward. Six turns of bonuses added up to about +0.49. Solving on turn 1 scored below solving on turn 3. A first-guess solve earned +0.99 and a third-guess solve earned +1.61, because the extra turns collected more bonuses. The fix separates a dominant outcome term from a small, bounded shaping term: reward = outcome + w * clip(shaping, -1, 1), w = 0.04 if solved, else 0.15 The outcome term is set entirely by how the game ended: Outcome Value Solved on guess n 1.05 + 0.5 * (6 – n) / 5, so 1.55 on guess 1 down to 1.05 on guess 6 Played all six guesses, unsolved -0.5 Never made a valid guess -1.5 The shaping term is that per-guess scoring, summed over the game: Penalties for contradicting a known green, yellow, or gray letter, for repeating a guess, and for words outside the dictionary. An entropy bonus for a strong opening word. Bonuses for trying new letters and for shrinking the set of remaining possibilities. The sum is clipped to [-1, 1] and scaled by 0.04 for a solve and 0.15 for a loss, so it separates games with the same outcome but never moves a game into another tier. With typical shaping values: Scenario Reward Solve on guess 1 +1.550 Solve on guess 3 +1.375 Solve on guess 6 +1.069 Lost after six guesses -0.427 Never made a valid guess -1.500 A faster solve now always beats a slower one, every solve beats every loss, and never playing is the worst outcome. Our first fix used a single weight of 0.15, which let a guess-3 solve with full shaping (+1.45) outscore a guess-2 solve with the minimum (+1.25). Adjacent guess counts are 0.1 apart, so a smaller solve weight of 0.04 removes the overlap, and the worst solve (+1.01) still clears the 1.0 success threshold. Shaping still matters because GRPO learns from reward variance within a group, so two lost games that differ in clue consistency still teach the model something. As the SageMaker AI documentation advises, start with an outcome-based reward, add shaping sparingly, and check the reward on real trajectories. Deep dive: What went wrong, in the order you will hit it Each of these cost at least one training run. Bearer tokens under concurrency. Minting a token with a fresh botocore session per call starved the credential provider at 32 concurrent rollouts, and caching tokens for an hour returned 403 errors as credentials rotated. The fix is one self-refreshing session, a short cache, and a re-sign on 403. A rollout that never reaches the policy model fails the whole job. When every model call in a rollout failed authentication, the service ended the job with “No sampling requests were received.” Returning an error status fails it too, so always return a reward. A game where the model is sampled but never makes a valid guess is fine: it scores -1.5, and the 100-step run had 51 of them in about 105,000 rollouts. Tool calls drift into plain text. At too high a learning rate, the model wrote tool calls as text, every rollout got the same floor reward, and the gradient vanished. The agent now recovers guesses from raw text with a small formatting penalty. The plateau. Training reward stopped rising after about step 15 and validation stopped improving after about step 30, though at temperature 0 validation understates the model (Step 7). A curriculum that seeds games with prior guesses, or more rollouts per word than the default group_size of 8, is what we would try next. Conclusion MTRL on SageMaker AI trains a model on the outcome of a whole episode. That fits agentic tasks, where the right trajectory is unknown and only the result can be scored. We used a single episode-level reward. When intermediate steps can be scored too, MTRL also accepts one reward per turn through the UpdateReward API . In this post, an open-weight 20B model reached an 84 percent solve rate at serving settings, up from 61 percent, for about $339 in training tokens and about $79 in AgentCore runtime usage. The 37 percent the training curve reports is an artifact of how the training job scores validation, so evaluate at the settings you will serve at. The same pipeline applies to internal procedures, tools, and workflows that public models were never trained on. To get started, clone the sample repository , follow the preceding steps, and run the smoke test in Step 3 before committing GPU time. For the underlying APIs, see the SageMaker AI MTRL documentation . He holds a PhD in Computer Science from the University of California, Irvine, with a research focus on machine learning and bioinformatics. Hadrien Almela Hadrien is a Senior Frontier AI Account Manager in the AWS Startup team, helping top AI startups build technical integrations and global go-to-market (GTM) partnerships. He has eight years of experience in the startup landscape. Vinay Bhat Vinay is the Head of Solutions Architecture for Frontier AI at AWS, where he leads a team of technologists helping foundation model labs and AI-native startups build, train, and scale their models and applications on AWS. He brings more than 20 years of experience building technical teams across AWS, Google Cloud, and high-growth startups.

title: Austria orders expulsion of four Russian diplomats suspected of spying
body: Austria will expel four Russian diplomats suspected of spying. Three worked at the Russian Embassy in Vienna and the fourth at Russia’s mission to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). Austria’s Foreign Ministry said the diplomats “have engaged in activities incompatible with their diplomatic status” and had therefore been declared personae non gratae. Austrian authorities have long known about all four diplomats and have kept them on internal lists of suspects for some time, Profil magazine reported. An inquiry began in mid-August after the news outlet Proekt reported on ties between Russian diplomats in Europe and three Russian intelligence agencies: military intelligence (the GRU), the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), and the Federal Security Service (FSB). Austria previously expelled three Russian Embassy employees in May on suspicion of maintaining spying equipment. Profil reported that satellite dishes Russia could use to intercept communications traffic had been found on the embassy’s roof. title: US senator probes Tether after reported deal with ex-Trump crypto adviser
body:
The Democratic ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations asked Paolo Ardoino for records related to a reported deal between Tether and Nxum.
Update (Oct. 23, 6:27 pm UTC): This article has been updated to include a response from Tether.
Senator Richard Blumenthal has requested information from Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino after a Wall Street Journal report said that the stablecoin issuer had inked a $6.3 million deal with a marketing company co-founded by former White House crypto adviser Bo Hines.
In a Thursday letter to Ardoino, the Connecticut lawmaker said that the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations demanded “records and information related to contracts, payments, communications, and lobbying” between Tether and Nxum, Hines’ company. The probe into Nxum, Tether and Hines, according to Blumental, was part of what the senator called the Trump administration’s “self-enrichment and self-dealings with cryptocurrency firms.”
“While Hines failed to divest his one-third stake in Nxum [...] he worked closely over encrypted messaging applications with Nxum to coordinate lobbying, advocacy, and browbeating of members of Congress that were opposed to, or had sought changes to, pending stablecoin legislation,” said Blumenthal. “Those messages also reportedly demonstrate that Tether was directly coordinating Nxum’s lobbying efforts on the GENIUS Act which would regulate stablecoins, with CEO Paolo Ardoino demanding that Nxum ‘obliterate’ the legislation’s opponents.”
Hines worked as executive director as President’s Council of Advisers on Digital Assets from January to August 2025, when he left the White House to join Tether as a “strategic adviser.” He later became CEO of Tether US. Harry Jung, another crypto adviser in the Trump administration, left his position in July 2026 and joined Nxum as a managing director in August.
A Tether spokesperson told Cointelegraph that the company was aware of the allegations and an external counsel ”found no evidence of wrongdoing” after a previous ”in-depth internal investigation into the matter.”
Related: Trump didn‘t mention ‘crypto’ once in White House cybercrime roundtable
Trump, his family and members of his administration continue to face scrutiny over accusations that they are reaping financial windfalls from crypto policies on laws over which they have control or influence. The president disclosed earning $1.4 billion from investments related to crypto in 2025.
While Blumenthal has limited authority as the Democratic ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, the results of the 2026 midterm elections could potentially change party control in the House of Representatives and Senate. This could give the Connecticut lawmaker and other Democratic additional authority to conduct investigations into Trump and his administration’s ties to the crypto industry, including those which could present conflicts of interest.
As of Friday, event contracts on prediction market platforms Kalshi and Polymarket favored Democrats retaking majority control of both chambers of Congress in 2027, with 92% and 68% chances on Kalshi for the House and Senate, respectively. US Election Day is on Nov. 3.

title: What if Flávio Bolsonaro wins? High stakes for the environment in Brazil’s 2026 elections (commentary)
body: Fear and disbelief prevail among those in Brazil who are concerned about the environment. A climate denier and voluble supporter of dismantling Brazil’s environmental agencies may well be the country`s next president. Brazil’s current president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (known simply as “Lula”) faces Flávio Bolsonaro, one of former president Jair Bolsonaro’s sons. In the first round of the election on October 4th neither reached the required 50% plus one vote needed, and they face each other in a runoff on October 25th. Flávio was two percentage points ahead for valid votes in a poll released on October 21st, although one poll released on October 18th showed Lula ahead by two points. Flávio’s father Jair Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 term was an environmental disaster, and Flávio frequently claims that his father was the best president Brazil has ever had and that, if elected, he will bring back his father’s policies. Under Jair Bolsonaro the annual deforestation rate in the Amazon rose sharply, peaking in 2021. He made good on his promise not to demarcate “a single centimeter” of Indigenous land. He appointed openly anti-environmental figures to head the Ministry of the Environment and IBAMA (the Brazilian Institute for the Environment and Renewable Natural Resources), who largely dismantled these agencies and blocked enforcement of environmental laws. Jair Bolsonaro’s constant rhetoric supporting illegal loggers, goldminers and deforesters resulted in surges of these activities, including in Indigenous areas. Most notorious was the invasion of the Yanomami Indigenous Land by over 20,000 goldminers who converted…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: Canada-Türkiye Strategic Partnership Includes Defence MOU
body: The world is changing rapidly. Global trade is being rewired and the institutions that underpinned our security for decades are under threat. In response, Canada is focused on what we can control: building our strength at home and deeper partnerships with reliable partners abroad to create greater certainty, security, and prosperity for Canadians. As a NATO Ally and G20 member, Türkiye is a critical partner in this mission, and one with significant untapped potential. Türkiye is one of the world’s most dynamic economies, with a market of more than 85 million people. It sits at the crossroads of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, with a network of 24 free trade agreements. It has NATO’s second-largest standing military and one of the world’s most important and innovative defence industries. To deepen the Canada-Türkiye partnership, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, concluded a successful visit to Ankara and Istanbul. This historic occasion marked the first bilateral visit to Türkiye by a Canadian Prime Minister, opening a new chapter in the relationship between our two countries. In Ankara, Prime Minister Carney met with the President of Türkiye, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, to launch an ambitious Canada-Türkiye Strategic Partnership . Supported by a three-year action plan , this partnership will deepen cooperation in key areas, including trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and people-to-people ties. On trade and investment, the leaders announced that the first round of negotiations toward a comprehensive free trade agreement (FTA) will take place from November 30 to December 4, 2026, in Ankara. Trade between Canada and Türkiye has grown by almost 50% since 2020, but this has only begun to realise the full potential of the relationship. An FTA will build on that momentum and open new doors for Canadian businesses. To further unlock new opportunities for trade and investment, Export Development Canada and Türk Eximbank signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to cooperate on projects in third countries. The MOU will help Canadian and Turkish companies team up on projects in international markets across a range of sectors. In Istanbul, Prime Minister Carney met with Turkish business leaders and investors to build on this momentum and further catalyse investment in Canada’s energy, mining, aerospace, and defence industries. To seize these opportunities, the Prime Minister announced a Canadian trade mission to Türkiye in 2027 , to be led by the Minister of International Trade. As NATO Allies, Canada and Türkiye deepened collaboration in defence, announcing a new MOU on defence sector partnerships. This agreement will connect Canadian and Turkish companies so they can build together, creating good jobs at home, export opportunities abroad, greater security for Canadians, and a stronger NATO Alliance. On energy, Canada and Türkiye signed a joint statement to strengthen cooperation in LNG, civil nuclear and renewable energy, and critical minerals. This will facilitate investment in major energy and resource projects, strengthen supply chains, and build greater energy security and economic resilience in both countries. Beyond trade, energy, and defence, the Strategic Partnership will also deepen people-to-people ties between Canada and Türkiye. To that end, the two countries signed the recently expanded Air Transport Agreement , which increases weekly passenger flights from 12 to up to 21 and allows unlimited cargo flights between Canadian and Turkish airports. This agreement will make travel easier and more affordable for families visiting loved ones, for students, and for tourists. It will also create new opportunities for Canadian exporters to Türkiye and the markets beyond. At this pivotal moment, Canada and Türkiye are launching a broader, deeper partnership – opening new markets, strengthening our defence industries, powering our economies, and bringing our people closer together. Together, we are building a more secure, resilient, and prosperous future. “In a rapidly changing world, Canada is diversifying our trade and building stronger partnerships to create greater security and prosperity for Canadians. Türkiye, a NATO Ally, a G20 economy, and a gateway to Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, is an essential partner in that work. Our new Strategic Partnership will open new markets for Canadian businesses, connect our defence industries, and strengthen our energy security, creating good jobs for Canadian workers. This is a new chapter in our partnership, and we are only beginning to realise its potential.” — The Rt. Hon. Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada ADDITIONAL INFO Prime Minister Carney was accompanied on this visit by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Anita Anand, and the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Tim Hodgson. This visit builds on earlier engagements undertaken this past year to advance cooperation between Canada and Türkiye, including on trade and defence: In July 2026, on the margins of the NATO Summit in Ankara, Prime Minister Carney and President Erdoğan announced the launch of negotiations toward a comprehensive Canada-Türkiye FTA. Public consultations in Canada on this agreement concluded last month. In July 2026, the two countries also signed a Statement of Intent on Defence Cooperation. This arrangement establishes a framework to expand collaboration in areas of mutual interest, including military-to-military dialogue, operational support, and defence industrial collaboration. Canada and Türkiye will continue to deepen their cooperation on climate-related priorities, including electrification and methane emissions reduction, ahead of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), which Türkiye will host in Antalya next month. Prime Minister Carney expressed Canada’s full support for Türkiye’s COP31 Presidency. The Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Julie Aviva Dabrusin, will represent Canada at the conference. Canada and Türkiye are NATO Allies with longstanding diplomatic relations dating back to 1944. Both countries work closely together on today’s most pressing global challenges through a number of multilateral forums, including the United Nations, the G20, the International Energy Agency, the International Civil Aviation Organization, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe. The expanded Canada-Türkiye Air Transport Agreement allows unlimited access to all points in each country, up to 21 weekly passenger-combination flights per country, and unlimited weekly all-cargo flights. Two-way merchandise trade between Canada and Türkiye reached $4.3 billion in 2025, including $1.1 billion in Canadian exports and $3.2 billion in imports from Türkiye. The post Canada-Türkiye Strategic Partnership Includes Defence MOU appeared first on Canadian Defence Review .

title: Cyprus police investigate Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich for possible tax evasion after reports implicate accounting giant Deloitte
body: Police in Cyprus have launched an investigation into reports that Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich may have evaded taxes with help from the accounting firm Deloitte. A Cypriot Justice Ministry official told a parliamentary committee meeting on combating money laundering that the investigation was underway, the BBC reported. The police financial crime unit is conducting the investigation. “We will look at any company or person who may be involved. We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated,” Cypriot police spokesman Andreas Anastasiades told the BBC. The BBC, The Guardian, and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ) previously published investigations reporting that Deloitte, one of the world’s largest consulting and accounting firms, helped falsify documents to conceal Abramovich’s wealth and help him evade taxes. According to the journalists, Deloitte’s Cyprus division helped him conceal $672 million in assets, including mansions, yachts, and private jets. Abramovich’s lawyers denied any wrongdoing. Deloitte Cyprus said it had always complied with local laws. title: Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
body:
Last week, Starshield — the version of SpaceX’s Starlink used by the Ukrainian military — was throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds from accessing the service. The Ukrainian army’s interceptors, which counter Russian drones carrying bombs, suddenly stopped working at high speeds, making it easier for Russia to attack the country’s energy infrastructure and leading to a reported two deaths and at least 17 injuries.
The Ukrainian military reported receiving no advance warning about the Starshield speed restriction. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was a direct message from the US amid rising tensions between himself and President Donald Trump. The abrupt nature of the cutoff and its potentially dangerous military and humanitarian ramifications led to widespread public outcry focused both on Trump for pulling the rug out from under Ukraine and on SpaceX CEO Elon Musk for enabling him.
Since then Musk and Trump have traded denials back and forth. Musk first said that SpaceX has no control over Starshield and decisions are made by the US military, while the White House denied taking action. Then reports emerged that Musk was the one who suggested the slowdown tactic to Trump, who then accepted it, followed by a further report that Musk himself unilaterally ordered the restrictions.
The finger-pointing is of little interest to Ukrainians, who are focused on trying to defend their country from a brutal ongoing Russian invasion. Zelenskyy is well aware that he is being used as a scapegoat as Trump flails around attempting to blame Ukraine for the rising oil prices caused by his unpopular war with Iran.
But Ukraine needs to play nice to some extent, given how dependent it is on US technologies like Starlink/Starshield that enable it to mount a defense against Russian attacks. Starlink access has been deliberately restricted there before, including in 2022, when coverage was not extended to cover a counterattack operation in Crimea. If Musk decided to pull the plug completely, the effect on Ukraine could be devastating.
This amount of geopolitical power being wielded by an unelected tech oligarch is the direct result of consolidating so much of the space industry into just one company, and one man’s hands. And the scope of Musk’s control goes well beyond Ukraine. From the defense of nations to the ability of NASA to launch its astronauts into space, SpaceX has been irreplaceable — and that means Musk has the space industry in his grip.
A de facto monopoly
SpaceX’s recent IPO positions it as one of the most valuable companies in the world. And while the company has generated most of its recent revenue from its Starlink service, it made its name as a company that launches rockets into space.
SpaceX’s Falcon 9 is the most successful rocket in history, and its “rideshare” program, which lets small satellite operators share space on a rocket, has dropped the price of launches to historic lows. This has helped organizations from small startups to university research departments launch their own satellites and has been hailed as a democratizing force in the space industry.
However, that success has come at a cost, which is that SpaceX now holds all the cards when it comes to access to space.
“For all intents and purposes, SpaceX has a monopoly on launch right now,” said Wendy Whitman Cobb of the School of Advanced Air and Space Studies at Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama. “There are competitors out there,” she said, such as United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, and Rocket Lab, “but nobody comes even close to SpaceX in terms of frequency, mass, scale, cost. I mean, they’ve got everything in the bag.”
Space economist Oğuz Karasu of the Oxford Space Initiative concurred. SpaceX doesn’t have a monopoly on launch in the legal sense, he said, but in practical terms it does. And that gives the company tremendous pull over the industry as a whole.
“The rocket launch industry is around 8 percent of the entire [space] industry,” Karasu said, “but without that 8 percent, you can’t have the rest of it.”
The gatekeeper for space
SpaceX, which didn’t respond to a request for comment, has a tremendous advantage in providing space-based services like satellite internet. The company has been able to build out its network of over 10,000 Starlink satellites currently in low Earth orbit by launching them cheaply and efficiently using its Falcon 9 rockets.
“This is almost like an antitrust issue,” said defense expert Andrew Reddie of the University of California, Berkeley. “The issue is that SpaceX launches support Starlink constellations that are owned by SpaceX. There is no incentive for a SpaceX launch to be used to provide constellations for other countries that would compete.”
Interestingly, SpaceX has previously launched Amazon Kuiper (now Leo) satellites on a handful of missions — arguably as a preemptive defense against antitrust complaints. Or perhaps SpaceX is simply so confident in its position that it can afford to be magnanimous (or to flex a little on its rival) by launching a few competitor satellites.
The downside of a monopoly, at least for the customer, is that eventually prices rise.
SpaceX doesn’t share prices for its launches publicly, but both Whitman Cobb and Karasu say they’ve heard complaints that Falcon 9 launches are getting more expensive, particularly for low Earth orbit deployments. And the Starlink service has seen considerable increases in price since its beta launch in 2020.
Of course, there are plenty of reasons for a company to increase its prices, from inflation to rising costs, but when a company has enormous market dominance (and now shareholders to please) there isn’t much incentive against raising prices to increase profits.
If this business model sounds familiar, it’s because it’s one of Silicon Valley’s favorite and most destructive tactics. Uber perfected the art of predatory pricing, whereby investor cash is used to artificially lower prices so that a company can corner a market and push out competition. Then, with the monopoly safely in place, the company can jack up its prices and lower the quality of its product or service, secure in the knowledge that customers no longer have any other viable alternatives.
The unseen power of space
This might sound like an obscure problem, something that might make life more difficult for a few high-tech operations but has little relevance to the day-to-day lives of most people. But space infrastructure is now embedded in the mechanisms of our most essential technologies, in the form of satellite communications and GPS data.
“If GPS goes down, you’re not going to be able to get gas at the gas pump, you’re not going to be able to get money out of the ATM,” said Whitman Cobb, “let alone not be able to do financial transactions or get an ambulance to the right place on time.”
It’s not that space experts are realistically worried that Elon Musk is going to lose his mind and cut off Starlink access worldwide, or cause a collision that could take down GPS. It’s that the space industry is woven, unseen, into so many parts of our everyday lives that allowing one company or one person to control access to space hands them enormous power.
“All of our current economic activities are based on space technologies right now,” said Karasu. “Giving this much control, or this much power, to one person is not good for society’s future.”
Even huge agencies like NASA and the Space Force face risks from being too dependent on SpaceX. With the company deciding to retire its workhorse and extremely reliable Falcon 9 rocket, reportedly not taking any new missions from 2028, the Space Force is struggling to find launch options for its military satellites, and NASA now faces a potential future in which it doesn’t have access to the Crew Dragon capsule for carrying its astronauts to and from the International Space Station.
History has shown the dangers of having only one launch option. After the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003, which cost the lives of seven astronauts, the entire program was canceled and no humans were launched into space from the US from 2011 until 2020.
That’s why NASA is continuing to support beleaguered Boeing in its slow and troubled development of the Starliner capsule, because dependence on a single launch provider means putting all of your very expensive and delicate eggs into one precarious basket. That was demonstrated in February this year, when issues with the usually rock-solid reliability of the Falcon 9 temporarily grounded it, leading to concerns that NASA’s launch of the Crew-12 mission to the space station could be delayed.
This was a timely reminder that even the most impressive and reliable of technologies — and, to be clear, the Falcon 9 is both an incredible feat of engineering and outstandingly successful — can have failures or outages. NASA continues to contract with smaller companies like Rocket Lab and Blue Origin, and has repeatedly stressed its desire to have multiple commercial providers for services like transporting astronauts to the space station.
“Even NASA is realizing, okay, we are putting all our bets on a single player,” said space business expert Michele Scataglini of the Oxford Space Initiative and University of Oxford. “The market needs to have more competition, otherwise it’s not a market.”
Whether any of these companies will be able to catch up and provide a meaningful, affordable alternative to SpaceX remains to be seen. It will be hard for any company to keep pace with SpaceX’s sister companies developing complementary technologies as well.
“The complementarity of the assets that SpaceX has built — artificial intelligence, the batteries, the launch capabilities — these are all self-reinforcing capabilities for the firm, that I would say none of the other players alone possesses,” said Scataglini.
Too much power in too few hands
For now, with Starlink access restored in Ukraine, the country will continue to walk the tightrope of trying to defend itself using technology it does not ultimately control. Unlike previous restrictions of Starlink usage there, which were arguably more about limiting offensive capabilities, “what seems to have been impacted in this most recent episode is Ukrainian defensive capability,” said Reddie, the defense expert. “And then you end up with all the harrowing images of apartment blocks on fire and people getting pulled out of the buildings.
“And so that’s the major security challenge, that you’ve effectively got a non-state actor making decisions as if they’re a government.”
Scataglini concurred, describing the events in Ukraine as a global wake-up call. “There’s a single entrepreneur that has more power than governments in deciding how strategic defense capabilities can be used,” he said.
In times of stress and uncertainty — and between ever-climbing costs of living, a decimated social safety net, fears about AI coming for our jobs, and rising global populism and extremism, there’s plenty to be stressed and uncertain about — it is tempting to turn our gazes inward, to look out for our own interests and prioritize the needs of our own nations.
But space does not respect national boundaries, and what happens in orbit around our planet affects us all. The risk, Scataglini said, is that “we are moving into one firm dominating the launch market and deciding who goes up, and who doesn’t. Which country has access to space, and which one does not, because not all nations around the world, especially if you think about the Global South, will have easy access to these capabilities.”
Looking to the future, experts hoped that out of the brutal events in Ukraine could come more public awareness of the dangers of too much power held in too few hands.
“I’m cautiously optimistic that, at least in this case in particular, it is highlighting the dangers of being reliant on a single company, a single individual,” said Whitman Cobb. “It took something bad happening — people dying — for people to realize, oh, wait, maybe there’s a problem here.”

title: Russian anti-war rock musician Andrey Makarevich endorses Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of election, drawing backlash
body: Israel will hold parliamentary elections on October 27. Recent opinion polls show Likud, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, trailing Yashar, the party led by former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot. Neither party has a decisive lead, however. A few days before the election, Netanyahu posted a recording of a conversation with musician Andrey Makarevich, who has lived in Israel for the past several years. Makarevich, who holds both Israeli and Russian citizenship, expressed support for Netanyahu during the conversation. Many people in Israel and beyond were unhappy with Makarevich’s support for Netanyahu, who divides opinion among Israelis. Some Israelis are dissatisfied with the prime minister’s domestic policies, as well as his government’s actions before, during, and after the Hamas terrorist attack on October 7, 2023. “Wow, what a storm this has stirred up! A typhoon! A tsunami!” Makarevich wrote on social media. Critics noted that the musician had supported Vladimir Putin in the early 2000s and that in 2008, his band, Mashina Vremeni, had taken part in the “Forward, Russia!” rally and concert on Moscow’s Vasilyevsky Spusk to celebrate Dmitry Medvedev’s presidential election victory. Makarevich later publicly criticized the Russian authorities on many occasions. In 2022, the musician, who spoke out against the war with Ukraine, was designated a “foreign agent” in Russia. “God, what an absolute disgrace,” blogger Rustem Adagamov wrote , pointing out that the International Criminal Court had issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu and that the prime minister faces corruption charges in Israel. Adagamov stressed that Makarevich had “spent years condemning the crimes of Putin’s regime, Russian aggression, and the killing of civilians,” but was now “having a friendly chat with a politician accused of extremely serious international crimes,” helping him “build a favorable public image.” “This isn’t about principles anymore — it’s hypocrisy and double standards,” the blogger wrote. Some users on Facebook, where Makarevich’s conversation with Netanyahu has drawn the most discussion, supported the musician, saying that “everyone has the right to freedom of speech and freedom of choice.” Makarevich responded to the comments: Once again, my opponents have proved that their emotions run about a hundred times stronger than their brains — assuming they have any — and that they can outdo even the worst Kremlin trolls when it comes to being obnoxious. Pretty much what I expected. Building politics in our country around those attitudes is a bad idea. Take my word for it. I reserve the right to think what I think and say what I say. Enjoy the elections. title: Air Purifiers as White Noise Machines
body:
Instead of spinning a fan in free air to make noise, you can have it pull air through a filter. A small purifier sounds a lot like a classic noise machine, is only a bit larger and more expensive, and removes smoke and infectious particles from the air. For example, here's a $47 purifier with a 6.5" diameter, cleaning 34 cubic feet of air per minute ("CADR") at 45dB. For most circumstances where someone would use a white noise machine, this kind of small purifier is all-around better.
Now, 34 CFM is not very much air cleaning. I usually run an AirFanta 3Pro and it cleans ~6x more air for the same amount of noise, or ~12x more air with much more noise (~56dB). On the other hand it's more expensive ($165) and bulkier (12.6" square), and arguably uglier.
Still, even a 34 CFM purifier helps a lot with smoke. If you have a 10ft square room with an 8ft ceiling and a reasonably typical 0.5 air changes per hour through leakage from outdoors, this small purifier will cut particulate levels to 16% of the outdoor level. In AQI terms (not linear) this is like going from AQI 200 to 72 or AQI 100 to 31.

title: Northrop Grumman CEO says factory expansion will increase B-21 Raider bomber production
body: “We will be investing in that acceleration capacity over the next couple of years and then expect to see the translation into higher volume later in the decade,” Warden told analysts on October 20. She said sustainment and modernization work would also contribute to the program’s growth. Chief Financial Officer John Greene said Northrop expects companywide capital expenditures of approximately $2.1 billion in 2027, equivalent to about 4.5% of sales. That spending includes the capacity needed to support a higher B-21 production rate. The company expects stronger operating performance, working capital management and tax optimization to offset the additional capital spending associated with B-21 acceleration. It maintained its forecast for adjusted free cash flow of $3.3 billion to $3.7 billion in 2027. Warden said B-21 testing and production would increase in 2027 while the company invests in the longer-term expansion. Work on supporting and upgrading the aircraft is also developing alongside manufacturing. “We have sustainment starting to come into the program,” Warden said. “We also have modernization that is ongoing in the program.” Asked whether Northrop faced further charges on its fixed-price, low-rate initial production contracts, Warden said the aircraft was meeting key performance parameters during testing. Successful tests were reducing the risk of discovering problems late in development, she said, while manufacturing experience was improving production performance. “The program is performing very well,” Warden said. She nevertheless acknowledged that risk remained while Northrop completes its outstanding low-rate initial production aircraft. Greene said the continued B-21 production ramp contributed to higher sales in Northrop’s strike aircraft portfolio during the third quarter. He expects the bomber to support further growth in the Aeronautics Systems business in 2027, although its increasing share of sales will put some pressure on the division’s operating margin.

title: Texas Senate race: New Talarico ad rips Elon Musk 'dark money' push
body:
James Talarico 's campaign hit back at Elon Musk Thursday, calling the 2026 election cycle's top spender out for his cash infusion in the Texas Senate race amid an ongoing feud between the Democratic nominee and the world's richest man.
A video posted by the Talarico campaign's account on X Thursday of a new ad targets Musk for his record spending in favor of Republican nominee Ken Paxton, telling him "Texas is not for sale."
"Do you keep seeing these attack ads against James Talarico? Look a little closer. The same super PACs are paying for nearly all of them," the video's narrator intones. "But who's funding these dark money groups? Elon Musk."
"He's almost single-handedly bankrolling the effort to install Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate," the narrator continues.
"Elon wants to buy up our land, he wants to buy up our water, and now, he wants to buy his own personal U.S. senator. He knows that if his millions drag the most corrupt politician in Texas across the finish line, Ken Paxton will owe him everything."
The new ad dropped with less than two weeks until the midterm election and amid an ongoing feud between Talarico and Musk.
In a post Wednesday on X, Musk said, "There is something deeply wrong with James Talarico." And on Thursday, he wrote on X that "Talarico hates Texas and America" while reposting a video about voter-ID requirements.
Talarico fired back Wednesday, replying to the earlier post, "There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator."
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has spent around $366 million across 40 races so far in the midterms, based on CNBC's calculations, making Musk the largest individual donor of the cycle. Much of that spending is based in Texas, where he moved his corporate headquarters and personal primary residence.
At least $189.6 million of Musk's political spend has been, through various methods, in support of Paxton, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Texas and Talarico's opponent. An average of polls aggregated by FiftyPlusOne show Talarico with a 3-percentage-point advantage over Paxton as of Oct. 23.

title: Arab and international leaders condemn deadly funeral attack at church in Jordan
body: Regional and international leaders have condemned a shooting at a church in Jordan that killed eight people and injured 34, sending shockwaves across the kingdom. Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, expressed the Emirates' full solidarity with the kingdom during a phone call on Friday with Ayman Safadi, Jordan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates. He affirmed the UAE’s support for Jordan's measures to safeguard its security and stability and protect the safety of its citizens, residents and visitors. Sheikh Abdullah also extended his condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a speedy recovery. In a separate statement, the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs reiterated the country's strong condemnation of terrorist and criminal acts, reaffirming its rejection of all forms of violence, extremism and terrorism aimed at undermining security and stability. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah El Sisi expressed his "unequivocal condemnation of these heinous acts, which violate all human values" in a statement on X. He stressed his country's solidarity with Jordan "in confronting this deplorable attack and all forms of violence and terrorism". Saudi Arabia also condemned what it described as a "cowardly terrorist attack" in the strongest terms. It expressed its solidarity with Jordan and rejected all acts of terrorism aimed at undermining the country's security and stability, the kingdom's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said. Iraq condemned "all forms of terrorism and violence, which threaten the security and stability of societies and seek to sow division and incite discord among their communities". It also called for "enhanced regional and international co-operation and solidarity to combat terrorism and strengthen security and stability". Syria stressed its "unwavering support in confronting any threats to Jordan's security, stability and national unity", while rejecting "all forms of terrorism that threaten the safety and security of civilians", the Foreign Ministry said. Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun said the attack on a place of worship "violated the sanctity of death and mourners" and "all religious and humanitarian values". He said “terrorism has neither a religion nor a homeland" and warned that such actions sought to undermine co-existence and sow discord. Qatar said it rejected "violence, terrorism and criminal acts, regardless of their motives or causes", as well as "attacks on places of worship and the terrorisation of innocent people". Bahrain's Foreign Ministry affirmed its support for Jordan's efforts to "safeguard its security, combat terrorism and extremism, and apprehend those responsible for the attack". Oman and Kuwait also condemned attacks on "places of worship and acts that terrorise civilians", expressing solidarity with Jordan and extending condolences to the families of the victims. International reactions The US embassy in Amman said Washington stood with King Abdullah II against those seeking to sow division and harm people practising their faith. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney described the attack as a terrorist act and condemned the violence. Germany's Foreign Office expressed shock over the attack and emphasised the importance of protecting peaceful co-existence between religions. The EU condemned the "cruel attack" and offered its "full support to the ongoing security investigation by the Jordanian authorities". UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also strongly condemned the terrorist attack. "It goes without saying that an attack not only on a place of worship, but during a funeral procession is especially heinous," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. The shooting took place during a funeral at Hamoud Church in Karak governorate, where gunmen opened fire. Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said 27 of the injured were receiving treatment in hospitals, while security forces continued to search for the attackers. King Abdullah II described the incident as a terrorist attack and said the attack would be met with force. He vowed to crack down on those responsible and said the shooting would not undermine national unity. “Every Jordanian life is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation,” he said. Opened fire on mourners Gunmen arrived in a vehicle and opened fire on mourners before fleeing, a relative of one of the deceased told The National . They continued shooting for about five minutes, according to a witness quoted by Al Mamlaka TV. Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding that most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70. A video broadcast on Al Mamlaka that appeared to be from a security camera mounted on the church showed three people firing at it from a pavement and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. A member of the Halasah family in Karak told The National that three doctors were among those killed. “This was a direct attack on the church. Christians were the target,” the relative said.

title: Russia announces October 27 ceasefire on southern Ukraine’s Kherson front to evacuate residents of occupied Oleshky
body: Valery Gerasimov, chief of the Russian military’s General Staff, said Russian forces would cease fire on the Kherson front starting at 4 a.m. on October 27 for a humanitarian operation in Oleshky (Alyoshki in Russian). “To ensure people’s safety and deliver essential supplies, arrangements will be made to conduct engineering reconnaissance and provide safe passage for a humanitarian convoy into Alyoshki in the Kherson region,” Gerasimov said. On the afternoon of October 23, the White House said Russia and Ukraine would temporarily halt hostilities in Oleshky, in the Russian-occupied part of the Kherson region, so residents could leave the city safely. U.S. first lady Melania Trump was involved in reaching the agreement. The ceasefire was scheduled to begin on October 29, the White House said. Oleshky was occupied at the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. By the fall of 2026, conditions there had become dire — residents had no food, electricity, or adequate medical care. Civilians cannot leave the city safely. Pope Leo XIV also appealed to Russian President Vladimir Putin regarding the situation in Oleshky, calling in a phone call for a ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the safe, voluntary evacuation of residents. title: 6 Million Barrels in Two Minutes Draws CFTC Scrutiny
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
Oil traders sold futures equivalent to at least 6 million barrels of crude in just two minutes on March 23, shortly before President Donald Trump backed away from threats to strike Iranian power plants. Now, the federal regulator overseeing those trades says it has been looking into the activity.
Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael Selig said Friday that the agency's enforcement division has been examining oil trading during the Iran war, including the unusual surge preceding Trump's announcement.
"Our enforcement division has been looking at all these trades," Selig told Bloomberg Television. "We take this stuff very seriously."
The March 23 selling involved Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures. Trading volume during the two-minute window was more than 8.5 times the volume recorded during the same period over the preceding week, according to Bloomberg.
The timing has raised questions about whether some traders had advance knowledge of Trump's plans.
Oil markets have been particularly sensitive to presidential announcements since the Iran war began in February, with threats of military strikes and subsequent reversals capable of triggering sharp price swings.
The March 23 trades weren't the only unusual activity. Bloomberg previously reported several spikes in oil trading volumes ahead of major Trump announcements this spring, raising concerns about the possible use of nonpublic information.
Selig did not identify any traders involved or disclose whether investigators had uncovered evidence of wrongdoing.
"We are on top of this and, rest assured, people can have confidence in the markets as long as I'm in the seat," Selig said.
The CFTC chairman also addressed oversight of prediction markets, which the agency is monitoring for possible manipulation ahead of November's midterm elections. Selig expressed disappointment that Congress had failed to pass the Clarity Act, legislation addressing cryptocurrency regulation.
The CFTC has yet to announce any enforcement findings.
