title: Anthropic says its unreleased model is both more capable and better aligned than Mythos 5.1
body:
Anthropic has an internal model that outperforms Mythos 5.1 in both capability and alignment, according to an analysis that revisits a cybersecurity test by the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) . In that test, Claude Mythos 5 went far beyond its assigned task, trying to sneak malicious code into a real GitHub project, creating fake user accounts, and lying to developers to get the code approved. This happened in 9 of 43 runs. Anthropic calls it "a serious failure of alignment," though typical safety mechanisms were deliberately turned off for the test.
Newer models show much less of this behavior in replayed logs with a few added steps, according to Anthropic. Opus 5.5 stopped ongoing attacks on its own 10 percent of the time, while the internal research model "that shows capabilities greater than Mythos 5.1" did so in 67 percent of cases. Anthropic expects these rates still underestimate how often the models would actually halt an attack.

title: Tom Skerritt, Air Force veteran and ‘Top Gun’ star, dies at 93
body: Versatile actor and U.S. Air Force veteran Tom Skerritt, who starred in the war comedy M*A*S*H and the action drama Top Gun , has died at the age of 93. Skerritt, a Detroit native whose Hollywood career spanned from the 1960s to the 2020s, died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement. “While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” they said. “He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world, and helping others find and share their own voices.” Born on August 25, 1933, in Detroit, Skerritt served in the Air Force before becoming an actor, making his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Robert Redford in War Hunt . Tony Scott cast Skerritt in the key supporting role of naval aviation instructor Viper Metcalf in the 1986 blockbuster Top Gun that helped star Tom Cruise soar into Hollywood’s stratosphere. “Hollywood knew him as Viper. We remember him as an American Veteran. Rest in peace, U.S. Air Force Veteran Tom Skerritt,” Department of Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins wrote Friday on X. Known for his rugged good looks and ability to shine in a variety of genres, Skerritt delivered memorable performances in leading and supporting roles in film and television. Skerritt’s breakthrough role was a roguish U.S. Army surgeon in director Robert Altman’s 1970 Korean War black comedy M*A*S*H , a film whose ensemble cast also included Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman. Skerritt played Southerner Duke Forrest as the doctors at the Mobile Army Surgical Hospital who stitched up wounded troops. The film, whose popularity coincided with American unease over the Vietnam War, was nominated for five Academy Awards. In director Ridley Scott’s claustrophobic 1979 sci-fi horror Alien , Skerritt played Dallas, the captain of an ill-fated spacecraft whose crew encounters a deadly parasitic extraterrestrial creature with a surrealist look and a bad attitude. In the film’s famous and bloody “chestburster” scene, Skerritt’s character is seated next to cast mate John Hurt when a baby alien violently exits the torso of Hurt’s character. Alien , an influential masterpiece whose ensemble cast also included Sigourney Weaver and Ian Holm, earned two Oscar nominations. “It is spontaneity and impulse that make the difference, and that is what I felt we had with ‘Alien.’ Every one of us had that immediate rapport with each other — the respect that I had for the other actors and the respect that they had for me,” Skerritt told interviewer Peter Sobczynski in 2019, while also lauding Scott’s directorial brilliance. Alien was one of several films in which Skerritt appeared that featured strong female characters, in this case Weaver’s courageous character Ripley. That was considered pioneering at the time. “When I read the script, one of the things that I liked most about it was that the woman becomes the hero. I loved that,” Skerritt said. “The sight of women being in positions of strength and fortitude to make the right connections and decisions was what appealed to me. I experienced that as well in ‘Steel Magnolias,’ with the women in that. I liked the idea of women being tough and strong and influential.” In Steel Magnolias (1989), Skerritt played Drum Eatenton, husband of Sally Field’s M’Lynn Eatenton. Skerritt also played Shirley MacLaine’s husband in director Herbert Ross’s 1977 ballet drama The Turning Point , and starred alongside another emerging star in Brad Pitt in Redford’s beautifully shot 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It . Among other films in which he appeared were: Harold and Maude (1971), Ice Castles (1978), The Dead Zone (1983), Poltergeist III (1988), Contact (1997), Tears of the Sun (2003) and Ted (2012). On the small screen, Skerritt starred in the offbeat CBS series Picket Fences from 1992 to 1996, playing a Wisconsin town sheriff and claiming an Emmy as outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. He was a father of five children and was married three times.

title: A ‘super’ rebrand: Navy mandates dropping ‘artificial intelligence’
body: Artificial intelligence may one day destroy the human race, but if and when it does, there will be nothing artificial about it. In fact, it’ll be super. That is, at least, the proper terminology in this great American age of rebrands, one that has borne witness to such seismic overhauls as the Gulf of Mexico becoming the Gulf of America, Lake Ontario becoming Lake America, and a push to call New Mexico … New America. U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sept. 29 the term “artificial intelligence” would henceforth be retired in favor of “super intelligence.” “As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence,” the executive order stated. The president followed that “SI” declaration up with an Oct. 8 Truth Social post asserting that anyone who uses the previous moniker would be branded “THE ENEMY!” The U.S. Navy this week became one of the first services to avoid that traitorous designation, cementing the super initiative and calling on “all Navy echelons, commands, activities, and personnel [to] use ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in place of ‘Artificial Intelligence’ and ‘AI,’” a service memo stated. “This policy applies effective immediately across all official Navy correspondence, flag letters, OPORDs, wargame documentation, instructional material, fleet advisories, public communications, official websites, strategic assessments, congressional reports, and non-statutory internal and external policy documents,” the memo continued. As part of the super overhaul, echelon II commanders, type commanders and systems commanders will be required to review all “public releases, intranet portals, and external presentations for compliance” no later than 30 days after the release of the super memo. These personnel will then be required to submit a super report on completing the task. The directive does not require retroactively amending previously published documentation or contracts, the message noted, while existing laws and statutes “will continue to be cited as statutorily required until conforming congressional amendments are enacted.” A Military Times request for comment from the sea service regarding what consequences might result should “artificial intelligence” be used was not returned as of press time.

title: U.S. Rig Count Holds Steady as Oil Prices Surge
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Brazil's ambitious data center expansion…
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
The total number of active drilling rigs for oil and gas in the United States remained unchanged for the second week in a row this week, according to new data that Baker Hughes published on Friday, with the total rig count in the US staying at 603, up 53 from this same time last year.
The number of active oil rigs rose by 1, to 460 during the latest reporting period, according to the data. This is 40 above this same time last year. The number of gas rigs fell by 1 to 132, which is 11 more than this time last year. Miscellaneous rigs stayed the same at 11.
The latest EIA data showed that weekly U.S. crude oil production fell during week ending October 16. US crude oil production averaged 13.269 million bpd during the reporting period, down from 13.679 million bpd last week and down 360,000 bpd from a year ago.
Primary Vision’s Frac Spread Count, an estimate of the number of crews completing wells, fell for the first time in six weeks during the week ending October 16, losing 4 crews and sinking to 199. This is up 24 year over year.
The number of active drilling rigs in the Permian Basin stayed the same during the reporting period, at 272. This is 22 rigs above year-ago levels. The count in the Eagle Ford rose by 2 to 51, which is 8 more than this same time last year.
Oil prices were up on Friday prior to the data release, with Brent now trading at $116.52 (+2.96%) per barrel, and up $11 per barrel from this time last week. WTI was also trading up on the day at $102.88 (+3.43%), although this is up nearly $5 per barrel from this time last week.

title: Bitcoin Core Rewrites Its Security Policy for a World Where AI Finds Bugs in One Prompt
body:
Bitcoin Core developers have changed how the software handles certain security flaws, acknowledging that AI has made some vulnerabilities so easy to find that keeping them secret no longer makes sense.
The project merged the policy update Thursday, after Chaincode Labs developer Antoine Poinsot opened it earlier this month citing a spike in reports of bugs that can be “easily (re-)discovered.”
The reason, Poinsot wrote, is that large language models have “drastically reduced the bar” to find certain classes of issues or to spot a quietly shipped fix in the code.
The change targets a tension at the heart of any disclosure policy. Bitcoin Core, which runs most of the nodes underpinning the network, has long favored a lengthy embargo period, keeping security fixes quiet and often holding them until the next major release.
That cautious approach reflects Bitcoin’s famously slow upgrade culture, where rushing node operators to update carries its own risks. But developers concluded that for bugs an attacker can surface with a single AI prompt, a long embargo “achieves little but delays the availability of a fixed release.”
Under the new policy, Bitcoin Core may flag a reported vulnerability as “easily discoverable,” a label it expects to apply to issues findable through a simple LLM query.
For those, it will backport a fix to every maintained release and cut a new version as quickly as possible, publishing details in a security advisory alongside the patched software, rather than sitting on it. The logic, as Poinsot put it in the discussion, is that covertly patching such a bug “would achieve little,” since a trivial AI scan can find it and an aggressive backport gives it away anyway.
The shift reflects how sharply AI has reshaped the security landscape around Bitcoin. Over the summer, a volunteer “ Bitcoin Red Team ” began racing to find AI-discoverable flaws before attackers do. In early August, an AI-driven audit logged nearly 5,000 findings across hundreds of crypto projects, and developers have scrambled to patch AI-surfaced bugs in Lightning implementations and hardware wallets .
One Bitcoin bridge even shut down after concluding AI was finding bugs faster than it could fix them.

title: Doctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reaction
body:
Leaked confidential data. A major stock sell-off.
Beneath the chaos surrounding Moderna and Merck 's latest data on their personalized cancer vaccine, oncologists see something else: an important milestone in melanoma treatment.
The companies on Thursday released detailed results from a phase 3 trial on their mRNA-based shot after partial data leaked on social media platforms earlier that day.
The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% when given alongside Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda, compared with Keytruda alone. The combination also reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy, according to the trial on roughly 1,100 patients whose tumors were removed by surgery.
The stock market's reaction contrasted with the assessment of six melanoma specialists, who told CNBC the results represent a clinically meaningful advance that could eventually become a standard of care for patients who undergo surgery first and have not received immunotherapy before their operation.
"This has the potential to be a major breakthrough in melanoma treatment and also cancer immunotherapy in general that will open the door to greater outcomes for patients," said Dr. Sekwon Jang, a melanoma specialist at Inova Schar Cancer and principal investigator at one of the trial's U.S. sites.
Dr. Janice Mehnert, NYU Langone skin cancer specialist and trial investigator, added that "this is the first time we're seeing that when you add something to immunotherapy, you actually boost the efficacy of the immunotherapy."
The vaccine is not far from potentially entering the market for the first time and reaching melanoma patients. In an interview ahead of the results, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the company is finishing a filing with regulators as it aims to get the drug fully approved next year.
"It's a very, very happy moment for the field, for patients," he said.
An immunotherapy like Keytruda wakes up the immune system to detect and attack cancer cells. Unlike preventative vaccines, which protect against infections that can cause cancer, Moderna and Merck's treatment acts like a blueprint to train the immune system to recognize and hunt residual cancer cells based on the specific mutations in an individual patient's tumor.
The significance of the phase 3 data extends beyond delaying a recurrence, doctors said. Melanoma can become much more difficult to treat when it returns after surgery and spreads to distant parts of the body, such as the lungs, brain or liver. Patients with advanced disease may require additional treatments, including immunotherapy, radiation or further surgery, and those methods are not guaranteed to work.
Preventing the cancer from returning could spare patients from ever facing the risks and complexities of metastatic disease altogether.
"If we can essentially cure more patients with earlier-stage melanoma and never have to deal with unresectable metastatic disease — that's a wonderful advance," said Dr. Michael Postow, chief of the Melanoma Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and an investigator on the trial.
Ideally, patients in the future may be able to undergo surgery and receive the vaccine and Keytruda without needing further melanoma treatment, Postow told CNBC.
Still, questions remain about whether the combination ultimately helps patients live longer, what the benefit looks like over longer periods of time and which patients benefit most.
The results also leave open where the personalized vaccine would fit into a changing melanoma treatment landscape, some experts said.
The trial tested the vaccine after surgery, alongside Keytruda, rather than against immunotherapy regimens given before surgery. That's an approach increasingly used for eligible patients with resectable melanoma, where the primary tumor can be removed. The data does not show that using the vaccine approach is more or less effective than receiving immunotherapy before surgery.
The medical community will get more clarity after Moderna and Merck present the detailed results at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference on Saturday.
Moderna shares fell as much as 25% Thursday, before regaining some ground, after partial data from the trial leaked on social media. The sell-off came despite the positive results, underscoring the gap between the treatment's clinical promise and investor expectations for its commercial potential. Moderna shares are also up nearly 600% this year due to the cancer shot optimism, creating more potential for a Wall Street letdown.
Investors had hoped the vaccine and Keytruda would replicate the results of an earlier phase 2 trial, which showed a roughly 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death at five years, RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh wrote in a note Thursday. Huynh described the phase 3 results as clinically meaningful and likely to support regulatory approval, but said the primary efficacy result landed at the low end of investor expectations.
But there was a key difference in the studies: The phase 3 trial included patients with a broader range of risk profiles, including some at lower risk of recurrence than those enrolled in the earlier phase 2 trial, said Dr. George Ansstas, who leads the melanoma department at Washington University in St. Louis. That may have slightly tempered the results, since patients considered lower risk have less chance of recurrence to begin with.
"It's great data actually. It's overall consistent with what we've proven in the phase 2 trial," said Ansstas, who also worked on the phase 2 trial.
The combination showed little difference from Keytruda alone during the first six months of treatment, the companies said. But a separate analysis of the phase 3 data offered a more encouraging signal about the treatment's effect after the six-month mark. The vaccine and Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 58% after that point, compared with Keytruda alone.
The 42% figure comes from the primary analysis, which included patients' outcomes throughout the trial's follow-up period. The median follow-up was about two years at the time of the analysis, so the result reflects the overall treatment effect, not just what happened before or after the six-month mark.
Ansstas said the benefit of the personalized cancer vaccine may take several months to emerge because each shot must be custom-manufactured, a process that can take roughly six weeks, while patients begin Keytruda in the meantime. After vaccination begins, the immune system also needs time and repeated doses to develop a response against tumors.
That timeline could help explain why the group that received the combination regimen saw even greater benefits around six months, Ansstas said. Still, the explanation is a hypothesis rather than proof of when the vaccine's effect begins.
Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD ​Anderson Cancer Center, also highlighted the relatively mild side effects associated with the vaccine, including injection-site reactions, as a positive.
Keytruda and other cancer therapies can cause potentially serious immune-related side effects. Detailed safety results released on Saturday should help clarify the trade-offs of adding the vaccine to the immunotherapy regimen.
For Moderna, the stakes extend beyond melanoma. The company is working to build a business beyond its Covid vaccine, while Merck is preparing for the eventual loss of patent protection on Keytruda.
The companies have several hurdles ahead of them, including selling an individualized therapy that takes several weeks to create for a patient at scale.
"I think the downside is that it's super labor-intensive, and you're gonna have to make vaccines for each person, and so you can't just stockpile a million vaccines and then just ship it out when somebody needs it," said Dr. Adil Daud, professor of medicine and melanoma oncologist at the University of California San Francisco, who was the lead investigator on the phase 3 trial. "There is the time and expense, and it's probably going to cost like a lot of money."
Moderna and Merck have not disclosed any details about the manufacturing costs for the vaccine.
He added that most people who walk into the clinic with a tumor that has not been surgically removed may stick to receiving Keytruda before an operation because "that approach is simpler and doesn't put the patient through the delay" of creating the vaccine.
Daud said he expects the vaccine combination to be used primarily in the adjuvant setting, after surgery, rather than replace established immunotherapy regimens given before an operation. For patients who receive immunotherapy before surgery but show little or no response, the vaccine combination could offer another option, he said, though that would likely be for a smaller group of patients.
Moderna and Merck still need to validate the approach in other cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma. Success in melanoma does not automatically guarantee that the approach will work in other tumors.
"I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Merck Research Laboratories President Dean Li said in an interview ahead of the results. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."
Moderna's Bancel sees a bright future for the vaccine, saying he believes it will eventually be able to help "literally thousands and then tens of thousands and then hundreds of thousands of people across different tumors around the world."

title: Can we replace a $150k Looker with a bucket of HTML files?
body:
Like a lot of companies, we pay for Looker. Let’s say $150k a year, the average Looker licence 1 , roughly 300 seats. We are 3 data platform engineers at a company of about 500 people, and most of our week goes on the unglamorous stuff: keeping Snowflake fed, babysitting a dbt project that passed 2,000 models a while ago, and running the Airflow, Airbyte, DataHub and Kubernetes plumbing underneath it all.
In February, one of us built a thing on the side to host HTML files. It took an afternoon. 8 months later, and it’s already got as many weekly users as Looker in our company, maybe even more and Looker’s down a third.
Tech influencers keep posting about software being dead , and some say they’ve cancelled and vibecoded all their SaaS subscriptions . They say AI is going to kill B2B SaaS. 2
SaaS is dead, apparently, so can we replace our enterprise BI tool?
Left: share of new GitHub repos described as "self-hosted". Right: share of Hacker News comments saying "slop". 3
A year ago I thought most AI output was slop, and most of it was. We made a few “chat with your data” demos, and they looked great on a toy schema with 4 tables, but never really worked at our scale. The SQL ran without errors, but the numbers were wrong. That’s much worse.
Then Claude Code with Opus 4.5 got really good. Like, really good. In early January adoption across the company skyrocketed. It could work in our repos and use our tools. Also, it could run a query to check the numbers before answering. That mattered a lot more than getting a clever-sounding response. Within a few weeks, people in finance, ops and marketing who had never opened a terminal were prompting all day. All of a sudden everyone was prompting, and nobody was clicking.
Around this time, Claude started spitting out a lot of HTML. You would ask for an analysis and you’d get a single file with charts, and honestly, some of those pages looked better than our Looker dashboards. The problem was that it would live in someone’s Downloads folder. To share it, they would attach it in Slack and hope. This was way before Anthropic shipped shareable artifacts for Team and Enterprise (June 2026), and we really needed a way to share this new kind of dashboard.
One day Maddy from our team said she’d just put them all on a web server, with an internal domain name. By the end of the day she had vibe-coded the whole thing: a small service that stored the files in S3, SSO in front of it, and (some) tests. We already run everything on Kubernetes, so deploying a service was mostly a matter of adding a Terraform module and a Helm chart. Having all that plumbing in place made the whole thing much easier.
She wrote a small Python script and packaged it in a Claude plugin. Users would get their Claude to write the HTML, the script would push it (behind SSO), and anyone in the company could open the link. Initially, the files were just plain, static HTML. In March we thought, why not, and added a live query API using the viewer’s Snowflake OAuth token: best decision of the year.
Turns out, we didn’t need to write a permission model. Snowflake already had one all along. It had roles we’d been maintaining for years, and if Snowflake says you can’t read the sales table, then neither can the dashboard. By April, Snowflake OAuth was the only login.
A Looker tile is a box with a fixed list of chart types and a fixed set of colours, and it looks like every other Looker tile ever made. Ugly, and no personality.
Free-form LLM-generated HTML in less than 1 minute
By getting rid of the rigid fixed tiles, our users could produce free-form HTML and prompt it until it looked neat. They loved it. Email and Slack exports came in April, parameters in May, and weekly viewers went from 23 in March to 136 in June. The exec team started to send links around. People also made the tool their own. They found use cases we would never have thought of, set dashboards to regenerate themselves on a schedule, added buttons, and built some wild designs and UX that no BI tool would have let them.
Security, at this point, was bad. Like, really bad. Dashboard JavaScript ran on the same origin as your session, nothing had permissions, and every employee could read every dashboard. It was basically one big XSS hole: any dashboard could run code as whoever opened it and pull data out in their name. We knew, and we shipped it anyway, because it was internal, behind VPN and SSO, and nothing else did this job.
In our team, “let’s just build a BI tool” became a running joke. It stayed a joke for a few months, until it became clear we were in too deep. We had piled months of vibe-coding onto something with a security model we weren’t proud of, and half the company was using it. We stopped joking and said it properly: let’s build a BI tool. We got in front of a whiteboard, mostly to work out how to fix the security model, and to agree on what we didn’t want to lose: the same S3 bucket, no migration, nothing breaking for the people already using it, and publishing that stayed as easy as before.
The one thing everyone agreed on: anyone can still push any HTML in one prompt, with no review step, no template and no list of approved widgets. We’d still defend that.
Every constraint you put between people and their dashboard sends them back to the Downloads folder.
One connector instead of a script. The upload script had been copied into 2 repos and a plugin, and every copy was a bit different. We replaced all of them with one remote MCP connector for the whole company, so claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude in Slack and our own analyst agent all call the same tools. The connector passes your Snowflake token along, and the API checks who you are with SELECT CURRENT_USER() . Whatever an AI uploads lands as a draft, and a human has to click Publish.
Assume every dashboard is hostile. This is the part we needed to actually think about. The whole product is basically XSS by design: anyone can upload JavaScript that runs in a colleague’s browser, nobody reviews it, and the colleague might be the CFO. We can’t block the XSS, because the XSS is the product, so our job is to make sure it can’t reach anything. Our security model starts with “We assume it is hostile” for that reason. Each dashboard runs in a sandboxed iframe on its own origin, which gets no cookies and a strict CSP. The only thing it can talk to is the parent page, through postMessage , and the parent checks who sent the message, attaches the session and calls the API. Content tokens last an hour and work for one dashboard, one viewer and one host.
The sandbox protects the browser. We also created a separate metadata service that reads every new version of a dashboard async. It pulls out the whole HTML and the Snowflake queries. It checks for the scripts the page loads and where it sends data. Then a set of rules judges those facts. Most rules only report. They flag a dashboard that reads raw data instead of a dbt model, a script that isn’t pinned to a version, or a dashboard nobody has opened in 90 days. Some rules can block a dashboard: a script from a package nobody here has used before, or a WebRTC connection, which is the one way out that CSP can’t block. A blocked dashboard doesn’t load. The viewer sees a warning and has to accept it before the page runs.
Let Snowflake do identity and permissions. Every query runs with the viewer’s own token. Sharing a dashboard never shares data access. That’s a security feature, and it’s also a laziness feature: we never had to build or maintain data permissions, because everyone who logs in already has a Snowflake user with the right roles.
Content management. This part we vibe-coded in about a week, and it barely needed any design. For spaces, folders and sharing we copied Google Drive, because everybody already knows how Google Drive works: viewer, editor and owner, grants flow down the folder tree, and the strongest grant wins. Versions are stored by content hash, and restoring one gives you a draft. Then search, likes, scheduled exports, and teams synced from the HR system every hour. Compare that with the security model, which is where nearly all the real thinking went.
It took a few weeks of dev, and we got there.
Then it spread. People started tagging Claude in Slack threads and getting a dashboard back. Our analyst agent publishes its own, some repos publish straight from CI, and most people just publish from their own Claude, so every dashboard ends up looking a bit like the person who made it. These days it’s everywhere.
That’s the whole bill on our side: 8 months, 3 engineers doing it on the side, plus a few friends who sent PRs. Claude wrote most of the code. We did the whiteboarding, argued a lot, and reviewed everything.
Looker’s usage leaked rather than crashed. We haven’t moved everything: some teams still live in Looker, and some of its dashboards have no replacement yet. What made people use this instead of Looker is that building a dashboard stopped being expensive. That made us curious: how cheap, exactly? The good thing about paying in tokens instead of engineering time is that it’s easier to measure.
We use our analyst agent as a proxy here, because it’s a builder we can measure exactly. Every run is logged with its tokens and its cost, and every publish links back to the run that made it.
We found that each dashboard takes the agent around 1 million tokens, from the first question to the finished page. Now that we’ve moved it to Opus 5.5, the cost of a dashboard has dropped from about $2.50 to about $0.50. The agent does the same work; the tokens just got cheaper. That’s the real story: building software now costs whatever tokens cost, and that price keeps falling.
Here’s the bill for the whole thing, from the first commit in February to now.
Running it costs about $6k a year in AWS now that it has its own database, plus whatever Claude we spend to keep adding features, which has been around $1.3k a month since July. Call it $20k a year, against $150k for Looker, and most of that $20k is us building new stuff rather than keeping the lights on.
When we bought Looker we were buying 4 things: a UI to draw charts, a permission model, a semantic layer, and somewhere to host it. Claude now draws the charts, one dashboard at a time.
Take those away and what’s left is a $150k invoice.
We’re not the only ones, either. You hear it more and more often: solid, established businesses cancelling very expensive analytics subscriptions. Amjad Masad told Platformer the same story about Replit: once he could join the warehouse to production Postgres and build the report himself, they “canceled or downsized most of [their] analytics products”.
In our case, building a dashboard tool around our existing stack has cost a fraction of what we were paying for Looker. For us, the important bits were already in dbt and Snowflake: the models, permissions and data. Looker sat on top of that and turned it into dashboards. That’s the part we’ve found we can replace.
The bill above also leaves out the biggest cost, which is us: 3 engineers spending 8 months on this, on top of everything else a data platform team does: the pipelines, the dbt project, the warehouse, the Kubernetes clusters, the on-call. None of that stopped. We can’t put an honest number on the hours, because they were spread across everything else we did. If you need to hire a team to build this, the maths is different.
I’d argue the line is scale. AWS and Snowflake sell things nobody can vibe-code: data centres, storage at petabyte prices, compute that’s cheap because millions of other customers share it. I think BI is particularly exposed because a lot of its value, at least for us, was in building and presenting dashboards. Claude can now do that for pennies. Products with a real scale advantage are a different story, but I wouldn’t be surprised if more companies start replacing parts of their BI stack themselves.
Anthropic announced Claude Dashboards in beta on 8 October, a week before this went up. So the obvious question: should we have just waited and bought that?
We couldn’t really. We started 8 months ago and it didn’t exist. If we were starting from scratch today, honestly, we’d probably look at it first. It’s AI-native, and it doesn’t have the rendering problems Looker has. If your team has nothing today, it’s probably the right call.
For us, the dashboards are only part of it. The tool is wired into the way our team already works: it talks to our agent control plane, our analytics platform and Slack, with a bunch of workflows we’ve built ourselves. Claude Dashboards might cover some of that, but we’d still have to work out how to connect it all. And if a feature changes or the price goes up, we’d have to deal with it.
So it’s still the same answer. If you need software that fits what you do, and you already have a platform to run it on and a dedicated team, build it, unless the moat is scale.

title: Newmont prices Red Chris expansion at up to $4.8B
body: Newmont (NYSE, ASX: NEM) put a price of up to (C$6.4 billion) $4.8 billion on taking its Red Chris copper-gold mine underground in British Columbia, with commercial production targeted for 2033. The project, about 1,030 km northwest of Vancouver, would produce an annual average of 275,000–325,000 oz. gold and 65,000–85,000 tonnes copper from 2035 through 2040, the company said Thursday in its quarterly results . Newmont owns 70% of Red Chris and operates it alongside Imperial Metals (TSX: III), which holds the balance. “The cave is now larger and it’s also orientated to prevent any intersection with major fault lines,” President and CEO Natascha Viljoen said on Thursday’s third-quarter analyst call, noting that engineering is at least 60% complete. The update sets out the funding needed for a major Canadian copper expansion backed by Ottawa . The $4.2-billion to $4.8-billion estimate includes contingency but excludes the cost of transitioning from open-pit to underground mining. It also assumes a C$500-million federal contribution, whose terms have yet to be finalized. It puts development spending well above the $2.1 billion estimated in Newcrest’s 2021 prefeasibility study, although the scope has changed: that plan covered three mining blocks over 31 years, while Newmont’s initial stage covers two blocks over 13 years. Newmont beat Scotiabank’s earnings forecast and outlined lower capital spending for 2027 than the bank expected, analyst Tanya Jakusconek said in a Thursday note. But “these estimates may be overshadowed by the higher capex” at Red Chris, she wrote. Even so, changes to the project’s scope make direct comparisons with Newcrest’s earlier study unhelpful, Jakusconek said. Red Chris represents about 2% of Scotiabank’s estimate of Newmont’s net asset value. Shares in Newmont fell 2% to $111.81 on Friday morning in New York, valuing the company at $116.1 billion. The stock has traded in a 12-month range of $76.04 to $135.29. Construction decision The feasibility study is nearing completion, with an investment decision expected early next year, Viljoen said. B.C. granted key permits in June through a consent-based process with the Tahltan Nation. Construction could begin in 2027, subject to board approvals. Ottawa referred the Red Chris expansion to its Major Projects Office in September last year, placing it among the first five selected for help coordinating regulatory approvals and financing. The initial stage is to produce 3 million oz. gold and more than 850,000 tonnes copper. Newmont sees potential for a mine life of up to 70 years through further development, including East Ridge, but those additions aren’t included in the initial plan. The company expects to fund construction from internal cash flow. Australian progress Down Under, Newmont brought forward commercial production at Tanami Expansion 2 in the Northern Territory to the end of June next year from the second half of 2027. Shaft construction is complete, mechanical completion is expected by year-end and commissioning should begin early next year. The $1.7-billion to $1.8-billion expansion adds a 1,460-metre hoisting shaft and supporting infrastructure to improve underground productivity and extend Tanami’s life beyond 2040. At Cadia in New South Wales, gold output recovered to 61,000 oz. from 34,000 oz. in the second quarter following April’s seismic disruption . Newmont completed the final blasting step needed to develop Panel Cave 2-3 in September and expects to hand the project over to operations by year-end. Cave-establishment work at Panel Cave 1-2 has resumed after regulatory approvals following the earthquake. That project remains on schedule. Water risk Lihir in Papua New Guinea faces a less certain fourth quarter. Newmont expects higher grades and throughput after completing September maintenance but warned that El Niño conditions affecting water supply could intensify through year-end and hurt production and costs. Water shortages haven’t yet affected operations, Viljoen said. If conditions worsen, Newmont will prioritize community supplies while continuing mining and stockpiling ore and could bring forward maintenance scheduled for next year. The company maintained its annual production outlook for the operation. It continues to advance Lihir’s Nearshore Barrier project, due for completion in 2028, to unlock access to additional ore and extend the operation’s life beyond 2040. At Mexico’s Peñasquito, fourth-quarter silver output is expected to fall to about half the third-quarter level as planned lower grades and throughput reduce production. Peñasquito’s silver output is expected to fall roughly 30% next year because of planned mine sequencing, chief financial officer Brian Tabolt said on the analyst call. The decline would reduce the revenue credits that offset Newmont’s reported gold costs. Brucejack in B.C. increased quarterly gold production to 72,000 oz. from 53,000 oz., helped by improved access to mining areas and fewer underground bottlenecks. Cerro Negro in Argentina lifted output to 55,000 oz. from 49,000 oz. as mining rates and grades improved. Growth returns Across the portfolio, Newmont expects gold production to grow by a low-to-mid single-digit percentage next year, supported by Tanami’s expansion, higher grades at Lihir and Boddington, and extended mining at Yanacocha in Peru. Development spending is expected to rise by about $500 million next year from this year’s $1.4-billion budget as investment increases at Red Chris and Lihir. Red Chris accounts for half that increase, or about $250 million, Viljoen said, subject to project approval. About $200 million of the overall increase would be offset by lower reclamation spending as Yanacocha’s water-treatment plants near completion. Unit costs are expected to rise next year because of inflation, diesel prices, currency movements and lower by-product credits. For this year, however, Newmont cut its gold all-in sustaining cost forecast, after by-product credits, to $1,520 per oz. from $1,680, while maintaining production guidance of about 5.3 million ounces. Third-quarter gold production was essentially unchanged from the previous quarter at 1.3 million ounces. Adjusted earnings rose 23% to $2.3 billion, or $2.20 a share, from $1.9 billion, or $1.71 a share, a year earlier. Free cash flow totalled $1.9 billion. Newmont ended September with $8.8 billion in cash, before a planned $1.95-billion payment to Barrick Mining (TSX: ABX; NYSE: B) this quarter under their amended Nevada Gold Mines agreement . The August deal provides for adding Barrick’s Fourmile and Newmont’s Fiberline and Mike properties to the joint venture. BMO Capital Markets analyst Matthew Murphy put Newmont’s $1.9-billion quarterly free cash flow above his $1.4-billion forecast. The company’s preliminary 2027 production outlook implies 5.4 million to 5.5 million oz., below BMO’s previous 5.7-million-oz. estimate, he said in a Thursday note. He is watching for a path back to annual gold production of 6 million ounces. “Overall, we feel NEM continues to track well versus expectations,” Murphy wrote.

title: Romania blames Russia for drone strike that sinks cargo ship in Black Sea, killing one sailor and leaving three missing
body: The Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv sank in the Black Sea off Romania’s coast after a drone attack, Reuters reported. The ship had 13 sailors from Ukraine and Azerbaijan aboard. One crew member was killed, nine were rescued, and three remain missing. “It is part of Russia’s escalation process in its war in Ukraine,” Romanian President Nicusor Dan said. He told reporters that the ship had sunk after being hit by a drone. Romania’s naval authority said the Khoryv sent a distress signal 24 kilometers (about 15 miles) from the port of Constanta, just outside Romania’s territorial waters. At least seven cargo ships have been attacked off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, Reuters reported. About 30 sailors have been killed or gone missing. Most of the ships attacked were near the Sulina Channel, which connects the Danube to the Black Sea. After strikes on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, the channel became the main export route for Ukrainian grain and vegetable oil, Reuters reported. title: UNRWA teacher tells ‘Post’ she was threatened for challenging pro-Hamas rhetoric in Gaza schools
body: The antisemitic and pro-Hamas indoctrination of Gazan students has a “profound impact” that extends far beyond the classroom, a Gaza-based UNRWA teacher told The Jerusalem Post, after school administrators threatened her with scissors for confronting extremist rhetoric being pushed onto young girls.Speaking on Saturday anonymously due to the risks she faces, T. said she decided it was her responsibility to speak out after repeatedly witnessing a colleague attempt to blur the “boundaries between education and political and religious indoctrination within the school environment.”“I believe that remaining silent in the face of such practices means abandoning our moral and educational responsibilities,” she said, saying that Palestinian students deserved an environment where they could study and dream of a future uncolored by conflict.“They have already experienced more than enough war, fear, and death,” T. said. “No one has the right to rob them of their childhood or predetermine that their future must be an extension of the conflict.”While T. said that she did not consider her attempts to challenge the indoctrination to be anything special, she acknowledged that confronting radicalization had put her at risk. She said she became more aware of the danger recently, when a school administrator threatened her with scissors after she intervened in an attempt by another teacher to promote support for Hamas.School administrator threatened to cut teacher's tongue for mentioning Hamas“I had confronted several teachers on more than one occasion over their attempts to indoctrinate children with extremist ideas. During one of these incidents, I became involved in a heated argument with a female teacher who was promoting such views,” she recalled.“Shortly afterward, a school administrator confronted me, pushed me into a room, pulled a pair of scissors from his pocket, and threatened me, saying: 'I'll cut your tongue out if you ever mention Hamas again.'”T. said she decided not to file a formal complaint with UNRWA because she could not trust that the matter would be handled confidentially or that the organization could guarantee her safety, particularly given the extent of the radicalization she had witnessed within the agency.“Some people abroad imagine that UNRWA, because it is a United Nations agency, operates in Gaza the same way international institutions operate in Western countries, with an independent administration to which employees can turn for protection. But the reality I experienced was very different,” she said.“I also believe that UNRWA operates in an environment where it cannot simply ignore Hamas's influence and control on the ground. In my view, employees who openly oppose Hamas may put themselves at risk and potentially create pressures affecting the agency's operations.”Even as she explained that UNRWA had to navigate a complex political terrain to be able to operate in Gaza, and was not responsible for the creation of the culture in its facilities, T. said that the UN agency has not done enough to confront it and has failed to enforce strict boundaries on teachers, allowing the problem to enter the classroom.T. said that not all UNRWA employees supported or were affiliated with Hamas, but noted that the agency lacked adequate structural safeguards to protect her and other whistleblowers.“If a school administrator could push me into a room, pull scissors from his pocket, and threaten to cut out my tongue because I spoke about Hamas, how could I feel confident that filing a complaint would not expose me to an even more serious threat? What guarantee would I have that next time they would not stop at threatening to cut out my tongue, but might actually kill me?” she asked.Hamas uses punishment beyond physical intimidation“For me, this was not simply a matter of administrative procedures or filing an official complaint. It was a matter of life and death. That is why I did not report the incident. Not because what happened was insignificant, and not because I accepted the threat, but because I did not trust the available system to protect my identity or my safety if I spoke out.”Beyond physical intimidation, T. said Hamas could use other means to punish her for speaking out, including accusations against her honor and threats against her family, to silence dissent.“There are dissenting voices, and there are people who reject these ideas. But most people are afraid for their families. Not everyone can bear the consequences of confronting an organization that holds political power, influence, and security authority,” T. said.“For this reason, I do not believe what happened to me was an isolated incident. In my view, it reflects a much broader problem within Gaza's educational environment. I believe Hamas understood, from the time it came to power, the importance of education in shaping the minds of future generations.”Asked how Hamas-oriented education was affecting Palestinian children, T. said antisemitism and the romanticization of martyrdom were shaping their worldviews in psychologically damaging ways.She added that the schooling system's emphasis on memorization and repetition to answer exam questions failed to equip students with the critical-thinking skills that could help protect them from radicalization.“When an educational system built around memorization is combined with an ideological discourse that discourages dissent, the problem becomes even more dangerous,” she said. “A child who has never learned to ask questions, challenge assumptions, or examine information critically may become more vulnerable to extremist narratives.”T. said that Palestinian students should not be defined by the conflict or viewed solely as potential fighters but as children who are also victims of war who have the ability to choose a different future if given the chance.“The children of Gaza have lived through years of war, fear, destruction, and the loss of loved ones. They need an education that gives them hope and helps them build their lives, not one that makes hatred and conflict permanent parts of their identity,” she said.“I fear that continued extremist ideological indoctrination could produce generations who believe violence is the natural solution to disagreements, and that a person's religious or national identity alone is enough to judge them…“I want Palestinian children to dream of becoming doctors, engineers, teachers, or artists. I want them to know that their future does not have to be confined to a choice between war and death.“Reforming education is not simply about changing textbooks. It is an essential part of building a society that can live in peace and dignity, and give its children a genuine opportunity for a better future.”

title: Time Nuts (2005)
body:
Time-Nuts ™ is a mailing list for amateurs who are interested in precise Time & Frequency. Topics include stability of quartz oscillators, measurements of rubidium and cesium atomic clocks, using WWVB, Loran-C, and GPS for long-term comparisons.
Most of the members are hams or electronics hobbyists. Topics also include acquisition, repair, and operation of surplus electronic instruments related to precise time; nanoseconds; picoseconds; results of homebrew hardware and software T&F projects, etc.
Please join if you have questions or expertise to add to the group. If you have an interest in precise time & frequency or are getting the "time bug" here are some suggestions:
In the pre-web 1990s Tom Clark set up a gps-timing mailing list at NASA for those interested in his pioneering work with the Motorola Oncore-series GPS receiver. That list was an inspirational example of one man freely sharing a wealth of experience and information with a group of interested GPS timing newbies. The list was specific to his home-brew TAC hardware (now TAC-2 ) and SHOWTIME software (now TAC32 ). The list moved to TACGPS and is still around but quiet (now hosted by TAPR ).
However, there were other precise time & frequency topics not covered by tacgps . Over the years several of us — tvb, DougH, StanP, CorbyD, JohnA, BrookeC — were exchanging private emails that I thought deserved wider audience, participation, and archiving. So in 2001 time-nuts began. It was once cesium-nuts at Yahoo, then time-nuts here at LeapSecond.com, then John Ackermann graciously offered to administer and host it on his site so that's where it is today. title: A whirlwind tour of systemd-nspawn containers (2025)
body:
In the last yearly update , I talked about isolating my self-hosted LLMs running in Ollama as well as Open WebUI in systemd-nspawn containers and promised a blog post about it. However, while writing that blog post, a footnote on why I am using it instead of Docker accidentally turned into a full blog post on its own . Here’s the actual post on systemd-nspawn .
Fundamentally, systemd-nspawn is a lightweight Linux namespaces-based container technology, not dissimilar to Docker . The difference is mostly in image management—instead of describing how to build images with Dockerfile s and distributing prebuilt, read-only images containing ready-to-run software, systemd-nspawn is typically used with a writable root filesystem, functioning more similarly to a virtual machine. For those of you who remember using chroot to run software on a different Linux distro, it can also be described as chroot on steroids.
I find systemd-nspawn especially useful in the following scenarios:
In this post, I’ll describe the process of setting up systemd-nspawn containers and how to use them in some common scenarios.
Update (2025-05-19) : added safer Alpine container creation instructions and some more guidance on setting up Alpine Linux containers.
systemd-nspawn , like all containers, requires a separate rootfs in a directory. Since it doesn’t come with an image manager to build images for you, you’ll need to use the traditional Unix approach of creating a chroot . It is, after all, chroot on steroids.
For systemd-nspawn , the typical convention is to put these rootfses under /var/lib/machines/[hostname] , where the hostname is that of the container. For this exercise, I’ll just use the name of the OS as the hostname.
Each Linux distro has its own way of creating a new rootfs, so we’ll go through some of the more common ones. I am testing all this on Debian, but there’s no reason why you wouldn’t be able to do any of this on another distro by substituting the equivalent packages. Still, I’ll probably go deeper into Debian because I am more familiar with it.
debootstrap has featured on this blog many times, mostly when doing crazy things like installing Debian by hand from rescue systems . For Debian-based distros like Ubuntu or Debian itself, this is the tool to use to create a rootfs.
On a Debian-based OS, install it with sudo apt install debootstrap . It may also be packaged on other distros, or you can just download it from Debian’s repositories:
Either way you installed debootstrap , let’s create the rootfs in /var/lib/machines/debian :
Here, we’ve installed bookworm , but feel free to substitute this for the latest Debian release. To avoid silly issues, I ensured that systemd and dbus are installed, along with locales to avoid weird warnings in apt , bash-completion so I don’t hate my life when typing in commands by hand, and curl so you can download stuff later. Some of these require a bit of additional configuration later, which we’ll do once we boot into the container.
First, install dnf and rpm if you are on another distro, e.g. on Debian:
Then, we make a Fedora 41 chroot as an example:
Alpine Linux is commonly used in Docker images due to its lightweight size, so I thought I might as well try creating an Alpine Linux chroot. The usual tool for this sort of thing is alpine-chroot-install , but its default behaviour is horrifying for our use case. For example:
It is possible to run a crazy umount command afterward to clean up after alpine-chroot-install , such as:
However, I deem this a ticking time-bomb waiting to explode in someone’s face, so instead, I forked the script and created alpine-nspawn-install . My version removes all the crazy “features” of alpine-chroot-install that don’t make sense for systemd-nspawn , e.g. the mounting, chroot helper scripts, qemu support, etc. 2 , while installing a more sane list of packages by default. You can use it like this:
Now let’s see if Alpine lives up to its reputation:
Well, that’s certainly impressive… Alpine is an order of magnitude smaller than the other two, while Fedora is quite bloated with the list of packages I have installed. I am not a Fedora user and copied the package list from the Arch Linux wiki guide on systemd-nspawn , so I am not sure if it’s because I’ve installed bloat, but they all seem pretty necessary… It’s certainly bigger than what dnf claimed to be, so I took a look, and dnf created 260 MiB of stuff under /var/cache/dnf .
Also to be fair to Debian, I did install a bunch of “bloat” like locales for a more pleasant experience. Removing the “bloat” results in 305 MiB, which is slightly smaller.
First, install systemd-nspawn with sudo apt install systemd-container or your distro’s equivalent.
Then, you can get a root shell in a container by running the following command:
And we are in the newly created Debian container. Note that this is just a root shell and isn’t a proper way to deploy the container long term. There is no init process even.
If you are going to be using a root shell for a significant amount of time and want autocomplete to avoid typing entire commands:
If you are just using the container to run a single application, it can get really tedious to manage your own users and then sudo, so I just opt to do the management as root and having a functioning .bashrc works wonders. This is technically not best practice, but I basically never run commands in single application containers that don’t require root anyway, so it makes no real difference.
debootstrap also copied the host’s hostname into /etc/hostname . Let’s fix that:
If you exited the root shell for some reason, you can go back by doing:
Running the container like this isn’t a long-term solution. You probably want to set it up to run properly in the background. However, this leaves the question of how to access the container. If you are using a systemd-based distro, you have a few options:
Note that because we only have a root shell right now, not a proper boot, systemd (or any other init system) isn’t actually running—so don’t expect to be able to start sshd for the moment. The next step will boot the container properly.
Note that console and shell access through machinectl requires systemd to be running inside a container. This will not be possible when using a non-systemd distro, such as Alpine. If you are using Alpine, you’ll need the openssh-server route.
The default Alpine Linux install created by alpine-chroot-install is configured exclusively for chroot use and doesn’t even include a functioning init system. To run it in a systemd-nspawn container properly, we’ll need to install openrc , their init system, as well as openssh-server :
If you are using my alpine-nspawn-install script instead, this is all done for you . All you have to do is some basic configuration:
Alpine uses ifupdown-ng to configure networking, and the syntax should be compatible with Debian’s, so you can just copy the examples below. You’ll need to do the networking configuration before starting the container, or you will be unable to log in via ssh .
We can create /etc/systemd/nspawn/[name].nspawn to manage the container with machinectl , e.g. machinectl start [name] . Note that the /etc/systemd/nspawn directory isn’t created by default, so you may need to:
The .nspawn file is a text file in INI format that contains the equivalent of command line arguments to systemd-nspawn . For the basics, do the equivalent of --private-users=yes :
There are many other options, such as networking, resource limits, and bind mounting directories on the host system into the container. We’ll cover those later.
For non-systemd distros like Alpine, add KillSignal=SIGTERM to the [Exec] section to ensure that init can terminate properly when the container is stopped. The default signal of SIGRTMIN+3 is only understood by systemd, and SIGTERM is understood more broadly.
For now, let’s try starting the container in the background, with a full init system:
And we are logged in! To leave, press Ctrl + ] three times to disconnect from the console, like machinectl suggests.
You can also just get a direct shell with machinectl shell :
To stop this container, use sudo machinectl stop . For non-systemd distros, use sudo systemctl stop systemd-nspawn@[name] .
To run this container on boot, you can simply run:
To undo this, use sudo machinectl disable .
Note that machinectl just controls the underlying systemd unit, systemd-nspawn@[name].service . This will become important later. Note that you can configure additional options on the unit by running sudo systemd edit systemd-nspawn@[name].service .
Networking is configured under the [Network] section in the .nspawn file. There are several options:
This means that the container shares the same network as the host machine. There is no network isolation anywhere. This is the easiest option to set up, but it’s not very isolated, so I wouldn’t recommend it if you want isolation.
This is the default with invoking systemd-nspawn directly, which is why apt install worked earlier without any networking config. This can be enabled with VirtualEthernet=no in the .nspawn .
A Linux bridge is basically just a virtual ethernet switch. On Debian, you can create one with ifupdown by installing the bridge-utils packages and modifying your /etc/network/interfaces .
If you are running a PC behind a router at home (or somehow have a lot of IPs from your hosting provider), you can add your current interface (we’ll use eth0 as an example) to a bridge. It’ll be like connecting both the cable that goes into eth0 and your PC into a virtual switch, along with any containers. You’ll need to replicate the IP assignment currently on eth0 onto the bridge, since it effectively pulls eth0 out of your machine. Your IP configuration will need to be done on the bridge interface instead, which connects to the virtual port on the switch for your machine.
For static IPs, add the following stanza to /etc/network/interfaces and delete (or comment out with # ) the block for eth0 :
Alternatively, if you prefer DHCP for IPv4 and SLAAC for IPv6:
You can of course name the bridge anything you’d like, though you are advised to start the name with br . Also note that this turns off the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) to make new connections go online faster, but you really shouldn’t be involving this virtual bridge in a loop topology anyway. Doing bridges on any other platform or networking tool is left as an exercise for the reader. The Arch Linux wiki may prove helpful here even if you aren’t using Arch Linux.
Then, you can just use Bridge=br_test in your .nspawn file ( --network-bridge=br_test on the command line) to hook up the virtual interface host0 inside the container to the bridge. You can then set up /etc/network/interfaces inside the container (or your distro’s equivalent) as follows:
Alternatively, if you prefer DHCP for IPv4 and SLAAC for IPv6:
Note that you can hook up multiple containers to the same bridge, so you only have to do this once.
If you are using systemd-networkd in the guest, create /etc/systemd/network/host0.network with the following content in the container:
You may need to enable systemd-networkd :
Alternatively, if you can’t bridge your current network (e.g. you are using a VPS and only have one IP assigned), all is not lost. You can create a bridge with your own custom network and route it instead. This is bridge is new virtual network and the real network interface isn’t plugged into it.
For IPv4, I would recommend allocating yourself a random /24 from the RFC 1918 range. We’ll use 192.0.2.0/24 as the example, since it’s reserved for documentation.
For IPv6, ask your ISP to delegate you a /64 (or a bigger block, but you only need a /64 for this), which most competent 4 VPS providers should be able to do. If you are running this at home, see if your router can use DHCP-PD to request a large block and delegate a /64 to the host machine. We’ll use 2001:db8::/64 as the example.
In either case, assign the first address in the subnet to the bridge per convention.
You’ll then need to set up NAT by running the following iptables command:
Alternatively, if you have a static IP on the host, say 198.51.100.123 , you can also use a SNAT rule, which is faster:
You’ll need to run this every boot. Doing so is left as an exercise for the reader. You can use one of the prebuilt firewalls, a systemd unit, or even rc.local . For more details, consult your distro’s documentation on iptables .
You’ll also need to configure the following sysctl s. You can do so by adding them into /etc/sysctl.conf or uncommenting the line that already exists:
Then run sudo sysctl -p . This will allow the host machine to act as a router.
Once that’s done, use Bridge=br_test in your .nspawn file like before to hook up host0 inside the container to the bridge. You can then set up /etc/network/interfaces inside the container (or your distro’s equivalent) as follows:
For systemd-networkd , use the same example as the bridge section above.
You can also use DHCP and SLAAC, but that requires running a DHCP and route advertisement server on the host. Options include dnsmasq . Doing so is left as an exercise for the reader.
Note that you can hook up multiple containers to the same bridge with NAT, so you only have to do this once.
Now that the networking is configured, you should be able to connect to the container. For example, with ssh and the bridge example:
Another common thing to do is mounting certain files and directories from the host machine into the container. This can be done in the [Files] section of the .nspawn file. Here are some examples:
The third parameter allows comma-separated bind options to be specified. There are two related to the style of bind mounting:
There are also four options related to UID mapping. Recall that containers are given y y UIDs in the range [ x , x + y ) [x, x+y) on the host. These options are:
You can use noidmap pretty easily to allow access to user z z inside the container by granting access to x + z x+z on the host. You can do this with traditional permissions, but I get lazy and just use POSIX ACLs instead, which are so much more flexible. For example, to grant UID 13333337 write access to everything under /srv/example , you can simply run (after installing the acl package on Debian or the equivalent):
If you want to also have this apply to new files created under the directory, you can also run:
I may write an introduction to POSIX ACLs one day, but there are plenty of resources online and figuring out the details is left as an exercise for the reader for the time being.
Also note that you don’t have to bind mount directories. You can bind mount files also. Needless to say, don’t grant the container more access than necessary.
Another interesting use is sharing the host’s GPUs with the guest. Note that unlike doing VFIO passthrough on a KVM virtual machine, the device can be shared between the host and multiple guests. This is accomplished by bind mounting device files.
You’ll need to make sure the driver version inside the guest matches that on the host. You’ll also need to allow the systemd unit access by systemctl edit systemd-nspawn@[name].service and putting in the following lines:
Note that this will share access of all GPUs. Passing through a specific GPU is left as an exercise for the reader.
You can limit CPU cores by setting CPU affinity like this:
You can also add CPU and memory limits through standard systemd mechanisms by editing the unit, such as:
For more details, see the systemd documentation on resource control .
And that’s a quick whirlwind tour of systemd-nspawn . We went over a lot, but that was mostly because there were so many valid ways of setting things up. With systemd-nspawn , you are free to configure things in a way that pleases you with full control. In the end, it’s just like a virtual machine. You can do whatever you want!
Once you figure out a setup that you like, you really just need a name and an IP address allocation, before running a few commands to prepare the image during the first boot. Everything else just requires editing the .nspawn file. You can even make your own script to automate everything. Doing that, of course, is left as an exercise for the reader.
Even if nested virtualization is available, it typically has weird limitations and stability issues. It’s usually not recommended to run it in production. ↩
Other crazy features deleted include the way it copies the user running sudo into the chroot , or the way it randomly calls apt to install packages on the host system, or the way it screws around with sudo rules inside the container. ↩
For those of you who think in binary, this is effectively using the bottom 16 bits for UID/GIDs inside the container, and setting the high 16 bits to a value between 0x8 and 0x6fff . ↩
VPS providers who fail to grant you a /64 at least—either by default or by request—for your own uses have failed to deploy IPv6 properly and should be ashamed of themselves. For the uninitiated, IPv6 specifically doesn’t use NAT, but instead allocates all hosts on a network with a globally unique IP address. For this reason, and to facilitate SLAAC, every L2 network needs to have a /64 block assigned to it. Good ISPs know this and assign such blocks on request, or even hand out larger blocks like /56 or /48 so you don’t need to bother them all the time. ↩
While unmappable UIDs are shown as nobody inside the container, it doesn’t mean the nobody user can actually access those files. The real UID as seen by the host is checked for access. Remember that root is mapped to UID x x on the host. If UID x x doesn’t have access, even the root user inside the container will be denied access. ↩

title: Organized Crime Postponed Democracy in Haiti, Again
body: Organized Crime Postponed Democracy in Haiti, Again As criminal governance becomes entrenched, the question about Haiti’s return to democracy is not when but how. In a briefing on October 19, the United Nations’ top delegate to Haiti, Carlos Ruiz Massieu told the UN Security Council that the country is still far from holding its first national elections since 2016. “Setting new dates for elections without a realistic assessment of their feasibility will only erode public confidence and the credibility of Haitian institutions,” he told the council. SEE ALSO: Haiti Gangs Push For Power Amid Political Chaos The stark assessment came just two weeks after the country’s electoral council (CEP) cancelled the general elections, the first round of which was set for December. No new date has been established for elections that have been postponed multiple times since Haitian President Jovenel Moïse was ambushed and killed by a group of Colombian mercenaries in July 2021. The assassination has been attributed to a fight among elites, but it is the country’s gangs that remain on the forefront of the battle for control over Haiti. And with each postponement, these gangs seem to notch another chaotic hole in their belts. The United Nations’ Security Council’s Panel of Experts said in its final report issued in September that the gangs control 70% of the nation’s capital and have spread deep into the countryside. Violence has become particularly acute in the province of Artibonite, the country’s second-largest electoral district behind the capital, Port-au-Prince, where massacres and hostages are commonplace, the United Nations says. Forced displacement and rape have also become go-to tools of war. The UN says 1.5 million people have fled their homes, one-fourth of the country’s population; among these internal refugees are nearly 800,000 children. In final report, the UN catalogued nearly 2,500 cases of sexual assault, 64% of which they said were cases of “gang rape.” At the forefront of this gang violence is Viv Ansanm, the coalition that formed in 2023 by the G9 and the GPèp, then the country’s most formidible alliances. Another gang, Gran Grif, which operates independently in Artibonite, has surged in recent months to compete with Viv Ansanm. Both groups have been declared foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs) by the United States government. SEE ALSO: Haiti Violence Surges as Gangs Expand Influence The gangs are not operating on their own. In an annex of its final report to the UN Security Council, the Panel said close to a million rounds of ammunition from the stocks of neighboring Dominican Republic’s police were found in 2024, and it chronicled persistent connections and support from Haitian security forces. It added that political and economic elites, among them several former senators, were supplying Viv Ansanm with weapons and ammunition, as well as political and judicial top-cover. Among these former legislators is Youri Latortue. Latortue was called as a witness in the Moïse case but was cleared of any wrongdoing. Indeed, while there have been several convictions of alleged hitmen and some ancillary figures, the case has stalled as prosecutors seek the intellectual authors. The case got a break in September when Haiti extradited Joseph Félix Badio, a former anti-corruption prosecutor. US prosecutors say Badio coordinated the attack via radio, gave the Colombian mercenaries their weapons, and paid off enough Haitian presidential guards to open the path to the presidential suite where Moïse was killed. Badio was captured in 2023, after spending two years in hiding, and the hope is he may cooperate with US authorities to crack the case. Meanwhile, a so-called “National Pact,” cobbled together with what is left of Haiti’s political parties in February after the Transitional Presidential Council’s mandate expired in February, tries to keep order. Ironically, its mandate is dependent on its ability to engineer the country’s first elections in a decade. But how those elections will happen remains an open question. Haiti’s National Police has been decimated by departures and deaths of both on- and off-duty officers. The US has been scrambling to train new police, and the United Nations is trying to replace the Keynan police it once saddled with fighting the gangs with a so-called Gang Suppression Force. Private security, armed with drones, have also joined the fray. The results have been deadly and less than affirming. The UN Panel of Experts said in May that government and private security forces were responsible for 69% of the deaths and injuries during the first three months of 2026. But that ratio swung the other way in the second quarter, the UN said , illustrating the tit-for-tat nature of this conflict and the distance Haiti still must travel before its next democratic elections. title: German grocery wholesaler Metro’s Russian operation donates 1 billion rubles to a fund equipping front-line Russian troops, weeks after Putin placed its assets under temporary management
body: The retail chain Metro, whose Russian assets were placed under temporary management less than a month ago, said it had donated 1 billion rubles to the “People’s Front: Everything for Victory!” fund. The money will go toward “purchasing equipment needed by the military on the front lines,” the company said in a press release. The fund said the money would help meet “urgent needs” for vehicles, communications and reconnaissance systems, equipment to counter drones, and “other things needed by troops in the “special military operation.” “As part of Russia’s economic system, we believe it is important to take part in the state’s strategic initiatives,” said Johannes Tholey, Metro’s chief executive in Russia. Update: Germany’s Metro said it had not approved the transfer of 1 billion rubles to the Russian military. In a statement to Deutsche Welle, Metro AG said it “distances itself from any support for Russia’s war against Ukraine.” “Financing or supporting military operations runs counter to both our position and our business principles,” the company said. In late September, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree placing the assets of the German retail chain Metro under temporary management. The company had remained in Russia after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The appointed manager was JSC UK Torg Rus, a company registered three weeks earlier. Its listed owner was Johannes Tholey, who has headed Metro Cash & Carry since 2023. Le Monde later reported that Metro itself had proposed that the Russian authorities place it under temporary management, deciding to “act preemptively” to avoid the worst-case scenario.
