title: Bitcoin Core Ends Long Embargoes for Bugs AI Can Rediscover
body: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Core Ends Long Embargoes for Bugs AI Can Rediscover Bitcoin Core has changed its security disclosure policy to speed up fixes for vulnerabilities that large language models can find with little effort, ending the months-long embargoes those bugs once received. Maintainers merged the change to the project’s security policy on Thursday. Chaincode Labs developer Antoine Poinsot, who wrote the proposal, announced it in a message to the Bitcoin Development Mailing List the same day. “We recently experienced an increase in the number of reports for security vulnerabilities that can be easily (re-)discovered,” Poinsot wrote. “This is largely due to LLMs drastically reducing the bar to find certain classes of issues or identify covert fixes.” How the policy worked before Bitcoin Core , the software that runs on most nodes in the Bitcoin network, has graded each reported vulnerability by severity and timed its disclosure to match. Low-severity flaws were made public two weeks after the next major version shipped. Medium- and high-severity issues stayed under embargo until two weeks after the last affected release reached end of life, a span that could stretch to a year. The extended timelines gave node operators, many of whom upgrade at a slow pace, time to move to patched software before details became public. In practice, the approach meant fixes went unreleased for older maintained versions and arrived with the next major release. Poinsot argued that this tradeoff fails for bugs that are easy to rediscover. “The embargo period achieves little but it delays the availability of a fixed release,” the policy reads. What changes During triage, Bitcoin Core can flag a vulnerability as “easily discoverable,” a category the policy defines as issues that can be found “with minimal effort, such as through a simple LLM prompt.” The label is open to flaws found by other means as well. For those issues, the project will backport a fix to every maintained major version, cut point releases as soon as possible and publish a security advisory with some details at the same time as the fixed software. Poinsot acknowledged that such fixes will have less testing time before they reach users. Vulnerabilities outside that category keep the existing severity-based schedule. Critical bugs, those that could enable coin theft at the protocol level, inflate the supply or cause a permanent chain split, remain outside the standard policy and will be handled case by case. Developer Antoine Riard pushed for an option to ship a fix without an advisory and withhold details on a case-by-case basis. Poinsot declined, writing that alerting users without details “could create more risk unnecessarily” by prompting a rushed migration among users who would otherwise be unaffected. A summer of AI-driven reports The change follows months of heightened pressure on Bitcoin’s open-source projects. In late July, a volunteer group of 16 developers known as the Bitcoin Red Team ran AI models across 390 bitcoin repositories in about a day and logged 4,962 findings, including 85 rated critical . Within days, a BTCPay Server flaw the group had reported in private was exploited on live merchant servers, draining Lightning nodes. In August, Core Lightning developers told operators to upgrade or disconnect after AI-generated reports to the project proved accurate. The Red Team effort followed a Coldcard hardware wallet exploit in which attackers drained 594 BTC in 25 minutes on July 30. Losses across four sweeps approached $114 million. This post Bitcoin Core Ends Long Embargoes for Bugs AI Can Rediscover first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman .

title: AI bubble update: 79% of companies say their GPUs sit idle at least half the time, yet most plan new AI platforms
body:
Most surveyed companies running AI in production say the GPUs they use sit idle at least half the time, and most of those companies plan to add or switch AI compute platforms anyway, according to the latest data from VentureBeat Intelligence.
A whopping 79% of the 218 respondents who reported GPU utilization said their GPUs are busy half the time or less, across three monthly VB Pulse surveys from July through September . Among those companies, 70% said they plan to adopt a new, additional or replacement AI compute platform within the next 12 months. The share with idle GPUs held between 77% and 81% in each of the three months. We reported the September results Thursday ; the three months of data show the pattern holding steady.
Those numbers matter because Wall Street is arguing over whether AI is a bubble. On October 13, the International Monetary Fund warned that a sharp fall in AI share prices could threaten global financial stability . Most of that argument has focused on the companies selling AI compute, such as Nvidia, cloud giants Microsoft, Google and Amazon Web Services, and specialized GPU clouds like CoreWeave, and on whether they are building more capacity than their customers will pay for. We looked at what those customers are actually doing.
At first glance, the numbers look like a contradiction. Why would companies with so much unused GPU capacity plan to add or switch AI compute platforms? And why would they leave GPUs idle when, as technology leaders tell me, they are under heavy pressure in this fall's budget season to cut their AI bills?
The demand for AI is real, but it is landing in a different place than the idle GPUs. Professionals and consumers keep using more AI, and much of that work runs through the frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI. That demand will keep supporting those companies' spending on compute for some time. The mismatch sits one level down, inside enterprises that are paying for two kinds of AI that cannot easily stand in for each other.
The first kind is capacity. I believe many companies were scared by reports of GPU shortages in 2024 and 2025 and lined up GPU capacity so they would not be caught short. Much of the capacity companies use sits idle, our surveys show, though the surveys did not ask how companies got that capacity or whether they controlled it directly..
The second kind is frontier models. Engineers and other employees have preferred the most capable models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, paid by the token through those companies' APIs, through monthly subscriptions or through the big cloud providers. The thinking was that companies needed the best intelligence to race ahead, and they would sort out the economics later. Uber's chief technology officer, Praveen Neppalli Naga, said in August that "we're coming to the end of the so-called tokenmaxxing era," after Uber spent its 2026 AI budget within a few months, according to Fortune. An AI leader at a Fortune 500 company, speaking on background, told me in October that AI costs keep rising, and that while the company expects productivity gains to offset them eventually, it does not know that yet.
Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google now sell Anthropic's or OpenAI's models through their clouds, and OpenAI said on Wednesday that its models will reach Google Cloud in the coming weeks. OpenAI's frontier GPT models and Anthropic's Claude models are closed, so the cloud provider or the model maker runs them on its own infrastructure and bills by the token or for capacity reserved for that one model. A company cannot load them onto GPUs it already controls. To shift work onto those GPUs, a company has to switch to an open-weight model and run it itself. That is real engineering work, and the cheapest options raise questions of their own: In VentureBeat's own tests in October, DeepSeek was the cheapest of five open models we ran, and DeepSeek comes from a Chinese lab — and many companies are still reluctant to double down on Chinese models as their main workhorse models, for a variety of reasons .
Our data fits this reading in three ways:
Companies with idle GPUs are still planning new platforms. Within the next year, 70% of companies with idle GPUs plan to adopt a new, additional or replacement AI compute platform. That’s about the same as the 74% of companies whose GPUs are busy, a statistically insignificant difference.
Companies with idle GPUs are considering cloud platforms or model providers. Among those planning a new platform, 90% named a cloud platform or a model provider among their options, and only 8% named an on-premises or colocated GPU cluster or a self-managed open-source stack.
Companies that run their own stack report higher GPU utilization. Among companies running AI on an on-premises or colocated GPU cluster or a self-managed open-source stack, 56% said their GPUs sit idle at least half the time, against 83% of all other companies running AI in production. We did not ask why. My guess is that a team running its own stack sees every idle hour directly and has the engineers to fill it.
Few companies planning a new AI compute platform have a finance-reviewed ROI figure. In the September survey , 91% of all companies planning a new AI compute platform had no return-on-investment figure their finance team had reviewed. To be sure, some idle capacity may be deliberate, since a company may reserve GPUs for spikes in demand, and a planned platform may replace an older one.
I expect a growing share of companies’ AI spending to go to model usage. By this, I mean the per-token charges that model makers and cloud providers collect on every request. Those charges are likely to grow because companies are shifting to AI agents, which plan and carry out multi-step tasks. Inference costs per agentic workflow will rise more than fivefold through 2028 , Gartner has predicted. Inference is the work a model does to answer each request. The price of each token is falling, but agents use so many more tokens, and more expensive ones, that the falling prices do not keep up.
Most of the tokens a coding agent processes are context, meaning the instructions, documents and history it rereads at every step. That is why caching matters so much. In a technical guide first published in March, two Nvidia engineers reported that after the first call in a Claude Code session, later calls reuse 85% to 97% of their context from a cache. Reusing that context is far cheaper than processing it fresh: Anthropic charges between one-fortieth and one-tenth of its normal input price for cached tokens, depending on the model.
Adding agents multiplies the bill, too. Coding-agent teams, with a lead agent running up to five subagents at once, cost 1.8 to 5.1 times as much as a single agent, and only one of four team setups improved benchmark scores by a statistically significant margin, according to Vals AI .
Companies should get more finished work out of the compute and tokens they already pay for before they sign the next contract. In practice, that means six things:
measuring the cost of each completed task, across both GPU capacity and API spending;
testing which model and effort level to set as the company default, judged by the cost of each finished task rather than the price per token, since a cheaper model can use so many more tokens that it costs more per task;
sending each agent only the context it needs, and caching repeated context, whether through model-provider APIs or on companies' own infrastructure;
adding a second agent only when the task splits into parallel pieces;
moving routine, high-volume work, such as classification, extraction and summarization, from frontier model APIs to open models running on idle capacity;
filling the remaining idle GPU hours with work that can wait, such as batch inference, model evaluations and fine-tuning.
Those choices are the agenda of VentureBeat's Agentic Infrastructure Stack Summit on October 28 in San Francisco, under the theme "Smarter Agents Need More Memory. The Best Teams Will Use Less." The day runs in four parts:
How many agents to run: Jeff Simon, chief information officer of T-Mobile; Val Bercovici, chief AI officer of WEKA; Deepika Khera, senior director of AI at PayPal; and Ben Kus, chief technology officer of Box, on coordinating agents while controlling cost and risk.
How much context to give them: Anjul Bhambhri, senior vice president of engineering at Adobe, and Vijoy Pandey, senior vice president and general manager of Outshift by Cisco, on memory, context and coordination.
What inference really costs: Micah Hill-Smith, co-founder and CEO of Artificial Analysis, and Uday Kiran Medisetty, distinguished engineer at Uber, on inference economics, model routing and the cost of completed tasks. The track also includes a WEKA-sponsored panel with Sudhanshu Bist of Upwork and Val Bercovici of WEKA.
Whether to build your own AI factory: Reynold D'Sa, corporate vice president at Microsoft, on infrastructure for agentic workloads, alongside a session featuring Omni and Acxiom.
VentureBeat Intelligence pooled its July , August and September 2026 VB Pulse surveys on AI infrastructure and compute. The surveys drew 385 qualified respondents at organizations with 100 or more employees, including consultants answering for their main client. Each month's survey drew a different self-selected group of VentureBeat readers and panel respondents, so the results describe those respondents rather than every company.
Companies running AI in production whose GPUs are busy half the time or less
Companies with GPUs busy half the time or less that plan a new, additional or replacement AI compute platform within 12 months
Companies with GPUs busy more than half the time that plan a new, additional or replacement AI compute platform within 12 months
Companies with idle GPUs planning a new platform that named a cloud platform or a model provider among their options
Companies with idle GPUs planning a new platform that named an on-premises or colocated GPU cluster or a self-managed open-source stack
Companies running AI on an on-premises or colocated GPU cluster or a self-managed open-source stack whose GPUs are busy half the time or less
All other companies running AI in production whose GPUs are busy half the time or less
September only: companies planning a new AI compute platform with no return figure reviewed by their finance team
The utilization figures cover companies running AI in production that gave a utilization figure. They leave out companies that said they do not measure GPU use or do not operate GPUs, and July respondents who chose more than one utilization answer. Respondents could name several platforms they use and several they are considering. Cloud platforms are AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure; model providers are OpenAI, Anthropic and Google's Gemini. July and September use the screening rules of their published reports. August leaves out respondents whose written-in job titles fall outside AI work, so its total differs slightly from the August report. Month-to-month differences in the idle share are statistically insignificant. Differences between groups count as statistically significant only when a Fisher's exact test or chi-square test gives p below 0.05.

title: Ukrainian commanders report first known aerial drone rescue of wounded soldier
body: Ukraine’s armed forces have evacuated a wounded soldier from the front line by drone for the first time, Reuters reported . The news agency recounted the rescue of 49-year-old Kostiantyn Vlasenko in the Kharkiv region, based on his account. Vlasenko had been on the front line since May 2025, holding a position in a trench with a fellow soldier whose call sign was Basky. They received food and supplies by drone. There was no other way to deliver them — the sheer number of drones made any movement near the front line potentially deadly, Reuters reported. They were due to rotate out in the fall of 2025, but the two soldiers sent to relieve them were killed on the way to their position. Two more soldiers sent to retrieve their bodies were then killed. Vlasenko said that was when he realized that “no one would get out anymore.” In mid-February, after 10 months in the trench, Vlasenko and Basky were forced to abandon their position because it had flooded. They moved into a partially destroyed school building. One day, when they went out to collect a package of food and clothing dropped by their fellow soldiers, a Russian reconnaissance drone spotted them. Another drone then struck their position. Basky, who turned 50 that day, was killed. The blast shattered Vlasenko’s left foot and left his right leg broken and twisted. He managed to crawl into shelter — a pit measuring about 80 by 60 centimeters beneath a metal boiler used to heat the school. Vlasenko said his left foot gradually “rotted away,” while a bone protruded from his injured right shin. He decided to cut off his right foot as well. “I had to amputate it because it was just dragging along behind me. The leg was dragging so much that the bone was sticking out further and further,” he said. As Vlasenko “started losing hope,” Reuters reported, his commanders began looking for ways to evacuate him. Using an armored vehicle was impossible because of the drones, so they initially planned to rescue him with unmanned ground vehicles. But drones destroyed two of those vehicles as they tried to reach him. The commanders then decided to try a new heavy-lift drone capable of carrying a 90-kilogram load for up to 25 kilometers. That was enough: The officers estimated that Vlasenko weighed about 70 kilograms after a year on the front line, and a safe location behind the lines was 15 kilometers away. Vlasenko was evacuated in early October after spending months alone awaiting rescue. The day before, a supply drop brought him a harness to put on and attach to a cable, along with a phone containing instructional videos. During the evacuation, the drone carrying Vlasenko climbed to an altitude of 70 meters. Three other small drones escorted it to distract Russian drones. Before and during the evacuation, four FPV drone crews, fixed-wing drones, and artillery struck nearby positions identified as those of Russian drone operators. The flight lasted 15 minutes. “I wasn’t afraid of falling, say somewhere into the forest, I wasn’t afraid of that. But I was afraid of falling into the water, because I can’t swim,” Vlasenko said. He is now undergoing rehabilitation at a hospital in Kharkiv. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. title: Animations for System Builders
body:
One of the things I love using LLMs for is helping me understand systems better. In the Strands Decider post I wrote about how I often ask ask me questions to check I understand this . The other technique Iâm enjoying right now, and am delighted to see folks around me using too, is building animations.
Animations can help us build an intuition for how and why systems work, or how and why they fail.
Hereâs one example: did you know that a Raft cluster can lose writes if even one of the cluster members has a storage layer that lies about fsync() ?
When I built Stability Sim , I wanted to help engineers understand metastable failures better. That worked pretty well on an abstract level (e.g. retries and queues make metastability really easy to trigger ), but I still hear doubts that these behaviors happen in real systems. After all, those real systems are production-proven, and wouldnât we have shaken out the behaviors by now if they existed?
In this example, captured from traces on real Postgres 16 running in a real MicroVM. Before a load spike, the database is easily able to handle its 20 queries-per-second load, thanks to the whole working set sitting in the page cache. But after the load spike, weâve filled up a lot of the memory running queries (each takes 12MB), which now run slower because theyâre served off the disk rather than the page cache. I like this example, because it shows that even simple, non-distributed systems have these behaviors.
Again, we have load spike triggering the metastable state. Writes, in this case. The overloaded peers look like theyâre unavailable, which triggers a storm of application-level resends. I like this example, because etcd is widely-used quality software. Operational experience doesnât seem to effectively shake out these kinds of issues.
When I wrote Garbage Collection and Metastability , a widely-known systems academic told me that it was a fantasy . Iâve seen it happen in the wild in ways I couldnât share, and I can forgive people for not believing this can happen based on the hand waving in the blog.
So itâs nice to have a real world example, picking on etcd again.
At the start, weâre ticking along nicely at 500 reads/second, before spiking load to 1000 reads/s. The read spike increases the time spent in GC, increasing average tenure, and making less CPU available for the read workload. This is a self-reinforcing loop, and the system doesnât recover without intercession.
I believe the same thing could happen on a runtime without GC, due to increasing work in the allocator, but havenât been able to reproduce that yet.
The animations here are all generated with Kiro and KiroCrew , mostly with Opus 5.5. The actual results came from a real test environment, which captures the traces that back the animations.

title: 2026.43: A New Era
body: Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! This week marks a new era for Stratechery, which is now presented by Stripe . I’m excited about what this partnership can unlock, starting with in-person on-video episodes of Sharp Tech. Check out the YouTube video above (or watch it on Stratechery ); and, for subscribers, look forward to a bonus episode showing up in your subscriber feed every Sunday morning (add your feed on sharptech.fm ). Here were a few of our favorite topics this week: The Best iPad; The Worst Phone. John Gruber wrote a great review of the iPhone Duo, which we broke down on Dithering . In short, it’s an iPad that fits in your pocket, and it’s awesome at that; just don’t expect a good phone. Plus, on Monday we discussed Apple’s surprising partnership with Meta for edge AI, a topic I also covered in Tuesday’s Update . — Ben Thompson The SS Sarandos in a Storm. The past week has seen a flood of bad news for Netflix: layoffs, executive departures, another disappointing round of earnings, and another hit to a share price that has taken a 40% hit over the past 12 months. Wednesday’s Update provides a comprehensive state of the union , and we doubled back on the topic for a fun conversation on this week’s Sharp Tech , where we divided the company’s problems into areas that can be fixed (the content) and what may be much trickier (growing the business in a world where Meta and YouTube are primary engagement competition). — Andrew Sharp You Can See Everything, But Can’t Trust Anyone. Allow me to be the 1,000th person on the internet to recommend Nathan Fielder’s new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything . After declaring on Sharp Tech last week that I wasn’t interested in seeing it, I did in fact check it out, and wound up loving it. I wrote about my experience on Sharp Text , with 5 spoiler-free notes for anyone still on the fence, and 5 more reactions for anyone who’s seen it. Compulsively watchable (and worth seeing in a theater), I think it may have also been the most effective document of our modern media environment I’ve ever seen. — AS Presented by It’s kind of weird to be the Internet’s number one fan of ads. What makes it even weirder is that I have been the Internet’s number one fan of ads without actually having ads on Stratechery . That second part is changing: I’m super excited to announce that Stripe is going to be the presenting sponsor of Stratechery. And, at the end of the day, for me it couldn’t be any other company. One of my hangups in terms of advertising is that I take my ethics super seriously, and ultimately, if a company is helping pay the bills, it’s hard to be truly objective about them. What I realized, however, is that it’s hard for me to be objective about Stripe anyway. I wanted to be a professional blogger long before I started Stratechery; however, I thought I had missed my chance, particularly as it became clear that advertising was not a long term business model for a one-person site. However, when Stripe launched with support for recurring billing, I realized there was a better model: subscriptions. 13 years later, and I’m still a happy customer. Or, to put it another way, I’m already conflicted because I love Stripe. I’m not the only one: more than 5 million businesses use Stripe, accounting for 1.7% of global GDP. Moreover, a lot of those businesses are Internet native and accretive to the world’s economy, which is to say that Stripe is literally making the world a better place. That’s an easy company to get behind, especially since they have been behind Stratechery from the very beginning. — Ben Thompson Stratechery Articles and Updates Do You Trust Apple? — Apple has a lot of trust in terms of delivering integrated products and preserving privacy; the real trust question is if you think Siri AI will justify investing more in their ecosystem. Muse Spark Open, Meta + Apple, Thin and Thick — Meta has a new open source model, and to everyone’s surprise, they are are partnering with Apple to make sure you can run it locally. Netflix Earnings, Business or Franchise, Disney’s Deal — Netflix has a solid business, which is exactly the problem: the company increasingly seems like a business and not a franchise, at least in terms of growth. An Interview with Craig Moffett About SpaceX and Bubbles — An interview with Craig Moffett about SpaceX, from launch to broadband to mobile, plus how he is applying the lessons of the dot-com bubble to today. title: Iran sent bomb-making manual as it organised plots in the UK
body: An Iranian plotter transferred bomb-making instructions to the UK as it sought agents to carry out an atrocity in a major city. A court heard on Friday that investigators uncovered steps for making a “powder chlorine and rake oil fluid bomb” in a document prepared in Iran. Prosecutors alleged that a terrorism suspect was found to have instructions on his phone for making a home-made bomb to attack Jews in the UK. Salam Ahmadyan, 36, and Rahman ⁠Salehi, 34, are accused of plotting acts of terrorism at the behest of a regime agent believed to be in Iran . The targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue, the scene of a deadly attack a year ago in which two Jewish worshippers were killed. Mr Ahmadyan, who had a Kurdish Sorani interpreter, and Mr ⁠Salehi, were told they would face trial in June in Manchester, charged with terrorism offences relating to the alleged plot. Both deny the charges. At a preliminary hearing at the Old Bailey in London, prosecutor Lydon Harris told the court that Mr Ahmadyan was asked by a third party to buy components for a home-made bomb around September 8 this year. Ten days later he recruited Mr Salehi to help him. He subsequently purchased various materials online, Mr Harris said. “On September 20, that being the date of the Jewish celebration of Yom Kippur, both defendants were seen by police officers driving around areas of Manchester, taking photographs and video recordings of various areas,” the prosecutor said. “The Crown’s case is that this was reconnaissance conducted for the purposes of a future attack on the Jewish community in Manchester.” Mr Harris told the court that the “police investigation has revealed Mr Ahmadyan was in contact with a third party who appears to be located in Iran”. “Analysis of his mobile telephone shows that it contained a file, the title of which, when translated into English, is steps for making a powder chlorine and rake oil fluid bomb.” Both suspects were interviewed by police and Mr Salehi denied any involvement in a terrorist plot, said Mr Harris. He said that Mr Ahmadyan made no comment on the questions he was asked. At a previous hearing, the court was told both suspects had come to Britain from Europe in small boats. Mr Salehi had arrived in 2020 and had been granted asylum, while Mr Ahmadyan came in 2023 and his asylum claim was still outstanding.

title: Air Defenses at Russian Drone Factory Linked to Forced Labor Rival Putin’s Residence
body:
Russia’s main Shahed drone factory has become one of the country’s most heavily defended sites, alongside President Vladimir Putin’s Valdai residence, according to satellite imagery published on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
The expanding defenses surround the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, where a separate US research report describes forced labor involving North Korean workers and the exploitation of foreign women recruited largely from Africa.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Radio Svoboda identified 33 air-defense positions around the complex, including new concrete towers and raised platforms intended for Pantsir or Tor air-defense systems.
The site also has towers for heavy anti-aircraft machine guns and structures supporting anti-drone barriers over production buildings.
The concentration of defenses puts Alabuga alongside Putin’s Valdai residence, where Radio Svoboda identified 31 towers and two S-300 or S-400 missile positions. The outlet reported more than 100 new air-defense positions across Moscow and the surrounding region since the full-scale invasion. Its findings do not establish a definitive national ranking of the best-protected sites.
An investigation by the Institute for Science and International Security , updated on Sept. 25, used high-resolution Vantor and Airbus imagery to document two defensive perimeters around Alabuga’s production facilities.
Shorter towers surround the main production buildings. A taller outer ring encloses a wider area, including the neighboring Alabuga-Volokno plant, which supplies carbon fiber used in drone manufacturing.
Cables strung between the towers are intended to intercept incoming drones or cruise missiles before they reach the buildings, or force them to fly higher and become more exposed to air defenses, the institute said.
Satellite images also show new production buildings being hardened with layers of earth and reinforced concrete.
Kyiv Post previously reported on Alabuga’s expansion , including new industrial buildings and dormitories for foreign workers.
A report published on Oct. 14 by the Center for Strategic and International Studies and the George W. Bush Institute describes Alabuga as a site of human trafficking and serious labor abuses.
The report cites Ukrainian intelligence estimates of up to 12,000 North Korean workers assigned to the complex. Its underlying source, however, is a November 2025 intelligence announcement describing plans to bring in that number, previously covered by Kyiv Post .
The figure therefore should not be treated as an independently verified count of workers currently at the factory.
According to the report, North Korean laborers earn approximately $2.50 an hour, while their government withholds 70–90% of their wages. At that rate, a 12-hour shift would generate $30 before deductions, leaving the worker between $3 and $9.
The authors describe the arrangement as state-sponsored trafficking, with minders restricting workers’ movements and Pyongyang collecting most of their earnings.
The report also notes that the overseas labor arrangement violates UN sanctions requiring countries to repatriate North Korean workers by December 2019.
Alabuga also recruits Russian students as young as 15 under a “work experience” program, according to the CSIS–Bush Institute report. They reportedly face long shifts, production quotas and threats of fines if they tell their families what they build.
Foreign women recruited through the Alabuga Start program are promised hospitality jobs, educational opportunities and salaries starting above $500 a month, the report said. Some instead find themselves assigned to weapons production.
Their pay is reduced by deductions for flights, accommodation, medical care and mandatory Russian-language classes. The report also describes passport confiscation, restrictions on movement and threats against workers who discuss their jobs.
Kyiv Post previously reported on African and Asian women misled into assembling drones , drawing on interviews with recruits who said their actual work differed from what they had been promised.
These accounts distinguish between agreeing to travel to Russia for employment and consenting to the work and conditions encountered after arrival.
Located more than 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine, Alabuga is a principal Russian production center for Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones and their Russian Geran variants.
The CSIS–Bush Institute report describes a complex capable of producing more than 5,500 drones a month, with extensive construction supporting its growing workforce and output.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the site. An April 2024 strike injured 13 students employed at the complex , according to reports at the time.
Ukraine’s General Staff also confirmed a strike on the facility in June 2025 . The publicly available reporting does not establish the extent of any lasting reduction in production.
The drones manufactured at Alabuga form part of Russia’s long-range bombardment of Ukraine. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission recorded 165 civilians killed and 1,119 injured by long-range missiles and drones in September 2026 . Those figures cover multiple weapon types and cannot be attributed solely to Alabuga-made drones.
Ukraine has sought US Tomahawk cruise missiles to strengthen its ability to strike military-industrial targets deep inside Russia. President Volodymyr Zelensky pressed the request during his October 2025 visit to Washington , but the meeting ended without a commitment to supply them.
Putin had warned that providing Tomahawks would damage US-Russian relations , while Trump publicly raised concerns about escalation and American stockpiles.
Stefan Korshak is the Kyiv Post Senior Defense Correspondent. He is from Houston Texas, is a Yalie and since the mid-1990s has worked as correspondent/photographer for newswire, newspapers, television and radio. He has reported from five wars but most enjoys doing articles on wildlife and nature. You can read his weekly blog on the Russo-Ukraine War on Facebook, Substack and Medium. His new book on the 2022 Siege of Mariupol is available on Amazon UK and Amazon US .

title: Denmark To Buy Anthem Munitions, Joint Strike Missiles In Dual Long-Range Strike Push
body: Denmark is set to acquire Anthem long-range strike weapons from U.S.-based defense startup Covenant, as well as Joint Strike Missile (JSM) cruise missiles from Norway’s Kongsberg Defense & Aerospace. The twin-track approach by the Nordic NATO member will give it all-new options for launching long-range strikes from the ground and air. Furthermore, Denmark’s move reflects a broader European push to acquire longer-range strike options , especially by NATO allies seeking to deter Russia . Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus announced the planned purchases yesterday. He said the new weapons would strengthen Denmark’s ability to respond to an attack and strike targets “behind enemy lines,” according to Reuters . Copenhagen has not disclosed the number of missiles involved, the value of the purchases, or expected delivery dates. A stock picture of Covenant’s Anthem long-range strike weapon. Covenant “We’re in a serious and deteriorating security situation, and that is why we are building up the defense and strengthening our combat power,” Bruus told reporters . The planned acquisitions are a “strong signal that we have the ability to strike back,” he added , without explicitly naming any particular adversary. The Danish government did say last year that it would pursue new long-range offensive precision weapons, in general, in response to the growing security concerns in Europe amid Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Bruus’ announcement comes amid a new surge in geopolitical friction between Russia and members of the NATO alliance . A stock picture of a Joint Strike Missile (JSM), seen here being loaded onto a US Air Force F-16 Viper during a test in 2018. USAF The two new acquisitions will provide Denmark with important complementary strike options. Anthem is a ground-launched weapon, while JSM is designed to be air-launched, including by stealthy F-35 fighters just like those in Danish Air Force service today. Together, the weapons are set to expand the range of platforms from which Denmark can deliver stand-off precision strikes and give its armed forces additional options for attacking high-value military targets. A Royal Danish Air Force F-35A takes off for a Red Flag-Nellis 24-2 mission at Nellis AFB, Nevada, on March 13, 2024. U.S. Air Force photo by William R. Lewis William Lewis Anthem is being developed by Covenant, a U.S.-based defense company that has also outlined plans to establish missile production in Germany and Israel. The system’s selection by Denmark gives the company an important European customer as NATO members seek to expand their inventories of long-range weapons. Covenant’s Anthem is in a category of munitions that increasingly blurs the line between long-range kamikaze drones and traditional cruise missiles. It is designed to offer a lower-cost, longer-range strike capability that can be produced more easily and at greater scale than many existing systems. Covenant has not publicly disclosed the weapon’s range. Still-unconfirmed reports put it at roughly 740 miles (1,200 kilometers). It is also said to carry a warhead weighing more than 200 kilograms (441 pounds). It also uses a solid rocket motor to provide an initial boost at launch before transitioning to a heavy-fuel jet engine for cruise flight. Currently, it is unclear how exactly Anthem is launched. It has already undergone testing with the U.S. Army , and images from those trials show the weapons being handled on the ground using a tricycle undercarriage. This may point to rocket-assisted takeoffs from runways. A Covenant cruise missile is prepared for a live-fire demonstration at the Africa Multidomain Training and Experimentation Center in Tan-Tan, Morocco, August 5, 2026. U.S. Army photo by Capt. Jordan Beagle Last month, Covenant announced it had already conducted more than 200 test flights of Anthem and had secured roughly $150 million in orders. It also disclosed that an unidentified international customer was expected to begin receiving German-built weapons before the end of this year. This may well be Denmark, though there could also be other customers that have yet to emerge publicly. Meanwhile, U.S. Army deliveries are expected in 2027, under an accelerated qualification contract. Anthem reflects a broader push, globally, for new long-range strike weapons that can be manufactured rapidly and in large quantities , potentially trading some of the performance and sophistication of more expensive, ‘exquisite’ weapons for affordability, scalability, and mass availability. Recent conflicts in the Middle East , as well as the war in Ukraine , have underscored the challenges of bolstering stockpiles of critical munitions and replenishing them during prolonged fighting. JSM, developed by Kongsberg in cooperation with U.S. defense contractor Raytheon, is a traditional air-launched cruise missile capable of being employed against targets on land and at sea. It is capable of being carried internally and externally on the A and C variants of the F-35. The design has also been fit-checked for external carriage on a variety of other tactical jets. As already mentioned, JSM will provide an entirely new stand-off precision-strike option for Denmark’s F-35As. These are the only tactical jets in Danish service today following the retirement of the country’s F-16 Vipers in January. Pictures showing work on integrating the Joint Strike Missile on all three variants of the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter, as well as the F-16. Kongsberg Kongsberg has identified Denmark as the seventh country to select JSM , although the final contract scope and value remain subject to negotiations. JSM is an enlarged derivative of the surface-launched Naval Strike Missile (NSM), which has also seen growing worldwide sales in recent years, including to the U.S. military . Since 2025, Denmark has also been fielding NSM on its Iver Huitfeldt class frigates and as part of a ground-based coastal defense system. Since JSM is designed to be air-launched, its maximum range is dependent in part on the altitude at which the missile is released, as well as the speed of the aircraft carrying it. Kongsberg has said in the past the missile can fly out to a range of more than 300 nautical miles, but also that its reach is significantly cut back when it is employed in its low-altitude penetration mode. A briefing slide with various details about the JSM’s capabilities. Kongsberg The JSM carries a 260-pound warhead and uses a combination of GPS, inertial navigation (INS), and terrain mapping to guide it toward its target. The terrain-mapping capability provides an additional means of navigation, helping the missile maintain its course even in environments where GPS connectivity is degraded or unavailable. The missile switches over to an imaging infrared seeker to provide precise target discrimination during the terminal phase of flight. Because the seeker operates passively, it does not rely on emitting radiofrequency signals, reducing the risk of detection and making it immune to conventional radiofrequency jamming. The agile JSM’s overall design also includes reduced-signature features to help limit its detectability and improve its survivability on the way to the target. A U.S. Air Force F-35A releases a Joint Strike Missile (JSM) during a test. Norwegian Defense Materiel Agency A two-way datalink also allows the missile to receive updated targeting information while en route, or to be redirected toward an entirely different target during the mid-course phase of flight. The dual purchases build on a broader Danish effort to field new options for holding targets at extended ranges at risk. Denmark previously operated eight M270 Multiple Launch Rocket Systems (MLRS), but retired them in 2004. The country is now introducing Israel’s PULS rocket artillery system , which can employ different rocket and missile types depending on the mission. Presently, the Danish military looks to be fielding PULS just with artillery rockets. In terms of Denmark’s current and future ground-based capabilities, PULS – which stands for Precise and Universal Launch System – and Anthem will serve different. In Danish service, PULS provides a flexible rocket artillery capability, while Anthem will offer a cruise-missile-like option for longer-range precision attacks. The acquisition of JSM also reflects the importance of Denmark’s F-35 fleet to its future combat capability. Air-launched weapons offer mobility and flexibility, but their employment depends on available aircraft. In this context, Denmark’s planned expansion of its F-35 fleet from 27 to 43 aircraft, announced in October 2025 , will provide a larger platform base for its emerging long-range strike capability. There could be some overlap here between Denmark’s growing array of air- and ground-based strike capabilities, as well. Dutch F-35As demonstrated their ability to provide targeting data to PULS launchers during a NATO exercise last year. A ground-launched weapon like Anthem also provides an alternative long-range strike option that does not require a fighter to carry it aloft, creating additional operational flexibility. For Denmark, acquiring JSMs and Anthems also offers the appeal of adding a capable higher-end munition alongside a more affordable, readily available long-range strike weapon. Reuters has reported that Covenant expects Anthem to eventually cost in the mid-six-figure range, although a final unit price has not been disclosed. Meanwhile, the JSM has a reported unit cost of approximately $2.8 million . As mentioned, the announcement of the Anthem and JSM purchase is fully in line with prior statements from the government in Copenhagen about acquiring new long-range strike options. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen previously urged the military to accelerate procurement across the board after years of comparatively limited defense spending. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen meets conscripts during a visit to Air Base Karup, the main air base of the Royal Danish Air Force, in Jutland, Denmark on March 7, 2024. (Photo by Mikkel Berg Pedersen / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP) / Denmark OUT MIKKEL BERG PEDERSEN The long-range strike acquisitions also fit into a broader NATO effort to strengthen deterrence across the Baltic region and the alliance’s northeastern flank. Denmark occupies a strategically important position linking the Baltic Sea to the North Sea, while its forces contribute to NATO’s regional presence and reinforcement plans. The ability to strike targets deep behind enemy lines will provide a new ability for Denmark to threaten an adversary’s military infrastructure, command facilities, and other critical targets. Denmark is far from alone in pursuing new long-range strike capabilities. In September, Latvia moved to acquire Anduril’s Barracuda family of long-range strike missiles , building on its earlier order for Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) short-range ballistic missiles. Poland is expanding its own layered strike capabilities , while France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Sweden and the United Kingdom are working on the European Long-Range Strike Approach (ELSA) initiative to accelerate the development and procurement of next-generation weapons. The efforts reflect a wider shift across Europe toward restoring deep-strike capabilities that have been relatively scarce among NATO’s European members since the end of the Cold War. All of this is happening while the Baltic states, in particular, increasingly voice their concerns that Russia could seek to exploit vulnerabilities along NATO’s northeastern flank. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have all warned about the risks posed by Russian force expansion, airspace incursions, sabotage, and other potential provocations. In response, NATO has stepped up its regional posture through initiatives, including Operation Eastern Sentry . Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus (right) speaks with military personnel during a visit to the Antenna Park in Nuuk, Greenland, on August 26, 2026. Photo by Thomas Traasdahl / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP THOMAS TRAASDAHL The news about Denmark’s new long-range strike plans has already drawn a heated reaction from Moscow. Russia’s embassy in Copenhagen accused Denmark of pursuing confrontation with Russia and warned of “inevitable disastrous consequences,” Reuters reported . Many details about the planned Anthem and JSM acquisitions still remain to be learned. However, the announcement yesterday is a clear signal of Copenhagen’s intention to give its armed forces a more substantial ability to threaten targets at distance, and reflects still-growing trends elsewhere in Europe. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Denmark To Buy Anthem Munitions, Joint Strike Missiles In Dual Long-Range Strike Push appeared first on TWZ .

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
body:
We're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.
We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.
Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai , Kimi Work , Kimi Code , and the Kimi API . The full model weights will be released by Nov 4.
Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.
Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%) . And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon , our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2% , above K3's 55.95% .
K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.
K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot , combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:
K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.
K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools , approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%) . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.
K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout.
Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences:
3D Make is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere.
With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis.
K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks:
Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's factual accuracy on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.)
The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice:
As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness.
Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example.
Evaluation and results. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.
On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance.
Open-weight principles. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure.
Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API .
Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026.
Kimi Enterprise administrators can enable K3.1 Pro for their organization; access is off by default at launch.
Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95.

title: Canadian Space Act Consultations Launch at SpaceBound 2026
body: This week, at SpaceBound 2026, the Honourable Mélanie Joly, Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, launched consultations on a new Canadian space act, aimed at modernizing and streamlining Canada’s in-space regulations, and Canada’s first Positioning, Navigation and Timing (PNT) Resilience Frameworak. As the world becomes increasingly complex, dangerous and unpredictable, with growing competition in space and shifting geopolitical dynamics, the Government of Canada is taking the necessary steps to modernize Canada’s space regulatory frameworks, strengthen our national security and safeguard Canada’s interests. Building on the Canadian Space Launch Act introduced in 2026 to enable commercial space launch, a space act would aim to establish a modern and comprehensive regulatory framework for Canadian activities in outer space, supporting Canada’s continued leadership as a responsible spacefaring nation and helping Canadian companies compete on the global stage. Canadians can help shape the space act through public consultations this fall. Minister Joly also announced the release of Canada’s first PNT Resilience Framework, which aims to bolster the resiliency of vital space infrastructure that is fundamental to building a strong, sovereign and secure Canada, for Canadians. The framework reflects a modern, coordinated approach by governments, industry and researchers to diversify Canada’s PNT sources, strengthen sovereign dual-use PNT capabilities, drive investment and innovation, and improve awareness and preparedness. The new framework enables initiatives that will do the following: Diversify Canada’s PNT sources : Recognizing the importance of advancing multiple sources of PNT such as space- and terrestrial-based technologies, sensors and emerging PNT technologies Strengthen sovereign dual-use PNT capabilities : Reflecting the role of domestic companies and technology development to support Canadian civilian and defence requirements Foster investment and innovation : Highlighting the importance of the right conditions to support companies developing and deploying dual-use PNT technology Improve awareness and preparedness : Reinforcing that resilience is strengthened by fostering collaboration, knowledge sharing and best practices PNT underpins nearly every aspect of our digital and physical infrastructure, and the new framework will help support and protect critical services, northern and remote operations, and Canada’s long-term competitiveness. By modernizing Canada’s space regulatory framework and strengthening the resilience of critical dual-use PNT infrastructure, our government is safeguarding Canada’s sovereignty, strengthening our national security and ensuring Canadian businesses and innovators are positioned to succeed in an increasingly competitive global space sector. “Building a strong Canada means supporting the industries that underpin our economic and national security. These initiatives will bring governments, world-leading space companies and innovators together to seize emerging economic opportunities and strengthen our position as a global leader in space. Our government is building a strong, resilient space sector that advances Canada’s economic security, space capabilities and national interests and will continue to do so for decades to come.” – The Honourable Mélanie Joly, Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions “Whether it’s to defend our sovereignty in the Arctic or operate alongside our allies, the Canadian Armed Forces depend on reliable positioning, navigation and timing systems. As threats evolve, strengthening the resilience of these critical capabilities is essential to our national security. This new framework will help advance Canadian-made, dual-use technologies, strengthen our defence readiness, and ensure the women and men who serve Canada can depend on the tools they need to carry out their missions.” – The Honourable David McGuinty, Minister of National Defence ADDITIONAL INFO In 2024, Canada’s space industry contributed $3.8 billion to Canada’s economy and supported more than 28,000 jobs across Canada. PNT technologies and systems provide the information we need to understand where we are (positioning), to determine how to get where we need to go (navigation) and to synchronize networks, or time-stamp (timing). An example of PNT systems that many Canadians rely on daily is global navigation satellite systems, such as the global positioning system (GPS) and Galileo. These everyday uses for PNT systems are diverse and critical. They include phone-based navigation and ride-sharing, payment processing and fraud prevention, first responder dispatch and communications, and power grid operations. title: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
body:
Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's being described as "Black October."
Nearly 70% of all websites use PHP, according to some estimates.
"In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year," John Milinovich, senior director of product management at Figma, wrote in a post on X on Thursday. "Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out."
Researchers at Google's Wiz and the AI firm Calif discovered major vulnerabilities in PHP in August by using advanced AI models from OpenAI and Google. But by Tuesday, the warnings had spread online, prompting governments and businesses around the globe to scramble to contain the fallout .
Major AI companies have been warning about the technology's advancing cybersecurity capabilities since April, when Anthropic announced a limited rollout of its powerful model called Mythos . Concerns mounted in July, when OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached a company called Hugging Face .
Experts believe the PHP security flaws serve as the latest example of what's to come.
Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, wrote in a post on X on Thursday that the cybersecurity landscape is likely to get "a lot worse" before it gets better.
"Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now," Clinton said. "Not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)"
While many large companies have access to advanced models that they can use to harden their systems, serious bugs could be more challenging for small- and medium-sized businesses to address, Chris Krebs, former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told CNBC on Friday. He encouraged smaller companies to "constantly" scan for vulnerabilities, deploy patches as fast as possible or take legacy systems offline.
"This is a significant week or two in cybersecurity," Krebs told CNBC's "Squawk Box." "As I mentioned, 3% of all critical vulnerabilities ever discovered have been found in the last month."
Figma's Milinovich encouraged individuals to set up two-factor authentication for "everything," use a password manager, set up an identity protection app and move smart devices to their own network. He added that people should lean in and experiment with AI to understand how powerful the tools have become.
"While I still firmly believe that AI will be a net positive for humanity, it's more clear to me than ever that the societal and individual risk is very real, and is playing out NOW," Milinovich said.
Krebs added that company leaders and employees should check in on their security teams.
"Make sure they're doing okay," he said. "They've had a heck of a week."
—CNBC's Isabel O’Brien contributed to this report

title: Initial shipment of Russian diesel heads to the US after Trump-Putin deal
body: A Malta-flagged tanker carrying 40,000 metric tonnes of Russian ⁠diesel is heading towards New York following an agreement with US President Donald Trump , LSEG data showed on Friday. Mr Trump has made several moves to try to ⁠bring down diesel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections ​, including waiving ⁠parts of a new ‌sanctions law against Russia and threatening Europe with a US diesel export ​ban unless countries release more from their emergency reserves. The medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel in the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the US on November 7. Russia agreed to lift a self-imposed ban on diesel exports and supply the fuel to global markets, including the US, after the agreement reached between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Mr Trump. Mr Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 ​tonnes in November and one million tonnes "immediately thereafter". Russia ‌will be able to increase ⁠diesel exports to between three million ​tonnes and 3.5 million tonnes per month by the end of the year, ​the country's ‌usual export volume of the fuel, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said last ⁠week. Last week, export diesel cargoes were loaded in the Russian Baltic ⁠port of Primorsk, but their final destinations are not clear, with most vessels signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, according to LSEG shipping data. Since the full EU embargo on the import of ​Russian oil products came into effect in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Brazil and Turkey, as well as to African countries.

Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority , adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”
That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.
Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.
“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”
“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”
If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

title: HD Hyundai–Kiewit Shipyard Plan Signals New Phase in South Korea’s U.S. Shipbuilding Push
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
A general view shows HD Hyundai Heavy Industries Ulsan Shipyard in Ulsan, South Korea, December 29, 2023. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries/Handout via REUTERS/File Photo
South Korea’s push to help rebuild the American shipbuilding industry is moving beyond investments in existing shipyards and toward the development of entirely new production capacity.
The latest example comes from HD Hyundai, one of the world’s largest shipbuilders, which has announced plans to develop a new U.S. shipyard in partnership with American engineering and construction giant Kiewit.
The proposed joint venture, HD Kiewit Shipbuilding, would combine South Korean shipbuilding technology with American engineering, fabrication and construction expertise. The companies are targeting construction beginning in 2027, with full-scale operations by 2029 and the potential to create up to 3,000 jobs.
But the significance extends beyond another planned shipyard. The project represents a potentially important step in South Korea’s $150 billion commitment to rebuilding U.S. shipbuilding capacity under the Make American Shipbuilding Great Again, or MASGA, initiative.
It also highlights two different approaches emerging among South Korea’s shipbuilding giants: Hanwha is investing heavily in expanding an existing American shipyard, while HD Hyundai is pursuing an entirely new production facility built around modern manufacturing technology.
HD Hyundai and Kiewit first announced a strategic partnership in July, laying the groundwork for cooperation on U.S. shipbuilding projects, including the fabrication of ship blocks and modules.
The latest agreement takes that relationship considerably further. Rather than simply supplying technology or helping modernize existing facilities, the companies envision a purpose-built shipyard on an existing industrial site with deepwater access to the Gulf of Mexico.
Although the companies have not formally identified the location, Kiewit already operates a major offshore fabrication complex in Ingleside, Texas, near Corpus Christi, where it has spent decades constructing large offshore energy structures.
The facility has the waterfront access, heavy industrial fabrication experience and infrastructure needed for major marine construction projects. Kiewit has previously fabricated enormous offshore production modules there, including the 35,000-ton topsides for Shell’s Appomattox platform.
The companies signed their initial shipbuilding partnership agreement at Kiewit’s Ingleside headquarters in July.
For HD Hyundai, the attraction is clear. Kiewit brings established U.S. industrial capabilities, while Hyundai brings the vessel design expertise, production systems and shipyard management experience developed through decades of building ships at scale in South Korea.
The companies intend to introduce HD Hyundai’s “Future of Shipyard” model, which incorporates digital twins, automated production systems, robotic welding and other advanced manufacturing technologies intended to improve productivity and reduce costs.
That approach could be particularly important in the United States, where labor shortages, aging infrastructure and production inefficiencies have contributed to some of the world’s highest shipbuilding costs.
The venture is initially targeting U.S. Navy auxiliary vessels, commercial ships and the fabrication of ship blocks and modules for other American shipbuilders.
The latter could prove especially important. Supplying prefabricated sections to existing yards would allow the venture to contribute to U.S. shipbuilding programs without necessarily waiting for an entire vessel construction program of its own.
The HD Hyundai–Kiewit project is the latest in a series of increasingly ambitious moves by South Korean shipbuilders to establish a permanent presence in the United States.
Hanwha got an early start with its $100 million acquisition of Philly Shipyard in 2024, becoming the first major South Korean shipbuilder to take ownership of an American shipyard.
In August 2025, Hanwha unveiled a $5 billion infrastructure plan aimed at transforming the Philadelphia facility into a high-volume production center.
The plan includes additional docks, new quays, expanded block assembly capacity and advanced manufacturing technology. Hanwha has set an ambitious goal of increasing annual production from fewer than two vessels to as many as 20.
The company has also begun building a commercial order pipeline, including plans for 10 Jones Act-compliant product tankers and LNG carriers, while pursuing opportunities in U.S. naval construction.
HD Hyundai, meanwhile, has been building its own network of American partnerships.
In July, it signed an agreement with Fraser Industries to explore shipyard modernization, including integrated design, production and management systems.
Other South Korean shipbuilders are pursuing similar arrangements. Samsung Heavy Industries has established partnerships involving advanced shipbuilding technology, automated production and workforce training, while Hanwha Ocean has expanded its cooperation with U.S. defense and engineering companies.
Those agreements gained additional momentum in July with the launch of the Korea–U.S. Shipbuilding Partnership Center in Washington, D.C.
The center was established to coordinate investment, technology transfer, workforce development and industrial cooperation under the $150 billion MASGA initiative, which emerged from the broader U.S.–South Korea trade agreement reached in 2025.
Its opening was accompanied by 15 agreements involving shipbuilders, technology companies, research institutions and other organizations from both countries.
The proposed Hyundai–Kiewit yard offers one of the clearest examples yet of how that cooperation could translate into new industrial capacity.
The investments are arriving at a time when the gap between American and Asian shipbuilding capacity remains enormous.
According to new BIMCO analysis , Chinese shipyards now control 64% of the global shipbuilding order book, compared with 19% for South Korea and 6% for Japan.
China also secured 74% of the compensated gross tonnage contracted worldwide over the past year, further strengthening its dominance across major commercial vessel sectors.
The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge facing Washington as it attempts to restore domestic shipbuilding capacity after decades of decline.
The United States is not starting from the same industrial position as its Asian competitors. South Korean and Chinese shipyards benefit from mature supplier networks, experienced workforces, established production systems and the economies of scale that come from building large numbers of ships.
Rebuilding those capabilities in the United States will require more than new docks and modern equipment.
An April report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that American Navy and Coast Guard shipbuilding programs have consistently suffered from cost overruns and delivery delays, with workforce shortages and infrastructure constraints among the major contributing factors.
The report also warned that efforts to expand naval and commercial shipbuilding could increase competition for many of the same skilled workers and suppliers.
That makes the involvement of established industrial contractors such as Kiewit particularly noteworthy.
Unlike a traditional shipbuilder entering a new market, Kiewit already has an American workforce, complex fabrication experience and relationships across major industrial supply chains.
Combined with HD Hyundai’s advanced production methods, those capabilities could offer a more practical starting point for expanding American shipbuilding than attempting to create an entirely new industrial operation from scratch.
Still, significant questions remain about the proposed venture.
HD Hyundai and Kiewit have not disclosed the project’s expected investment cost, identified the final shipyard location, announced construction contracts or provided production capacity targets.
The proposed 2029 opening also leaves a relatively narrow window to develop a facility capable of undertaking complex commercial and naval construction.
And while the companies have identified naval auxiliaries and commercial vessels as potential markets, neither has announced specific vessel orders for the new yard.
That distinction matters. New shipbuilding capacity will only be sustainable if it is supported by a dependable pipeline of orders, a competitive cost structure and a workforce capable of maintaining production schedules.
For Washington, the challenge is to ensure that the growing number of international partnerships becomes a durable American industrial base rather than a collection of high-profile investment announcements.
For South Korea, the opportunity is substantial. American shipbuilding ambitions could create a long-term market for Korean technology, engineering expertise and industrial investment, while helping strengthen ties between two major maritime allies.
The proposed HD Hyundai–Kiewit venture is another indication that the relationship is moving from government-level commitments toward concrete industrial projects.
Whether those projects can deliver ships competitively, on schedule and at the scale Washington hopes to achieve will ultimately determine how much of America’s shipbuilding revival becomes reality.
