title: BBC profiles Russian exile who says his surveillance network tracked General Staff officer Fanil Sarvarov before his assassination in Moscow
body: A blast-damaged Kia Sorento at the site where Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov was killed In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Russian Armed Forces General Staff’s Operational Training Directorate, was killed in a car bombing in Moscow. A Russian man who left the country in 2022 and now coordinates a network of volunteers tracking Russian military personnel says he helped prepare the killing. His role is detailed in the BBC documentary ” Traitors, Patriots, Spies: Shadowmen Helping Ukraine Inside Russia .” The film introduces the man as Foma. His face is hidden — viewers see only his silhouette and hear his voice. The filmmakers say that in early 2022, Foma warned Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, about Russia’s planned invasion. He then fled Russia, and the Ukrainians helped him settle in Warsaw. He now lives in Poland. Foma says he coordinates a network of about 30 people operating in Russia, Ukraine, and several European countries. He says he also maintains ties with sources in Russia’s intelligence services. According to the film, years of working among Russia’s elite gave him a unique network of contacts and a steady flow of inside information. Foma says his network gathers intelligence on where storage depots and headquarters are located, where units are stationed, where generals live, where officers working at those headquarters live, where strategic bomber pilots who attack Ukraine live, and who gives the orders. The HUR confirmed that it had worked with Foma, the investigative outlet iStories reported . One scene shows Foma training volunteers to conduct surveillance in Moscow. He tells them not to bring a phone. He also warns that if they are caught, they face terrorism charges and 25 years in prison. In the film, Foma says he wants Russian soldiers and officers who order the shooting of prisoners and the rape and murder of civilians to think long and hard before giving such orders, to be scared, and to stop. Those who turn into animals and those who kill people, he says, need to be punished. The next segment covers the December 2024 killing of General Igor Kirillov, head of Russia’s Radiation, Chemical, and Biological Protection Troops. Foma told the BBC that he was not involved in that killing but confirmed that his network passes information about Russian military personnel to Ukraine. He insists the people his volunteers follow are war criminals. Sarvarov was killed a year after Kirillov. When the BBC filmmaker asked Foma about Sarvarov’s killing, he said: “Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule.” Foma stresses, however, that his group does not take part in the killings themselves. A man using the same pseudonym has appeared as a military expert on The Breakfast Show’s morning broadcasts since mid-September. On September 19, after regular military expert Yuri Fyodorov left the channel, The Breakfast Show founder Alexander Plyushchev wrote that the morning show would have a new military commentator: Foma, co-founder of the Telegram channel Volya, who appears on camera with his face hidden. The BBC film does not explicitly link Foma to Volya. But Agentstvo journalists noticed that several shots show him sitting in front of a computer monitor displaying Volya’s donation page on Patreon. Plyushchev told Agentstvo that he contacted Foma while looking for a replacement for Fyodorov. “All I knew about Foma was that he did analysis on Georgian political scientist Gela Vasadze’s show and ran the Telegram channel Volya… We understood the risks of having an anonymous commentator, but we decided to try it, since he was providing commentary rather than serving as a source. Foma is now one of four military commentators who regularly work with The Breakfast Show,” Plyushchev said. Agentstvo received no response from Foma, who had been sent an editor’s contact information. title: Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried
body:
Fewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high and climbing , airline executives say that's just fine.
At the New York Hilton in Midtown Manhattan on Friday night, the aviation industry held its annual Wings Club gala, honoring Ed Bastian, CEO of profit-leader Delta Air Lines .
North American airline CEOs and other executives at the black-tie bash told CNBC that demand trends aren't worrying them, but persistently high, profit-crimping fuel prices are.
The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares matters more than fully filling planes or flying record numbers of travelers.
"We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making," American Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday.
American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.
Plane ticket prices have skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.
Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects this holiday season to come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.
The average Southwest Airlines fare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane.
The airline's revenue passenger count, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago to about 33.5 million people.
Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations.
"Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.
Since April — when airlines began warning in earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints than in the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. That's down less than 2% from last year, but it follows years of growth.
With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices at $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible.
Despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that overall travel demand is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.
And not every carrier is seeing a decline. United Airlines flew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than a year ago and said its unit revenue rose 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic.
"I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company's earnings call Wednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."
Most airlines expect fuel costs to keep biting, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.
United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 per gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from $3.90 per gallon in the third.
American, United, Delta and Southwest all cut their 2026 profit forecasts this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.
American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back its capacity expansion goals, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds.
The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.
"Today, we find ourselves yet at another inflection point for our industry and the world. ... Geopolitics affecting our business, driving the price of jet fuel to historic highs," Bastian said in his award-acceptance speech, adding that artificial intelligence makes it hard to predict months or weeks ahead.
"It causes many people to question yet again the durability of our industry. But I'm not worried because I know the people in this room, and I know your resilience and how you've demonstrated that time and time again," he said.
Smaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, starting with JetBlue Airways next week, followed by Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air , have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.
One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May.
"Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.
Many of the problems that plagued the airline industry for years are starting to abate.
In some cases, aircraft deliveries are still years behind schedule. But Boeing , whose CEO, Kelly Ortberg, attended on Friday night, and its main rival, Airbus, have ramped up production. Boeing will update investors on its production outlook when it reports quarterly results Tuesday.
The Federal Aviation Administration has approved Boeing's Max 7, a key smaller jet for Southwest Airlines, and the Max 10, which Alaska Airlines and United Airlines have been waiting for for years.
Pratt & Whitney parent, RTX , and GE Aerospace say they're improving engine durability and shop visit turnaround time, though customers say more improvements are needed.

title: An LLM judge passed renders with defects I planted
body:
My vision-model judge passed and failed the same code. On a newer model it was steadier, so I planted defects in five components and scored them with it and with Cloudflare Clef. The 0.85 pass gate let about half of the defect runs through.
The pipeline I wrote about in the harness post started reporting regressions that weren't there. A button would pass on one refinement attempt and fail on the next. Four times. I hashed the code for its Secondary variant from each attempt's output, and in two of those four cases the code was byte for byte the same. The refiner had changed exactly what its changes_made list said it changed, which didn't touch that block, and the score had gone down anyway.
Quick recap if you haven't read the earlier post. The pipeline turns a Figma design into a React component, renders it, and asks a vision model to compare the render with the design. The model scores four things (layout, colors, typography, spacing) up to 0.25 each, and the component passes when the total is at least 0.85 and a handful of hard checks are green. If it fails, a refinement agent edits the code and the whole thing runs again.
If the code didn't change and the score did, whatever moved it came after the code, so I took the refiner and the writer out of it entirely. I took one run's stored artefacts for that same button, which comes from Untitled UI's Figma kit: the code, the rendered screenshot and the Figma reference image. Then I had the reviewer score the same version eight times. Before each call the inputs were hashed and asserted identical, so nothing upstream could have changed.
A fixed seed was already in place. The pipeline passes seed=settings.AI_AGENT.SEED to every agent, with SEED set to 42, and sets no temperature. The reviewer at the time was gpt-5.6-terra at medium reasoning effort. Here's what came back:
Seven of the eight runs cleared 0.85 and one landed at 0.82, so the same code, the same screenshot and the same design both passed and failed depending on which call you happened to look at. The yes-or-no fields the reviewer also returns (whether the schema is valid, whether the structure is complete) were identical on all eight runs.
I also ran one component through the whole pipeline three times, with the same design and the same pipeline code each time:
The loop stops at the first attempt that clears the gate, so a passing score tends to sit right at 0.85, inside the band the reviewer wanders around in. That undid a lot of my own reasoning. Most of the comparisons in my build log at the time were between scores 0.03 to 0.09 apart, including the four button regressions I started with, and none of them can be told apart from the reviewer disagreeing with itself. The harness post had the same problem: it read dips of 0.01 to 0.02 in refinement trajectories as refinement going backwards, and I've added a note there.
Not every drop was noise, though. One nav went 0.81, 0.68, 0.76, 0.87 across four attempts because the refiner really had broken a version: its instructions said "A fix for one version must not regress a version that already passes", and the trace showed it received none of the component's seven labelled designs, while the writer got all seven on every call. I changed that, so the refiner now gets all seven too.
In the harness post I made a point of deriving the verdict in code so the model never gets to decide it. This is the current version:
Every line in that property held steady across the eight runs except one. The llm_review_score line is the model inventing a number on the spot, and the code compares it with a constant, so the verdict really is computed in code and it still inherits all of the model's variance through that one comparison. The loop also picks which attempt to keep by sorting on (review.passed, review.llm_review_score) , and the noise reaches both parts of that key.
I'd picked 0.85 after running a number of Figma designs through the pipeline, because above it the output mostly looked good, and it's still the gate today.
Since then every agent in the pipeline has moved to gpt-6.1-sol at high reasoning effort, so I ran the eight-call study again. This time I used a nav from Untitled UI's free Figma community kit, so I can show the images, and two of its versions: the closed mobile header, and the open panel, the menu opened with its subnav expanded, whose render is over 4,000 pixels tall.
The terra rows are the old reviewer on the same code and the same two images. On the open panel its spread was 0.10, about what I saw the first time, and sol's was 0.03. On the closed header both spreads were 0.04. I changed the model and the effort together, so I can't say which of the two did it.
The top row of that image is the design and the render, and they're very close, so a steady score at or above 0.90 was the right answer. When I gave the reviewer the wrong design to compare against (the closed header's render against the design of a third version, the open menu with its subnav collapsed), it scored 0.46 to 0.54 and failed all three runs.
That covers a render that's right and one that's completely wrong. The refinement loop mostly deals with the cases in between, so I planted some small defects whose answers I knew. Each defect is one Tailwind class changed in the generated styles, font-semibold to font-normal on the nav labels, px-4 to px-10 on the rows, a hidden on the menu button and so on. Each one was rendered in the same sandbox as the real thing and scored three times by the reviewer. The bottom row of the image above shows two of them.
Freshly rendered and clean, the two versions scored 0.93 to 0.95, and the 30 defect runs scored 0.82 to 0.90:
The reviewer noticed every defect, in the sense that the score went down. The gate failed all three runs on only 4 of the 10, and never failed the regular-weight labels, the wider row padding or the missing "All blog posts" link. A defect costs 0.04 to 0.11, and how much it costs doesn't follow how visible it is: the regular-weight labels are obvious in the image and cost about 0.04. On these runs a gate at 0.91 would have separated every clean run from every defect run, and I took that number forward without noticing that the eight-run study above had already scored the same clean panel 0.90 once.
Planting known defects to test a judge isn't new. Finding Blind Spots in Evaluator LLMs with Interpretable Checklists (opens in a new tab) (Doddapaneni and others, EMNLP 2024) built 2,400 perturbed text answers across 22 kinds of perturbation, and the evaluator LLMs they tested "failed to identify quality drops in over 50% of cases on average". The result looks similar, since the 0.85 gate here let about half of the defect runs through, but the cause is different: their judges didn't notice the drop, and my reviewer's score went down every time and the threshold let it through. Their paper also found judges did better with a reference answer to compare against, which is how my reviewer works.
The plan after the first study was to stop asking the reviewer for a number, because its yes-or-no fields had held still. I wrote 15 checks across the same four dimensions (every element present, text colors match, font weights match, padding matches and so on), asked gpt-6.1-sol with the same settings to answer each one true or false with a sentence of evidence, and computed the score in code with each dimension still worth 0.25.
Over eight runs on the open panel it scored exactly 0.50 every time, failing the same 7 of 15 checks. On the closed header it moved between 0.646 and 0.792, with two checks flipping between runs. The open panel's failures point at differences that are real but small, like this one:
The render uses neutral black and grey text where the reference uses dark navy and blue-grey.
The instructions say a visible difference is a fail, and on a render this close the checks fail anyway on differences too small to matter. So it caught only 4 of the 10 defects, the ones whose check had passed on the clean render. Two of those four, the regular-weight labels and the missing link, are defects the 0.85 gate never failed.
I tried Cloudflare's Clef next because it's built for this kind of classification and it's fast. It takes the two images, a sentence naming the version and the same 15 checks, and returns a probability of yes for each check in 0.7 to 2.7 seconds, with the same answers on every call. It doesn't get the code or the Figma data, and any image over 300,000 pixels has to be scaled down to fit its window, so it sees the open panel at a much lower resolution than the reviewer does.
On the nav it was sure about three defects: the grey background, the missing menu button and the red labels, at 0.05 to 0.16, where the lowest answer it gave any clean render was 0.476. It missed the rest, and on the missing link it was confidently wrong, at 0.858.
By this point I had two ideas from one nav: raise the gate to 0.91, and fail a render whenever Clef answers any check below 0.2, which I'll call the Clef veto. I wrote both down, then took four more components from the same Untitled UI kit (a desktop FAQ, a desktop hero, a call-to-action strip from a homepage and the open mobile menu of a different nav) and planted 27 defects of the same kinds in them. The reviewer scored each clean render five times and each defect three times, and Clef scored each render once. The veto held up, and 0.91 turned out to be too high.
The hero scored 0.73 to 0.78 with nothing planted in it, so I compared it with the design:
The cards are flipped and stacked the wrong way round, and the reviewer said so: "The illustration differs substantially: the purple card slopes upward instead of downward". The older reviewer had passed this render at exactly 0.85, the new one fails it every time, and Clef answered every check above 0.55. A broken render underneath says nothing about the defects planted on top of it, so I left the hero out of the table, a call I made after seeing its scores.
The table covers every clean run from the current reviewer except the hero's (37, across the nav's two versions and the clean FAQ, CTA and menu) and the 60 defect runs on the FAQ, CTA and menu:
These scores are the reviewer's alone. The experiment doesn't run the TypeScript compiler, so the reviewer guesses ts_compiles and the hard checks in passed aren't the ones production would apply.
On the nav, the FAQ, the CTA and the menu, every defect run scored below every fresh clean run of the render it was planted in, one by only 0.02, less than the 0.03 to 0.04 the score moved on one clean render scored eight times. So the score reacted to every defect, by amounts one fixed gate can't separate from its own noise. Clef's veto caught 6 of the 8 color changes and 3 of the 5 missing elements, and never fired on a clean render. With the gate at 0.88, which I picked after seeing these scores, the two together fail 45 of the 60 defect runs on the FAQ, CTA and menu and pass all 37 clean runs, which come from seven renders.
What gets through 0.88 with the veto is all on the FAQ and the menu: bolder questions, a larger heading, larger footer links, regular-weight rows and two grey backgrounds. The clean FAQ scored 0.99 on all five runs and its bolder questions 0.92 to 0.94, so the reviewer saw that change, and one absolute gate can't sit right for a component that starts at 0.99 and one whose clean runs dip to 0.90. Gating on the drop from a component's own clean score would need a known-good render to compare with, and while the pipeline is generating a component it doesn't have one.
Comparing two images might work better than scoring one. In MLLM-as-a-Judge (opens in a new tab) (Chen and others, ICML 2024), multimodal judges "demonstrate remarkable human-like discernment in Pair Comparison" while their scores diverge from people's. The loop already has two renders to compare whenever it picks which attempt to keep, and I haven't tried asking the reviewer which one is closer to the design.
The other limits: five components from one free kit, and 37 defects that I designed, 7 of them on the hero and left out of the rules table. I haven't measured what the higher gate costs in extra refinement attempts, or what a Clef call costs next to a reviewer call. The veto's clean record is 37 runs but only seven renders, since Clef gives the same answer every time. And Clef saw every desktop render, the open panel and the other nav's open menu scaled down to 300,000 pixels, so I don't know how it does on those cut into full-size pieces.
Written by Yaman Ahlawat . New posts arrive in the RSS feed .

title: Bitcoin ETFs Lose Over $635M In One Day Following Oil Price Spike
body: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin ETFs Lose Over $635M In One Day Following Oil Price Spike U.S. investors quickly reversed course on Thursday, cashing out over half a billion dollars from spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds as risk-off sentiment surfaced again. A total of $635.6 million left the funds on Thursday, data from Farside Investors shows. The redemptions put downward pressure on the price of bitcoin , which dropped under $81,000 at one point. The coin has since rebounded and was recently trading for nearly $81,669, down just 1% over a 24-hour period. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust saw the biggest outflows, with investors cashing out over $254 million. Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund followed, losing close to $218 million. Over $109 million left the ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF; Morgan Stanley’s fund and Bitwise’s ETF lost nearly $30 million and over $27 million, respectively. But the investment vehicles this week have this week received net positive investment of over $439 million. Investors went into “risk-off” mode after flare ups in the Middle East sent the price of oil higher. Brent crude hit its highest price in five months after Yemeni rebel group the Houthis on Thursday attacked Saudi Arabia, sparking concerns over more disruption to energy supplies. Bitcoin’s price has been rattled this year since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, halting oil supplies as ships have struggled to pass through the strategic Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil passes through. A higher oil price can hurt the price of bitcoin and other “risk-on” assets because it increases the chances of the U.S. central bank raising interest rates. Bitcoin has typically done well in a low interest rate environment because it means the asset has more liquidity to rally. Investors on Thursday also sold off tech stocks, which had rallied earlier in the week off the back of SpaceX’s impressive earnings. Analysts are saying bitcoin is entering a bull market again. Data last month showed that the leading cryptocurrency crossed above its 365-day moving average — a typical sign it is out of a bear market — following a strong run in August. Bitcoin notched a record of $126,080 in October 2025 but then began to sink later that month after the biggest liquidation event in crypto history saw over $19 billion in bets closed. The coin spent the first half of 2026 trading well below that level but picked up again in August and September, having its best quarter in years. This post Bitcoin ETFs Lose Over $635M In One Day Following Oil Price Spike first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Mathew Di Salvo .

title: Nearly all the world’s coral reefs are at risk of collapse within 50 years, IUCN warns
body: Nearly every shallow-water coral reef ecosystem on Earth is at high risk of ecological collapse by 2075, according to the first coral reef assessment of the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems (RLE). The RLE is a scientific framework for assessing the risk of ecosystem collapse. More than 250 experts assessed shallow water coral reef ecosystems across 127 tropical and subtropical ecoregions worldwide including the Great Barrier Reef in Australia and the Coral Triangle of Southeast Asia. The Oct. 22 report concluded that 24% of coral reefs are already critically endangered. When scientist include projected heat stress from climate change, they found 96% will be critically endangered in the next 50 years. One coral reef ecosystem, the Western Galapagos Islands, has collapsed already, the assessment found. The assessment identified heat stress from climate change as the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide. Heat stress causes coral bleaching, a process in which corals expel the symbiotic algae living in their tissue. Algae provide most of the coral’s food via photosynthesis and prolonged bleaching events leave coral weakened, vulnerable to disease and lead to death. Coral reefs are crucial for marine biodiversity; they “cover less than 1% of the ocean floor,” but support approximately 25% of marine life. In an email to Mongabay Marcos Valderrábano, programme manager for the RLE at IUCN, said that if climate projections are accurate, most corals will suffer repeated severe bleaching, resulting in a less biodiverse ecosystem as corals are replaced by algae and turf.…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: Seven killed as gunmen open fire at church in Jordan in 'terrorist' attack, authorities say
body: Seven people were killed on Friday when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan, said the head of the country's Public Security Directorate, in a rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority that authorities described as a terrorist act by extremists.Speaking at a press conference, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak governorate were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing. Jordan's health minister said 40 people were wounded.Shooting attack carried out by 'extremists'Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists," but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though authorities in the US ally say that in recent years they have repeatedly foiled attempted attacks by Islamist terrorists.There was no immediate claim of responsibility.A video aired on Jordan's state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station that appeared to be from a security camera on the church showed three people firing at it from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as well as other details."This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism, and we will not allow society to go down this path," Jordanian Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said in a post on X/Twitter.Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes.Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station he saw bloodied people collapse on the floor after the attack. "People were crying, wailing, screaming — it's hard to describe," he said. Attackers will be punished with 'iron fist,' King Abdullah saysJordan's King Abdullah, a major US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished "with an iron fist.""The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," he said in a statement.Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.In a post on X, United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable.People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the wounded expressed shock."What happened today has left people unable to speak or raise our voices. But our only reproach to the state is that it must investigate these dark ideas — where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children," said one of them, Hani Al-Mbaydeen.Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.The US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz described it on X as a "depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship."Jordan was among the US allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

title: Air Force suspends rappelling events for special ops training unit after fatal fall
body: An Air Force unit that trains special operations airmen suspended rappelling and ropes training after an instructor in the squadron died during a demonstration at a college football game in San Antonio, Texas, officials confirmed to Task & Purpose. Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a 15-year Air Force veteran and instructor at the 6th Combat Training Squadron, fell during a rappelling demonstration before the University of Texas at San Antonio’s Oct. 17 football game against Navy at the Alamodome. Patterson fell from the stadium’s 160-foot-high rafters onto the playing field. He was transported to a hospital, where he later died. “Tech Sgt Patterson’s squadron, 6th Combat Training Squadron, has paused all rappel and ropes training events and demonstrations until further notice,” the U.S. Air Force Warfare Center Public Affairs office said in an emailed statement. Patterson was assigned to the 6th CTS’ Detachment 2, at Joint Base San Antonio. The detachment selects and trains candidates for the service’s tactical air control party, or TACP, roles, one of four Air Force special warfare jobs. Students are taught the basics of rappelling, which is a core skill for TACPs. The Air Force did not specify when the training suspension began, who ordered it or what conditions must be met before training resumes. Officials also did not say whether the suspension extends to other units. The circumstances surrounding Patterson’s fall remain under investigation. Nellis Air Force Base officials previously said they would not discuss operational details or potential causes while the investigation is ongoing. Rappelling is a common portion of military training to move personnel down steep terrain, structures and other elevated positions using ropes and specialized equipment. Demonstrations of those skills are also conducted at public events. According to a GoFundMe organized by his brother-in-law, Mitch Blunn, Patterson is survived by his wife, Niki, and their two young sons, who the Pattersons homeschooled. “Our hearts are broken for Niki and her two young boys following the tragic loss of Ian, a beloved husband and father whose life was taken far too soon,” Blunn wrote. The fundraiser will help the family relocate closer to relatives, cover potential legal expenses and navigate the financial consequences of Patterson’s death. The suspension follows Patterson’s death during one such public demonstration, though the Air Force has not explicitly stated whether the fatal fall prompted the decision. The post Air Force suspends rappelling events for special ops training unit after fatal fall appeared first on Task & Purpose .

title: Pentagon issues guidance on AI procurements to support Trump’s ‘truth-seeking’ and ‘ideological neutrality’ directives
body: The Pentagon issued new guidance this week focused on implementing the Trump administration’s so-called “truth-seeking” and “ideological neutrality” principles in AI procurements. A memorandum dated Oct. 20 from Principal Director for Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy John Tenaglia noted that the initiative is “in direct support” of a previous executive order from President Donald Trump on “Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government” and a White House Office of Management and Budget memo on “Increasing Public Trust in Artificial Intelligence Through Unbiased AI Principles.” Trump’s EO, issued last year, laid out the administration’s “truth-seeking” and “ideological neutrality” edicts for AI procurements, stating that large language models purchased by federal agencies “shall be truthful in responding to user prompts seeking factual information or analysis” and “prioritize historical accuracy, scientific inquiry, and objectivity, and shall acknowledge uncertainty where reliable information is incomplete or contradictory.” The models must be “neutral, nonpartisan tools that do not manipulate responses in favor of ideological dogmas such as DEI,” Trump wrote, adding that developers “shall not intentionally encode partisan or ideological judgments into an LLM’s outputs unless those judgments are prompted by or otherwise readily accessible to the end user.” Tenaglia noted in his memo that compliance with the White House directives is mandatory. The new Pentagon guidance includes three attachments for personnel involved in acquisitions of artificial intelligence technologies. The issuance “provides contracting and program personnel with adaptable templates and standardized language to document, solicit, and enforce these Unbiased AI Principles in our procurements. It is designed to be flexible, allowing DoW Components to tailor the language to fit the specific context and risk level of their individual AI acquisitions,” Tenaglia wrote in his memo to acquisition leaders at the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force, U.S. Special Operations Command, U.S. Cyber Command, U.S. Transportation Command, DOD agencies and field activities. (The term “DoW” refers to the Department of War, which is the Trump administration’s preferred name for the Department of Defense.) The templates include a memorandum for the requiring activity to select the appropriate transparency requirements for the procurement; standardized solicitation language that instructs vendors on the specific documentation they must provide to demonstrate compliance; and formal contract language that could be included in the Statement of Work or Performance Work Statement in solicitations and final contracts. When buying an LLM, the Pentagon must obtain sufficient information from the contractor to determine whether its tech complies with the principles in Trump’s EO, according to an attachment to Tenaglia’s memo. “The amount and type of information available will vary depending on the contractor’s role within the software supply chain and its relationship with the LLM developer itself, with more information generally being available from sources closer to the original LLM developer,” the document noted. The memo suggests that contracting language should define key terms, clearly communicate submission requirements to potential vendors and make the provision of related documentation a formal part of the proposal process. The post Pentagon issues guidance on AI procurements to support Trump’s ‘truth-seeking’ and ‘ideological neutrality’ directives appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: First Russian Diesel From Putin-Trump Deal Heading for US
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Oct 23 (Reuters) – The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.
Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US mid-term elections.
Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.
The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel in Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7.
The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.
Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”
A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.
“As far as I’m aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.
The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.
RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTS Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.
Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signaling trips to Turkey and Brazil.
It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signaling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port-Said, LSEG data showed.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.
Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.
Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.
(Reporting by Reuters; editing by Philippa Fletcher and Jason Neely)

title: 1 Killed, 11 Injured as Russia Strikes Dnipropetrovsk Region Nearly 70 Times
body:
Russian forces struck four districts of the Dnipropetrovsk region nearly 70 times on Friday, Oct. 23, killing one person and wounding 11 others.
The head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration reported the number of casualties in his latest update on Telegram.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The regional center, Dnipro, sustained the heaviest damage during today’s strikes.
One private house was destroyed, while at least five others were damaged, Hanzha said in an earlier update. Two people were initially reported injured, with warnings that another person might be trapped under the rubble.
Less than an hour later, rescuers pulled a body from the rubble of the destroyed house.
Eight people injured in the city have been hospitalized, including a 26-year-old man in extremely serious condition.
The strikes damaged other infrastructure, businesses and vehicles in Dnipro as well.
In the Pidhorodne community of Dnipro district, two men aged 66 and 46, and a 55-year-old woman were injured. According to Hanzha, they received outpatient treatment.
In Nikopol district, which lies across the Dnipro River from Russian-occupied territory, Russian forces targeted the city of Nikopol and the Marhanets, Chervonohryhorivka, Pokrovske and Mozolevske communities.
The attacks damaged infrastructure, an administrative building, private homes and vehicles.
In Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown, Russian forces struck the Karpivka and Hrushivka communities, damaging infrastructure.
The Pokrovske community in Synelnykove district was also attacked.
The strikes followed an overnight assault in which Russian forces attacked Dnipro and the surrounding region with drones nearly 20 times, injuring two people, Ukrinform reported.
That same morning, a strike on a business in Dnipro district started a fire and injured two more people.
The region continues to face near-daily barrage, with Russia frequently attacking civilians and civilian infrastructure, although such attacks are strictly prohibited under international humanitarian law.
On Monday, Oct. 19, Russian drone and artillery attacks killed two people and wounded at least 10 others, including a 15-year-old boy, in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
Around the same time, regional authorities began preparing for the upcoming winter and possible power outages by adding more than 125 megawatts (MW) of alternative generation this year to keep heat and water running. “We are all working together: utility workers, energy workers, businesses and communities,” Hanzha said.
Just a week prior, on Oct. 13, Russia attacked the region with guided aerial bombs (KABs), injuring a 64-year-old man and damaging apartment buildings, vehicles, and transport infrastructure.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Two ex-FBI officials charged with allegedly lying about Hunter Biden probe: DOJ
body:
Two former senior FBI officials were taken into custody on Friday after being charged with lying to Congress about their roles in investigations into Hunter Biden , top Department of Justice officials announced.
The former officials, 46-year-old Nikki Floris and 56-year-old Bradley Benavides, surrendered on arrest warrants Friday morning, the DOJ said in a press release .
The charges were filed less than two weeks before the midterm election , breaking with longstanding DOJ guidance discouraging actions that could affect upcoming political races.
The announcement also comes amid growing concerns that President Donald Trump — who refused to accept his 2020 election loss and tried repeatedly to overturn those results — is looking for ways to challenge potential Republican midterm losses.
On Thursday, the DOJ filed an unusual lawsuit against Alaska seeking to preemptively challenge the results of that state's Senate race if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses.
The charges unveiled Friday morning accuse the two ex-FBI agents of lying in 2023 testimony before the House Judiciary Committee about their agency's probe of Hunter Biden, the now-56-year-old son of former President Joe Biden .
The agents were "actively involved" in federal investigations of Hunter Biden, which began in 2019 on tax- and money-laundering-related matters, but said otherwise in separate interviews before the House panel, according to an FBI special agent's affidavit in support of the charges.
"Floris and Benavides allegedly lied to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations, with one claiming they only learned about it from Wikipedia — despite evidence showing their involvement in helping shape the public narrative about Hunter Biden's laptop right before the election," U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in an X post.
FBI Director Kash Patel said on X that the charges "stem from an ongoing investigation into the since-dissolved FBI Foreign Influence Task Force."
Floris and Benavides, who both worked on that task force, testified that it "was not involved in the Hunter Biden investigations," Patel wrote. "Documentary evidence, contemporaneous communications, and witness accounts contradict their testimony."
Attorneys for Floris called the charges "nonsense," and accused the Trump administration of deliberately filing them just before the Nov. 3 midterm election in hopes of gaining political advantage.
" Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts," read a statement from her counsel, including Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle Freeny.
"It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they wrote.
"The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points," their statement added. "It's another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki's day in court."

title: Missile attack on Russia’s Oryol region may have targeted Proton, a factory producing military electronics, Ukrainian monitors say
body: Ukrainian forces launched a missile attack on Russia’s Oryol region. Preliminary reports from Ukrainian monitoring channels suggest the target was the Proton factory, which produces optoelectronic equipment and components for military use. A missile alert was issued across the Oryol region at about 5 p.m. local time. Local Telegram channels reported at least four explosions in the city of Oryol. Afterward, residents reported seeing thick smoke and hearing emergency vehicles. Storm Shadow cruise missiles were used in the attack on Oryol, according to preliminary reports from Ukrainian monitoring channels. The Telegram channel Exile+ reported that the factory’s products are used to manufacture S-71 “Kover” air-launched cruise missiles, 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and Pantsir-S1 air defense missile and gun systems. Oryol Governor Andrey Klychkov said Ukrainian forces had launched a missile attack on a civilian facility — a business in Oryol’s Sovetsky district. Details on casualties and the extent of the damage remain unclear. title: Crypto Scammers Who Used Prayer Groups to Lure Victims Must Pay $1.3 Billion, Says New York
body:
New York Attorney General Letitia James wants the founders of collapsed crypto trading platform NovaTech to pay nearly $1.4 billion. Collecting it may be another matter: The couple has fled the country, according to James.
In a filing in New York County Supreme Court on Thursday, James’ office asked a judge to order Cynthia and Eddy Petion, NovaTech and related companies to pay about $1.37 billion in damages, disgorgement, and interest.
The request follows an August 2025 default judgment issued after the Petions fled the U.S. and failed to respond to the state’s lawsuit. That judgment also banned them from the securities, commodities and crypto industries.
James also announced settlements totaling nearly $6 million with four of the scheme’s top promoters: Martin Zizi, Frantz Ciceron, Ricardo Roy Sr,. and James Corbett. They’ll pay the money to benefit victims and are permanently barred from those industries.
James first sued NovaTech and AWS Mining in June 2024, alleging they defrauded investors of more than $1 billion. Two months later, the SEC charged the Petions and others over what it called a $650 million fraud.
According to the attorney general’s office, the Petions targeted immigrant communities, particularly Haitian New Yorkers, through prayer groups, social media, and WhatsApp chats, using ads in Haitian Creole and religious messaging. More than 11,000 New Yorkers were among the hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide.
“These scammers targeted immigrant and religious communities with the promise of a better life but instead robbed them of their life savings,” James said in a statement .
NovaTech falsely marketed itself as a registered hedge fund broker licensed to trade crypto in the U.S. and advertised returns of 2% to 4% a week, or more than 140% a year, according to the state.
In reality, it sent just under $26 million to its trading provider between 2019 and 2023 and lost about $18.2 million of it. Weekly payouts and recruiting bonuses came from new investors’ deposits, the state said. When NovaTech collapsed in 2023, tens of thousands of investors couldn’t withdraw their funds.
Data from payment processor CoinPayments shows investors deposited roughly $1.16 billion in crypto into NovaTech’s wallet between August 2019 and May 2023, and Cynthia Petion was the only authorized user on the account. At least $134.5 million went to wallets belonging to the Petions. After subtracting the money sent for trading, the state is seeking about $1.13 billion in disgorgement, plus $232 million in interest.
Before NovaTech, the Petions were top U.S. promoters of AWS Mining, which promised monthly returns of 15% to 20% from crypto mining before collapsing in 2019. Cynthia Petion admitted in a WhatsApp chat to making at least $3 million from that scheme, according to the filing.

title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
body:
Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources. In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention. Why this problem occurs When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue. Changing the endpoint configuration with auto scaling registered CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error: The variant(s) "[AllTraffic]" must be deregistered as scalable targets with Application Auto Scaling before they can be removed or have their instance type updated. SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing only the endpoint configuration If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing auto scaling parameters If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists: Resource of type 'AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget' with identifier 'endpoint/
/variant/AllTraffic|sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount|sagemaker' was not found. This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover. Solution overview You can use this CDK construct to replace the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by node.add_dependency calls in CDK. The full sequence is: Deregister (custom resource): Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins. On first deploy, no scalable target exists yet, so the handler handles the error gracefully and continues. Endpoint update (CDK-managed): CDK updates the endpoint resource normally, swapping to the new endpoint configuration. Register Scalable Target (custom resource): Waits for the endpoint to reach InService status, then registers the scalable target. Attach Scaling Policy (custom resource): Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target tracking policy. Figure 1: Custom resource orchestration of SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling around a CDK-managed endpoint update. Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy use the CDK provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. Each custom resource has an on_event handler that returns immediately and an is_complete handler. The provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on an interval (every 30 seconds) until its readiness check passes. The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour for Register Scalable Target, 15 minutes for Attach Scaling Policy) bounds the wait, so it isn’t limited by the timeout of any single Lambda invocation. A ConfigHash property on each custom resource forces CloudFormation to re-invoke the Lambda functions whenever a configuration value changes. The endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters are defined together because a single ConfigHash drives the auto scaling orchestration. While the construct defines three custom resources, the deployed stack contains more than three Lambda functions. Each custom resource is backed by a CDK cr.Provider , and the provider framework generates its own helper Lambda functions. A synchronous provider (Deregister) adds one framework function. An asynchronous provider (Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy) adds three ( onEvent , isComplete , and onTimeout ) plus an AWS Step Functions state machine that drives the waiter. As a result, the deployed stack contains three custom resources, two Step Functions state machines, and twelve Lambda functions. Five of the resources hold the construct’s own handler code (one for Deregister, and an on_event and is_complete pair for each asynchronous resource), with the remaining seven generated by the provider framework. You don’t write or maintain the framework-generated functions, but they are present in the stack and worth accounting for when you review the deployed resources. Walkthrough In this walkthrough, you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with auto scaling using the provided example stack, then verify that configuration updates work correctly. The walkthrough includes the following steps: Clone the repository and install dependencies. Configure your endpoint and auto scaling settings. Deploy and verify. Test an update. The source code is available in the linked GitHub repository . Prerequisites For this walkthrough, you need the following: An AWS account with permissions for Amazon SageMaker AI, AWS Lambda, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Application Auto Scaling, and Amazon CloudWatch. AWS CDK v2 installed. Python 3.12 or later. uv for Python dependency management. A SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and a container image in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), or a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm container. Clone the repository and install dependencies Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling.git cd sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling Install dependencies: uv sync Configure your endpoint and auto scaling settings The endpoint and auto scaling settings are defined together in config/ config.yaml because a single config_hash drives the auto scaling orchestration. A change to either section triggers the full sequence. Edit config/ config.yaml with your values: endpoint: endpoint_name: "my-model-endpoint" image: "123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:latest" model_data_url: "s3://my-bucket/models/model.tar.gz" instance_type: "ml.m5.large" initial_instance_count: 1 environment: {} autoscaling: min_capacity: 1 max_capacity: 10 target_value: 100 scale_in_cooldown: 600 scale_out_cooldown: 120 The endpoint parameters map to the SageMaker AI CreateModel and CreateEndpointConfig APIs. The auto scaling parameters map to the Application Auto Scaling RegisterScalableTarget and PutScalingPolicy APIs. Deploy and verify Bootstrap your AWS environment if you haven’t already: uv run cdk bootstrap Deploy the stack: uv run cdk deploy InferenceStack CloudFormation creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint, then runs the three custom resources in sequence to register auto scaling. Verify that the deployment registered the scalable target: aws application-autoscaling describe-scalable-targets --service-namespace sagemaker --resource-ids endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic Verify that the deployment applied the scaling policy: aws application-autoscaling describe-scaling-policies --service-namespace sagemaker --resource-id endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic Test an update Change a value in config/ config.yaml , for example, update the instance type from ml.m5.large to ml.m5.xlarge , and redeploy: uv run cdk deploy InferenceStack After the deployment completes, verify that auto scaling is still registered and has the updated values: aws application-autoscaling describe-scalable-targets --service-namespace sagemaker --resource-ids endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic Integrating with an existing stack Use the example stack if you’re starting fresh or want a reference implementation. Use the construct directly if you already have a CDK stack with SageMaker AI resources. To integrate with an existing stack, copy the sagemaker_autoscaling/constructs/ directory into your project and add the construct alongside your endpoint resources: import json from sagemaker_autoscaling.constructs.sagemaker_autoscaling_construct import ( AutoscalingConfig, SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct, SagemakerAutoscalingProps, ) # Both endpoint and auto scaling values must be in config_hash so that # a change to either triggers the auto scaling orchestration. config_hash = json.dumps({ "endpoint": { "image": "123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:latest", "modelDataUrl": "s3://my-bucket/models/model.tar.gz", "instanceType": "ml.m5.large", "initialInstanceCount": 1, }, "autoscaling": { "minCapacity": 1, "maxCapacity": 10, "targetValue": 100, "scaleInCooldown": 600, "scaleOutCooldown": 120, }, }) SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct( self, "Autoscaling", props=SagemakerAutoscalingProps( endpoint=your_endpoint, # your CfnEndpoint autoscaling=AutoscalingConfig( min_capacity=1, max_capacity=10, target_value=100, scale_in_cooldown=600, scale_out_cooldown=120, ), config_hash=config_hash, ), ) How the construct works This section walks through the key implementation details of SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct . Deregister The Deregister custom resource calls deregister_scalable_target before the endpoint update. It handles ObjectNotFoundException for first deployments where no scalable target exists: def handler(event, context): resource_id = event["ResourceProperties"]["ResourceId"] if event["RequestType"] in ("Create", "Update"): try: client.deregister_scalable_target( ServiceNamespace="sagemaker", ResourceId=resource_id, ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount", ) except client.exceptions.ObjectNotFoundException: pass # No scalable target on first deploy return {"PhysicalResourceId": f"deregister-{resource_id}"} The dependency is established in CDK: props.endpoint.node.add_dependency(deregister) Register Scalable Target Even though CloudFormation treats the endpoint resource as complete once the update is accepted, the scalable target can only be registered after the endpoint reaches InService . Rather than block a single Lambda invocation on that wait, Register Scalable Target uses the provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. The on_event handler returns immediately, and the provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on query_interval until the endpoint is InService . The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour) bounds the wait, not the timeout of any single Lambda invocation: def handler(event, context): props = event["ResourceProperties"] resource_id = props["ResourceId"] endpoint_name = resource_id.split("/")[1] if event["RequestType"] == "Delete": return {"IsComplete": True} status = sm_client.describe_endpoint(EndpointName=endpoint_name)["EndpointStatus"] if status == "Failed": raise Exception("Endpoint in Failed state") if status != "InService": return {"IsComplete": False} as_client.register_scalable_target( ServiceNamespace="sagemaker", ResourceId=resource_id, ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount", MinCapacity=int(props["MinCapacity"]), MaxCapacity=int(props["MaxCapacity"]), ) return {"IsComplete": True} On stack deletion, the on_event handler deregisters the scalable target to clean up. Attach Scaling Policy There is a brief window after RegisterScalableTarget returns where the target isn’t yet queryable. Attach Scaling Policy uses the same asynchronous completion pattern: the on_event handler returns immediately, and the is_complete handler reports completion only once the scalable target is queryable, at which point it applies the policy. The provider’s total_timeout (15 minutes) bounds the wait: def handler(event, context): props = event["ResourceProperties"] resource_id = props["ResourceId"] if event["RequestType"] == "Delete": return {"IsComplete": True} resp = client.describe_scalable_targets( ServiceNamespace="sagemaker", ResourceIds=[resource_id], ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount", ) if not resp.get("ScalableTargets"): return {"IsComplete": False} client.put_scaling_policy( PolicyName=props["PolicyName"], ServiceNamespace="sagemaker", ResourceId=resource_id, ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount", PolicyType="TargetTrackingScaling", TargetTrackingScalingPolicyConfiguration=json.loads(props["ScalingPolicyConfig"]), ) return {"IsComplete": True} On stack deletion, the on_event handler deletes the scaling policy to clean up. Cleaning up To avoid incurring future charges, delete the resources: uv run cdk destroy InferenceStack This removes the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, model, Lambda functions, IAM roles, Amazon CloudWatch alarms created by the target tracking scaling policy, and deregisters the scalable target. Conclusion In this post, we showed you how to use a reusable CDK construct to deregister and register auto scaling automatically to orchestrate SageMaker AI endpoint updates. The construct uses three CloudFormation custom resources with explicit dependency ordering and a ConfigHash property to keep auto scaling intact across deployments. To get started, clone the sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling repository and follow the setup instructions. The repository includes an example stack you can deploy directly, or you can integrate the construct into your existing CDK stack. For more information about Application Auto Scaling for SageMaker AI, see Automatically scale Amazon SageMaker AI models . For more information about CloudFormation custom resources, see Custom resources in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide . About the author Lauren Eterno Lauren is an Associate Delivery Consultant with Amazon Web Services specializing in AI/ML. She works with customer teams to design, build, deploy, and scale machine learning and generative AI solutions. She holds a B.S. in Data Science & Analytics and an M.S. in Computer Science from Case Western Reserve University.

title: Wells Fargo, Arm, Intuit Keep Their Stock Off OKX-ICE Token Venue as Objections Reach 22
body: Wells Fargo , Arm Holdings and Intuit are among six more companies that have barred tokenized versions of their stock from OKXICE , the trading venue jointly owned by Intercontinental Exchange and OKX, Reuters reported on Friday, citing a regulatory document it reviewed. The additions bring the number of issuers that have objected to 22 , according to Reuters. Unchained has not seen that document and could not locate an updated notice on the venue’s website, where the most recent public version is dated Oct. 19. Reuters did not name the other three companies. Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . How an Objection Works OKXICE is set up under a five-year exemption the SEC issued on Sept. 17, which lets qualifying tokenized-stock platforms operate without being treated as an exchange. Before a venue lists a token of a company’s shares that the company did not create itself, it has to send that company written notice and wait at least 30 calendar days. A written objection inside that window keeps the token from trading, and the venue then has five business days to disclose the objection in a revised public notice. The venue plans to run permissioned Uniswap v4 pools on XLayer, pairing the stock tokens with stablecoins, and only wallets holding a soulbound token it issues can trade. Its disclosures state it is not registered with the SEC for these activities. From Nine to 22 The list has grown quickly. The venue’s Oct. 15 notice named nine objectors , among them Broadcom, Verizon and UnitedHealth. Its Oct. 19 notice raised the count to 16 , adding Goldman Sachs, Microsoft, Qualcomm, Caterpillar, McDonald’s, Western Digital and Alphabet. OKX and ICE had planned to offer tokens of 63 stocks through the venture and the venue has not announced a launch date. As of the Oct. 19 notice, companies on the original roster with no disclosed objection included Nvidia, Tesla, Apple and Amazon. Related Listen: Robinhood Tokenized AMC Stock Without Asking. title: $120 Oil Is Almost Here, and Trump Has Few Good Options
body: Brent crude nears $120 as escalating Saudi-Houthi tensions fuel another weekly oil price rally, putting fresh pressure on Trump.                Friday, October 23, 2026  The slow creep of oil prices towards the $120 per barrel mark is a nightmarish scenario for US President Trump, even though there has been little fundamental change in the crude oil markets. A slight drop in freight rates and a ubiquitous flattening of backwardated curves lowered differentials of most grades globally, offsetting some of the pressures coming from higher crude benchmarks. Be that as it may, an escalating Saudi-Houthi conflict paved the way for another 4% weekly gain, with ICE Brent trading around $117 per barrel.  First Russian Diesel Cargo Heads for New York. A non-sanctioned tanker, the Maltese-flagged Agioi Fanendes, left Russia's Baltic Sea port of Primorsk with New York listed as its destination, marking the first diesel cargo under Trump's deal with Moscow with final delivery expected on November 7.  Libya Oil Output Falls After Protests Reemerge. Libya's NOC said unauthorized individuals shut a pipeline valve serving the Hamada and Tahara fields, cutting output by 50,000 and 40,000 b/d respectively, as recurring protests jeopardize crude production that provides 90% of state revenues.  Europe Enters Winter with Gas at Four-Year Highs. Europe's TTF gas benchmark rose above 93/MWh $30 per MMBtu, the highest since December 2022, as restricted Qatari LNG supply coincided with colder weather and storage peaking below 75%, leaving Europe highly exposed ahead of winter.  Aramco Evacuates HQ After Houthi Attacks. Saudi Aramco TADAWUL2222 ordered staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and temporarily work from home after the HQ was attacked by the Houthis, the first such move since the Iran war began, with drone strikes also killing two at the Shaybah oilfield.  Qatar Looks to Rebuild Its LNG Supply Base. QatarEnergy is seeking additional long-term cargoes from the US and potentially Asia after securing its first agreement with US developer Cheniere NYSELNG, locking in 4 million tonnes of LNG per year until 2054, as domestic LNG outflows remain constrained.  Trump Taps Emergency Diesel Stockpiles. The US Energy Department is offering 315,000 barrels of diesel, one-third of its Northeast reserve, to ease regional disruptions as global diesel exports decline, while portraying the loan as temporary relief, with first Russian cargoes arriving in early November.  Japan Weighs Phasing Out Gasoline Subsidies. The Japanese government is considering phasing down gasoline subsidies from December as the program costs billions monthly, rapidly depleting a $20 billion budget, with average prices potentially rising from $4.1 per gallon now to $4.35 per gallon in January.  Trump Sees Wind Turbines as a Security Threat. US President Trump declared imported wind turbines and components a national security threat over cybersecurity and foreign dependence concerns, citing a Commerce Department investigation, ordering trade officials to discuss the issue with trading partners.  Indonesia Considers Halting Gas Exports. Indonesia may halt pipeline gas exports to neighbouring countries as Jakarta seeks to prioritize rising domestic demand, potentially a great blow to Singapore as such a move would remove some 7 bcm of supply, equivalent to 45% of the city-state's consumption.  Mexico Doubles Down on Oil Exploration. Mexico's state oil company Pemex pledged to direct $99 billion towards its upstream business in 2025-2030, 80% of its entire investment budget, seeking to counter declining production as crude oil output hovers at a meagre 1.34 million b/d in 2026 to date.  Kashagan Arbitration Court Rejects $12bn Cost Claims. The Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague rejected the Kazakh government's $12 billion cost claims against international oil majors operating the giant Kashagan field, claiming it is too late to claim costs incurred between 2011 and 2015.  EU Starts Work on 22nd Russia Sanctions Package. The EU's draft 22nd sanctions package would add 12 individuals and 105 entities tied to Russian oil production, trading, refining, shipping and logistics, doubling down on pressure as Washington and Moscow discuss broader bilateral economic issues.  UAE Oil Spill Threatens Civilian Infrastructure. UAE authorities closed coastal areas around Umm Al Quwain and launched containment operations after a tankerthe Gem No.2 VLCC struck by missiles two weeks agobegan leaking oil, with currents carrying contamination towards desalination plants.  Beijing Orders a Nationwide Oil Supply Boost. The Chinese government instructed state oil companies PetroChina, Sinopec and CNOOC to expedite oil exploration and production to shield the country from supply shocks, going beyond the 2% annual growth rate with current oil output at 4.43 million b/d.  America's Gas Glut Defies the Global Rally. Henry Hub gas futures fell to a two-month low of $2.66 per MMBtu as mild weather, recovering offshore supply and above-average US inventories outweigh record LNG demand, with the calendar year 2027 futures falling to a 5-year low of $3.09 per MMBtu.  By Tom Kool for Oilprice.com

title: Exceptional state visit elevates UK-Oman strategic ties
body:
LONDON: Stephen Doughty, UK Minister of State for the Middle East, affirmed that the Royal visit of His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik to the United Kingdom celebrates centuries of deeply rooted ties. In an interview with the Oman News Agency (ONA), Doughty noted that the official reception and state banquet hosted by King Charles III reflected the profound depth of these historic relations. Doughty emphasised that a central pillar of the "exceptional" visit is economic, as His Majesty’s ambitious vision for Oman closely aligns with the UK’s agenda for economic growth and modern technology. The visit focuses heavily on strategic minerals, renewable energy, artificial intelligence, and space technology, with new bilateral partnerships being forged across these domains. To strengthen future-focused people-to-people ties, the minister announced the resumption of the prestigious Chevening Scholarship programme for Omani students. Discussions also centred on university-level collaboration in renewable energy, AI, and space, positioning both nations to provide global leadership in cutting-edge industries. Addressing regional security, Doughty highlighted Oman’s diplomatically vital role amid ongoing Middle Eastern tensions. Having stood side by side through decades of turbulence, the UK and Oman continue intensive defence and security collaboration while maintaining joint diplomatic efforts to resolve regional and global challenges. Doughty commended Oman’s long-standing ability to keep channels of communication open among diverse nations. A primary focus remains maritime security and enhanced information-sharing to protect the free flow of trade and uphold freedom of navigation. Doughty noted that regional disruptions impact not only Middle Eastern economies but also the UK and the wider global economy. The two nations will continue working closely within international institutions, such as the United Nations, to advance peaceful, diplomatic solutions to regional conflicts. Doughty concluded by stressing the expansion of broader economic ties through the impending GCC-UK Free Trade Agreement. Bringing this agreement to its final stages, alongside establishing new strategic partnerships, remains essential for securing shared economic interests, regional stability, and long-term prosperity for both nations.
