title: Oman and UK forge ambitious future partnership
body:
LONDON/MUSCAT: The Sultanate of Oman and the United Kingdom have pledged to build an ambitious, future-forward partnership following a landmark state visit by His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik to the UK as a guest of King Charles III. The three-day visit, held from October 20 to 22, culminated in a joint statement outlining a bold agenda to deepen bilateral ties, align Oman Vision 2040 with the UK’s economic growth goals, and tackle shared global challenges. Strengthening Ties During a high-level bilateral meeting at 10 Downing Street on October 21, His Majesty the Sultan and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham reaffirmed the historical depth of Omani-British relations. The leaders agreed on a wide-ranging road map prioritising defence modernisation, green industries, advanced technology, and regional stability. To drive economic collaboration, both nations unveiled the "Sovereign Partnership for Investment Cooperation and Encouragement." The initiative connects the Oman Investment Authority (OIA) with the UK Office for Investment, aligning Oman’s Future Industries Ecosystem with the UK’s Modern Industrial Strategy. Major priority areas include green growth, critical minerals, space, and industrial clusters. In a major financial boost, UK Export Finance (UKEF) announced an additional £1.6 billion in financing capacity for Oman, bringing the total available funding to £7 billion to back British exports and high-priority development projects across the Sultanate of Oman. Tech Frontiers Defence collaboration remains a cornerstone of the alliance. Both governments reaffirmed their commitment to modernising military capabilities, deepening defence industry collaboration, and bolstering cybersecurity. Preparations are officially underway for Swift Sword 4 (Al Saif Al Saree 4), the latest instalment in the flagship joint military exercise series. On the technological front, Oman’s National Space Programme signed a partnership agreement with the UK Space Agency to share best practices in space launch vehicles and commercial technology. Both countries also introduced the "UK-Oman Innovation Initiative" to help emerging tech startups access both markets. In commitment to climate goals, both nations reiterated their target of achieving Net-Zero emissions by 2050. The Oman Net-Zero Centre partnered with Net-Zero Industry Wales and UKEF, while announcing plans for an "Oman Green Growth Tour" delegation to visit the UK in 2027. Peace and Maritime Security Addressing international issues, Oman and the UK renewed their shared commitment to peace and peaceful dispute resolution in the Middle East. Both nations firmly reiterated their support for the two-state solution as the only viable path to lasting peace between Israelis and Palestinians. The joint statement also underscored the necessity of upholding international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The UK reaffirmed Oman’s sovereignty over its waters in the Strait of Hormuz, emphasising the critical importance of maintaining maritime security and freedom of navigation through the international shipping lane. Investing in Education The visit also marked significant steps in cultural and educational diplomacy. A key highlight was the official resumption of the Chevening Scholarship programme for Omani scholars for the first time since 2021. Furthermore, the British Council launched a pilot programme to integrate artificial intelligence into Omani schools, while Cardiff University and the Oman Net-Zero Centre announced new joint research scholarships. Highlighting the role of youth leadership, HH Sayyid Theyazin bin Haitham al Said, Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs, and William, Prince of Wales, emphasised their joint patronage of the Anglo-Omani Society to foster intergenerational ties between both nations. KEY POINTS 1. UKEF raised Oman’s financing capacity to £7 billion for priority development projects. 2. Launched joint investment frameworks targeting Net-Zero carbon emissions by 2050. 3. Advanced military ties with "Swift Sword 4" exercises and space agency cooperation. 4. Reaffirmed the two-state solution for Palestine and Omani sovereignty in the Strait of Hormuz. 5. Resumed Chevening Scholarship and launched AI initiatives for Omani schools. 6. Cardiff University and the Oman Net-Zero Centre launch new joint research scholarships.

title: Oman condemns church attack in Jordan
body:
MUSCAT: The Sultanate of Oman expressed its strong condemnation and denunciation of the shooting incident that targeted a church in the Karak Governorate of Jordan, which resulted in a number of casualties and injuries. In a statement issued by the Foreign Ministry on Friday, the Sultanate of Oman reaffirmed its firm stance rejecting all forms of violence, the targeting of places of worship, and the terrorising of innocent people. Expressing solidarity with Jordan, Oman extended its sincere condolences and heartfelt sympathies to the families of victims and to the brotherly government and people of Jordan, wishing the injured a speedy recovery.

title: Agent cloud startup Daytona hits $1B valuation backed by FirstMark and a who’s who of angels
body:
Daytona Platforms announced on Friday that it had raised a $60 million Series B round at a $1 billion valuation led by FirstMark Growth. The company says it has now raised a total of $91 million.
The New York-based startup has attracted not just FirstMark (which also led its $24 million Series A in February), but also a host of well-known angels in this latest round. Daytona says they include Stripe’s Patrick Collison, Shopify’s Tobi Lütke, Perplexity’s Aravind Srinivas, Zoom’s Eric Yuan, Datadog’s Olivier Pomel, Quora’s Adam D’Angelo (who is also an OpenAI board member), and Mercor’s Brendan Foody. It also names Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next, and Okta Ventures as participants.
Three-year-old Daytona is building a cloud specifically for long-running agents, which have different infrastructure needs than yesteryear’s software, the startup contends. “Agents don’t work like the long-lived services today’s cloud was designed for. They spin up thousands of short, stateful jobs nobody planned in advance, and they need a cloud built for that,” founder Ivan Burazin wrote in a blog post announcing the new round . Daytona’s cloud, he said, is like giving every agent its own computer, where agents have access to sandboxed versions of Linux, Windows, macOS, and GPUs, among other services, on the one platform.

title: Defense giant Saab sees orders triple after Gripen fighter jet deal with Ukraine
body:
Swedish defense giant Saab reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year earlier, boosted by a deal to supply Gripen fighter jets to Ukraine.
New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor ($6.6 billion), up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier, beating FactSet expectations of 56.4 billion kronor.
Third-quarter sales reached 20.6 billion kronor, ahead of FactSet expectations of 20 billion kronor. Earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) came in at 1.95 billion kronor, also beating forecasts of 1.9 billion kronor.
Stockholm-listed shares closed 1.8% higher Friday, amid a mixed defense sector. The Stoxx 600 index ended the session down 0.3%.
The results come as European governments race to turn defense spending pledges into military capability.
Saab's order intake included a 24.6 billion kronor contract for 16 Gripen E fighter jets with the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration for Ukraine, signed in June and booked in the third quarter. Deliveries are scheduled for 2029-2030.
"The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said in a statement.
Orders booked in the quarter also include a 10.1 billion kronor order for its military surveillance aircraft GlobalEye to an undisclosed customer in the Middle East, and an 8.7 billion kronor order to equip warships for the German Navy.
Saab, whose products range from Gripen fighter jets and submarines to missiles and advanced electronics, has seen exponential order growth since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Even with an ever-growing order book , booming sales, and increasing profitability, Saab stock, like many of its peers, has taken a hit in recent months as some investors question whether valuations have run ahead of the industry's ability to deliver.
Rising geopolitical tensions, including recent airspace violations, drone incidents and ongoing conflicts, are driving demand for defense capabilities, Johansson said. He added that Saab is expanding production capacity and investments to help it meet growing customer needs.
"The long-term market outlook remains favourable," he said, as Saab reported that the order growth was driven by a more than sixfold surge in large orders to 52.1 billion kronor, while small orders rose 84% and medium-sized orders fell 16%.
The total order backlog amounted to 364.2 billion at the end of September, up from 274.5 billion at the beginning of the year, marking a sixth consecutive quarter of order book growth.
In July, Saab said it was looking to boost its production of jets from 15 per year to between 20 and 30.
"We can go further than that if we now get sort of partners involved in a more substantial way," Johansson told CNBC at the time.
Johansson also emphasized that European governments must fundamentally rethink how they buy weapons, moving away from fragmented national procurement toward long-term partnerships with industry.

title: UAE researchers win award for AI tool that helps surgeons during operations
body: Researchers in Abu Dhabi have won an international award at a robotic surgery conference in Italy for an AI tool designed to assist surgeons during operations. The team at Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) in Abu Dhabi won the accolade for developing Janus AI, which will show surgeons footage of similar past procedures. The technology analyses video footage captured during robotic surgery and selects a 30-second clip from a previous operation that matches the current stage of the procedure . The system works like a Google search for robotic surgery clips, letting doctors access relevant examples while operating. The footage can help surgeons see how other doctors approached the same task and guide them through subsequent steps. “While performing robotic surgery, we can have superimposed a number of small videos that show similar procedures, successful procedures, good procedures, in the exact same moment, so there is a guideline to follow,” said Cesare Stefanini, a professor of robotics at MBZUAI, who oversaw the technology’s development. “Sometimes surgeons may need some assistance; they would like to discuss with a colleague what they are doing, but they are not there, so this is a way to bring some human content to another human.” Janus AI takes its name from the Roman god Janus, depicted with two faces: one looking to the past and the other to the future. The name reflects the system’s aim of using previous surgical experience to help doctors make decisions during current procedures. The technology won the Robotic Urology Breakthrough Innovation Challenge award at Erus 26, a robotic urology surgery conference held in Padua, Italy, in September. “It’s very rewarding to be acknowledged by a community which is not only the computer science, AI, and robotics community, but also the medical community, [as it shows] that we are doing something that can be useful in the future,” said Prof Stefanini. The project was developed in collaboration with surgeons at the University of Illinois Chicago, and the University of Turin in Italy also contributed. Edoardo Fazzari, a postdoctoral researcher at MBZUAI, carried out much of the system’s development over about five months this year, following initial discussions with doctors. He said the project was particularly rewarding because it offered practical benefits beyond academic research. The system can show surgeons footage from three previous operations at the same stage of a procedure, letting them compare different approaches. “Why it’s helpful for the resident, for the surgeons, is that you can look at the future. We are using past experience to help humans make the next steps,” he said. “It should be very quick – we try to make it in milliseconds. You just click your button, make your query, and it pops up with three previous experiences that you can learn from.” The current video library covers robotic urology procedures, including nephrectomies, in which a kidney is removed. The researchers hope to expand the system to other surgeries, particularly robotic procedures, as the library grows. However, Janus AI is not yet ready for use in live operations. The technology needs further refinement and regulatory approval before it can enter clinical practice. When development is complete, the researchers hope to secure a commercial partner to bring the system to market. Prof Stefanini, whose group plans to recruit new postgraduate students, including Emiratis, said the project is a source of pride for the UAE. He said MBZUAI had created an environment in which AI researchers can exchange ideas and develop new technologies. “We’ve proven we can produce world-class results in the UAE, with the talent and vision that we have here. It’s encouraging for the future,” he said. “It’s not just something that individually we are proud of, but it can become a platform for future developments here.”

title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
body: With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched , you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them. Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString . Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports. Amazon Quick Sight , the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick , is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies. In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically. Dataset structure considerations A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized. Prerequisites The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight: A GeoJSON file describing your geometry. A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions. A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB. Structure of the GeoJSON file GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines. { "type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [{ "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [88.4, 22.6] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }, { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [88.2, 22.4], [88.9, 23.1], [89.5, 22.8], [90.1, 23.6] ] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }] } The structure of the file is as follows: FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array. Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key. geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates . The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point , and an ordered list of positions for a LineString . Configuring the Quick Sight dataset and its GeoJSON In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize , which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. The second is matching the Shape file key field to the Dataset key field , which links each Feature in the GeoJSON to a row in your Quick Sight dataset. The field names don’t need to be identical, but the values do. The following two examples show this end to end, first a LineString layer and then a Point layer. Example: LineString layer Consider example data showing a flight from JFK to a destination city like Los Angeles. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows: { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [-73.7781, 40.6413], [-85.5627, 40.6407], [-97.1415, 39.4569], [-108.1612, 37.1753], [-118.4085, 33.9416] ] }, "properties": { "route_id": "JFK-LAX" } } The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information: Figure 1: Dataset row for the JFK-LAX route, keyed by route_id The route_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per route, and the dataset one row per route. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Lines. Figure 2: The JFK-LAX route drawn as a LineString layer Example: Point layer Consider example data showing a retail store location like Long Island City. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows: { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [-73.9490, 40.7447] }, "properties": { "store_id": "S-109" } } The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information: Figure 3: Dataset row for a store, keyed by store_id The store_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per store, and the dataset one row per store. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Points. Figure 4: A store plotted as a Point layer Lines on layer map visuals Layer map visuals now support LineString geometry, connecting an ordered list of coordinates into a single path. As covered in the data structure section, each route is one feature, and its coordinates are the ordered positions the map connects in sequence. Use lines when the relationship between locations is what you want to show, such as flight paths, delivery routes, shipping lanes, or pipeline segments. The visual draws each path from the coordinates in your GeoJSON file rather than generating it from your data at load time. A field from your joined dataset can determine the line color encoding, so you can group routes by whatever that field represents. In addition to color, you can customize lines with width and opacity controls to adjust visual prominence and clarity on the map. The join key in the GeoJSON properties object ties each LineString to the dataset row behind its tooltip and color. For example, an airport operations team might map the flights leaving New York (JFK) on a given day. The GeoJSON file holds one LineString per route, keyed by a route ID that joins to the dataset. Each line starts at JFK and ends at its destination, such as Los Angeles, Chicago, or Miami. The dataset supplies the origin, destination, and carrier that show up in the tooltip. Figure 5: Flights leaving JFK drawn as LineString routes to multiple destinations Points on layer map visuals Amazon Quick Sight offers a native point map visual type that geocodes location names automatically and refreshes with your SPICE schedule or Direct Query connection. It supports dynamic point sizing, color encoding, and point styles such as cluster points and heatmap density gradients. It works best with data that changes frequently and where you want the map to respond to those changes visually. With the added support for GeoJSON point layers in layer map visuals, Quick Sight now offers a second point mapping capability with a few key differences. Layer map visual points use a uniform marker size and don’t support geocoding, so you provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file. In return, you can control the viewport precisely, locking the map to an exact geographic region, and disabling panning and zooming. The following table summarizes the key differences: Feature Point map Layer map visual points Data source Latitude/longitude values or geolocation names in your dataset GeoJSON Point features joined to your dataset by a shared key Geocoding Recognizes city, county, state, country, and postal code automatically Not available. Must provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file Location updates Mapping updates automatically with SPICE refreshes or Direct Query as location values change Visual uses a static GeoJSON file for point locations. Requires manual re-upload or API call to update geometry Viewport Auto-fits to your data, panning and zooming always enabled Auto-fits by default, can configure if panning and zooming is allowed Appearance Size and color can be encoded from the dataset. Point style configuration available (basic, cluster, heatmap) Customizable uniform marker size, fill opacity, border color and thickness. Color can be encoded from the dataset Choose layer map visual points when: You require a locked, non-scrollable viewport. Your locations are fixed and curated (such as regional offices, distribution centers, retail stores) rather than changing with each data refresh. You plan to combine points with other geometry types (covered in the advanced use cases section). Consider a retail brand whose regional managers use a Quick Sight dashboard to track store performance across a metro area. The GeoJSON file contains a Point feature for each store with a store ID property that joins to the dataset. The dataset holds the metrics (store type, monthly revenue, daily foot traffic) that drive the tooltip and color encoding. You position the map at the zoom level covering the metro area, then disable map navigation so the map renders at a consistent view on every load. Managers can’t accidentally zoom out to a national or global view. Figure 6: Store locations as points with map navigation disabled to lock the metro-area view Advanced use cases The previous sections cover a standard layer map setup. Use the following techniques when you need more control over what readers see, want to combine geometry types in a single view, or need geometry that changes over time. Controlling the viewport When you need to control the viewport in layer map visuals, you can pan and zoom to the view you want manually. Then disable map navigation to lock it in place. For use cases where you need more precise boundaries or programmatic control, you can set the exact viewport coordinates through the visual definition using the Quick Sight APIs. The layer map visual stores its viewport configuration in the MapState property within ChartConfiguration . This property accepts two fields: Bounds : The geographic coordinates defining the minimum visible area (North, South, East, West). MapNavigation : ENABLED or DISABLED to control whether readers can pan and zoom. Although the bounds property is not exposed on the console, you can set these bounds when working with the dashboard definition JSON for programmatic asset management. For example, to define the bounds, modify the MapState block in the visual definition, then call the CreateDashboard or UpdateDashboard APIs. The bounds define the minimum area that is guaranteed to be visible. The map zooms to make sure this entire area fits within the visual container. For the tightest fit with minimal extra space added to the map, match the aspect ratio of your bounds to the shape of your visual container. Layering geometries For use cases that require combining multiple geometry types into a single view, you can layer visuals on top of each other. For example, the following screenshot demonstrates plotting customer locations as points within US regional boundaries defined by polygons. This composition shows which territories have the highest customer density and can be used to correlate with other metrics present in the dataset like performance. Figure 7: Customer points layered within polygon regional boundaries This second example demonstrates combining points as stops along a delivery route path. The LineString draws the planned route, and Point features mark each scheduled stop along the way. Figure 8: A delivery route drawn as a LineString with Point markers for each stop To layer geometries, you stack multiple layer map visuals on top of each other, following these steps: Use free-form layout: Change the sheet layout setting to free-form so that visuals can overlap and stack. Create two layer map visuals: Create the two layer map visuals that you combine into a single view, such as one using a Point GeoJSON file and one using a LineString GeoJSON file. Use matching bounds: Using the approach previously described for controlling the viewport, verify all layer map visuals use identical bounds to have the same underlying map view. Disable panning and zooming: For each layer map visual, disable the panning and zooming under Map options so that alignment stays the same. Hide the base map and background on upper layer: Set the upper visual’s background to hidden under Display settings and disable the base map under Map options. Stack the visuals: Move the top visual on top of the base layer using drag-and-drop or by matching precise size and position coordinates under Display settings. Layer ordering follows the visual stacking order in the free-form layout. To change a visual’s position in the stack, choose the menu icon (three dots) on the visual, then choose Send backward or Bring forward . Readers can access the tooltip of the topmost visual, so place the layer that readers need details from on top. Each sheet supports up to five layer map visuals. Dynamically updating GeoJSON Unlike other Quick Sight visuals where data refreshes through SPICE or Direct Query, layer map geometry lives in the GeoJSON file itself. When your dataset refreshes on schedule, the metrics update (for example, colors change and tooltip values refresh), but the geometry remains at its original position. To update what appears on the map, like a new route, new point locations, or updated boundaries, you need to update the GeoJSON file and republish the dashboard. You can replace a GeoJSON file manually through the Quick Sight console by editing the layer map visual within the Analysis and uploading a new file. This works for infrequent changes such as updating territory boundaries quarterly or adding a new store location. For automated, on-demand, or dynamic updates, the process involves Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the Quick Sight APIs outlined in the following steps: Upload the new GeoJSON to Amazon S3: Generate your updated geometry and save it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Custom solutions can use other AWS services such as Amazon Location Service to create the GeoJSON files. Reference the file on the dashboard definition: The dashboard definition contains a StaticFiles array with a SpatialStaticFile entry for each GeoJSON file. Modify the file reference to the S3 location of your updated file entry for each GeoJSON file. Call the UpdateDashboard API: Submit the updated definition with the new file reference using the UpdateDashboard API. Call the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API: Publish the change so it is visible to dashboard readers with the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API. The following example uses this pattern to support on-demand map updates in an embedded dashboard to generate optimal routes between locations and waypoints. Although outside the scope of this post, this represents an advanced use case that combines each of the preceding approaches. Figure 9: On-demand route generation in an embedded dashboard Conclusion In this post, we showed how to use Point and LineString geometry in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps to plot specific locations and the routes between them. We covered the GeoJSON structure and dataset join that layer maps require, and compared layer map points with the native point map. We also walked through advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering separate visuals into one view, and refreshing GeoJSON files with Amazon S3 and the Quick Sight APIs. To learn more about layered maps, refer to the Amazon Quick Sight layered maps documentation . Visit the Amazon Quick Community to connect with peers and stay updated on the newest features and resources. About the authors Amit Makashir Amit is a Software Development Engineer on the Amazon Quick Suite visualization team, where he helped build Quick Sight’s layer maps and the geospatial mapping stack behind them. His work spans the mapping visuals customers see and the geocoding, data, and service infrastructure that power them. Drawn to maps, places, and spatial problem-solving, he brings that curiosity to much of his work. Outside the office, he enjoys the outdoors—hiking, exploring new destinations, and taking long scenic drives. Jackson Dowden Jackson is a Worldwide Generative AI Solutions Architect for Amazon Quick at AWS. He began at AWS as a Partner Solutions Architect and now focuses on helping ISV and healthcare & life sciences customers implement AI-driven analytics and embedded insights with the Quick service. Koushik Muthanna Koravanda Ganapathy Koushik is a Specialist Solutions Architect for Amazon Quick at AWS. He helps customers design, implement, and scale Quick across their organization, from architecture to everyday use. Salim Khan Salim is a Senior Worldwide Generative AI Solutions Architect for Amazon Quick at AWS. He has over 16 years of experience implementing enterprise business intelligence solutions. At AWS, Salim works with customers globally to design and implement AI-powered BI and generative AI capabilities on Amazon Quick. Prior to AWS, he worked as a BI consultant across industry verticals including Automotive, Healthcare, Entertainment, Consumer, Publishing, and Financial Services, delivering business intelligence, data warehousing, data integration, and master data management solutions.

title: Omani engineer’s journey to the Bundestag
body:
When Mohsin al Shukaili sat in the Bundestag gallery on September 9 to watch the Chancellor defend Germany’s 2027 budget, the Omani engineer was a long way from the oil and logistics world he works in at home. He was also, by his own account, in the right place. Mohsin, 26, has just returned from a month in Berlin on the International Parliamentary Scholarship (IPS) Programme for Arab States 2026, which places participants in the office of a Bundestag member and gives them a close look at German democracy at work. He was selected after an interview at the German Embassy in Muscat. “For me, the IPS programme was much more than a study visit,” he said. “It was an opportunity to engage directly with policymakers." For Mohsin, the programme’s value lay in what it could mean for Oman. Sessions on Germany’s energy transition, its partnerships with the Middle East and North Africa, and green hydrogen struck him most. “As an Omani, I found particular value in the discussions on cooperation between Germany and the Gulf region, especially in renewable energy and green hydrogen,” he said. Such topics, he added, feed into “the wider conversation about economic diversification, international partnerships and the future of energy in our region.” He is careful not to overstate the comparison. “Although Germany and Oman have different political systems and institutional structures, learning from other countries’ experiences can provide valuable perspectives and encourage constructive exchanges of ideas,” he said. He hopes to apply “the knowledge, connections and insights” he gained “in my professional development and future contributions to Oman.” He said he was proud to have “represented Oman in this international setting,” describing the trip as "an important personal and professional milestone.” Placed with the office of Enrico Komning, an AfD lawmaker, attorney and the party group’s Parliamentary Managing Director, Mohsin helped prepare a parliamentary question on wind energy and assisted with a draft speech. He sat in on the group’s economic affairs and energy working group, a committee meeting and several plenary sittings, including questions to the government. Enrico said the Omani visitor made the most of a short stay. “He was an exceptionally pleasant, motivated and intellectually curious participant,” he said, noting Mohsin’s “open-mindedness, his thoughtful questions and his genuine interest in understanding how our institutions operate in practice.” What stood out, Enrico said, was that Mohsin came "not as a student, but as an established professional seeking to broaden his personal and intellectual horizons.” Mohsin finished school in Oman, then studied petroleum engineering at Montanuniversität Leoben in Austria, graduating in 2023. The years there gave him fluent German, which he says let him talk to Berlin’s politicians “without a language barrier.” He joined ASYAD Group’s graduate programme and now works as a planning officer at its unit Mwasalat. He also presides over the ASYAD Group Toastmasters Club and regularly attends German and Austrian embassy events in Muscat. In Berlin, he joined participants from Egypt, Tunisia, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Algeria for workshops on anti-corruption, press freedom, artificial intelligence and transitional justice, and visited Deutsche Welle’s Arabic newsroom. Ines Dlih, a participant from Algeria, said the programme’s worth outlasts the visit. By bringing Arab participants together, she said, it builds “a foundation for informed engagement with political and societal issues,” with lessons applied to “the particular circumstances, priorities and traditions” of each home country. Mohsin now eyes a career in diplomacy. Enrico sees him going far. “Talented and internationally experienced young professionals such as Mohsin can make an important contribution” to Oman’s future, he said, adding that Berlin would be “delighted to welcome him back.” Photos by Franz von Winterfeld and German Bundestag

title: COP17: Open letter urges governments to keep extractives out of protected areas
body: YEREVAN, Armenia — More than 80 conservation, Indigenous and civil society organizations have called on governments meeting at the COP17 U.N. biodiversity summit in Armenia to keep mining, oil and gas operations out of protected areas. “Meeting a numerical target will mean little”, if areas designated for conservation remain exposed to industrial activities, the organizations warn in a joint letter released in advance of COP17 on Oct. 2. An Oct. 8 report by Earth Insight and partners says that nearly 62 million hectares (153 million acres) of protected and conserved areas across the tropics overlap with oil and gas blocks, while mining concessions overlap with 43 million hectares (106 million acres). World leaders agreed in 2022 to protect 30% of the planet’s land and waters by 2030, a commitment known as “30×30” or Target 3 of the Global Biodiversity Framework. The signatories argue that this commitment must be achieved “not just on paper, but in reality.” Conservation officials argue that mining has no place in protected and conserved areas. “Protected areas are protected areas,” Nadège Nzoyem, WWF’s Congo Basin regional director, said in a recent interview with Mongabay. Madhu Rao, chair of the IUCN World Commission on Protected Areas, has echoed that concern, arguing that “some places are so critical that they have to be secured against extractive industries.” The head of Nigeria’s National Park Service also acknowledged in a recent interview with Mongabay the challenges posed by illegal mining and insecurity in the country’s national parks. title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
body: Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls. As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models. To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations . The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch. Architecture overview ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility. Amazon DynamoDB stores LangGraph checkpoint state. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL stores session records, user feedback, and analytics. Amazon ElastiCache caches agent responses with a time to live (TTL). Domain content in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and indexed in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Amazon CloudWatch captures runtime and application telemetry. AgentCore Gateway exposes backend APIs to agents as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code. Figure 1: Agentic Decision Engine architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ADE runs 22 specialist agents in production, each scoped to one domain with its own tools and data sources. For example, the Domain Expert Agent answers conceptual questions through RAG. The Operational Agent retrieves live workflow status and results from CDE. The Troubleshooting Agent analyzes operational telemetry. The Visualization Agent generates charts or returns existing dashboards. A customer-specific Models as Skill pattern converts model code and documentation into skill definitions stored in a central registry, so agents answer model-specific questions from the model’s implementation instead of generic model knowledge. When a breeder asks, “Why did my phenotyping workflow fail yesterday?”, the supervisor classifies the intent and routes the request to the Troubleshooting Agent. That agent reads the workflow’s telemetry in CloudWatch and its status from the CDE API through AgentCore Gateway, identifies the failure point, and returns a diagnosis through the supervisor (Figure 2). The breeder doesn’t search logs directly. With the Troubleshooting Agent, a diagnosis that once took over an hour of manual log-hunting and waiting for engineer support now takes under 10 minutes. Figure 2: ADE request flow: intent classification, cache lookup, specialist routing, and response Five design decisions on the path to production The Unified Operations TAM and DSE took part in the following decisions as members of the working team, not as an escalation point after the fact. That let Bayer test each design against AWS service behavior before committing to it, while keeping ownership of the architecture and the final call. 1. Externalize orchestration state without treating the runtime as stateless AgentCore runtime provides isolated sessions that preserve execution context across invocations within a session’s lifecycle. That context isn’t a durable store for a multi-step workflow. ADE writes LangGraph checkpoints to DynamoDB so the graph can resume after scale-out events, restarts, or session boundaries without depending on one execution environment remaining available. Principle: Use the runtime session for active execution, and persist the state required to resume or reconstruct the workflow in a durable service. 2. Separate enterprise identity, gateway access, and downstream authorization Bayer standardizes on Microsoft Entra ID for user identity, while ADE’s services authorize each other with AWS-native mechanisms. Rather than force one token across every trust boundary, the team gave each boundary its own mechanism. Entra ID remains the source of user identity. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) authorizes service-to-service calls. AgentCore Gateway outbound authorization handles access to downstream CDE services. A request interceptor AWS Lambda function performs custom validation and passes the authorization attributes that downstream tools require. The team worked through the token contract at each hop with the DSE. Principle: Identity failures in agent systems cluster at the transitions between user identity, agent identity, and tool identity. Define the issuer, audience, claims, scopes, and credential lifetime at every hop instead of reusing a token that is valid for one boundary at the next. 3. Treat model selection as an interface contract During the build, the team evaluated a newer model version with reasoning mode enabled. For that version, the combination of tool use and structured output that ADE depends on was not compatible with how its agents were implemented. The DSE confirmed the constraint, and the team retained the current model for the release. Principle: For tool-using agents, model choice is constrained by the full interface: tool calling, structured output, streaming behavior, reasoning features, latency, quota availability, and model-specific request semantics. A newer model is not automatically a drop-in replacement. 4. Control the tool surface before it controls the prompt CDE manages more than 500 model configurations. A dedicated MCP server per API would have added deployment, authentication, and version management overhead. ADE instead registers OpenAPI specifications with AgentCore Gateway, which exposes the REST operations as MCP tools. Adding or changing an API becomes a schema and gateway configuration change instead of a new server deployment. Tool schemas and descriptions also consume input tokens and compete with the user’s request and retrieved context. ADE scopes tools by specialist agent instead of giving every agent the full catalog. For larger catalogs, AgentCore Gateway supports semantic tool search, so an agent can find relevant tools without loading the entire catalog on every turn. Principle: Scope the tool catalog per agent. Every tool definition adds tokens and widens the model’s decision space. 5. Promote complex capabilities from tools to agents Visualization started as a tool invoked by other agents. As it grew, it needed its own data retrieval, chart selection logic, retries, error handling, and a decision about whether to generate a chart or return an existing dashboard. The team moved it into a specialist Visualization Agent. The agent generates on-demand charts with matplotlib and Plotly in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides a sandboxed code execution environment, and exchanges data with it through Amazon S3. When a prebuilt dashboard is the better answer, the agent returns the existing Amazon Quick or Power BI asset. Principle: A tool performs a bounded operation. When a capability starts to own state, retries, planning, policy, or presentation decisions, model it as an agent. Preparing ADE for production As the build moved toward launch, the focus shifted from design to operability: detecting agent failures, attributing inference cost, and hardening the deployment. Observability: Measure task failures, not only exceptions A supervisor architecture turns one user request into a chain of model calls, tool calls, and agent handoffs. The final answer can be wrong even when every HTTP request succeeded. ADE encountered this directly: application exception handlers caught agent errors and returned responses that monitoring counted as successful. After reproducing the issue with the DSE, the team added custom CloudWatch metrics inside failure paths and alarms on agent-specific conditions: tool call errors, throttling, model timeouts, and structured output validation failures. Traces and invocation logs follow each request across the supervisor and specialists. Principle: Distinguish transport success from task success. Agent observability should show whether the task completed, which agent or tool changed the outcome, and whether the response used the expected source. Cost attribution: Combine billing attribution with request-level telemetry One ADE request can invoke several models and tools, so account-level Amazon Bedrock spend doesn’t explain unit economics. The team designed the attribution approach with the DSE using three mechanisms that answer different questions. Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles attribute billed model usage to an application or workload. Request metadata and model invocation logging associate token usage with a specific agent, feature, or request. IAM principal attribution adds an identity dimension. Together they let the team estimate cost per interaction, identify expensive agents, and determine whether prompts, retrieved context, or tool definitions drive token use. In practice, the Visualization and Operational agents, which rely on MCP tools and multiple tool calls, consumed the most tokens. The same telemetry surfaced a workload during launch preparation with a large repeated input prefix and no prompt cache activity. For supported models, placing stable instructions and tool definitions in a cacheable prompt prefix reduces repeated input processing, which lowers latency and token cost. For ADE, caching the stable prompt prefix cut input-token cost by 20–30 percent. Security and launch readiness IAM roles are scoped to each agent’s responsibility. The Troubleshooting Agent can read the operational data it needs for diagnosis but can’t modify workflows. The Domain Expert Agent can query its retrieval index but cannot call unrelated CDE APIs. In production today, ADE’s agent responses are governed by least privilege, read-only tool access scoped to each agent, structured output validation on agent responses, and answers grounded in retrieved CDE data and telemetry rather than open-ended generation. Bayer also plans to evaluate Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as an additional layer on these controls, complementing the custom safety checks already used in CDE multi-turn workflows. Before launch, Unified Operations ran a Critical Workload Review and a Well-Architected review with the Generative AI Lens alongside the ADE team. Because the DSE already knew the workload, both reviews targeted ADE’s specific failure modes, capacity risks, and deployment gaps rather than generic best practices. Findings included gaps in failure visibility across the supervisor and specialist agents, mutable container image tags, limited image traceability, and missing vulnerability scanning. The team responded with stronger alarms, immutable versioned images, scan on push in Amazon ECR, and lifecycle policies for unused images. The DSE also reviewed scaling and quota requirements with the team. Load testing validated both the application and its service quotas and exposed a networking failure mode that returned empty responses, which the team fixed before the production event. By launch, the team had tracked 35 blockers to resolution with Unified Operations. Launch, operations, and next steps Bayer launched ADE to a gated group rather than opening it to the whole organization at once. Since launch, more than 100 users across Bayer Crop Science have used ADE, including breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and engineers. Alongside its 22 specialist agents, ADE exposes about 20 API tools and can host third-party agents as it expands. Exposing those APIs through AgentCore Gateway rather than a dedicated server per API cut per-API integration overhead by more than 99 percent. In its first phase, ADE has resolved about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. CDE remains the governed execution layer for analytics. ADE adds a natural language layer over it, so users can ask about workflow status, results, model behavior, and failures without learning the location or interface of each underlying system. The engagement then shifted from launch readiness to ongoing operations. The DSE continues to meet with the team, so issue triage and operational reviews start from existing knowledge of ADE instead of a new ramp-up. ADE’s critical CloudWatch alarms, including the agent-specific alarms described earlier, are onboarded to AWS Incident Detection and Response. When one fires, AWS Incident Management Engineers engage within 5 minutes and start from the workload’s context rather than from scratch. On the security side, AWS Security Incident Response engineers support the team during potential or active security events, so ADE has AWS monitoring and response coverage for both operational and security issues. With agent-to-agent communication already in place, Bayer is focusing next on hybrid cloud agent interoperability. The team is exploring how agents running in different environments can discover and communicate with each other without manual configuration. Conclusion Bayer didn’t replace its analytics platform with ADE. It made CDE easier to query and operate. Most of the production work sat outside the prompts: durable state, identity boundaries, tool scoping, task-level observability, cost attribution, and launch readiness. Bayer owned the architecture and each of those decisions. Working with a designated DSE and TAM through AWS Unified Operations, the team tested those decisions against AWS service behavior during design and carried the same context into production. To learn more, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Bedrock cost attribution , AWS Well-Architected Generative AI guidance , and AWS Unified Operations . The authors would like to thank Sijie Shi, Jorge Gomes, Naveen Reddy, Iago Fonseca, Mateus Silva, and Sushimitha Jarugula for their contributions to the design, development, and launch of ADE. About the authors Subbu Dandamudi Subbu is Head of MLOps for R&D at Bayer. He leads the development of scalable platforms and AI capabilities and has played a key role in building the Connected Decision Engine (CDE) and its evolution into the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE) to accelerate AI-driven innovation across R&D. Dr. Leo de Melo Leo is a Staff ML Engineer at Bayer Crop Science, where he helps shape the future of AI-powered R&D through scalable platforms, agentic systems, and advanced analytics. With a background in Computer Science and Computational Mathematics, he specializes in building AI and data platforms that enable researchers to transform complex data into actionable insights and accelerate scientific discovery. Mahnoor Hussain Mahnoor is a Senior Solutions Architect specializing in Generative AI and cloud architecture. She helps customers operationalize GenAI by translating emerging capabilities into production-ready solutions across agentic systems, governance, security, and cloud operations. Her work focuses on helping organizations move from experimentation to enterprise adoption. Outside of work, Mahnoor enjoys spending time with family and traveling. Ram Pamidimukkala Ram is a Senior Technical Account Manager at AWS, specializing in Generative AI, agentic workloads, data analytics, multi-cloud, and cloud operations. He helps organizations design, modernize, and migrate workloads to the AWS Cloud efficiently and securely. As part of Unified Operations his work focuses on building resilient architectures that balance performance, cost optimization, and long-term sustainability. Sai Pavan Kasani Sai is a Domain Specialist Engineer for Generative AI at AWS. As a technical advisor and customer advocate, he helps teams move generative AI proofs of concept into production, with particular focus on agentic AI workloads. He also works with customers on inference optimization and cost efficiency as their generative AI applications scale. Outside of work, Sai enjoys exploring new coffee shops and spending time with family.

title: Commonwealth Fusion Systems gets $85M to build better fusion-ready semiconductors
body:
Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) announced on Thursday that it would receive $85 million from the U.S. government to develop advanced chips for the fusion power industry.
Fusion power startups have been racing to complete their first demonstration devices, with CFS aiming to turn on its Sparc reactor sometime next year. But building one reactor is just a proof point. If fusion startups want to build dozens of commercial power plants, they’ll need more durable power electronics and a robust supply chain.
The new CHIPS Act award from the Department of Commerce, which also grants the government a stake in CFS, will help boost R&D and manufacturing capacity for semiconductors in the U.S., the company said.
“Ultimately, that means a more capable, economical power plant and a stronger U.S. supply chain to build it,” Brandon Sorbom, co-founder and chief science officer at CFS, wrote in a blog post .
CFS’s award will go toward supporting five different initiatives.
The first is the advancement of silicon carbide power electronics. The semiconductors are widely used to manage high voltages, and they’re found in everything from LEDs and EVs to cell phone base stations and data centers. It’s also used in fusion machines, where intense bursts of electricity are used to drive the superconducting magnets that confine plasma inside a reactor.
CFS will also use the award to develop next-generation radio-frequency power generators, which the company uses to heat fusion fuel, and advanced electronics that will enable faster control of the reactor and be hardened against radiation. The latter could help extend the lifespan of electronics within a fusion power plant, reducing operating costs.
Lastly, CFS plans to use part of the CHIPS award to adapt AI hardware like GPUs and TPUs for power plants.
“The funding would help improve the U.S. chip and power electronics industries at the same time it accelerates fusion energy’s progress toward the electrical grid,” Sorbom said.

title: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with making false statements about Hunter Biden's laptop
body:
Two former FBI intelligence officials who specialized in foreign election interference have been charged with making false statements about their roles in investigating the origins of Hunter Biden’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election
WASHINGTON -- Two former FBI intelligence officials who specialized in foreign election interference were charged on Friday with making false statements to Congress about their roles in investigating Hunter Biden’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election .
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides surrendered Friday and made their first appearance in federal court in Washington, where their lawyers pressed for a speedy hearing at which they could contest the allegations against them.
The Department of Justice says Floris and Benavides lied to Congress in 2023 about the involvement of a specialized foreign-influence task force in investigations into Biden as well as their knowledge of the laptop.
Floris' attorneys called her “a patriot” and said she has “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years.”
"Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts," her attorneys said in a statement. “It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.”
The case was filed 10 days before the Nov. 3 elections and marks the latest in a series of splashy and politically charged investigative actions the Department of Justice has undertaken in the run-up to the midterm contests.
The prosecution, a rare Department of Justice criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and peculiar saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race. It also comes amid a broader, backward-looking effort by FBI Director Kash Patel, who before taking over the nation’s premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it , to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau’s recent past that for years have animated President Donald Trump’s conservative base.
“Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system. No one is above the law,” Patel said in a statement posted on X.
The revelation of the laptop’s existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump, the Republican incumbent, and Hunter Biden's father, Joe Biden, Trump's Democratic challenger, who went on to win the race .
The laptop’s contents were publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop. The laptop contained emails that appeared to show discussions of the younger Biden’s foreign business dealings.
The peculiar circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian disinformation, particularly when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community was assessing that Russia was attempting to interfere on Trump’s behalf in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens.
Hunter Biden was subsequently charged with, and convicted of, gun and tax offenses during his father’s administration. Joe Biden pardoned him in his final weeks in office.
The Justice Department historically looks to avoid public and overt investigative acts in the direct lead-up to an election that involve candidates or that risk influencing an outcome. But officials in the last two weeks have made a series of bold moves in cases with political undertones, including a search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s house in an immigration fraud investigation and a corruption indictment unsealed Thursday against powerful Democratic Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Floris and Benavides, two experienced intelligence officials, led the FBI's since-disbanded Foreign Intelligence Task Force, or FITF, when the laptop was discovered. They are accused by the Justice Department of making false statements in Congress in 2023 by saying that the FITF was not involved in investigations related to Hunter Biden when contemporaneous messages proved otherwise, according to a criminal complaint filed against them.
The case brings renewed attention to the work of the task force, which was established in the first Trump administration to police influence campaigns staged by Russia and other nations aimed at sowing discord, undermining democracy and spreading disinformation. The task force became a magnet of congressional Republican criticism during the Biden investigation and was disbanded in February 2025 by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi in one of her first acts on the job.

title: F-35 multiyear production framework proposed for 850 U.S. aircraft
body:
ARLINGTON, Virginia. The Department of War and Lockheed Martin announced a framework for potential multiyear F-35 production and sustainment covering 850 U.S. aircraft over 10 years, along with initial spares, modification kits, sustainment, and international customer orders across Lots 21 through 30.
The framework calls for continued production at 156 aircraft per year and would combine aircraft procurement with spare parts, modification kits, and sustainment planning. Lockheed Martin says the approach is intended to give suppliers longer-term demand visibility, support bulk purchases of materials and components, and improve parts availability and readiness metrics.
The framework is not yet a final contract award. If multiyear procurement authority and associated appropriations are approved, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin would negotiate final contract terms, pricing, and schedules. The company says the arrangement is expected to reduce lifecycle costs through volume purchasing and more predictable production and sustainment planning.

title: AI-enabled EO/IR sensor to be integrated with Do228 NXT special-mission aircraft
body:
OBERPFAFFENHOFEN, Germany. General Atomics AeroTec Systems and HENSOLDT will offer the ARGOS-15 electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) gimbal as a mission-system option for the Do228 NXT special-mission aircraft, the companies announced in a statement.
The ARGOS-15 is a single line-replaceable unit equipped with multispectral sensors and onboard artificial intelligence capabilities for object detection, classification, and tracking. Mounted ahead of the aircraft’s retractable main landing gear, the sensor is designed to provide an unobstructed 360-degree field of view. Available payload options include long-range multispectral cameras, a laser pointer, illuminator, range finder, and designator.
The companies say the integration is intended to expand the Do228 NXT’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities while reducing operator workload through onboard detection and tracking. The aircraft can remain on station for up to eight hours and operate from short grass or unpaved runways, according to the statement.

title: Melania Trump says she negotiated ceasefire in Russian-held Ukrainian city
body: US President Donald Trump's wife Melania Trump has secured a ⁠localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled ⁠city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, the White House announced on Friday. The ceasefire will begin on ​October 29. Oleshky has been occupied by Russian forces since February 2022 and residents there have reported a deepening food crisis. In a statement, the first lady described the situation in Oleshky as “dire” and on “the brink of disaster”. The White House said that Russia and Ukraine agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter ⁠and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway. “Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water,” Ms Trump said. “The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads and endure regular military attacks.” She added that it was “abundantly clear” that without her intervention, the possibility of bringing humanitarian aid into the city and evacuating the elderly would have been “impossible”. The development comes as ‌Mr Trump appears to be increasingly on Russia's side in its war against Ukraine. He has repeatedly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for not making a peace deal and has waived sanctions to allow the US to import Russian diesel as he tries to lower prices ahead of the November 3 midterms. Of his wife's announcement, Mr Trump said it was “not the worst idea I've ever heard.” “What she wants to do is save children ... It was her initiative, and they contacted both sides, and both sides wanted to do it,” he told reporters. Ms Trump has been active in trying to have Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families. Last year, she said she and Russian President Vladimir Putin had an “open channel of communication” to discuss the welfare of children caught up in the war. Oleshky, which is across the Dnipro River ​from Kherson, has a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people – ​primarily elderly residents ‌along with about 50 children – down from roughly 24,000 before the war, the White ⁠House said. About 90 per cent of the city was flooded following the destruction ⁠of the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White House. The White House said Ms Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and ​transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia and some to Ukraine,” Ms Trump said. The suffering in Oleshky came to Ms Trump’s attention during a private discussion at an event during the UN General Assembly in New York, the White House said.

title: Taiwan shuts schools and grounds flights as Typhoon Champi brushes by
body: TAIPEI, Taiwan (AP) — Taiwan shut down schools and offices and grounded hundreds of flights as Typhoon Champi brushed by the island Friday, packing strong winds and torrential rains. Champi peaked at 298 kph (185 mph) maximum sustained winds earlier this week but has weakened to 155 kph (96 mph) winds as it approached Taiwan from the southwest. Its center is forecast to remain offshore as it sweeps by the island’s northeastern tip before turning north toward Japan’s southwestern islands. Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration urged residents in coastal areas to avoid outdoor activities and driving and be cautious of falling objects. One person was killed Thursday after being swept away by waves in Liuqiu, a small island off the southeastern coast of Taiwan’s main island, according to the fire department. More than 170 other people were injured in the storm. More than 2,600 people have been evacuated from vulnerable, mountainous areas, the government said. All of Taiwan’s 262 domestic flights were canceled, along with 669 international flights, according to the transport ministry. High-speed rail services on the western coast were operating normally. The capital Taipei, in northern Taiwan, saw light showers and gusts of winds. Transportation services including the subway remained open. Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te visited the island’s Central Emergency Operation Center in New Taipei City, which spans from near the capital to Taiwan’s northern coast. Champi has a massive radius of around 320 kilometers (200 miles), large enough to engulf most of Taiwan. Experts expect its biggest effect…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: OpenVPX backplane from Pixus adds 100GbE support and optical interface cutout
body:
KITCHENER, Ontario. Pixus Technologies released a single-slot power and ground backplane using the RT3 version of the OpenVPX connector, enabling support for 100 Gigabit Ethernet plug-in cards, the company announced in a statement.
The backplane is based on the VITA 66.4 standard and includes a cutout for optical interfaces, allowing different fiber housing options to be implemented. Pixus says the design is intended for development systems, including standalone board testing and configurations in which the single-slot backplane is used alongside other backplanes.
The company also offers RT3 backplane versions with a VITA 67.3c cutout designed to accept modules using the 14.6.11 Sensor Open Systems Architecture, or SOSA, Technical Standard slot profile. Pixus develops SOSA aligned, OpenVPX, and other VITA-based backplanes and enclosure systems for embedded defense applications.

title: SEC flags tokenization as high-risk area in 2027 market examinations
body:
The SEC’s latest priorities highlight tokenization as an emerging market risk, while cryptocurrencies remain absent as a standalone examination category.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has added tokenization to its fiscal 2027 examination priorities, placing tokenized securities alongside quantum computing and extended trading hours among emerging trends it plans to examine.
In its 2027 examination priorities , released Friday, the SEC identified tokenization as an area of focus for examinations of critical market infrastructure. Tokenization was not explicitly mentioned in the agency’s 2026 priorities .
The report addressed the security and reliability of critical market infrastructure, stating:
The SEC also listed tokenization among the high-risk areas it will examine at clearing agencies, alongside default management, securities lending and operational risks.
Cryptocurrencies, meanwhile, remain absent as a standalone examination priority for the second consecutive year. The SEC last included a dedicated section on crypto assets in its fiscal 2025 priorities.
The new priorities come as traditional financial institutions move further into tokenized securities. Earlier this month, an OKX and Intercontinental Exchange joint venture filed to launch a platform offering tokenized shares in more than 60 US-listed companies.

title: Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine has received more than 50,000 rounds of 20-mm ammunition from Denmark for the onboard cannons of its F-16 fighter jets, with Ukrainian pilots already using the rounds to intercept Russian jet-powered Geran attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said. The accelerated delivery addresses a key need in Ukraine’s air defense as Russia increasingly deploys faster jet-powered drones that challenge conventional interceptors. Ukraine has also relied on F-16 cannons when stocks of air-to-air missiles are limited, making ammunition supplies important to keeping the aircraft effective against incoming aerial threats. Denmark responds to ammunition request The Defense Ministry thanked Denmark for responding quickly to Ukraine’s request for additional ammunition, saying the delivery directly strengthens the country’s air defenses and helps protect civilians from Russian aerial attacks. The delivery follows a broader effort by Ukraine’s European partners to replenish F-16 cannon ammunition. On October 2, it was reported that Spain, Belgium, and Poland were also sending 20-mm rounds for Ukrainian F-16s to counter Russia’s jet-powered drones. Belgium is also expanding its support for Ukraine’s F-16 fleet. On 16 October, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever pledged to deliver 10 F-16s by the end of 2026, up from three previously planned, and discussed supplying additional ammunition, including 20-mm rounds produced by Belgian defense company FN Herstal. Jet-powered drones pose a growing challenge Russia’s faster attack drones are harder to intercept than older, propeller-driven Shahed-type models. Their speed gives air defenders less time to respond and makes them more difficult for many interceptor drones and conventional short-range weapons to catch. Ukraine’s air-to-air missile shortages have also increased the importance of F-16 cannon ammunition. Ukrainian pilots have sometimes relied on their aircraft’s built-in 20-mm cannon when air-to-air missiles are scarce. Explore further Ukraine’s F-16s are so short of Western missiles that pilots fall back on jet’s built-in M61A1 Vulcan cannon, which risks killing civilians below The threat from jet-powered drones is growing. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late September that Ukraine was intercepting about 55% of Russia’s jet-powered drones, compared with more than 90% of older models. Denmark’s ammunition delivery gives Ukrainian F-16 pilots more rounds to engage these faster targets, as Ukraine works to strengthen its defenses against Russia’s expanding drone campaign.
