title: UK power supply forecasts warn of 'tight winter days' as costs soar
body: The UK’s power supply could have “some tight days” in December and January, despite energy prices more than doubling, one of the country’s energy operators said on Friday. At the same time, a last-minute deal with a Belgian interconnector firm would provide for an additional five per cent of forecast demand, maintaining gas import capacity and allowing more flexibility for the grid at times of demand strain. Supply agreements should mean there is enough gas and electricity to meet peak demand through winter, according to forecasts published by National Gas and National Energy System Operator (Neso). Front-month gas and power prices have risen about 180 per cent and 120 per cent since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February of this year, and this is set to have a rising impact on consumer bills. Neso predicts a “small number of low surplus days”, which balances supply and demand across the grid in real time. This would require routine balancing tools such as electricity margin notices, and did not indicate a risk to electricity supplies, Neso said. Peak gas demand is expected to reach 493 million cubic metres per day this winter, 2 per cent higher than last year, according to a separate report by National Gas, also published on Friday. This is largely due to stronger demand from power stations. Overall gas demand is expected to fall by 1 per cent as a result of consumer switching. Peak gas supply capacity is estimated at 592 mcm/day, leaving a buffer of 99 mcm/day but a “highly unlikely” stress scenario, such as the failure of the largest single part of the transmission system, would shrink the buffer to 18 mcm/day. National Gas said its forecasts were improved by a deal it reached on Thursday with a Belgian Interconnector pipeline to boost gas import capacity. Gas imports to the UK through interconnectors with Europe declined in recent years because of their maintenance costs, including the capacity of the two-way Belgium- Britain Interconnector. Yet lower levels of gas storage in Europe – also as a result of the war – would probably restrain imports. The British energy regulator Ofgem said it would launch a consultation on how to recover the costs of this capability, as it approved the agreement on Thursday. Disruptions in the global liquefied natural gas (LNG) market could also still affect supplies. “Our ​analysis shows that Great Britain is expected to have sufficient gas ‌supply capability to meet demand throughout winter ⁠2026/27, even under a range of ​very unlikely high-stress scenarios,” said Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, National Gas's director of energy systems and ​resilience. The UK's gas storage levels were estimated to be the lowest in Europe – at 48 per cent of its capacity – according to analysis by the European network of transmission systems for gas (Entsog) earlier this month. On the power side, there will be spare capacity of 5.9 gigawatts above peak demand – the equivalent of 9.5 per cent of peak demand – during a typical cold spell, according to Neso. That margin is similar to recent winters, and is wider than during the 2022 energy crisis. Higher peak demand has largely been offset by additional battery storage, gas-fired generation and wind power, Neso said. The margin is also higher than its June estimate because it now expects more wind generation to be available during ​peak periods. Neso said some days in December and January could be tight and require routine balancing tools such as electricity margin notices. It stressed that such notices signal a need for additional generation and do not indicate a risk to electricity supplies.

title: What some of Anthropic’s backers are reportedly worth before its IPO
body:
Anthropic’s public listing, which is expected this year at a valuation of as much as $2 trillion, is bound to be a windfall for both early-stage and later-stage investors. But even at the company’s latest private market valuation of $965 billion, the stakes held by many of those VCs and early backers already total billions.
Coatue , which first backed Anthropic in 2025 at a $183 billion valuation and co-led the AI lab’s last two funding rounds, has poured a total of $4.75 billion into the company. That stake, based on the last round’s price, is now worth roughly $7.5 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter. Coatue declined to comment.
Below is what some other backers of Anthropic are worth based on the last round’s price, according to Bloomberg :
Eric Schmidt: The former Google CEO invested in Anthropic’s Series A in 2021, when the startup was valued at $461 million, according to PitchBook data. Today, Schmidt owns about 1% of the company, and even at its current private valuation, his stake is worth nearly $10 billion.
Iconiq: The investment outfit wrote a $6 billion check to Anthropic last year when the company was already valued at $183 billion. That massive late-stage bet is now worth $17 billion and has the potential to double at the IPO.
Menlo Ventures: The VC firm led Anthropic’s Series D and has invested more than $1 billion in the company over time, a stake now worth $14 billion.
Sequoia: The famed VC firm backed the AI lab for the first time only earlier this year, when the company was already valued at $380 billion. The $3 billion investment gave it about 1% ownership, which means it has already more than doubled its investment.
Sound Ventures: The firm, launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, invested $35 million in Anthropic’s 2023 Series C round and has since funneled an additional $400 million into the company, resulting in a stake that’s worth billions now. (Kutcher left Sound Ventures this year to launch a new VC firm .)
Spark Capital: The only VC firm known to hold a board seat at Anthropic invested $75 million in that same 2023 Series C round, when it was valued at $5 billion. That position has ballooned more than ninetyfold to $7 billion.

title: ‘Buying Czech aircraft is part of Armenia’s air force modernisation’ — military expert
body: Expert opinion on Armenia’s Czech aircraft purchase Armenian Defence Minister Suren Papikyan is on an official visit to the Czech Republic. He began his visit with a trip to Aero Vodochody, a Czech defence industry company. According to reports, he discussed the possibility of further cooperation with the company’s management. He also examined Aero Vodochody’s products in detail. “These marvels will soon take to the skies over Armenia,” the defence minister wrote in a caption accompanying a video he posted shortly after visiting the company. Papikyan also shared photographs , captioning them: “One of the landmark days in the history of the Armenian Armed Forces’ aviation.” Experts have speculated, based on the video and photographs he posted online, that Armenia is preparing to receive Czech-made L-39 Skyfox aircraft. These are a new generation of jet trainers. Military expert Eduard Arakelyan believes that Armenia, which has a limited fleet of aircraft, could use the L-39 Skyfox not only for training but also for certain operational tasks: “As a result, the purchase could become a practical step towards modernising the air force. However, its scale does not yet justify claims that it would significantly change the combat capabilities of Armenian aviation. For training purposes, four aircraft could serve as the first batch in a transition to a new training system and curriculum. If the Skyfox purchase forms part of a broader restructuring of the air force, expanding the fleet further would be the logical next step.” The L-39 Skyfox is a new-generation jet trainer designed for advanced pilot training. It features modern digital avionics, multifunction displays and an integrated virtual training system. These capabilities allow pilots to simulate various tactical scenarios during training flights. According to Defense Mirror, one Skyfox costs less than $10 million. The final price depends on the aircraft’s configuration and delivery terms. Depending on its configuration, the aircraft can carry air-launched weapons, reconnaissance equipment and additional external systems. This allows it to perform limited military and reconnaissance missions. Azerbaijani soldier enters Armenia, fires at local residents Suicides in Armenia’s military: the statistics and debate over who should be held responsible Armenia’s army to continue acquiring advanced weaponry, defence minister says What we know about the defence minister’s visit The defence minister arrived in the Czech Republic on 20 October. During his visit, Suren Papikyan attended the opening ceremony of the Future Forces Exhibition & Forum. He toured the exhibition halls and viewed the latest technologies and advanced military equipment on display. The Armenian minister also held talks with Czech Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Jaromír Zůna. Armenia’s Defence Ministry said the two ministers discussed: Armenian-Czech defence cooperation, including military-technical cooperation; reforms in the Armenian Armed Forces and cooperation in military education. “Both sides stressed the importance of cooperation in multilateral formats, including within the EU and NATO,” the statement said. Papikyan also discussed bilateral military-technical cooperation with Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade Karel Havlíček. ‘New army, new weapons’: military parade in Yerevan marks Republic Day The government showcased new weapons and military equipment acquired from foreign partners in recent years, as well as systems produced in Armenia itself. Commentary Military expert Eduard Arakelyan noted that a Czech defence industry source had reported a month earlier that AERO Vodochody Aerospace was producing four L-39 Skyfox aircraft for Armenia. Specialist publications had also circulated the information, but none identified the customer or disclosed the terms of the deal. Meanwhile, Arakelyan said, the Armenian Air Force already operates Czech-made L-39 Albatros trainers. Armenia acquired these second-hand aircraft in 2004 and 2010–11. It purchased some of them from Ukraine. “However, the exact number of aircraft that remain in service with the Armenian Air Force and can still fly regularly is unknown,” the expert said. In Arakelyan’s view, the Skyfox purchase fits Armenia’s strategy of diversifying its arms suppliers and expanding cooperation with European defence manufacturers: “An Armenian-Czech agreement on military-technical cooperation, which has been in force since 2023, provides an additional basis for collaboration.” Arakelyan believes the Armenian defence minister’s statement signals that the Skyfox acquisition has reached a practical stage. “Nevertheless, until the parties officially disclose the terms of the deal, questions remain about the actual cost, delivery schedule, configuration and maintenance. These include technical support from the manufacturer and specialist training. “The delivery of four Skyfox aircraft would represent a generational shift in Armenia’s training platform rather than a numerical expansion of its air force. The deal’s significance will depend on whether it remains a standalone purchase or marks the first stage of a broader overhaul of pilot training and air force capabilities. In the latter case, the Skyfox could bridge the gap between existing training aircraft and future combat platforms, with the four aircraft serving as the first batch in an air force modernisation programme.” 'New doors are opening for Armenia': expert on country’s developing defence industry Military expert Leonid Nersisyan believes that in three to five years, Armenian defence companies will be able to earn most of their revenue from foreign markets. title: Razer Basilisk V4 Pro Review: Tried and true and now with AI
body: Razer has been updating its gaming mouse lineup systematically over the past two years, and it's finally the Basilisk's turn to get a real update. The last update we saw to the Basilisk line was the Basilisk V3 Pro 35K in October 2024, which was basically just the Basilisk V3 Pro with a new sensor. The Basilisk isn't Razer's most popular gaming mouse line, but it is the more versatile, all-rounder line for people who aren't chasing performance above all else. The Basilisk V4 Pro maintains the general design of its predecessor — a contoured, right-handed gaming mouse with bright RGB lighting and a handful of extra buttons, for the serious gamer who isn't trying to break esports records. It features Razer's newest Focus Pro 50K optical sensor, gen-4 optical mouse switches, and up to an 8,000 Hz polling rate, plus multiple forms of connectivity and up to 200 hours of battery life (over 2.4GHz at 1,000 Hz). It is admittedly pricey, like all of Razer's flagship mice, at $169.99 for both colorways (black and white), and it launched with Razer's Mouse Dock V2 Pro — which is sold separately for $69.99. Design and Comfort of the Basilisk V4 Pro Following in the footsteps of its other recent next-gen mouse launches, Razer has kept the design of the Basilisk V4 Pro largely the same. The Basilisk V4 Pro has basically the same size and shape as its predecessor — it has a right-handed ergonomic shape with a contoured thumb rest and a hump that sits slightly back and to the left. It has large primary mouse buttons with shallow finger grooves, and a slight contour on its outer edge that makes it relatively easy to pick up and move. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) It's not exactly the same as the V3 Pro, however. The V4 Pro has two new buttons, for a total of 12 programmable buttons on the mouse: the left and right primary buttons, three thumb buttons (instead of the usual two) and a trigger button in the thumb groove, a clickable tilt wheel (three "buttons" — center click and left/right click), two buttons above the tilt wheel, and an extra button on the left side of the left mouse button. The third thumb button and the extra button on the left mouse button are the new ones; the third thumb button sits in front of the first two and is set to open up Razer's AI prompt by default, while the extra button on the left mouse button is set to switch through profiles by default. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware I'm... actually not a big fan of the new buttons. Or, well, I don't really think they're necessary — the Basilisk already had plenty of buttons for a mouse that's not all about having buttons, and I don't really see myself incorporating these new buttons into my workflow in the near future. The extra button on the left mouse button is a little too far forward — this is a very long mouse (it measures 5.02 inches / 127.5mm long), and the extra button is right at the front edge. I have medium-sized hands and relatively long fingers, and the button felt too far for me to press comfortably. It's not a big deal if you plan to leave it set as a profile switch button (which are often located on the bottom of mice), but it's not really viable as a real extra button. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Worse, however, is the location of the third thumb button — the AI prompt button — which is located in line with the other two thumb buttons. I generally have no issue with three rows of thumb buttons, as my daily driver is the Razer Naga V3 Pro , but this new AI button is the same size as the other thumb buttons and it pushes everything back a little. This puts the first thumb button (MB4) back too far to press comfortably (and that's a mouse button I use often). And while you can swap the buttons around, the AI prompt button is slightly too far forward. Basically, there are now three buttons where there should be only two, and they all feel slightly off. The tilt wheel has three different modes you can switch through with the button right above it: two tactile modes (24 and 48 steps), and free-spin mode. I generally love free-spin mode, but the tilt wheel on the Basilisk V4 Pro is a little too sensitive and will backscroll if you even think about moving your finger near it. The precision-tactile scroll hits a great balance and feels great, however, so this didn't bother me too much. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The Basilisk V4 Pro comes in both black and white colorways; ours came in white, which has shiny black accents so it's a little more Stormtrooper than iPod. It has a smooth matte white body with dimpled rubber texturing for grip on both sides. While it's nice to have built-in side grips, I suspect they will wear down like the grips on the V3 Pro — and then you'll have to find or make your own grip tape, as the mouse comes with none. The mouse is roughly the same size as its predecessor, but it weighs less: the black version weighs 3.53 ounces (100g), which is almost half an ounce lighter than the V3 Pro 35K (3.95oz / 112g). It's not an ultralightweight mouse (or anywhere close), but the weight difference is noticeable and the mouse is definitely easier to pick up. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware On the bottom of the mouse, you'll find pure PTFE feet — two near the front, a strip at the back, and a strip under the thumbrest, as well as a strip around the sensor, a power switch, and a connection switch button that is not programmable. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) In the box, the Basilisk V4 Pro comes with a USB-A dongle, a USB-A to USB-C converter, and a 6-foot (2m) braided USB-C to USB-A cable. While the cable is braided, it is not one of Razer's flexible HyperFlex cables — it's meant for charging the mouse and plugging the dongle into your PC, not for using the mouse in its wired form. Specs Sensor Model Focus Pro 50K Gen-3 optical sensor Max Sensitivity 50,000 DPI Max Speed (IPS) 930 IPS Max Acceleration 90 G Polling Rates 8,000 / 4,000 / Programmable Buttons 12 LED Zones 7 Cable USB-C to USB-A Connectivity 2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth, wired (USB-C) Measurements (L x W x H) 5.02 x 2.98 x 1.68 inches / 127.5 x 75.8 x 42.5 mm Weight (excluding cable) 100g MSRP / Price at Time of Review $169.99 Release Date Oct. 2026 Performance of the Basilisk V4 Pro The Basilisk V4 Pro sports Razer's latest optical sensor, which is the Focus Pro 50K Gen-3 optical sensor. It has a maximum resolution of 50,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 930 IPS, and it can handle up to 90 G's of force. This is the third Razer mouse to feature this sensor (others are the Viper V4 Pro and the Naga V3 Pro), and it's a solid sensor that works with Razer's dynamic sensitivity (the sensitivity can be set up to change based on how quickly you move your hand) and rotation tool in Synapse. It tracks well across just about every surface, including glass that's at least 4mm thick. The Basilisk V4 Pro isn't an ultra-lightweight mouse, but its shape and grippiness mean it's pretty easy to pick up and move quickly if you're playing an FPS. The trigger button is right under your thumb, however, so you may accidentally trigger (haha) it if you have a tendency to pick up your mouse a lot. The Basilisk's shape isn't quite as natural-feeling as that of the DeathAdder V4 Pro, but it's a comfortable mouse for a variety of games — from multi-button-needing MMOs to competitive shooters (though, perhaps not for peak competition). While I still take issue with the placement of the new buttons, it is nice to have a few extra buttons without jumping straight to 19. The Basilisk V4 Pro sports Razer's Gen-4 optical mouse switches, which are rated for over 100 million clicks. The switches have a nice, crisp sound that's not too loud (not as loud as Logitech's, anyway), though it's not a mouse for those trying to minimize mouse clickiness. The primary buttons have a solid, tactile feel, and I had no issues with misclicks or double-clicks while I was testing. While the tilt wheel's free-spin mode was too sensitive for me to get to work properly, I love the precision tactile mode — it blends speed and tactility perfectly. Features and Software of the Basilisk V4 Pro The Basilisk V4 Pro is programmable with Razer Synapse 4 (not Razer's web-based version of Synapse). You can use Synapse to remap the mouse's 12 programmable buttons (14 programmable controls, if you include scroll up/down; the connection switch button on the bottom of the mouse is not programmable). Synapse has a variety of remap options, as well as a built-in macro recorder / editor. Synapse is also where you'll be able to customize the mouse further by tweaking things like the scroll wheel, DPI stages, and surface calibration. There's also a sensitivity matcher that will match the Basilisk V4 Pro's sensitivity to match that of your old mouse. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware You can also use Razer's Chroma Studio to customize the mouse's lighting and sync it with games and/or your other Razer peripherals. The Basilisk V4 Pro has seven RGB lighting zones: a five-zone underglow strip along the bottom curve of the mouse, as well as one in the scroll wheel and one in the logo on the palm rest. The lighting is bright and the underglow's five zones blend nicely — the underglow strip is tilted outward so it's pretty visible when the mouse is just sitting on your desk. Wireless Experience and Battery Life of the Basilisk V4 Pro The Basilisk V4 Pro has three forms of connectivity: 2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth, and wired (via USB-C), though it doesn't really come with a mouse-ready USB-C cable. Razer rates it at 200 hours of battery life over a 2.4GHz wireless connection with a 1,000 Hz polling rate, which is excellent. This number does drop to 54 hours at an 8,000 Hz polling rate, which is... still pretty good, to be honest. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Basilisk V4 Pro launched alongside Razer's Mouse Dock V2 Pro, which is a wireless charging dock with built-in RGB lighting and an integrated 8,000 Hz wireless receiver. The Mouse Dock V2 Pro is sold separately for $70, and comes with a wireless charging puck that slots into the bottom of the mouse. It sits on your desk (it's small — 3.28 x 2.2 x 1.71 inches / 83.5 x 56 x 43.5mm) and serves as a magnetic dock and wireless receiver for your mouse. It has eight RGB lighting zones around the base, and it lights up to indicate battery level (flashes red when the battery is low). It's made for the Basilisk V4 Pro and V4 HyperSpeed, but it will also work with the Basilisk V3 Pro 35K , the Basilisk V3 Pro , the Cobra Pro , the Cobra HyperSpeed, the Naga V3 Pro, and the Naga V2 Pro (up to 8,000 Hz polling rate for all except the Naga V2 Pro). The Basilisk V4 Pro is also compatible with Razer's HyperFlux V2 charging mouse pad , but you'll need to connect to your PC via the mouse's dongle for 8,000 Hz polling. Bottom Line The Razer Basilisk V4 Pro is an expected update to the Basilisk V3 Pro / 35K. The bump in battery life, from 150 hours in the Basilisk V3 Pro 35K to 200 hours in the Basilisk V4 Pro, is very nice (and 54 hours with an 8,000 Hz polling rate isn't bad, either). While I didn't like the new buttons, I'm sure some people will (although I find it difficult to believe that every mouse and keyboard needs a dedicated AI prompt button), and the reduced weight feels good even if, at 100g, it's still nowhere near the ultra-lightweight category. The Basilisk V4 Pro is a great gaming mouse for gamers who want something a little more exciting and versatile than a DeathAdder V4 Pro , but not as button-heavy (or as heavy) as a Naga V3 Pro.

US officials publicly accused Russia of threatening a Finnish-operated commercial satellite that provides imagery and intelligence to Ukraine and other nations, calling the move "deliberately reckless."
In response to the accusations, made during a United Nations debate on October 21, Russia broadly described US claims as "absurd" and accused Washington of its own "aggressive military space ambitions."
The back-and-forth came days after a Russian military satellite known as Kosmos-2612 moved "dangerously" near to ICEYE-X36, a satellite registered in the United States and operated by a Finnish company called ICEYE.
The Russian satellite came "exceptionally close" -- within 200 meters, by some estimates -- something that space officials and amateur satellite watchers said was extremely unusual.
"This was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by,'" LeoLabs, an aerospace intelligence company, told RFE/RL. "The behavior is consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations."
ICEYE-X36 carries a radar technology that can gather detailed terrestrial images, even through cloud cover. The Finnish company in January signed a contract with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry to provide intelligence.
Kosmos-2612 "exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite," Brian Hardesty, an adviser to the US Delegation to the Conference on Disarmament, said during a meeting in New York of the UN First Committee, a body that debates arms control and disarmament issues. "These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation."
"The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless," he said.
Russia's representative who could not be immediately identified, did not directly address the assertion.
"We call on member states to give the proper response to the aggressive military space ambitions of the United States," he said.
He also referenced comments made last month by the secretary of the US Air Force, the top civilian official for that military branch.
As just announced in the @UN First Committee, Russia’s COSMOS 2612 military satellite has been exhibiting threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite, behaviors consistent with on-orbit weapons operations. This violates long-established safety thresholds in low Earth orbit. The United States will continue to secure and defend American vital national security interests in, from, and to space.
Speaking to a conference outside of Washington, Troy Meink's comments that Washington has in fact deployed actual weapons in space -- "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action" -- caused a jolt among policy experts.
Other longtime space watchers, however, said the announcement merely stated publicly what had already been obvious for some time.
"The United States did not suddenly weaponize space by acknowledging that it possesses these capabilities," wrote Mallory Stewart, a former top arms control secretary at the US State Department. "An arms race in space has been under way for years."
